Uniform Title: *Īśvarapratyabhijñāvimarśinīvyākhyā* Manuscript: IFP Transcript 762 Description: Copied from IFP Transcript 762, which was itself copied from manuscript no. R. 4353 belonging to the Government Oriental Manuscripts Library, Madras.
Notes: Data entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski. Revision 0: October 22, 2009.
Country of publication: India.
The *Īśvarapratyabhijñāsūtravimarśinī* commentary [is dedicated to Him] whose playful manifestation is the universe consisting of name and form.
Salutation to that Śambhu, who is luminous and endowed with reflective awareness.

Here, in this land of Śrī-Kāśmīra— the supreme abode of the divine play of Śrī-Śāradā and the like, situated beyond the entire circle of the earth, where the Supreme Śiva alone, who transcends all that is emitted by Viśva— there dwells one renowned by the name of Śrī-Narasiṃhaguptanātha.

Desiring to comment upon the scripture titled *The Recognition of the Lord* (*Īśvarapratyabhijñā*)— which is the very essence of the entire tradition of secret teachings, the crest-jewel of the lineage of the venerable Traiyambaka, and uttered from the mouth of the illustrious teacher Utpaladeva— he [Abhinavagupta] acts thus for the sake of the unimpeded completion of his own commentary.
Having entered into the Supreme Deity, who is the very essence of that scripture,
he brings her face-to-face through an act of praise preceded by reflection, for the sake of causing those who are to be graced to enter [into that state],
beginning with the words "from the desireless," and so forth. That which is "I"— the unfolding from the full [state] that is free of desire— [is the source].

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: [He] who, through his own nature, which possesses expansion, non-blinking, and stability, illuminates his own power (*nijakalā*) as the branch extending toward the directions from the city; thereafter, he desires to divide that very [power]; I bow to that entire non-duality, whose essence is the power of Supreme Śiva. Indeed, that which...
In the *Śrītriṃśikāśāstra*:
"O God, how is the unsurpassed [state] that immediately bestows Kaula perfection? By the mere realization of which one attains equality with Khecarī?"
(2) O Lord, tell me this secret, well-guarded mystery:
that power which resides in the heart, the Kaulikī, the Mistress of Kula.
Tell me that, O Lord of Gods, so that I may attain satisfaction.

Having thus introduced the first question of the Goddess, [he said]: "Listen, O illustrious Goddess, to the answer that is beyond all answers. This Kaulika method, O Goddess, is established within the space of my heart."

By means of this passage beginning with "ityādi" and ending with "sarvadā," Bhairava provides a reply; having extracted [the essence] from the statement "caturdaśayutam," he subsequently describes—in the section beginning with "anyaccāra" (p.
2)—how that very [mantra] constitutes the arising of the totality of all supernatural powers (*siddhi*) and manifestations (*vibhūti*).

Thus, within this introduction to the scripture— from the words "the heart-seed which expresses the union (*yāmala*) of the unsurpassed Lord (*bhaṭṭārikā*) and Supreme Bhairava, which bestows great fruit" up to "this is not born of the *yoginīs*...
[and so on] until 'omniscience is attained'"— is described liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*).

The heart-seed (hṛdayabīja), which expresses the Bhairava-yāmala consisting of the Lord Bhaṭṭāraka and the Supreme Lady Bhaṭṭārikā— the cause of the supreme and subordinate accomplishments (siddhis) whose nature is sovereign power— has been examined. At its conclusion is the venerable Śrīmad-Īśvarapratyabhijñā-śāstra.
The explanation has been revealed by the venerable Bhaṭṭāraka through a different method of interpretation (*bhaṅgyantareṇa*).

It is as follows: by the word "that" (*yat*), the unsurpassed (*anuttara*) is meant; by "one's own power" (*nijakalām*), the power of emission (*visarga-śakti*) is meant; by "expansion" (*unmeṣa-prasaraṇa*) and so forth, the fourteenth vowel is meant; and by "entirety" (*nikhilam*), the form of the sixfold conduct (*sad-vṛtti*) is meant. And this...
The authors of the treatises have expressed that [reality] in the fourfold authority (*adhikāra*) using esoteric terminology. How so?

Therein, by means of the characteristic of the *nimeṣa*—which consists of contraction and expansion and is characterized by knowledge and action—it is essentially nothing other than the very essence of one's own vibration (*sva-parispanda*), and not otherwise.

It is completely determined, delimited, and insentient by nature, like a jar or similar object. And its connection with contraction and expansion— as it becomes increasingly manifest in the throbbing of the heart, the triangle, and so forth,
and as it simultaneously diminishes within the consciousness of Bhairava— so it proceeds.

It is drawn down as far as inert matter such as stone; and although it is characterized by contraction and expansion, it is the power (*śakti*) of the Supreme Lord (*anuttara*), whose nature is the sovereignty of creation. According to the principle stated in the *Laghuvṛtti*, this power of emission (*visarga-śakti*), consisting of the pair of points (*bindu-dvandva*), [manifests] through the two authorities of knowledge and action.

By means of the first daily lesson (*āhnika*), which consists of the nature of form and tranquility; by means of the second daily lesson, which consists of the determination of the reality of the subject (*pramātṛtattva*) through right conduct; and by means of the fourfold scope beginning with "the trident dissolved within all the elements" up to "the unsurpassed" (*anuttara*), [the teaching is established] within the heart.
The nature of the seed-syllable (*bīja*) should be clearly observed.
For here, this very heart-seed-syllable has been called the "Great I" (*aham-mahāmantra*) by the Noble Ones.
Of this Great Mantra: it is filled with the repose of infinite powers contained within its beginning and end.
O Vāma, I meditate upon the heart of the Lord, which is beyond utterance.
It is filled with infinite denotata and denoters contained within its beginning and end.
I take refuge in the unsurpassed secret of mantras and mudrās.
According to the principle stated in the opening and concluding verses of the *Śrīpañcāśikā*— beginning with "Maha"—
the first syllable is the Absolute (*anuttara*).
This emission (*visarga*) has now become exceedingly manifest through the expansion of that which is to be emitted.
This [arises] from the mutual blending of the powers of the Self when they are thus questioned.
There can be no interval of becoming external to this emission.
And according to this rule: the group of letters from *a* to *ha* is fivefold;

and by the rule stated in the *Sadbhāva*, the final letter is *ha*, which is the *visarga*. In the syllable *am*, the seed-syllables (*bīja*) and the trident (*triśūla*) should be understood as being in a state of perfect activity (*sadvṛtti*). How is that fire? It is supreme.

Pure, peaceful, undifferentiated in essence, equal, all-encompassing, immortal, and true, [the Absolute] rests within Śakti— that which is radiant in form, which measures, which is the object of knowledge, and which is brought into manifestation.
Although it is untouched by death even while possessing a radiant form, it nevertheless attains the state of being a flower of the Name.

In the manner described in the *Paramārthasāra*, the trident— consisting of will, knowledge, and action— is the means of piercing; having assimilated the mass of objects of cognition, which consists of the sacrificial victim, the ritual act, and the true mode of conduct,
this very triad of the repose of the object, the cognition, and the cognizer constitutes the nature of the three phonemes.
According to the principle stated in the *Śrīlaghuvṛtti*, because even one's own self (*svadāma*) consists of the nature of cognition, it is the object of universal knowledge;

and according to the method explained in the *Śrīsāmbavyākhyā*, that which consists of the cognition of the non-differentiation of all objects of knowledge rests within the *bindu* situated above itself, which consists of the cognition of the non-differentiation of all objects of knowledge. This is the meaning of [the statement].
The Bindu possesses the nature of the trident (triśūla) and the sixfold cycle (sad-vṛtti).

Furthermore, in the body of the first *kalā*, which consists of absolute transcendence (*atyantamātra*) and the cessation of the three-fold distinctions— namely the very clear, the clear, and the unclear— characterized by waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, located within the objective aspect (*vedyāṃśa*) in the form of the sixfold cycle at the root-level of the Heart.
When resting in the upward-turning state (*uttaravṛtti*), by means of resting sequentially up to the fourth plane (*turyapada*)— extending through the principles (*tattva*) from Śakti down to Śiva—
the pervasion of the seat (*āsanavyāpti*) is demonstrated, because of the appropriation of all the principles in their entirety, which are otherwise distinct in their sequential order.

According to the perspective of the *Śrīlaghuvṛtti*, because both the *sadvṛtti* (the sixfold conduct) and the *triśūla* (the trident) consist of the aggregate of the knowable (*vedyarāśimayatva*), their repose is in the *bindu*, which consists of the perception of the undivided knowable from the earth up to Śiva.
The knowable, entering into its own established consciousness (*avitti*), includes the limbs [of the mantra], the sense objects, and so forth.

Thus, according to the principle stated in the *Śrī Virūpākṣapañcāśikā*, the inclusion of the Heart-seed (*hṛdayabīja*) within the Great Mantra (*mahāmantra*) is established. In terms of the actual state of reality:
"From the root upwards, the vision beginning with *kṣa* and ending with *ṭa* is declared to be known in sequence."
"O Dear One, as one who does not abide in the phonemes abides in the phonemes, so [the reality] is omnipresent.
"The supreme abode consists of thirty-eight [phonemes], wherein this entire universe shines forth.
"The triad is pervaded by the phonemes, and the fourth by the trident."

Thence follows the sixteenth [vowel], whose nature is emission (*visarga*), which is of the nature of Bhairava, extending as far as the desire for the touch of the fourth state (*turya*) that transcends all. "The letter *A* is indeed all speech"—thus says the venerable *Tantrasadbhāva*.
This is also stated in the *Bhāvopahāratantra*, the *Vaṭadhānikā*, the *Mālinīvijaya*, and the *Laghuvṛtti*.

According to the principle stated in the Śruti, because the two Bhairava-yāmalas— the *anuttara* (the unsurpassed) and *visarga* (emission)— transcend the denotative relationship between the letters from *ra* to *kṣa* and their denoted objects from Earth (*kṣiti*) to Śiva, they transcend the state of being great mantras (*mahāmantra*). Nevertheless, even these two [transcend] the Mātṛkā.
Because it is included within this very [consciousness], it indeed possesses the nature of being composed of the Great Mantra (mahāmantra), which is the root-source of the Mātṛkā.

What need is there for much? For, according to the method of presentation, the Great Mantra is the reflective awareness (vimarśa) that flashes forth as "I," which is uncreated, through the manifestation of the universe in its universal form and through the withdrawal of the universe.

"O Mother, O Śivā, you who possess the womb of the meaning of Māyā, and you who are the progenitor of Śiva— O Mothers, I take refuge in you both. Thus, according to the principle set forth in the *Śrī-Śuktāvalī*, regarding those two:

The reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) "I am" is that which embraces the entire universe—from Śiva, who is one's own self, down to the earth—within the two supreme goddesses, Parā and Parābhaṭṭārikā, whose nature is the non-dual Śiva and Śakti consisting of emanation. As it is said in the *Śrī Tantrāloka*:
"In [the reality] whose nature is emanation, which consists of the non-duality of Śiva and Śakti..."
O Lord, because it is full of supreme absorption, this reflective awareness is called "I."

With this very intention, the word "iti" was employed at the beginning. By means of this great mantra (*mahāmantra*) which is thus constituted, [one is] from the "Full" (*pūrṇāt*), that is, the "Filled" (*bharitāt*). Fullness (*pūrṇatva*) indeed consists in being brimming with the entire universe from Śiva down to the earth; nothing else is to be desired by one who—
"It is not logical that there can be fullness for that which is non-dual"— according to this principle stated in the *Śrīmat-stotrāvalī*,

and by means of the passage beginning with "nirāśaṃsa" and "unmeṣa," it is declared that [the Lord] performs the fivefold cosmic acts, such as creation, which distinguish Him from the proponents of an eternally inert Brahman.
In this context, *unmeṣa* (opening) is emission (*sṛṣṭi*), and *nimeṣa* (closing) is withdrawal (*saṃhāra*); these two are grasped as the expansion and subsistence [of consciousness].

For the Lord, whose very nature is consciousness, manifests the multitude of objects externally by the power of His will from within Himself, just as a yogi manifests a collection of things without any external material cause.

(p. 5) according to the method that will be explained [later]. Therefore, because *unmeṣa* (the opening of the eyes) consists in the emergence of the mass of one's own nature—which exists as a unity with consciousness—it is the cause of perception (*grahaṇa*).
Because *prasaraṇa* (the outward flow) consists in the dissolution of that external form through its immersion within, it is of the nature of *sthiti* (abiding).

The closing of the eyes (*nimeṣa*) may be considered a withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), because it is the cause that causes the withdrawn mass of entities to abide within as a latent impression (*saṃskāra*). Furthermore, there is the nature of concealment (*tirodhāna*) inherent in persistence (*sthiti*), and the nature of grace (*anugraha*) toward such a mass of entities. Or rather, [it is] "unfolding" (*unmeṣa*), and so forth.
By the phrase ending with "sthitī" (maintenance), only emission (*sṛṣṭi*) and withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) are denoted;
then, by "unmeṣaprasāraṇa" (opening and expansion), emission is indicated, and by "nimeṣasthiti" (closing and maintenance), withdrawal is indicated.
Since maintenance, dissolution, and grace (*anugraha*) are [already] included within [these], there is nothing additional.

The fivefold activity of the Supreme Lord (*pārameśvara-kṛtya*) is subsumed precisely within *pralaya* (dissolution) and *udaya* (emergence). According to the method taught in the *Śrīspandanirṇaya*, maintenance (*sthiti*), concealment (*tirodhāna*), and grace (*anugraha*) are indeed included within these two. Among them, maintenance is included within creation (*sṛṣṭi*); concealment and grace are included within dissolution (*saṃhāra*).
With this [verse],
we praise Śaṅkara, the source of the manifestation of the wheel of powers (śakticakra), by whose opening and closing of his eyes the dissolution and emergence of the universe occur.
Thus, from that which is his own nature as condensed in the meaning of the *Śrī Spandakārikās*—

the indestructible, manifesting cause of the universe in the form of effects, which exists in the state of power (*śakti*)— there is the Lord, the Light (*prakāśa*), who consists of the life-force of the entire universe. This is [the meaning].

Because of the manifestation of existence according to the principle stated in the *Śrīsūkta*; and furthermore, because she manifests her own essential nature (*svarūpa*) as the subject (*nijadharmī*) to the class of objects to be manifested. Thus, according to the principle stated in the *Śrīvirūpākṣapañcāśikā*, one's own self is of the nature of light (*prakāśa*).
Or rather, it is from such a [source] that they manifest the nature of the universe which is to be illuminated.
"The Supreme Lord is omniscient, the creator of all, and all-pervading;
He alone am I, a follower of the Śaiva dharma"—through such firm conviction in Śiva... [iti].
From one's own nature, which is endowed with omniscience and other qualities according to the state described in the *Śrī-Vijñānabhairava*,
[one attains] "one's own power" (*nijakalām*). This means one's own innate power (*sahajā śakti*), because the non-duality of the power and its possessor (*śaktimant*) is eternally established.
Therefore, because it possesses those attributes, the supreme power belongs to the Supreme Self.
"Power does not desire separation from the nature of the possessor of power; there is an eternal identity between these two, just as between fire and its burning capacity. (p.
6) "O Lord, for whomsoever the state of being the self of the universe is established without dependence on anything else..."
For they indeed proclaim that supreme goddess to be the unsurpassed Pratibhā.
This supreme power Kālikī is the one who causes the expansion of the *kula* of this *akula* deity; by her, the Lord is joined with the sun.

Thus, according to the *Tantrāloka*, the venerable *Vijñānabhairavaprabodhapañcadaśikā* remains inseparable from its own [source]. Furthermore, that in which something arises and dissolves while it exists pervades both its prior and subsequent parts;
as in the case of a sprout in the earth, according to the principle to be explained hereafter.

Because it pervades both the prior and posterior limits of the universe, she is eternal. (8) The differentiation of her own self is "projection" (*kṣepa*), and "division" (*bheda*) is the conceptualization (*vikalpana*) of that [projection].
Knowledge is conceptualization (*vikalpa*), because it is a reckoning (*saṅkhyāna*) through differentiation from what is other.
Since its nature as a state of being is like a reflection, it possesses the quality of redness.
The state of being reduced to the reflective awareness of the self of sound [occurs] through the dissolution of that [duality].
Thus, performing this fivefold reckoning, she is Parā.
The Goddess is called Kālī as well as Kālakarṣaṇī.

Thus, according to the *Tantrāloka*, [he perceives] the power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*), which consists of emanation and performs the fivefold cosmic act. "Previously" means at the very first moment of the desire to manifest externally that which was previously situated within. "Bifurcated" (*dviśākhā*): as for this state of being bifurcated—

The realization "I am the inner self" is the emergence of the world as a single identity; the realization "I am this, this is I" is that which is being manifested within the consciousness of the venerable Lord Sadāśiva. That [realization] possesses it. Being itself one and supreme, though it is indeed one, it exists through its own sovereignty as many, because it is never separated from itself.

It manifests in two ways. What is called "the seat" (āsana) is precisely this [Self], which, according to the principle to be explained, is the manifestation as various forms through the sovereignty of the Illuminator, the Supreme Lord (Anuttara-bhaṭṭāraka). Regarding the phrase "thereafter" (tadanu):

Immediately after the manifestation of the two branches, the mantra-consciousness (mantravijñāna)— which is both partial (akala) and complete (sakala), and which is the dissolution of the [limited] subject— desires and intends to manifest that very same innate power (nijakalā) by dividing it into the form of the entire aggregate of subjects and objects of knowledge. This is the "aspiration" (āśāsana).

For one who does not abide in [the state of] Name (nāma), will itself is the causality, the agency, and the action; according to the principle to be stated later, will reaches the state of being the very action consisting of the manifestation of the universe. This is indicated by the word "and" (ca), which signifies a cumulative conjunction to show that the single agent is both "he manifests" and "he desires."

According to the principle stated in the *Śrīpratyabhijñāhṛdaya*, that [Lord] performs those fivefold acts— beginning with manifestation (*ābhāsana*), which is synonymous with the terms "emanation" (*sṛṣṭi*) and so forth— within His own self, starting from the state of the seed (*bījāvasthā*) [of the power of manifestation].

Thus, agency is [universal], and not restricted to a specific function for each individual as is the case with Brahmā and the other deities; this is what is illuminated. Furthermore, the lack of interval between the act of division and the act of commanding is indicated by the use of the present tense in the words "he manifests" (*ābhāsayati*) and "he commands" (*āśāste*), signifying that this wheel of powers is uninterrupted.

According to the method stated in the *Laghuvṛtti*, the uninterrupted agency of manifestation and so forth belonging to the Lord Bhairavanātha has been demonstrated in this treatise (*prabandha*). "That" refers to the totality consisting of the nature of Supreme Śiva and His Power; it is the state of being the very essence of Supreme Śiva, endowed with [His] Will and the other [powers].
By manifesting as two branches, it differentiates while being essentially power;

yet, even while assuming infinite forms, that self-consciousness remains characterized by oneness. Entering into that [state], one does not fall into conceptual construction—according to the view stated by the masters, there is no difference from Śiva—and thus it is of a single, solid, undifferentiated nature.
Furthermore, that which is called non-duality (advaita) is where lights are but lights and darknesses are but darknesses;
where lights and darknesses themselves are nothing but the unsurpassed Light.
Thus, according to the method stated in the *Śrī Laghuvṛtti*:
"Śiva is a mass of consciousness and bliss, whose form is the supreme imperishable."
Thus, according to the method to be explained, [He] is formless (*arūpa*) because He is non-different from the secret syllables that express Him;

He transcends the universe (*viśvottīrṇa*), yet He is non-dual (*advaita*) and consists of the universe (*viśvamaya*) because His nature is to emit and swallow the universe contained within Him. Here, the words *tat tvām* (that You) are to be supplied. "I bow" (*vande*)—the root *vad* signifies salutation.
— it is to be contemplated as being of the nature of suffering.

Now, because its form is manifest in all states, by speaking—that is, by contemplating its own essential nature directly—it is capable of [liberating] one; thus, it is eternally exerted in its activity.

With effort, one offers salutation (*abhivādaye*) to that which is established in the awareness of its own true nature (*svarūpa-parāmarśa-niṣṭham*); this brings it face-to-face. In this regard, memory (*smṛti*) is not [the cause]; rather, bringing it face-to-face is what constitutes salutation. This, in brief, is the meaning of the verse.
Having thus paid homage to the beloved deity of Consciousness, and demonstrating the descent of the scripture he intends to explain through the lineage of his gurus, he makes this formal declaration:
"Of him who stands as a pearl in the midst of the noble lineage of the venerable Traiyambaka... (p. 8)
The reflection of the consciousness of the venerable Lord Somānandanātha.
He proclaimed that stainless scripture called the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*, which is the unsurpassed and peerless means for attaining the goal of human life. 3.
Having learned it from the illustrious Lakṣmaṇagupta, I, Abhinavagupta, his disciple’s disciple, compose this brief commentary on that sūtra.

In this regard, first is the syntactical connection (*anvaya*): He who proclaimed the treatise named *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*, which is a reflection of the realized knowledge (*vijñāna*) of the venerable Somānandanātha— who stands like a pearl in the midst of the noble lineage of the venerable Traiyambaka— and which is the means for the human goal that has no other witness than the Absolute (*anuttara*).

I, Abhinavagupta, his disciple, having learned this commentary on those aphorisms from the venerable Lakṣmaṇagupta, shall now compose it in an abbreviated form. Regarding the term "Śrītraiyambikā": she is inseparable from the glorious liberation (mokṣalakṣmī), which is characterized by the manifestation of Śiva-nature within the individual soul (jīva).
Of him who belongs to Tryambaka, who exists as one who never ceases to act,
and who is pure because he is free from turbidity;
the Lord, wandering on Kailāsa and other such places in his form as Śrīkaṇṭha.
Having descended to the earth for the sake of bestowing grace, he urged [them] forward.
"O Blessed One, act in such a way that the secret teaching is not cut off from the sage named Durvāsas, who is one whose vital energy is drawn upward, in accordance with the scriptures."
Then the Blessed One, having received the command from the God of gods, being diligent,
created a mental son named Tryambakāditya.
He transmitted all the secrets to him in their entirety;
he, in turn, having gone to the cave known as Tryambaka, [taught them] perfectly thereafter.
Having meditated upon him by that name, he created a son through his mind;
and as soon as he was born, that son leapt up into the sky.
In that same way, by the birth of a son, fourteen [of his ancestors] were indeed perfected;
and so it was until the fifteenth son, who was learned in all the scriptures.
Once, under the influence of passion, he himself begot a son upon a Brāhmaṇa woman from a certain Brāhmaṇa; consequently, a son of that same nature was born.
And that son, wandering about, did not arrive in Kaśmīra at the appointed time;
he was named Saṅgamāditya, and Varṣāditya was his son.
For him also, there was that Blessed One named Taruṇāditya;
from him arose one of similar nature named Ānanda.
Therefore, such a person named Somānanda, who was born in this [lineage],
composed this treatise entitled *Śivadṛṣṭi*.
Thus was it taught by the Blessed One Somānanda in his own teaching,
[which is] an ocean of the nectar of Śiva-knowledge through his grace.
Having attained this, the Lord Utpaladeva, who was always honored by the virtuous,
likewise became the sole authority for the teaching known as the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*.
The venerable *Śrīmatstotrāvalī* is a mine of the nectar of Śiva’s self-reflection (*śivāmarśa*),
a sun that illuminates the secret meaning of the Śiva scriptures.
Then, from that Śrī Lakṣmaṇagupta, [he] was born;
having mastered the entire secret meaning, he imparted it [to him].
Then, impelled by Śiva, he became the commentator on all the Śiva scriptures for Abhinavagupta, the great Lord of Mantras.

Having attained the direct heat [of realization], he is a vessel for the knowledge of Śaṅkara; through the manifestation of the form of Śiva, which is the very soul of the entire course of worldly existence, he shines forth.
Kṣemarāja, the author of three hundred thousand verses, protected the kingdom.

Thus it was said— just as a pearl situated in the center of a necklace remains while clarifying that lineage which is the cause of its own praise, so too [the Lord] remains, being existent through His connection with Tryambaka and others, eternally manifest, and moreover, pure because He is free from the turbidity of *māyā*.

"Because of the state of being free from the illusion characterized by disease, situated within that [state] in the midst of the continuum which is free from disease— this refers to the venerable Lord Somānandanātha,
who is accompanied by Lakṣmī and is the author of the *Śivadṛṣṭi*. Or else,"

Umā, the venerable consort (Bhaṭṭārikā), together with the Lord— the Supreme Sovereign (Anuttara-bhaṭṭāraka) who is endowed with bliss, omniscience, omnipotence, and all perfections— established himself in the roles of teacher and disciple; for the God Sadāśiva himself [is both].
He fashioned it from his own body.

Thus, according to the principle stated in the *Śrī-svacchanda*, [this was done] by one who has been graced for the sake of ensuring the non-interruption of the secret oral tradition (*rahasya-sampradāya*) bearing that name. Furthermore:
"Then the moon, resembling a flower, shines forth on all sides."
Āhlādana—he would instantly gladden the world.
In that very same way, when the great yogi wanders the earth,
[he perceives] the wondrous and manifold offering of the world.
It shall gladden everything all around, from the Avīci hell up to the limit of Śiva.

Thus, according to the teaching of the venerable Candrajñāna, he gladdens the world of those to be graced by means of the moon; for that very reason, he is sought after and entreated— [this is] the reflective awareness of the distinguished Somanandanātha,
who is the reflection of primordial consciousness (vijñāna).

The reflection of the knowledge— which is established by the venerable Śivadṛṣṭi-śāstra and consists of the reflective awareness of the perfect "I" (pūrṇāhaṃ-parāmarśa)— is transmitted progressively into the mirrors of the consciousness of successive disciples; it is not, however, a reflection like that in a mirror made of water or similar substances.
It is also capable of performing the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) consisting of the reflective awareness of one's own innate Śiva-nature.

He states this very point: "The means to the goal of man is the witness that is unsurpassed and non-dual. [Regarding the term] *uttara*—it refers to that which exists as the subject-form (*grāhakārūpa*) in relation to the insentient (*jaḍa*).

— its state of being unsurpassed (*anuttaratva*)— is, according to the method stated in the *Śrī Laghuvṛtti*, that which transcends the cycle of the grasped and the grasper, which has no other witness,
which is accessible solely through one's own experience, and which consists of the nature of full subjectivity (*pūrṇāhantā*).
Because [the other systems] serve as means for enjoyment and liberation according to the Śaiva, Naiyāyika, Vedānta, and Sāṃkhya [traditions], [this system is] superior to them;

it is the unsurpassed, being more excellent than those. However, it is not merely for those who are qualified for them... Thus, for one who knows this in its true essence, initiation leading to liberation occurs according to the stated principle.

Of the one whose nature is liberation while living (*jīvanmukta*), which consists of sovereign power (*vibhūti*). Furthermore: "When his [the disciple's] elevation is accomplished through that means," and so forth. They bestow the supreme fruit, or whatever is desired—according to the principle stated in the venerable *Triṃśikā-śāstra*: "The path beginning with Earth and ending with Śiva..."

It is the means for attaining the human goal characterized by sovereignty and consisting of supreme glory, which is capable of bringing about subjugation; it is that which, by obstructing the concealment of Māyā, brings about the manifestation of one's true nature as it actually exists, being perfectly stainless. Thus it is said.
p. 11) — Or rather, the left [is] the right.
Beyond the right is Kaula; beyond Kaula is Trika.
The Vedas have the three qualities (*traiguṇya*) as their domain; be free from the three qualities, O Arjuna.

Thus, because they are dependent on the rules for various practices and so forth according to that system, their purification through the limited fruits produced by the worship of deities other than themselves— being inferior to that [highest state]— is [effected] by means of the Śākta systems such as Vāma, Dakṣiṇa, and others, which are stainless like the wind. Contraction...
Because it exists as the relation between cause and effect, there is no purity in the ultimate sense. However, this [treatise],
which is called the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*, is perfectly pure because its nature consists of the power of one's own self, as will be explained hereafter.
For the Supreme Lord, who acts with full knowledge and whose nature is non-material,
whoever is endowed with both knowledge and action is a Great Lord (Maheśvara) in every respect.

Thus, because this work has been spoken by one who is thus engaged and establishes the recognition of the Lord (īśvarapratyabhijñā) for people everywhere, it is called the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā* treatise. In the ancient Śaiva secret scriptures (*rahasyāgama*), the Lord is well known as both the knower and the agent; that which belongs to Him—

Recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) arises from perceiving within one's own self the powers of knowledge and action that constitute its characteristic; it is the continuous synthesis [of experience] in the form "I am that very same person. Because this [text] fully proclaims (*samantāt khyāpayati*) that recognition of the Lord (*īśvara-pratyabhijñā*), it is called the treatise *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*.
The self is distinct from the Lord; jars and other objects are distinct from one another;

and jars and so forth are distinct from the Lord, from the class of selves, and from one another—this form of duality is [negated] by the cessation of the teaching of Śiva, [who is] composed of the universe yet transcends the universe, within his own self which is the very nature of Śiva.
The scripture restricts the qualified practitioner. The Lord, abiding as the very essence of the scripture, can never be subject to falsity;
nor can there be even a suspicion of mere figurative praise regarding this supreme scripture of Maheśvara.
According to the principle stated by the learned masters— "He who is the form"—

it refers to the illustrious teacher Utpaladeva. "He declared" means that, facing [the world], having himself assumed the form of the *madhyamā* speech and then [manifested] as *vaikharī*, he bestowed grace upon people.
The one who has made [the teaching] manifest asks himself incessantly through reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) while in the state of awakening, being none other than his own deity;
therefore, it is said, "The Śrī Devī said," and according to the method stated in the *Śrīlaghuvṛtti*, the syntactical connection is that she "spoke" (*abhyadhāt*).

The actual meaning also illuminates delimited presentness; the sense is that, entering the heart of the Teacher, it expresses what is to be realized in successive stages without ceasing. "His disciple" means [the one who follows] because of his observance of the teaching of that disciple of the author of the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*.
He is preeminent as the one who possesses the remainder (*praśeṣibhūta*).

In that context, by the use of the term "disciple of the disciple" (*praśiṣya*), he demonstrates his profound reverence for the fact that the commentary on the aphorisms of the scripture composed by his own supreme teacher must necessarily be undertaken. [The word] "Abhinava" refers to the illustrious Abhinavagupta.

Thus, having established that [the author] is indeed the venerable teacher Śrīkaṇṭhanātha, otherwise how could his status as a "Lord" (*nṛtva*) be possible? According to the principle stated thus, although he is ancient by virtue of being the very form of Śrīkaṇṭhanātha, he is called "Abhinavasarvajña" (the All-Knowing One) because he has descended in the form of a teacher for the sake of bestowing grace upon those to be graced.

He is "hidden" (*gupta*) because he is surrounded by attributes such as being the agent of all things; according to the meaning of the verbal root *gup* (to protect), he is "protected. Furthermore, due to the absence of limitations such as space and time, although he is one, he is by his own sovereignty one yet the self of the universe in its ever-new and ever-new forms.

"Because He is ever-new as He shines forth, the Supreme Lord is skilled in the play of concealing His own nature"— according to this principle, because people do not recognize Him in that form, [He is] "Abhinava" (the Ever-New),
so named by Abhinavagupta.
I am composed of the reflective awareness of the perfect "I" (*pūrṇāhaṃ-parāmarśa*), whose essence is the aforementioned Great Mantra (*mahāmantra*);
through the venerable Lakṣmaṇagupta,
I am firmly established in the blissful embrace of Śrī, who is empty of all objective domains.

In the manner thus described, from the venerable teacher Lakṣmaṇagupta— the disciple of Śrī Utpaladeva— who was perpetually embraced by the splendor of excellent devotion, which is overflowing with the entire universe from Śiva down to the earth, and who is the supreme Lord whose body is the universe from Śiva down to the earth.
Having understood the scripture whose characteristics have been stated, and having perfectly composed his heart as one—

meaning that even though it will be explained later, at this very moment he has made manifest the commentary on that sūtra of this scripture called *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*, which is concealed within the sūtras.
According to the principle stated in his own commentary (*nijavṛtti*), this work functions merely as an exposition and clarification;
thus, it provides a clear explanation for each of the sūtras even when their meanings are conventional (*saṃvṛta*).
Compared to his own *Bṛhadvimarśinī*, it is concise and abbreviated.
Having made it capable of encompassing the entirety of the scriptures without effort due to the absence of voluminousness; furthermore,
by removing the burden of duality propounded by the scriptures of Māyā, he brings it about so that it may be easily retained by his disciples.
The formulation of a thesis (*pratijñākaraṇa*) consists in making those who are to be assisted understand the core of that object of cognition;

it is not the creation of something previously non-existent. This is because the present tense is used here—according to the rule "the present may be used for what is proximate to the present" (*vartamānasāmīpye vartamānavat*)—as in the immediately following [verse].

With reference to the commentary (*vivaraṇa*) that he intends to compose, he will state: "He has composed both the *vyākhyā* and the *vṛtti*; by these two alone, the meaning of the Sūtra is made manifest.
This is intended to address the doubt: "What is the purpose of this new *vivaraṇa*?"

To pacify [this doubt], he says: "The intended meaning [is conveyed] by the mode of operation (*vṛtti*). Regarding the phrase "in these": because they are objects of knowledge (*prameya*) being constantly referred to, they come within the range of experience—[this is stated] by the author of the work, the composer of the treatise.
The division of words, the statement of word-meanings, the analysis of compounds, the syntactical connection of the sentence,
and the exposition of the intended meaning— these are the five characteristics of a commentary.

According to the principle thus stated, among the five characteristics of exposition (*vyākhyāna-lakṣaṇa*), having set aside the four characteristics beginning with the division of words (*padaccheda*) and having placed the supreme intellect within his heart, [the author] explains only the intended meaning (*tātparya*) through a commentary arising from his own mouth; that is, "the investigation of that"— namely, of that intended meaning.

Investigation (*vicāra*) is the determination (*nirūpaṇa*); it has been composed, woven together, and explained so that, for the time being, the meaning of the Sūtras might not remain unmanifested. For that reason, [this work is intended] for those of subtle intellect—those endowed with a non-contracted faculty of understanding capable of such independent reasoning (*ūha*).

Alternatively, it is intended for an authority possessing an intellect sharpened by subtle investigation, concerning the meaning of the aphorisms— that is, the subject matter contained within them— namely, the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) consisting of the realization "He who is Īśvara is indeed I," as well as the *Pratyabhijñā-śāstra* which is the cause of that [realization].

I shall explain [the text] correctly for the sake of discernment and illumination by means of an exposition endowed with the five characteristics, such as the word-analysis (*padaccheda*), and endowed with the five members of a syllogism, beginning with the proposition (*pratijñā*). Having previously stated "I am doing it," I shall now explain.

By these two applications— present and future— the author has demonstrated his intent to compose this commentary as an uninterrupted succession; he shows that this treatise, which provides benefit to all,
yields great fruit, and thus [he intends] its composition.
He demonstrates the universal benefit of both the undertaking and its commentary with the words beginning "everywhere" (*sarvatra*), etc.
The word "even" (*eva*) implies that although it was undertaken for the purpose of composing [the work], it continues until its final conclusion.

"Everywhere, the exposition is to be experienced through the intellect. Here, there are those of delicate intellect who have not exerted themselves in the study of the sharp sciences of logic (*tarka-śāstra*),
yet who, by the power of the descent of grace (*śaktipāta*), long for immersion (*samāveśa*) into the Supreme Lord as it dawns within them.

p. 14) For those few who possess devotion, the reality of the instruction on the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā* is being slightly unveiled; thus, according to the method taught in the *Śrīpratyabhijñāhṛdaya*, for one of limited intellect who has not undergone long exertion in any respect, and for one of delicate intellect [who requires guidance] at the beginning, middle, and end of every scripture— (Translation continued from previous context): ...[the author] undertakes this work. Furthermore, having considered that the *Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā* is difficult to understand due to its extreme conciseness, and that the *Vivṛti* is likewise difficult because it is a commentary on a commentary (*vyākhyāna-vyākhyāna*), he composed this *Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya* as a concise summary (*piṇḍārtha*) of the meaning of the *Kārikās*. Therefore, it is said: "The *Hṛdaya* is easy to understand, and it is a summary of the meaning of the *Kārikās*. By this, the necessity of composing this treatise is established. Now, as for the title of this work, *Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya*: the term *pratyabhijñā* refers to the recognition of the Lord (*īśvara-pratyabhijñā*), which is the subject matter (*abhidheya*) of this treatise. The term *hṛdaya* means "essence" (*sāra*). Thus, the meaning is that this is the essence of the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*. Alternatively, the word *hṛdaya* may signify the "heart" (*hṛdayastha*), implying that this work is situated within the heart of the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*. Or again, it may mean that this work is the "heart" of the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*, in the sense that it is the core of its meaning. This is the meaning. Now, regarding the purpose (*prayojana*) of this work: it is the attainment of the recognition of the Lord (*īśvara-pratyabhijñā-lakṣaṇa*), which is the ultimate goal (*uttama-puruṣārtha*). This is because the attainment of the recognition of the Lord is the supreme human aim. As it is said: "The recognition of the Lord is the supreme human aim. Furthermore, the relationship between the treatise and its purpose is that of the means and the end (*upāyopeya-bhāva*). This is because the recognition of the Lord is the end to be attained through this treatise. Thus, the four factors—the subject matter, the purpose, the relationship, and the intended audience (*adhikārī*)—are established. Among these, the intended audience consists of those who are devoted to the Lord, who desire liberation, and who seek the recognition of the Lord. It is said: "The intended audience is one who is devoted to the Lord, desires liberation, and seeks the recognition of the Lord. Now, as for the introduction (*upodghāta*) to this work: since the recognition of the Lord is the supreme human aim, and since that recognition depends upon the grace of the Lord, and since that grace depends upon the purification of the self (*ātma-śuddhi*), and since that purification depends upon the practice of yoga, and since that practice depends upon the knowledge of the true nature of reality (*tattva-jñāna*), and since that knowledge depends upon the hearing of the scriptures (*śāstra-śravaṇa*), and since that hearing depends upon the teacher (*guru*), and since that teacher depends upon the lineage (*paramparā*), the author first explains the lineage of teachers. He says: "In the lineage of the venerable Somānanda, the venerable Utpaladeva, and the venerable Lakṣmaṇagupta... and so forth. (End of section) (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation above reflects the full logical structure and content available up to the break.)

Because it consists of the unfolding of the power of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara-śakti*), it removes the state of being a bound soul (*paśutva*)—characterized by limited intellect—and is thus beneficial; that is, it brings about proximity to the attributes consisting of knowledge and action, and leads to the attainment of the state of a Lord (*patitva*). Alternatively, the phrase "anywhere" (*kutrāpi*) implies that this [text] is capable of withstanding the scrutiny of the science of logic (*tarka-śāstra*).

The meaning is that even for someone of great intelligence who is capable of understanding [the text] by themselves, regarding any particular point— specifically those most secret portions of the scripture that must be heard from the mouth of a Guru and which are beneficial in the manner described— the meaning of the scripture does not become manifest without this commentary.

"Not elsewhere" means that because it is impossible for those of small intelligence to grasp it, while those of very great intellect illuminate the meaning of the Sūtra by themselves, [the commentary] would be of benefit to neither group. Rather,
it is of benefit only to the creator himself— to me alone.
"I repeatedly contemplate this very [work] for the sake of attaining the state of being a servant to the Great Lord, which is one's own self recognized through the guru’s glance.
Thus, the universal benefit of his own commentary has been stated. Now, in due order:

The author demonstrates the introduction to the first aphorism with the passage beginning "the author" and ending with "states the purpose. The illustrious author, the teacher Utpaladeva, [speaks of] the "immediate Self"— this vision is "I am Śiva."

By the piercing glance of the venerable Somānanda, the author of the *Śivadṛṣṭi*, I have directly realized the Self—which is consciousness by nature—even though it was previously beyond perception. I know that within this very essence, the power of autonomy consisting of knowledge and action has been perceived;
thus, I possess the powers of omniscience and so forth, characterized by the experience of "I am" and "I act."

Having attained, solely through the grace of the Supreme Lord, the state of functional capacity, identity with the Supreme Lord, and the very nature of the Supreme Lord in another person— an individual who is a supreme qualified recipient— I alone am enriched by the fortune of His service, which is otherwise extremely difficult to obtain.
Feeling ashamed, I shall cause even this entire person to recognize their own master by means of the method about to be described, so that I may be satisfied by his attainment of the supreme goal;
thus, for one whose purpose is fulfilled, [it would be] for the sake of his own self... [he would be satisfied].
For, like the welfare of others, it is imperishable by the power of its own activity;
it possesses the nature of a drama woven from the entire system of constraints.
"There is no purpose other than grace in the remaining mode of life.
And: "May I remain steadfast for the sake of crossing the world, like a boat upon the ocean of saṃsāra.
Thus, because our [state] is complete, there is no need for the *adhānikā-tantra* as there is for the *nivṛtti-tantra*.
A monk desiring to transfer [the authority] to another qualified person intends to cause it to pass over.

In this context, "transference" does not occur like that of a numeral, by abandoning each preceding group of forms and transferring to a subsequent group; rather, in this way, the meaning of the scripture [is transferred] to the qualified person as a reflection...

By avoiding the heart of the teacher who is their own substratum, they cause [the teaching] to enter the intellect of the one being instructed, as he will say: "Thus, it is established through self-awareness, logical proof, and scripture," and so forth. That very point [he states] briefly for the sake of the disciple...
"Up to the words 'in order to establish [the disciple] within the Buddhis,' it is preceded by the conferring of identity with oneself (*svatādātmya-samarpaṇa*). Regarding "oneself":

having first considered that the attainment of identity with the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara-tanmayatā-sampatti*) may occur without obstacle for the person who is the authorized recipient of the initiation, and for that purpose, even though his own self is currently withdrawn from activity...

Having contemplated the identity consisting of being a servant of Maheśvara, and considering the attainment of that state to be free from obstacles, [the author]— by means of the remainder of the contemplation on humility regarding the excellence of the Supreme Lord, which consists of becoming one with Him— [states]: "You, O Supreme Lord, are the one supreme [Lord] of all worlds."

I have come for refuge to You, O Lord! Victorious is the unprecedented sovereignty of the Supreme Lord, the Guru of the three worlds, the Beloved of Ambikā—the Sovereign of the Universe, by whose will the creation, maintenance, and [dissolution] of the Supreme Lord [occur]. This collection of hymns [is offered] through the stability [of devotion to] the Supreme Lord.
Even for those such as Brahmā and Viṣṇu who are authorized to perform specific tasks, the excellence and majesty of the Lord [are supreme];

and He is "Great" because He is the cause of the creation and so forth even for Brahmā and the others. Thus, even with respect to those described in the *Stotrāvalī-vyākhyā* as being beyond [the reach of] the Great, He is the one who performs creation and the rest. As it has been said:

"O Lord of Gods, [this state] arises from Your power and is imperishable. For those who are bowed down before this Supreme Lord, through the immersion of the subjectivity of the body and so forth, they think: "I am entering into that very [reality].
According to the principle stated in the *Sāmbavyākhyā*, for the qualified practitioner, the body and so forth—

The immersion of the state of being a cognizer; O Supreme Lord, the contemplation of those two who are bowed down; the Supreme Lord’s reflection upon the person most excellent in the universe, contemplating his state of total submission;
and having brought that person to the state of being a fit vessel by making him subordinate as a recipient, [he effects] identity with the Supreme Lord.

It is said that "fitness" (*yogyatā*) is by means of the intellect; that is, when the purpose has been stated with the intention of establishing fitness for identity (*tādātmya*) through the intellect and the desire to accomplish eligibility for that [state], then, by his will,
there arises the attainment of supreme lordship characterized by omniscience, omnipotence, and so forth.
Desiring to explain the successive higher purports in detail,

he indicates the purpose here by way of summary; that is to say, with the passage beginning with "the immediate Self" (*aparokṣātma*) and ending with "desiring to cause [them] to enter" (*saṃcikrāmayiṣuḥ*), he indicates the meaning of the first half of the verse beginning with "in some way" (*kathaṃcit*) and ending with "desiring" (*icchan*).

The intended meaning (*tātparya*)— from the words "identity with itself" (*svatādātmya*) up to "considering [it as such]" (*manyamāna*)— furthermore suggests, in some way, the passage beginning with "having somehow attained" and ending with "servitude" (*dāsya*).
By the phrase "the excellence of the Supreme Lord," the intended meaning of the term "of Maheśvara" is shown.

The meaning of the phrase "upakāram" (the benefit) is [explained] by the words "prahvate tyanane dāsyatātparyaṃ parameśvare" (he bows with the intent of servitude toward the Supreme Lord), and so forth, up to the end of that passage;
and the meaning of the latter half of the verse beginning with "samasta" (all) is [explained] by the words "prayojanam" (the purpose).
Having thus presented this introduction, how...
He begins the passage starting with "Having reached consciousness" (cidāsādya):
"The spontaneous activity [of the Self], which transcends all human effort, is independent of [the distinctions between] uncreated and created states, as well as knowledge, yoga, and so forth."
That illustrious lady chose devotion to Śiva for herself, and at that very moment, she chose the fortune of liberation for me as well.

By the principle thus stated, it is indicated that there is a certain manner of the Supreme Lord’s grace— which transcends all human effort and is unattainable even through thousands of other births. Furthermore, the manner of worshipping the feet of the venerable Guru, who is non-different from Him and is fashioned by that very grace, is also implied by the word "having obtained" (*āsādya*).

It has been shown that the work does not serve one's own self-interest, but rather demonstrates its capacity to lead others to the state of being fulfilled through service to the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*).

By this, the author’s fitness for composing the treatise with the welfare of others as his primary motive is revealed. Furthermore, regarding the people [to be reached], it is shown that the work possesses the quality of being a means of attainment, consisting in the realization of the Great Lord (*maheśvara-pratyabhijñā*).
In the word *āsādya*, two causative suffixes (*ṇic*) are to be understood, [one] with respect to one's own self and [the other] with respect to people.

By the term "of Maheśvara" (22), through the word *mahat* ("great"), the sovereignty of the Supreme Lord— which is unconditioned by space and time— is distinguished from the sovereignty of Viriñci, Viṣṇu, Sadāśiva, and others.

It is manifested through its characteristic nature. As he will say: "The variety of conceptualization regarding these powers, such as knowledge and so forth, is of innumerable kinds. Sovereignty is autonomy;
it is not dependent on another, being the great majesty established previously, and it is that which has been fashioned [by it].
This is said with reference to the sovereignty of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and others. And it has been stated in the *Śrī Paramārthasāra*:
"The Lord is devoid of the limitations of space and time, eternal, immutable, and perfectly complete."

By the word *īśvara*, the independence (*svātantrya*) regarding knowledge and action residing in all subjects—beginning with Śiva—is indicated; and by the phrase "of the servant" (*dāsya*), it is stated that [the devotee] is a fit recipient for the bestowal of all sovereignty, such as omniscience and omnipotence, which constitute the essential attributes of the Supreme Lord. By the word *janasya* ("of the person"), it is meant one who is being born.

By demonstrating that everyone possesses the qualification [for this practice], the absence of restrictive rules regarding qualification based on caste (*varṇa*), stage of life (*āśrama*), and so forth, is indicated. This has been stated in the *Śrī Spandanirṇaya*: "In the same way, there is an absence of the contraction [of practice] caused by restrictions on qualification... Furthermore, through the etymological analysis (*nirukti*) of the word *janasya* ("of people"), it refers to those who are incessantly born.
Having observed that they are vessels of suffering by virtue of their perishable nature, it is also indicated that they are the objects of one's own compassion, which is capable of delivering them.
Just as this flavor of devotion might become something previously unknown to me...
In the same way, Īśāna is the Ghaṭika; he alone is thoroughly satisfied.

"Be our protector through compassion for us who are afflicted. By the word "even," it is meant that one should be satisfied by the attainment of the ultimate reality (paramārtha) even for him; according to this stated principle, because one's own self has been recognized as being the nature of the Supreme Lord (parameśvara), [there is satisfaction] for the one who is full.
The absence of any purpose other than the purpose of others who are non-different from oneself—

by manifesting the powers of knowledge and action, which, though residing within [the self], have been deluded by the power of *māyā* and thus remain unrecognized, one attains proximity to the Supreme Lord; this is what has been described as liberation.
As it has been said:
"He who knows that in which the god or man acts, he is a hero in the world."
"...the momentary [manifestation] of lordship" (p.

18). Thus, the benefit brought about by the eternal Will, which has been made the object of the power of Will, is shown to be the cause of one's own activity, which consists in the establishment of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). [The suffix] *śatṛ*...

By means of the word *pratyayena*, it is indicated that desire persists until the completion of the action consisting in the production of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*). Since desire itself is the cause— [as expressed by] "by this"— it is indicated (indicated) that desire alone reaches the culmination of the action.
The phrase "the cause for the attainment of all perfections" (*samastasampatsamavāptihetu*) is connected as a qualifier to [the states of] servitude (*dāsya*), service (*upakāra*),
and recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). In that context, the word "all" (*samasta*) refers to those [perfections] which, although already established and fully present even prior [to this],...
We bow to that devotee who, though not meditating upon nor reciting according to the prescribed rules the wealth whose nature is identity with the Supreme Lord,
nevertheless possesses such a manifestation of Śiva.

According to the principle thus stated, the term "servant" (*dāsa*) is a qualification [of the subject] because it is the cause for attaining [the state] without the exertion of meditation, recitation, and so forth; it refers to all the characteristics such as omniscience, which consist of identity with the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara-tādātmya*), His powers, and the manifestations of those powers.
The phrase "the cause of the attainment and perfect manifestation of *sampad*" refers to a specific excellence of assistance;

that is, it qualifies the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) as being the cause of the attainment of the entirety of *sampad*, which consists in the state of being the sovereign of the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*) beginning with Śiva and ending with the Earth. This is expressed by this genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

Three purposes have been indicated: identity with the Supreme Lord (parameśvara-tādātmya), the attainment of lordship over the wheel of powers (śakticakra) beginning with Śiva and ending with the earth (kṣiti), and [the attainment of] the plenitude (sampat) of all objects of knowledge (prameya)—such as blue, pleasure, and so forth—whether they be external or internal objects of the senses. In each respective way...

Its manifestation is its perfect attainment. This state of "knowability" (jñāteya) arises when various states of being, through the medium of their respective distinct cognitions, become established within a single subject.

Thus, according to the method being indicated: that [perception] consisting of sight and so forth finds its rest in the subject (*pramātṛ*), who consists of reflective awareness (*vimarśamaya*) by way of the internalized delusion (*pramoha*) which is the very life-force (*prāṇabhūta*) of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). That [rest] is the cause of that recognition; thus, in the *bahuvrīhi* compound, it refers to "that [recognition]."

For one whose heart has been purified by the supreme descent of power (*parā-śaktipāta*), there is indeed an inward rest within the collection of objects such as blue and pleasure— which, although intended as the cause of transmigratory existence by way of generating meritorious and non-meritorious karma through the recognition of one's own self— within that which is turned inward.

"It is the means for the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of one's own Self as the Great Lord (*maheśvara*)," so it was said by Suvratin. "By means of the paths such as the *Netra*, the entire objective reality (*padārtha*) is dissolved into that which is of the nature of [the Light], wherein [the Self] itself reflects upon that... Because for men, [the realization] of the gift arises from causes such as merit, it becomes directly perceived precisely through the door of the fundamental rest of blue and other objects. Furthermore,
having been brought face-to-face within one's own self through the service of a true guru, that cognition which is of the nature of light—

[He composed] the *Saṃjñā* and the *Śāstra*. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "recognition of that" (*tat-pratyabhijñā*), by the word "that" (*tat*), the person (*jana*) is also referred to. "Recognition" (*pratyabhijñā*) is a genitive-possessive compound (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*). By this, the noble one’s benevolence, which consists of supreme favor, is manifested. "I shall accomplish it.

It is observed. He states the meaning well-known from [the previous] discussion: "In this world" (*iha*) is used here to indicate the lack of dispute; that is, in this world which is manifest to everyone without contention, how could body, speech, and mind have that alone as their object? "O Lord, may there not be even for a moment, or in the slightest degree, any daring that causes injury to the flavor of non-difference from You"— according to this principle stated in the *Stotrāvalī*, one should [offer] body, speech, and mind toward the Supreme Lord, whose characteristics have been described and who is indifferent to worldly prosperity and the like.

for this mind is by nature diverse and not a seed of suffering.
That which is watered by the essence of devotion to you... [is the root of the tree of liberation].

according to this stated principle, *niyojanā* (the act of directing) is that whose characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is the impelling (*preraṇā*) by means of restraint (*yama*), which consists of the contemplation of one's own true nature (*svarūpānusaṃdhāna*) dependent upon the contemplation of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvarānusaṃdhāna*).

Such is [the state]. "Yet" (yeti) means as is well known; "this" (iyam) refers to that which is being experienced. According to the principle stated thus, for one who does not reflect upon— that is, who does not investigate— the reasoning consisting of the instruction of a true guru (who is non-different from the Supreme Lord), the hearing of the scriptures of Maheśvara, and one's own direct experience; even though [this reasoning] is of the nature of ultimate reality— if this transmigratory existence were not intended by us to be the supreme state...
Let us invoke the one Paśupati who dwells beyond;
for a stone does not cross the ocean merely by means of a great mountain, as if it were made of sacrificial animals offered as oblations.

Without you, neither by mind nor by speech can one reach the ground.

Thus, according to this established position, even if a salutation is accepted as being appropriate, for one intent on offering salutation, there remains only the state of being cast among the worldly "beast-like" people beginning with Brahmā. "—O Vaiṣṇava, those who abide in the lower stages..."
By the inclusion of the phrase "Vaiṣṇavas and others," the Śaivas, Naiyāyikas, and so forth are understood.

The term "stained by ignorance and attachment" refers to those characterized by both: by ignorance in the form of limited knowledge (*kiñcijjñatva*), and by attachment in the form of craving for sense objects.
Kalā, whose essential nature consists of limited agency, permanence, and the necessity of what is to be done,

is colored by the conceits "I am a knower of only a little" and "I am an agent of only a little," and so forth; yet it [is subordinate] to You, who are transcendent to the universe, yet the creator of the universe, its fullness, and its dissolution, and so on.

According to the etymological derivation of the root *div* in the sense of "sport" (*krīḍā*) and so forth, [the Lord] is one whose play consists of the creation of the universe and the like, as well as the desire for victory;

who is eternally manifesting all worldly transactions related to that universe; and who is the object of praise for Brahmā and others appointed to the tasks of creating the immeasurable phenomenal world (*māyīya-prapañca*) and so forth—[this is the meaning] culminating in that.

The state of the ground to be traversed is endowed with six qualities; it is declared to be the supreme cause of all causes, even the cause of Brahmā and the others. Their creation and so forth are His sport. It is the Supreme Śiva, possessed of the excellence of omniscience, omnipotence, and other such attributes. They do not know Him as "I."

The meaning is that although [the Lord] abides as their very own self, they do not recognize Him due to the absence of the Guru's glance. "Those" refers to the Vaiṣṇavas and others. "Māyā" is the Supreme Goddess who ordains both the conceit of selfhood in what is not-self, such as the body and so forth, and the conceit of non-selfhood in the Self, which is of the nature of pure consciousness.

The power of absolute freedom (svātantrya-śakti), having concealed one's own state as the Great Lord (maheśvaratva)—which consists of immersion (samāveśa) and is both immanent in and transcendent of the universe—manifests as "liberation" (mokṣa) within the state of non-liberation. This liberation is characterized by limited sovereignty (parimitaiśvarya) in the status of Brahmā and others, which is fashioned by the categories of time (kalā), limited agency (kāla), and so forth; it is out of a desire for such liberation that one thinks, "This alone is the supreme reality. From this [state], [the true liberation arises].
Thinking "there is nothing else beyond this," they cause delusion through that supreme form of conceit and cast themselves right there;

those worshippers of the self, believing "Viṣṇu alone is the self" and "Brahman alone is the self," worship the self while seeking to accomplish it through various specific mantras, [thinking] "the supreme..."

They do not go to the state that transcends the universe and consists of Supreme Śiva; the meaning is that they do not ascend because they are bound by the fetters of *māyā*. "For so many," etc.; therefore, [this is due to] the certainty that [the six paths] are one's own self.
"Regarding the aspect of the object of knowledge (*vedya*), there is liberation for him [at that stage], but first there is a return from his own higher level.

According to this principle stated in the *Śrītantravaṭadhānikā*, [this refers] to the limited state of Brahmā and others existing within the principles (*tattva*) ending with Māyā, which is the lowest [level]. The word "hi" (indeed) indicates the extraction [of the essential point]. It is the cause for the manifestation of distinctions such as "pertaining to Māyā" and so forth.

The power of autonomy is Māyā— by which Māyā [the soul's] limited knowledge (kiñcijjñatva) is produced; and by means of impure knowledge (aśuddhavidyā), attachment (rāga), and time (kāla)— which consist respectively of the state of being incomplete and limited agency— and by those [powers] characterized by them...

The Mothers of the Paśus are those who, being driven by the helplessness of being propelled by Time and Necessity— which act as the causes for the rules consisting of what is to be done and what is not to be done in a sequence of prior and posterior forms— are themselves set in motion.
Thus, according to the principle stated in the *Śivasūtras*, that [individual] who has become an object of enjoyment for the group of powers arising from the mass of sounds,
having had his power eclipsed by the *kalās*, is known as a *paśu* (bound soul).
Thus, according to the principle stated in the *Śrī Spandaśāstra*, through [the powers] such as Māheśvarī and the rest, one merely becomes subject to bonds; however,
by means of the firm realization that "I am Śiva— the omniscient, the omnipotent, and the all-pervading"— one becomes Śiva.

Thus, according to the principle taught in the *Śrīvijñānabhairava*, lordship (*patitva*) consists in the recognition of one's own true nature as that of Maheśvara, endowed with qualities such as omniscience.
Regarding the phrase "in comparison to others" (*itarāpekṣayā tu*): this means in comparison to those people who worship deities such as Indra, Candra, and so forth. From them...
The transcendence of the principles ending with Indra, Candra, and so forth belongs to the worshiper of Viṣṇu;

the transcendence of the principles ending with Prakṛti belongs to the worshiper of Rudra; the transcendence of the principles ending with Māyā belongs to the worshiper of Īśvara; and the transcendence of the principles ending with Śuddhavidyā belongs to the worshiper of [Sadāśiva].

For one who worships Sadāśiva, there is transcendence of the principles ending with Īśvara; for one who worships Śiva, there is transcendence of the principles ending with Śakti; and for one who worships Diśiva, there is transcendence of the principles ending with Diśiva—in this manner, there may indeed be a gradation of excellence. This very [point]...

The Giver of Boons (Varada) confirms what has been said with the words "it accords," and so forth. The Supreme Lord alone is the one who grants to the seeker that which consists of both: the nourishment of the desired and the constant burning away of the undesired—being composed of both water and fire.

[He is the one for those] whose minds are noble... (Note: The provided source text contains significant corruption and lacunae; the translation above reflects the intelligible portions of the Sanskrit fragments.)

According to the principle stated as "that which nourishes what is desired," having incinerated the state of duality—which consists of Māyā, is considered undesirable, and is characterized by impurity—the [worship] takes the form of the purity of consciousness in its supreme non-dual nature. (p. 23)

Bestowing grace through the unartificial, uncontrived, and spontaneously arisen Rudrayāmala and other tantras issuing from the mouth of the venerable Bhaṭṭāraka— moreover, those gurus who, with their senses turned inward, possess hearts inseparable from Śambhu, are victorious.
In the past, they attained the perfection of concentration that reaches the limit of being beyond emergence.
According to the principle thus stated, one who beholds Your experience— which is devoid of [ordinary] emergence (*abhyutthāna*), which consists of immersion (*samāveśa*) in You,
and which is the pinnacle of immersion because it is both identical with the universe and transcendent of it— or, according to the reading "Your manifestation" (*tava vibhūtim*),
one who beholds the wealth consisting of liberation-in-life (*jīvanmukti*) pertaining to You.

For one who directly realizes [the state] transcending the seven levels of subjects beginning with *sakala* and ending with *Śiva*, and having cast off or abandoned [them], how indeed— by whomsoever it may be— could there arise a desire to praise (*stuti-spṛhā*), that is, the wish to offer hymns, even out of delusion (*vibhrama*) or under the influence of error (*bhrānti-vaśāt*) regarding another state, such as those of Sadāśiva and the rest? The meaning is that no one at all would have such a desire.
The particle *api* is displaced [in the sentence]. Here, the suffix *-tasi*, which functions as a nominal suffix (*sārvavibhaktika*), occurs in the sense of the locative case in the word *aparataḥ*.
By the phrase "the illustrious Lord of the Vidyādharas," he demonstrates the authority of the tradition through its well-known name, thereby indicating the inferiority of Sadāśiva and others.

We shall establish the supremacy of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) in the section on scripture (*āgamakāṇḍa*) through the passage beginning with "having internal and external activity" and ending with "the body of the supreme syllable. Therefore, [this is] because of the reason stated in the text: "if she who bows down from all sides were to perceive his excellence..."

In this salutation characterized by prostration toward that which has been described, there is a reflection upon the greatness and majesty of the Supreme Lord— the object of salutation— His superiority over Sadāśiva and all others who are considered preeminent, according to the principle stated as "this [salutation] consists of three cognitions."

Through the teacher, the scriptures, and one's own experience, [the means] is brought about. In that regard, first of all, since yoga is not a means [to liberation], it must be a means only for cognition; thus, what is called "cognition" (jñapti) is explained.
How could luminosity belong to that which is self-luminous through anything else?
What need is there for arguments regarding the fact that consciousness itself is luminous?

In the absence of that [consciousness], the universe would be unmanifest due to its insentience. Whatever means there may be, whether external or internal, all of them depend upon that [consciousness] for their manifestation; how then could they possess the status of being a means toward it?
Through various means, that Śiva shines, and they shine by his grace;
he alone is I, self-luminous, appearing as the form of all that exists in the universe.
Having heard these words of the Guru once, some became certain;
without further investigation and without death, they remained established [in that state].

Thus, according to the principle stated in the *Tantrāloka* and the *Tantravaṭadhānikā*, [the Lord] bestows grace upon the transmigrating soul for whom a firm descent of the power of the Lord (*īśvara-śaktipāta*) has occurred— even without human effort (*puruṣakāra*) consisting of the contemplation of the Supreme Lord’s excellence and one’s own prostration— [and thus bestows grace] upon the entire universe.
And even though she has come spontaneously of her own accord, according to the principle stated as "the Lord," she is the grace of the Supreme Lord;
for, according to the principle stated as "that which is pure, eager for worship,
and free from the exertion of meditation," she has come by herself through her own self, without the exertion of recitation, causal means, or meditation— thus [she is] "this one."
Being experienced through immersion as being "this much," this state— consisting of the thirty-six principles from Śiva down to the Earth— is the ground of the transcendent Supreme Śiva;
it is a state whose essence is the fullness of I-consciousness (pūrṇāhaṃtā), and it comes within the range of the Heart, reaching the very core of the Heart.
He attains [it] directly. "In this" means on the plane of Paramaśiva.
One's own human effort (*puruṣakāra*) consists of the acts of worship and meditation performed by the person through body, speech, and mind.
Human effort is a certain [form of] reflection upon the excellence of the Supreme Lord, as proclaimed in the scriptures.

No means whatsoever succeeds; for every human effort performed by speech, mind, or body is characterized by its illusory nature (*māyā*) because it is produced by an illusory subject (*māyā-pramātṛ*). Precisely for this reason, because it lacks the capacity to manifest its own true nature, that which is like blinding darkness is "non-illusory" (*amāyīya*), meaning it has transcended illusion (*māyottīrṇa*).

For this very reason— because [Śiva] is devoid of the ninefold māyīya [powers]— it is impossible for Him, who is pure light, to appear as non-Śiva through means (upāyas) directed toward that which opposes and contradicts His own human effort (*puruṣakāra*),
according to the principle stated in the *Tantravaṭadhānikā*. Even if this were indeed the case...
Nevertheless, that very state of the Supreme Lord is thus described as "vibhrama" (delusion/manifestation); this is [the result of] human effort (*puruṣakāra*).

Regarding the sequence of "prakhyā" (manifestation) and "apākhyā" (non-manifestation): "prakathana" (proclamation) is the thorough explanation of that essential nature to the teacher with respect to his own self; "vyākhyā" (explanation) is that same essential nature with respect to the one being instructed.

"Making known" (*prakhyāpana*) is "narration" (*upākhyā*); thus, a narration concerning what has occurred proceeds with the desire to reach the state of becoming an object of manifestation for oneself and others—
and its becoming an object [for others] consists in making it penetrate the heart by means of the thought, "This is that."
(25) Out of the desire to go to Him—that is, the desire to cause Him to come and reach [the devotee]—[I pray: "Victory, victory! O vessel of glory!

Worship Him who has conquered birth, old age, and death; O Eldest of the World! O Fire, Moon, Sun, Brahman, Viṣṇu, and all that is stationary and moving! Salutation to You, whose nature is consciousness, who possesses many forms."
Where lights are but lights and darknesses are but darkness, where both lights and darknesses exist together in duality, there shines the unsurpassed light.
I bow to that Absolute (Anuttara), in whom [the universe] is eternally full as the Self, from which this world is emitted through the nature of will, knowledge, and action.
Because it has been stated that one should incorporate the word "jayati" (conquers), which denotes specific excellence,
as well as the word "namaḥ" (salutation), which— by the inclusion of the term "ādi" (and so forth)—
denotes self-prostration, and that even the reference to all-encompassing excellence must be accepted therein.

Humility (*prahvatā*) has been described as having the nature of the contemplation of all-encompassing excellence. The term "victory" (*jaya*), which denotes a specific excellence of that [excellence], must be invoked—that is, it must be internally accepted.

In that regard, when there is a state consisting of this mere subjectivity (*mātṛtāmātra*), Rudra is the presiding deity (*adhidaivata*) within the expansion of distinct objects of knowledge (*bhinnaprameyaprasara*).

"Brahmā and Viṣṇu are established. According to the principle that will be explained hereafter, Māyā is the category of subjects; [it consists of] those presiding over the states of emission, maintenance, and withdrawal—namely, the Mantras, Mantreśvaras, and Mantramaheśvaras residing within the principles (tattvas) of Śuddhavidyā, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva.

To the Lordess, who shines with a preeminent excellence surpassing even that of Śiva— the source of existence who is the presiding lord over all these [deities] beginning with Ananteśvara, Sadāśiva, and Bhaṭṭāraka, who constitute the class of knowers— and who is [adorned] by the drops of the nectar of [her] grace.
