Obeisance to the Blessed One, the Great Lord (Maheśvara), whose ultimate reality is uninterrupted light, bliss, and sovereignty; even though this is an invocation for victory regarding the Great Lord who possesses such characteristics as will be described hereafter, I intend to refer to that very Maheśvara who partakes in such victory.

According to the stated principle— that the meaning of *namaskāra* (salutation) is the state of being bowed down (*prahvatā*), characterized by the application of body, speech, and mind toward that single object— for one who thus bows down their own self-knowledge in the form of body, speech, and mind, and is consequently detached (*taṭastha*), everything is given to him by the Lord.

"According to one's desire" means for one who has not yet attained the state of servitude (*dāsya*) to the Supreme Lord, as will be described later [in the verse beginning with] "the servant. Therefore, by establishing his station here, having contemplated his own agency over the worlds, and constantly entering into that which consists of Śiva-nature, he attains perfection.

Thus, due to the absence of both *jīvanmukti*— which consists of the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of one's own self as the form of the Supreme Lord to be described hereafter— and the two-fold *siddhi* consisting of the power of practice and immersion (*samāveśa*),
there is only a supreme excellence in the sense of being beneficial to others, according to the previously stated definition.
Since the salutation (*namaskāra*) has been specifically implied and forcibly drawn in by the word "victory" (*jaya*), it must necessarily be internalized;

for it is impossible to employ both "the Supreme Lord is victorious" (*parameśvaro jayati*) and "I bow to the Supreme Lord" (*parameśvaraṃ namāmi*) at one and the same time. By this reasoning, there is an exclusion of one of the two—either victory or salutation.

One must necessarily admit that for one of the two [the unmentioned], there is an absence of words that would be appropriate expressive forms for its own subject matter, and that this is necessitated by the implication of the meaning. One must admit that the meaning of the other is contained within this [unmentioned element]. [This is expressed through verbs such as] "I revere," "I understand," "I remember," "I mutter," or "I meditate."

Since even acts such as saluting, contemplating, and remembering the Supreme Lord possess the nature of the subject— the one who salutes, contemplates, remembers, recites, and meditates— and because the ultimate reality consists in the continuous flow of homage within the subject's own self, the object of veneration must be understood [as being identical with that subject].

This path, which consists of the nature of bowing to one’s own self— characterized as "this [is it]" because its ultimate reality is the meaning of sacrifice expressed in the excellence of the Supreme Lord who is to be remembered, recited, and meditated upon— is the supreme, ultimate method (*vartanī-pāramārthikī-paddhati*). It is *namaskāra*.

The meaning is that there is no path other than victory over the objects [of sense]. Thus, when either "victory" (*jaya*) or "salutation" (*namaskāra*) is employed, the purpose of the other is already fulfilled. However, thinking that there is no reference to the specific word appropriate for that [other term], the author of this work has adopted such an order, in which—

The term "both" refers to the sense of victory and the sense of salutation; both are indeed indicated by their respective appropriate words. The meaning of these two phrases—“this” and “servitude to Maheśvara”—will become manifest during the occasion of their detailed exposition. [This concerns] the appropriate words for victory and salutation.

And this reference (*parāmarśa*) is logical because it is for the benefit of all people; that is, because it is accessible to the hearts of everyone. For that very reference by its own word (*svaśabdaparāmarśa*), as soon as it enters the path of hearing, becomes heart-pleasing even to one of extremely dull intellect, by means of a word expressive of itself that is appropriate to it.
Without the word "anyatama" (one of many), the phrase "some" (*katicit*) would be implied by the sense;

however, it is employed for the sake of distinction regarding those of the highest capacity who are capable of discernment. It becomes heart-pleasing for those of delicate intellect who have undergone the exertion of sharp reasoning. The reason for this lies in the fact that [the word] expresses the sense of "victory" (*jayati*).

When the word *jaya* (victory) is employed directly, the sense of *namaḥ* (salutation) is implied by its meaning; [this is so] because it is impossible for there to be a reflective awareness (*avamarśa*) of the reality of speech (*vāktattva*) while one has performed [an act of salutation]. Likewise, even when the word *namaḥ* is employed directly as the expressive signifier of the sense of salutation, the sense of *jayati* (he is victorious) is implied by its meaning.

Because it is impossible to refer back to the word "victory" (*jaya*) as something arisen from one's own intuition, the meaning of that word does not immediately enter the heart of those with sharp intellects; therefore, [the author] has simultaneously expressed this extraordinary path,
which conveys both the sense of victory and salutation.

He followed [the path] correctly and without effort; that is, he accepted it. In such statements, the word "jaya" (victory) is used by the Ācārya for the purpose of salutation (*namaskāra*). Having thus explained the meaning of this word, [he proceeds]:
the Buddhists (*saugata*) assert non-dual consciousness (*vijñānādvaita*) as being devoid of both self (*ātman*) and Lord (*īśvara*).
The non-duality of Brahman, accompanied by the adjunct of ignorance and thus indeterminable, is the conclusion of the Vedas;
this very freedom of consciousness (saṃvitsvātantrya) is the intended heart of all the scriptures.
It is taught by means of recognition.

According to the principle stated by Abhiyukta, demonstrating that the vision of the non-duality of the Lord (*īśvarādvaya*) is distinct from the dualistic views such as those of the Vijñānavādins, he states the following thesis, which constitutes the essence of this system: "Whatever exists in the world as subject (*pramātṛ*) or means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*..."
Some object in the form of a cognizable entity manifests; that is merely the manifestation of one's own Self in its various forms as the Lord (Īśvara) which will be described hereafter.

"It is merely the manifestation of this or that" is the view of the Buddhists (Saugatas). "It is merely the manifestation of one's own Self" is the view of the Vedāntins. To exclude both of these, [in our] system...
It has been stated that the nature of the Lord is merely the manifestation of one's own self. As it is said: "Blue, yellow, pleasure—these are only the Light, which is Śiva. And:
"Whatever manifests through the gateway of the senses, that very form arises as the Lord."
That which is manifest is not something other than manifestation— what is this [object], for it is non-different from manifestation?
That very manifestation which shines forth in the form of a jar also shines forth in the form of a cloth.

"In this way, the independent Light alone, manifesting as the body of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), expands itself"— with these words, [the author] will explain, in the section beginning with "action, relation," and ending with "the causality, the agency, and the action," how this expansion consists of the various objects of knowledge (*prameya*), means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and subjects of knowledge (*pramātṛ*).

The relationship consisting of the state of means (*upāya*) and end (*upeya*), which takes the form of the relationship between the signifier (*jñāpaka*) and the signified (*jñāpya*), is also, like light, ultimately nothing other than light itself. The means is the path; the end is the village.
The state of means and end is established in both of these; the knowledge beginning with that [means] and so forth is the signifier.
The object to be made known (*jñāpya*) is a jar and so forth; the sun and so forth are the means of making it known (*jñāpaka*); the earth and so forth are the knower (*jñātṛ*).
Caitra is the cause; his son is the effect.
The seed is the cause; the sprout is the effect. Such are the two [categories]. (p. 28)

The relationship of cause and effect, which is grounded in real entities, is also a connection; for instance, according to each respective manifestation, it is in the ultimate sense merely the unfolding of one's own Self in the form of the Lord. This is the meaning. [This is understood] from the word "tu" (but/only).
Because that which exists in two places has multiple forms, because this [agent] is not observed in what is already established,
and because it is impossible for it to be dependent on others and so forth— by whom has such a "creator" been conceptualized?

Thus, he dispels the doubt regarding the non-reality of the relationship as asserted by the proponent of consciousness (*vijñānavādin*) which is about to be stated—by means of the phrase "of that which is manifesting. This is because a relationship manifesting in such and such a manner cannot be denied by anyone; for if it were denied...
Otherwise, because consciousness itself would be subject to denial, the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*) would follow.

To show that consciousness here cannot be denied, he provides a point of agreement (*saṃvāda*), as stated by the venerable Bhaṭṭa Divākaravatsa in the *Vivekāñjana*: "Of entities such as earth and the rest..."

If those entities such as jars and cloths that constitute its own acceptance— manifesting perceptibly to everyone as "this"— do not dissolve through the power of negation (śāpiktyā) nor by means of a declarative oath (śapathavacanena), stating that they do not appear in any other manner, then [they remain] as related to those respective entities such as jars and cloths.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the absence of all conventional discourse such as relinquishment and acquisition. Thus, having established that the causal relationship existing within that phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is likewise ultimately real (*pāramārthika*),
the author intends by the phrase "in some way" (*kathaṃcit*) to refer to an effect that is non-illusory (*amāyīya*).

In order to demonstrate the nature of causality, [the author] states the nature of that causality—of which Māyā is the cause and which has worldly convention as its counter-correlator—by first presenting its counter-correlate: "Causality is twofold: the worldly and..."

And it is supramundane; and it is illusory—thus, in that context, regarding the relationship between cause and effect. Such being the twofold state, in some cases—in the aforementioned relationship of cause and effect—it is complete.
Here, however, it is of this present form; that which is unconditioned by space, time, and shape.

Sovereignty (*svātantrya*) is its defining characteristic. Therefore, that Maheśvarī sovereignty—which is distinct from the lordships (*aiśvarya*) consisting of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra—is, by virtue of being inseparable from it and dependent upon it, made *kaula* (belonging to the Kula), having its form accepted as such. Thus, [it is free from] spatial, temporal, and formal limitations, as well as hardness.

Those entities which are presided over— that is, touched— by that infinite and undivided wheel of powers (*śakticakra*), which consists of fluidity, heat, motion, measure, the granting of space, and so forth, and which takes the form of limited agency (*kiñcitkartṛtva*) and limited knowledge (*kiñcijjñatva*).

(29) Earth and the other [elements], as well as Caitra, Maitra, and others—by means of a different manifestation (*prathāntara*) produced or brought about by these, there is the causal materiality (*mṛtkāraṇa*), which he will state later: "In the doctrine of causality and so forth, cognition is produced from a plurality of blue and other [objects]. This refers to the insentient object of knowledge (*jaḍasya prameyasya*).
This causal relationship belonging to Māyā—which is non-inert, immeasurable, and differentiated by hundreds of intermediate distinctions—is "produced by that" [the Supreme Lord].
Thus it is said: "The Supreme Lord is the creator of objects common to all."
But the potter and others are the creators by means of the clay and other materials fashioned by them.
The capacity for the creation of the universe belongs to Viśva; [the capacity for] the creation of the universe does not exist in weavers and the like.

Thus, according to scripture, this [notion] "this is so" is perceived by everyone; it consists of all worldly transactions, such as: "the jar is the cause and the fetching of water is the effect," or "the potter and others are the cause, and the jar is the effect," and so forth.
Alternatively, by means of a specific manifestation other than the causal relationship free from *māyā* which will be described later,
it is the Supreme Lord alone who is the cause and the universe is His effect; that causal relationship, which shines forth as being free from *māyā*,
is the [causal relationship].
However, it will be established in such passages as "The insentient [entity] does not possess that power" that this pertains to the realm of *māyā*.

For an insentient object such as a jar, the cause is an insentient material such as clay; for a sentient being such as Caitra, the cause is a sentient one such as his father; and for an insentient object such as a jar, the cause is a sentient one such as the potter. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*),...

For insentient cognition, which is of the nature of a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there is the relation of producer and produced with respect to its insentient form, such as blue; having brought about [the object], the appearance of the relation of the known and the knower is the manifestation of the producer and the produced. The produced is the jar and so forth, while the producer is... [omitted].

The knower is the one who makes known by means of the instrument of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Thus, through their mutual relationship characterized as the states of producer and produced, and signifier and signified, there arises the manifestation:
"I am the producer; this is the product," and "I am the signifier."

That which is to be made known—namely, that which takes the form of worldly convention—is, in its various sub-divisions numbering in the hundreds, rooted in this [relation]; thus, the reality of that relation is twofold:

from the perspective of ultimate truth, it consists of the state of being the object of cognition (*jñāpyatā*) and the state of being the means of cognition (*jñāpakatā*), as well as the state of being effect and cause (*kāryakāraṇatā*).

With the intention of what is to be explained hereafter— namely, that [the agent] both knows and acts— the twofold nature of the relationship has been stated by means of the opening and conclusion of the treatise (śāstra), as well as through the passage beginning with "to be produced" (*niṣpādya*), etc., based on the perspective of the one who knows and the one who acts.

Having thus explained the illusory relationship of cause and effect which is the basis for worldly convention, he now defines the non-illusory relationship of cause and effect with the passage beginning with "But where... and ending with "...by the construction of the Supreme Lord alone."

The word "but" (*tu*) serves to highlight the distinction between that which belongs to *māyā* and that which does not. Regarding the phrase "wherein": it refers to the state characterized by the purity of the causal relationship, which is distinct from the previously mentioned [state] belonging to *māyā*. It is pure—meaning free from the turbidity of *māyā*—consisting of one's own self-manifestation, having the nature of self-luminosity, indestructible, and indeed the innate light itself.

He is praised for possessing that power which is beginningless, supreme, and the most excellent, consisting of both knowledge and action. Furthermore, he is endowed with the essential nature of light and awareness (*prakāśa-vimarśa*), which consists of the unsurpassed emission (*visarga*) arising from the union of Śiva and Śakti.

The Self alone, manifesting within all existents, is Śiva, whose nature is consciousness free from objective activity, whose flow of will is unobstructed, and who possesses expanding vision and action.

Thus, according to the principle set forth in the *Śivadṛṣṭi*, there is an unrestrained and unimpeded expansion of the powers of knowledge and action, which consists of the assumption of the essential nature of all things from Sadāśiva down to a mere insect. Regarding the phrase "by the one possessing Māyā" (*māyīya*):
how could agency belong to anyone else when it is possible [only] for You, the Lord who is the agent of all, while remaining awake?

Thus, by this principle, [the Self] is devoid of any obstruction consisting of the manifestation of difference—characterized by limited agency and so forth—which would obstruct its great manifestation as all-agency, omniscience, and the like.
Since that [manifestation] belongs to Him by His very nature, how could there be any restriction by means of the vital breath (*prāṇa*)? Thus, He is non-inert (*ajaḍa*).

According to the reasoning established in the *Pramātṛsiddhi*, even this manifestation of "I" (maya) is of the nature of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), because it is itself manifest; otherwise, manifestation would be impossible, as it could not be separated from that great manifestation which is the self-luminous light of the Self. Thus, this [world] has the Supreme Lord alone as its cause.
He states that the manifestation of one's own Self is the cause of the supreme human goal with the words "And this": *eṣa ca*.

This refers to the manifestation of one's own Self, which is established through one's own direct experience (*svānubhava*). It is called "the last" because it is the fifth in relation to the [five] cosmic acts beginning with emission (*sṛṣṭi*). Beyond that, the supreme state of the Lord (*pārameśvara*) is the end of all objective existents (*bhāva*).
The specific function characterized by grace (anugraha) is as follows:
from grace up to creation, the power of the Existent (sat-śakti) is ever-arisen;
[the Lord] acts by bestowing grace, not bestowing grace, withdrawing, establishing, and creating.
According to the principle thus stated, creation (*sṛṣṭi*) is also found among the five [categories].

To exclude this, it is said that the final fifth is characterized as grace (*anugraha*). "Supreme" (*para*) means that which brings about for the person (*puruṣa*) the supreme human goal whose nature is Supreme Śiva (*paramaśiva*). "That" (*tat*)...

Because ultimate liberation—which consists in the manifestation of one's state as the living Śiva (jīvacchivatva) and so forth—is dependent upon such grace; "elsewhere" refers to the states of the *pralayākala* and *vijñānākala*.
The liberation intended by the *mantras*, *mantreśvaras*, and others is a liberation from something specific, not from everything.

In that regard, there is liberation for the *pralayākalas* who abide in the principle of *māyā* from the aggregate of principles beginning with earth and ending with *kalā*. Then, for those situated in the plane of *vidyā*, there is liberation from the five principles beginning with *vidyā* and ending with *śiva*, which exist above them.

For those who take the mantra as their means of valid cognition (*pramātṛ*), there is liberation from *māyā*—beginning with *akṣiti*—but not from the four *tattvas* situated above it. This should be understood in other cases as well. "Therefore" [means]:
each respective liberation is merely a semblance of the ultimate good (*niḥśreyasa*), but it is not the ultimate good in the absolute sense.
Thus it has been said:
"He alone is liberated in truth by virtue of abandoning all limitations;
others are not liberated in truth because there remains a portion of limitation."

Thus it is stated in the *Tantravaṭadhānikā*. We shall explain this in the section on the goat-skin [chapter], during the occasion of defining the reality of the subject (*pramātṛ*). And as for "this very one":
[it refers to] that where there is self-manifestation (*svaprathā*), and so forth. "This" is established by one's own experience within me.

The second [type of dependence] is with respect to the relationship between cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). When causes consisting of both the insentient and the sentient—such as clay and a potter—exist, effects such as jars arise; when they do not exist, the effect does not arise. Thus, it lacks the well-known relationship of cause and effect established through worldly positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
It is not perceived as a cause in a manifest form, like a potter is [perceived] in relation to a jar; nevertheless, it shines forth at some time like a flash of lightning from the Lord,
anointed with my nectar.
Thus, when a longing for Śiva indeed arises in bound souls (paśus) according to the method taught by the Guru— this is the secret— then,
through the identification with Śiva, [they attain liberation].
According to the principle taught in the *Vāgāmokta*, at that time, by means of the occasional manifestation— impelled by the will of the Lord—

of the reality that exists within, which consists of consciousness and is of the nature of "I," the ultimate realization is determined; and it is precisely this [realization] that constitutes its unsurpassed capacity to accomplish the impossible.

"Autonomy, sovereignty, and likewise both—what can the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) not accomplish in this world? It is capable of unifying them. According to this stated principle, because the universe—which is essentially of the nature of "I"—is manifest, it appears as "this" to the class of illusory subjects (*māyīya-pramātṛ*), thereby becoming limited.
The manifestation of the body and so forth as "I" [is explained as follows]. As it has been said (p. 32):

"In the theory of self-manifestation (*ātmakhyāti*), one projects the non-self as the self due to the flashing forth of the cognition of 'I'; furthermore, because of the manifestation of the self, even the distinctness from what is other [is projected]. This very [theory] is difficult to establish...
What could the divine Māyā, the consort of Maheśvara, who acts as the very form of the sovereignty of another's consciousness, not manifest? For she is non-existent [as an independent entity].

Thus, through the manifestation of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) and autonomy (*svātantrya*), characterized by the performance of what is difficult to accomplish, [the Lord] bestows grace; this state of wonder (*adbhutabhāva*), whose very nature is marvelous, is not [ordinarily] contemplated. Regarding the phrase "the first limit": it refers to the accumulation [of merit] from the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).

According to the principle stated by the venerable Sāmbabhaṭṭāraka— "of those who rely on the bondage of actions, whether existent or non-existent," and so forth— the first possibility is that which is void, beginningless, established, and of the nature of Kālikā;
that which is the form of impurity (*mala*), the subtle impurity here that obscures both one's own and other natures.

The fivefold [sheaths] beginning with *māyā* are gross and external, consisting of forms of restraint; for the Self is indeed enveloped by the three sheaths, according to the principle stated in the *Śrī Paramārthasāra*:
"That which resides within the sheath of *kalā* and the rest, enveloped by the body, vital breath, and so forth."
The Self alone of the worlds is defiled by the impurity of beginningless time.
According to the principle stated by the learned, there is the concealment known as *āṇava*, *māyīya*, and *kārmika*;

furthermore, as will be explained later, there is the concealment of one's own true nature (*svasvarūpatirodhāna*) belonging to the bound soul (*paśu*), which consists of the *māyā* called *tirodhānakarī*. Upon the removal of that [concealment], [liberation occurs].
Even by hundreds of desires,
nor by the Vedas, nor by austerity, nor by charity, nor by sacrifice,
can one such as this be seen.

Thus, according to the principle stated in the *Gītā*, that which is difficult to attain through hundreds of desires fulfilled by the study of the Vedas, asceticism, charity, and sacrifices such as the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*)—
meaning it is impossible to obtain except solely through the grace of the Supreme Lord— is of this nature.

From the words "the worldly sequence" (*laukikānvaya*) up to "difficult to attain through hundreds of desires" (*manorathaśataduṣprāpa*), [the text] describes the extraordinary mode (*alaukikaḥ prakāraḥ*) as stated in the treatise. This very mode is indicated by the phrase "in some way" (*kathañcit*), which is uttered together with the first quarter of the root aphorism (*mūlasūtra*) that is invariably concomitant (*avinābhūtayā*) with it. Thus it is.
It is defined by a suffix joined with the indeclinables *laukika*, *alaukika*, *prakāra*, *cetana*,
*cit*, *iti*, and *nipāta*. Having thus stated one meaning of the word *kathañcit*,
he states another meaning of that same word which is useful for its primary sense, using the phrase "by some" (*kenacit*).

Because he is non-different from the Supreme Lord whose characteristics have been described, and because he has attained identity with Him through constant immersion (*samāveśa*) therein, he perceives and teaches the true meaning of the reality of mantra, mudrā, and the vital force of right knowledge and action exactly as they are; for this reason, he is the Guru.

Thus, according to the principle stated in the Vārttika on the *Śrīśivasūtra*, in order to perceive the nature of Śiva— the supreme goal for those to be graced— one should, by means of the two rays of knowledge and action, [worship] the pair of lotus feet of the Guru, which are essentially identical with that [reality] and constitute its true meaning through their qualities. (43)

According to the principle stated in the *Śrīmatstotrāvalī-vyākhyā*, since you are the one whose feet consist of the rays of knowledge and action (*jñāna-kriyā*), O Lord, it is solely by Your will that I have become Your servant; for there is no power here belonging to another—
this being according to the principle stated in the *Śrīmatstotrāvalī* beginning with "When there is indeed a longing for Śiva," and so forth regarding initiation (*dīkṣā*).

"They attain [the goal], O Guru," according to the principle stated in the *Śrīnandiśikhāgrantha*, and by means of worship performed for the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) with devotion and faith— otherwise the two feet [of the Lord] would not be attained— one should serve with service endowed with devotion and faith, in accordance with the tradition of the venerable Sāmba.
The particle *ca* indicates a conjunction of other modes;

the particle *eva* indicates the exclusion of others. The venerable teachers [state] that Rādhā can be united with the Supreme Lord alone; for even those who seek refuge [say], "You are the Supreme Lord of the worlds," and so forth.
According to the principle stated that "it is the refuge," [one does not rely] on any other group of causal deities from Brahmā down to Śiva;

nor is any practice of yoga, austerity, or ritual worship prescribed by them. According to this principle, one relies instead upon one's own activities such as yoga, austerity, and worship. Regarding this point, there is the statement of an authoritative scholar:
He provides the proof with the words "as it has been said," and so forth.

The ellipsis is to be supplied as "of the disciple who has turned away from the desire for enjoyment and longs solely for the path to liberation. And [it is said]: "The connection with a teacher who is perfectly awakened is exceedingly difficult to establish."
The disciple, having turned away from the desire for enjoyment regarding worldly fields, wife, sons, friends, and so forth,

and being solely intent on the longing for the means to liberation— which consists of identity with Supreme Śiva— is well-awakened, having recognized the nature of his own self as the Supreme Lord through *pratyabhijñā*.

Such a Guru is difficult to find; likewise, a disciple possessing the aforementioned characteristics is difficult to find. Thus, without the grace of the Supreme Lord, the relationship between Guru and disciple is extremely hard to establish.
"In this way, somehow"—so it is said.

Having set aside two possible meanings of the word *pada*, he explains *āsādya* as follows: "Having attained" (*āsādya*) refers to the service (*dāsya*) characterized by the [great] pride that will be described hereafter. Even for one who has attained such great pride, [the state of] being subdued (*damayam*) toward the Lord is appropriate for one in the condition of a servant, according to the principle stated [in the verse]. (44)
Śivadāsa, through his identity with Śiva, shall moreover attain happiness;
for by him, even the foremost gods are satisfied with nectar-like offerings.
According to the principle thus stated, by being free from the obstacles consisting of emergence (*vyutthāna*),
and having brought [the practice] to completion in its fullness even during times such as the past (*bhūta*)— which are characterized by your own particular command—
one attains the unimpeded state of one's own self, which is identical with Śiva, and [destroys] that which is called *māyā*, the concealer.

Furthermore, having led [the soul]— which is enveloped by the five [principles] beginning with *kāla* and so forth, up to being shrouded by *tirodhāna*— to a state of fitness for enjoyment (*upabhoga-bhoga-yogyatā*) consisting of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) "I am Śiva," "I am the Lord," "I am Paśupati," "I am Bhairava," and so on, [and which is thus] freed from the bolts of *māyā*, *kāla*, and the rest;

First, one strives for the state of being a servant of Maheśvara; thus, through the attainment of the nature of Maheśvara, there is the realization. "Realized" means that the secret of the Vedas has been known, and that this body and so forth are not the Self, and that Śiva is the Self—what more is there [to be known]?
According to the principle stated that "the supreme fruitfulness of human birth [consists in this]," by means of realizing the nature of the Great Lord (Maheśvaratva) within one's own self,

the author has demonstrated his qualification for composing the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā-śāstra*— which bestows grace regarding the ultimate reality— and has manifested his fitness. Otherwise, it would be mere servitude.
Because the state of being that which is to be known has been realized through the attainment of perfection, both self and other are liberated;

thus, according to the principle to be explained, the very recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of one's own nature as the Lord bears fruit. By the word "having attained" (*āsādya*), priority in time is indicated.

The term "immediate succession" (*sāmanantarya*) is intended here not as the mere immediate existence of a subsequent person who provides assistance, but rather as the establishment of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) consisting in the act of seating the servant.
By the word "agent" (*kartṛ*), the entire manifold (*prapañca*)— comprising the object of cognition, the means of cognition, and the cognizer— is [denoted] by itself.

It has been stated that because He is the creator of such a manifold universe (prapañca) and because He pervades its prior and posterior limits, the Great Lord (Maheśvara) is eternal; therefore, the operation of causal agents is not possible with respect to Him.
By the term "the Knower" (jñātari), it is indicated that He Himself [is the agent] because He illumines His own created universe in such a manner.
Furthermore, because its nature is luminosity (*prakāśarūpatva*),

it has been stated that the operation of a cognizer (*jñāpaka-vyāpāra*)— consisting of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) which establishes limited objects of knowledge (*parimita-prameya*)— is not possible here in the Supreme Lord. This being so, [what then of] the person?

Regarding the activity stated as "I cause Maheśvara to be recognized," one might wonder whether that is the activity of an agent (*kāraka*), the activity of a signifier (*jñāpaka*), both, or something else entirely.
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "But the Self of people is Maheśvara."
"Thus, by the power of delusion, you somehow [perceive] these [beings] fashioned by His will and consisting of *māyā*";

this refers to the verse previously cited, because even though Maheśvara— the subject of that verse— is being perceived as "I," He remains unobserved due to the power of delusion, despite being directly seen (*sākṣātkṛte*) as "I myself am Maheśvara."

When [the reality] has not yet reached the state of being felt in the heart, this recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), established through one's own experience, is taught by means of the manifestation of the power consisting of knowledge and action belonging to that Great Lord (*maheśvara*) whose nature is knowledge and action. Thus, the realization "I am indeed the Great Lord" is demonstrated and revealed.
To people, I appear as form, yet my true nature is that of the Lord alone; even while appearing as the Lord's own nature, this Self possesses absolute freedom. As it has been said:
"If the Great Lord were to abide with a body of a single, fixed form..."
The state of being Maheśvara and the state of consciousness—that he abandoned like a jar or other such objects.
Thus, the meaning is that it does not fail to manifest in any form whatsoever; rather, it manifests in its entirety.

He demonstrates this very manifestation in its entirety by saying "therein": in the manifestation in its entirety, [there is] the consciousness whose nature is light, manifesting as "I" even while having a nature that is not [objectively] manifest.
It manifests as having a void and insentient nature; it also manifests as having the nature of light—that is, as the nature of Śiva.

In that regard, even while manifesting as the nature of light, [it appears] through the nature of the Mantramahēśvaras, Mantreśvaras, and Mantras, due to the predominance of their "I-ness" (*ahaṃprathā*) in parts. (46) Thus, from this "I-ness"...
Even though this manifestation exists as the "not-this" conceit fashioned by the will of the Supreme Lord,

and even while it shines forth, there is a dissolution of the manifestation of "I" through the nature of *kalā*— that is, apart from the manifestation of "this"— and a partial [dissolution] of the full manifestation of "I" apart from that.

It manifests as the self of all subjects, from the gods down to the animals. The term "self" refers to seven types, beginning with the insentient manifestation up to Paramaśiva. He explains these seven types starting with the words "In that [context]," etc., ending with "the Kalā. The middle... [ends] with the Kalā.

That very freedom (*svātantrya*) which is described as the appearance of individual souls (*jīvābhāsāḥ*) is the power of the Lord known as Māyā, the deluder. By its force— that is, by the force of Māyā— the [soul] remains perpetually within itself as the Great Lord, whose nature is self-luminous.
Even while [the world] is manifesting, Maheśvara is not [fully realized] because of the partiality [of perception];

due to the power of gradual [unfolding], [this state] is not perceived, and thus fullness has not reached the state of being felt within the heart. Precisely because it has not been attained, the manifestation of "I am Maheśvara" occurs as fullness.
Regarding that which does not produce the intended wonder, there is a specific form of conceit (*abhimāna*) consisting of the manifestation of fullness in the form "I am Maheśvara.
This has not been explained previously; it is now shown as belonging to Power (*śakti*).

The Pratyabhijñā system is so called because it demonstrates— that is, reveals— through the manifestation of that [power] which resides in the Possessor of Power (the Lord), which is well-known as consisting of knowledge and action, and which exists as inseparable from the individual soul; thus, for those things to be accomplished...

Because the manifestation of wonders is not established without the accomplishment of the conviction in one's own possession of power, he provides an illustration for this point with the words "And thus," and so forth.
This is what is meant: [it is] the recognition of Maheśvara toward people.

This activity belongs to Maheśvara; however, [the statement] "I am not the Lord, but Caitra alone" is merely for the purpose of removing delusion. As will be explained according to the method to be presented, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establish the conventional usage of impermanence and so forth have never before been set in motion here.
Since the means of establishing conventional designations such as "lordship" and so forth—which consist of the scriptures—rest upon valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [we state]:
the pot is the subject (*pakṣa*); "being in front" is the property to be proven (*sādhya*);
and in the proof of being in front, the fact that the pot is perceptible (*pratyakṣatva*) is the logical reason (*hetu*). Wherever there is a pot...
The state of being "in front" (purovartitva) with respect to the cognizer is its being foremost in each respective instance, as in the case of a cloth and so forth;

and this cloth is likewise [presented]. Therefore, by such a sentence, the jar is made known (*jñāpyate*), but the jar is not manifested (*prakāśyate*). The jar is [known] precisely through perception.

It is not [established] by means of a sentence, because it is being made known [by another means]. Otherwise, since the subject (pakṣa), which is the form of the pot, would not be made known by perception alone, the reason "because of being perceived" (pratyakṣatvāt) would be unestablished (asiddha).
Thus, only delusion consisting of the absence of that [perception] is removed; the Great Lord is not [the object of this inference].

This delusion, which is the lack of refuge in delusion caused by the glance of the Teacher, and that which is the veiling of one's own true nature as Maheśvara and its subsequent manifestation, is merely the unfolding of the Lord’s absolute freedom (*svātantrya*);
it is nothing more than that. Thus, in the same way... [tathā]

"It was previously set in motion here" (p. 37). By stating "by the manifestation of power," it is said that the power of a certain [entity] is manifested toward a certain [object]. In that regard, because the mass of existing things perceived as appearing through the distinction between the insentient (*jaḍa*) and the sentient (*ajaḍa*) is twofold, there are the forms of the insentient and the sentient.

In this world, one might raise the doubt with the words "But surely" (*nanu*), considering the two possible alternatives: that the power of the insentient manifests toward the insentient, or that the power of the sentient manifests toward the sentient—and [concluding] that in neither of these two positions is this tenable. [The question is:
"Whose power is it?"—is it the power residing in the insentient or the power residing in the sentient? And toward whom does it manifest—is it toward the insentient or [the sentient]?

The meaning of the term "non-inert" (*ajaḍa*) is that which possesses cognition. He states "of inert things" (*jaḍānām*) because the manifestation of power is simply impossible for inert things. Power consists of both knowledge and action;
among these, the cognition "I am" does not exist for inert things such as stones and the like.
The emptiness of form is indeed admitted by everyone. Knowledge has reflection (*vimarśa*) as its life-force;

reflection itself is action. In that regard, there arises the internal exertion (*saṃrambha*) of the yoga [expressed as] "I know," and so forth. That exertion is called the power of the action of reflection. Knowledge has reflection as its life-force. (48)

Furthermore, it will be stated that reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) itself is action; thus, the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), which consists of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and is characterized by the autonomy (*svātantrya*) of such movements as "I do" or "I go," is not far removed.
For this very reason, certain figurative grammarians (*lākṣaṇika*) have accepted a metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) in expressions such as "the chariot goes. This is not [the case here].

Since, from the perspective of ultimate reality, there is no activity of motion in an insentient chariot, the meaning is that it is the occupant of the chariot who moves. Nor is it appropriate to establish the conventional usage of "Lord" (Īśa) and so forth for insentient things on the grounds that they possess the capacity for cognition; for instance, when one says to a jar, "Come here."

Just as movement and so forth are not observed [in a jar], because it is insentient (*acetana*) and inert (*jaḍa*), the application of proofs such as "desire" (*īśā*) and the like to establish its agency is untenable. As he will state: "A jar does not produce wonder within itself; it does not perceive itself, nor is it illuminated by itself."
It does not appear as something delimited; therefore, it is said that it is not an object of cognition (*cetya*).

Thus, the power residing in the non-inert (*ajaḍa*) is manifested toward the non-inert. This is the second position, which is adopted [as follows]: the state of possessing power (*śaktimattva*) is established with reference to the non-inert individual soul (*jīva*), who is a person capable of both [perceiving and being perceived].

"Both [the power and its manifestation] are [of the nature of the non-inert]," so it is said. Now, if the view is that both are [of the nature of the non-inert] by virtue of the authority of the living being (*jīva*), who is non-inert—this is the meaning:
even in that position, since there are many non-inert beings, does the power of the non-inert Caitra belong to the non-inert Maitra?

Or rather, it is said that "it is manifested to [the individual]. That is to say, the supreme power of the Lord (*pārameśvarī svaśakti*), which is not recognized by one or another—such as Caitra or anyone else—is manifested to that very person. In both these positions, according to the manner stated in the *Naijavṛtti*, there is the "Self of all" (*sarvātman*) as you intend, namely, the Self of everyone.

"Great Lordship (maheśvaratva) is not established, because of the absence of possessing power in insentient things whose powers are unmanifest, and because of the exclusion of [other] insentient things"— thus the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvavādī) refutes [the argument]. "In that case," [and] "therefore this very [point]"...

In the manner described above, it is not possible to establish recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) through the manifestation of power in every respect; anticipating this objection, he explains the method of its establishment in the subsequent sūtra beginning with "tathā hi" (for thus...). Now...

Regarding the view that the power of a sentient being is manifested toward another sentient being who is insentient for the purpose of accomplishing worldly transactions: in that case, it follows that the insentient Caitra is manifested [toward the sentient Devadatta],
and so forth.

And since it has already been stated that [the manifestation] elsewhere is impossible because the difference between those two is established by perception—and thus it is impossible to establish a recognition of non-difference—this very position is untenable; as he says: "Not so, because the power of one thing cannot [manifest] elsewhere..."
The power [of consciousness] is manifested toward that very [individual]; thus, one raises the objection:

"adhikāriṇi" (toward the qualified person). Both the possession of power and its manifestation are intended with respect to the qualified person who is capable of recognition; this is what the proponent of consciousness (saṃvidvādin) intends.

Once the status of Maheśvara as the agent has been established through recognition, the proponent of the previous position states "Then... in order to demonstrate his own intended point: that because other individual souls (*jīvas*) and insentient things (*jaḍas*) lack that nature, Maheśvara is the Self of everything.
Introducing the subsequent sūtra as a resolution to this doubt:

"I shall first examine the reasoning for what was stated—that [the nature of] sound is being demonstrated. Thus, one meaning of the word *tathā* (thus) is "in that manner," referring to the subject at hand (*prakṛta*), namely, the probandum (*sādhya*).

For the recognition of the very subject as the Lord (īśvara) is established as being endowed with the causal reason characterized by the possession of the powers of knowledge and action; this is according to the principle of the Sūtra [I.3.1], "Not those which have been perceived... (*na yān...*). Likewise, that [recognition] has become the object of memory and is present in the intellect (*buddhi*).
All this, as will be explained in the manner to follow, is possible through [His] power (*śakti*) regarding the manifestation of objects;
thus, what was stated—that "this is all illogical for you"—is indeed consistent, because your objection does not apply. This is clear: even in His unmanifest nature, He is the Supreme Lord alone.
According to the principle stated as "it shines forth," although there is an absence of inherent insentience [in the Self], through the power of its *māyā*,

insentient things such as the body and jars appear here as if submerged in consciousness; for the reflective awareness of "this" is indeed the awareness of the insentient, while the reflective awareness of "I" is the awareness of pure consciousness itself.

The meaning is that, according to the principle to be explained later, there is no self-sustained foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*); rather, it exists by being oriented toward the subject (*pramātṛ*) in such a manner as "my body appears," which has its locus in the living subject.

(39) It is well known in the Āgamas that for living beings—who are composed of consciousness, real, and possessors of life—their very life consists of a dual power consisting of knowledge (*jñāna*) and action (*kriyā*), which is the nature of the vivifier. And it has been said: "The presence or absence of consciousness and activity are the causes of sentience and insentience, respectively."

Therefore, although the plural form "may they live" (*jīvatām*) is used due to the influence of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the body— and because even the body and its like are attached to the individual soul (*jīva*) just as a jar or other objects are— the soul is ultimately established as being one. Thus, the unique characteristic of Maheśvara, who is the foundation of the entire universe characterized by jars, bodies, and so forth, is revealed.

The essential meaning is as follows: since the state of being the Great Lord (maheśvara) is established for everyone through the manifestation of the powers of knowledge and action, the state of being the Great Lord is thereby established for all; thus, by resorting to the position that [the self] is non-inert (ajaḍa), the objection is resolved. This refers to the possession of the power that constitutes the higher knowledge of the Great Lord with respect to living beings.

"Let it be seen, so to speak"—the meaning is that this is well-known. "For instance": the object belongs only to a word that is capable [of signification]. When [the word] is split, there are two natures: the non-insentient (*ajaḍa*) and the living being (*jīva*). [The phrase] *hṛdayaṅgamā* is made to mean "reaching the heart. This refers to the second alternative intended by [the author] himself.

In order to state the reason for not accepting the first position— that which was spoken by the opponent regarding the fault of non-establishment due to Maheśvara being the self of all— he establishes that the existence of the mass of insentient entities depends upon the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the conscious subject (*pramātṛ*): "Here," and so forth.

In whatever manner the aggregate of entities such as blue and so forth is reflected upon—that is, contemplated by the subject through its own self-ascension—it exists in that very manner; it does not transcend its own being, nor does it exist independently of such reflection or by itself. Such is the nature of the universe.

Anticipating the objection that "surely, when examined from the perspective of ultimate reality, its existence must be intrinsic because it is manifest," [the author] states that this is not so, because the non-inert [consciousness], though it is "I am," does not cognize the existence of its own self by itself.

He states the reason for the proposition—that "it is thus"—namely, that its nature is doubly purified and dependent upon the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the subject, because it shines forth in such a manner: "of existence," "seeking refuge in light.
For that which is unmanifest does not exist at all; indeed, existence is nothing but manifestation. Therefore, [existence] is dependent upon light.
"Existence here is eternal. According to the principle of the *Tantravaṭadhānikā*, existence—which is dependent upon manifestation—is as if animated by manifestation.
This is in accordance with the principle that will be stated later: "The nature of manifestation is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*); otherwise, it is a mere point (*bindu*)."

When consciousness (*vimarśa*), which is the very life of light (*prakāśa*), takes hold [of it] through its unfolding, there arises the reflective awareness "this is blue"; thus, the blue shines as blueness. It does not, however, shine by itself as "I am blue.
For this reason, whatever object is reflected upon in whatever manner, it exists in that very way—this alone [is the truth].

This is the ultimate truth; therefore, the meaning is that the proposition stated is indeed logical. He establishes this very point by demonstrating the sublation [of the opposite view] through the following: "For if it were unexamined," etc. This means that if one were to admit the existence of objects such as blue and so forth by themselves, even without the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the subject (*pramātṛ*).

The conventional name "blue" and so forth, which is the object of linguistic usage through its form—whether as existent or non-existent—is not the cause for the heart of the cognizer [to settle upon it].
Thus, when someone asks: "Why is it blue and not yellow? Why is it existent and not non-existent? [the answer follows].
No answer whatsoever can be given because [the object] has not entered the heart;
rather, an answer preceded by reasoning is appropriate because, upon the acceptance of inquiry, it is being inquired into. As he will say:
"In this world, why does a jar exist? [Because] a sky-flower does not exist, whereas the jar indeed manifests."
He concludes the established point with the words "Therefore": by that [reasoning], the existence of an object is dependent solely upon reflective awareness (vimarśa).
One might object: "But surely, even when being examined, things such as silver in a mother-of-pearl shell or a second moon do not possess reality; therefore, there is no pervasion.
Anticipating this, he says: "As long as... [up to the point of attaining causal efficiency].
That which is examined—provided it remains free from sublation in the interim, unlike the case of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell and so forth—for that long...
The meaning is that there exists a sublation (*bādha*) in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), such as silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, when it is being investigated; this is what is stated here.

The subject under dispute (*vimata*), such as blue and so forth, possesses an existence dependent upon the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of an uncontradicted cognizer, because, while being manifest in dependence upon that [cognizer], it serves as the locus for the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) of the form "blue."
The application [of the argument] should be seen as "distinctly, like a shell-silver" (*śukti-rajatādivat*).

By this, the refutation of the views of the proponents of the unreality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-mithyātva-vādins*), the Śūnyavādins, the Vijñānavādins, those who maintain that insentient things exist by themselves (*svato jaḍāstitva-vādins*), and the Naiyāyikas and others, has been accomplished. [This applies to] blue, pleasure, and so forth.
This teaching on the attainment of the ultimate knower by means of the investigation of the [empirical] knower is the true state of affairs;
[these cognitions] are self-evident.
The doctrine asserted by the Buddhist proponents of the *Śrutyanta* (Ultimate Scripture) is not at all tenable;
for reality depends solely upon the uncontradicted reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the single cognizer.
Therefore, let the wise accept that the status of being a qualifier exists conventionally, though not in reality; for if it did not, there would be no conventional usage whatsoever.
Because they are the objects of uncontradicted reflective awareness—
[it follows that] even the cognitions of substance and so forth, which are considered unreal by the Vijñānavādins and others, will be shown to possess ultimate reality as will be explained.

He states that it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) "precisely because of that. Since [the object] exists when examined as uncontradicted, for that very reason there is the substance extended in space, the action extended in time, and the relation of form— by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [one includes] universals, direction, and so forth— as being uncontradicted in their oneness.

Since it is established that the existence of an object depends upon reflective awareness (vimarśa) precisely by virtue of its being an object of such awareness, then—even though [the universe] is expanded out from Śiva down to the earth—it is, in the state of reflective awareness, to be considered in brief as follows: the inert [objects] such as earth are gross; [qualities] such as odor are subtle; and [colors] such as blue are subtle [in another sense].

The nature of Caitra, Maitra, and others is examined as being both living and non-living. Let there be this twofold division; however, what does that have to do with the present subject? To this, he says:
"(53) Therein. It means that its establishment is based upon the living subject (*pramātṛ*).
The cognition of diversity— appearing in the forms of blue, yellow, pleasure, and pain— shines forth as if it were a single consciousness,
just as the notion "this is a woman with a deep navel and high breasts" arises from a flat surface on a painting board.

As it has been said: the phrase "in the *Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi*" is to be understood as the ellipsis. Within the Self, which is one's own non-inert nature, [objects] are like non-existents because they lack the reflective awareness of their own being. They exist only through their relation to the Light, which is the nature of the subject, as in the thought, "this jar is manifesting."

The meaning is that the existence of objects such as a jar is dependent solely upon the cognizer. Establishing that insentient things lack existence in themselves (*svataḥ sattva*), he states the criterion for existence in itself: "That alone" (*sa eva*).
Manifestation in its own nature, unconditioned by anything else, is the criterion for existence in itself. And that...

[The capacity for manifestation] belongs only to the cognizer, because of the manifestation [of the self] as "I. Since that [manifestation] is absent in the insentient, it is said to be "of the nature of light.
This is because the insentient manifests only by ascending into the light of the form of the "I.
By this [statement], the first position—that insentient things possess existence in themselves—is not accepted at all; such is the meaning.

Now, one might object: "Even in the second position, since there is a plurality of individual souls (jīvas), the previously mentioned defect remains as it was. Anticipating this, [the author] states, "But those others... and "The eightfold city (puryaṣṭaka)... to show that the insentience belongs to the body and so forth which serve as limiting adjuncts (upādhi) by way of distinction among souls, whereas being a soul (jīvatva) belongs only to consciousness (caitanya) distinct from those adjuncts. [The term] "prāṇādayaḥ" refers to the vital breaths and the rest.

The five vital airs (vāyu), the two groups of sense organs— the cognitive and the active— and the intellect (buddhi); or alternatively, the pentad of subtle elements beginning with sound, along with the mind (manas), ego (ahaṃkāra), and intellect (buddhi)—
this constitutes the "eightfold city" (puryaṣṭaka).
O Mother, the states of being the grasped and the grasper are non-different within the subject.
Thus, according to the method to be explained, that which constitutes one's own body and so forth is the *lagna* (the point of attachment).

(54) Now, one might object: "Since the cognizer (*pramātṛ*), though having as its locus the inert body and so forth, is perceived as being manifold in forms such as Caitra and others, the aforementioned fault has not been avoided. To this, he says: "And of that... Even though it is being perceived...
Regarding the reason why [the plurality] is ultimate, he states: "Because of mutual dependence" (*anyonyāśrayāt*).
He clarifies this very point:

"The individual souls (*jīva*), etc. [This means that] once the distinctions between bodies and so forth are established, [there arise] Caitra and others as qualified by their respective bodies and so forth.

The establishment of difference: once the difference between Caitra and others is established, there follows the establishment of the difference between the body and so forth, such as "I am that particular body.

Thus, because of the existence of the Supreme [Self], difference is merely imagined; this is the meaning. This is because we observe such linguistic usage as "this blue cloth belongs to Maitra alone" or "the yellow one belongs to Caitra alone," and so forth, regarding blue and other qualities.

It may be suspected that there will be a distinction between individual souls (*jīva*) due to the distinction between objects; however, since blue and other such qualities lack inherent existence (*svataḥ sattva*), this cannot be so. In the case of the body and so forth—expressed as "I am fat" or "I am thin"—there is no self-subsistence. Since blue and the like are the locus of the "this-ness" (*idantā*), they cannot possibly possess inherent existence. Thus, the very possibility of such inherent existence does not exist.

The word *tu* serves to highlight a distinction. It has been established that the power of the Supreme Lord is manifested toward the individual soul (*jīva*) by way of removing the defects previously mentioned regarding the soul's own nature.
In that regard, what is the nature of the power being manifested, and how does it belong to the individual soul?

Anticipating the objection that [the self] is merely "gone" (or transmigrates), he says: "And life. Because it possesses the power of knowledge and action, its nature as a living being (*jīvatva*) is distinct from insentient things such as stones.
Consequently, the cognizing subject (*pramātā*), while knowing and acting, [exists] by means of which power...

Since she alone gives life to that which is insentient in nature, such as stone and the like, there exists indeed a power belonging to the individual soul (*jīva*) that enlivens it, consisting of the forms of knowledge and action. Therefore, this *jīva* [is related] to the Lord (*īśvara*)— he is the Lord,
as well-known from the Purāṇas and other sources— and likewise, this *jīva* is never separated from the powers of knowledge and action.

Therefore, the proposition that "it is indeed Īśvara" is endowed with the five members [of a syllogism]; yet, the nature of Īśvara is not established by inference. Regarding the Sāṃkhya and Buddhist schools, which maintain the absence of Īśvara, he says here that in their view, the subject (*pakṣa*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) are devoid of a substratum (*āśrayahīna*). (55)

Regarding the phrase "even if that is not established": the meaning is even if the Lord (Īśvara) is not established by means of such sources as the Purāṇas and Āgamas. [For example: "I see form with the eye, I hear sound with the ear, I speak what is to be spoken with speech, and I go to what is to be gone to with my feet."

It is universally accepted that the possession of the powers of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) and action (*kriyā-śakti*) regarding all objects—whether they be those of the *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice or those pertaining to the *jñeya* (the knowable)—constitutes lordship (*īśvaratva*). This lordship is well-established even through the consciousness of the *purāṇas* and other such sources; thus, by relying solely on the powers of knowledge and action, the aforementioned fault does not arise.

If one does not accept a transcendent Lord (*alaukikeśvara*), there is indeed the example of Viśeṣa and so forth. This Self ought to be the Lord over all, because it is the knower and the agent of all.
Whosoever is the knower and the agent of whatever extent, he is the Lord over that extent; just as a king is the Lord within his own realm.

Likewise, this self is the knower and the agent in all things; therefore, it should be understood through inference that it is indeed the Lord (Īśvara) in all respects. He states the subverting argument against the subject (*pakṣa*): "of one who is not the Lord," meaning that if the individual soul (*jīva*) lacks the status of being the Lord, then its status as a knower and an agent would not exist, just as in the case of a jar or similar objects.

The meaning is that because there exists a subverting proof (*bādhaka*), therefore the existence of God is established. He states the application (*upanaya*): "And the Self... [The verse continues: "The eater [of all] is the root of the world; no one exists who is not measured by that."
Thus, in the *Śrīmahārthamañjarī*, the conclusion is stated: "The Siddha [is present] everywhere, from Śiva down to the earth.

To establish that the Self is the knower and the agent everywhere, he states the pervasion of the powers of knowledge and action, beginning with the word "jñāna" (knowledge). He says, "the two are innate," meaning "I..."

Indeed, in the Lord Śrī Paramaśiva, who is of the nature of primordial expansion (*prathā-rūpa*), there is no discourse whatsoever regarding an object of knowledge (*prameya*); according to the principle to be explained, in the state of Śiva, even the talk of duality does not exist.
Although in the states of Sadāśiva and Īśvara there exists the mere duality expressed as "I am this" and "this is I," [in the supreme state, such distinction is absent].
Because the ego-sense (*ahaṃtā*) has come to rest and its manifestation has not yet fully emerged, it is designated as Sadāśiva and Īśvara.
As it is said in the *Śrī-tattvagarbha-stotra* (56): "O Śivā, you who have proceeded forth in the form of knowledge and action..."
Those who know the truth always sang of Śiva as the reality called Bhoga.
The power of the knower exists as a subordinate quality, while the nature of action exists as a manifest individuality.
Regarding the phrase "that which belongs to the Lord": it refers to the state of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), which serves as the cause for those two.
As will be stated: "The instrument residing in the two presiding deities is the principle of Knowledge (*vidyātattva*).
This concerns the two cognitions of "I" and "this," which have distinct substrates, expressed as "I am indeed I" and "this is indeed this."

When there is the manifestation of specific qualities such as blue and so forth, and when the generic differentiation has sprouted in the form of "this," there exist the two impure powers of limited knowledge (*vidyā*) and limited agency (*kalā*), characterized by being a knower of only a little and a doer of only a little. As it is said in the *Śrīparyantapañcāśikā*:
The power of consciousness, whose nature is action and knowledge, is the cause for the threading together of distinctions; having reached the stage of *vidyā*, it is called *kalā*.
Thus, when differentiation has sprouted through the forms of conventional particulars such as Caitra or blue, and has arisen in the form of the intellect,

the organs of action, and the qualities— as well as in the form of the principles (tattvas) ranging from the subtle elements like sound to the gross element earth as their respective objects— it is said in that very [text]:
Furthermore, in the emergence of differentiation,
there may arise various modes of valid cognition, actions, and conceptual constructions;
when that very [cognition] manifests as an effort through the illusion of action, whether uninterrupted or interrupted.
"Having reached the state of being a Buddha through karma.

Thus, the pervasion of the universe—from Śiva down to the Earth—by the powers of knowledge (*jñāna*) and action (*kriyā*) has been demonstrated. Therefore, the Self (*ātman*), endowed with such powers of knowledge and action, exists everywhere.
"It has been stated that the knower is not an agent" (p.
44); the meaning is that this is indeed logical. As for the phrase "it will be so": therein, knowledge and action are established by their own nature.

"Since the pure powers of knowledge and action belong to the Lord precisely as his reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), [his] activity is thus both internal and external... and so forth, in the section concerning the scriptures (*āgama*).
Now, [one might object]: since the individual soul (*jīva*) has consciousness alone (*saṃvinmātra*) as its essential nature, because of its unity, [how can there be...]?

(57) Regarding the state of being the subject (*pramātṛtva*), because the intended body and so forth are not attached to the "I," and because—according to the principle to be stated later—there is no difference from consciousness in terms of place, time, or essential nature due to its unity, it is considered the "life" (*jīvana*) of consciousness. When the term *jīvatām* ought to have been used in the instruction, why was the term *jīvatām* [or *jīvatām*] used? [Note: The text appears to contain a scribal error or intentional variation here.]
Anticipating this objection, he says "insentient" (*jaḍāḥ*) to show that the designation "moving" (*jaṅgama*) is established.

Regarding "at first" (*āpāte*): it is well known in the world that in the state of non-recognition due to the absence of the teacher’s instruction, consciousness itself appears in the form of both the insentient and the sentient. Therefore...
Pure consciousness (*saṃvit*), which serves as the foundation for both the insentient and the sentient, is well known to be permeated by consciousness due to its manifestation;
thus, it is precisely the moving beings that are indicated by the word "let them live" (*jīvatām*) with this underlying intention.

He raises the objection with "But [how]? (*nanu*), suggesting that the reason—characterized by the possession of the powers of knowledge and action, which is intended to prove that the individual soul (*jīva*) has the Lord (*īśvara*) as its self—is itself unestablished (*asiddha*). How so? If [the powers] are established through a connection with something else, or if they are established intrinsically (*svataḥ*), then, given that their establishment depends upon a connection with an object, they cannot serve as proof for the Lord-hood of those two.

It could not be so. For if [the self] were established by itself (*svataḥ-siddhatva*), then even in the absence of the coloring of objects (*viṣayoparāga*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the empirical usage "I know" and "I act" during deep sleep and similar states. Therefore, the meaning is that the reason is not established in either way.
With this as the response to the objection, he introduces the subsequent sūtra, which serves to support the reason:

This is said in order to quell such a doubt. Regarding the word "therein": for the individual soul (jīva)—or rather, as long as the knower lives—knowledge is self-established, continuous throughout the three periods of time, and self-luminous; it does not [depend] on anything else, such as the coloring by an object, because the object lacks inherent existence in itself.
As it is said in the *Śrīmatstotrāvalī*: "O Omniscient One, O Omnipotent One, while You are thus [the ultimate reality], the manifestation of the world occurs within me."

In this view, however, it will be stated that even the object consists of reflective awareness (*vimarśamayatva*). Nor does there follow the consequence of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) during states such as deep sleep; for, although [the world] is self-established, the group of sense organs—which constitute the expansion of the activity of consciousness—is dissolved, and thus it remains unmanifest until once again...

"It would be characterized as self-established..."—this is the summary of the meaning of the sūtra: that the action is not performed by one's own self alone, but rather the cognition of another is inferred. (p. 45) He explains the introduced sūtra with the words "I" (*aham*): it is fully established and rests [in itself].

In this regard, regarding this cognition, [the opponent might argue] that there is another existence, non-existence, and so forth. He demonstrates the refutation of this position from the perspective of the counter-argument (vipakṣe bādhakamukhena) with the words: "that would not be manifest. If it were not manifest, even blinding darkness—such as a jar and the like, which is being manifested in its own form—would be [known] through the non-manifestation of the cognition, [in the form]: "this is blinding darkness."
As it has been said by the learned:
"Whatever appears, all that would indeed be blind darkness without her; yet even that [darkness] is not capable of existing."

He says "even a child" (*bālo'pi*) to show that the claim that knowledge is self-established (*svataḥ-siddha*) is well-known even to a suckling infant who has not yet mastered conventional linguistic usage. [The infant] experiences the repose of knowledge within the light of the "I" (*ahaṃ-prakāśa*) through the drinking of milk and so forth.

He makes known his desire through the sign of weeping. Indeed, a child performs such acts as weeping only preceded by the knowledge: "This drinking of breast milk and so forth is the means for the cessation of hunger and other needs.
Therefore, it is known by all that he possesses cognition. Thus, from childhood until old age...

The meaning is that he is indeed renowned as a wise man (*paṇḍita*). Regarding this, he states that scripture (*śruti*) is also an authority, saying "it has been said. In the *Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa* of the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*, it was said by Yājñavalkya: "O dear one" (*are*)—with affection, he thus addresses his beloved wife, who is fit for instruction in the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*)—"of everything..."

In what manner could one know the Self as the knower? For even the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), which establishes objects of knowledge (*prameya*), finds its ultimate rest in that very [Self]. As it is said in the *Śrī Tantrāloka*:
"Even the means of valid cognition, which extend the life of all things—their supreme life-force is that very same Supreme Lord. (59)

Therefore, regarding this object, since there is the consideration that "this means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) establishes it" and "this [other] negates it," what is the means of valid cognition for the existence of this object in its form as a cognizer who possesses both establishing and subverting cognitions? This is the point concerning the object.
Having granted the existence [of Maheśvara], the question "What is the proof for such a nature?

is posed; yet, the self-luminosity of Maheśvara, who was previously established as the subject of inquiry, is proven by everyone through their own self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). Furthermore, even a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) depends upon him.
"Is it a means of valid cognition? and so forth—
up to "In the case of the variegated painting of the universe's diversity, which is like a level wall-surface," and so on,
ending with "Is it not the case that manifestation partakes in all forms of valid knowledge?"

And it will be stated [later]: "This is also established by the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the questions and answers," as he says: "In the concealment of that" (tannihnave). This refers to the concealment—that is, the denial—of that cognition which constitutes the very nature of the knower, on the part of the questioner.

The intended meaning is that if there were an absence of knowledge regarding what is to be asked, a reply would be impossible. To address how the accomplishment of this very knowledge occurs, he says "therein" (*tatra*). Since the self-evident nature of knowledge is established by all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [the text discusses] knowledge and [qualities] such as whiteness.

Even though there is no difference in their status as qualities (*guṇatva*), the distinction of cognition (*jñāna*)— characterized by the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) consisting of internal dynamism and the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)— is its non-inert nature, which rests upon the non-inert cognizer (*pramātṛ*), whereas [qualities] such as whiteness are themselves inert and rest upon inert objects such as jars.

Since it arises through the conjunction with the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), by what means do I know this? Herein, the internal power of action—characterized by reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) and consisting of the intensity of knowledge—is established as "I" (*aham*). Action, being dependent upon time, [is explained further]. He states the remainder of the meaning of the aphorism, beginning with "That very... and so forth.

That very power of action (*kriyāśakti*), although both [the self and action] are equal in their self-luminosity, the word [“action”] highlights a specific distinction characterized by being an object of perception and other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), due to action having the nature of vibration (*spandana*). By its own power, it serves as the cause for the conceit of [agency] in one's own capacity.
Subsequently, within the vital breath (prāṇa), there is the activity of inhalation and so forth; and within my pentad of prāṇa and the rest,

as well as within the "eightfold city" (puryaṣṭaka) characterized by the two groups of sense organs— knowledge and action— and by intellect, ego, mind, and the five subtle elements (tanmātras) such as sound, [the Self resides].

Having transferred [itself] and entered even the body, it causes movement and other activities such as speech; this is established through perception and other means of knowledge. Thus, he explains that the cognition of another is to be inferred. And "that" refers to [the inference] from the movement and so forth of another body, such as that of Caitra, by means of its association with breath and the like.

The knower, having made himself directly manifest through the entry [of consciousness] into the body and so forth, makes known to another that knowledge which is his own inherent nature. If it is argued that this activity of one who is moving—namely, that knowledge is made known by means of an action—then how can its self-luminosity (svaprakāśatva) be maintained? To this [it is replied]:

He says: "And it is not knowledge. If this [cognition] were perceived as having the nature of that [object], like a knowable object such as a jar which is of the nature of ignorance (non-knowledge), then its very status as knowledge would not exist. For a jar never appears in the form of a cloth. Therefore, [if this were so], the jar being perceived in the form of "this" [would cease to be a jar].
Because this manifesting cognition lacks the nature of being "this," its very body— its essential form— is "I" alone. Since that which is perceived as "I" finds its rest in the knower,
even cognition shines forth as "I" itself, just as whiteness and other qualities shine when perceived as "this."
The meaning is that it shines forth in that very manner, by its own form alone.
[Objection: Let it be so for that which resides within itself; but how is it so for that which belongs to another? To this, he says: "Thus, even the cognition of another... and so forth.

The distinction between self and other is, first of all, adventitious (*aupādhika*). At the time of the manifestation of cognition, even for the Supreme [Self], its form is simply "I" (*aham*), because it shines forth as "I" within itself. He states that there is no difference in the perception of the cognition of self and other even due to the power of adventitious distinctions: "And that... [sa ca...]
— because the cause, consisting of limiting adjuncts such as the body and so forth, being insentient, does not in reality differ from the non-insentient Self, since it rests within it; for,
according to the principle stated [in verse 61], "of those things that have become insentient," of that which has become insentient...

The entire universe—from jars and the like, as well as bodies and so forth, up to the locus of rest, extending from Sadāśiva down to the smallest insect—consists of the class of subjects whose ultimate nature, in its absolute mode of being (*paramārthavṛttyā*), is the single subject that is Supreme Śiva. Only that supreme subject exists eternally, and nothing else does. The proof for this is as follows:
This is the remainder of the verse previously cited in the *Jaḍapramātṛsiddhi*: "The very light that constitutes the essential nature of one's own self—
which is of the nature of the perfect, self-luminous reflective awareness of 'I'—
is indeed [the same] as that which is perceived by oneself through one's own form of 'I-ness,' and by others..."

The Universal Self exists in the form of "this-ness" (idantā); however, there exists no nature of the knower—whether its own nature or another's—that is distinct from it. Consequently, [it is] the Supreme Lord alone, whose nature is consciousness pervading bodies from Sadāśiva down to a worm, [who exists].
Since primary consciousness is the state of being a knower, by that very same reasoning, his status as the creator of all is also established.
There is no knowledge devoid of action, nor is there action devoid of knowledge.

This is because of the statement of the learned masters: "I desire," [is used] here through the interpenetration of the three powers (*śakti*).
