Likewise, in the cases of "I know" and "I act," knowledge and action powers are also joined, according to the principle beginning with "the appearance of connection" (*yuktatvābhāsa*). By this, knowledge and action are the cause for a person's recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of their own self as the Lord.

The characteristic of being an activity (*vṛtti*) has been established. He states the intended meaning of the use of the word "is inferred" (*ūhyate*): "being an application" means being an object of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) through the form of "this-ness" (*idantākāra*). What is called "inference" (*ūhana*) is the manifestation of knowledge—which exists inherently within another self—through action. Of this...

This is to demonstrate that there exists some knowledge which is the very root of action. And since that knowledge manifests only in the form of "I-ness" (ahantā), it is not an object of cognition; for if it were inferable, there would be the undesirable consequence of its appearing in the form of "this-ness" (idantā), like fire and other objects. With this intention, it is said to be "inferred."
It has not been stated.

Thus, the first chapter (*āhnika*), consisting of the four verses beginning with "kartari" and following, which are devoted to supporting the meaning of the proposition stated in the introductory sentences beginning with "kathaṃcit," has been explained.

(48) For those who, preceded by a restatement of that [very] purpose, proceed with necessity toward this vision of consciousness (*saṃvid-darśana*)— setting aside other philosophical systems such as the Nyāya and others— and who are devoid of the inert sense of "I" regarding the body and so forth, there occurs the manifestation of Śiva-nature from the state of the individual soul (*jīva*).

Stating that "the accomplishment of the goals of human life (puruṣārtha) indeed occurs," he provides an introductory statement (upodghāta) for this chapter by declaring its well-known subject matter: "Thus, therefore... Since the lordship of living beings is established through the conjunction of the powers of knowledge and action, for that very reason, it is thus.

In this path of consciousness, according to the manner described in the four verses, one realizes the lordship of one's own self through one's own direct experience alone; thus, it is on the path of consciousness (*saṃvinmārga*) that the very self in its form as a living being (*jīva*) is made to recognize its own nature as the Great Lord (*maheśvaratva*).
Those who are firmly established— purified by the ultimate reality of consciousness—
even though they are established in the state of ultimate reality, their means [of attainment] remain constrained.

Thus, according to the method taught in the Śrītantra, one’s own self (*svātmāna*) is the Lord (*īśvara*); for there is no distinction in the reality of the Self between that which is conventionally known as inert and non-self—such as a jar—and that which is denoted by the terms body, vital breath, pleasure, and sound, including the intellect (*buddhi*), its absence, the void (*śūnya*), and so forth, up to the Lord, because they are all equally non-Self in essence. In that very [Self],...
Plunging [all things] into their very own nature— which is the Supreme Lord himself, who is the source of all diverse manifestations and transcends the universe—

and thereby immersing them thoroughly up to the limit of the object of knowledge (*prameya*), they make them identical with Him; thus, even though the state of being the Self of the Lord is eternally present, by means of His power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*).

These [souls], having been reduced to the state of bondage characterized by the egoity of the body and so forth, once again become the lords of their own selves—made manifest through the recognition [of their true nature] via the glance of a true Guru, fashioned by His grace.
As it is said in the *Śivasūtras*: "He becomes equal to Śiva."

Having entered your own path through innate compassion, O Guide, with a gaze whose rays are beyond counting as they shatter the mass of darkness of the six-fold path, you instantly bestow the supreme command— the hand of Śiva— which is itself unknown.
"svamā... [etc. Thus, in the *Śrīsakalajananīstotra* (verse 63): "By the word of the true Guru, I am indeed Śiva while still living, through the powers of knowledge and action."
Even though I am acting like an ordinary person through the wisdom that has been imparted to me,
once all the fruits of my previously commenced good and evil karmas have been exhausted through experience, this body will fall away.

It has also been stated by others: "In this context, by the term *tārkika* (logician), all disputants whatsoever are included—those who rely solely on the power of mere reasoning (*tarka*) and are devoid of self-realization (*svātmānubhava*). As he will say:

The Cārvākas, who abide on the level of the measurement of the body (*dehamāna-bhūmikā*), hold that the person (*puruṣa*) is the body characterized by consciousness; thus, they consider the body alone to be primary, and not [the other] states. This is stated in the *Śrī-Pratyabhijñā-hṛdaya*.
"The Buddhists are established in the principle of consciousness (*buddhi-tattva*), while the Ārhats (Jainas) are established in the *guṇas*";
thus it is stated in the scriptures. The Buddhists are proponents of the non-existence of a permanent, perceived self;
and although there exists a stable self, the Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas are proponents of its being non-divine (*an-īśvaratva*).

In this vision of consciousness (*saṃvid-darśana*), all those who maintain doctrines of a single or multiple self and who assert that the self is insentient (*jaḍātma-vādin*)—even if they belong to other philosophical systems—are included. Their various assertions are merely the mutual babbling of the dull-witted, like the spray of dust. As it has been said by the learned:
Aiming at this arbiter, those afflicted by the fear of the fever of logic [have said]:
"By the nets of your hair-raising arguments..."
"...they inevitably go to their destruction through mutual strife," and so forth;
"the constructions of logic end in mutual hair-pulling combat and death," and so forth;
[he refutes] those [doctrines] well-known as worldly, Vedic, Śaiva, Vāma, Dakṣiṇa, Kaurvaka, and others.
The functions of doubt, contraction, cause-and-effect, and ritual injunctions— and so forth—

are merely obstacles to that single-flavored immersion (*samāveśa*) which consists of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) [of reality], since doubt has as its essence uncertainty and conflicting views. (64) [O] you whose doubt is utterly exhausted...

And by the phrase "because of its being real" (*bhūtatvāt*), according to the *Śrīlaghuvṛtti*, those who are themselves obstructors of the path to wisdom— those for whom the state [of reality] has become grey due to that fall and whose true nature has been covered— are, by this very statement, [revealed as] those fortunate ones who are otherwise perverted by the habituation to false views.
It has been shown that here the authority belongs to the intellects alone.

As it is stated in the Āmnāyas: "One who has abandoned the scriptures of the Paśus and is devoted to the scripture of Śiva," and: "Having abandoned the engagement with other systems of philosophy, one should always abide by the doctrine of the Lord (Patimatam) alone."

Regarding the word "tat" (that): because it bestows the immersion (*samāveśa*) into the Lord upon those who contemplate its meaning in the manner described, this collection of texts receives the designation of "introduction" (*upodghāta*). He explains its status as an introduction with the word "upa": [the prefix] *upa* [refers to] the Self.

The meaning is "in the vicinity. The prefix *ud-* signifies excellence (*utkarṣa*). This refers to the supreme pre-eminence of Sadāśiva and others who reside within the [lower] principles (*tattva*), consisting in the state of transcending all principles (*sarvatattvottīrṇatā*). [This pertains to] the Lord who transcends the universe (*viśvottīrṇa*) [and his relation to] the three worlds.
p. 50) That which is *prakāśa* (light) and that which is *vimarśa* (reflective awareness)—these two alone constitute knowledge and action, according to the principle to be stated later.
In this context, the word *ghāta* means "that by which one is struck" (*hanyate yena saḥ*). The suffix *dhañ* is used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*).
The verbal root is *hana*, meaning "to strike" or "to go" (*hiṃsā-gatyoḥ*). Here, "going" (*gati*) refers to the attainment characterized by internal repose.
It is intended [to be understood] thus. It has been stated that "one rests," as in the case of a chisel:
just as an axe driven into a mountain or great mass of earth becomes firmly stuck therein and cannot be extracted again, so too this excellence, once made known by the Guru, cannot be taken back.
One meaning, according to the function of its constituent parts, is that it does not produce the delusion of being a bound soul (paśu).

This much alone—the purport expressed in these four verses—is the primary subject to be established in this work titled *Pratyabhijñā*; the subsequent text serves only to elaborate upon this very point.

The meaning of the term *upa* as a conventional whole is "the principal introductory section" (*upodghāta*), because it consists in stating the intended purport after having established the principal subject matter by way of refuting the previously mentioned positions in an extensive manner. It is called *upodghāta* because it has been made "low-voiced" (*upāṃśu*) and "concise" (*saṃkṣipta*).

This is an adverbial modifier (65). *Ud* means "upward"; it refers to the confusion regarding the subject matter of the doctrines to be explained, which pertains to the upper portion of the treatise. This delusion—consisting of the listener’s inquiry as to what kind of primary object of knowledge (*prameya*) is intended by the cause of sharp dialectical arguments—is destroyed by this very [work].

It has been established that, according to the principle that "one who takes up [an object] for the purpose of harming is moved away," [the roots] have the meanings of motion and cognition; thus, by relying on the sense of motion, it is also understood as having the meaning of "knowing.
Consequently, this too is a derivative meaning [of the term].

Thus, there are three meanings of the term *upodghāta*. Relying on the maxim: "Whether stated in brief or in detail, when the subject matter is explained, it reaches the inner organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) of men of dull, middling, and superior intellect; therefore, it is called [an *upodghāta*]," the primary subject matter is here stated in brief.
The meaning of the treatise has been entered into the heart.

Thus, in our own system, it is understood that one "rests" (*viśramyate*). To this effect, having explained the root *han* as meaning "to know," [the author] adopts the sense of "going" (*gati*) according to another school's view and states that the word *hanyate* means "manifestation" (*khyāti*), as in "it is manifested by someone. When it is said, "he goes to a woman," the going has the woman as its object.
Some say that what is perceived here destroys the understanding whose object is the Self;

by the word "but" (tu), he indicates that such a view is not to be respected. For that understanding is not of the nature of identity, since difference is being perceived. Such an understanding is not intended here.
Because it is precisely the state of rest in non-duality that is intended as the goal, he concludes with the word "evam" (thus).

Since it is established that this introductory section— the composition of the new text— is a summary of the entire meaning of the scripture to be expounded, [it follows that] "I am always attained" by virtue of one's own essential nature.
That which was already attained appears as if unattained due to the power of delusion; by the removal of that delusion, it is attained, meaning it is entered into non-differently.
[This refers to] the nature of the Teacher who is always and everywhere... p. 51).

Through the firmness of contemplation upon the fourfold reality—beginning with the waking state and ending with the fourth (turya), and beginning with emanation (sṛṣṭi) and ending with the inexpressible (anākhyā)—and through the stability of immersion, Paramaśiva, who is beyond the fourth, the performer of the five cosmic acts, is to be recognized according to the scriptures. "Śivam" means: of such a nature.

The object of knowledge (*prameya*) is of the very nature of Śiva because it is produced from Śiva, because its essential nature is non-different [from Him], and so forth; thus, at the end of this chapter, the use of the word "Śiva" is for the sake of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*). As it has been said in the venerable *Pātañjala-bhāṣya*:
"Treatises that begin with auspiciousness, have auspiciousness in their middle, and end with auspiciousness, attain success," and so forth.
May there be auspiciousness!
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Vimarśinī* commentary on the *Śrīpratyabhijñāsūtra*.
Now begins the second chapter.

Now, by the logic of "driving in a post" (athasthūṇānikhananyāya)— that is, by means of objections and their resolutions— he wishes to explain this objection in order to further strengthen the very point already stated as the introduction: "For that Bhairava doctrine is indeed composed of the prima facie arguments."

Thus, according to the principle stated by the venerable Pañcaśikha at the conclusion [of his work], the construction of the sentence is as follows: "I praise that Śiva," who—though manifesting even in the form of the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa)—is contemplated as Śiva himself; and having been made to appear as the prima facie view, he is then subsumed within the non-dualistic final position (siddhānta). Regarding the word "by whom" (yena): [it refers to the means of realization].
I alone am the universal form; just as the body has the nature of hands, feet, and so forth, I alone manifest within all things as their luminous essence—the seer, the hearer, and even the agent.
It is I alone who compose the various conclusions, aphorisms, and arguments.

According to the principle stated in the *Śrīparamārthasāra*, the author of all philosophical systems (*sarvadarśanakartā*) [declares that] the universe, which manifests in the form of both difference and non-difference, and the entire range of objects of knowledge (*prameya*) mentioned in the introduction— the entire collection of subjects (*pramātṛ*) and objects (*prameya*) from Śiva down to the earth— is "difference" (*bheda*). This is by way of differentiation (*bhedena*).
And through mutual difference as well—
(67)— O Vimalatara-carabhairava, because of awakening, although [reality] is devoid of division,
it nevertheless appears as mutually distinct from that very form of Śiva.
Having created a multitude of objects whose appearance is distinct from its own, yet which are entirely non-different from it—
a mass of knowables that it manifests as non-different from itself— this [Self] shines forth.
O Mahātripurasundarī, all that is the activity of that [reality].

According to the principle stated [on] p. 52, because [the opponent's view] is presented as a prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)—either by way of being distinct from the supreme subject (*paramapramātṛ*) or by way of mutual distinction—it is manifested, that is, made to appear, and then rejected;
having merely caused it to appear, [it is not accepted].
Alternatively, the phrase "by revealing the object" (*vastuprakāśya*) is included within the latter position of non-difference; that is, by means of the nature of consciousness,

it is brought into and reached within the interior of the latter position— which is of the nature of non-difference and will be stated as the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) starting with "But [the truth is]..."— through the refutation of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

It is formulated as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). Thinking that there will be an opportunity for the presentation of the conclusion once the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) has been set forth, it was stated that non-difference is included within the latter part of the response. Furthermore, regarding "non-difference" (*abheda*): because non-difference is of a single nature, being unconditioned by space and time—
That wherein all this effect resides and from which it is produced— such is the nature of Light, perfectly complete,
resting within its own self; it is great bliss, filled with the breath, consciousness, and the instruments of action, and replete with infinite power.

According to the principle stated in the *Śrīspandaparamārthasāra*— that "the world consisting of thirty-six principles shines within that Supreme Reality which is devoid of all conceptual construction, pure, tranquil, and free from arising and passing away"—
the universe, which transcends the world, is internalized within the Light of the nature of full *ahaṃtā* (I-consciousness), which constitutes the final position.
We praise, in a state of non-duality, that Śiva— who is indicated by the word "that" (*tam*), who is well-known from the sacred scriptures (*āmnāya*) and so forth,

and who removes the inauspicious delusions of worldly existence— by union with whom one attains the ultimate reality of the supreme and subordinate goals of life, consisting of the essence of bliss and the fruits of enjoyment and liberation. (68)
We reflect upon this. The justification for the plural number is as before.

Now, [this occurs] precisely through the firmness of the cultivation of the meaning of the fourth daily lesson (*āhnika*), which consists of four verses and is designated as the "Introduction" (*upodghāta*).

Raising the objection that since it was previously stated that "Supreme Śiva is attained," what is the purpose of the subsequent textual composition, [the author] replies that it is meaningful because it serves as an exposition by means of raising and resolving that very objection regarding its meaning.

By stating that the presentation of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) must necessarily be performed first for the sake of establishing the final doctrine (*siddhānta*), he shows the purport of the immediately following chapter (*āhnika*) with the word "here" (*iha*). That which is of the nature of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-rūpa*) has been explained here in this introductory chapter (*upoddhātāhnika*).

The passage beginning with "that" (*tad*) and so forth has a clear meaning. Here, he provides a corroborative statement, saying "as it was said. With the vocative "bhava," he addresses the Supreme Lord to draw His attention—*bhū* meaning "existence. By the etymological derivation of the verbal root, He is one whose nature is to exist incessantly as the self of the universe.
Salutations to You, who are eternally present as the nature of Being, the Lord of the wheel of powers such as creation and the rest,
and the ground that culminates in the state of rest; salutations to You who manifest the subjectivity of the body and so forth.
"I enter into you alone eternally. To what kind of one? He says: "To him who is bewildered by existence (*bhava*)," etc.
"Homage to Śambhu, whose sole cause is *saṃsāra*, whose sole adversary is *saṃsāra*, who has the form of *saṃsāra*, yet is himself free from *saṃsāra*."

Thus, according to the principle stated in the *Śrīmatstotrāvalī*, for those who are bewildered within this worldly existence (*bhava*)— which ranges from *māyā* down to the earth (*kṣiti*) and is a manifestation of one's own sovereignty— and who, due to the failure to recognize their own true nature, experience the miseries of hell and other realms consisting of the enjoyment of suffering, they are devoid of the bliss that consists in the perfect contemplation of one's own Self.
"By the principle that those who fall for a moment and then rise upward for a moment do not remain stable due to their incessant coming and going,
they wander; thus, the delusion [of this wandering] is knowledge bound by ignorance, which is bondage."

According to the *Śivasūtra*, this is that darkness which, even though objects are not distinct from the Self because they are of the nature of light, there arises this conceit of non-Self (*anātmābhimāna*). This is a great cataract (*timira*)—
this is a great explosion (*sphoṭa*)— that [this occurs] even with respect to the Self.

The conceit of selfhood (*mānitva*) consists in identifying with the body, the vital breath, and their absence. Thus, according to the method of the *Śrī Paramārthasāra*, [the ego] is a form of knowledge consisting in the non-self-nature (*anātmatā*)—such as "I am not Śiva"—with respect to the Self, which is of the nature of consciousness;
whereas with respect to the non-Self, such as the body and so forth, it takes the form of "I am thin," "I am stout," and so on.

Having first dispelled that appearance of the nature of one thing in what is not that thing— a pair of delusions consisting of both such a nature and the form of cognition— the Supreme Self dissolves the error of non-selfhood within the Self.

By the phrase "the Lord thus cuts away [everything] along with its root," he further indicates that this [Lord] possesses the power over both of these as well. According to the etymology of the verbal root *div*— meaning play (*krīḍā*), worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), brilliance (*dyuti*), splendor (*śrī*), praise (*stuti*), and movement (*gati*)—
"play" (*krīḍā*) here refers to the surging forth [of consciousness] through its density of self-bliss when devoid of discourse concerning what is to be rejected or accepted.

Sovereignty (*svatantratvam*) is the desire to exist in a state of absolute pre-eminence; it is the manifestation of one's own self even while remaining undivided. Since everything—from the very moment of its own acquisition—is directed toward that [sovereignty], the entirety of what is to be done is essentially of the nature of consciousness (*bodhātmaka*).

In the *Śivatanuśāstra*, the Guru has explained the Lord through such etymological definitions as "the aggregate," "consisting of action," "vision," "action," "attribute," and "motion. According to this perspective, He has triumphed by virtue of His supreme excellence over the universe and His play consisting of the creation and other processes of the world.
"Shining with the nine jewels, it is to be praised by all, to be attained, and free from duality. (p.
54) Through those various forms, ignorance shines forth both externally and internally;
for no entities have ever been made objects of experience apart from knowledge.
Knowledge has attained identity with that; therefore, let it be understood from this.
According to this principle, having embraced non-dual knowledge— which is bliss because no entity exists apart from itself—
they conceal it by assuming the position of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) through *māyā*. Then,
relying on the established doctrine of consciousness (*saṃvitsiddhānta*), they reveal it by casting aside that *māyā* and bringing it forth.
By the phrase "it pierces and, having enveloped, it reveals," the Lord's nature as a revealer is expressed through the description of his incessant manifestation and differentiation.
In that context, the words "and here" mean that only when there is the rejection of opposing views does the previously mentioned form of ultimate reality [become manifest].

Since it has been established that there is no self (anātman) or Lord (īśvara), for those who maintain that consciousness alone is momentary, there exists no permanent self distinct from that [consciousness] which could serve as its substratum. Due to the absence of such a self, it cannot possess lordship; this is the case for you, the proponent of consciousness (jñānavādin).
Having accepted the existence of the self (*ātman*),

the atheistic Sāṃkhyas and Bhāṭṭas— who deny the existence of a Lord (*īśvara*)— accept both the self and the non-existence of a Lord; because of the distinction between these two, they maintain that the self lacks lordship and thus assert a plurality of selves.

The Naiyāyikas, Vaiśeṣikas, Śaivas, and others—though they maintain the oneness of the Self—hold that because the universe is insentient, it lacks the independence characterized by being the creator of the universe;
thus, those who know the Upaniṣads maintain that the Self does not consist of the powers of knowledge and action. Of these...
When examined from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), that which is accepted by all is nothing but an illusion (*bhrānti*).

Preceded by the piercing of that [illusion], the ultimate reality is the true sovereignty (*īśvaratva*) of one’s own self alone. Thus, while debating through successive chapters beginning with "But what... (*kiṃ tu*), [the author] proceeds with the eleven verses beginning with "Now... (*atha*).
The purport of this collection of verses is that by means of this chapter, he demonstrates its non-erroneousness.
He states the purport of each verse, beginning with "Therein" (*tatra*). Regarding the word "dṛśya" (*dṛśya*):

by means of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), which is the sixth means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the non-existence of the self is asserted on the grounds that it is capable of being perceived [but is not so perceived].
This refers to those such as the Mīmāṃsakas and Naiyāyikas who maintain that the self is not known through mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*).

It is untenable to claim that there exists some self (*ātman*) which is inferred because the synthesis (*anusandhāna*)— in the form of recollection, memory, conceptualization, and so forth— is established through the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of prior experience;
for this refers to the proponents of an inferable self, namely the proponents of consciousness (*saṃvidvādinaḥ*), who maintain that the self is directly perceived (*pratyakṣatva*).
And both [of these] are considered to be objects of inference (*meyatva*).

For the Vaiśeṣikas and others, it is held that the self is eternally inferable through qualities such as cognition; this is established by three verses. Furthermore, the self exists as the cause of all worldly transactions, such as abandoning and acquiring.

Having raised the objection— “How could there be a memory of an object previously experienced?”— in a single verse against the position of those who maintain the existence of a self (*ātman*), [the author] establishes that very memory, without a self, through the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) by means of the following two verses.

It has been stated that [the argument] is not sufficient for the inference of a self. Consequently, by means of the verse, the following inference is refuted: that the cognition and other qualities of entities lead to the apprehension of the self as their possessor through those nine qualities. "In this way" means having asserted that the self does not exist either through perception or through inference.

In this regard, in order to refute [the notions of] the power of knowledge and action, relation, and sovereignty within the self, the view of the Naiyāyikas and others is that the self is distinct [from these], that the self is eternal and of the nature of consciousness (*cit*), and that knowledge—which is of the nature of consciousness—is impermanent; [they hold] that knowledge is insentient (*jaḍa*) while the self is of the nature of consciousness. The view of the Sāṃkhyas is that knowledge is insentient and the self is of the nature of consciousness.

It is agreed by both [parties] that cognition is distinct from the self; however, it has been demonstrated that this is not tenable. By this, it is stated that while mere cognition exists, there is no such thing as a self distinct from it with which it could be related. Regarding the phrase "by another proponent": the self is of the nature of consciousness (*acid-rūpa*).

The Mīmāṃsakas, Naiyāyikas, and others who maintain that consciousness is distinct [from the self] argue that eternal cognition is likewise [non-existent], because it has the nature of a power (*śakti*) similar to that [action]. Therefore, [the text says] "by one" (*ekena*). Action, however, does not exist by itself like the self, because—unlike effects and so forth—it lacks visibility (*dṛśyatva*). "In some cases" (*kvacit*)...

There is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the existence of action (*kriyā*) as something distinct from Caitra, Maitra, and so forth, in any place, time, or form. Furthermore, there is a subverting argument (*bādhaka*): if action were a single unity, the sequence of prior and posterior [moments] would be untenable; if such a sequence exists, its unity is untenable.
The subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) is that multiplicity is untenable when there is a relation with a single substratum;

for if one were to accept the unity of an action through its relation to a single substratum, then because that substratum is characterized by space and time and thus assumes different forms at every moment, the unity [of the action] would be untenable.

By the Master who has adopted the Buddhist position, who asserts that there is no mutual relationship between cognition, action, and the self, and who thus maintains the absence of any means of valid cognition— consisting of perception and inference— to establish the existence of such a relationship, [the following was said regarding] the relationship: (72)

Non-existence has been established. By stating that there is an absence of a proving means of valid cognition (*sādhaka-pramāṇa*), the opponent (*pūrvapakṣin*) has presented the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) that a relation cannot be unitary because it resides in two [relata]. [This applies] to the cognition "the self is not stable," etc., [arising] from its own causal complex (*svasāmagrī*).

Because it is an effect—since [the existence of] an agent is not established, the entire preceding prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) that "there is a knower" is indeed untenable; this is the meaning of both the struck and the unstruck verses.
Now, as for the two verses beginning with "nanu svalakṣaṇabhāsaṃ nityasya kasyacid":
Now, regarding the experience [of the Self], since there is an obstacle even when the Self exists, there follow three verses beginning with "yataḥ hi" (p.
56); then one verse beginning with "bhinneṣu";
then two verses beginning with "athārthasya"; and finally one verse beginning with "kriyāpyarthasya," each situated in its respective place.

"One [says] 'that and that' because of the manifold nature of what resides in two; thus, having stated the purport for each verse, he begins the commentary on the text with the word *atha*. [He explains] the state of being the Great Lord (*maheśvaratva*) of the Self by means of its powers of knowledge and action..."

By this [verse], it is stated that cognition and action, which reside in the subject (*pramātṛ*), are established by themselves. In that regard, there is no permanent self (*ātman*) distinct from cognition. Furthermore, cognition is not of the nature of a power (*śakti*) as intended by you (the Śaivas), nor is it of the nature of pure consciousness (*saṃvit*) as favored by the Vijñānavādins; rather, it is strictly momentary.
The statement "but action itself does not exist by its own nature" raises an objection against the point stated in the first chapter— that [the appearance of the particular] is not untenable—
by means of the word "not" (na) and the phrase "the appearance of the particular" (*svalakṣaṇābhāsa*) and so forth, which first expresses his own intended view regarding cognition.

Having demonstrated their own nature, they establish the non-existence of both the cognition favored by the proponents of consciousness (*saṃvidvādins*) and the eternal self (*ātman*) that serves as its substratum—
[the latter] which will become manifest at the time of the conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*) occurring immediately thereafter.
The characteristic [of an object] consists of what is called place, time, and form.

At this point, qualifiers such as "present," "now," or "having such a form" first exist solely within themselves at the time of indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*), residing in the blue and so forth, but not [yet in the conceptual cognition].

The "I," which is considered to be of the nature of the perceiver, has attained the cognition of blue—[and so forth]—in the moment of indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*). At that time, the perceiver is not reflected upon (*parāmṛśyate*), because at that moment there is the manifestation of the mere object (*vastumātra*) alone. As it has been said: "There is the manifestation of the mere object."
Regarding the term "non-conceptual" (*nirvikalpaka*): that which has as its object an entity qualified by names and so forth is conceptual (*savikalpaka*);

whereas perception (*pratyakṣa*) that has as its object an unqualified entity is non-conceptual. Thus, by virtue of its essential nature—[it is] possessed of characteristics such as space and so forth.

The internal manifestation of blue and other [objects], which occurs within that cognition that is itself turned outward due to its orientation toward grasping an external object in the form of light—
that is the cognition called "non-conceptual" (*nirvikalpa*), which is the manifestation of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*). This is one [type].

Because it is the root of all subsequent cognitions, it is the primary among those that arise thereafter. Furthermore, although its objects—such as blue and so forth—are manifold, it is supreme insofar as it is devoid of internal differentiation within itself, like this very cognition of conceptualization; thus, it is that which arises immediately following this [initial state].

Because its object is different from [the previous] object, it is distinct due to this difference in objects. Furthermore, the word "again" (*punaḥ*) indicates a specific distinction. "Accompanied by verbal expression" (*sābhilāpam*) means accompanied by verbal expression—that is, by speech consisting of internal discourse such as "this is that" or "that is this. For this very reason, it is manifold conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

(p. 57) There exists only two kinds of cognition, distinguished as non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) and conceptual (*savikalpaka*), the latter being the so-called conceptualizing cognition which takes various forms such as the recollection of memory and so forth.
There is no eternal cognition distinct from these. [Objection: Let it be exactly so.

"There are two types of cognition; by means of these as well, recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is indeed established. To this he says: "Nor even... That pair [of cognitions] does not belong to any eternal seer.
For at the times of experience, conceptualization, memory, and so forth, it is that very same one who, in the form of a synthesizer (*anusaṃdhātṛ*), [thinks], "I..."

Due to such synthesis as "I clearly experienced that very same thing, and now I remember it," the [self]— which you maintain to be a persisting, eternal perceiver and the substratum of cognitions such as experience— does not belong to [the self]. In this regard:
He states the reason: "of that" (tasya). Here, between the two types of knowledge mentioned, it is because that seer does not appear—that is, because he is not manifest.
[Objection: But surely there is the experience, "I know," "I conceptualize," which serves as the locus for these two types of knowledge.

Regarding the claim that "the self indeed manifests [itself]," he says: "I. This very notion of "I," which is well-known to everyone and intended by you as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for establishing the self, actually terminates in the body and so forth;
it determines the body and such as being the self itself, as in "I am happy" or "I am suffering."

Or rather, for this reason, there is no self (ātman) characterized by the notion of "I" that is accessible through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as a continuum of cognition (*jñānasantāna*), distinct from the body and so forth; because if the self were the object of the cognition "I," it would be visible,
and according to the view of those who maintain external objects (*bāhyārthavādin*), that which is visible [is not the self].

The summary meaning of the verse is that there would only be the pair consisting of "seeing" (*darśana*), but not a "seer" (*draṣṭṛ*); thus, the absence of a self (*ātman*) is established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). He begins to explain the two introduced verses word by word: The summary meaning of the verse is that there would only be the pair consisting of "seeing" (*darśana*), but not a "seer" (*draṣṭṛ*); thus, the absence of a self (*ātman*) is established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Regarding the phrase "nānvityākṣepe" (in the objection beginning with "not so"): by this, the characteristic of the object of the objection and the objection itself are indicated, thereby demonstrating the connection between the preceding and subsequent sections (*āhnika*). Having restated what was said—namely, the permanence of the self by the word "kartari" (as agent) and its self-luminosity by the word "jñātari" (as knower)—he now reveals the objection to that:

Regarding the word "here" (*iha*): the use of the particle *tāvat* is made with reference to the refutation of sovereignty—which consists in the nature of knowledge and action that will be treated immediately hereafter.
*Tāvat* means "first. "Here" refers to the preceding chapter (*āhnika*). The Self (*ātman*) is by its very nature consciousness (*saṃvit*). Itself...

Regarding the term "illumination" (*prakāśa*): what was stated by the word "in the knower" (*jñātari*) and what was stated by the word "stable" (*sthira*) as referring to the agent (*kartṛ*) is incorrect.
The reason for this is given by the phrase "of that which is eternal" (*nityasya*). The commentary on "of the stable one" (*sthirasya*) is as follows;
the commentary on "the seer" (*draṣṭṛ*) and so forth is "of that which is self-luminous" (*svaprakāśasya*); [and the commentary on] "not appearing" (*anavabhāsataḥ*) is as follows.

"Because it does not manifest as an object of perception. [Objection: "But surely... [Response: The thesis here is the opposite of what was stated previously; the reason is that no eternal perceiver ever manifests.
If such a self does not manifest, then due to its non-existence, would it not simply be a void?

Since they are manifest, it follows that they alone are denotable by the word "Self"; therefore, he says: "For instance. Regarding the phrase "the manifestation of the jar": indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) has all things as its object, whereas conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—which is sustained by the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), such as "it is a jar and not a cloth"—is the thought "this is that very jar."
[The definition of] *pratyabhijñā* (recognition) consists of both the forms of recollection and direct experience.

Because it is included within perception (*pratyakṣa*), like [other types of perception], recollection is presented first. Recollection of a jar (*ghaṭasmṛti*) is a cognition produced solely from the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of a prior experience; it is certainly not a conceptual construction (*utprekṣā*) regarding the jar.
[The cognition] takes the form "there must be a jar here," and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), volition (saṅkalpa) is included.
Regarding the phrase "occurring at different times": at the time of the mere manifestation of the object as "this," there is one [cognition];
at the time of recognition as "this is blue," there is another; and at the time of the imaginative construction (utprekṣā) "surely it is blue," there is yet another.
Regarding the phrase "having different objects": the object of indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpa*) is the mere thing (*vastumātra*), undifferentiated by space and time, indicated as "this.

On the other hand, the object of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is the blue [object] which has the same form [as the previous one], but is qualified by space, time, and form—such as "being here," "existing now," and "having such a shape"—expressed as "that blue. Thus, they have different objects.

The aspect of manifestation (*bhātarūpa*) is the object of memory. That which is being conceptualized as "it is generally blue" is the blue that is the object of conceptualization (*utprekṣā*). The blue of identical form is the object of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
That [aspect] "this is blue" is the aspect of manifestation that is the object of memory; it is generally blue.
That which is being conceptualized as "it exists" is the blue object of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). Furthermore, there are distinct forms:

the non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) cognition having the form "this," and the conceptual (*savikalpaka*) cognition such as "this is indeed blue," and so forth—the distinction between these being both a distinction in [subjective] state and a distinction in form. Likewise, there are the manifestations of the jar and so on.

The meaning of the two verses ending with "bhinnākārāṇi ca" (and having distinct forms), beginning with "iha" (here), is as follows: it is the cognitions themselves that manifest as denotable by the word "Self," and not these [cognitions] as belonging to a seer distinct from them. This is the intended sense.

He states that the object of the word is the appearance of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) with the words "therein" (*tatra*). Since it is established that cognitions alone are what manifest,

and since it is well known— according to the reasoning in the *Śrītriṃśikā-laghuvṛtti*— that the manifestation of an object-entity is itself the experience (*saṃvedana*), [it follows] that because cognition is dependent upon the object of knowledge, [the cognition] of blue...

It has been stated that [consciousness] is "light. Of what kind? It is said to be "not following after others," meaning it does not follow after the subject (*pramātṛ*). Regarding the phrase "its own nature" (*svarūpa*): its characteristic is that it abides in a state of contraction within the mere nature of blue;
its own domain (*sva*)—space and so forth—is blue only for itself and does not extend to the observer. This refers to such [an object].

The appearance of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—that which is blue and directed outward—is oriented toward its apprehension; for this very reason, having proceeded by way of that [appearance], its manifestation within is non-conceptual cognition (*avikalpaka-jñāna*).
He states the meaning of the word "one" (*eka*) as follows: "even though there is a difference in objects," it has a single form within its own nature.
The reason: (p.

59) (76) "That variety" [is mentioned] in order to demonstrate that there is no variety of intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) in non-conceptual [cognition], by means of this [argument] regarding its counter-correlate, the non-conceptual [cognition], which possesses variety.

"lpahīti" [is the beginning of the verse]. He establishes the non-existence of the object in non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*), which is the cause of diversity in verbal expression (*abhilāpa*), by means of the words "nahi" [and so on]. According to the principle that "verbal expression (*abhilāpa*) is that which directly denotes the object as it has been designated by convention (*saṅketa*)," this [expression] such as "this is blue" is conventional (*sāṅketika*).
Linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*), which resides in the cognizer and is apprehended by the auditory organ, is not a property of the blue object that is the domain of the visual organ.

This verbal expression is already accessible [to the mind] because it has been conceptualized by those who accept valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*); thus, there is no absence of the apprehension of blue and so forth. For this very reason, it must be recollected at that time.

Recollection of that which is to be remembered depends upon memory; and the awakening of memory depends upon the perception of an object similar to the previously experienced object. Thus, at the time of non-conceptual [cognition], which consists in the perception of the mere object, there is the absence of verbal expression mediated by these various factors.
Since memory itself does not exist, it cannot be the cause of its own diversity; therefore, it is established that [the self] is of a single form.
Because the word "para" (subsequent) requires a point of reference (*avadhi*), the phrase "tataḥ" (from that) was stated; that is, from that [non-conceptual cognition].

Regarding the fact that conceptual cognition occurs immediately after non-conceptual cognition, he states the reason for the conceptual cognition's posteriority to the non-conceptual by saying "sarvasya" (of all). This refers to... [the following].

Immediately following the appearance [of the object], there arises a conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) in the form of the exclusion of others (*anyāpohana*), such as "this is blue indeed, not yellow. This conceptual cognition, which occurs immediately after the non-conceptual [perception] (*nirvikalpaka*), has that non-conceptual perception as its direct and immediate basis; this refers to the cognition whose form is "that" (*tad*) and so forth.
Since memory and the like are based on conceptual cognition, which itself is rooted in non-conceptual cognition, they are indirectly rooted in non-conceptual cognition through an intermediate step;

that is, they are rooted in non-conceptual cognition by way of the immediate awakening of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of prior experience. He states another meaning for the word "supreme" (*para*): "paramiti" [meaning "the supreme"].
The object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is an object distinct from the non-conceptual form of the object;

he explains this very nature of being a different object with the words "the universal" (*sāmānya*). That [conceptual cognition], which is accompanied by conceptual construction, has as its object something distinct from both the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*)—which is the object of non-conceptual perception characterized by the universal—and [the universal itself].

The object [of conceptual cognition] is a thing (*vastu*) characterized by the features known as space, time, and form, which are common to all cognizers; it is that which effects worldly transactions such as rejection and acquisition. Now, one might ask: "Why could the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) itself not be its object? Anticipating this doubt, [the author states] that it [the particular] is conventional (*sāṅketika*).
He says "the particular characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*) to show that this is not so, because [the particular] is not within the scope of conventional discourse (*vyavahāra*).

For, in the case of the object of non-conceptual [perception], which is extremely restricted by being unqualified by space, time, and form, there is the awakening of the object to be accomplished— which is merely the thing-in-itself— by means of conceptualization, even though it is conventional.

Because it is impossible to establish a convention for that which is well-known through worldly usage, for that which is established through instruction, for that which is established through the teacher’s oral instruction,

or for a secret designation (p. 60), if one were to establish such a convention, it would become a general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), thereby losing its status as a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Because it would follow [absurdly] that, even if a convention were somehow established for one thing through delusion as being another thing— which is merely a bare reality— the convention would be useless,
since it cannot serve as a basis for linguistic usage. Therefore, [the object] which is fit for the making of a convention is not a non-recurrent entity, nor is it dependent upon the cognizer.

If [the object] were defined as being restricted solely to its own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), then there would be no subsequent conventional usage following the apprehension of the linguistic convention (*saṅketa*); therefore,
the object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is precisely the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) that is serviceable for conventional usage.

Thus, it is established that conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*) has the nature of another object. He explains the meaning of the word "in many ways" (*bahudhā*) with the words "and that" (*tac ca*). That conceptual cognition is of many kinds through its divisions such as memory (*smṛti*) and so forth. He makes the word "since" (*yataḥ*) the reason for this [statement] with the words "because."

The meaning of "that" (*tat*) and so forth is clear. "This" (*idam*) refers to the present form. "That" (*tat*) refers to the past form. "That-this" (*tad-idam*) refers to the past-present form. "This or that" (*idaṃ vā idaṃ vā*) is of the nature of a mental construction (*utprekṣā*).
"Designation" (*śabdanam*) refers to that which manifests as "this" at the present moment.

Even in the case of a blue object, from moment to moment, there arises a different blue form; thus, "this" and "that" become distinct forms. This is the meaning of the expression "it knows this" or "it knows that.
Now, one might ask: does the multiplicity of conceptual constructions (vikalpa) arise merely through the difference in words applied to the object?

To the question "How so?", he says: "And that" (*tac ca*). The meaning is that this very act of denotation (*śabdana*), because it is a property of the cognizer (*pramātṛdharma*), produces a variety in the form of recollection, synthesis, and so forth, with respect to insentient objects such as blue and the like, which are the objects of conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*). (78)
Having summarized what was stated from "the appearance of the specific characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇabhāsa*) up to "in many ways" (*bahudhā*), he demonstrates it as follows:

"In this way. Cognitions themselves constitute, in the manner previously described, a continuum consisting of a succession of experiences, such as the memory of a jar and the mental synthesis (*anusandhāna*) of a jar.

The same applies to cloth and other such objects. As for the series of experiences and conceptual cognitions, does it arise through something else, or by itself? In the first case, there is an infinite regress (*anavasthā*); in the second, there is a contradiction regarding the agent [of cognition]. Therefore, he says: "by virtue of self-luminosity" (*svaprakāśatvena*). The first position is rejected by its own non-acceptance; as for the second, [he speaks] of "self... [the text continues].

This is because it is accepted that self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) consists precisely in the independence from anything else for its manifestation; however, it is not [defined] by the characteristic of being self-luminous [in the sense of being a substance], nor is it both of those.
This is in order to explain the passage beginning with "of the eternal," and so forth.
He raises a doubt to be refuted with the words, "It might be thus. Just as a painting appears fixed to a wall,
so too this succession of experiences and conceptualizations appears fixed—
that is, it appears— within that which consists of the experiencer and the conceptualizer.

The meaning is that it would follow from your own position that if that [cognition], which is its own substratum, were not manifest, then itself too would not be manifest. He introduces the subsequent passage beginning with "taddvayam" as a response to this doubt, stating: "That is not so," because [there is] some eternal [entity].

The meaning is: [it refers to] that which you assert exists as the substratum of the visible object— being inseparable from the two cognitions— and which, being inextricably woven through all times, cannot withstand rational analysis as a "seer" (*draṣṭṛ*).
Since conceptual constructions such as memory are rooted in direct experience, by the mention of the "experiencer" as the substratum of that experience,
the substratum of memory and the like is also included. Therefore, the meaning is that apart from these two cognitions, there is no other substratum for them whatsoever.

Now, one might object: since, according to the *Vijñānapāda*, even the object of perception (*dṛśya*) does not exist apart from the duality [of subject and object], it must be said that it cannot belong to the perceiver (*draṣṭṛ*). To this, he says: "But as for the object... Even the non-existence of the object, according to his own view, [is established].
Even if it were related to the object of perception according to the view of the proponents of external objects (bāhyārthavādin),
that too would be untenable when subjected to analysis. Nevertheless, even while granting this for the sake of argument,
the emphasis here is that the [object] accepted by the Sañcayavādins and others certainly does not belong to the perceiver.
The meaning is: "having spoken thus. This is intended to state the reason why there are not two cognitions and no seer.

Introducing the passage beginning with "of that" (*tasya*), he explains it as follows: "herein. By the root word "of that" (*tasya*) and by the phrase "since there is no manifestation" (*yata ābhāso nāsti*), it is indicated that [the absence of manifestation] is the reason for the statement "it does not appear as a seer" (*draṣṭur anavabhāsate*).

This has been explained. Now, [the opponent] objects: "The non-manifestation [of the self] is due to its being unfit for manifestation by the seer, not because of its non-existence. To this, he says: "For this very reason," etc. According to the proponent of consciousness (*saṃvidvādin*), the seer is admitted to have consciousness as his essential nature (*svabhāva*). And consciousness is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*). Therefore...

Because its nature is self-luminous consciousness (*svaprakāśasaṃvitsvabhāva*), it is logical that its self-luminosity must be accepted by those who maintain [this view]; therefore, he says: "For this very reason. [The opponent] says: "[By the proponent]...". "Attained" (*āpannā*) means arrived at or perceived (*upalabdhi*).
The meaning is: "of one who has [the state] whose nature is the comprehension proximate to the two types of knowledge. Alternatively:

*āpanna* means "attained," and *upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpti* means "the attainment of the characteristic of perception. The meaning is: "of one by whom there is the attainment—that is, the fitness—of that which is the characteristic cause for perception. Regarding this fitness:
The non-apprehension of something everywhere is the cause for knowing the absence of that particular object.
In this context, "attainment of the conditions for apprehension" means fitness (*yogyatā*). Thus, [an object is perceived] because of the fitness consisting in the illumination of the perceiver;
and when there is fitness, it is due to the presence of all the constituent parts of its definition. Conversely, there is no manifestation because of unfitness.
The meaning is that because it cannot be described and because it does not manifest, its very existence is non-existent. Here, "in this" means within these two types of sublation of the root-term.
Within the two types of cognition mentioned in this sūtra, the phrase "the cognition 'I'" refers to the latter half [of the verse] (80).
He shows the doubt to be set aside with the words "Now, [nanu]":

the non-perception of that which is capable of being seen—that is, of that which has reached the conditions for perception—is presented by you as proving the non-existence of the seer; however, this [reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*), and thus there is no non-existence of the seer.
Certainty. It establishes the very existence of manifestation—namely, "tathāhi" (for instance), "vid-ādi" (beginning with *vid*), etc. *Vid* means "to know";
*ci* means "to gather"; *smṛ* means "to remember. Thus, from the suffix [attached] to a verbal root (*prakṛti*) such as *vid* and the others...
That which is produced first is the *prakṛti*, a specific word;

its [manifestation as] "I" occurs in experiences such as "I know," with respect to the object of that [word], and with respect to the mental modification (*vṛtti*) consisting of knowledge— which has the form of experience— arising from the object of speech which has the form of the meaning [of the word].

The meaning is that, since in the light [of consciousness] there appears a form called the "self"— which persists through time, which is the basis for the cognition of "I," and whose nature consists of being a knower, a determiner, and a rememberer— the non-perception of such a visible object is unestablished; thus, the existence of the seer is proven.

"Even the word 'api' (also) in the Sūtra, keeping in mind the meaning that the self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) of this [notion] 'I' does not exist at all, states the refutation: 'One'. He says, "Who indeed [says] thus?"—referring to one who knows the truth of reasoning and examines the nature of the follower. Furthermore, from knowledge alone... [it is] thus.

The word "what" (*kiṃ*) has the sense of an objection, as in "you say. To state that, in reality, this "I" lacks even the nature of pure luminosity, he describes the nature of luminosity with the words "for manifestation... [and so on].
It is indeed free from verbalization and conceptual construction (*nirvikalpaka*).

This is the meaning of the word "manifestation" (*prakāśa*). The cognition "I" is likewise permeated by the verbal form "I"; for this very reason, it is a conceptual cognition (*vikalpapratyaya*). Let it be, according to your reasoning, that "I" is a conceptual cognition; nevertheless, that cognition is...

"—te---- nanu iti. What is the nature that is conceptualized? The meaning of the doubt is: must some form distinct from the conceptual cognition (*vikalpapratyaya*) be admitted as the object of conceptualization (*vikalpya*), namely, the nature of the self (*ātmarūpa*)?
He says "the body, etc. to state that the body and so forth alone are the objects of conceptualization, and that a self distinct from them must be admitted.

It has been stated that the "body" refers to the continuum (*santāna*) of the body and so forth at every moment. He states the reason why this continuum is subject to conceptual construction (*vikalpyatva*) with the words, "I am thin. [Objection: But surely, in the expression "my body," the self (*ātman*) exists as distinct from the body.
Since it is being perceived, how can the continuum of the body be considered a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of the notion of "I"?

Because the Vijñānavādin is not satisfied by the [previous] objection against the doctrine that the body is the self, he states another position—beginning with the word *jñāna*. He provides the reason for the fact that the continuum of cognition is a conceptual construction:
"I am happy.

Now, [one might object]: "A 'happy person' (sukhī) is so called because he possesses happiness; thus, taking the possessive suffix (*matvartha*) prescribed by the rule *tad asyāsty asmin* [Pāṇini 5.2.94], the suffix *ini* is applied according to the rule *ata ini ṭhanau* [Pāṇini 5.2.115]. To this, [the response is: "No..."

He states that a self (*ātman*) distinct from the continuum of cognition (*jñāna-santāna*) must be admitted as its substratum, saying: "And [the suffix] expressing possession" (*matvarthīya*). Having explained [the passage] beginning with "the cognition 'I'" according to its underlying intent, he analyzes it in accordance with the connection of the words, saying: "This very [point]. "Ascertainment" (*avasāya*) means conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). The reason for this is as follows:

Regarding the term "similar": it refers to entities that, although having different forms in each successive moment, are perceived through delusion as being similar to the preceding moments because their subsequent forms resemble the forms of those preceding them.

Because it is permeated by the latent predisposition (*vāsanā*)— which will be described later and which possesses the capacity for the erroneous appearance of blue and other objects as having a single form when they are actually possessed of distinctions—
the meaning of the word "this" (*eṣā*) is stated: "In this view, [it] does not establish the self."

This [self] has been accepted by us and not denied; for it is perceived by everyone as established through their own internal cognition that "I am emaciated. However, it is indeed subsumed under the category of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

He states the summarized meaning of "I" and so forth: this is what is meant—it must be stated by one who seeks to establish the self as a knower distinct from knowledge and the like, which have the functions of discerning and so on, and from their objects: is the self merely the cognition "I," or is it the subjective awareness of that [cognition]?
Having thus considered both alternatives, he states that neither is possible: "The cognition 'I'.

This is because, through such instances as "I am fat" at one time and "I am thin" at another, the cognition possesses a different form at every moment; therefore, a single uniform cognition is unstable.

In the cognition of a jar and so forth, there is no self distinct from the body that is to be cognized as "I," just as the form of the jar itself is cognized. Even if one were to accept a self distinct from that [body], the self as you intend it would not be established; this is the meaning of the word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "even if existing" (*bhavann api*).
Because it is an object of cognition like a jar or other objects, and because it is accepted as being the object of the cognition "I," one might ask:
in the absence of a denotative word, how is this meaning understood? To this he says: "This too [is understood] by means of a word. (p.
64) He concludes the meaning stated in the two verses with the word "evam" (thus): "Thus, by perception..."

There is no cognition of a self; having stated that its non-existence is understood through the non-perception of a perceptible object, he says "here" (*atre*) to show that inference (*anumāna*) is also raised as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the self in the following verse, in order to state that it is not established even by inference. Thus, [he refutes] perception with respect to the self.

Having stated that [the self] is established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he introduces inference with the following verse in order to assert that inference also exists as a proof; thus he says: "In this regard" (*atre*). When it is said that the self is established by perception, the proponent of the self (*ātmavādī*)—who maintains that there exists a self distinct from consciousness and its objects—[responds].
Thus, the inference based on the mark of memory is presented as a proof for the self.

The word *atha* marks the commencement of an objection: [the opponent argues] that the self (*ātman*) must be eternal because it is the experiencer (*anubhāvaka*). If that is so, then how could there be a memory corresponding to an experience once that experience has perished? This is the connection of the argument. Regarding the term *nitya*: as before, it refers to the self as the experiencer, the agent of experience, or the one possessing experience.

"Experience me as having the nature of 'I'. [The author replies: How, and in what manner, could there be a memory—characterized by the non-loss (asaṃpramoṣa) of the experienced object—that conforms to the experience "this is a jar," "this is a cloth," once that experience has perished? It could not exist.
In the absence of a cognizer, since there would be no object being remembered, the occurrence of memory could not be accounted for by an object that is itself non-existent.
Nor can memory be established through experience alone, precisely because [the experience] has perished. Therefore, memory cannot be established by any means whatsoever.

In the absence of memory, all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), which depend upon the recollection of conventional linguistic signs, would also cease to exist. Furthermore, worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) would be impossible through mere non-conceptual cognition alone. For even that which is perceived here by non-conceptual perception remains unapprehended as long as it has not been touched by a specific reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).

Otherwise, because it would be remembered only through [mere] cessation, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the collapse of all worldly transaction (*sarvavyavahāra*). Therefore, for the sake of establishing worldly transaction, memory must first be accepted. Consequently, the eternal conscious self (*cidātman*), which is the substratum of that memory and the locus of experience at the time of the experience—the one who experienced—must also be accepted.

Just as there is an inference of fire by means of the mark of smoke, so too is inference stated here by means of the mark of memory (*smṛti*). This is the concise meaning of the sūtra: "What is it that you desire? Regarding the word "here" (*iha*):
it refers to the object already experienced which is intended to be remembered at the time of memory, occurring immediately after the time of the original experience.

Whether [the object] perishes or does not perish, whether it is destroyed or undestroyed, what purpose does that object serve for memory? The meaning is that it does not become a generator of the recollection of the object.
"That very same" means that the absence of the object is itself made the object of one's own self by the very fact of having been experienced.
To establish the experience in this very way—(p.

65)—one might object: "Since the experience occurs spontaneously in accordance with the object, why should it not have that [external] thing as its object? To this, he says: "For instance" (*tathā hi*). "Manifestation" (*prakāśa*) means as a mere thing (*vastumātra*), in the form of "this."

Vibration (*sphuraṇa*) is the intermediate determination; "this alone" is the certainty. When there is the state of being manifested through the coexistence of the experience and the object—such that one says, "This is the experience, this is the object"—just as one says "Devadatta is qualified by a staff," so too is "this object qualified by the experience. The reason for this is as follows:

"In all cases" means: whether it be the manifestation of an object in memory, the determination [of an object], the simultaneous manifestation of both experience and the object, or the manifestation of an object qualified by experience—that is, when there is a determination [of the object]—it is due to the manifestation and determination [of the object]. And it is not...
In memory, there is the manifestation "this is that object," such as "that is the jar," because in that case, the object itself appears without distinction [from its prior state].
But if, in memory, the object does not manifest by itself, how can there be an appearance of the object?
Anticipating this objection, he says "But rather...

(*kiṃ tu*) to show that [memory] must conform to experience; the word "but" (*tu*) indicates that memory’s conformity to experience is required with respect to the manifestation of its own object, as distinct from [the original] perception. [This occurs] by way of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*).

Even at the time of recollection, that which persists (84) is primarily the illumination of the experience itself. The reason for this is stated as "of the experience. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "In the experience"—only when there is the illumination of the experience in the form of a latent impression (*vāsanā*) does it exist in recollection.

The meaning is that there occurs an appearance of the object. "By all means" means even by way of its latent impression (*saṃskāra*). "Experience" [means] having ascended into the cognizer by way of its latent impression, [it is] destroyed by that impression. "Its illumination" means having the nature of the illumination of experience. "By means of that" means...
[The objection is: "How could there be memory of objects through the medium of the manifestation of experience?

Let there be no memory"—this must not be said; thus [the author] says: "By that. By means of that memory, having remembered with the mind the object previously experienced, all worldly activity such as rejection, acquisition, and so forth, is carried out.
Memory, which is the root of all worldly transaction, is well-established for everyone;

its own nature cannot be denied. Even when the experience that constitutes its cause has perished, memory—though its own substratum has also perished—testifies that there exists some form [of that experience].
If it is argued that "only cognitions shine forth," that which you have asserted has already been refuted.

Now, as to how the existence of an eternal seer is not established by that much alone, he says: "That very [form] indeed. That very form, which is undesirable [to the opponent], is established through the impossibility of otherwise accounting for memory (*smṛti-anyathānupapatti*).
It is the agent of experience from the outset; for this very reason, it is called the "experiencer," the eternal self (*ātman*). Regarding the term "experiencer" (*anubhāvaka*):
it is an analysis of the root word [as] "the agent of experiencing," with the suffix *ṇvul*.

And by means of that [recollection], it is established that [the self] has the nature of memory. "Only this much" means: only mere memory. To the question, "If so, why has it been explained here at such length?", he says: "In that regard," etc.
Here, in this very prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), the self has been established through the power of memory; by that self...

The meaning of the objection is: "How could there be recollection (*smṛti*) of an object? The word "how" implies that since the self is not admitted, one must explain how recollection is possible through the experience of an object.
In that regard, first, for an object appearing in this manner as "this," [recollection occurs] in the form of a reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) as "that."

It has been established that memory is not possible in any way whatsoever, because it is of no assistance [to the process of recollection] and because the foundational experience (*anubhava*) has perished. It was stated that if the self (*ātman*) is not accepted, memory would not exist; let there be no such memory—this is the fault [in that position]. In this regard, [the opponent claims] that there is an absence of that [fault].

Recalling the previously established conventional term in the form of a name for each respective object, such as a jar and so forth—all things that are possible are seen as being composed of that [consciousness].
Or, as will be stated later, there are twenty modes [of perception]. This alone is it, and nothing else; "this is that," and so forth.
Even conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), which consist of verbal discourse and the like, have come to an end; let there be no conceptual constructions at all.
To the objection that "let there be only one non-conceptual knowledge," he replies: "non-conceptual" (*nirvikalpaka*).
Because non-conceptual [knowledge] is the motivator of conventional discourse, it is described as "vision" (*darśana*).

It would follow the conventions of hearing and so forth. As it was said in the *Śrī-tattvagarbha-stotra*: "And therefore, because all activities and linguistic conventions would be abolished, this entire world would certainly become blind and mute."
This very notion of transmigrating beings exists both externally and internally;
for even when one has departed [from the body], this notion is still perceived, like wood or a wall.

Thus, in the manner taught by the venerable Bhartṛhari, there would be nothing at all—devoid of lamentation, resembling a corpse, and lacking visual, verbal, and auditory activity. The word "iti" indicates the conclusion of the inquiry concerning the proponent of the Self (ātmavādin). In this way, that which was raised for the purpose of establishing the Self...
The inference of the self-advocates, characterized by the impossibility of explaining memory and its effects otherwise, is refuted by showing that it can be explained otherwise; for in the world,
a cause postulated on the basis of an effect is postulated only as something capable of producing its own specific result, and the self is not such.

It is capable of accomplishing the function of memory; therefore, it is not the volition (*saṃkalpa*) that is so capable, but rather the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) itself, which is the prior experience, that is capable of accomplishing it. To this he says: "In this world" (*iha*). That is, in this world; "without the effect" (*kāryavyatirekeṇa*), meaning in the absence of an effect—by what impossibility otherwise?

p. 67) Such a cause is fit to be postulated. Whatever cause is being postulated must be capable of producing that effect... [as in the case of] Devadatta, who does not eat during the day; here, by the effect characterized as corpulence—which is devoid of daytime eating—one infers a cause capable of bringing about that [corpulence] itself.

Just as eating at night is observed to be postulated as the cause [of certain effects], so too the self, when postulated by means of memory as its effect, is not capable of that [function]. Therefore, he says: "For the object... You accept the existence of a self for the purpose of remembering an experienced object.

An object is remembered precisely by way of the manifestation of its experience; it is not remembered by way of the self. It has been stated that the experience, which serves as the gateway for the memory of the object, has perished; therefore, the object cannot be [remembered] by the self through the experience.

What is the purpose of memory? Even if the existence of the self were postulated, since experience perishes and there would be no manifestation of that experience, memory—which depends upon it—would not arise; thus, the meaning is that the self serves no purpose whatsoever. [This is said] because the function of memory would not be accomplished.
Regarding the existence of a capable self— the sense is that there is no distinction between the self and space in terms of their capacity for cause and effect—
although the self alone is not useful for memory.

He raises the objection that this criticism is unfounded because it lacks the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of experience— introducing it with "Now" (*atha*). Even if one does not accept that this effect, which has the nature of memory, arises from the word alone, [the point remains] that without a latent impression, the effect does not arise.

Since you have also stated this, the proponent of the previous view replies: "In that case, it is the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) alone—accepted by both disputants—which must be postulated on the basis of the effect of memory; it is not the self (*ātman*). He explains: "This very thing [is] one's own mental impression"; thus, apart from the observed effect here, there is no object of knowledge (*prameya*).
He demonstrates this with two verses, beginning with "iha" and ending with "kiṃ tena. By the phrase "even though," it is stated as follows:

even though the self exists, since perception has perished, by what means could there be remembrance of those objects previously seen? This is the grammatical connection (*anvaya*). Regarding the term "by that means": [it refers to] the perceived object.
Since [the cognition] is connected with the door of experiencing your form through contact, it is called "vision" (*dṛk*) because of its destruction;
for, like experience, it possesses selfhood as that which serves as the door for manifestation.
Thus, the term "vision" is employed. Even though the Self exists at the time of its destruction, what purpose does that [destruction] serve for the Self? It accomplishes nothing for it.
Because you yourself have stated that the foundational experience has been destroyed; since the experience is lost, even the manifestation in the form "this is it" is severed, and thus,
due to the absence of a memory qualified by the aspect of reality, if there were some experiencer— then...
What could memory—which is capable of arising immediately after the destruction of the experience—possibly do?

Since that [self] is the experiencer, it has perished along with the very destruction of the experience; for even if one were to accept its stability, it would be of no use here, whether by means of the object, the experience of that object, or the self itself.

The meaning is that memory would not occur. In the phrase "in objects" (*dṛṣṭeṣu vastuṣu*), the locative case is used in the sense of the object (*viṣaya-saptamī*). The term "through that" (*taddvārā*) is a *bahu-vrīhi* compound. According to his own philosophical system, experience (*anubhava*) has the nature of perception (*dṛg-ātman*);
thus, for every cognition, one part is the object, while the other part is the constituent known as cognition itself (*jñāna*).
Thus, because both components exist, it is said that [the memory] pertains to a portion of the object (*arthaṃśa*).

Having stated the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) regarding the contrary position, he establishes the very fact of its being lost, beginning with the words "of that" (*tasya*). Here, "uninterrupted" (*atruṭita*) means unbroken. Regarding the phrase "what kind of memory?": it would not even have the nature of a memory in the form "that" (*sa iti*). [This is so] because of the experience (*anubhava*).

When destruction occurs, the experiencer himself is also destroyed; even if he remains according to the opponent's view, he is not the cause for memory in our own system. Since there is no state of being a rememberer apart from the state of being an experiencer, what purpose would the experiencer serve for memory? He raises the following objection: "Memory arises precisely with respect to the object that was experienced."

Regarding "atha": here, experience itself is that "word" (pada); the object of that experience, such as blue and so forth, exists at the time of experience, and while being experienced at that time, it becomes something remembered [later].
Thus, the meaning is that this very [object] is the producer of memory. Regarding "pada": the meaning is "object" (viṣaya).

That [object] is the very locus (*pada*) of the experience; that memory which has that as its object is called "that-locus" (*tatpada*), according to a *bahuvrīhi* compound. Anticipating the question of how it can be the locus of that [memory], he introduces the first half of the following verse as the reason for this, beginning with "nanu": [of the object] of the cognition of a jar...
