Having raised the objection that "since it is not an object of the cognition of a cloth, it is not possible for what is an object of direct experience to become an object of memory," he introduces the second half of the verse as a response to that, beginning with "nanu" and so forth. [He explains] "viṣayitve" [as follows]: by means of one thing being the object of another... [the other].

The state of being an object is merely a matter of conceit; it does not exist in reality. (88) Regarding the doubt as to what the cause for this conceit of being an object is, the answer is given by the words "for" (*yataḥ*).
This is because the occurrence of memory arises from the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of prior experience.
Therefore, it is appropriate that it was stated, "by those very words. The word *hi* (for/indeed) indicates universal renown.
He explains the text that has been introduced with the words "by experience" (*anubhavena*). Regarding the phrase "suited to itself" (*svocita*):
by whichever experience of blue, pleasure, or the like has arisen, by that very experience...
A mental impression (*saṃskāra*), which is synonymous with *vāsanā* and serves as the seed for the re-emergence of such experienced objects as blue or pleasure through being remembered, arises.
Since memory is born from a mental impression, it is possible for it to have the same object as the original experience.

He shows that the state of being "established" (*sthita-sthāpita*) is well-known in the world as a *saṃskāra* by saying, "And the *saṃskāra*... The *saṃskāra* is called "the establisher of what is established. Regarding the word "drawn back" (*ākṛṣṭa*)—as in "for a long time" (*cira-kālam*)—it refers to something that has remained coiled for a long duration and is subsequently being extended.
Because it is well known in the world as "the bark of the birch tree" (*bhūrjakaṭādi*), for that reason,
even in this case of experience, the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produces from itself a memory born of it,
which causes the prior experience; [it is understood that] "this prior experience grasped the object."

Memory also grasps that very same object and acts accordingly; whereas at the time of experience there was the cognition "this," at the time of memory there is the cognition "that. This alone is the distinction; in every respect, however, the experience of the cloth is one and the same.

The sense is that because the [cognition] produced by the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of the cognition of a jar does not arise from the jar itself, it does not have the jar as its object; whereas, since memory arises from the latent impression of a prior experience, it is possible for it to possess an object through the object of that prior experience—thus, the example you have cited is dissimilar. This is the point. Even by [the opponent] himself...
Since it does not produce recollection, the efficient cause of the effect that is recollection is indeed the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) alone;
thus, he says "If this is so" to show that the self (*ātman*) serves no purpose whatsoever. If it is thus, then...

What purpose would there be in an internal, non-existent self? Thus [you argue]: "The mental impression (*saṃskāra*) is itself devoid of an object; it is by you stated that [the impression] is the cause of memory. If that is so, then the objection you raised—beginning with "Alas! [if this were so], it would follow that...
and so forth—is also refuted. He says:

"All" refers to the formative forces (*saṃskāras*). Since all conventional usage is based on the fact that these [formative forces] are the cause of memory, the presumption (*arthāpatti*)— which takes the form of "memory would otherwise be inexplicable"— cannot serve as an inferential mark for a self (*ātman*), because it is vitiated by the fault of being capable of being explained in another way.
It has been stated:

now, since it is impossible for a formation (*saṃskāra*) that has not yet arisen to have the lower elements such as earth as its substratum (*āśraya*), by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), it must be the self (*ātman*).

Having raised the objection that [the self] is established as the substratum of the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), he introduces the following verse as a response to it: "But of what? It has already been stated that memory belongs to the impressions themselves, independent of a self; for the impression itself, being a quality (*guṇatvāt*), [requires a substrate].
He raises the objection that [the impression] leads one to infer its own substrate, the self, which possesses the quality—this is expressed by "not so" (nānviti).

Regarding the word "of that" (tasyeti): since the latent impression (*saṃskāra*), which is the cause of memory, is a quality, it requires a substrate just like color and other qualities; therefore, the meaning is that the self is inferred as its substrate.
Therefore, regarding the subject— the self (ātman)— if its attributes,

such as the qualities of knowledge and so forth, which are non-different and non-distinct from it, are accepted as being distinct [from it], then, while those [attributes] are eternal, the subject, the self, which is not intended to be eternal, would [become] impermanent due to its having those attributes.

(p. 70) Because there would be no distinction from the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of cognition and so forth due to the absence of difference, it would follow that there is no distinction between their being eternal and non-eternal. [The phrase] "because there would be no distinction from the essential nature of cognition and so forth due to the absence of difference" implies that non-eternality would also accrue to that [essential nature], since [non-eternality] occurs in things that are distinct and separate.

Because there is no distinction within that nature of the self; for indeed, no distinction is produced in the nature of a jar by means of a cloth, since they are mutually distinct. Furthermore, just as the inference of a jar [is not made] from a different [object], so too the inference of the self does not occur through a distinct mental impression (*saṃskāra*); nor is it memory.

It must be stated that there exists a relationship between the two formations (saṃskāra) consisting of the state of being the locus and the located; for a relationship distinct from the entities themselves cannot be established in various instances, as it would follow that a single thing possesses multiple forms—a point which will be refuted by the following two verses. Nor can those two [formations] belong to something eternal.
Just as a "seer" (draṣṭṛ)— who, according to the stated principle, is conceived as the substratum for both non-conceptual and conceptual perception—
is imagined, so too is an "rememberer" (smartṛ), who is conceived as the substratum for memory, imagined. Thus it is with memory.
Success arises from the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) alone.

The meaning of the passage beginning with "here" (*iha*) is as follows: regarding the claim that the self (*ātman*) is inferred through its own substratum by means of the mental impression, this must be examined. Even when the mental impression is being produced, [the existence of] the self is established from the very state of its production.

Is there a distinction [between the self and its attributes], or not? If the former, this distinction must either be distinct from the self or non-distinct from it—just as a cloth is neither distinct nor non-distinct from a pot. Since the production of a distinction within the self is impossible, and because the relationship [between them] is difficult to define, it is impossible to say "this is a distinction of that [self]."

And if there were no distinction [between the cloth and its quality], then because that which is produced would be eternal, it would follow that even the self, which is non-different from the impermanent particular, would be impermanent. Regarding the second position— that there is no particular—
[it follows that] in the substrate, such as the cloth, there would be only the whiteness and so forth which produce the particular.
Because the quality of conferring a specific characteristic is itself absent in a quality,
the inference of the self by means of *saṃskāra* (latent impression) is not possible, since the reason (*hetu*) of "being a quality" is unestablished (*asiddha*). In this context,
regarding the position that the self is inferred by means of *saṃskāra*, [it is argued] when a sprout is being produced...

The "entirety of the seed's swelling" (*ucchūnatā-śeṣa*) refers to a specific excellence; it is a certain particularity existing at that time, an excellence that is superior to its prior state due to the production of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*). It does not exist as something distinct from the self (*ātman*). Regarding the "opposite side" (*vipakṣa*): in the case of the position of distinction (*vyatireka-pakṣa*), [the proof fails] because of the absence of a relationship.

Since it is impossible for [the self] to belong to that [body], if one accepts that it is non-different from it in order to establish its belonging to that body, then the self—like the impermanent particular—would itself not be eternal.
Thus, your position that it is eternal (p. 71) is not established; for that which is non-different from an impermanent particular would necessarily be impermanent itself.
"Of this" means of the self (*ātman*). "By that" refers to the impression (*saṃskāra*) which effects a specific quality within the self that serves as its own substratum;

what then happens to the self? Its state of being a quality (*guṇatva*) and its state of being a possessor of qualities (*guṇitva*) do not [arise] for the self, because the reason for its being a quality is unestablished when the impression is produced. Thus, there is no inference of the self.

"Let there be no other distinct quality (*viśeṣa*) of the self; let that very [impression] itself be the quality. For a 'quality' (*viśeṣa*) is that which distinguishes its own substratum from other entities. Therefore, it is merely a quality (*guṇa*). Thus he raises the objection with "Now, if... Since a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) is impermanent, if one accepts it as a quality of the self, then the quality would belong to that [impermanent impression].
For the sake of establishing [the point], non-distinctness must be accepted.

He offers the following reply—beginning with "In that case"—to the objection that if the self were non-different from impermanent mental formations (*saṃskāra*), it would follow that the self itself is impermanent.
(91) Now, regarding whether the mental formation is non-distinct or distinct [from the self], let us consider the first alternative.
"The fault is not that [the self] is non-distinct. Regarding the word "by that": by means of that specific impression (*saṃskāra*), this self does not become something distinct.
Because it lacks the state of being qualified by a distinct, separate qualification (*viśeṣa*), it would again fall into the form of cognition, as was stated in the case of other qualifications.

Since conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, it follows that the self (*ātman*), being non-different from them, must also be impermanent. With the intention that there is no eternal conditioned phenomenon existing apart from cognition itself, [the text speaks of] the conditioning of cognition.

Thus it has been said. In order to exclude the permanent mental impression (*saṃskāra*)—which is of the nature of an entity (*bhāva*) and accepted by the Vaiśeṣikas and others—the term "cognition" (*jñāna*) is used to indicate that which resides in insentient objects such as jars.
Now, one might object: cognition is indeed a distinct quality (*guṇa*), whereas mental impression is another quality altogether.
To the question, "In what way does it have the nature of knowledge?", he says: "From experience.

From experience—that is, from non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*)—there arises, through a succession, a cognition that is distinct because it possesses a conceptual form (*vikalpa-rūpatva*), which is indirect (*parokṣa*) in nature and characterized by a specific object.

The term "saṃskāra" (mental impression) is what is expressed by the word; because the object is singular, there is a succession [of its apprehension], and because the experience of being the grasper of that [object] and so forth belongs to cognition, there is also a succession for the cognition of the saṃskāra which produces that [primary] cognition. The particle *eva* is for the sake of clarity.
This is the sense.

He adopts the second position—that the *saṃskāra* (mental impression) is a specific quality of the self and thus distinct from it—by stating: "Now, if the *saṃskāra* is distinct, it is indeed a specific quality of the self."
He says "of that" [tasya] to show that there would be no [improvement] for the impression (*saṃskāra*). The meaning is: what special quality (*viśeṣa*) would this impression bring to that self?
[The implication is] that an impression distinct from the self—like the whiteness of a jar and so forth—[cannot belong to it].
[Objection: "Since there exists a relationship of the locus and the located (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*), there would be a distinction between them. To this, he says:

"And the relationship... [The position that] there exists some kind of relationship distinct from the entities themselves and residing within those entities will be refuted—this being established therein.

Because that which resides in two [substrata] possesses multiple forms; thus, with these two verses, he states that the self is not inferred by means of qualities such as cognition (jñāna) and so forth, just as it is not inferred by latent impressions (saṃskāra): "In this way, cognition... and so on.
Just as cognition, pleasure, and the like—which are distinct from the self—are qualities of the self, so too is latent impression.

To this he replies: "In the same way, regarding knowledge," and so forth. When knowledge, pleasure, and the like arise, does a distinction exist in the self or not? One must refute [the opponent's position] by examining the alternatives: whether knowledge, pleasure, and so forth are distinct from the self or non-distinct from it. [The opponent's] example is unaccepted.
Such is the intended meaning (*bhāva*).
Having thus stated the essential purport (*tātparyārtha*), he joins the verse to the subject matter at hand with the words "therefore" (*tataḥ*).
The word "root" (*mūla*) has the sense of "the Self" (*ātman*). The terms "in non-different things" and "in different things" involve the elision (*praśleṣa*) of the vowel *a*.
By means of these two [verses] on conjunction (*praśleṣa*), [the fault] has been explained regarding the qualities beginning with knowledge (*jñāna*) and ending with mental formations (*saṃskāra*);

for when it is accepted that the self (*ātman*), the possessor of qualities, is either distinct from or non-distinct from those qualities, one must supply the remaining portion of the argument: "this [self] is the locus of all [these qualities]. Thus ends the seventh verse.
"Even when these [attributes] exist"—this is the meaning.

If non-difference were accepted, it would follow that the Self is also impermanent, just like its impermanent attributes; consequently, there would be no distinction between the nature of the Self and those attributes such as knowledge regarding permanence or impermanence.
As a consequence,

the position that the self is inferred through those qualities by means of the relationship between quality and qualificand— which is impossible— is already refuted. [This is so] because there is no inference of a self [as a substance] in the absence of the self's own activity.
He states that memory is established from the *saṃskāra* (latent impression) and so forth—namely, "first of all" (*tāvat*). This means, for now, in the absence of doubt.

Furthermore, it is not the case that the self (*ātman*) is the substratum [of memory] because the cognition of memory is a quality (*guṇa*); for under the view of non-difference (*abheda-pakṣa*), [the self] consists of attributes (*dharma-mayatva*), and under the view of difference (*bheda-pakṣa*), there is no connection [between the self and the cognition], and thus there is no memory.

The state of being the agent of conceptualization and so forth is merely its prior form; thus, the experience free from all conceptualization (*nirvikalpa-anubhava*) alone is the innate nature of the Self, because that [nature] never departs. Since there is no purpose for a memory of a self distinct from that, and since memory is established through latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), the "rememberer" is merely a mental construct, just like the "seer."

By the two verses beginning with "nanu," direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) has been refuted; then, by the verse beginning with "athānubhavavidhvaṃsa," inference (*anumāna*) has been rejected. Furthermore, by the phrase "tato bhinneṣu," the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) has been indicated.
He states that very subverting argument as "dharmayoga" [in the sense of] the connection of qualities such as cognition (*jñāna*) and so forth with the self (*ātman*).
If a specific quality (*viśeṣa*) were to be imparted [to the self], then because it would be subject to modification, that specific quality would be impermanent like a hide;

otherwise, like space (*ākāśa*), it would be as good as non-existent. (p. 73) Now, was not the self already refuted previously? [The answer is: In the subsequent verse, its nature as consciousness (*jñāna-svarūpa*) [is established].
It is being examined. Therefore, having raised the doubt that there is no logical connection between what precedes and what follows,

[the author] intends to refute the sovereignty (*aiśvarya*)— characterized by the possession of the powers of knowledge and action— which was previously attributed to the Self (*ātman*) as the agent and knower in the statement "in the Great Lord who is one's own Self."

The definition of the nature of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) is indeed relevant to the present context; thus, reiterating the previously mentioned attribute, he states the purport of the following verse with the words "in this way" (*ittham*).
In this manner, by means of the aforementioned method through the presence of valid means of cognition consisting of perception and inference, together with the Self—
This indicates a conjunction: just as the self (*ātman*) is of the nature of consciousness (*cit-svarūpa*), so too is knowledge (*jñāna*) of the nature of consciousness;
therefore, how could that knowledge be impermanent? Why should it be impermanent? It should be eternal, just like the self.
The sense is that because there is no difference in their being of the nature of consciousness, the desired impermanence cannot be established.

One who asserts that there is knowledge distinct from the self which is impermanent should be questioned: Is the knowledge you accept of the nature of consciousness (*cit*), as in the systems of the Prābhākara school and others, or is it insentient (*jaḍa*)? In the first case, knowledge must be eternal, just like the conscious self.

In the second alternative, like a jar or other objects, it would lack the capacity to illuminate its own desired object. Having raised the dilemma as to whether the power of cognition (*jñānaśakti*) is of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*) or insentient (*jaḍa*), the refutation follows.
Even if the power of cognition is admitted to be of the nature of consciousness, if its impermanence is accepted—[the following refutation applies].

Furthermore, if [knowledge] were impermanent, there would be a mutual dependence between them; since bondage would thus be impossible, the statement that "knowledge is a quality of the self" would not hold—this is the meaning.
Now, one might object: if knowledge has the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), it would be eternal like the self; therefore, its impermanence—(94)

Anticipating the objection that the Vijñānavādin might be attempting to impose an unwanted consequence (*prasaṅga*) upon himself by his own admission, [the author] states: this imposition of a consequence is not based on what is established in our own system;
rather, it is directed at those others, such as the Vaiśeṣikas and Naiyāyikas, who maintain that the self (*ātman*) is distinct from consciousness.

Thus, an undesirable consequence is produced by him: if cognition were of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), it would follow that it is eternal, like the self; yet eternity is not accepted [for cognition]. Therefore, if its impermanence is admitted despite its being of the nature of consciousness, then it follows that the self too would be impermanent; thus, for the sake of the self’s eternity—
The power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) belongs to the Supreme; since [the Supreme] possesses both its own will and attainment, this is indeed logical.
Thus, he states that this is an application by way of a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*): "even in the case of knowledge being of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*)."

The logical consequence (*prasaṅga*) would be that [the self] possesses permanence like the Self (*ātman*). Its opposite, however, is impermanence; thus, in this reversal of the consequence, even if it were of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), it would be accepted as impermanent, whereas the Self is permanent.

(74) "If knowledge were eternal, it would lack causal efficacy (*śakti*); this is the gain for the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvavādin*). [Objection: "But does it not follow as a logical consequence (*prasaṅga*) that it would be eternal like the Self (*ātman*)? [Response: Since the consequence has been established, and since even the opponent possesses the gain [of the argument], the very admission of the opponent is demonstrated therein. Thus says the proponent of the Self (*ātmavādin*).

In order to establish the impermanence of the self—which he will later declare to be permanent—he states that time is the instrumental cause for its opposite, impermanence, with the word "here" (*iha*). Time (*kāla*) is so called because it "measures" (*kalayati*), that is, it delimits an entity by means of its own form. This [entity] is "being" (*bhāva*); it is "this-ness" (*idantā*).

For one who is attached to that [object] and for whom a jar or the like is being referred to as "this" by the cognizer, there is this distinction: [the object is qualified] as "belonging to that time" or "belonging to now"; thus, by qualifying that entity with that specific time—such as the present—it undergoes limitation (*saṃkoca*).
By causing the non-entry of one's own time [into others], it renders them impermanent. By this, it is stated that time alone is the cause of the impermanence of all entities.
To the question, "What follows from this in the present context?", he says: "of the Self" and "consciousness. (95)
Since I am of the nature of light, how could there not be a state of being qualified for the Self? To this he says:
"By the qualifier," and so forth. In cases such as "this is a blue lotus," one might think that "this is the blue" is the qualifier and "this is the lotus" is the qualified;
however, it is not those two themselves that connect them, but rather some cognizer distinct from both who performs that conjunction.

[The two] understand their own relationship as qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyabhāva*). Therefore, if the Self were the qualified object, some further unifier would have to be required for that purpose. To the objection, "Let it be so," he replies: "And not [so]" (*na ca*). If another unifier were required, its self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) would be lost, and there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Thus...

Because there is no other unifier [to connect the moments], and because there is no state of being a qualified object [of cognition], and because there is no delimitation by time, impermanence is self-evident; such is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the proponents of the Self (*ātmavādin*).
Having thus stated the permanence of the Self according to the opponent's own admission, [the author proceeds] by means of that same illustration.
He brings this [objection] against knowledge as well—“it is thus.

We ask: is the knowledge that constitutes an attribute (*dharma*) of the self, which is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), itself self-luminous or not? Regarding the first case, he states the flaw: “knowledge,” etc.

Even in that case, regarding cognition (*jñāna*), since its nature is consciousness (*cit-svabhāvatva*), if there is no manifestation as "this," then the argument stated by the proponent of eternality is merely a triviality; nothing more need be said. [Otherwise] cognition would be eternal just like the Self (*ātman*).
To the objection, "Let both be eternal; what is the fault? he says: "And not... [because they are] two eternal things.

One should not say, "Let there be no relation," because the relation of cause and effect is impossible and because, according to your own view, there exists no relation distinct from those two; thus he says:
"tat" (that). Due to the absence of a relation, the genitive case is used in the sense of a relation [to express] the absence of a relation.
This is logical. Therefore, this view, being untenable, is rejected. Having restated the second position, he states its defect with the words "atha" (now/if).
If it does not manifest its own nature, then it certainly cannot manifest that which is distinct from itself.
The author [explains] that consciousness is thus luminous, stating: "self-luminous" (*svaprakāśa*).

By effecting the cognition of itself—which is of the nature of light—it imparts its own luminosity to another, thereby becoming the luminosity of that other as well, unlike other entities such as a jar.

(96) Just as an insentient object, such as a jar, being dependent on something else for its manifestation and thus incapable of manifesting itself, is all the more incapable of manifesting another thing such as a cloth; in the same way, if cognition were insentient in nature, it could not manifest its own object. Therefore, it must possess self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*).

Because of the consequence that [knowledge] would be eternal like the self, there would be no mutual relationship; and because it is insentient, it lacks the capacity to illuminate objects, and thus knowledge itself would be non-existent. In either case, knowledge is not a power of the self, since the self does not exist by its own nature apart from knowledge.

Even though [the soul] exists, because there is no mutual relationship and because it lacks that capacity, it has been stated by you that it is rightly called the "Self-Lord" (Ātmeśvara) due to its connection with that capacity; this is what is meant.
Even if knowledge is insentient according to the Sāṅkhya school...

The meaning of the intent of the following verse is stated as follows: "Even though [the intellect] is insentient... This addresses the objection raised against the position of insentience—that the manifestation of objects could only occur through the reception of a reflection in consciousness—and thus offers a rebuttal.
"In this way" means by the method that is about to be described. "This cognition" refers to the intellect (*buddhi*), which is the very nature of the object.

Just as it assumes [a form], so too does it bear the reflection of the consciousness of the Self. Precisely because it bears the reflection of consciousness, its insentience and other such qualities are established; thus, the nature of cognition, which is distinct from those [qualities], is superimposed upon the intellect by means of reflection, thereby [establishing] the object.

Having stated the worldly convention to establish the example of "illumination," he says "here" (*iha*) to show that the illumination of an object is not devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) while being independent of anything else. Here— in the intellect (*buddhi*)— is the reflection (*pratibimba*).

When there is an approach by means of form (*rūpa*), the worldly conventions such as "I know the jar" or "the jar appears to me" become logically possible; however, this is not the case for an object that lacks [such] form. Furthermore, if the form of a jar or similar object were itself of the nature of luminosity (*prakāśa*), it would follow that it is visible to the eye (*cākṣuṣa*).

Otherwise, in the absence of cognizers who apprehend the jar and so forth, it would follow that even those other than them would have its manifestation; or else, it would either manifest to those others or not manifest to them at all. Since no distinction between manifestation and non-manifestation is possible for light itself, it would result in everyone being omniscient.

It would be characterized by ignorance. For one who has the conjunction of the eyes and other senses, there would be no distinction such that luminosity exists only with respect to him, while it is non-luminous with respect to others.
Therefore, the meaning is that luminosity is not its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). From the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*)... [text fragment]
It is not even slightly less [inconsistently] to say that this very form has arrived at the object;

for even if one accepts that it has arrived from something else, since manifestation is dependent upon the object, there would be no distinction between manifestation and non-manifestation with respect to specific subjects. Thus, this alone...

There is a fault. Therefore, because it is one's own essential nature (*nijasvarūpa*) and because of its existence, this property called "manifestation" (*prakāśa*) must be accepted as the very nature of that reality (*tattva*), whichever one it may be.
Even if it were a property of something else, when the question arises as to how there could be manifestation of an object—
In whichever particular reality (tattva-viśeṣa) that [object]— such as a jar or a cloth— is located, its cause of production,
such as earth and so forth, and its subordinate qualities, such as odor and so forth,
enter [the consciousness] by way of the sense organs through reflection, like [an image] upon the surface of a mirror. In that other reality...
"It is certainly determined that the manifestation of that object occurs. Regarding how the object enters [the mind] by means of a reflection within that specific reality, he says: "That" (tat).
Because of the predominance of *sattva*, which is of the nature of light (*prakāśa*), it is capable of receiving the reflection of the mental construct (*saṃkalpa*).

To the objection that there would then follow the perception of everything at all times, he says: "By darkness" (*tamasa*). Because it is enveloped by darkness, which is of the nature of non-luminosity, it perceives only the reflection of the *sakala* (the manifest).
Due to the predominance of the quality of *sattva*, there is the capacity for the apprehension of the *sakala*; however, due to the predominance of the quality of *tamas*, this does not occur.

The capacity for apprehending only a portion [of objects] arises from the association with the quality of *rajas*. Apart from universal apprehension and being the grasper of all—which result from the association with the quality of *sattva*—there occurs the state of being a grasper of only a portion due to its intermediate position;
this is the meaning of the phrase "the three qualities. Nevertheless, the intellect (*buddhi*) assumes the form of the object.
Regarding how his own established doctrine [is formulated], he says: "That very... [tadeva]. Now, one might ask:
"How can there be knowledge of an object through the apprehension of a reflection? To this he replies: "The object... [artha].
The knowledge consisting of the modification (vṛtti) of this intellect is the jar and so forth residing within its own self.

When the intellect (*buddhi*)—which is essentially the grasping of a reflection—takes on the form of an object such as a jar as a reflection within itself and functions in that very form, it is then called "the cognition of that jar" and so forth. This functioning is a transformation into that form; and regarding this transformation:

Regarding the objection that there would be a loss of the form of the intellect (*buddhi*), he says "the previous," etc. "Previous designation" refers to conventional usage such as "milk" and so forth. In the statement "the milk has been measured" (98), [one might think] there is a sweet substance-form, a sour substance-form, a liquid form, or a solid form, according to the principle to be explained hereafter.

The cause, having cast off its designation as milk and so forth, transforms into a state distinct from it due to its modification into curds and so forth. This "modification" (*pariṇāma*) consists in the assumption of a different designation without abandoning the previous form's designation. In this context, [the transformation] of the intellect (*buddhi*) into a jar and so forth—

The meaning is that the transformation consisting of cognition whose nature is the apprehension of a reflection does not obscure the designation of the intellect (*buddhi*) as being of the nature of its cause. "In this way" means by the aforementioned method, because of the predominance of *sattva*, which possesses a slight degree of luminosity. If that is so, then it is the intellect alone [that acts].
Because its nature is luminosity (*prakāśa*), there is no self other than that; to the objection that "there is no self other than this," he says: "And this...

Since sattva and the other guṇas are objects of experience by virtue of their being pleasure and so forth, the intellect (*buddhi*), which consists of sattva and the rest, is also included within the experienced, which is indeed insentient (*jaḍa*). Thus, it is precisely the mirror of this insentient principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*) [that reflects the Self].

Although the intellect (*buddhi*) possesses the nature of *dṛśya* (the object of seeing), just as a mirror— which is insentient— possesses the capacity to receive reflections, it is not logical for it to have a nature consisting of the manifestation of a subject (*bhoktṛ*) that is opposed to its own character, because it is an object of experience (*bhogya*) and lacks luminosity (*aprakāśatva*). Therefore, there must be a subject distinct from itself.

It follows that there exists someone; he is the enjoyer, whose essential nature is nothing but self-luminosity. Whatever is asserted by others to be his essential nature as something distinct from this self-luminous form is entirely non-luminous and of the nature of an object of enjoyment (*bhogya*). It does not exist as the essential nature of the enjoyer.
The meaning is that one need not postulate another intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) because it is logically possible [otherwise]. As for the phrase "if he":

if he were the illuminator of the entire universe—from primordial nature (*prakṛti*) down to the earth—by his own nature alone, without casting his own reflection into the intellect (*buddhi*), then, since he is of the nature of light, he would always...

If [the world] were manifested as a single entity, then— since there would be no other cause for manifestation in the sequence of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the great principle (*mahat*), the ego-principle (*ahaṃkāra*), and so forth— the entire universe would necessarily be manifested all at once. Consequently, because there would be no mutual distinction in the manifestation of jars and other objects, such that one could say "this is a jar" and "this is a cloth," [there would be no differentiation between] jars and the like.

The sublation [of the opponent's view] is shown as follows: if it were accepted that the Self is the illuminator of the universe, then there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasajyeta*) of a confusion (*sāṃkarya*) consisting of the mutual intermingling of the entire universe, such as the performance of purposeful actions like fetching water for the sake of what is to be accomplished.
Thus, having first [presented] the refutation regarding the Self’s status as the illuminator of the universe... [the text continues with the argument concerning] the universe.

Having demonstrated the subverting argument characterized by the confusion [of categories], it is now shown that because this [consciousness] lacks a relationship with that universe, its capacity to illuminate the universe is simply impossible—
(99)— [arising] from the object such as blue, which exists in the form of a reflection within the intellect, distinct from the physical sense organs.

How could that which is distinct from both the reflection and the intellect-principle (buddhitattva), which serves as the substratum for that reflection, be the illuminator of the object? For the scripture states, "This Puruṣa is indeed unattached"; thus, it is by means of the manifestation of the Puruṣa, whose nature is unattached, that [the object is known].

He states the established conclusion: "Therefore" (tasmāt). Since it is not possible for the *puruṣa* to illuminate objects while being self-luminous, therefore it is *buddhi* alone—due to its clarity resulting from the predominance of *sattva*—that [illuminates] objects as if they were reflections of light.

It also receives a reflection. To the question of how the worldly convention—established by the common experience that an object is manifested merely through the reception of the reflections of the intellect (*buddhi*), the object, and consciousness (*caitanya*)—is established, he says: "From that" (*tataḥ*). This is because both the object and consciousness receive a reflection.

Therefore, because that consciousness— which is the reflection of sentience— undergoes the transfer of the blue and so forth existing as the original object (bimba) by means of the transfer of the reflection into it, the linguistic usage "I know this blue" or "the blue manifests to me" is established. [This is] manifestation.
By virtue of the apprehension of the reflection, even though the principle of the intellect (*buddhitattva*) is inherently insentient, it becomes permeated by light; thus,
through the superimposition of blue and other objects, and by means of that reflection,
the permeation by light is transmitted all the way to the external object— such as the blue thing— which serves as the original prototype (*bimba*) that presents itself.

The Sāṃkhya concludes his established position with the words "tadevam" (thus, therefore). Since the principle of *buddhi* (intellect) receives the reflection of consciousness (*caitanya*) just as it does the reflection of an object, its capacity to manifest objects occurs in the manner just described—
namely, by way of being a transformation of the insentient *buddhi*.

Because it is distinct [from consciousness], the mental modification (*buddhivṛtti*), though itself insentient, becomes the illuminator of the object through its connection with the reflection of the consciousness residing in the intellect (*buddhi*) which is distinct from itself.
Even so, how can that which is insentient have the capacity to illuminate an object?

Thus, the refutation of the faults alleged by the Vijñānavādin is to be considered insufficient from the perspective of the Sāṃkhya. To state that the word "atha" (now/then) in the Sūtra indicates a lack of conviction arising from the emergence of logical inconsistencies within this Sāṃkhya system, he states the inconsistency: (100) "etadeva... [and] "prakāśātmā pumān."

That the intellect-principle (*buddhitattva*), which is bound by nature, should project its own reflection as the Self—this alone is initially improper. Having provisionally accepted this, the fault will be stated later; it is with reference to that [later critique] that the word "firstly" (*tāvat*) is employed here.

He states the reason for the impropriety: "having qualities equal to its own. Here he provides an illustration: just as a beautiful form is seen as a reflection of an object such as a jar in a spotless mirror—which possesses qualities equal to those of the object and is clear with respect to the jar and so forth—so it is in this case.

It must be stated that the self casts its reflection upon the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*), which is pure and possesses qualities equal to those of the self in relation to itself. To the objection that this is not the case, he says: "The self," etc.
Because the self consists of the nature of consciousness (*cit*) while the intellect is insentient (*jaḍa*), there is a contradiction between the sentient and the insentient.
Because it possesses a nature opposed to light, because it lacks the quality of equanimity (*sattva*), because the intellect (*buddhi*) is veiled by darkness (*tamas*),
because the Self (*ātman*) is not so veiled, and because it lacks the purity relative to the Self which serves as the original image (*bimba*).
(p. 79) That the intellect (buddhi) lacks the capacity to reflect the Self is indeed untenable;

this is what was stated by the Sāṃkhya. [The author’s] lack of approval is that one might first grant that consciousness (caitanya) is reflected in the intellect. Nevertheless, even while provisionally accepting this for the sake of argument (prauḍhyā), the refutation is now stated; such is the meaning.

He indicates this with the word "matha" (it implies). To the objection that "if even what is improper is accepted out of boldness, our desired goal will be achieved," he replies with the words "But what [of it]? (*kiṃ tu*). The word "atha" indicates a statement of censure, meaning "let it be so for now. Then, by the remainder of the aphorism, it is stated that the previously mentioned fault is indeed impossible to avoid.

He shows the intended meaning with the words "But rather" (kiṃ tu). The meaning of the word "but rather" is: "Even if we were to accept this as improper, we shall state a specific distinction such that what you desire does not succeed. It is not only by means of [the arguments concerning] causes and so forth that our stated refutation is not [established].
Even by means of the theory of reflection (pratibimbavāda), which is favored by you, this has been somewhat resolved.

In this way, she (the intellect) would be non-inert. For if there were inertness, there would be no manifestation of objects; yet, since it is accepted that the intellect—due to its transparency—receives the reflection of consciousness (caitanya), that reflection...

Consciousness (*caitanya*) is either of the nature of primary illumination (*prakāśa*). (101) If it is of the nature of primary illumination, then that intellect (*buddhi*), possessing primary consciousness, would likewise be pure and of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpinī*), just like the conscious self (*cid-ātman*).
In that case, your own position that "the intellect is insentient" (*jaḍā*) would not hold. [It would become sentient] by virtue of receiving the reflection of the self, just like the self itself.

Since one's own self is also composed of consciousness (*cinmaya*), it would be non-inert and, like the Self, eternal; however, the Self would likewise not be eternal. If both were eternal, there could be no mutual relationship between them. If, on the other hand, that [consciousness] were of the nature of a secondary light, then the intellect (*buddhi*) caused by it would necessarily be non-eternal.

The very same fault already stated—that an object does not shine forth as something distinct from its own nature—would recur once again. Furthermore, if there were the apprehension of a reflection of the object, then by means of that apprehension of the object's reflection, it would follow that consciousness consists of the object itself;
thus, there would be a lapse into the doctrine of Vijñānavāda, resulting in a contradiction with one's own established tenets (apasiddhānta). This is the meaning of the remainder of the Sūtra.

In the position that the person (*puruṣa*) is of the nature of light (*prakāśātmā*), there arises the doubt as to whether the consciousness reflected in the intellect (*buddhi*) is of the nature of primary light or not. Intending to state that it is not of the nature of primary light—arguing that [if it were], it would follow that one's own cognition is established [as the self]—he says: "it is not of the nature of primary light."

The refutation of the second position: first, the claim that "the object is manifested by its own dullness" is explained as follows—because the original object (*bimba*) is not seen to perform its well-known purposeful action while maintaining its status as an original object, it cannot maintain the reflection of consciousness (*caitanya-pratibimba*). (The original object [cannot maintain the reflection]).

It should be understood that since no causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) corresponding to the well-known [external] object is observed, there arises an opportunity for the following dilemma: whether the illumination of an object by the intellect— which consists of the reflection of consciousness— is itself the primary form of illumination, or something else.
If it is admitted that there is a connection between the intellect (*buddhi*) and the reflection of consciousness (*caitanya*),
then the reflection residing in the intellect— just like the consciousness which serves as the original object (*bimba*)—
would not possess the nature of primary illumination. If that is so, then...

By means of that non-primary form of illumination—the reflection of consciousness residing in the intellect—nothing at all would be accomplished toward the intellect's manifestation of objects. You have stated that even by bearing the reflection of consciousness, the intellect possesses the capacity to manifest objects; yet, as for that reflection...

Because it lacks the nature of being a primary illuminator, if consciousness were to possess only a secondary form of illumination, the intellect would be unable to illuminate objects. He demonstrates this very point through an analogy: "For not... and so forth.
This very point is established by means of an *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroborative illustration): "For not...
[etc.]. Because that which is reflected—the form of fire—is not a real entity, the meaning is that just as it is perceived, so it is in the case at hand as well.

Having raised the first position, he says "atha mukhena" in order to explain the root text beginning with "ajaḍa," which demonstrates an undesirable consequence for the opponent in that regard: "If it is held that the reflection of consciousness in the intellect is itself of the nature of primary luminosity, then... [the opponent's view leads to the following].
Apart from the intellect which has become the substratum,
nothing exists; just as in the reflection of a mirror, a variegated array of cities, villages, and so forth appears as undivided,
yet it does not appear as distinct from one another nor even from the mirror itself.

As it has been stated, although a mirror and the like, by virtue of their nature of extreme transparency, do indeed receive a reflection, that reflected object exists merely as a presence apart from its own substratum—the mirror and so forth; yet in reality, there is no actual separation. And just as this is so in that case, it is likewise with consciousness.

If the reflection were of the nature of the primary light (*prakāśa*), then the intellect (*buddhi*) which perceives it— being non-different from it— would also necessarily be of the nature of the primary light; for this reason, according to our own system, since the intellect is established as being insentient (*jaḍa*),
its being of the nature of primary consciousness (*cit*) is impossible, and thus the object of enjoyment would not be light.
The occurrence of a nature consisting of the manifestation of a subject that is opposed to that [object] is not logically tenable;

for, according to the reasoning previously stated, there can be no superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the contradictory—the insentient and the conscious—within a single entity such as the intellect (*buddhi*). This is because, due to the defect of superimposing contradictory attributes, both parties would be at fault.
In order to avoid that very fault, the Sāṃkhyas argue that because contradictory properties would otherwise follow—

since it is contradictory for the *buddhi*-principle, which is the object of experience, to possess the nature of an experiencer, and for that [Puruṣa], whose nature is luminosity, to possess the nature of luminosity [again]— therefore, the states of being an object of experience and being an experiencer must be non-luminous in nature.

If one were to accept that the intellect (*buddhi*) is the self, there would result the defect characterized by superimposition (*adhyāsa*)—the coexistence in a single locus of "luminosity" and "form," which are mutually contradictory. This follows from such a superimposition of contradictory attributes.
Furthermore, if one were to accept that impermanent cognition (*jñāna*) is of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), [there would be further difficulties].

There would follow the consequence of [the self] being eternal like the self. For, there would be the superimposition of the attribute of eternity—which is contradictory to it—upon a cognition whose nature is consciousness and which is impermanent; or, there would be the superimposition of the attribute of impermanence—which is contradictory to it—upon a self whose nature is consciousness and which is eternal. Thus, because of the superimposition of contradictory attributes. Furthermore:

This was said by you, who are afraid of error, for the sake of avoiding it. "In this way" means that even though the intellect (*buddhi*) is insentient (*jaḍa*), its capacity to illuminate objects is asserted to arise from the conjunction with the reflection of consciousness (*cit-pratibimba*).
This was stated without investigation, out of fear; however, it is not logically tenable according to your own principles.

Furthermore, that very same fault— which you yourself have just now stated in your own words— is now fallen upon you once again with even greater force than before: namely, the superimposition of contradictory attributes (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*),
by way of [positing] consciousness (*caitanya*) as the primary form of light (*prakāśa*) being the substratum for the reflection.

The meaning is that since you yourselves have stated that the nature of cognition (*buddhi*) is primarily luminosity (*prakāśa*), these two contradictory properties— insentience (*jaḍatva*) and the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpatva*)— have nonetheless once again fallen upon this very cognition.

"In that case, let the intellect not be insentient; let it be of the nature of primary luminosity itself—what is the fault? To this, he says: "And therefore," etc. Since consciousness, being of the nature of primary luminosity, is non-different from its reflection, the intellect also must be of the nature of primary luminosity; and for that reason...
That very intellect, which you maintain to be insentient, must itself be composed of consciousness (*cinmayī*).

He asks "What? to exclude [any other possibility] by means of the particle *eva*. Having postulated the insentiency of the intellect, what is the use of a postulated Self (*ātman*) distinct from it—an enjoyer whose nature is luminosity—[expressing thoughts such as] "I know this" and so forth?

For the functioning of worldly transactions, the intellect consisting of consciousness alone is sufficient; for that purpose, a self need not be postulated. [Objection: If the self were established as distinct from the intellect, then the Vijñānavāda position—that the intellect is the self—would be reached. [Response: This is not so, for even then, an object is admitted as distinct from the intellect.

To the objection that [this] is not the doctrine of consciousness (*vijñānavāda*) because of its causal nature, he says: "In this way. Just as the intellect (*buddhi*) consists of consciousness because it bears the reflection of consciousness, so too, by bearing the reflection of objects, it would likewise consist of objects; this must also be understood.

To the question—"What is the answer to the doubt: 'If, by the force of your own statement alone, one does not admit [the existence of] two things distinct from cognition (buddhi), how could the nature of being composed of consciousness (cinmayatva) and being composed of objects (arthamayatva) be established in the Vijñānavāda?'"—he says "From what? because cognition is momentary.
Since the preceding moments— which serve as the respective causes—

possess both the nature of consciousness (*cinmaya*) and the nature of materiality (*arthamaya*), it must be stated in response that the intellect (*buddhi*) assumes that form through the succession of prior causes; thus, [the world] is composed of materiality (*maya*).

The sense is that since the theory of the reflection of an object (*bimbapratibimbavāda*) is not to be accepted, the Vijñānavāda alone remains tenable. ... [the word] "thus" (*evam*). That very cognition (*buddhi*), being primarily of the nature of light, is as before; and thus it is knowledge (*jñāna*).

It has been stated that the nature of consciousness (*cit-svarūpa*) is [self-luminous]; thus, what was previously mentioned—that the reversal of the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga-viparyaya*) will be obtained—is now established. He states the purport of these two verses in brief with the word "evam" (thus). Now, [it may be asked]: is it not twofold?

[Knowledge] is both conceptual (*savikalpaka*) and non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*). Since that twofold knowledge is not a power belonging to the knowing self (*ātman*), and because the self exists in the manner already described, there is only knowledge itself. Having thus examined knowledge, he now examines action (*kriyā*): "Furthermore—"

Regarding the [objection] that "knowledge of the self arises through sound," he says: because, according to the principle to be explained, that [knowledge] does not exist by itself, there is no action of the body either;
and by the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), this also applies to objects such as milk. [This occurs] in various places—such as in a house or outside it on its courtyard.
Outside of that, in areas such as the pathways and so forth, there is the first [period] at the time of morning, followed by midday, and subsequently the evening,
and so on— this refers to the time. By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), one includes the state of having arisen in the form of curd and so forth,
the fact of its having arisen, and its presence in various locations, as well as the distinctness of the body and other such things from their respective locations.
There is no such thing as an action (*kriyā*). This is because that action is not perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) nor through inference (*anumāna*) following upon it.
In this world, what appears within the range of cognition is only in the form of "going," "moving," "turning," and so forth.

Regarding that which has become an object of the means of valid cognition (pratyakṣa-pramāṇa) in the form of motion— such as the movement of going and so forth— it is perceived that Devadatta, who was previously staying at home,
exists in a body accompanied by Devadatta in an external location immediately after his body [has left]. This much is apprehended.
It is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). We do not recognize, nor do we see, any action whatsoever other than the body of Devadatta situated in an external location.
Therefore, like the body of Devadatta, it [the action] possesses a gross form characterized by qualities such as blue, long, and so forth.

In the common usage "Devadatta remains for a day because he is not seen," Devadatta’s body appears as having been occupied by the time of dawn previously, and subsequently occupied by the time of midday, and so forth. Even here, there is no action apart from Devadatta’s body being occupied by those respective times.
Something is indeed perceived. In the statement "the milk transforms," during that transformation, the milk appears as having a sweet form, an acidic form, a liquid form, a solid form, and so forth.
Even there, apart from the curds and other products characterized by acidity and solidity, no action consisting of transformation exists.

A body is seen. Thus, by virtue of being located in such-and-such a place, by virtue of being situated in such-and-such a place, by virtue of being occupied by such-and-such a time, and by virtue of having such-and-such a form of transformation, it is the entity itself that appears. This is because each preceding form is occupied by time.
Even in the case of destruction, that very body which previously went into the house is this same one now standing in the courtyard;
that which was pervaded by the time of dawn is this same one pervaded by the time of midday;
and that object which previously existed in the form of milk is this very same thing transformed into the form of curd and so forth.

Recognition (*pratyabhijñā*): The meaning is that the recognition which occurs regarding hair, nails, and so forth—wherein each successive form has been replaced by a preceding form—is the very recognition that "this is that same time," "this is that same hair," or "this is that same nail"; it is merely a form of error (*bhrānti*).

When there is a difference in location, and given that there is a difference in time and form, and that they possess reciprocal forms, a difference in time is necessarily entailed; for in the absence of a difference in time, there would likewise be no difference between those two. Thus, when the mutual distinctness of space and time is accepted, [the following ensues].

Since the form (*ākāra*) alone constitutes place, when there is a difference in time, the form itself becomes different; thus, place, time, and form ultimately resolve into the form alone, resolving within the nature of the form itself. Therefore, it is not necessary to say "born in such-and-such a place"; that much alone is sufficient. Nevertheless, from the perspective of gross observation, they maintain that there is a distinction.

The Master has employed such phrases as "the Buddhists assert that [entities] are distinct and separate precisely through the differences of place, time, and form. Thus, in the case of direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*), no action is observed in any particular place, at any particular time, or in any particular form.

Because there is an absence of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The meaning is that it is not seen even by inference (*anumāna*) which is preceded by that direct perception. If it is argued that no such action exists, [the response is: for Devadatta who is going, there is the attainment of the village and so forth; however, the subsequent effect, which consists of his own successive moments, is the object located in space.

Since there is no such thing as an effect that exists apart from the nature of objects such as a jar— which is their very own form— that activity (*kriyā*) cannot be postulated even on the grounds of the inexplicability of the effect otherwise (*kāryānyathānupapatti*). Furthermore, it has been stated that there is an absence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), namely perception and inference, which could establish that activity, because such an activity is not observed.
He states a further refutation with the remainder of the sūtra: "It does not become one. [If it were] something, it would not be successive. It is not appropriate for a single cognizer.
Furthermore, it does not become one by virtue of having a single cognizer as its locus, because that [cognizer] is also conceived as being one.
Because the mother is manifold due to being occupied by various places, times, and forms—
[this jar was born previously, this jar was born later, this jar...]

"This jar is situated in the eastern region" and "it is situated in the northern region"— such states of being prior and posterior belong to those moments of the jar and so forth only through the synthesis of the cognizer’s conceptualizing intellect (*vikalpabuddhi*),
because their own essential nature (*svarūpa*) was previously [devoid of such qualities]; thus, that object possesses qualities such as priority and so on.

Because they lack the state of being fixed [in a single moment], their essential nature—which is merely the object graspable by the eye and other senses—is not touched by the entity such as a jar, whose characteristic is action: namely, a sequence consisting of a succession of prior and posterior states animated by the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of the cognizer. This is because of that [action].

The cognizer of an entity that possesses priority and posteriority cannot be mutually permeated by each other’s essential nature; therefore, how could there be a single action related to them? For succession is pervaded by mutual difference, and that [succession] is absent in an undivided entity.

Because there is no sequence of prior and subsequent [moments] constructed by the cognizer (*pramātṛ*), if [the object] were divided, the unity of that division would be lost; thus it would follow that it is one. Because it abides within a single cognizer, even though it is manifold, it is treated as one in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).
No substratum distinct from the momentary characteristics of Devadatta is experienced by anyone.

The body and so forth of Devadatta appear as a continuous succession of moments; because they are pervaded by time, they appear as distinct and diverse. Furthermore, [this is so] because of the unity of the continuum...

He says that there is something else as well which indicates [the existence of] a real entity (bhāva), beginning with the words "Furthermore" (*kiñca*): how could Devadatta’s body be one, if it were permeated by moments (*kṣaṇa*)—which are intended to be actions—that are of such a nature as to have different locations, times, and forms? For in every moment, its...

Because it possesses a different form [at each moment], and precisely because the substrate lacks oneness, the recognition that arises from a semblance— which is of the nature of an error— due to the thought "He who departed from the city is this very same person who has reached the village," [is the recognition] "This is that very Devadatta."
It is capable of establishing actual identity;

for, in the manner thus described, because it is occupied with the perception of differences between successive similar states, the "I" [is perceived] as similar to the subsequent and prior pots, cloths, and so forth, within the scope of cognition.

There exists only knowledge whose nature consists in the apprehension of entities. Since such knowledge is not a power belonging to the self—according to the principle stated [previously] because of its non-existence as an entity—the action [of that knowledge] arises from the self itself. Furthermore, because it is an entity, that [action] also is not a power belonging to the self.

Having examined knowledge and action along with the self, [one should consider] that relationship between knowledge and action, in the presence of which those two— knowledge and action— are capable of establishing sovereignty in the form of omniscience and omnipotence; that very relationship...
To refute that [position], the proponent first states the absence of valid means of knowledge regarding its object:

when a thing exists in the form of a lump of clay, a bundle of grass, a palanquin, and so forth, or likewise in the form of fire, a seed, and so forth, it arises through the sequence of a jar, a sprout, smoke, and so on; thus, each of those is produced.

Nothing other than what is perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is seen; thus, among objects such as a lump of clay and the like, no entity whatsoever—distinct from each respective object and consisting of a mutual relationship between them—is observed through direct perception. Just as action (*kriyā*) is not seen through either direct perception or inference (*anumāna*).

Likewise, even by means of inference, no entity called "relation" is perceived; for there is no relation other than that of cause and effect. Thus, the existence of the sprout immediately following the seed [is established].

Only the momentary states of the lump of clay are perceived; apart from these momentary states of the lump of clay and so forth, no additional entity called "relation" is perceived by the means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). It must be stated that even by means of inference (*anumāna*), there is no relation, just as there is no action. (108)

This same path applies even in the absence of a stream [of causal succession], as in the case of "there is smoke when there is fire. The Vijñānavādin states the nature of the cause-and-effect relationship according to his own doctrine: "After two things, such as a basin and a jujube fruit, which previously existed separately, have come together due to the force of wind's impulsion..."

When the jujube fruit has fallen into the pit, there arises the manifestation of the jujube as qualified by the pit with which it is inseparable. This entity, the jujube, is invariably concomitant with another entity, the pit, through a relation of priority and posteriority; thus, immediately after the moments of the distinct forms of the pit and the jujube, that which is inseparable [arises].

The causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is said to be that which is conventionally designated by the cognizer’s conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) as "the production of jujube fruits characterized by a bowl. Regarding this prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*),
he refers back to what has already been introduced with the words "If not," and so forth, [and] regarding the mutual [relationship] between self-cognition and action...

He demonstrates the very nature of the causal relationship [between them] with the words beginning "If not" (*na cet*). And he demonstrates that between self-knowledge (*ātmajñāna*) and action (*kriyā*) there is indeed a mutual causal relationship with the words beginning "If not.
In the world, regarding the self—which is considered to be the agent—and knowledge—which is considered to be the cause—[he shows their relationship].

Anticipating the objection that "in that case, let knowledge be the effect of the self," he states that even this is not so: because knowledge is the effect of its own causal complex consisting of the contact between the object and the sense organ, and because action itself is inherently non-existent, [knowledge] cannot be the cause of the self.
Since there is no connection of action with the self, through which connection its status as knower and agent might arise; having thus refuted the means of proof (*pramāṇa*) for such a connection,
he demonstrates it by way of its own specific characteristics:

By the statement, "Because that which resides in two related entities lacks a single uniform nature precisely due to its residing in two related entities," all [objections regarding] relation have been refuted.
If the jar were already established prior [to its production], it would have no dependence on clay and so forth. Of that—

If it is argued that a pot is unestablished precisely because it is [already] established, then all the more there is no dependence on anything else. Because it is non-existent, for that which is established, dependence on another and so forth has been ruled out.
By the word "and so forth" (ādi), [is meant] the mutual form of two things being established, such as a king and his servant.

Even a relationship characterized by conjunction does not exist in the case of non-existence, as in the example "the woman with breasts" (109); for how could two things that do not exist conjoin? This is because the oneness of two [non-existent] things is untenable. Alternatively, even if there were oneness, a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) has been established regarding the relationship, such as the "wave. [Furthermore,] between the two related entities, there is mutual...

The definition of that [inherence] is as follows: when two related entities possess mutual inherence, there exists a single relation in the form of their own nature; and how can that single relation abide in both places?

It would be so. That relation whose entire nature rests upon one related entity cannot rest upon another related entity. If that same relation were to rest upon another related entity as well, it would follow that there is a difference in its essential nature (*svarūpa-bheda*).
Because the true nature of a relation would result in a twofold [ontological] consequence, if it were to rest in both [relata], then—
since this would entail a difference in their essential natures— there would be no such thing as a "relation" existing apart from the two related entities. Thus,
cognition which consists of firm experience is non-inert knowledge.

It is distinguished from objects of knowledge such as jars and cloths. The reason for this is that, because cognition has the singular nature of self-luminosity (*svaprakāśa*), jars, cloths, and the like are insentient (*jaḍa*). Since illumination belongs to sentient beings, by way of conceiving the opposite of the sentient within the sentient, the insentient is [defined] as that which is dependent upon the sentient.

Dependence regarding fields, wealth, and so forth; the dependence of the insentient upon the sentient—regarding that relationship which is conventionally designated, there is no mutual dependence between the sentient and the insentient, because it is precisely due to their being established [as independent]. As for an unestablished entity, there is none.
[The dependence] is even less [possible]. Because it is unestablished (*asiddhatva*), that which lacks its own nature (*niḥsvarūpa*) cannot be subject to dependence (*pāratantrya*).

For an established entity (*siddha-vastu*), there is no relation consisting of mutual expectation; this is because it is already established. For an unestablished entity, it is even less so. He states the purpose of including the word "etc. (*ādi*): how [could there be dependence] in the two forms consisting of the king and the servant?

Regarding the two who embrace: since it is impossible for two persons to be one, what kind of embrace could there be if two forms were to become one? For both would then possess a single nature. He explains this very point:
[the self] is imagined as having the nature of a knower through its connection with cognition and so forth, but this is not the ultimate reality.
"Because it is connected with such an action, the object consisting of an agent is not the ultimate reality. This is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).
(110) Thus ends the second chapter in the *Pratyabhijñāvimarśinī* commentary.
It is finished.
Now begins the third chapter (*āhnika*).

Regarding what was stated—that non-duality is subsumed within the position of the subsequent [view]—that is the subsumption of non-duality within the position of the subsequent view. Starting from this chapter, by which Self, namely Śiva, all [things] exist without exception...
Views consisting of experience, conceptualization, recollection, synthesis, and so forth, as well as cognitions,
would not exist at all without an experiencer, a conceptualizer, a rememberer, a synthesizer, and so on;
for even though they are capable of illuminating their respective objects, they do not attain their own initial existence [without such a subject].

They exist. "Without having set" means that because they are conditioned by place, time, and form (p. 87), they are pervasive—[we] praise Śiva, who is the nature of the light of the perfect "I. When it is stated that accomplishment arises from memory through the mere presence of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), [it is as follows].

In order to refute that which was stated in the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), there are these seven verses. Regarding the refutation of action (*kriyā*) and relation (*sambandha*)— namely, [the arguments] "action also [is not established] because of the object" and so forth, as well as "it remains in each respective case"— the removal of that refutation of action and relation is presented in the three verses beginning with "it remains in each respective case."

This will appear in the second chapter on Action (*kriyādhikāra*). Here, in this very chapter on Knowledge (*jñānādhikāra*), the refutation of the object of the power of knowledge is extracted. By means of two verses beginning with "Knowledge is of the nature of consciousness" (*jñānaṃ citsvarūpam*), the opponent—the Buddhist—[asserts] that knowledge is distinct from the self, [and so forth], as do the Sāṃkhya and others.
The author’s intended refutation is one that has already been rejected by [the opponent’s] own view;

thus, within those seven verses, the entire discussion ends in a mere critique, for even though all cognition— by virtue of being self-cognizing and having its own form— is produced from the impressions of experience...

Just as memory has experience as its object, so too experience is not the object of memory; since [experience] is not cognizable by another cognition, one might first suspect— by means of the first verse— that memory is an error, then refute that erroneous nature by means of the second verse, and finally, by means of the third verse, address the consequence regarding memory.

In the view of consciousness (*saṃvid-darśana*), which is our own position, it was stated in the verse that if all perceptions of forms and all determinations were suspected of being erroneous, then worldly activity such as rejection and acquisition would be abolished.

Regarding the statement that it was not mentioned in the verse beginning with "smṛtyupapatti," he says: "It is true. By means of this word, which consists of a partial acceptance (*ardhāṅgīkāra*), it is stated that the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) must be accepted. If one asks why that is so, it is because knowledge distinct from the self (*ātman*) has been refuted.

The meaning is that this must also be accepted by me. By the word "but" (*kiṃ tu*), which expresses a distinction, it is stated that what was previously [by me]—namely, the memory-cognition intended by you, which is self-luminous and based on prior experience—is [what I] tolerate. Memory...

Knowledge does not become a cognizer—that is, a revealer—of its own prior experience or knowledge, just as it is of an experienced object; for that too is self-luminous, and because [the knowledge] is firmly established in the experiencing subject, the self, at the time of recollection. In this system...
In memory, the manifestation of mere restriction (*niyama*) does not need to be established;

for whatever object is manifested is established solely through the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of experience, and thus it does not require further justification. Therefore, he first examines the logical possibility of this, saying "this [is so]."

Memory follows upon experience; therefore, how could there be memory in the form "that" immediately after that [experience]? It cannot be said, "Let there be no memory," for without memory, there can be no [processes] such as rejection or acquisition regarding an object previously experienced.

How could practical activity (*vyavahāra*) occur? For it is through the experience of this object that its status as a means to pleasure is determined. From that [determination], there arises the cognition "this is a means to pleasure," and from that, one desires it; from that desire, one undertakes its acquisition, which involves the re-engagement with the previously experienced object. In this process, memory [plays a role].
If [recollection] were produced from a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), then the knowledge of recollection would arise from the impression of a prior experience;
that knowledge of recollection, unlike the original experience, is not indeed produced by the object itself.
Nevertheless, it has the object of the original experience as its domain solely through the mental impression of that recollection.
Thus it is established:

nothing at all has been produced for memory by the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) which effects the relationship between the experience and its object as being the object of that [memory]. For in that memory-cognition, which resides in the self and is self-luminous, there is no manifestation of the past experience, just as there is none of the experienced object.

If that experience manifests in memory, it does not possess self-luminosity; like a jar, it becomes an object of knowledge. Experience is dependent upon the experiencer; memory is dependent upon the rememberer, who is the form of the previous experiencer.
The meaning is that cognitions are dependent upon the knower. Thus is memory.
Anticipating the objection that "since it is produced by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of a previous experience, let it also take as its object that which was previously experienced," he says:
"The Seer (*dṛk*), whose nature is experience, is self-luminous (*svaprakāśā*) through its own manifestation alone; it is not something other than that which is manifested by another."

If it were to be manifested by another, its self-luminosity would not be possible. Therefore, it is self-manifesting; moreover, that which illuminates and makes manifest its own clearly perceived object is not to be known by another cognition, such as memory.
If it were knowable, then [it would follow that] the eye itself would be knowable by the eye, just like milk or clouds, which are objects of the eye.

Furthermore, the tongue would have to grasp the taste of the fruit as well as its odor. Therefore, [the object] is not cognizable by another cognition. As for the fact that memory arises from a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), it is similar to direct experience because it takes as its object the same object-field as that experience; this is because experience and memory share a single object-field.
There is merely a similarity to the experience; there is no apprehension of that [object], nor is there an apprehension of the experience itself.

It does not become an object of the knowledge of existence (*bhavajñāna*). Even through the word "that" (*tat*), there is no comprehension of identity with it. Memory does not even know, "I am similar to the previous experience," nor does it know its similarity to that.

Memory is similar to a prior experience because that similarity depends upon the cognizer alone. Furthermore, memory does not know that "this jar, which is the object [of the present cognition], was the object of a prior experience."

Since that knowledge as well is dependent upon a knower, it must be stated to be distinct from the light that consists of consciousness; the phrase "in the state of worldly transaction" (*vyavahāra-daśāyām*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
