Because even the insentient (*jaḍa*) is, in the ultimate sense, manifest, [consciousness] is distinguished from the insentient by its nature as seeing (*dṛk*).

"From its own manifestation" (*svābhāsāt*). Manifestation (*ābhāsa*) means the state of being manifest (*prakāśamānatā*). That manifestation is the "own form" (*svarūpa*) of that vision (*dṛś*) which does not deviate from it. Furthermore, it is also "from its own manifestation" because its nature consists in manifesting as "this" externally an object that resides within itself.

The meaning is that it is "self-manifesting" because it shines by itself and because it illuminates its own object. Even when the object is external to the cognition— such as being described in this manner— the nature of that cognition is nonetheless transferred onto the body of that external object.

It cannot be so. He states the reason for this: the manifestation of one's own essential nature—which is conceived as being other than itself—is indeed what constitutes knowledge. Therefore, let that experience of knowledge be self-manifesting in the manner described; nevertheless...

It will appear in the recollection that occurs subsequent to itself. [The opponent objects: "If so, there would be a loss of the self-luminous nature (*svābhāsatva*) of the experience-knowledge (*anubhavajñāna*) as it proceeds toward recollection. To this he says:
"Experience-knowledge is not an object to be known by the subsequent recollective knowledge."

If the cognition of experience (*anubhavajñāna*) appears during the recollection of something else, then that cognition of experience does not become manifest. For this [recollection] manifests as the manifestation of the very nature of the experience itself; at the time when the experience is self-manifesting, the experience—

How can the locative case in the phrase "saṃbandhapramāṇāparatra" be justified as denoting the locus of cognition? For within that recollective cognition (*smṛtijñāna*), there is no manifestation of the original experience (*anubhava*)— as there would be if one were to mount upon it like one mounts a jar—
and thus they do not become mutually cognizable through that cognition.

If the knowledge of the taste of an object—which has taste as its domain—were not perceived by the tongue, then by implication (phalataḥ), that is, through the force of the circumstances, taste would effectively be perceived by the eye alone. Furthermore, if there were no restriction of sense faculties, then the taste of an object belonging to the domain of the tongue would be grasped by the eye from objects such as clouds and so forth. Thus, there would be an absence of the fixed correspondence between sense organs and their respective objects.

What, then, would be accomplished by a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) for the cognition of recollection? By the words "the object in the example" and so forth, he indicates that it is the cognition of form (*rūpa*). Furthermore, the cognition of form does not arise from the latent impression produced by the cognition of taste.

Memory arises from the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of an experience. Therefore, how can it serve as an analogy? How could it be that [memory] is known by another [means], such that the fault you have alleged would follow? It is the latent impression alone that has the power [to produce memory]. What is being said? That the latent impression alone makes the experience the object of memory.

The meaning is "it produces. "This is not so" means that what has been stated by you does not hold true. From a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by an experience, [memory arises]. Memory is a cognition arising from the knowledge of an object similar to that which was previously experienced;
it is one's own awareness. Therefore, the cognitive state of memory would be similar to the original experience.

It is not a single entity like the experience itself. Because each successive arrangement of branches produced at later times arises from the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the preceding arrangements of branches, the cognition of memory regarding these later times is as if identical to the preceding arrangements of branches.

Because it is produced from the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of a prior experience, an impression belonging to a later time is not equivalent to the experience of that prior time. In the world, whatever entity is produced from the impression of a certain entity, that [later] entity does not possess the nature of being the experiencer of that [prior] entity. This is because of the impression that is the producer...

The son is born; for instance, there is no existence of that past father who was the knower. Just as a sprout born from the conditioning of a seed does not exist with the same nature as the seed whose own form has perished, so too the cognition of memory born from the conditioning of experience does not exist with the same nature as the prior experience.

It cannot be the knower. Furthermore, how can even the cognition of the similarity between memory and experience not lead the cognitive act of experience to understand its own similarity with the cognitive act of memory?
Likewise, the cognitive act of memory [should] also [understand] its own similarity with experience.
It does not convey that the experience and the cognition are equal.

For, if the experience and the cognition are not mutually perceived, it would be impossible to determine a similarity residing in both within the cognition of memory; thus, there would be no cognition of similarity.

Or rather, it resides in the cognizer. Just as when one says "the face is like a lotus," there is the cognition of both [the face and the lotus], because there is no other knowledge distinct from those two;
therefore, from the latent impression (*saṃskāra*), it is established that there is merely the state of having the same object as the original experience.

The experience itself does not become the object [of the memory]. It is certain that even the fact that this jar or other object—which is the object of the knowledge of memory—was previously made an object of experience is not established by the memory [itself]. This is the conclusion.

(115) Now, one might suspect that memory is an error: even though the jar or other object in a memory-cognition that follows upon the experience "this is a jar" has perished along with that experience, [the memory] takes as its object that perished jar and so forth, such that one thinks, "that is the jar," or "that is the cloth."
When memory and knowledge arise regarding what has been done, there would be a manifestation as "this" of the experience itself as real;
and by way of that experience, there would also be a manifestation as "this" of the object of that experience as real,
if it were identical to that experience.

Since it has an object—namely, because it has as its sole object that very thing which was the object of experience—it illuminates that experienced object as "that"; thus, there is room for what you have stated. The indeclinable *yāvatā* indicates the absence of a resolution regarding the matter under discussion; likewise, the meaning is "not so," [refuting] memory and conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

(91) According to the principle stated that "conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) do not touch their objects," because conceptual construction does not touch its object, memory— which is of the nature of conceptual construction— determines (*adhyavasyati*) only a non-manifest experience and its object. "Determination" (*adhyavasāya*), as in the phrase "the superimposition of B upon A when it is not B," and so forth...

Like the superimposition of silver and so forth, it has the nature of an error because it does not touch the actual object. In that regard, what is the insistence on the claim that without such [superimposition], linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) is not possible in memory? This is the point of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) which [the author] demonstrates... [of] memory.
Even though existence (*bhava*) and the experienced object lack the status of being [actual] objects [of cognition], because they are determined through that— namely,

through a determination consisting of the cognition of one thing as another— the meaning is that, due to error, the state of having the experienced object as its support (in the thought "there is a jar") is not ultimate.

The experience of the object of memory is not... [the object of perception]... because it is not the object of both; nevertheless, even in the absence of being the object of both, it is determined by memory through its nature as an error. He refutes this suspicion that memory is erroneous.

He states the refutation itself with the remainder of the verse: "Regarding what you have said—that it is a 'mistaken memory'—here, by means of the subsequent verse-sūtra, he provides the reasoning for this inconsistency:
first, as for the claim that it is 'mistaken,' how can it even be considered a memory at all? [The author] will explain the nature of memory below.

How could there be a characteristic of error? For memory, which is suspected of being erroneous in some respect—how could it have the status of an establisher [of an object]? Because there is no establishment of the object. [This is because] of the prior experience...
And why is dependence on a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) required for memory?

He defines the characteristic of memory as follows: "Memory is the non-erroneous recollection of an experienced object. According to the system of the *Yogasūtra*, [memory is] that which pertains to a jar revealed by experience—
Likewise, this manifestation of memory— namely, the manifestation of an experienced object such as "this is a jar" in exactly that same way, neither deficient nor excessive—
is the very nature of memory itself. Even in the absence of the manifestation of the experienced object in that manner [at the time of recollection], [memory remains distinct].
Just as in the case of a jar, that which grasps non-existent silver and so forth in an error appears as the form of existent silver and so forth through that error; yet by that error,
the object is not truly accepted, because a non-existent object does not manifest, whereas that which is real in nature is the ultimate reality.

Because it is manifested by that error, the object is not established at all. Since there is no manifestation of an object that has been established, if [the error] were produced from a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), then for an erroneous cognition (*bhrānti*) arising from a mental impression of a prior experience, there would be no purpose whatsoever.

This is precisely because error lacks the quality of being produced by a latent impression (*saṃskāra*). For if it were produced by a latent impression, it would have to rely upon a similarity with its object in order to be classified as memory—as it has been said: "The state of being produced by a latent impression is what makes it similar to that [object]. Regarding the object...

There is not even the slightest resemblance between error and an experience whose nature is illumination, which in no way touches upon an object— whether as "this" or as "residence. Therefore, for an error that arises from a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), there is no purpose whatsoever.
Anticipating the objection that error possesses the capacity to manifest an object, it is argued:

since both the experience and its object are determined (*adhyavasīyate*) by that error, there is a similarity [between them] based on that determination; thus, for the sake of establishing that [object], there is a similarity between the experience and the memory.

For the sake of [cognitive] accomplishment (*siddhi*), there is the grasping of a mental impression (*saṃskāra*). Therefore, that which establishes the object, as well as the similarity to the experience for the sake of its accomplishment, and the grasping of the mental impression—all worldly discourse is accomplished through mere error; having raised this doubt, he states the answer: "it is determined" (*adhyavasīyate*).

(117) What do you mean by "is determined" (*adhyavasīyate*)? If you say that the object appears through error, then it does not constitute an error. If you say that by "is determined" you mean "is manifested," then once again the object is not clearly established.

As previously stated, since the object is not clearly established due to error according to the logic already explained, the similarity of experience to that of delusion is merely a verbal赘 (redundancy); it is not the actual object.
He demonstrates this very point of the object of cognition: conceptualization belongs to the determination of cognition.

If error is admitted, then from that inert determination (*avasāya*), there can be no established stability of the object. In the case of a memory-illusion or any other erroneous cognition, there is no error with respect to the manifesting aspect of consciousness—the aspect consisting of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). As for the object, [the situation is as follows:]
Because there is no state of contrariety (*vaiparītyābhāva*), when one sees a distant mother-of-pearl shell and,

due to its quality of translucence, a delusory cognition arises— namely, "this is silver"— the delusive nature of that cognition which manifests as "this is silver" is established by self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) precisely because there is no state of contrariety.

If all cognition of silver is erroneous, then it is a mistaken cognition. In that erroneous cognition, one's own form—which is the form of silver—is determined; and that form of silver is superimposed upon it by means of that cognition, being perceived erroneously as if it were not one's own form.
Because it determines the object as having the form of silver—that is, as having the form of the object—it is the very form of the mother-of-pearl that is determined as being silver;

thus, that cognition of silver is erroneous with respect to its objective aspect (*viṣayāṃśa*), not erroneous with respect to its cognitive aspect (*jñānāṃśa*). That [cognition] takes the form of the object, such as mother-of-pearl or silver.
Whether by way of the form of a cognition such as that of two moons,

or by way of memory, it is not touched [by the object]; thus, being silent regarding the objective aspect (*arthāṃśa*), this consciousness of erroneous recollection does not illuminate anything else, and its insentience (*jaḍatva*) has ensued with respect to that objective portion.

The cognition of silver arising with respect to a mother-of-pearl shell possesses insentience (*jaḍatva*) in its own objective aspect, namely the silver portion, because it lacks the capacity to illuminate that [silver]. However, in the case of the cognition of a jar, since it lacks the capacity to illuminate a cloth— which is the object of the cognition of a cloth— the insentience resides only in the object of the cognition of a cloth, and not in its own object.

[This is] the remainder: there is no function whatsoever for insentient cognition (*jaḍa-jñāna*), because it lacks the quality of self-luminosity (*tatprakāśatva*). Consequently, even the capacity to illuminate memory and error would be lost. Therefore, if it is then admitted that the cognition of memory and error is not insentient—

When the mother-of-pearl is being delineated by the cognition of "silver" with respect to its own self-cognized aspect (*svasaṃvedanāṃśa*), there is then a subsistence (*niṣṭhatā*) in both its own form and the form of silver; consequently, there is no state of being otherwise established (*anyathāsthiti*). Now, the word "atha" is used in the sense of a question regarding memory that takes the form of an error (*bhrānti*).

Is the nature of space (khāya rūpa) admitted to be insentient by taking as a basis either that which consists of conceptualization (vikalpātmaka), which is the aspect of cognition (saṃjñānāṃśa) within self-awareness (svasaṃvedana), or the form of space (khākāra) being delineated by the cognition of it? Even so, this would be of the nature of an error (bhrānti).
When memory exists, it delineates its own portion of cognition— its own form and its own object— which are both ultimately unreal; thus,
this memory is established in both respects as being incapable of manifesting an object in the form of real silver, and therefore unable even to grasp its name.
For one who is unable [to perceive directly], memory becomes a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

Its capacity consists in bringing about the state of being communicable (*vyavahāryatva*) for that object. Even though a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) exists, the capacity to bring about the communicability of an object—such as its rejection, acquisition, and so forth—is [what constitutes memory].

How could it not be consistent with memory? Because of the absence of the manifestation of the object [at the time of recollection], immediately following that, by the words "the truth," etc., [it is shown that] cognitions are devoid of mutual connection. First, experience, because it becomes the object of memory, [would have to] have its own object as an object of memory as well.

And because there is no offering [of the object], it is devoid of connection with memory. This should be understood to apply equally to memory and conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Thus, they are mutually disconnected. Regarding the statement "of experience and so forth...

that is the subject at hand," it means that since memory does not occur when the self exists as the subject under discussion—as indicated by the passage beginning with "Now, experience..."—[the self must be distinct from them].
In the present context, it is argued that in the absence of memory, there would be an absence of worldly transactions such as rejection and acceptance.

Thus, in the manner described, conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*) is distinct from perceptual experience (*anubhavajñāna*), and memory-cognition (*smṛtijñāna*) is distinct from that; thus they are mutually differentiated.
"Of those that are distinct and mutually unaware" (119).
(p. 94) The cognition of experience does not know the cognition of memory, nor does the cognition of memory know the object of memory;
and the cognition of memory does not know the experience, nor does it know the object of that experience.

The conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*) that exists between those two is also exactly like this; thus, for cognitions that do not mutually know one another, there arises a synthesis (*anusandhāna*) through experience and so forth. "This" is the experience (*anubhava*).
"This is a jar, not a cloth" is the conceptualization (*vikalpa*). "That is the jar" is memory (*smṛti*); that itself is the synthesis.
The state of existence for those born [from that] consists of worldly activities such as rejection and acquisition.

This would be impossible if the Supreme Lord were not the one to be described in the immediately following verse. Furthermore, if one accepts your position—that "thus it would perish"—this is merely a possibility; let it not perish.

It does not perish merely by your desire, because it is manifest. The maintenance of worldly existence—the activity of taking and rejecting arising from the synthesis of cognitions—does not perish even if Maheśvara were not present; for Maheśvara certainly exists. Therefore, the maintenance of worldly existence does not [cease].

The meaning is that it perishes. Whatever state there may be for a person—that is, for the world—such as the worldly transaction of taking and giving, all such states consisting of worldly transactions are, for a single cognizer, attained in the form of memory, which is established by the existence of objects. Furthermore:

The fact that perceptual experience, conceptual construction, and recollective cognition share a single object is established by the nature of the cognizer as the rememberer; for the state of being a memory depends upon that [rememberer], and the synthesis—which consists in the attainment of that [object]—is produced from it. Thus, all cognition, including perception and so forth, is dependent upon that synthesis.

And he demonstrates that worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is indeed dependent upon memory with the words "For instance" (*tathāhi*), and so forth. Every worldly transaction depends on memory; for example, the perceptual cognition "First I know the jar"—that "I," who previously experienced the jar and so forth prior to seeing a cloth.

The thought "I, who was that very same person, now experience the jar" is not possible without the synthesis (*anusandhāna*) consisting of the unification of prior and subsequent cognitions under the form of "I"— a synthesis sustained by the memory produced from the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of that experience. If it were possible without that, then for the direct perception "I know," [the subject] would [not be established].
Otherwise, the non-existence of the universe within the cognizer would follow as a consequence, and there would be the undesirable contingency of it being imperceptible.
Without the cognizer, its perception does not occur;
for the cognition "I am experiencing pleasure"—which is a perceptual knowledge consisting of pleasure—occurs in the cognizer who possesses that pleasure.

(120) Without rest, nothing is possible; for if there were no repose within the subject who experiences pleasure, pleasure could not become manifest, as it would follow that it lacks perceptibility. Thus, in all cases—whether regarding conceptualizations such as "jar" or "pleasure," or all worldly transactions such as rejection and so forth—all are essentially of the nature of memory.

Whether insentient or sentient, whatever state was previously experienced as adverse must be abandoned because it is undesirable; whereas that which was experienced as favorable must be accepted because it is desirable. That Caitra who was seen previously—[in him... p. 95).

The impulsion, "One capable of the task should be urged toward this," is also based on memory; likewise, the universally accepted consensus is also based on memory. Thus, the stability of the world arises from such a synthetic reflection (*anusaṃdhāna*). Furthermore, it is as follows:

By way of implication (*ākṣepa*), the word expresses another meaning: if one accepts the views of those who maintain that consciousness is devoid of a self or a Lord (*ātmeśvara*), the stability of the world would not perish;

rather, it is the possibility of its perishing that is intended—because, as will be explained later, [the world] is dependent upon the Great Lord (*maheśvara*), and thus it does not perish in an ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*).

He states the reason for this possibility with the words "From where," etc. The existence of people [is established] in the context of the possibility of destruction. By means of the two qualifiers—"mutually distinct" and "not cognizing one another"—this refers to cognitions (*jñāna*).

He states the reason: "mutually" (*anyonya*). This [cognition] called "this" is a perceptual cognition (*anubhava-jñāna*) distinct from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and memory (*smṛti*). The conceptual cognition "this is blue indeed, not yellow" is also distinct from perception and memory. The mnemonic cognition "that is blue" is likewise distinct from perception and conceptual construction; thus they are mutually distinct.

To that extent, these cognitions belong only to the state of conceptualization (*vikalpa*), for it has been stated that the manifestation of the connection and disconnection of time within cognition is what constitutes "the present. These very cognitions occur in succession as: "this," "this is a jar and not a cloth," and "that is a jar."

The meaning is that these cognitions, whose nature consists solely in the manifestation of their own respective objects, are like those born blind, infants, or the mute with respect to the objects of others; apart from their own [objects], they are incapable of seeing, discerning, or speaking regarding the objects of others. "And not... [is the beginning of the next sentence].

Recollective cognition (*smaraṇajñāna*) does not illuminate conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*). Conceptual cognition does not illuminate experiential cognition (*anubhavajñāna*). Furthermore, experiential cognition does not illuminate conceptual cognitions; [nor does] conceptual cognition [illuminate them].
Recollection-knowledge does not manifest [other objects],

and thus, according to the manner described, they do not possess the nature of mutual manifestation. In this way, there is no synthetic unification (*anusandhāna*) among cognitions— whether by way of their own respective intrinsic natures or by way of their objects— such that one cognition would be identical with another.

The state of being the subject; and for the other [the object], there is no state of being the subject. There is the state of being the object for experience (*anubhava*) and the state of being the object for conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

Alternatively, there is the state of being the object for conceptual construction and the state of being the object for experience. Likewise, even for memory (*smṛti*), there is no relationship of object and subject. Apart from experience, conceptual construction, and memory...
The fourth knowledge (*turīya-jñāna*), having become the binding cause for these [states] such as experience and so forth,
is conceived as that which establishes the synthesis by abiding in the position of the synthesizer. Such is the fourth as well.

(96) [If it were so,] knowledge would cease to exist; all worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*) would perish. Since it is your mere wish that they should perish, yet they actually perish and manifest—because these transactions are manifesting, the following consequence ensues: [that which is about to be stated].

This very [process] is striving to justify the manifestation of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*); that which has resulted in the necessity of performing an application (*ayoga*) is intended as being manifest within the agent who knows—that is, in the form of one's own self whose nature is the Supreme Lord (*maheśvara*). Without this, [the manifestation would not occur].
He shows that even for Brahmā it would be impossible to provide a justification:

"If the one Great Lord—who has within himself the infinite forms of the universe, whose body is consciousness, and who possesses the powers of knowledge, memory, and the removal [of ignorance]—did not exist, the stability of the world would perish; thus it is conceived. He certainly exists."
Therefore, by the final verse beginning with "it perishes," there is a reversal of the [preceding] consequence.

Within the internal fullness of the I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*), that which has been made—that which has been brought to the state of identity with it—is the universal form (*viśvarūpa*) extending from Śiva down to the earth; for since space and time are also included within the principles (*tattva*), it is undivided by them.

By whom— that Maheśvara who is of such a nature, whose body is consciousness, a single mass of light, endowed with the three excellent powers consisting of experience, exclusion, and memory, and who is the sole substratum of those powers— he effects the conjunction and disjunction of those powers. (122)
Resting is said to be *svacchanda*. If it were not so—as connected with the preceding verse by the phrase "if it were not thus"—then how could this aphorism (*sūtra*) be reached?

This refers to the chapters (*āhnika*) which consist of the determination of Maheśvaratva, which is the sole locus for the removal of memory, knowledge, and [other states], as will be explained in such passages as "having somehow attained this."
Above that, it is the very essence of the sūtras belonging to the chapters on Action (Kriyā) and the chapters on Means (Upāya);
some say it shines forth as mere consciousness (*saṃvitti*), while others say it shines forth as consciousness whose nature is knowledge (*jñāna*).
All disputants agree that it is the manifesting consciousness which is accepted by all; therefore, there is no dispute regarding it.

They do not deny that which is manifesting; they are unable to conceal it. If that consciousness (saṃvit) consists of its own self alone and rests solely within itself, how could it be the illuminator of an object? For there would be no contact with the object. If it is the illuminator of the object, then that light is of the nature of consciousness.

The object would indeed be the very nature of consciousness (*dharma*), just as [the capacity] is [inherent in the thing]. Therefore, because the object is of the nature of consciousness, its manifestation is consciousness itself; thus, consciousness, being essentially the manifestation of the object, culminates in the object alone.
This is the state of the grasped and the grasper—the relationship between the object and the subject. Hence...

For one who maintains that consciousness is essentially the illumination of objects— lest there be the consequence of the dissolution of the relationship between the grasped and the grasper— it follows by the force of that [consciousness], that is, precisely through the power of that consciousness, that the object too is indeed contained within the nature of consciousness; for consciousness is essentially illumination.

Moreover, abandoning the identity in the form of "that very same [consciousness] which previously had the manifestation of a jar as its nature is the manifestor of a cloth," one must consider that— just like the view of the Vijñānavādins— the [manifestation] resides in the jar and [the manifestation] resides in the cloth.
If it is argued that "it is that very same [consciousness] which has become [the object] that is remembered," then the recollection of an object previously experienced would be impossible;

and because such recollection would be impossible, that [consciousness] must be one, and since it is one, the entire aggregate of all objects of knowledge must be accepted by the Vijñānavādin who desires [to maintain his position] as being encompassed by that single consciousness.

"Even so" means: if consciousness, having embraced the entire mass of all objects of knowledge (*vedyarāśi*) within its single fold, remains perpetually emergent, then it would manifest simultaneously externally as the universe, from Śiva down to the earth; if, however, it remains submerged within, then [it would manifest] simultaneously internally from the earth—[down to the individual soul].

Because it has such a nature, it is exactly so from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Nevertheless, due to its sovereignty (*svātantrya*), it does not manifest in that way. Therefore, for one who desires to bring forth the mass of entities (*bhāvarāśi*) which are embraced within the interior of the nature of consciousness (*sāṃvitsvarūpa*), the object—which is non-different in form from his own self—is distinct from that [manifestation].

Having grasped [the object] within itself, someone perceives an object such as a mere jar or a mere cloth, manifesting it as "I" or "this form," emerging as the nature of form; thus, consciousness consists of manifestation (*ābhāsa*).

The power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) is that nature of consciousness which, though distinct as the appearance of an emerging jar, is by its own self not turned outward; yet, because it is oriented toward objects manifested as external, it possesses an outward-facing character. Thus, it is variously turned outward, ever-new, and mutually distinct.
Knowledge itself is said to be ever-new through its coloring by the reflections of various objects;

thus, even though it is ever-new, the cognitions of jars, cloths, and so forth—appearing as ever-new—undergo arising and passing away at every moment. Therefore, it is precisely this state of undergoing arising and passing away at every moment [that constitutes its nature].

There would be a loss in the maintenance of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). This is because, due to the absence of the synthesis (*anusandhāna*) consisting of the recollection of various previously experienced objects, there would follow the consequence of a failure in transaction;
for regarding an object previously grasped, there was a self-awareness directed outward, such as "this is a jar" or "that is another."

The inward-facing awareness of that outward-turned [consciousness] is the nature of consciousness as the subject; and that state of being the nature of consciousness, which persists even at a later time following the wakefulness of that experience, is situated within one's own self and established in one's own self.

The outward-directedness toward objects such as a jar, which occurs at the time of experience, manifests that specific outward-directedness— distinguishing "this is a jar" from "this is a cloth"— by way of the object being qualified by its particular place and time, such as the jar seen as outward-directed at that specific time and place.
The very non-apprehension of that inward-turned nature of consciousness itself is memory (*smṛti*).
It manifests that object anew as "this is blue"; it remembers that object as "that is blue.
For that object, which is the form of the referent of both experience and memory, shines forth in ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*).
Since one functions in a state of identity with consciousness— which consists of the entire universe from Śiva down to the earth— one is oneself already composed of that universal consciousness;
thus, nothing new or previously non-existent, such as a mere jar, has been manifested by experience.
It would be considered manifested as memory. This too must be accepted: by means of the stream [of consciousness], consciousness is [itself] a stream;
this also must be accepted. Even so, it does not happen that at the time of experience, that object which is merely a jar is first separated from consciousness.

The consciousness that has the apprehension of a jar as its nature is distinguished from [other] consciousnesses; the consciousness that establishes the jar is distinguished from the consciousness that has the establishment of a cloth as its nature. And the object of cognition consisting of a jar is distinguished from other objects of cognition such as a cloth.

Because everything consists of a single consciousness, there is ultimately no separation; thus, the appearance of the non-existence of mutual separation between cognitions and objects of cognition— that is, their "separation"—
is merely an appearance, and as such, that separation does not exist even as an appearance.

In the ultimate sense, this very mutual distinction of the object being manifested—which consists of the grasped and the grasper—is the ultimate reality. First, there is the distinction of the consciousness that is the grasped from other objects of grasp and from the grasper. Thus...
There is a separation of consciousness from another consciousness, from the class of objects of consciousness, and from the knower;
and there is a separation of the knower from another knower, from consciousness, and from another object of consciousness.
This very separation is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), because this separation arises from the act of delimitation (*paricchedana*).

Determination (*pariccheda*) is said to be the manifestation of that [object]. Thus, the manifestation of the determination of reality is *apohana*, which is incapacity. "This" is the linguistic usage [of] "this very thing is that. By this, capacity—[namely] those three capacities.

Because power belongs only to the Lord who possesses power; and by the statement that these three powers belong to the Lord alone, the meaning of the word "one" (eka) employed by the author of the Sūtras is established. As it has been said:
"Power is of the same nature as the possessor of power; it does not seek separation from it."
The identity of these two is eternal.
The dependence of the triad of powers upon the Lord means that, being such, the Great Lord alone— possessing those three powers—
by his own will manifests Caitra, Maitra, and others, whose nature consists of experiencing, remembering, and conceptualizing,
in their respective bodies as Caitra, Maitra, and so forth.

As stated by the author of the Sūtras himself: "The establishment of the meaning of words such as 'jar' (125)—the determination of objects—is restricted to the *jīva* who is constrained by the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*); even when that [restriction] is suspended, it remains fixed in the Supreme Self. This applies to these powers of knowledge and so forth."
The experience of a jar, the memory of a jar, and so forth, are conceptual constructions of the variety of objects.
That capacity to accomplish [effects] independently of anything else is the sovereignty created by its own freedom;
it is the sovereignty of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, which, when compared to that of Sadāśiva and Īśvara, is [inferior].

The full [state] is called "I" (*aham*). This very sovereignty is composed of consciousness (*cinmaya*). Considering it as a "body" (*vapuḥ*), from Śiva down to the earth—when [it is so conceived], this [sovereignty] of the Supreme Lord takes the form of being endowed with knowledge, memory, and so forth, [as opposed to] the insentience that arises from a single uniform nature.

The state of Maheśvara has been fully attained. Thus, there is the following reductio ad absurdum: if such a Maheshvara were not accepted, this variegated universe would not appear as anything at all.
It is because [Maheshvara] is the ground of rest that the universe shines forth—indeed, it is He alone.
The state of being the Great Lord (Māheśvarya) must necessarily be accepted; otherwise, there would be a reversal of the logical consequence (*prasaṅga-viparyaya*).

For if it were not so, such a Great Lord as described would not exist, and consequently, the stability of the world would not exist—this follows from what was stated previously. Thus, in the verse beginning with "mutually distinct" (*anyonyabhinnām*), there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). This is indicated by the phrase "if it were not so" (*na cet*).
The consequence [is established] by means of a verse.
Thus ends the third chapter in the commentary *Pratyabhijñāsūtravimarśinī*.
Now begins the fourth chapter.

It has been stated that [the Lord] possesses the power of knowledge (*jñāna*), memory (*smṛti*), and non-removal (*apohana*). According to this sequence, since the power of knowledge is the first to be defined when it is appropriate to do so,
there arises the occasion— already indicated by the previous aphorism *athānubhavavidhvaṃsaḥ* (now, the destruction of experience)— to establish its opposite.

(126) First, the determination of the direction, memory, and capacity is undertaken. For instance, immediately after the definition of the nature of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), in order to refute that prima facie argument, it was begun with the words "Indeed, [it is] true, however... because [the work] is titled *Padārtharatnanikara*.

Regarding the term *padārtha*: the subjects (*pramātṛ*) range from Śiva down to the *sakala* [limited subject]; the objects of their cognition (*prameya*) are the principles (*tattva*) ranging from Sadāśiva down to the earth (*kṣiti*). Because these very principles—along with their transformations such as jars and so forth—are the root of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) and because they produce delight, they are "jewels" (*ratna*). [This refers to] experienced objects...
According to the principle stated in the *Yogasūtra*, "unconfused mindfulness" (*sampramoṣasmṛti*), the jewels are their collection—

which consists of many common aggregates and is of the nature of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*)— and one's own heart, which is inherently indestructible like its own self, is the contraction and expansion of the universe.

Through the application of *līlā* (divine play), the lotus is the effect (*kārya*). The "grove" (*kuñja*) is the heart itself, because it provides space for the entire universe from Śiva down to the earth. As it has been said:
"Having obtained this wealth of knowledge within the cave of the heart, though it is difficult to attain," and so forth, because of its reality.

We praise Śiva, who, through his continuity, makes the infinite thread of memory—which is the very lifeblood of all worldly transaction—hang down as a continuous string within the midst of the [otherwise] severed [states]. "In this way" means: by the manner described as being "possessed of the powers of knowledge, memory, and the removal [of ignorance]. Memory...

The power of *apohana* (exclusion), which is preceded by knowledge and favors both recollection and perception, illuminates that [object] as new or remembers it; however, because it functions through identity with consciousness—which is essentially the universe—it is entirely full of the universe. Thus, nothing is illuminated or remembered as "new."
This too must be accepted as a necessary consequence of the [monistic] stream:
namely, that whatever is manifested is severed from consciousness, and consciousness [is severed] from another consciousness, as is the object of cognition (*saṃvedya*).
According to the principle beginning with "from within the object of cognition" (*saṃvedyāntarāt*), the power of *apohana* (exclusion), which favors both [cognition and its object],

was first demonstrated through the sequence of the emergence of objects such as pots and cloths that become the domain of experience. Now, however, in accordance with the introduction "But [it is] true, yet it is the knowledge of memory" (*satyaṃ kintu smṛtijñānam*), [the same is shown again].

First: "How could it not be that the self would be non-eternal if it were the experiencer? This should be examined as being similar to the support of the reversal of the context of the Sūtra. Regarding this prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), in order to refute what was stated—that memory is established from the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) alone—(127) [the following is said].

According to the method stated [in the text] beginning with "satyam" and ending with "jñānasmṛtyapohanaśaktimān," this group of seven verses, you must first establish that memory arises from the mere latent impression (*saṃskāra*) as asserted by you.

However, this must be stated: in order to dispel the doubt that even the power of the Blessed One— acknowledged by you and mentioned in the Sūtra as "being thus" (tathābhūta) provided it is not "internally grasped" (antah-kṛta)— might produce this memory, [the following is said] for the purpose of determining the true nature of memory (smṛti-tattva).

The daily lesson (āhnika) begins with eight verses. Therein, by the first [verse], it is stated that the doctrine of consciousness (*saṃvidvāda*) alone is established as the nature of memory, according to the expression "the agent who knows" and so forth. By the second [verse]:
"Now, even though memory has that [past object] as its object, its determination is directed toward that [present consciousness]."
According to the principle stated that "the object of perception must be something previously seen," [memory] is of the nature of an error of recollection;

therefore, in order to refute the view of the Vijñānavādins and others, it is stated that memory has the capacity to manifest the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of jars, cloths, and so forth, which were made objects of prior experience. This is expressed by the word "that" (*sa*) in the phrase "recollection of that" (*tatsmṛti*).
Through the experience "this," and through its object, immersion (*āveśa*) is said to extend up to the point of unification.
Memory enters into that experience and its object up to the point of unification.
For this very reason, an object experienced as "this" becomes "that" in memory; thus, memory is an experience.
If there were an absorption (*āveśa*) extending to the point of unification with those two objects, it would be like a previously experienced jar; yet,

fearing that even the experience itself might become an object, it was established in the fifth [chapter]— concerning the past, future, and present— that because experience is of the nature of self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*), there is no manifestation [of it] through memory.
By asserting that [the yogi] does not apprehend even the experience of Caitra, Maitra, and others as distinct entities, the meaning of the fourth verse itself is reinforced.
If it is argued that the yogi does apprehend the cognitions of Caitra, Maitra, and so forth, then [that cognition would have to apprehend] the bodies of Caitra, Maitra, and the rest—

"—I am experiencing the pot. Now, by asserting that one's own cognition takes as its object another cognition—such as that of Caitra or Maitra—who is distinct from oneself, you have merely reinforced the meaning of the fourth verse. Just as in the case of the sixth [verse], "there is a pot," the experience "it was like this for me" is [explained] by means of a suspected memory.
...makes them distinct objects—(p.

101)—just as memory makes its object conform to a previous experience, so too does conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which follows in the wake of experience, make its object conform to that experience. Memory...
In this context, even regarding memory and mental construction (*kalpa*), the state of identity with the prior experience has been demonstrated.
By the eighth [verse], it is shown that the object to be remembered— such as Caitra or Maitra—
and the rememberer are essentially a single consciousness (*ekacittatva*), whose nature is the full, undivided light of the "I" (*pūrṇāhaṃ-prakāśa*) unconditioned by space and time.

Rest has been described. By way of connection with mindfulness (*smṛti*), the meaning of the intent of this chapter (*āhnika*) concerns the object of perception (*dṛśya*), the act of seeing (*darśana*), and the seer (*draṣṭṛ*), which precede that [mindfulness] and will be examined in the form of the subsequent chapters.
Now, the verses are stated: "He who is the perceiver of the object previously experienced.

By the perception (*upalabdhi*) of an object such as a jar that was previously experienced as "this," there arises within the self (*ātman*) a consciousness (*bodha*) turned inward, whose nature is "I" (*aham*). As for the word "he" (*sa hi*): it refers to one who has internalized the infinite.

Maheśvara himself, endowed with the universal form (viśvarūpa), exists even beyond that; thus, at the time of experiencing that [form], he is present even during the time of the subsequent memory directed toward it. "Sva" refers to his own instrument, consisting of will, knowledge, and action, for his own creative activity.

He is called *svairī* because he impels [the universe] at the beginning of creation by his own will; furthermore, he is *svairī*—that is, independent—because he impels his very self toward its own duties. Thus, due to this independence, when he reflects upon an object previously experienced as "this," it is designated as "remembering. This designation consists in the contraction of the various temporal divisions, such as past and future.

The assumption of the contraction of the state of the subject consists in the persistence of that which was previously [experienced]. "Previously" refers to the inward-turned consciousness that perceives an object already experienced;
"even now" means that even at the time of recollection, subsequent to the time of that experience, pure consciousness (saṃvinmātra) indeed persists.
"Of the nature of the self, which is the cognizer of form;
where that cognition of time might occur— neither as 'not then,' nor as 'always,' nor even as 'at one time,'" according to the principle stated in the *Śrīmat-stotrāvalī*.

Because it is impossible for experience to be delimited by distinctions created by time, it follows—by the very fact that it is "the perception of an experienced object"—that the internal object also exists inseparably from the experience; this is established without effort. However, this much remains to be considered: namely, that what was stated as "reflecting 'it is that'" refers precisely to the arising of memory whose essence is the reflective awareness "it is that."

It is to be contemplated: "unconditioned by time. And according to the principle that will be stated later—namely, that within the eternal, supreme subject whose nature is perfect I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*), and which shines at all times as the primordial cognizer—the entire collection of entities from earth up to Sadāśiva exists; such is the nature of that [reality].

If that [perception] of what has arisen is a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) by virtue of its consisting of consciousness (*cinmayatva*), then it must necessarily be accompanied by the full reflective awareness "I" (*aham*). Therefore, for that multitude of objects existing within it, [the awareness] arises from that [subject].

If there is a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of cognition and so forth as being distinct through the modality of "this-ness" (*idantā*) from the nature of the subject (*pramātṛ*), then even in that case— where there is an appearance of distinctness through "this-ness"— there are two possible courses:
if [the object] is related to the state of being that [subject] in its full form as "I" (*aham*).

In that case, since that which has arisen as an entity rests because it is veiled by the sense of "I," one must abide in the state of the venerable Sadāśiva and Īśvara, characterized by the thought: "I am this, and this is I."

Now, if the aspect of "this-ness" (*idantā*) were to rest within that portion which is "not-I" (*ahaṃ na*), then the entire collection of objective phenomena (*bhāvajāta*) would have to appear as "this" (*idam*) alone, through the consciousness of the subject who is the power of illusion (*māyā-pramātṛ*).
As for the term "novelty" (*apūrvatā*): because they appear in ever-new forms, there is this manifestation as "this is it" (*idam-idam*).

It would be mere mental representation (*manubhavana*). Fearing that there might be no recollection in the state of Śiva expressed as "I," nor in the states of Śrī Sadāśiva and Īśvara expressed as "I am this" and "this is mine," nor even in the state of the subject (*pramātṛ-daśā*) where "this-ness" (*idantā*) belongs to Māyā, he says:

He necessarily impels his own instrument—consisting of will, knowledge, and action—which belongs to him, toward his own tasks such as creation and the rest. Furthermore, he is by nature one who employs instruments; moreover, he himself impels his own self toward its own task by its own will upon its own ground.

According to the principle stated—that he unfolds the universe—he does not require another impeller for his own duty, as Brahmā and others do; thus, he is *svairī* (acting according to his own will) and *svatantra* (independent). Because of this independence, the subject (*pramātā*) [remains] even at a time immediately following the experience. (130)

Having remained [in that state], one reflects upon the object experienced as "that. This reflection as "that" consists precisely in this: the reflective awareness of one's own nature as delimited by time;
and that very same [awareness] is also the reflective awareness of internal distinctions such as "this" and "not this," or "prior" and "subsequent."
At the time of recollection, by means of the assistance of another cognition regarding that place and time— namely, the place which serves as the locus for the object of experience such as a jar,
appearing as its qualifier, and the time at that moment, together with Caitra, Maitra, and others residing in that place— [the recollection occurs].

Having been separated from consciousness and subsequently dissolved into that very fullness of I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*) by becoming one with it, he remains exactly as he was— that is, possessing a form that was previously separate. Because that knower (*pramātṛ*) is engaged in the experience of objects other than that [original object], he is awakened by the sight of something resembling the experienced object.
Concealed by the service of time (*kāla*),
that which is denoted by the term "latent impression" (*saṃskāra*) remains within the sphere of the experiencer; then,
through the awakening of that latent impression arising from the sight of a similar object, [there occurs the recollection] of that object at that time.
It casts aside that which conceals it, namely, the form of intervention.
Therein—the object [appears] as before, at the time of experience, appearing as if entirely separated from the knower. If it appears as entirely separated from the knower...

Regarding the phrase "as before," one might suspect that [the object] would appear as "this" (*idantā*) at the time of its experience; having raised this doubt, he refutes it with "not so. He demonstrates that "it"—[the object]—is distinguished from the time of its experience by the appearance at the time of recollection, which belongs to the present.
The manifestation of that which was previously experienced occurs without disregarding its connection to the body, vital breaths, and so forth of the remembering subject.

Regarding the phrase "and therefore": because it manifests by relying precisely upon the connection with the body and so forth of the present remembering subject, that previously experienced object [is manifested] at the present time of recollection.

"Even the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) does not close its eyes. Regarding the phrase "that reflective awareness": based primarily on the wall of reflective awareness of the present time, there is a reflective awareness of the time of the prior experience; thus, it is a contradictory reflective awareness of both prior and subsequent times.

The reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) is said to be his very own nature (*svabhāva*). And thus, it is the Supreme Lord alone who remembers that which was experienced as qualified by such a reflective awareness of contradictory preceding and succeeding times. That this very remembrance of the Supreme Lord takes such a form is what is called "contradiction."

The state of the subject (*pramātṛ*) consists in the assumption of the nature of *māyā*, which is capable of enduring the contraction of time, its divisions (*kalā*), and so forth, characterized by the non-apprehension of what preceded and what followed. As it has been said: "That very [Self] knows, remembers, and conceptualizes through this or that form"—thus the subject consists of both *māyā* and *vidyā*, as well as their non-duality.

Because its object consists of entities distinguished by separate space and time, it is called *māyā*; because it is attached to the light of the subject consisting of consciousness (*saṃvinmaya-pramātṛ*), it is called *vidyā* from that very light. Thus, remembrance is of the nature of a synthesis of both *māyā* and *vidyā*, and for that very reason, it bestows all supernatural powers (*siddhi*).
"Resembling the fourfold wish-fulfilling gem (caturacintāmaṇi)" means: "From that very source" refers to the fact that [the Lord] consists of both Māyā and Vidyā, as well as their non-duality.
Māyā is that which takes the form of the manifestation of duality for the subject; Vidyā is the longing for accomplishment and the bestowing of that [accomplishment].
Thus, it is "resembling the wish-fulfilling gem" because it is skilled in bestowing such accomplishments.
The followers of the Āgamas consider it to be recollection (*smaraṇa*); having observed its nature as a prior reflective awareness (*pūrvāmarśatva*),
it attains a state of being solely composed of internal reflective awareness (*antarvimarśa*).
Recollection alone, having attained the state of meditative absorption and the like, manifests that wealth just as a wish-fulfilling gem does.

By the compound *pūrvānubhūtārthopalabdhi*—an instrumental-tatpuruṣa ending in a *tṛn*-suffix—the experience, like the subject, consists of consciousness (*saṃvinmayatva*); thus, although it lacks contact with time, by the word *anubhūte* (in the locative), there is a contact with past time. By the word *artha*, there is the state of resting in the object.

By the term "perceived" (*upalabdha*), he demonstrates that both [the object and the subject] find their rest in the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) through the two relations of difference and non-difference established with respect to the object of cognition (*prameya*) and the cognizer (*pramātṛ*).
This is shown by the phrase "the perception of an object previously experienced. In this [definition], the experience and the object reside in a single cognizer.
Because it consists of a single unified state characterized by rest, its nature is one of non-differentiation from the various subjects;

we shall explain this in the section beginning with "action, relation," and so forth. The remaining seven verses are intended to establish this very principle of memory. In that regard, concerning the object of memory, [it says] "someone," and so on.
If one among those who deny the self and the Lord were to say, "In this case, memory exists;

therefore, it is a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) consisting of superimposition," then for that very reason, the object experienced through the conceptualization of memory is not manifested by it.
This is what was stated in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the object which is cognition in the form of manifestation.

Since only direct experience (*anubhava*) illuminates an object, conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), which do not touch the object, [cannot do so]. Previously, by whatever experience that object—the domain of experience—was brought to illumination as "this," at the time of recollection (*smṛti*), it now becomes a mere form of renown (*kīrtimātramūrti*). At that very moment, [the object] is [re-presented].
Because it has perished, that [object] remains as a mere story and is not manifested through memory of experience; for,

according to the principle stated that "vision is self-manifesting and is not known by another," one cognition cannot be cognized by another cognition, and since that [cognition] no longer exists, there can be no manifestation of the object manifested by it.
Because there is no manifestation of the object manifested by that [cognition] due to its non-existence,

the claim "I remember an experienced object" would likewise be a case where, even though the memory has that [past object] as its object, it is determined otherwise; thus, as was stated, it is merely an error regarding the basis of what was seen, and consequently, it results in being nothing but an illusion.
"It was previously stated that [the object] is mere illusion; that very point has now returned.
To one who speaks thus, it is replied:
"That which was called the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) in the form of a rememberer is [present] at its own time; by implication, this means at the time of the recollection."
The previously manifested— that is, previously revealed through experience— particular (svalakṣaṇa) characterized by specific place and time,
which consists of a collection of various universals such as "gold-ness" and so forth; reflecting upon that [particular] as "this," [one perceives it] not merely as the appearance of a golden jar.

Alternatively, the phrase "the memory which, by its power, would manifest [objects] endowed with appearances such as gold" indicates a restrictive rule (*niyama*) through the injunctive form of the verb "would manifest," meaning that it necessarily manifests them. Even though you have stated that memory— which follows upon experience— is of the nature of error (*bhrānti*), [it nonetheless manifests the object].

The meaning is this: when the determination of the object is overwhelmed, that conceptual memory reaches a state of deep sleep or fainting characterized by dullness, and thus it does not manifest the experienced object. Therefore, as long as the determination of the experienced object occurs within the conceptual memory, to that extent it is "from that [object]," namely, that memory.

By implication, it follows that "that experienced object is manifested" (p. 105); for if there were no manifestation, the determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*) would be like that of a blind person, since it is that [manifestation] which makes the object manifest.

Therefore, when an object is manifested in memory or conceptual construction, that manifestation of the object as "that" occurs through the exclusion of the time of the present experience. If it were through exclusion, there would follow the consequence of the absence of the reflective awareness "that"; [thus, it must be] by way of accepting the time of the experience.

If it were the case that this [object] appears as "this," then such an undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) would follow. Therefore, in the manifestation of a remembered object, the time of the previous experience—which serves as a qualifier for the experienced object—depends upon the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇya) of that previously experienced entity; thus, with respect to the objective portion within the domain of experience, [the memory does not apprehend the object as "this"].
It must be taken into account. For that portion of the object to be known, which is now being clung to as having the nature of manifestation and experience,
one must also take as an objective support the time of the appearance of the body, vital breath, and so forth of the subject who is the rememberer at that very moment.

In the state where there is a knower and a form of the object to be known, the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of that portion [of the cognition] is established as being non-different from the determination (*abhiniveśa*);

therefore, it is remembered as the manifestation of the object. Furthermore, even the contact with both times must be required for the category of "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*), which is the object of knowledge such as memory, direct experience, and so forth.
The essential nature [of an object] is merely the appearance of one or another form, such as gold-ness;
likewise, the existence, pot-ness, substance-ness, brilliance of gold, and so forth [are its forms].
This is because the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) extends to each individual appearance.
The locus of that sound is that which produces an object undivided from the distinctions of its own manifestations.

Thus, according to the principle to be explained later, the manifestation of "golden-ness" and so forth— which resides within the manifestation of the jar as its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)— is, through the operation of the respective means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*),
that very same manifestation of the jar itself; it is merely that manifestation of the jar, with the manifestation of golden-ness and so forth serving as its qualifying attributes (*viśeṣaṇa*).
Through the blending [of perceptions], it becomes manifest, as if by the coalescence of the light of a thousand lamps.

Even though that manifestation of a jar lacks manifestation through the blending of other manifestations such as its being made of gold, it nonetheless [becomes manifest] precisely through the intermingling with the manifestation of the time of the experience "that."

The subject (pramātṛ) renders that manifested appearance which has been experienced into the state of being an object of memory by means of its specific characteristic (svālakṣaṇya); this is the ellipsis to be supplied. It will be stated later that "it is precisely the power of time (kāla-śakti) that effects the differentiation of entities. He reiterates here the very point already stated in the passage "in every case there is a difference of manifestation" regarding the experienced [object]. Thus, first, concerning the experienced...
The statement "the jar exists in the earth as its own specific characteristic" (svalakṣaṇa) means that it possesses the status of being an object.

Through the conjunction with the temporal manifestation of the experience arising from the assistance of the previous perceiver’s form, body, and so forth, there is merely the manifestation of the jar within that [experience].

Or rather, even when memory is distracted by other appearances such as gold and so forth, the memory of that [object]— the jar— is extremely clear; for even when there is an extreme clarification through the recollection of parts such as the face and so on of an experienced object, [the memory remains vivid].

At that time, the reflective awareness of "this is his" does not break off from its continuity. This is because, due to the non-manifestation [of the object] in common to others, there is no such manifestation;
that is, an object experienced by one subject is not manifested as being common to the class of other subjects.

Thus, that kind of manifestation shines forth by means of the teeth; such a manifestation for the yogin is indeed a creative transformation (*nirmāṇa*), and not the illumination of an object previously experienced.
"Brahmā said" refers to the scriptures (*āgama*) and so forth, which consist of manifestations spoken by Brahmā and others.

The means is the continuous succession of recollections regarding the essential nature of Brahmā and others as experienced through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Even in that case, the manifestation of the appearance of non-Brahmā and so forth would manifest only as an experience for the practitioner who is fully immersed in the essential nature of that Brahmā and others.
The rule is stated that [consciousness] manifests [the object] precisely through an application in a positive form (*vidhirūpa*). "At its own time" means at the time of recollection.
By the word "perceiving," it is indicated that there is contact with the aspect of the object previously experienced.
"Of the pure" means of the manifestation of the jar, which is the object of cognition even when devoid of qualifiers such as gold and so forth; "that" refers to it.

Time, which is the cause for the attainment of specific characteristics (*svālakṣaṇya*), has been shown. "Only this much" means that the very manifestation of the mere appearance of the experienced jar is the unerring body of memory; yet, due to the intention of the cognizer's desire, it takes on the form of the experienced object as qualified by its various attributes.
The word "atha" (then) indicates that clarity arises.

He states this very point with the word "tat" (that): it [the consciousness] would manifest that clarity through a body mixed with the appearances of all things, such as the self and so forth—the object previously experienced.

And according to the stated principle that "it is that very Supreme Lord who remembers [the object] as qualified by the gold and other attributes which serve as its qualifiers," the Supreme Lord Himself, having assumed the form of the rememberer, would manifest the experienced object through the power of memory (*smṛti-śakti*). That [object] is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

It has been stated that [the object] should appear through memory; thus, when the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is manifested in memory, that particular characteristic would appear to that memory as "this-ness" (*idantayā*), with an external differentiation just as it did in the original experience.
This very appearance of the particular characteristic externally within memory is what constitutes the manifestation of the particular characteristic in memory.
To dispel the doubt that [the object] appears as something external, he explains with the words "And not...

Since there is a distinction between the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) which is the object of memory and the direct experience of it as "this," it is not logical for that which is being remembered to appear as "that. Only that which is being directly experienced [could so appear].
"It does not belong to that" refers to the external manifestation of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). "Of those belonging to different times" means:
"this one," "this very one," and "that one. There exists a unity among the cognitions of experience, conceptualization, and recollection, even when they pertain to different or non-different times.
(107) This is because the object already experienced is indeed the object of both conceptualization and memory;

for what is called "synthetic integration" (*anusandhāna*) can only be established through two cognitions that are aware of the preceding and succeeding moments. And yet, it is established by the preceding...

When there is an identity between the two supreme cognitions in the form of "I," that alone is shown to be the Knower through grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). This is expressed as "this is he," which is the manifestation of the clarity of the very nature of the subject (*pramātṛ*) that had been concealed— thus [it is said] regarding the cognitions of experience and so forth.
The agent is one who possesses independence regarding the severing of fetters and so forth.

If this experienced object, like the experience itself, were to appear as "this" from the memory-cognition as something distinct— separate [from the subject]— then that appearance of the remembered object as "that" [would not occur].

That very [particular] would not exist. That object of memory would necessarily be an object of cognition. If this were so, how could there be the manifestation of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) in memory?
By the phrase "previously manifested," it is implied that at the present time of recollection, that particular does not [exist].

[Objection: But was it not stated that its manifestation occurs precisely at the time of the prior experience? That [word] "then" refers to the time of experience. "This" refers to the jar, which is of the nature of a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). "This" [in the present context] refers to the very external appearance. [Reply: Then, what [happens] now at the time of recollection regarding that particular characteristic which was manifested "then"?
We say it is "investigation" (*vimarśana*).

Now, by the very sentence you have stated, it follows that the two illuminations related to the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) occur at different times; why is this so? Because they are at different times, what [is the consequence]?
A refutation follows: "Both" refers to manifestation (*prakāśana*) and investigation (*vimarśana*).
According to the principle that will be stated later—that nothing could exist without the reflection of its own nature—both of these are mutually dependent for their very existence.

Not so. It is cognitions alone that manifest. According to the principle stated—that [cognitions] are of different times, different objects, and different forms—cognition alone, which consists of momentary states mutually distinct from one another, is reality for that proponent of the theory of the stream of cognition (*jñāna-santāna-vādin*). For him, there is the experience "this."

Regarding the two acts of recollection— illumination and discernment— the state of being born from the synthesis of cognitions such as direct experience, characterized by the temporal distinction expressed as "this," constitutes the persistence of the non-born. Just as this is to be resolved through the acceptance of one's own Self in the form of Maheśvara, who possesses the powers of cognition, memory, and exclusion, so too is direct experience [to be resolved].

Furthermore, the difference in time between the two acts of manifestation and reflective awareness— corresponding to recollection and its form— is indeed irreconcilable. According to the principle stated as "the agent is the knower," [the subject] consists of the Great Lord in the nature of both agent and knower.
In our own philosophical system, which asserts the existence of one's own self (*svātman*), there are cognitions such as direct experience (*anubhava*) and so forth.

[The thought] "this is this very thing" or "that"— even though these refer to different times— by not abandoning their respective distinct times and by appearing as a unity within one's own self, the independent cognizer (*pramātṛ*) is that which persists through those three times.

By the principle that will be explained— that [the object] shines through the superimposition of the "I" upon the Self— for as long as one, having inwardly turned, superimposes the experience and the experienced object onto one's own Self and reflects upon that experienced portion of the object, for that long, of the light which consists of the experience...

The manifestation of an external existence at that moment becomes a present, inwardly directed state within the reflective awareness (*vimarśana*) which is of the nature of recollection; this very reflective awareness constitutes the superior leading power (*netṛtva*) of that subject over the sensations of experience and so forth, regarding those experiences of perception and the like.

In the conjunction of recollection and experience as "this is that," in the separation of conceptualization and recollection as "this," and in the separation of experience and recollection as "this alone"— by means of such operations according to one's will, autonomy (svātantrya) is realized.
Since the states of being a knower and being an agent are inseparable from one another, this very state of being a knower is called agency.
He demonstrates that very point with the words "they experienced the jar.

By superimposing both the experience and the jar upon their own self, there arises a reflective awareness (*vimarśana*) that rests solely upon the experienced object; this is the realization of the identity of consciousness and the self, which is non-different from the one who realizes it.
In order to demonstrate their identity, it is stated through grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) that "He alone is to be known.

Through this synthesis— in the form of recollection and experience imbued with wonder, expressed as "This is He"— there occurs the manifestation and flashing forth of the true nature of the subject (*pramātṛ-tattva*), which had been concealed by the power of *māyā*.
Recognition itself has been indicated. As the author himself stated in the *Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi*:
"Thus, by those who deny self-awareness..."
"That reality of the subject (pramātṛ-tattva) which was defiled by those who spoke [otherwise], has now been made manifest by silencing them with clear arguments," and so forth.
Now, according to the principle you have stated— that the manifestation [of an object] is its simultaneous external appearance—

if it is the very prior experience itself that constitutes the "this" at that time, then the nature of the external appearance of the object— which was experienced as "this" and is now being remembered as "that"— is established.
Prakāśa (138): Since there can be no manifestation of that which is being remembered as "that" without a prior experience,
let it be said by the rememberer that this experience— just like the object previously experienced— is now made an object of the memory.

(p. 109) According to the principle stated—that the seer himself is merely imagined—since there is no cognizer, what is the point of the "oneness of consciousness" with that which is not worldly, i.e., with that which is well-known in the world as being of the nature of resting within that [consciousness]? To dispel this misconception held by others, he says: "Previously," etc.
Just as at the time of experience, the object— which is the objective content of that experience—
appears as distinct from that experience,
so too at the time of recollection, the experience appears as something separate from that memory-cognition, as "this was a prior experience."

"It does not appear" is a dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). Furthermore, just as in the case of recollective cognition (*smṛti-jñāna*) an object experienced as it was appears as "that," so too the experience itself does not appear as "that. This also serves as a dissimilar example—[distinguished] from recollective cognition.

This is the object previously experienced. "Previously" means having the nature of appearing externally as before. Nor is a distinction from memory logical; according to the principle just stated, it does not appear as distinct because, at the time of recollection, the object that is the content of memory lacks external appearance, unlike the object that was the content of the original experience. This...
For that very reason—[as stated in the previous verse]—even the prior experience does not appear as distinct from the memory;

this is the corroborative instance (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). If so, what is "both"? It is the experience and the experienced object both [appearing] in the memory. Now, in what manner do they appear? He says: "I experienced. [This refers to] the sense of "I" (*asmadartha*).

They appear precisely as resting within [the Self]. The connection with the preceding verse is that both—the notion "I" and the unity of preceding and succeeding cognitions—[rest therein]. Furthermore, at the time of recollection, the subject whose nature is "I" experiences both [the past object and the past cognition] having brought them to rest within himself, and it appears as "I experienced. This is what is meant by "I experienced."

Because the time of speaking (*būtakāla*) is indicated by the verbal suffix (*luṅ*), the word "previously" (*prāk*) has its syntactic order altered. Because the meaning of "we" (*asmad-artha*) is indicated by the first person plural ending (*uttama-puruṣa*), the word "I" (*aham*) also has its syntactic order altered.
In this context, there is a point of contrast (*vaidharmya*) regarding the fact that in memory (*smṛti*), the direct experience (*anubhava*) does not appear separately.

He states an example by way of similarity: just as at the time of experience, this jar appeared as distinct from the experience itself, so too it is at the time of recollection. Therefore, this experience does not appear as something separate from the cognition of recollection.

Furthermore, just as at the time of recollection the object being remembered does not appear as distinct from that [recollection]— as he will say: "That which was seen by me is remembered as such," and so forth— and therefore, due to the cognition of memory, it does not shine forth as separate under the form "that," in the same way, the experience (*anubhava*) also does not shine forth as a separate object under the form "that."

Thus, in both ways, there is a dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). An object experienced at the time of recollection is its "prior nature" (*pūrva-svabhāva*) from before. Therefore, just as in the case of the cognition of recollection, an external object does not appear; for at the time of recollection, that object lacks an external manifestation, just as it did at the time of the original experience. Thus, [it is] of the object.
