Because of the absence of separate existence, even the prior experience does not appear as something separate; this is the corroborative instance (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
If that is so, how do both [the experience and its object] appear at the time of recollection? He says: "I experienced."

(110) It appears as resting solely within our own self. If one asks what is meant by this: it is because the Self—which has the nature of being inward-turned (*antarmukha-svabhāva*), consisting of the consciousness of prior and subsequent experience, conceptualization, and recollection, and whose essential form is "I"—is that wherein those two [the object and the subject] ascend and find rest; therefore [it appears so].

Because, by means of that [subsequent] cause, the self-luminous nature of the prior experience—as consciousness—is made manifest. Regarding the phrase "of that which was dissolved therein": it is stated that even objects such as a jar, having been dissolved into that subsequent experience, are manifested through their own self-luminosity. Furthermore, the cognizer, whose nature is that of a rememberer, [perceives] the experience and the object...

It has also been stated that the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is "it appears as if superimposed upon the self. He clarifies this very point by means of the maxim: "The base and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix together. Regarding the phrase "projected by number":
in the case of *anvabhūvam*, it is projected by the singular number; [the term] "possessing that" refers to that which possesses number, namely, that which has become the agent.
In our view, the experience—which is the form of the meaning of the base (prakṛti)—is augmented and intensified within the meaning of the suffix (pratyaya).

Through that experience, the object experienced is likewise augmented right there; it is not [augmented] independently. Without the mediation of experience, this experienced object cannot [exist] by itself.

(140) It does not come to rest in the sense of "us. Regarding the phrase "for that purpose": because there is no resting in the object itself that was experienced in the sense of "us," it comes to rest precisely through the medium of the experience. In the expression "I experienced," [resting occurs] by means of the object of experience (*anubhāvya*) as its own object.

Action has been specified because it is not yet established [as a distinct entity]. Furthermore, at the time of the experience "this is a jar" regarding cloth and so forth, the sense of the past tense (*bhūtārtha*)—namely, "I experienced"—does not apply to the referent of the word "I.
For indeed, the experience and the memory do not appear as separate.

Because it appears through the superimposition of the self in the form "I have experienced," as stated in the previous verse [beginning with] "aparārdha," there is therefore an identity of cognitions; this is the connection with the preceding verse. In the word "anvabhūvam" (I have experienced), the *luṅ* suffix indicates the past tense. The word "prāk" (previously) is displaced in its position [and should be understood as applying to the first person]. It is the first person (*uttama-puruṣa*).

Since the meaning of "we" (asmad) is already expressed by the word *puruṣeṇa*, the term *aham* ("I") is also displaced [from its expected position]. As for the word *ārohaṇam*, the root *ruh-* also carries the sense of the causative (*ṇij*)—[as in] "he causes to ascend. Who has ever said that the meaning of "he says" (*āha*) does not exist separately from experience and memory? If it is argued that it does not appear as having a separate meaning, then the meaning itself [does not appear].
If it is argued that the experience does not appear [as the object], then why does it not appear by way of its own nature as having the form of a broad base and belly (i.e., the shape of the object)?

To say "it appears" is common to both the object and the experience. Even if there is no similarity between the object and the experience, the objection—that the experience shines forth like the object—is not [valid].

It occurs as follows: one must first admit that both [the object and its cognition] manifest within memory. The following passage, beginning with "For instance" (*tathā hi*), demonstrates precisely that the experience does not appear separately.
Just as [it is accepted], so too is it accepted by all proponents of philosophical systems that the past and the future... [are perceived].

(p. 111) By the [Yoga] Sūtra, "The knowledge of another's mind through its mental modification" (*pratyayasya paracittajñānam*), it is stated that even the mind of another becomes an object [of cognition]. In that context, regarding the sūtra "The knowledge of another's mind through its mental modification," it is *sattva* alone—whose nature consists of the qualities (*guṇa*) transformed into the form of momentary cognitions such as those of a pot or a cloth—that [becomes the object].
If it is argued that [the mind] is not denoted by the word "citta," then why is it said that the object of the yogi’s *saṃyama* is the mental modification (*pratyaya*)?
In this context, *saṃyama* refers to the [restraint of] the sense organs with respect to their objects.

If [the yogic cognition] were produced from sense-contact, then the cognition of Caitra, Maitra, and so forth would be possible as having an objective support (*sālambana*), yet it would not be possible for that [cognition] to have an objective support [in the case of the yogi]. Therefore, the yogi’s cognition of another person’s experience (141) [would be impossible];
[this applies] even to his own prior experience.

Anticipating the objection that "let it be made an object [of cognition]," [the author] shows by means of the final sūtra that the example— "it appears thus"— is unestablished (*asiddha*) because one experiences what belongs to another. Alternatively, even if the example is established through admission, in the present context of the meaning "I experienced," this Caitra—
He indicates this by the remainder of the aphorism: "Or even in the state of the object.
Even for yogis, such [objects] do not appear in other systems of perception;
rather, they appear as being based solely on their own self-awareness, whether in the state of the subject or even in the state of the object. (5)

Even for Caitra, Maitra, and others who possess the application of cognitions such as experience and the like, these do not appear as objects possessing external reality when there arises a specific, world-transcending knowledge through the awakening of *bhāvanā* in another system of vision.
As it has been said: "And this cognition does not shine as 'this-ness' (*idantā*). This "this-ness" [is the characteristic of the object].

Ignorance is not something other than that which appears as another body; yet when that [other] is known, it does not appear at all. That which shines forth as the supreme is the very body of the "I"; thus, even the knowledge of the supreme is one's own self. Therefore, perceptions such as Caitra and others have consciousness alone as their sole means of proof, and are thus of the nature of self-luminosity.

The subjects (*pramātṛ*)—such as Caitra, Maitra, and others—are self-luminous forms of "I. Furthermore, because the yogin enters the bodies of others such as Caitra and Maitra, he assimilates those subjects into his own self, thinking, "Caitra, Maitra, and the rest are not [other than] I.

Thus, for that yogin, those Caitras, Maitras, and others appear as having the singular form of his own "I-ness" (*ahantā*), since they are measured solely by his own self-awareness (*svasaṃvid*). Indeed.

If these [objects] appear as "this one experiences," they fall into the status of the object of knowledge (*meyapada*); however, when it is "I experienced," this appears in the form of the object within the state of the subject (*mātṛpada*). Here, for yogins, this is limited consciousness (*parimita-cit*), which is distinct from the cognition of subjects such as those practicing loving-kindness (*maitrādi-pramātṛ-vijñāna*), and for that very reason, it is capable of making that [object] its own domain.

There exists a supramundane knowledge (*lokottara-jñāna*) arising from meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), mnemonic concentration (*dhāraṇā*), and so forth. Within that yogic knowledge, Caitra, Maitra, and others appear as objects under the aspect of "the seen.
To demonstrate that this is indeed the case, every proponent establishes it through corroboration, beginning with the words "for instance" (*tathā hi*).

For the Sugatas, as stated by the phrase "the Sugatas [hold that] the continuum of cognition alone is reality" (p. 112), for those who maintain that the continuum of cognition is the sole reality, cognition is of a single nature consisting of self-luminosity; such is that [cognition].

Regarding the statement "knowledge [is known] by another knowledge": if the yogin’s knowledge were something to be known, then that very nature of his knowledge—which consists in its manifestation through being un-knowable by anything else—would itself have to be manifested. Therefore, even for the Buddhists, knowledge must be knowable by another knowledge.
It does not exist.

Even for the Sāṃkhyas, [the reflection] belongs to the Puruṣa, who is of the nature of consciousness, who has transcended the insentient principles beginning with Earth and ending with Primordial Matter (prakṛti), and who is therefore beyond the stage of being an object of cognition; it is of the nature of a reflection.

Apprehension is merely a reflection (*chāyā*). Since the *puruṣa* is by nature imperceptible and does not fall within the category of the perceptible, how could that reflection—which is of the nature of apprehension—be an object of cognition?
[This is so] for those who maintain that the self, being distinct from each individual perceiver, is eternally inferable.
For the Vaiśeṣikas, since [the soul] is distinct [from the body], just as [properties like] "possibility" reside in milk and so forth,

how could knowledge residing in Caitra, Maitra, and others— which belongs to another [substratum] as its inherent cause— be grasped by the mind existing within the body of a yogi? [This would require] the yogi’s entry into the interior of those bodies of Caitra, Maitra, and the rest.

In that state, for the cognizer—such as Caitra or Maitra—the sense of "I" (*ahantā*) which manifests within the form of the cognizer as associated with the body, instruments, and so forth, causes the mutual distinction between selves (*ātman*) postulated by the Vaiśeṣikas to dissolve.
Furthermore, because the self is directly perceived by the yogi, its status as being eternally inferable (*nityānumeyatva*) also dissolves. This is [the nature of] experience.

If one cognition were to be known by another cognition, then that [second] cognition would also have to be known by yet another cognition, and that too would require another; this results in an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) that undermines the very root of the argument. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), it is meant that at the time of recollection, the [original] object would be non-existent; therefore, [the conclusion is] that cognition cannot be known by another cognition.

Because of the absence of objectivity (*vedyatva*), at the time when a yogi perceives the minds of others—such as Caitra or Maitra—the jar, pleasure, and so forth, manifest within that very manifestation accompanied by the "I"-form belonging to the cognizing subject (*pramātṛ*) who resides within the bodies of Caitra, Maitra, and others. "To this extent" means: the manifestation is precisely of this much. "In that" means: in such a manifestation.

The light [of consciousness] shines as "this" with respect to that jar, pleasure, and so forth; yet it is said to be "the light residing therein"—meaning that the light residing within the bodies of Caitra, Maitra, and others, shines for the yogin precisely as "I" by virtue of its self-luminosity. Even though they are insentient, when Caitra, Maitra, and the rest are made into subjects of cognition...
Even while perceiving [the world] as being in a state of impurity, the yogi conceives of this as "supreme knowledge" because he has not yet dissolved the distinction between self and other. However,
having attained the pinnacle of yoga, he perceives everything as being of the nature of the state of the Supreme Lord.

If it is argued that one perceives the distinction between self and other as merely imagined by oneself—thus, let the cognition of Caitra, Maitra, and so forth be identical to the cognition of a yogi—nevertheless, the point at issue remains: "I experienced [it]. By the words beginning with "for instance" (*tathā hi*), the author demonstrates that this [ordinary experience] is not similar to the experience of a yogi.
In the cognition "this Caitra experiences the cloth," it is the experience residing in another— such as Caitra or Maitra—
that is manifested. In the [cognition] "I experience," which occurs through the appropriation of the self,
the repose within the "I" portion of the experience remains untouched by the "this."

(113) Since experience does not appear as something separate from the being itself, it is said that the unity of cognitions occurring at different times is what is known. For experience indeed does not appear separately in memory like the former object; rather, it appears through the superimposition of the self in the form, "I experienced [this] individually."
If it is argued that due to the influence of fatigue, the experience does not appear as distinct from the memory, then [we reply]:

in that case, a certain specific reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) in the form of memory is perceived as reflecting upon that experience, thinking, "This was an experience. Or else, what more need be said?

The opponent’s intention is as follows: "Since the lotus-like face is seen, the form of 'this-ness' (idantā) is the beloved's feet; no other distinct reflective awareness (parāmarśāntara) is perceived. Therefore, even according to the distinction between these two types of reflective awareness, why is it not conventionally designated as appearing separately in experience and memory?"
She denies it, saying, "I did not see that. Yet, this experience is remembered as distinct and separate:

"This was my experience," or "That was seen by me. Such a memory—that "it was seen by me"—is formed together with the object seen (the jar), the act of seeing, and the experience thereof; thus, the meaning of "me" (asmat) is "seen by me" (dṛṣṭam).

The analysis and clarification of memory once it has come to rest—that vision was mine—is here also [to be understood] as a vision consisting of experience; the meaning is that the vision rested within my own self (*asmadartha*).
Furthermore, the phrase "that vision was mine" and "it was seen by me" are used with a different word order.

He connects them: here, both of these are of the nature of recollection— the mere reflective awareness in the form of "that was sight" (which is pure sight alone), and the reflective awareness of the act of seeing which rests upon an object in the form of "I saw."
This is the grammatical analysis of the memory characterized by the appropriate reflective awareness, "I experienced. The word *api* is used in the sense of "also.

For a person who has attained proficiency, that perception—such as "this vision was mine"—does not occur in the same manner as the perception of common worldly objects like jars or cloths being perceived by the world. That [vision] is not some ordinary worldly thing...

One does not consider one's own vision to be separate [from itself]; nevertheless, when something is remembered in this way through differentiation— as if it were the discernment of some other [subject]—
such a recollection is the "explanation" (*vyākaraṇa*), that is, the manifestation (*vyaktīkaraṇa*) of the memory (*smṛti*) that is about to be described.

If one reflects upon the aforementioned foundational realization of memory, thinking: "Just as the analysis of the meaning of a word's base and suffix is merely conceptual, so too here [in this context] is there a mere analytical presentation for the sake of the qualified practitioner; even I, though possessing discernment, have experienced this."

Then, one does not experience the perception "that likeness was mine" as something separate, because apart from the head there is no Rāhu; just as the manifestation "this is the head of Rāhu" is considered conceptual by the discerning person, so too is the thought "that likeness was mine."
(p. 114) Even that distinctness of the experience as "this" (idantā) is considered conceptual;

one who considers himself a discerning investigator treats it as ultimate. Otherwise, if he does not consider this difference to be conceptual, then in the case of "this is a jar," the jar being remembered in its own manifestation—

It depends upon a prior experience; likewise, for its own manifestation, that experience too would have to depend upon another prior experience, leading to an infinite regress. [This applies to the world, which is like the perceived objects such as jars and cloths, and is unestablished.]

He clarifies the very meaning already stated: by the use of the pronoun "that" (*tad*), which indicates that both the object seen and the act of seeing have been experienced, he refers to the visible jar and the nature of its perception as "that jar" and "that experience."

The attainment of the status of being an object of a prior experience is said to consist of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*); otherwise, in the absence of such verbal reflection, there would be only "seeing" (*dṛk*). Therefore, it follows that having established the experience, it has been reached by means of another experience. In that case as well, it consists of seeing.

Regarding the statement "experienced by another visual perception" (*dṛgantareṇānubhūtam*), even if that [first] perception is experienced by another perception, you have stated that this is not in consideration of that other perception, but rather while reflecting upon the original cognition (*mūlapratīti*).
If one asks what kind of original cognition that memory has as its basis, he says: "By me..."

The fundamental cognition consists in resting upon the referent of the word "I" as "this was seen. Regarding this, he raises an objection: even in the case of the thought "I saw it before," there must be a refinement consisting of the experience of that very object which you yourself accept as the fundamental cognition.

Just as whiteness does not rest within the mouth [of a woman], it has been said that vision, too, is "seen" because it has become a qualifier of the visible object; thus, the beloved’s face itself becomes the very object of vision. It is not, however, that the beloved’s face is the object of the act of seeing as something mounted upon the self.

Even the perception of the completion of an action, because it rests upon the visible object, is similar to the visible object itself—[as in the phrase] "because the completion of the action arises. Thus, he does not know his own words, the speech issuing from his own mouth, as the ultimate truth; he does not know the meaning of those words in their ultimate sense.

He does not understand this statement that "the object (*karman*) is that which is pervaded by the action of the agent (*kartṛ*). And so he explains it further: [the author] says that the action resides in the agent alone—just as it was stated that the act of seeing comes to rest in the king who is the observer, and not in the servants. By the action of the agent...

In the statement "the object is that which is pervaded," the action merely rests upon the agent and not upon the object; therefore, the acts of cognition and action depend upon the subject (*pramātṛ*). By the followers of Jaimini—that is, even by the Mīmāṃsakas—it is held that the ritual procedure itself bestows the respective fruits of the actions; thus, their view consists of a creative intuition (*dṛśi*) whose nature is the realization of the fruit (*phala-bhāvanā*).
Consciousness—by implication—is said to rest solely within the subject in the form of the illuminator.
(p. 115) The "seen-ness" or manifestness of forms such as a jar is not a property of the object, such as the jar itself.

Even in the Prābhākara view, because consciousness is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), although it is independent, the word "object" (*meyā*) is stated in the Sūtra merely to explain that the object of cognition culminates in the cognizer (*pramātṛ*).
Therefore, these two expressions— "I experienced" and "it was experienced by me"— are merely verbal [distinctions].

There is merely a difference in phrasing, but no difference in meaning between these two. Others, however, join them by reversing the order; for [the word] *anvabhūvam* is the appropriate reference to what was just mentioned—namely, "I saw her in the assembly" (*dṛgāsīt sā me*).

Regarding the application [of the term] "prediction" (*vyākaraṇa*) to memory (*smṛti*): the word "also" (*api*) functions in the sense of "and. An object such as blue, which was previously perceived by non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*)—which directly perceives the mere thing as qualified by place, time, and form—is here [in the present]... having become thus.
As long as something has not been brought to rest within a particular reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the cognizer, it is not remembered.
For example, the grass, leaves, and so forth seen by a person running on a path in a non-conceptual manner are not remembered because they have not been grasped in their specific forms,
such as "this is this grass" or "this is straw."
Just as that which was not previously remembered is not later remembered, so too an object, even if seen,
is not remembered later. Therefore, at the time of the non-conceptual [cognition] immediately following the non-conceptual,
that non-conceptual cognition did not previously appear as having the nature of "blue" and so forth.

Or rather, this very point must be investigated. Regarding the phrase "that very thing": having raised the objection that while the manifestation of the experience may not occur in the *smṛti* (recollection), why should the *nirvikalpaka* (non-conceptual) [perception] not manifest in conceptual cognition (*vikalpa-jñāna*)?
He says "yā etat" etc., meaning: "I see this."
Furthermore, that which is primarily perception preceded by the recollection (*parāmarśa*) of a previously seen object,

as well as that which is primarily the recollection of a mere object— such as "this is a jar"— both of these types of conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*) depend upon a preceding non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpakadarśana*).

"Avasātarī" means that consciousness is inherent (*samaveta*) without distinction within the subject whose nature is that of the conceptualizer. According to the principle stated—that it appears during the ascent of the "I"-sense—it is just as [consciousness] is inherent without division in the one who experiences and remembers at the time of recollection; so too it is at the time of conceptualization.

The non-conceptual [cognition] is inherent in the conceptualizer; therefore, even the non-conceptual does not become an object for conceptual cognition—this is the meaning. Here, "vision" refers to non-conceptual cognition, which at its own time is imperishable and, for that very reason, innate.

By means of its own body, which consists of the nature of self-knowledge, it should manifest at all times— even during the time of conceptual cognition and the like— in such a form as "I am not this form," even during the time of conceptual cognition and the like.
(116) Such a body is not abandoned. And that perception, which consists of non-conceptualization (*nirvikalpa*), is at its own time an unending manifestation;

it is manifested by another cognition, such as conceptual thought (*vikalpa*), and for this very reason, it is the consciousness-light whose form is the mere utterance "I" (*aham*). This is the [nature] of that non-conceptual knowledge.

An investigation into the aspect of conceptualizing relations: at that time, in its own moment, it does not exist anywhere as a subordinate member (*aṅga*)—neither with respect to itself nor with respect to an object—but rather becomes the principal (*aṅgin*). If it becomes the principal, then that non-conceptual [state] is indeed a conceptual cognition. However, even the subsequent ascertainment (*avasāya*) following that non-conceptual [state]...

Conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*) as well [is such]. "Thus it has become" means that at its own time it is not illuminated by anything else; the word "also" (*api*) indicates that it is illuminated even in the form of "I. By that conceptual cognition which arises immediately after the non-conceptual [perception], [the object] is thus established.

Having reflected upon the object of cognition as "I perceive this," it is either reflected upon through the reflection of the experience itself— preceded by the reflection on the sense of "I" (*asmadartha*) within its state of presentness—
or it is reflected upon by means of the phrase "this," which, by virtue of appearing as if directly perceived, constitutes a conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*).

It has been shown that the function of perception is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*). [In the cognition] "this is a jar," it is merely the object itself that is apprehended by being restricted to its own essence. By the word "this" in this conceptualization (*vikalpa*), its appearance as if it were perception is stated. "Therein" means: it is seen in the final conceptualization, "this is a jar."

Since there is no separate reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of perception and so forth that possess such a form [as "this"], what room is there for the suspicion that "this" belongs to the perception? Consequently, in the final conceptualization, because there is an absence of a reflective awareness of the form of perception as "it is seen," by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), [the thought] "I see this" occurs through the "I-ness" (*ahantā*) alone.

"Apprehension (*parāmarśa*) is observed even in its absence"—this means that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) occurs even when there is no apprehension, as it is possible for one with closed eyes; for when the cognizer has his eyes closed, the object such as "blue" is not seen, yet a conceptual construction related to it [still arises]. Thus he says:
By the words "himself" and so forth:
thus, whether in memory, or in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), or even in a cognition whose ultimate aim is exclusion (*apohana*),
he is determined to be established within the internal manifestation itself.

Thus, according to the principle to be explained, the determination (*adhyavasāya*) which culminates in a clearly manifest object, when it itself does not touch the object, is like something closed; the manifestation (*bhāsa*) is the object as it is in its innate state. In a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) such as "I see," that which is expressed by "I see" is the act of seeing.
Because it is established in the object, it is included within the referent of "I" (*asmadartha*).

For this very reason, it is the locus of the state of "I. It rests in the cognizer, the subject (*pramātṛ*). Therefore, it is perceived as having the nature of "I," and thus [it is distinct from] other conceptual cognitions (*vikalpabodha*).

An existent thing does not cause its own self to be known; the meaning is that memory alone does not cause cognition to be known by another cognition, nor does conceptual construction (vikalpa) cause it to be known. "Ascertainment" (avasā) means determination (avasāya). By the word "inherent" (samaveta) — [the sentence continues].

He speaks of the non-distinctness of the *kalpa* (the cosmic cycle): "The independent one who brings [all] to rest. According to the principle stated in the *Śrī Virūpākṣapañcāśikā*, the knower (*jña*)—who is the knower of the knowledge that has its internal form within the one who brings [all] to rest—is such that his state is one; he thinks, "I am this [state], and nothing else."
The meaning is that [it] is not the locus of [such] cognition. Regarding the term "perception" (*darśana*):
non-conceptual experience has been stated, and this is also an elliptical indication for conceptualization, memory, and so forth.
This same principle applies when one cognition is reflected upon by another cognition; thus, that cognition—
At that time, it becomes inherent in the cognizer (*pramātṛ*), because it is attached to the knower. [The author] demonstrates this through cognition—[as in the expressions]:

"I conceptualize," "I remember," "it was conceptualized by me," and "it was remembered by me"—since conceptualization and the like manifest precisely by being mounted upon the "I" (*ahantā*). Thus. For this very reason...

Because experiences and so forth rest within the cognizer, whose nature is the "I-sense" (asmadartha), it has been shown in the passage beginning with "the possessor of the powers of knowledge, memory, and exclusion" that these— experiences, conceptualizations, and the like— are specific powers (*śaktiviśeṣa*), since they rest within the essential nature of the Self, the Supreme Lord. Thus far.

Thus [it is said]. For he says "that" (*tad*) in order to demonstrate by way of a conclusion the fruit of the object of cognition (*prameya*)— beginning with "by the apprehension of an object previously experienced" and ending with "the perception of the one who concludes"— while the word "that" functions as a reason in the sense of "therefore."
Having established [the preceding], at the end of the seven verses spoken, he indicates the basis for the eighth verse as follows:
"Since memory is not an appearance as something distinct from the object that was previously experienced,
and since it has been stated that the power [of memory] belongs to the Supreme Lord, therefore (149) here this..."

He reflects: "Its completion is being seen by me," "this is seen," "that was seen by me," and "he was seen by me. Thus, within the supreme subject who consists of consciousness and is of the nature of Śiva, the states of being the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*) appear as distinct; that is, they exist as the form of the grasped and the form of the grasper.
Two distinct objects—the jar and so forth, and the body and so forth—appear as knowable entities possessing their own inherent natures;
thus it follows that "they shine forth. Here, in the word *tat*, the connection is established solely through the resolution of the pronoun.
Furthermore, it is not tenable [to claim] that by the phrase "the difference from memory," it is said that memory encompasses direct experience (*anubhava*).
(p. 118) When one reflects upon the object of experience preceded by the reflective awareness of one's own self as the primary experiencing subject— thinking, "Sometimes it is seen by me"—
this constitutes the reflective awareness of the act of seeing, which is the reflective awareness of the referent "I" (the sense of "me").

Furthermore, whether upon the sudden encounter with objects such as a jar or a cloth, or when there is a specific insistence toward their functional efficacy, one reflects upon that which is to be experienced as "this," even without intending one's own self or the act of seeing; thus, experience is twofold.

Regarding the phrase "there too": even in the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) "this," which takes the form of experience, there exists indeed that which has the nature of the subject (*pramātṛ*), whose ultimate reality is light (*prakāśa*). Otherwise, the manifestation of "this" would be impossible. Thus, in the experience occurring in both ways—"I see this"—it proceeds sequentially.

There are two types of recollection: that which is preceded by the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the nature of the rememberer and the referent "I," as in "He was seen by me" (*mayā dṛṣṭaḥ saḥ*);

and that which is preceded by the reflective awareness of the act of remembering alone, as in the mere recollection "He was seen" (*dṛṣṭaḥ*) without the reflective awareness of the nature of the rememberer and the referent "I."
There are four varieties of recollection: first, "that one," which consists of a reflection upon the object alone; second, "one," which consists of a reflection upon the object as a single entity;

third, "this one," which consists of a reflection upon the act of seeing—the nature of the experience of the experiencer denoted by "I"—in the form "it is being seen by me"; and fourth, "this one," which consists of a mere reflection upon the visible object itself.
According to the principle stated that "there are two types of experience— recollection is the means of knowledge for an experience, and it is the means for the object; there is a synthesis of both"—
this [cognition] consists of a synthesis (anusandhāna) characterized by the unification of both this experience and recollection.
Recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) also occurs in this very context; it is the synthesis (*anusaṃdhāna*) of experience and memory that has not yet become distinct.

This [recognition] is eightfold due to the differences between those experiences and memories. He demonstrates that very point with the words "this is that" (*so 'yam*): one [type] consists of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the object to be synthesized through both memory and experience.

(150) "This has been seen" is one [cognition] primarily consisting of a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of an object to be connected with the experience of seeing, which is itself of the nature of memory; "this has been seen by me" is another, primarily consisting of a reflective awareness of the experience of seeing, which is itself of the nature of memory, concerning the referent of the first-person pronoun "me."

"This is that" is a single [cognition] primarily consisting of the recollection of an object previously experienced as the referent of "I," followed by a subsequent experience and a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*). This tetrad has the nature of an existing object; it is seen as being composed of both recollection and present perception.

One [act of awareness] has the primary function of reflecting upon the object (*vastu-parāmarśa*). This very [act], "this is being seen," has the primary function of reflecting upon the perception of an object that is experienced as present; and [the act] "this is being seen by me" has the primary function of reflecting upon the object as that which is being reflected upon by an experience consisting of the perception of the meaning of the word "I" (*asmadartha*), namely, memory.
The fourfold synthesis of "this is the primary [object]" occurs with respect to a present object;
thus, it is eightfold. This synthesis also occurs in eight ways even when the order is reversed.
For example: "This is that," "This has been seen by me," "That has been seen by me. (p. 119)
In this context as well, this tetrad— “This is seen by me,” “He is seen by me,” “This is he,” and “He is by me”—
is the synthesis that occurs regarding the present object;
thus, there are sixteen types, including the four previously mentioned varieties of recollection.
There are two types of experiential distinctions: synthesis (*anusaṃdhāna*) according to the direct (*anuloma*) and reverse (*pratiloma*) orders, which constitutes the sixteenth [moment].

Within the perceptions of experience and so forth among these [sixteen], that which appears as the form of the object of perception—namely, the experience and so forth—is the "grasped" (*grāhya*), because it is grasped from the light (*prakāśa*).
It is non-distinct from the Great Light (*mahāprakāśa*), which is the grace of the existence of all things (*viśvasattā*); otherwise, its manifestation would be impossible.

And it is distinct from that Great Light which is its object; otherwise, because of being external, [it would follow that] it does not exist. Nor is it [produced] from that alone, and so forth. From that...

"From the Great Light alone. "That very same thing" means that the object of apprehension is indeed that very same thing. It does not appear as both separate and non-separate at one and the same time. "Nūnam" (surely) indicates certainty;
it means that between the Great Light and the object of apprehension, there is no [separate entity] of its own, like a jar or other objects.

There is no other object whatsoever that is imagined as "this is burning" and whose nature is light, which exists in the form of the subject of Māyā; for in the absence of the subject of Māyā, the object would not be manifest, just as it was previously, since it cannot exist without having the nature of light. (151) Thus it is said.

According to the principle that will be explained, how could there be a state of separateness— such as "Caitra is one, Maitra is another, a jar is another, a cloth is another"— among objects that consist of the grasped and the grasper and are non-different from the Great Light? Therefore...

Between the Great Light (*mahāprakāśa*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*), there certainly exists some entity consisting of the limited knower (*parimita-pramātṛ*). Without that, things such as a jar or a cloth would become objects of knowledge; however, for the Great Light, because it encompasses the entire universe within "I" (*aham*), there is no object of knowledge.

There exists no mutual relationship of the object and the subject between things such as a jar and a cloth. As it has been stated in the *Śrīlaghuvṛtti*: "The limited person, whose very nature is that of the cognizer, is counted among the mass of objects of cognition; for without him, of what would that earth and so forth be the object? Therefore...

The nature of the manifestation of the object of knowledge (*vedyābhāsa*) is as follows: when the aggregate of objects of knowledge has not yet abandoned its objective aspect, the *tattvas* or *kalās*—which are of the nature of wind—are active in making that distinct object into a subject;
and *aśuddhavidyā*, which is of the nature of fire, impels it by bestowing a limited capacity for knowledge (*kiñcijjñatva*).

The power of passion (*rāga-śakti*) has the nature of fire, being radiant and brilliant; it is nourishing, having the form of water and the nature of *māyā*; it is characterized by attachment, consisting of one's own marrow, and has the inherent quality of immobilization (*stambhana*); it has the form of earth, as indicated by Indra. These are the four.
The powers (*śaktayaḥ*) sustain the person (*puruṣa*); they cause him to rest in the middle like the *triśaṅku* [pole].

Otherwise, he would either fall into the state of insentience like a stone or the like, or he would fly up into the sky of consciousness like the Supreme Lord. Thus, in both ways, Māyā [functions] even with respect to the object of knowledge (*vedya*) within the state of the subject (*pramātṛ*).

"Nothing" means that there is neither contraction nor expansion; he will also state later that "there is nothing," and so forth. Furthermore, even this subject (*pramātṛ*) here is indeed an object (*prameya*). However, when that [subject] is being made into a subject, its status as an object is concealed, and it is thus spoken of in this context. And as for the subject, such as the void (*śūnya*), which is distinct from the object...

In the statement "the mother, being this [limited] 'I', is enveloped by the pentad beginning with Time," the object conceptualized as "this is that" is essentially the nature of light; yet, due to its insentience (*jaḍatva*), it is merely one among the objects of cognition (*vedya*),
being entirely distinct from the Great Light and from one another— such as Caitra and Maitra, or a jar and a cloth.

In such states as "I am fair" or "I am thirsty," while the status of the body, the vital breaths, and so forth—as objects of cognition—is not yet abandoned, that very body and its constituents are cognized through a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) characterized by a light devoid of differentiation (*viccheda*). This will be described as "the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) by me. Regarding the body:

Regarding the word "in the Buddha" (*buddhau*), he is called the grasper (*pratigrāhaka*) with respect to that which is to be grasped (*grāhya*) as distinct from himself. Thus, because his own self is like a stainless mirror due to its capacity for reflecting the universe, this dyad— consisting of blue, pleasure, and so forth in the form of the object (*grāhya*), and Caitra, Maitra, and so forth in the form of the subject (*grāhaka*)— [is present therein].
The Supreme Lord, from His own inseparable and essential nature—

which is the light of consciousness consisting of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)— simultaneously brings forth the dyad of subject and object, which is non-different from that light because it is bound to it. This is according to the principle thus stated.
That which manifests [objects] simultaneously is said to be this very manifestation of the Blessed One,
which consists of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*)—
namely, his agency— and the power of memory (*smaraṇaśakti*), which is the agency of remembering objects previously experienced.

This is the intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*). As for the meaning of the words (*padārtha*): the subject (*pramātā*) is of the nature of the Great Light (*mahāprakāśa*). For it is by that very [Light], according to the principle stated—that "it knows, remembers, and conceptualizes through this or that form"—that, existing in the forms of Caitra, Maitra, and so forth, it is said, "I am experiencing this. Therefore...
Through the act of reflective awareness (*āmarśana*), the grasped and the grasper— the objects such as jars and the like,

and the subjects such as the body and so forth— appear and shine forth within that pure light, the experiencing subject who is the knower (*pramātṛ*). This is the definition of the nature of the knower.

Regarding the word "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*): that which one refers to as "that" is what is designated as "remembering. Therefore, even from the perspective of perception, within the pure Self—the subject (*pramātṛ*) whose nature is the rememberer—the object to be remembered and the nature of the rememberer appear; this alone is what is indicated. Thus, preceded by knowledge—

In accordance with the principle stated previously (*ktarityuktanītyā*), in order to strengthen the fact that memory depends upon experience (*anubhava*) as its basis, I shall here—in the context of defining the power of memory (*smṛti-śakti-nirūpaṇa-prasaṅga*)—demonstrate [this] by means of the phrase "this is seen" (*mayā dṛśyate ayam iti*) regarding what is yet to come (*bhaviṣyantyā*). (p. 121)

The unfolding of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) has also been accomplished. The term "perceiving" (*āmṛśan*) functions as a definition for the "night" (*rātri*) and so forth. The subject (*grāhaka*) who expresses the fragmented object of knowledge (*vedya*) is the constructed subject belonging to *māyā*;
however, the Great Subject (*mahā-pramātṛ*), whose nature is pure light, is one from the very beginning.
Thirty.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Pratyabhijñāsūtravimarśinī*, the commentary.

Now, the fifth section begins with "within the great cave" (*mahāguhāntaḥ*) and so forth. It is called "great" (*mahatī*) because it is unconditioned by space and time; it is called a "cave" (*guhā*) because it is the abode of Śiva and the other [deities]. Thus, according to the principle stated: "This entire universe, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, resides within the seed-syllable of the Heart."

The heart-mantra is the very form of Śrī Parāśakti; for one who is utterly immersed in identity with that [mantra] by virtue of being composed of consciousness, and who abides in a state of uniformity with it, there is the supreme non-differentiation of the entire multitude of objects— consisting of both subject and object— which are thus embraced within the interior of one's own essential nature.

According to the stated principle— that [the Light] grasps some object within itself and makes it appear as something emerging from its own nature— this [object], such as "Caitra" or "this jar," exists for the subject under the influence of *māyā* in the form of "thisness" (*idantā*), by means of the lamp that is the power of cognition (*jñānaśakti*).
We ever praise that Śiva, who is eternally manifest.

Thus it is said: for by the chapter beginning with "He indeed follows the previous [object]," the nature of the power of memory (*smṛti-śakti*) has been established. Now, however, [the author] provides a definitive determination of the ultimate reality of the power of cognition (*jñāna-śakti*), which is that upon which the power of memory rooted in experience depends.

He establishes this through twenty-one verses. Among them, with the first verse beginning "of those things appearing as present," he makes a formal proposition (*pratijñā*) regarding the reality whose nature is the power of experience (*anubhava-śakti*). [The subsequent verses state:
"the power of ignorance is thus constituted," and then "as before, the object" and "in the divided light."

With two verses, he states that the very nature of the objects within the scope of the power of that experience is the light (*prakāśa*) itself, whose essence is the perfect I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*): "Then, in each single [moment]... and "There is no awakening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) here... with these two verses, [he describes] the light whose form is the manifestation of the "I" (*ahaṃ-prathā*).

Having raised the objection— on the part of the proponents of external objects— that "the existence of external things is such that consciousness itself appears as the object of cognition (*vijñeya*),

and there is no external object of cognition distinct from consciousness," and having thereby strengthened the position of the proponents of external objects by refuting the arguments of the proponents of consciousness-only (*kevala-vijñānavāda*) through the critique of mental impressions (*vāsanā*), [the author proceeds] from that point...

This might be so; by the sixth verse, [the author] first shows that the entire range of worldly transactions, such as rejection and acquisition, is not obstructed in the various appearances. Then, in the verse beginning with "For indeed, the conscious self alone," he states that this is not the case for those who assert external objects such as jars and cloths to be contained within the light [of consciousness].
Since the entire range of worldly transactions, such as rejection and acquisition, is established through the appearances of reflections alone,

these entities— such as jars, cloths, and so forth, which are the objects of the sense organs like the eyes— are of the nature of reflections, because they manifest as being attached to the mirror of the consciousness of form within the "I."

Even if one accepts the existence of external objects, as in the view that there exist certain things such as jars— which are external to consciousness, eternal, inferable, and the original forms (*bimba*) that project these reflections—
it is shown that the aforementioned entire range of worldly activity (*vyavahāra*) is not in the least obstructed. Now:

By the verse beginning with "cidātmaiva hi," [the author] demonstrates that in the vision of one's own consciousness, the very nature of the universe is its being composed of consciousness; thus, he refutes perception as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the existence of external objects. Following that, he addresses inference with the words "anābhātapūrva" (not previously manifested), [referring to] manifestation (*ābhāsa*).

Furthermore, with the two verses beginning with "punarābhāsāt," [the author] refutes even the inferability of an external object on the grounds that there is no direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and consequently, no inference (*anumāna*) following upon it. Thus,
due to the absence of the means of valid cognition— namely, direct perception and inference— the very existence of an external object is negated.

The word "it exists" has arrived [in the context]. Then, by the statement "of the Lord who resides within the self," according to the principle to be explained later—that they know the nature of manifestation to be reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)—the essential nature here is that the Supreme Lord is of the nature of light (*prakāśa*), and light is of the nature of reflective awareness. This is his true form.

And according to the principle stated in the *Praveśikā*, because the Supreme Lord, whose nature is the conscious self (*cidātman*), consists of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), and because everything from Śiva down to the earth—
the objects of that awareness— is contained within that very awareness, the world of objects of awareness [is realized] by means of the awareness itself.

It shows that objects necessarily exist within the conscious self, as they rest in the unsurpassed Lord who is the object of supreme apprehension; thus it says: "Therefore, one should manifest one's own nature. For this very reason, the Self is consciousness (*caitanya*), and consciousness is of the nature of reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*). (155)

In the four verses beginning with "sāsphurattā mahāsattā," it is established through experience, scripture, and reasoning that for the light of the "I" (ahaṃprakāśa), which is the nature of the subject (pramātṛ), reflective awareness (pratyavamarśa) alone is the very life-force— according to the principle that will be explained hereafter.
Therefore, by means of definitions that characterize its own nature, it designates itself as "this" (ayam).

For this very reason, it is said to be the "Self" (ātman) out of its absolute freedom, and not from the perspective of reflective awareness such as "I" (aham) and so forth—this is stated in three verses.
Reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), which is the very essence of knowledge, [establishes] that which constitutes its own foundation...

Although the Self, whose nature is light and who has arisen through its own sovereignty, appears in acts such as summoning as an object of knowledge (*jñeya*) in the form of insentient blue, yellow, and so forth— manifesting as the form of "this-ness" (*idantā*)—
it does so without ever abandoning the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of pure "I-ness" (*ahantā*). Thus, it remains essentially [the Self] even while appearing as an object of knowledge.

And he states the logical justification for the primacy of that very reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*)— expressed by the verse beginning with "thence, by the power of Māyā, of the All-pervasive One" (p. 123)—
even though the manifold world consisting of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge is of the single nature of Light (*prakāśa*).

The very manifestation of differentiation is the cause; it is the sovereign power (*svātantrya-śakti*). By means of that power of *māyā*, [the subject] perceives himself as distinct from other knowers and from the object of knowledge; he says that cognition is distinct from other cognitions, from the knower, from other objects of knowledge, and from both the knower and the cognition—therefrom arises direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*).

Thus, with the two verses beginning "One should determine 'this is a jar,'" he states that in both knowledge consisting of pure conceptualization and that consisting of conceptualization, *vimarśa* (reflective awareness) alone is the vital principle; this he expresses in the concluding verse of the chapter, beginning with "Therefore, when the object of cognition is distinct... and so forth.

The purport of this chapter is as follows: it establishes that the "fragility" (bhaṅguratva) which was refuted in the two preceding verses—beginning with "And for the knower and the knowledge... (*jñātuḥ jñānasya ca*)—by means of the objection that knowledge is of the nature of consciousness (*citsvarūpa*), is actually rendered possible through the power of *māyā*. Now, the meaning of the verses is being examined therein.

Regarding the first verse, he states the introduction with the words "Now then" (*nanu*) and so forth: "Indeed, experience alone is the authoritative means (*pramāṇa*) for memory, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), synthesis (*anusaṃdhāna*), volition (*saṅkalpa*), and creative imagination (*utprekṣā*); therein, it is the very life-force of those [mental states] such as memory, conceptual construction, and the rest."

If objects such as jars and cloths, which are manifesting within that experience, appear as distinct from the great illumination, then it is likewise appropriate that the experienced object manifesting within recollections, conceptualizations, and so forth, should also appear as distinct from them. It is not [otherwise].
If experience appears as distinct, then objects also appear distinctly within those [states] such as memory and conceptualization;

otherwise, they would not appear as distinct—this is the meaning. Therefore, it is experience alone, in the form of the power of cognition (*jñānaśakti*), which serves as the cause for memory, conceptualization, and so forth.

This is for the purpose of defining [the world] by way of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*). With this intention, he says: "With respect to the subject (*pramātṛ*), 'this jar manifests' and 'this cloth manifests'—[this refers to] those objects of various experiences which exist as external manifestations."

The manifestation of entities such as jars and the like as external to the non-illusory subject—that is what is meant by "manifestation. As for "internally": that manifestation is possible only for those who abide in the ultimate subject, which consists of pure consciousness, and who do not abandon their identity with it.
The meaning is that the state of existing within [the subject] is established by valid cognition only for those things that do not abandon [their dependence on] the cognizer.
If entities were to manifest by themselves, having abandoned the cognizer, then even the manifestation as "this is that" would not occur; for without a cognizer, what [could be manifested]?

The manifestation as "this" (*idam*) is the appearance that clarifies [the object] through its presentness; for those entities whose manifestation has precisely this form of "this," that which is imagined as being external in nature is the illusory (*āyīya*).

p. 124) Because they are differentiated by the cause that is the state of being separate from the subject, and because they are thus severed from the subject by *māyā*, this manifestation as "this" and "that"—which is their very appearance—belongs to those things that reside within the ultimate subject, who consists of consciousness and is the Great Light; it is by means of that [subject] [that they appear].
This is only possible for those who do not abandon their identity with the ultimate subject (*paramārtha-pramātṛ*). This is the summarized meaning here:

thus, for an entity that does not lose its non-difference from consciousness—which is of the nature of the supreme subject due to its abiding within—it is [erroneously] conceptualized as "I am Caitra," "I am Maitra," and so forth.

It is said that the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) of the Lord Maheśvara consists in the manifestation of things as "this" through differentiation in relation to the subject (*pramātṛ*). Within [the subject], there is that which manifests as "this is it" regarding those entities which manifest externally as objects of experience in the form of "this."

It has been stated that for those who abide in the pure, conscious subject and do not fall away from that unity, [the existence of objects] is possible—that is, it is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). To demonstrate such a means of valid cognition which reveals the nature of the object, he says: "This," [referring to the object] as being within the range of experience externally.

An object that is manifest would, in the absence of the nature of Light— which is the form of the transcendent subject who bestows existence upon the entire universe from Śiva down to the earth— remain unmanifest even at the moment its own cognition arises, just as it was before the arising of the cognition of that object. This is because it lacks the nature of Light.
Because its own existence is non-existent, it would follow that even when its own cognition arises, there would be no manifestation.

The Light (*prakāśa*), which bestows existence upon the universe, is not distinct from itself in its own nature, nor does it possess a different form; the meaning is that it is one alone within itself. Furthermore, the Light—regarding the object...

Therefore, the meaning is that the light itself—the self-nature (*svarūpa*) or essence of the entire universe—shines forth as the universal self (*viśvātman*). As it has been said: "That which shines is of the nature of a single light. And as it has been stated: "If there were no universality, insentience would necessarily follow for consciousness (*cit*)."
If the body of vibration were distinct from light, [it would not exist];
and because consciousness is the self-nature of all, the world is likewise composed of consciousness.
Śiva is all, and all is Śiva; I go for refuge to Śiva.
The object is blue and so forth; the manifestation of that blue is precisely its nature as blue and so forth.
Manifestation is not something other than the body of the blue, nor is it a separate subject distinct from the blue.
[If it were otherwise,] then that blue would [be perceived] by all subjects who experience blue...

Just as one says "I perceive blue" based on a subjective apprehension, that statement is merely a conceptual presumption (*saṃbhāvanāmātra*). In ultimate reality, that blue exists only within itself as the very blueness of blue;
it does not belong to Caitra, Maitra, or others, because it is logically untenable for it to reside in them.

For a cloth that is distinct from matted hair does not reside within a jar. Nor is blue [blue] by its own nature alone, because it lacks the status of being an object of the perceiver's vision. Anticipating the objection that "if it is not blue, let it be yellow," [the author replies: it is not non-blue; even as yellow, it is not blue by its own nature.

The light of the subject... [is] precisely so. Thus, just as the blueness of blue [is perceived by all], so too this manifestation of blue would have to appear to everyone. Regarding the phrase "to everyone":
it would appear even to those subjects who do not directly perceive the blue, or else it would not appear even to those who do directly perceive the blue.

It may be that the blue object and so forth would become the domain of the group of sense organs, such as the eye, for the class of subjects. Prior to the momentary collection of the sense organs, the world, the lamp, and so forth, this [blue]— which is of the nature of light and was previously unmanifested—
arises as something distinct from the moments of the blue-characterized object, the sense organs, and the world.

Now, even if it were the case that this very same object characterized by the moment of the sense organ and so forth has become the blue object in the form of a manifestation, then—regarding this [objection]:

does that blue object, though qualified by the moment of the sense organ and so forth, manifest for everyone, or for no one at all? [This is because] the blue object is qualified by the moment of the sense organ and so forth.

Even regarding manifestness, since it does not manifest for everyone nor for nothing at all, this blue-characterized [object] is distinguished from the group of moments consisting of the senses, the world, and so forth, by its nature as manifestation;
in this case too, the previously mentioned undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) would ensue. The manifestness of the blue belongs to the blue alone.

If it were the case that the manifestation of an object (dharma) occurred with respect to all [perceiving subjects], then there would be no manifestation of blue whatsoever; or rather, if it were the case that the manifestation of blue occurs with respect to all [subjects] in every way, then the manifestation of blue— characterized by the momentary state of the sense faculty and so forth—
would be the manifestation of blue due to its contact with the visual faculty, and thus manifestation would be entirely dependent upon the objective entity itself.

If it is argued that the object appears to me once it has come to rest, then because the light [of consciousness] is attached to the knower (*pramātṛ*), its measurement is difficult to establish. Now, if the knower consists of the senses and so forth— that is, the knower consists of the sense organs such as the eye— then...

At that time, during the moment of contact between the sense organs such as the eye and the object, it would have to be the cause of the manifestation of the form of the object; however, just as a seed is the cause of a sprout that was previously unmanifest, the very example [you provide] is flawed.
He demonstrates this with the words beginning "And not," etc. The sprout is not non-sprout in relation to the seed;
rather, it is at that time a cognizer (*pramātṛ*) consisting of the sense organs such as the eye by the will of the Lord (*īśvara*).
Thus, at the moment of the mutual conjunction of the eye and so forth with the jar and so forth, [it perceives] the form of the object.

Anticipating the objection that the manifestation of the form of a jar might have a cause, he shows that the very example is flawed with the words beginning "na ca" (and not). A sprout does not fail to be of the nature of a sprout in relation to its seed; rather, it is so by the will of Īśvara, as he will state later:
(159) But that power does not belong to an insentient thing, since existence arises from non-existence;
therefore, the nature of cause and effect consists precisely in the state of being agent and object.
"For this very reason, the Supreme Lord is accepted as the cause even in the case of the sprout;
otherwise, it would not be possible for anything else, such as the seed, to be its cause," and so forth.
Therefore, just as the seed has not become the cause of this sprout...

In the same way, the cognizer (pramātṛ), consisting of the senses and so forth, cannot be the cause of the manifestation of the object because it is insentient (jaḍa). Therefore, there is contact with manifestation for the object; otherwise, such a defect as described would arise, whereby the object would not be of the nature of manifestation. As before...
Just as before the arising of the cognition "this is a jar," that jar remained unmanifest to the knower, so too it remains unmanifest even when the cognition arises. [Objection:
But surely, what is called "cognition" is precisely the manifestation of the object; therefore, the object—
How could there be equality between the object even when there is the arising and non-arising of cognition whose nature is luminosity?
When cognition arises, there is the manifestation of the object; when it does not arise, there is no manifestation.
How, then, could there be equality between its arising and non-arising? The object is manifested through the arising of cognition.

It occurs. This—that non-manifestation would occur even when knowledge does not arise—might be possible; however, by the word "yāvatā" (insofar as), he shows that there is no such logical possibility at all.
For knowledge is distinct from the object, because its nature is consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), whereas the object is...

Furthermore, since cognition is insentient by nature, how could that cognition— which is itself insentient— be related to an object that is also insentient? Just as a cloth is not related to a foot that is distinct from it,
so too cognition cannot be related to an object that is distinct from it.
It does not exist—[he states another alternative:

if the nature of cognition is such that "the object is manifested," then from that, the non-difference of the object and the cognition follows; [for] the very nature of the jar [is the manifestation].
Since it has been stated that [the object] is of the nature of cognition, if it is admitted that cognition possesses the same essential nature as the object,
then— by such arguments as "cognition would perceive the object" and so forth—
it would follow that cognition, which is of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), would become insentient (*jaḍatva*).
If the nature of cognition is that it "illuminates the object," then it follows that it "causes the object to be illuminated. In that case, how can that cognition— which is distinct from the object—
be related to the object such that one says, "the object is illuminated" or "it illuminates the object"?

The distinction between *yathārtha* (corresponding to the object) and *prakāśa* (manifestation), as well as their respective meanings, has been explained by me at length in the work *Bhedavidāraṇa*; therefore, it should be sought there. Consequently, the mere possibility that manifestation—which is distinct from the object—could be related to the object does not exist. Therefore, [it is] the form... [of cognition].
(127) Luminosity (*prakāśatva*) is the state of being manifest (*prakāśamānatva*), which is non-difference from the Great Light (*mahāprakāśa*).

If such a light were different in a jar and different in a cloth—if it were distinct for every object like the view of those who maintain that cognition is momentary—then [the question arises]: "Who am I" in relation to the jar?
"I was that very person, and I am experiencing this cloth"— such an experience [would not occur],
because while the two manifestations (the past state and the present cognition) rest within their own respective natures, they do not rest within a single subject.
This has been demonstrated at length in the passage beginning with "the stability of people would perish."

Therefore, because such a synthesis is impossible, it has been demonstrated by this [statement] that "light is one alone; light is not divided within itself"—this is also the object of knowledge (*prameya*). For it is not possible for a cognition that is distinct from its objects to be the illuminator of those objects.

Nevertheless, even while conceding that [cognition] illuminates objects, he states another subverting argument: "another subverting argument" refers to the confusion of objects; that is, the confusion of their objects would mean that at the very moment the cognition of a jar arises, there is the arising of cloth and so forth—the simultaneous arising of every object.

The state of limitation would be such that there is visual cognition of form by the eye alone, and olfactory cognition of fragrance by the nose alone. Since the light [of consciousness] is distinct from the object, and because it is therefore non-different within its own self—being a unity—there is an absence of any defining factor; thus, the impression belongs to the object. Furthermore, [the light] is distinct from the object...

Therefore, if the cognition, which is non-different from itself, were again to become connected with the object, then all objects would arise simultaneously, resulting in confusion (*saṅkara*). If that cognition is the illuminator of blue alone, it cannot be the illuminator of yellow and so forth. Furthermore, [if it were simultaneous,] they would indeed arise all at once.
When all objects arise for a cognizer situated on a mountain peak, following the experience of objects such as cities, villages, rivers, and fields,
there occurs the perception of something similar to those experienced objects; [in this state], of every single object previously experienced—

There would be the consequence of simultaneous recollection, and thus there would be confusion (*saṅkara*). Due to that confusion, the object—which is of the nature of manifestation—manifests by becoming the very essence of manifestation. If the object were to manifest while being devoid of the manifestation of the object, it would not be established; it would not be possible, meaning its very existence would not exist.

If the luminosity that is the nature of cognition is indeed distinct from the object, then—precisely because it is non-different from the object—it would follow that this cognition, being different from the object, possesses only the nature of luminosity within itself; thus, there is indeed non-difference, indeed identity. Indeed, non-difference.

He explains this with the words "For instance" (*tathā hi*), and so forth. In the expressions "the manifestation of blue" and "the manifestation of yellow," there are the blue and yellow components which constitute the nature of the object of cognition (*jñeya*). That [object] is not the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of the cognition, because the object of cognition is distinct from the cognition; for if it were the intrinsic nature of the cognition...

There would be an abandonment of the doctrine that there is a distinction between knowledge and the object of knowledge. If it is argued that "the blue portion and the yellow portion may respectively become the objects of the cognition of blue and the cognition of yellow," we too are investigating precisely that status of being an object. He states the method of investigation with the words beginning with "here" (*iha*).
p. 128) This distinction—that "this is blue" and "this is yellow"—must be accepted on the basis of the power of cognition.

Since blue is apprehended as "blue" by that very cognition through which it is manifested, how could yellow be apprehended as "yellow" by that same cognition? For cognition is non-different within its own self.

Because it is non-different from objects such as jars and cloths, and because there is no plurality of selves, the determination of a cloth does not occur through the cognition of a jar. Therefore, the blue aspect is neither the essential nature (*svarūpa*) nor the object (*viṣaya*) of the cognition of blue; rather, the manifestation produced by the blue is the manifestation of the blue, [and not] by means of the yellow.

The claim that light is produced by the yellow [object], and that light possesses the status of being the producer while the yellow possesses the status of being the produced, could only be established if a difference between blue and yellow were already proven. Since cognition touches upon its object, the cognitions of blue and yellow do not touch blue and yellow respectively; thus, there is no such thing as a single causal complex (*ekasāmagrī*) for the blue [cognition] together with the blue [object].

The conjunction of the eye with that [object], the capacity of the eye to apprehend blue, and the manifestation of the blue—just as in the case of mother-of-pearl appearing as silver—the manifestation occurs through the very nature of the blue; thus, it arises from a single causal complex (*eka-sāmagrī*). This is what is meant by such statements as "the manifestation is of the nature of the cognition of blue."

That statement of yours would hold true if the difference between blue and yellow were already established. For the eye, having contacted either the blue-colored object or the yellow-colored object, can only determine "this is blue" or "this is yellow" once the difference between blue and yellow is established; yet that very difference is what remains to be investigated, investigated.
In the sphere of investigation, the knower is not perceived directly by means of the object of knowledge;
this means that the eye does not touch blue and so forth.
Furthermore, he states another position: "This light, whose nature is cognition..."

Just as in a mirror, it is said that the light of the nature of cognition possesses a blue form (*nīlākāra*) like a blue reflection; by the reasoning already stated, that state of having a blue form arises through the power of the reflection. That which, by means of that reflection, offers itself as the second [pole]...
It has been rightly stated that it is improper for there to be no manifestation of reflections possessing a blue nature; for,

since cognition is distinct from the object of knowledge, the sense organs such as the eye do not "touch" their respective objects such as form, and the object— blue and so forth— is the very nature of the light that constitutes the essence of cognition.

There is no [simultaneous] existence [of the object and its cognition], nor is there the state of being produced by blue and so forth. The luminosity that is the nature of cognition [arises] from a single, complete causal complex (*sāmagrī*), [consisting of] the object such as blue and the sense organs such as the eye.

And since [the cognition] arises from a form of mutual contact, the essence of cognition is not like a mirror that grasps a reflection of an object such as blue; [this is stated] having observed five defects in the position that there is a difference between the object and the cognition. Thus, taking refuge in non-difference itself, he says: "Now, as for the difference..."
In that case, your doctrine of difference (*bheda-vāda*), which has become a mere axe against us, is abandoned;

for even if one accepts the non-difference between the object and its cognition, the relationship of cause and effect—like the sight of a mountain peak and the sight of a river or a field—is established. (p. 129) [163] It arises from the perception of the river and the field.

How could there be a distinction such that the cognition of one situated on a mountain peak possesses the capacity for sharp and clear apprehension near one peak, while another [cognition] near a different [peak] lacks it?
This is because the nature of cognition, which consists of luminosity, is non-different within itself.
Even though there was a prior experience, he says "tathābhūta" and so forth [to explain]. Regarding an object experienced through such an experience,
subsequently, [there arises] another object characterized by similarity to that experienced object.

If the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) were awakened by the mere sight [of an object], then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that one would forcibly remember in its entirety every object— such as a village or a city— that was previously seen as a whole while standing on a mountain peak; therefore, the latent impression must pertain to each individual object.

Because each individual object lacks causal efficiency for purposes such as desire when it is grasped in isolation, whereas the collection of all causal efficiencies for all objects arises through the recollection of all things, there is a confusion of the objects.

Even in the theory that the object (*artha*) and its manifestation (*prakāśa*) are non-different, he says "this might be so" and so forth, implying: "Let there be no manifestation; let it be the object itself," for even if one were defeated [in debate], the purpose is not served by a manifestation that merely results in faults for the object, whether in the case of difference or non-difference. What utility is there in such a manifestor? None at all.

To one who argues, "The object alone is ours," he replies: If the object were unmanifest, it would not be established even by itself, because that object consists solely of manifestation. Indeed, there can be no connection between a painting and the absence of a wall; if the object were unmanifest, its very establishment would be impossible.

He shows this very point by saying "sometimes [it appears] as blue within itself," and so forth: for within its own self—that is, within its own essential nature—it does not exist apart from manifestation toward the knowing subject.
Or rather, even within its own self, it may appear as yellow, or as nothing at all; such is the case regarding its existence.

Thus, due to this non-existence, nothing at all would exist. It was stated that "that blue [object] is by means of a manifestation that brings about a defect"; it was stated "by that manifestation. How could the object be corrupted by that manifestation? If it exists by itself, its state of being corruptible is simply non-existent because of its very existence. Therefore, if the object were not manifest by itself...

Because manifestation itself does not manifest as anything other than the universal self (*aviśvātman*), this very point was stated by the author of the treatise, the Master [Abhinavagupta], elsewhere in the *Jñānasiddhi*: "In this way, within the Self"— meaning that these insentient things such as jars and cloths are, within their own nature (*ātmani svarūpe*), like non-existents, since they cannot arise by themselves.

Because they lack independent capacity, non-existent things exist only through manifestation; thus, they belong solely to the Light of the Full *ahaṃ* (I-consciousness) Self. Therefore, the manifestation of the Supreme Lord—who is one’s own Self—is indeed that which exists as both the supreme Self, which is one's own essential nature, and as the universal Self. Regarding this, he states the summarized meaning:

Therefore, for the reason stated above, if there is manifestation—that is, if manifestation exists—then the object also exists. There is no difference between manifestation and the object. Or rather, the object is of the very nature of manifestation.
He establishes this very point with the words beginning "How... and so forth.
Now, is it not the case that the very nature of a jar is its manifestation, and nothing else?

And since that same manifestation is also the nature of a cloth and so forth, it follows that there is only one single manifestation which, by its own sovereignty, manifests as the self of the universe. As it has been said:
"The very same light that manifests as the nature of a jar also manifests as the nature of a cloth;
thus, the independent, singular light itself manifests as the form of the phenomenal world. Thus [it is said].

By his own will, he unfolds the universe upon his own screen— the Great Self of full I-consciousness, which is unconditioned by space and time— having painted the picture of the world within himself with the brush of his own nature.
"Having beheld it himself, the Supreme Lord rejoices. Thus:

"Salutations to that wielder of the trident, who, without any collection of material causes or a supporting foundation, weaves the variegated picture of the universe, and who is praiseworthy for his creative artistry."

(165) According to the principle thus stated, because it provides space for the entire universe from Śiva down to the earth, there exists within one’s own Self—which is like the ether—a certain such sovereignty; with this in mind, he states the conclusion in the form: "of such a nature. It is of manifold forms and of various kinds.
