The nature of sequence and non-sequence: the creation of potters and the like is of the nature of sequence, while the creation of the omniscient ones and the like is of the nature of non-sequence; such is the relationship between cause and effect consisting of sequence and non-sequence, and the relationship between the signified and the signifier—the state of being the universal form.

There exists sovereignty in the form of the capacity for manifestation. One must bring [the inquiry] to a conclusion within this ultimate reality; this limit, which constitutes the very essence of the finality, must be established.
If that sovereignty concludes in this manner—namely, as the single Light appearing in the form of the universe—[then it is established].
In its manifestation,

the proponent of external objects has established that the universe— which brings about the manifoldness of light— is external to light and independent of light’s own sovereignty. [However,] when there is the manifoldness of light, that which is eternally inferable as being external to it is [in fact] within that very [light].
The manifestation of blue, yellow, and so forth— which consists of the original object (*bimba*) that imparts the reflection—
is established as such because the original object that imparts the reflection is not perceived; thus,
the appearance of the reflection is established as suddenly adhering to the mirror of consciousness.

From each respective manifestation, one may infer an external object; however, the cause for the diverse appearance within one's own self is not [an external object], since consciousness is non-different from one's own self.

Having thus established his own position, he says— beginning with the word "vicitraḥ" (variegated)— in order to demonstrate through various powerful arguments that the variety of manifestations, which consists in the awakening of various latent impressions (*vāsanā*) as taught by the proponents of consciousness (*vijñānavādin*), belongs to his own counter-position.

Because the experiences of various objects such as pots and cloths are diverse, the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) resulting from those respective experiences become diverse; thus, the awakening of such latent impressions must be brought to the state of being the cause for the diversity of those respective cognitions. Furthermore, regarding the diversity of that very awakening of latent impressions—
What is the basis for the cognition of the cause?

It is that the mind becomes one alone. Its diversity—[arising] from space, time, and so forth—is, according to your view, due to the fact that these are composed of cognition (*jñānamaya*); whereas in our view, it is because [the mind] is one within its own self.

Alternatively, since there is no diversity even in the awakening of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) which consists of the refinement of knowledge (*jñāna-saṃskāra*), the awakening of the latent impression is not the cause of the diversity of manifestation (*prakāśa*).
In this established doctrine (*siddhānta*), [the subject] is indeed non-different and one; of that—

The ultimate reality of consciousness is its mere luminosity alone. If blue were the essential nature of this consciousness external to its luminosity, then that blue would be of a non-luminous nature;
consequently, because the blue within the body of consciousness would not be luminous, consciousness itself would not shine forth either. Now, the word "atha" (then/if).
The word "tathā" indicates an alternative view. [It means: The very nature of this consciousness is its manifestation as the essence of blue.
At that time, while consciousness is manifesting precisely as the essence of blue, how could there be a manifestation of yellow? It would be impossible.

Furthermore, with the words "Now again," he states another position: if the very nature of consciousness consists of the successive manifestations of blue, yellow, and so forth, then in states such as deep sleep or fainting,
because blue, yellow, and so forth do not manifest, there would be a non-manifestation of that manifestation which has blue, yellow, and so forth as its form.

It would follow [from your position]. Therefore, consciousness is of the single nature of luminosity alone; apart from its own self-luminosity, there is not even an atom’s worth of another form such as blue or yellow.
Thus, consciousness is non-different. This is because for non-differentiated consciousness, just as in the case of a crystal pillar...

Sometimes there is the appearance of blue, sometimes the appearance of yellow; these various appearances, through the grasping of their respective reflections, constitute the manifold manifestations such as "I am manifesting as blue" or "I know the blue. In that regard, [one thinks] "I know the blue," "I know the yellow," and so forth.
It is not tenable for a single, undivided nature of consciousness to be the cause of diverse appearances;

for if that causal nature of consciousness were non-different, it would be impossible for there to be diverse effects such as blue, yellow, and so forth, because the cause itself is non-different. Thus, that very [consciousness] remains attached to its own [undivided] state.

The appearance of a reflection, consisting of various forms such as blue, yellow, and so forth, is accidental; because an external object that could provide the reflection is not perceived, it is established through the perception of what is unknown. Being thus caused, [it appears] as something external to the light, such as blue or yellow, within the consciousness.

It is the producer of that which consists of reflection and possesses its own luminosity. Just as there is a visible object (*bimba*) resembling the reflection of a jar within a mirror, so too, by virtue of the diversity of that object,
the reflection— though fixed in consciousness— knows blue or yellow, which resemble its own form.

I know that "blue shines" and "yellow shines"; because it consists of the nature of darkness and concealment (*tamas*), it is composed of manifold distinctions, whereas from consciousness— which is itself of a single form of self-luminosity— it is in every respect non-shining and characterized by multiplicity.
The proponent of external objects (bāhyārthavādin) conceives that a reflection, being distinct and serving as a cause, allows one to infer [the original object];
however, for this proponent of external objects, this inference is not a mere possibility, but rather—
It results exclusively in certainty. If it is asked, "Why does it result in certainty?

he says [the answer] beginning with "For instance" (*tathāhi*). This is because the reason stated by the Vijñānavādin—namely, that which consists in the awakening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—is not tenable for the Bāhyārthavādin.

The reason stated by the Vijñānavādin—that which is characterized by the awakening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—is precisely the non-occurrence [of an object]; for it is well known that a latent impression is a mental trace (*saṃskāra*) produced by an experience that generates a memory immediately following that experience. However, in this case, [the subject] first [experiences] "I" with respect to consciousness.
The cause for the diversity of experience— such as "I know a jar" and "I know a cloth"— must be sought.
Thus, from the very outset, consciousness is like an axe to [the tree of] cows and other such objects.

Having refuted the claim that latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are not the cause for the diversity of experience, [the author] suggests again that there must be some power called "latent impression" belonging to consciousness. Even while accepting this, he states the refutation with the words "Or let it be," etc.,
regarding the production of the appearance of blue and other objects which serve as the content of cognition.

Let there be a certain power called *vāsanā*, which consists of capacity (*sāmarthya*). Its "awakening" (*prabodha*) is its readiness to produce its respective effects, such as blue, yellow, and so forth. "From that"—namely, from the awakening of the *vāsanā*—there arises [the cognition] "this is blue" within the cognitions of blue, yellow, and so on.
Having set forth the position that "this yellow shines" or "the appearance of blue and so forth shines," he speaks— beginning with the words "tatrāpi" (even there)— in order to refute it. Here,
in your own system, for those [objects] existing within cognition...

The non-ultimate nature of blue, yellow, and so forth— that is, their lack of present reality— has been stated. Likewise, the latent impression (*vāsanā*) which is the causal form of these [phenomena] such as blue and yellow is that very *vāsanā* which is devoid of objective referents (*ālambana*), because it lacks the defining characteristic [of an object].

Since a thing that does not exist in itself cannot possess an inherent nature characterized by the capacity to produce effects such as blue or yellow, and since it remains necessary to accept the existence of the object as the basis for the latent impression (*vāsanā*), [the following applies] to blue, yellow, and so forth...
Those very things which are intended as the causes of manifestation exist at present;
however, insofar as they exist at present in that form, it is logically impossible for them to possess causality consisting in the production of effects such as blue or yellow.

If it is argued that these latent impressions (vāsanās) possess causality in the same form in which they possess ultimate reality, then— according to the principle already stated— that [ultimate] form belongs to consciousness;
and since that [consciousness] is non-different [from itself], the distinction between effects such as the appearances of blue, yellow, and so forth, would be untenable.

Because latent impressions (*vāsanā*) consist of nothing but cognition, if they lack variety—that is, if they are one—then their awakening would also lack variety; what hope, then, can there be? Or, let us grant that the latent impressions are distinct; nevertheless, regarding those latent impressions...
Even if diversity (*nānātva*) is admitted,
since there is no such thing as space, time, or form apart from mere cognition (*jñānamātra*), and since space, time, and so forth are included within cognition, [they are not distinct from it].

The meaning is that there exists no location or other factor whatsoever distinct [from consciousness]. According to your own view, since the location, time, and so forth intended to be the awakeners of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are of the same nature as cognition alone, the awakenings of the latent impressions are non-variegated; thus, there is only one [awakening].

Regarding the phrase "the awakening of latent impressions" (*vāsanā-prabodha*): since the awakening of latent impressions—which serves as the cause for blue, yellow, and so forth—is one within its own self, when it arises, the variety of blue, yellow, and so on would appear simultaneously; thus, there follows the previously mentioned undesirable consequence of the confusion of objects.

If it is argued that the various other awakenings occurring within Caitra, Maitra, and others—each residing in their own respective mental continua—are the causes for the awakening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), then [the opponent asks]: "How is that so? [The response is:
Because of the pleasure and pain occurring within one's own continuum... (169)

If distinctions of space and time— such as blue, yellow, prior, and posterior— were of the nature of cognition, then there would be no difference between the awareness of pleasure, pain, and so forth, which are objects of the internal organs,
and the awareness of blue, yellow, and so forth, which are objects of the external organs.

Since pleasure, pain, blue, yellow, and other such qualifiers have existed previously, and since space and time are of the same nature as consciousness— given that consciousness has mere luminosity as its ultimate reality and thus no difference in intrinsic nature is possible— consciousness itself must consist of a single cognition.

It follows that even for [a cognition] that follows its own independent course, other cognitions such as pleasure and pain are the causes for the awakening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). This applies to those in the form of another cognizer—namely, those in the form of a cognizer belonging to a different continuum from Caitra, and thus to those in the form of a cognizer belonging to any one of the continua such as Maitra, and so forth. Therefore...

This same manner of non-distinction applies even to those things denoted by the word "other" within a continuum of consciousness characterized by friendliness (*maitra*). This "manner of non-distinction" means the impossibility of there being any difference in the nature of the cognition. In that case as well, this applies to other cognitions in the form of subjects who are conceived of as belonging to another.

Since there is no difference in their nature as pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*) among the qualities of the body— such as being emaciated or stout— the vital breaths— such as inhalation and exhalation— and the intellect— such as pleasure and pain,
we do not know to whom even an atom’s worth of transcendence (*paratva*) could belong. There is not even an atom’s worth of transcendence.

The meaning is that it does not exist. If it is argued that consciousness residing in the body and so forth possesses supremacy, [we reply]: if that consciousness is not established by the means of valid cognition (pratyakṣa-pramāṇa), then it is simply non-existent.
If it were established as an object of knowledge (prameya) by the means of valid cognition, like a jar, then—being an object of knowledge—it would be nothing but insentient (jaḍa), just like a jar.

Just as an effect such as a jar has as its nature the mere existence of cognition, so too, in the case of awakening (*bodha*), it has as its nature the mere existence of cognition; therefore, since there is no awakening in the form of the "I-notion" (*ahaṃ-pratīti*) which is the object of those various cognitions, we do not know whose "otherness" (*paratva*) could exist. Of that...
If cognition residing in the body and so forth were of the nature of pure luminosity alone, it would be unestablished for another;
and in the case of self-luminosity, the operation of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) belonging to subjects such as Caitra or Maitra is impossible.
Thus, it has been stated that it is not logical for cognition residing in the body and so forth to possess "otherness."

One might raise the objection— beginning with "But surely" (nanu)— that the state of "otherness" belongs only to the volition (*samīhā*), which is inferable through actions such as worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) and the like, and which resides within the subject (*pramātṛ*) consisting of the body and so forth.
[This refers to] the action of Maitra in his own self, such as "I transact" or "I desire."

Since this [intention] is observed to be pervaded by its existence as the cause of an action performed with the desire "I shall engage in such-and-such worldly transaction," and because that pervasion has been observed, therefore— in the case of Caitra’s body as well—
the desire "I shall engage in such-and-such worldly transaction" exists as the cause of that very action of transaction and so forth.
There is no such thing as an equal [state] that has fallen within the continuum of friendliness (*maitrasantati*), for this is certain through one's own experience.

And because it is thus certain, even in the body of Caitra, the exertion (*samīhā*) of another—namely, of Caitra who is distinct from ourselves—is established as the cause of activities such as conventional discourse. That very thing is what constitutes a different continuum (*santānāntara*).

If it is argued that [the other] is a different continuum (*santānāntara*) based on conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), it is said in response: For Caitra, who infers his own intention through the act of his own conventional usage, there arises a semblance of conventional usage in two ways. If one asks how, it is because of the mutual relationship between his own conventional usage and his own intention.
At the time of grasping pervasion (*vyāpti*), which consists in the state of non-separation (*vinābhāva*), the appearance "I" speaks;
and at the occasion of conceiving the inference of a cause that is imperceptible by means of its effect— such as when one says,
"This Caitra speaks," and there appears the appearance of being separated, namely, "He lives"— there is the appearance of separation (*vicchinnābhāsa*).

The phrase "I speak" refers to the volition "I shall speak," which serves as the cause for the appearance of speech in the form "I am speaking"— an appearance that occurs at the time of grasping the pervasion (vyāpti) as being uninterrupted and distinct.
The word "now" refers to the cause of the appearance of one who is currently speaking.

How could the desire of another serve as a logical reason (*hetu*) on an occasion when one is inferring [that desire]? It would be the reason for the fallacious appearance that "Caitra is speaking. [If you argue it is] because it is unknown by the inferer, then how could the desire be inferred from that appearance of "speaking"? How could that desire be the cause of it?

He states with the words "Moreover" (*kiṃ ca*) and so forth that there is no causal relationship between the appearance of "I am speaking" and the appearance of "I speak," because the latter occurs through the intention of another, which serves as its cause.
[The structure is: by means of the appearance "I am speaking," [the thought] "I shall speak" [arises].

How could a fragmented appearance— such as "this person speaks"— occurring in another cognizer who infers based on the absence of [the speaker's own] volition toward form, be the effect of that other person's volition? Indeed,
the appearance "Maitra speaks," which resides in Maitra, cannot be the effect of a volition residing in Caitra.

The meaning is that it comes into being. That appearance which "speaks"—having its life in non-interruption—is indeed the appearance of that supreme volition having its life in the thought "I speak"; for that which consists of the non-interruption of the appearance "I speak," [the subject] "speaks. [The state] consisting of interruption...

It is not logical to say that the appearance (*ābhāsa*) is the effect. For from the cause, which is the uninterrupted [consciousness] "I, Caitra, am speaking," there arises the effect, which is the interrupted appearance "he speaks. Such is the case.
The means for grasping the relationship of cause and effect [is as follows]:
because one perceives the manifestation "he speaks" immediately after the manifestation "from existence," it is so for the cognizer who is accepted by the inferer within his own self.

It is not established by any means of valid cognition that this uninterrupted manifestation—“I speak”—produces a manifested appearance of being interrupted, such as “the cognizer, who is regarded as inferable, speaks.
It is established neither by perception nor by inference. If it were established by a means of valid cognition...
The refutation consists of a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*).
Here, a portion of the text measuring two folios has been lost.

One point is that we have accepted [the existence of] a single object. Furthermore, another point is that even when it is established by us through such statements as "Indeed, the conscious self alone... and so forth, [the threefold nature] still exists. When the worldly transactions of rejection, acquisition, and so forth are completed within those appearances of reflections that you accept as being attached to consciousness—

"Outside of manifestation..."—since there is no scope for the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) other than these appearances, and since inference (*anumāna*), which follows upon that [perception], has no object at all, what is the purpose of something that is thus devoid of justification? The meaning is: "There is none whatsoever. [The opponent] might say this...

If it is explained by accepting the aforementioned possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*), then it should be interpreted as follows: "In that case, another possibility—concerning the lack of looseness [in the argument]—is shown in the manner about to be stated, beginning with the words 'For the conscious self alone... (172).

If the insertion of "but" (*kiṃtu*) and so forth in the middle of the verse were not counted [as part of the syntactical connection], then this would be another possibility; that other possibility is to be construed as a single syntactical unit with the passage beginning "for it is nothing but the Self" (*nakiñcidātmaiva hi*), etc. [This refers to] the external object.
Even though [the external object] is unestablished from its own side, you— who attempt to establish external objects through such strained conceptualization—

have no purpose, such as rejection or acquisition, regarding those external objects. For [your purposes], such as rejection and acquisition, are accomplished by means of the appearances of reflections that are admitted by you and which are attached to consciousness.

Since there is no worldly transaction whatsoever involving the rejection or acceptance of an object that is an external form (*bimbarūpa*) which is eternally inferable through linguistic convention, what purpose is served by such an object external to the manifestation? That in which [this occurs]— such as "this is fire"— is the case of fire and so forth, which are external objects relative to the manifestation.

It is not merely that there is an absence of any proving means of knowledge— such as perception, which establishes the existence of objects, or inference, such as "this mountain possesses fire because it possesses smoke," which establishes fire and so forth— but rather, he states that there is also a subverting [reason] for this: "tat..."
If it is asked why: because the object as described by you is not manifested (p.
136), even if an external object is admitted, there would still be an absence of manifestation through inference; this is the primary refutation of an external object *per se*.
Since these [arguments] are unestablished, they are merely additional refutations;
thus, even while accepting that there exists an object external to the manifestation, he demonstrates the refuting proofs: "When it is accepted that the object possesses parts... and so forth.

The persistence [of the whole] in its parts, such as the hands and feet, is impossible because the whole is insentient; due to this very insentiency, there is no inherence (*samavāya*) in the parts. The meaning is that, because it is insentient, there is no state of being inherent. When Devadatta’s hand moves while the other parts remain motionless, of that Devadatta—[the text continues with] "that lotus-hand"— *Note: The provided source text appears to be an incomplete fragment of a philosophical argument concerning the relationship between a whole (*avayavin*) and its parts (*avayava*), likely from a Nyāya or Vaiśeṣika context.*

If Devadatta’s head were to be covered while the rest of his body remained uncovered, there would necessarily follow for Devadatta the conjunction of contradictory properties—namely, being covered and being uncovered—which is impossible for a single entity. Thus, the nature of form cannot belong to that which is mobile. Furthermore, if the form were to move, it would result in the same contradiction regarding the states of being covered and uncovered. Therefore, the nature of form does not belong to Devadatta [as a whole].

When one part is red while other parts are not red, there would be for that [entity] a conjunction of contradictory properties consisting of being both red and non-red. This is like Devadatta, who occupies a single location, having one hand situated in the southern direction and the other in the northern direction; thus they are distinct.

Having refuted the proponent of external objects by stating that there is no object whatsoever to be inferred— such as [the claim] that there exists a pervasive entity characterized by the conjunction of contradictory properties occupying distinct southern and northern spatial divisions, and so forth— ...

He states— beginning with the words "the doctrine of external objects consisting of a collection of atoms"— in order to establish the external object as a collection of atoms, which is the position maintained by the Naiyāyikas.
Since a "collection" (sañcaya) is nothing other than the atoms themselves, when no other entity exists apart from them, only those very atoms remain.

If atoms, having placed one atom in the center, were to join with it without any interval, the conjunction of those atoms within that central atom would occur only due to the distinction of spatial directions (*dig-nāga*). He explains this very distinction of spatial directions as being in the four directions, beginning with the east.
When six atoms are being accumulated in the directions of up, down, and the four cardinal points,
if another atom were to adhere to that very same location where one atom is already adhered to the central atom, then for that central atom— [it would occupy no more space].
Because an atom has no spatial extension (*nikhaya*), [the six atoms surrounding it] would occupy the same space as a single atom;
yet the creation of the manifold world (*prapañca*) does not occur by means of a single atom alone.
He states another refutation with the words "otherwise," etc.: a single atom [occupying the center] of that which is situated in the middle...
If it is argued that [the atom] is joined at one part and joined at another part elsewhere,
then for this central atom, even though it is partless (*niraṃśatva*), a distinction of parts would necessarily follow;
for the very part of the partless central atom would be the ultimately real central atom.

Only the pentad remains. Thus, the pentad of atoms becomes a tetrad; the tetrad becomes a triad, that becomes a dyad, and that becomes a unity alone. Consequently, no external object whatsoever—composed of the manifold world derived from atoms—remains in reality.

In the conjunction of material atoms, because the central atom is attached to only one side, conjunction is impossible [with all others]. Therefore, due to the fitness for occupying distinct spatial locations and their mutual separation, the effect called a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) is established in the central atom.
It becomes a substance. You must not say that the large effects such as earth arise from those very same triads of atoms—whether intermediate or final;

this would be a direct contradiction of your own tenets (*apasiddhānta*). He states that [this position] has fallen [into error] with the words beginning "the doctrine of the whole" (*avayavivāda*), and so forth. And that doctrine of the whole...

It has already been refuted previously. Furthermore, since corporeal things cannot occupy the same location, when a central atom joins with other atoms, that which is called "non-pervasive occurrence" (avyāpyavṛttitva) would have to reside in that partless central atom; how could such non-pervasive occurrence possibly be consistent?

Because it is partless (*niraṃśatva*). In that case, it is not logical for atoms to exist [in conjunction]. If another atom inheres in the own-support, which is the very nature of the central atom, then what other part of this central atom's body remains for the atom that has entered? [There would be none.]

The meaning is that the body of the central atom would not pervade [the others]; thus, it follows that everything is not pervaded at all. This argument regarding the extreme minuteness (*paramāṇu-sva-aṇutva*) of the atom is also an additional refutation; however, we have placed no burden upon this supplementary argument by the Teacher.

In his own work, the *Prajñālaṃkāra*, Śaṅkaranandana has demonstrated at length this corroborating proof that serves as a sublation [of the opponent's position]: namely, that if the external object were distinct from the manifestation, it would follow—by virtue of being an object of inference—that there would be no manifestation of the external object; this is what you have stated as your primary intended point.

As for the subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*): likewise, the impossibility of the existence of a composite whole (*avayavin*) and so forth constitute further subverting proofs. However, these are incapable of affecting anything regarding the external object established by the proving means of knowledge (*sādhakapramāṇa*), which consists of various spontaneous appearances (*ākasmikābhāsa*); for that very [external object] is firmly established as being of the nature of spontaneous appearance.

Anticipating the objection that "the non-validity of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) which has been sublated by another means of knowledge is established as being merely an occasional appearance," he says [in verse 175]: "The Lord, whose nature is consciousness, abides within."

The connection with the preceding verse is as follows: "One should indeed manifest the apprehension of form through one's own intellect; what need is there for an external object, since it is logically untenable? In cases such as dreams, memory, mental fantasies, and volitions, consciousness does not manifest through an external object that serves as a prototype (*bimba*) for the reflection of awareness within it.

Thus, there is indeed the possibility [of such an experience]. Nevertheless, because the variety of blue and other objects appearing in dreams and so forth lacks stability upon reaching the waking state,
they are just like dreams.

(138) Since it is an object of perception, one might suspect that what appears in memory and the like is merely a product of impressions from prior experience; because such [an external object] is absent, it might be considered non-existent. However, this is not so, for the desire of yogins is established according to the consensus of all theorists.

Just as a variety of things such as cities and armies are seen [to arise] from mere [mental] intention, so too in the case of a yogi’s creation, a material cause (*upādāna*) consisting of clay and the like, which is well-known in the world, is simply not possible. Thus, omnipresent atoms, suddenly assembled by the will of the yogi, will commence the effect.

Even this cannot be said. As for the phrase "this": it is being examined in order to establish that the universally pervasive atoms, when suddenly conjoined by the will of a yogin, will begin to produce an effect, without overstepping the status of being causes consisting of atoms as established in the world.

It is not well-known in the world that gross objects such as jars arise directly from atoms alone; rather, they do not arise through the mere intervention of potsherds, litters, or bundles. Instead, the potsherd arises by intervening between the atoms, and the litter arises by intervening between those [potsherds].
Through that intervention, a cluster [of parts] arises; through that intervention, a jar is produced.

Even in that case, although the jar and so forth are produced through the intervention of potsherds and the like, there is a reliance upon constant auxiliary factors such as water and fire, as well as the activity of hands, feet, and so on, at an appropriate place and time.
When one relies upon these factors— past karma, the presence of the sense organs, the conjunction [of causes], time, training, and the excellence of practice—
if the yogi, desiring to fashion a jar, were to construct the pot preceded by knowledge of whatever well-known collection of materials the potter employs;
The yogi would be nothing but *kumbhaka* (the retention of breath), and it would follow that the yogi possesses no true state of being a yogi.

Therefore, the yogi’s transcendence of well-known causes such as clay and so forth—by means of contemplating other material causes (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) such as atoms (*paramāṇu*) and the like, which are unperceived yet visible—is [the point]. What is there [in this]?
The yogi possesses a power of manifestation (*nirmāṇa-śakti*) that is independent of material causes and so forth, such as clay or a potter, for the creation of cities, armies, and the like.

Since this power of manifestation enables the yogi to manifest the manifold variety of objects in the form of appearances— such as jars and lights— why is it accepted [as a proof] by means of the example of the yogi’s manifestation?
The Supreme Goddess Satī, whose sovereignty consists of the creative activity of the cosmic manifestation (prapañca),
by virtue of a specific power of will characterized by non-obstruction,
brings forth the multitude of existing things while they remain within the nature of consciousness, never abandoning their essential identity as consciousness.
Since there is no possibility for that which scatters the limited forms of consciousness— such as the vital breath, intellect, and body—
to appear as "this" or "that" as external objects to the knower, therefore,
the diversity of appearances in the form of the universe is established by one's own experience as belonging solely to the Divine, whose nature is Consciousness.

Why is autonomy (*svātantrya*) not accepted? Why is there such exertion in searching for other external causes? By the emphatic particle "only" (*eva*), he says this: the very self of consciousness (*cidātman*). Every proponent must admit that the determination of objects such as "this is a jar" and "this is a cloth"—the arrangement of jars, cloths, and so forth—is undeniable.
That nature of consciousness is established from the beginning; it is established even prior to objects such as pots and cloths,
and because it is established prior to objects such as pots and cloths, it is described as being liberated by its very nature of not requiring proof.

(p. 139) By the word *deva*, which denotes the agent of the cosmic play (*viśvakrīḍā*) and so forth of that whose nature is consciousness (*saṃvidrūpa*), the Teacher has indicated nothing other than the sovereignty (*svātantrya*) consisting of the nature of consciousness. What is the use of seeking external instruments? Therefore, the Self, whose essence is consciousness, is indeed God (*deva*). Thus...

Because it is conceived as "nurturing the universe" (*viśvaṃ bhāvayati*), the connection with the preceding [verse] is: "What need is there for an external conforming [object]? The phrase "in both ways" refers to the manner stated in the verse beginning with "Indeed, the non-dual Self alone... which establishes the doctrine of the proponents of external objects (*bāhyārthavādin*).

The inference based on probability (*saṃbhāvanānumāna*) emerges. In that regard, when probability is established through both modes of inference, one relies upon the example of a jar or similar object reflected in a mirror to understand the variety of appearances reflected within consciousness.

There is nothing other than the mirror of consciousness (*bodhadarpaṇa*). For this very reason, we might otherwise postulate that external things such as blue, yellow, and so forth, which are considered "external," are the cause for the appearance of the manifoldness of consciousness.

Alternatively, by relying on [the principle of] non-duality, [we may consider] the appearance of the manifoldness of the universe within consciousness—that is, the appearance of the manifoldness of consciousness itself in the form of the universe.

"We praise freedom alone as the cause. The statement "inference is not accepted at all regarding an object never before perceived by anyone" results in the sense that it is indeed not accepted; thus, it concludes with reference to the present state of affairs.
Regarding an object never before perceived, the acceptance of inference is desired without cessation—

Anticipating the objection, "In that case, how can there be a jar?", he states the following—beginning with the words "the sense organ also"—in order to resolve it: by the perception of effects such as sprouts from causal entities such as seeds, [the cause] is inferred;

and although it is unmanifest because it is eternally inferable rather than being a direct manifestation (*ābhāsa*), it is nonetheless perceived through the perception of its form and other qualities.

The sense organ indeed exists as something manifested; however, it does not exist as something external to manifestation. From manifestation—that is, from light—the manifestation of an object that is external and therefore not itself manifesting occurs in some way, whether by way of perception or by way of inference; it did not previously exist [independently].

It has indeed never been seen before. They [the opponents] say, "This is not so"—that there is no establishment of an external object through inference following upon perception, because it is distinct from that manifestation (*prakāśa*). If its establishment were through inference, then that object would necessarily be included within the manifestation itself; thus, even what you have stated [is untenable].
The external object, being non-external in nature, would result in nothing but light itself; thus, this is a fallacy of one's own tenet (*apasiddhānta*).

This was stated previously: "Light is of the nature of light; an object that is not light cannot be established. [Regarding the word] "immediately after": it is the very self of consciousness (*cidātman*).

By means of the arguments indicated in the immediately following verse, he states that what you have said—that [the object] does not appear as distinct from the light in perception—is not the very nature of perception itself: "That which appears as 'blue'—this alone is indeed perception; it [perceives] the presence of blue. (p.
140) It is this very thing that constitutes the manifestation of blue.

Since consciousness itself, being of the nature of pure luminous awareness, manifests through its own sovereignty as the blue object and nothing more, that manifestation of blue does not exceed pure luminous awareness. This is because there is no manifestation of an external object through perception.
The meaning of the word "also" (*api*) is that there is no establishment [of the object] even by means of inference that follows upon perception (*pratyakṣapṛṣṭhapātī*).

In that regard, "mere inference" regarding an external object means that inference alone, when deprived of perception, is not at all capable of proceeding toward an object; for if inference were to proceed [on its own] toward an object, [it would follow that] of inference...
Because it falls within the range of the manifesting entity,
even the sequence of blue, yellow, and so forth— which is intended to be external to that manifestation— is experienced [as falling within the range of the manifesting entity].

Because it has become an object (*viṣayabhūtatvāt*), it is manifest; therefore, by the very fact that its nature as blue, yellow, and so forth is established, one would not achieve the establishment of its externality. This is the summarized meaning seen through these two verses. Here, regarding the external—

Inference, which is considered to be presently occurring, is the conceptual operation of the cognizer who is the inferrer. All conceptualizations of one who has had experience are rooted in that experience.
As was stated previously:

"Is it not the case that one cognition has the appearance of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), while another is called conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and is associated with verbal expression (*sābhilāpa*)? and so forth. "By that" means by that object which is established through experience (*anubhava*).
That which has never been previously illumined is something never before experienced because it was not manifesting; regarding such an object never before experienced, inference—

defined as the cognitive operation of inferential cognition consisting of conceptualization— is not accepted by certain thinkers, such as the Cārvākas and others, just as [they do not accept] fire and so forth.

Regarding the means of valid cognition that is direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*)—let this discussion of yours concerning the entity be a mere conventional discourse; let it be so. But when you yourself do not perceive the cause of this effect, what will you say regarding the "inference based on general observation" (*sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa*) through the apprehension of that effect?

He dispels the objection— "How will inference proceed with respect to the sense organs, since they are not perceived, whereas inference proceeds with respect to an object generally perceived, as in the case of the perception of form?"— by saying "It is replied," and so forth.

Nevertheless, the established conclusion (sthiti) or certainty (niścaya) is this: although an object in the form of a sense-faculty is perceived by a conceptualization that is inferential in nature through the inference of the sense-faculty, that [object] is not [perceived] in the manner of tactile contact within the inference itself; rather, it is the conceptualization of the self [of the cognition] that is inferred in the very mode of tactile contact. This is the settled position.

Conceptual cognition, such as inference and the like, does not touch the object consisting of the senses and so forth through its specific configuration, color, grossness, and other such formal characteristics—that is, through that particular form of consciousness; rather, it [touches] the object of form and so on by means of [the thought]: "There is some cause of this kind."

By its own nature (*svabhāvena*), the sense-faculty characterized as a cause has as its intrinsic nature the direct perception of form and so forth. And likewise: even with respect to an object such as a seed that has been previously seen, [it is understood that] from the seed, a sprout [arises].
In cases such as "the cloth from the threads," when the sprout proceeds from the seed and the cloth from the threads,
one can determine this much by the force of perception and the force of non-perception— that is, by the non-perception of the seed and so forth—
once the causal relationship has been ascertained.

He states the distinction regarding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that possesses truth: "That perception (*pratyakṣa*)—which has as its object a sprout, a jar, or the like, appearing as swelling, goldness, redness, and so forth—possesses validity (*prāmāṇya*). By means of that..."

If it is asked how [the object] can be [considered real] since it performs purposeful action such as joy for the cognizer through a semblance of swelling and so forth, he says: for the cognizer whose characteristic is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*),
there is the swelling of the cognitive operation (*pramiti-vyāpāra*), which is the very life-force of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and whose characteristic is reflective awareness.

Because the meanings such as "swollen" (ucchūna) and so forth— denoted by each individual word such as "long," "golden," or "red"— rest [ultimately] upon that [single object], therefore, for every individual appearance (*pratyābhāsa*), perceptual validity (*prāmāṇya*) is possessed; thus,
the connection with color and so forth rests upon what is denoted by each individual word of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Regarding the statement that "the cognition concerning the object designated as the operation of valid cognition (*pramiti-vyāpāra*) is with respect to the thing (*vastu*)," [it means that] appearances such as gold and so forth are merely the universal (*sāmānya-mātra*), unqualified by space and time. For this very reason,
it will be determined later that [the object] is the universal alone, as experienced by all.

Thus, that [consciousness], being essentially reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), is internally undifferentiated by space, time, and so forth. In the first half [of the process], when it assumes states such as the sprout,
even the non-perception of the seed and so on is of the nature of the perception of something else— namely, the perception of the sprout and so forth.

In the cognition "the sprout [arises] from the seed," the cause such as the seed appears as something devoid of specific qualities such as length or thickness; it is apprehended precisely in this way. That entity from which another thing is not distinct, and for which there is a rule that "this arises only from this"—such that it does not arise without it—is of this nature.
That which conforms to the rule of a thing necessarily conforms to the effect of that thing; for instance, from the appearance of a cause such as clay and so forth— which possesses that [rule]—
and its effect, the jar, it follows that whatever conforms to the rule of a certain thing belongs to that very thing alone.

The term "effect" (kārya) refers, as previously stated, to the jar which appears as the effect-form of the clay—the material cause characterized by its broad base, belly, and neck. In the same way, the appearance of the seed and so forth certainly exists within the sprout and other such effects.
Therefore, your stated example—that the inference of the sense organs is based on the perception of objects as they truly are—is invalid.

This is indeed consistent, because [the object] is included within manifestation, whereas the meaning you have stated is external to manifestation. Nothing is external to manifestation as appearance (*ābhāsa*). For this very reason, it is non-appearance (*anābhāsa*).
It is a contradiction to say that something which is not manifest appears or is manifested. [In the case of] that which is non-manifest... (ṭp.)

142) Because it does not illuminate external objects, inference— which consists of conceptual construction— does not exercise its function regarding an external thing such as a village or a house by expressing it in the form "it is not a village" or "it is not a house. If it were expressed in the form of "non-village" and so forth, [it would follow that]...

Even that which exists within the village—[and so forth]—is not outside the manifestation; this is merely a variety of words. For there is indeed a difference in terminology regarding the existence of an object external to the village, [but in reality...]
Because [the object] is of the nature of form (*rūpa*) while the other [consciousness] is of the nature of luminosity (*prakāśa*),

the conceptualization of inference has arisen for you alone as something external; however, according to the principle that "in a conceptualization there is no real entity," the conceptualization of inference does not touch upon the actual object.

However, we have already established in this very sūtra that [the world] from Śiva down to the earth is determined as being of the nature of valid cognition (*pramā*). Regarding the phrase "by that": when an object external to the light (*prakāśa*) has not yet appeared, inference functions...

It would be merely inferred through conceptual construction (*kalpa*). If, however, it is held that external objects, when entered by the conceptualization of inference, possess the very nature of being manifest, then that [manifestation] alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for that object.
On the contrary, your very statement— that it establishes only the external— is a contradiction;
for the manifestation of the external occurs precisely through the mode of its own self-manifestation, and thus there is no manifestation of an object that is not itself manifest.

"It did not exist. Therefore, it has been stated that Māyā, by its own will, manifests the established universe externally to the subjects (*pramātṛs*). That universe [resides] within that Divine One, who is the conscious Self (*cidātman*).
For one who is established—

[in the state of] being situated within the nature consisting of consciousness— and who abides perfectly through identity with that [consciousness], there is indeed the manifestation of the entire collection of objects. Therefore, from the objects established in the Self...

The nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is its own essential being; this reflective awareness, whose form is will, exists precisely by internalizing that which is to be willed—that which is to be reflected upon. When such reflective awareness manifests even as an external form, such as "this," it does so by means of its own inherent power.
Even in manifestation, the internal nature—the nature of "I-ness"—is not severed; for the universe is [constituted by] that internalization.
And that internalization always exists even during external manifestation. Therefore, according to the principle to be stated later, "this [manifestation] is itself the Self" (p. 143).

The multitude of entities (*bhāvajāta*) shines forth by means of that [Light] which has arisen from its power; it does not break apart in the form of an end—this is the connection with what precedes. While that [Light] manifests as the very self of the subject (*pramātṛ*), the multitude of entities... [is connected] by means of that [Light].

Since the external world that appears is not ultimately real, the state of being situated within this collection of entities— namely, "here"— is indeed nothing other than the consciousness that is perfectly integrated with the "I. Otherwise, there could be no reflective awareness in the form of desire directed toward an object to be sought.
If the potter were constrained by the thought, "I shall make a jar," then why would there not arise from that unconstrained desire for a jar a desire for a cloth? [Therefore, it is a jar.]
The conventional designations for cloth and so forth would become confused; likewise, conventional expressions such as "the desire for a jar is restricted by the jar" and so on would become confused.
Now, even in that case of the desire "I shall make a jar," that [jar] would be the object of seeking.

At that very moment, the jar, being composed of will alone and fashioned by the internal cause, arises in such a way as to become the object of desire; if one thinks, "Let me fashion it," then its creation occurs at that very instant through his own will, assuming the role of a potter.
Since nothing whatsoever is possible for the Supreme Lord, whose nature is consciousness, without His will, it will be explained here that His will alone is the cause;
thus, His will is that very collection of entities which are to be desired and perceived.
"By means of [the subject's] reflective grasping (*parāmarśa*), [the object] becomes transferred to the Lord.
— This has already been stated: "The manifestation of the multitude of objects occurs while the Lord remains established in Himself.
At that time, even another will (*icchā*) intent upon internal creation is either constrained by an object or not.

If, when conceptualization has become the object, [the will] were not constrained by the jar, then even another desire for a cloth and so forth would not arise; thus there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Now, if at that very time another desire were produced and constrained by its own object—

A jar that has become the object of that [first] desire, having been created by another desire distinct from it, becomes the object of that previous desire. He concludes the state of being established by the words beginning with "tasmāt" (therefore). Regarding "tasmāt":

through the medium of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) whose nature is will, this entire mass of objects to be desired and contemplated possesses a body that is eternally luminous within the Lord, the Self of Consciousness, in the very form of "I."

Thus, the entire range of entities is established within the Self by virtue of its nature as the Sovereign Lord (*aiśvara*). According to the stated principle— that because of the state of being a master, because of being superior to the universe, because of sovereignty, and because of having the nature of possessing power, consciousness does not desire any separation from that master— consciousness, as the Supreme Goddess (Parābhaṭṭārikā), joined with that Master, the Unsurpassed Lord (Anuttara Bhaṭṭāraka), [pervades] this entire range from Śiva down to the earth.

Just as a potter and others create such a mass through a sequential process with respect to the creation [of jars], so too does the Yogin [create] the Omniscient One and others with respect to their manifestation. According to the stated principle that "the cognition 'this is to be grasped' belongs even to the bound soul (paśu)," there exists in the interim a subject (*pramātṛ*) consisting of the grasper (*grāhaka*), which is distinct from one another and from *Mayā*.

Through emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) and through their "this-ness" (*idantā*), which is mutually differentiated therein, He externalizes them as distinct from each respective subject. Regarding the phrase "therein also": even within the manifestation of the subject, He unifies the subjects who are spectators in certain instances, such as when witnessing a woman’s dance.

In this much alone— namely, the mere dance— the manifestation of those perceivers consists solely of appearances; [therein] the appearance of the body, vital breath, intellect, pleasure, and so forth belonging to the perceiver who is the spectator appears as the body of one person,
while that of another is endowed with youth, and that of yet another is decayed by old age.

For one person it is weak, for another it is powerful; for one, the intellect is endowed with the quality of *sattva*, while for another it is endowed with the quality of *tamas*; for one there is happiness through a wife, fields, and so forth, while for another there is unhappiness due to the absence of those things—of such a nature [is desire]. One...

Thus, through the vision of non-difference and the vision of difference, there is for the subjects a unification in the form of oneness; yet even therein, because the mutual distinction between the body, the vital breath, and so forth has not dissolved,
there is a disjunction— such is the manifold variety [of states].
Through the variety of binding and unbinding— by means of emanation, withdrawal, and so forth—
he elaborates, expands, sustains, withdraws, conceals, and again dissolves; thus, through the activity of ceaseless manifestation, he elaborates the universe.

The meaning is that he expands [the universe]. Because he is the creator of creation, maintenance, and dissolution at all times, he is one who finds delight in constant creation (*sadāsṛṣṭivinodāyate*). Because he is the perpetual sustainer of those [three], he sits in the bliss of constant maintenance (*sadāsthitisukhāsīna*). [to him]...

Or, according to the principle stated in the verse, "Does this wood not become fire once the fire has been placed within it?", the three worlds are dissolved into the Withdrawer by means of the act of withdrawal for the sake of that [dissolution].
Thus, the Supreme Lord is eternally satisfied by those three worlds which have become his food; such is the conceptualization.
By means of hundreds [of powers] beginning with *sṛṣṭi*, he repeatedly and without rest emits the three worlds—consisting of the earth and ending with *puruṣa*;
from *niyati* and ending with *māyā*;
and from *śuddhavidyā* and ending with *Śiva*.

Unceasingly and without rest, conceiving, creating, sustaining, withdrawing, concealing, and bestowing grace—He is someone beyond the reach of words, whom even Hari, Hayaśiras, and Viriñca await outside, according to the principle stated [in scripture]; thus He alone is beyond the reach of Hari, Brahmā, and the others. Because there is no other person like himself among existing beings, he is alone and without a second;

because he is free from such conceptual constructions as "I am Caitra and not Maitra," he is devoid of worldly discrimination and is therefore perfect. Unborn and free from transformations such as birth and so forth, the Supreme Lord is victorious through his absolute preeminence.
It exists. Thus, the fact that he exists as the most excellent one, constantly performing the fivefold activity (*pañcakṛtya*), is the point of agreement.
He concludes with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*). "The multitude of existents resides within"—that is, it abides therein.

The reason is that, without the multitude of entities situated within it, the multitude of entities belonging to the Lord could not exist; for it is impossible for the Lord— who is the subject of the non-existence of the multitude of entities [and] who is the nature of that which has become the reflection of the multitude of entities— to possess the status of being the Lord's own nature.

Mastery (svāmitva) itself is not possible [in this context]. A reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) is a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) because its life-force is language. That reflective awareness—consisting of conceptual constructions that exclude others, such as "this is a jar, not a cloth"—is non-conceptual (*avikalpa*), because there is no object to be excluded distinct from itself, since its own self is the nature of all things.

Anticipating the objection— "If the Lord, the Master, whose body is pure consciousness, is entirely full and free from blemish, how could [any lack of self-awareness] exist?"— he states that reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) alone is the essential nature of the light of consciousness: "Without this reflective awareness, there is no true definition (*svālakṣaṇya*) of the light."

It distinguishes [the subject] from other modes by means of the "giver" (dāyin). According to the method to be explained later, that which is the reflective awareness of "I" (*ahaṃ-pratyavamarśa*) regarding the manifestation— which is the light whose nature is full consciousness—

The reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*)— which consists of the acceptance of the destruction of all that is denoted and denotative from Śiva down to the end of initiation—
is like the burning power of fire; it is not something that was previously non-existent,
even upon awakening, within the *Śrīśivasūtra-āgama*, the *Śrīmallinīvijayottara*, and other primary scriptures of realization.

By Śiva, who declares that "consciousness is the Self," the state of equilibrium with the world is [established]; by him who declares that "the supreme power is Mālinī," the power of consciousness is seen to be unchanging, and for one who sees thus, liberation is the state of being pure consciousness alone.
And by the Blessed One Ananta, who declares that consciousness is the primary attribute of the Self whose nature is luminosity, it was said:
"There is no cognition in the world that occurs without the accompaniment of words."

(186) By the venerable Bhartṛhari, through stating such [verses], the primacy of consciousness (*caitanya*) has been demonstrated; hence the use of the plural form "they know" (*viduḥ*). "Otherwise" means: if light were devoid of the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), that light...

"In this world, the Supreme Lord is of the nature of light, and light..."

Its essential nature is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). For reflective awareness indeed consists in the vibration of "I" (*aham*) as the manifestation of the universe in the form of the universe. [For] it would follow that one who lacks reflective awareness would be neither a sovereign lord nor sentient, and so forth.
Even though it is transparent, this crystal and the like does not know its own internal manifold nor itself;
I, however, am capable of knowing the manifold.
One should not [conceive] the Self as residing within itself or as being independent;
consciousness is distinct from the insentient.
Thus, there is a distinction between light and the insentient objects such as jars, which possess the nature of light.

Intending to demonstrate precisely this point—that [the Self] is the giver—[the author], in order to refute other proposed modes [of manifestation] that lack this specific quality of being the giver of differentiation from the Light, says:
"In this world, the manifestation... and so forth. [He explains: "The manifestation of the 'I'-form is the Light... and so on.

If those two—the light and the jar, etc.—were to exist within their own selves through mutual exclusion, such that the light, being of the nature of "I," excludes the jar, etc., which are of the nature of "not-I," and remains established only within itself; and likewise the jar, etc., [excludes the light]... [187] ...and remains established only within itself.
If form, having abandoned manifestation, were to abide solely within itself,
then its distinctness [from consciousness] would be difficult to establish; for since manifestation is entirely contained within itself,
it would follow that objects such as jars and cloths are not cognized.

Like a jar or a cloth that exists solely within its own self, illumination (*prakāśa*) would also be insentient (*jaḍa*) for him. Thus, since illumination is of an insentient nature, how could it be distinct from non-illuminated things such as jars? This is one mode of objection. Manifestation (*avabhāsa*), however, is of the nature of cognition (*jñāna*).
If it is argued that light is not insentient because it is related to the object in the form of the knowable— and thus, by virtue of being related,
it is not insentient— then, by the mere fact of being related (as in the case of "related to a jar"), it would follow that it is not insentient;
this is one mode of refutation.

Alternatively, if it is argued that "awakening" (saṃbodha) is the manifestation of an object such as a jar, then it follows that awakening— which is of the nature of consciousness— is identical with the jar and so forth, which are of the nature of the insentient. For [otherwise] there would be no connection between awakening,
which is non-insentient in nature, and an object that is insentient in nature.

(p. 147) He says that manifestation by another nature is not appropriate: the manifestation of one thing, such as a jar, by a manifestation belonging to another nature is not logically possible. On the view that [objects] are insentient, a jar or a cloth does not manifest in its own nature; so how could cognition, which is of the nature of "I," manifest in the form of "this"?

"May it manifest"—this is the manner of mutual refutation: although a jar has a nature other than manifestation, by the mere act of its own perception, it becomes the cause for the arising of consciousness, which is of the nature of manifestation. In that case, the relation of cause and effect implies that the jar, as the cause, is insentient (*jaḍa*).

If it is argued that cognition, even though it is of the nature of an effect, is non-inert (*ajaḍa*), then the manifestation in the form of knowledge would be the cause of the jar, which is of the nature of the object to be known; consequently, the jar, despite being an effect, would likewise have to be non-inert. Just as inertness is accepted for light even when it is an effect, so too it must be for the jar.
Even if it were an effect, it would follow that it lacks insentience; this too is a fault of the same kind.

Now, when an appearance (*ābhāsa*) is manifested by another existing thing, such as a jar, its own clear shadow in the form of a reflection is imparted; bearing that shadow in the form of a reflection, this appearance is said to belong to the jar. And thus, the shadow—

If it is argued that [the Self] is called "non-inert" merely because of its capacity to sustain [objects], then even a crystal, water, a mirror, and so forth would likewise be non-inert simply by virtue of sustaining the reflection of an image. This is the manner of the ultimate refutation. Now, as for the claim that the crystal and such are of that nature, [it applies equally to] pots, cloths, and so on.
If it is maintained that the Self is insentient (*jaḍa*) because it is incapable of reflecting upon itself as the bearer of reflections or upon objects such as jars reflected therein,
then [the same would apply to] the reflection of the entire universe— from Śiva down to the earth— within the Self.

The reflective awareness (*parāmarśana*) pertaining to that universe which has been reflected is the life-force and the very breath of non-inertness; it consists of the sovereignty (*svātantrya*) of manifesting such a universe both internally and externally,
and is the natural, inherent nature of Light as "I" (*aham*).
The very act of supreme awareness (*paramarśana*), characterized by resting within one’s own self, is precisely what it means to not look toward another face.

Not looking toward another face means that because the universe—which is conceived as "other"—is embraced within one's own self, it is oriented toward one's own self alone. Being oriented toward one's own self...

He demonstrates its very reality: when the light shines as the manifestation of the denotable (vācya) from Śiva down to the earth and the denotative (vācaka) from speech-sounds down to the earth— provided that there is the arising of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) within this light— then the self-awareness of the light, which is its own experience, alone constitutes the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge.

He considers the manifold world (*prapañca*) to have fulfilled its purpose; because that manifold is manifested as the nature of the "I" (*ahaṃtā*), he considers his own consciousness alone to have achieved its aim. He who perceives this entire circle of objects as a conceptual construction sees the whole of existence as the body of the Lord.
When the world has been completely filled with his own nature, how could there be any fear for this eternally blissful one?

According to the principle thus stated, because the universe is assimilated into one's own self (*svātmīkāra*), one does not desire anything whatsoever as distinct from oneself; even when inert objects such as crystal and the like reflect images of perceived jars, cloths, and so forth, they do not appear as such [as separate entities],
for even these reflected jars, cloths, and the like perceived by the crystal are likewise [of the nature of the Self].

If it is established that this crystal and so forth, by virtue of its own nature, grasps a reflection as something excellent, then [that which claims] "this has grasped a reflection" must depend upon another cognizer distinct from itself;
thus, because it lacks self-awareness (*nirvimarśatva*), the crystal and so forth are insentient (*jaḍa*) and incapable [of such cognition].

The jar and other objects that project their reflections, as well as the other cognizing subjects who perceive both of them, rest within the reflective awareness of "I" (ahaṃparāmarśa) at the initial limit— which is the state prior to the creation of the universe from Śiva down to the earth— and at the final limit, which is the state of withdrawal.
It is indeed non-inert. Furthermore,

even in the middle category consisting of "this-ness" (idantā), such as a jar or a cloth, it is non-inert because it rests within the subject (pramātṛ) whose nature is "I-ness" (ahantā) in both its states prior to and subsequent to the arising of the respective cognitions.
As it has been said: "The fulfillment of the reflective awareness (*avimarśa*) of 'this'—which is differentiated from [the subject]—in its own essential nature;

[and] the so-called fulfillment of the reflective awareness of blue and yellow, which are mutually differentiated from the cognizer (e.g., 'this is blue,' 'this is yellow'), is indeed their resting in their own essential nature."

This reflective awareness is "I" (ahaṃ). It is that intermediate state which extends from the two extremes consisting of the prior non-existence and the posterior non-existence of the entire universe— from Śiva down to the earth— up to the state of withdrawal known as resting in the essential nature of the form of "I."
That very same "I-ness" (*ahantā*), when not reflected upon,

constitutes the prior and posterior limits of the state of "this-ness" (*idantā*); for those who are thus deluded and have not recognized their own true nature as the Great Lord, it is called *māyā* in the state of differentiation— that is, transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*).

It is established and certain that the supreme consort (*parābhaṭṭārikā*) of the Blessed One, the Supreme Lord (*anuttarabhaṭṭāraka*), in her very form, is the primary form [of consciousness]. By us, the followers of the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*, who are devoted to consciousness (*sāṃvidaḥ*), [this] nature of consciousness...

He shows that it is we alone who have stated that the primacy of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) belongs to consciousness, by pointing out that this has been stated by the venerable *Sūtras* and other texts which are to be understood. For this very reason,
because its nature is the power of reflective awareness, the activity of consciousness (*citkriyā*) consists essentially in the agency of consciousness (*citi kartṛtā*).
He has arisen as the wall of consciousness. The term "conscious activity" (citkriyā) refers primarily to the state of being the agent of consciousness;

intending that very agency of consciousness as the supreme [principle], the Self—whose nature is the substratum (dharmin) and who is conscious—is designated by the word "consciousness" (caitanya), which denotes the substratum. For this reason, by him...

Because consciousness is conjoined [with the self], it is distinct from the insentient; thus, due to the absence of such consciousness in that [insentient matter], its difference from it is indeed logical. As it has been said:
"Cognition is distinct from the insentient, because it is not measured by anything else."

Thus, in the sūtra, "The nature of manifestation is distinct from the jar and other objects—which are insentient and devoid of consciousness—because [the Self] has consciousness as its essence," it is stated that *vimarśa* (reflective awareness) alone is the primary and principal form of the Self's consciousness, with the intent of establishing the Self as the agent (*kartṛ*). For, [it is] of the Self... [p. 149]... [that this is so].
Taking this very inquiry— which is the very form of the purpose and constitutes valid means of knowledge— as the cause,

[it is established that] the nature of phenomena consists in being the source of origin for all attributes such as agency residing in Śiva, Īśvara, and others, and because it is the place of rest for those very attributes.

Even though the self (*ātman*) is the substance (*dravya*), by using a word expressing its attribute (*dharma*), one says "this self is consciousness" (*caitanya*) and "this, however, is its consciousness. Thus, setting aside this level of distinction, one resorts to grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), as in "Śiva is Śaṅkara," [saying] "the self is consciousness."
It has been declared in the scriptures that "consciousness" (caitanya) is [the Self]; this is the remainder of the statement.

He demonstrates this very point: by the Blessed Śiva, in the Śivasūtras, it was stated that "consciousness alone is the Self. The word "consciousness" refers to those qualities which are yet to be described.
"Citi" is an indicative term for words denoting properties such as the "object of sight" (dṛśya) and so forth.
Even when assuming the form of the universe, consciousness (citi-śakti) is not subject to the loss of its own essential nature;
it is the conscious seer, and the isolation (kaivalya) of seeing—that is, pure perception alone—is its true nature.

"The seer is of the nature of seeing, the power of consciousness, immutable; he is the seer of that seeing, being pure seeing alone"—in such sūtras, the teacher Ananta has shown the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the word "attribute" (*dharma*) with the Self (*ātman*). Regarding what was stated [by him]: "The Self is not a substance (*adravyabhūta*)," [the following applies].
He defines *dravyatva* (substantiality) itself with the words, "For that which is called substance," and so forth.

In that substantial nature of the Self, wherein all objects—such as pots, cloths, and the like—find their rest, everything shines forth within the indestructible consciousness. Likewise, according to the principle stated previously regarding those things that have become insentient (*jaḍa*).

In that imperishable substance which is the nature of the Self, the entire world of cognition has been completely and correctly set; for this very reason, it is at rest. It appears in forms such as "this is a jar" or "this is a cloth," and it is sought for purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) in the form of fetching water, covering, and so forth. That alone [is real].
It is called a "substance" (*dravya*).

Furthermore, in order to state once more that substance alone possesses ultimate reality (*paramārthatā*), he restates it following the previous [argument] with a touch of irony, beginning with the words "tadyat" and so forth. There is no anger in this.
If [the universe]— consisting of the dissolution of the entire totality of principles such as earth and the rest, and of entities such as the *kalās*, elements, jars, and cloths—

is brought to rest within the consciousness of the forest and other such collections, which is the nature of the Self, that is, within awakened awareness, it becomes thus; that is, it exists as the very nature of earth and the rest, existing in each of those respective forms.

Regarding the phrase "it manifests": it refers to a specific substance such as earth, which is of the nature of a distinct category of entity (padārtha) like earth and so forth, serving as the substratum for attributes (dharma) such as smell and the like, for actions such as supporting, and for universals (sāmānya) and other properties.

(150) Since she is the place of rest for the supreme arising of substances, one takes recourse in that very consciousness which is the primary form of substance; thus, that Blessed Consciousness itself is the substance.
Because it is that [consciousness] alone which possesses the nature of substance, it is the resting place for an infinite mass of attributes such as eternity and so forth.
Of that very consciousness (*saṃvit*), which is the supreme Bhaṭṭārikā and whose nature is volition (*cetanā*),
that very attribute consisting of self-reflection (*vimarśa*) is itself volition.

By means of the suffix *-tva*— which denotes the state of being volitional (*caitanya*) even while expressing a relationship— the state of being volitional (*caitanya*) is primarily [the essence of] the volitional (*cetana*).
It has been shown that consciousness (*caitanya*) is indeed volition (*cetanā*).

He demonstrates its very predominance with the words "for instance" (*tathā hi*), and so forth. Since the relation rests upon the related entities—and because [the agent] is expressed by the verbal root itself—the conscious one [is the primary factor].

Because it has been stated by the *pratipādika* [the nominal stem]. According to the principle that "it causes to perceive, therefore it is consciousness (*citih*)," even while making known the very consciousness—which is of the nature of the act of perceiving—as the related factor connected to the attribute (*dharma*), that [consciousness] is not determined correctly as being distinct. (192)

The agency within the category of knowledge is manifested in the collection of the intellect and its functions. In the case of a single jar, there is the conjunction of memory and perception through the thought "this is that very [jar].

In the case of a single jar, there is the disjunction of memory and the subsequent synthesis through the thought "this is [a jar]. Furthermore, in the case of a single jar, there is [the cognition of] its being made of gold...

And so forth, including "the people"—this manifold sovereignty exists solely within the Self, within the very nature of the Self alone. Like an insentient object such as a jar, it is characterized by non-resting due to its pervasion of all space and time; it incessantly performs the five cosmic acts (*pañcakṛtya*).

Since the Self, whose nature is uninterrupted luminosity, does not depend on the face of another— having set aside that state of being dependent on another's face which belongs to a Self existing as something other than that uninterrupted luminosity—
that [dependence] consists in the form of agency within consciousness.

Intending and determining autonomy (*svātantrya*) as the primary [attribute], it should be said that the Self (*ātman*) is consciousness (*caitanya*); however, in order to establish the permanence of that Self whose nature has been investigated, and to bring forth its attribute which consists of investigation (*vimarśa*), it is stated that the Self is consciousness (*caitanyam*). This is the activity of consciousness (*cit-kriyā*).

"Citi-kartṛtā-tātparyeṇa" is a compound word (*samasta-pada*). According to the convention in the science of poetry (*kāvyāśāstra*), a pause at the middle of a quarter-verse constitutes a compound. Therefore, it is stated that "the activity of consciousness (*cit-kriyā*) has as its primary purport the agency of consciousness (*citi-kartṛtā-tātparyeṇa*). Alternatively, just as one says "self-consciousness" (*ātma-caitanya*), so too is it called "the activity of consciousness" (*cit-kriyā*); in that case, [it is understood as] "having as its primary purport the agency of consciousness" (*citi-kartṛtā-tātparyeṇa*).

The word *pada* is not accompanied by the activity of consciousness (*cit-kriyā*). Just as there is no reading stating "consciousness is the self" (*caitanya ātmā*), there is nowhere a reading stating "the activity of consciousness is the self.
For example, luminosity is of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), while non-luminosity is of the nature of non-consciousness (*acid-rūpa*).
Both [the light] and the jar and so forth are "in their own self" (svātmani); thus, light rests in its own nature as light alone,
while even the non-luminous jar and so forth rest in their own self, which is insentient and consists of forms such as a broad base and a bulbous belly.
[The subject] rests [in itself]. For, according to the principle stated as "of those things that have become inert" (193), it is not the case that light alone rests [in itself];

rather, because of that, for the sake of each resting in its own respective nature, when it is said, "I am the light whose nature is the Self," then from that inert [object], there arises the light whose nature is the "I."

If the manifestation of the jar and so forth— which is light— and the non-manifestation of the jar and so forth— which is darkness— do not coexist within their own nature due to their mutual exclusion, then it would be as difficult to establish the distinction between them as it is between a jar and a cloth, such that one could say, "this is conscious" and "this is insentient. Thus, their difference would be impossible to justify.
