If there were no distinction [between them], then, as in the case of a jar and a cloth, it would be difficult to establish the difference between "this is conscious" and "this is insentient"; thus, the commentary on the Sūtra regarding the nature of manifestation takes the form of an objection concerning how such a distinction could be asserted.

It may be that, similarly, even in the case of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), it shines within its own self, whereas non-awareness (*avimarśa*)— which is the opposite of that— does not shine within its own self as "I. Therefore, by means of that reflective awareness which rests solely within its own self,
there is a distinction between light— which is otherwise considered inert— and inert objects such as a jar.

Anticipating the question "How so?", he says: "Citi. The Supreme Lord, the Self of the universe, is that which cognizes (*cetayati*). Here, the action of cognition (*citi-kriyā*) is the power of consciousness (*citi-śakti*); that [power] is the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) characterized by the wonder of one's own self, namely "I" (*aham*).
That reflective awareness is the very essence of the power of consciousness.

By its own inherent nature (*svarasa*), which is the form of consciousness (*cidrūpa*) and whose essence is repose in its own self, it is arisen as continuous, unceasing, and eternally supreme. Because other reflective awarenesses—such as "this is blue" or "this is Caitra"—have already become objects of measurement (*miti*), she transcends the supreme universe; having internalized within herself the entire universe from Śiva down to the earth, she speaks.

It speaks—that is, it reflects upon—as its own self, as far as [this process extends]. This means that within such consciousness, the primary sovereignty itself, which consists of the power of the Self, the Supreme Lord, is the supreme and ultimate nature of speech (*vāk*); it is full sovereignty, the state of being a ruler, which requires no dependence on anything else.
In the state of Śiva, which consists of that which transcends the fourth (turyātīta), the supreme sovereignty (parāvara-aiśvarya) is said to exist;
in the states of Sadāśiva and Īśvara, which consist of the fourth (turya), the form of the visionary (paśyantī) is the lower sovereignty (apara-aiśvarya);
and in the waking and other states, the forms of the intermediate (madhyamā) and the manifest (vaikhārī) constitute the [remaining] sovereignty.

In the state of *māyā*, which consists of form (*rūpa*), there exists that which pertains to Viṣṇu, Viriñca, Indra, and the rest; yet even that arises solely from the grace of the Supreme Lord (*pārameśvara*). Thus, it is entirely logical to say that the Self (*ātman*) is distinct from the insentient due to such sovereignty (*svātantrya*). He is both identical with the universe (*viśvamaya*) and transcendent of the universe (*viśvottīrṇa*).

According to the stated principle that the Supreme Lord, by His own will, dissolves the universe— from Śiva down to the earth— back into Himself as His own screen, that consciousness which reflects upon [the universe] as being within His own self is the consciousness whose very nature is the autonomy of the act of cognizing; of that consciousness, of that creative act of cognition...

Reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*)—characterized by the wonder of one’s own self which contains the entire universe from Śiva down to the earth—is the Self. Because consciousness is inherently active, its nature is that of reflective awareness; the insentient [lacks this]. (p. 152)

And he demonstrates this by way of the connection with insentient objects: "By means of the jar, one is wondrously affected within one's own self in the form of its broad base and belly; one's own self is perceived through that jar;
by that jar, one's own self is manifested; yet one's own self is not [limited] by it."
Because it rests in a single place and time,
it is not manifested as something unlimited by virtue of its nature of pervading all places and times; therefore,
since there is no manifestation of it as limited, it is said that "the self is perceived by Caitra through the jar."

But in one's own self, which is of the nature of consciousness, through the union with the glory of its form— the expansion consisting of the blossoming of the reflective awareness "I"— one is struck with wonder and filled with bliss;
such a nature of the self as "I" is thus reflected upon, independent of anything else.

It is manifested within its own self. That very determination which takes the form "this is blue" rests for the time being in the mere blue through that [externalized] form. Having become distinct from the determination "this," it is joined with the objects of the external organs—blue, yellow, and so forth—as well as the objects of the internal organ, such as pleasure and pain.
It is manifested through the conjunction with the appearances of blue, yellow, pleasure, pain, and emptiness. As it has been said:
"Blue does not exist in yellow and the like, nor does visual cognition exist therein;
auditory cognition and the rest do not exist in them either, yet the knower persists as a common factor throughout them all."

Thus, because blue, yellow, and so forth are manifested through the process of appearing as numbers, one's own self— which is endowed with the manifestation of those various numbers— is said to be "cognized by Caitra. In this way, because the cognition of Caitra is joined with such a reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of things as they have become, [the self] resides within the nature of that reflective awareness.

"Reflection within one's own self," as you have stated, is indeed established. Reflection, when ascended upon consciousness, is all-enduring; it does not rest solely within its own nature like a jar or a cloth. He demonstrates that very quality of being all-enduring: "This state extends up to the limit of the form of the object of knowledge. [He says], "Fearless."

"I" unifies this "form"— namely, the essential natures of both self and other— into a single identity within the state of "I-ness" through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), such that one says, "I am this" and "this is I. However, in the stages of Sadāśiva and Īśvara,
this duality consisting of "I" and "this" does not submerge its own nature.
He renders [the world] empty. This is the state of the *pralayākala*.
The unmentioned *avidyeśvara*s and *vijñānākala*s are included within the realm above *māyā*. As it has been said:
"The agent of the transformation (*parikartṛ*) and that which is to be transformed (*parikārya*)—both are made one's own by means of the causative suffix (*ṇij*)."
"Is deliberation (*vimarśa*) not capable of making everything one in this world?
Thus: "I am indeed I" is Śiva; "I am this" is Sadāśiva; "This is I" is Īśvara;
"I am indeed I, and this is indeed this" is Vidyeśvara; "Not this" is Vijñānākala; "Not this... [and so on].

Nor is there the state of dissolution (*pralayakala*) characterized by "I am not"; rather, there are seven subjects, beginning with "I am this body" and "I am all these things. Furthermore, the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*), which consists of internal speech, is the very nature of the activity within consciousness.

It is the nature of sound (*śabdana*), consisting of the discernment of the entire universe— from Śiva down to the earth— as being one's own self; and likewise, there is the conventional designation (*saṅketa*) of "jar" for an object with a broad base and a bulbous belly,
and the conventional designation of "cloth" for a substance consisting of warp and woof, and so forth.

It is independent of those various conventional words; for this very reason, it consists of uninterrupted aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*), and thus its nature is full bliss (*pūrṇānanda*). Because it abides in its own self, it is oriented toward the form of the full I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhantā*) within, and it takes the form of an internal approach that is like the pointing of a finger.

Because it is complete, being the very life-force of conventional words consisting of the manifestation of differentiation— from the letter 'a' to 'kṣa'— which issues forth through the medium of various individual subjects, and because it serves as the internal reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) consisting of the grasped and the grasper, such as "this is blue" or "I am Caitra."

She is transcendent beyond the universe; she is called *vāk* because she speaks—that is, having internalized the aforementioned form of the universe, she expresses it and contemplates it directly. "For this very reason" means: because she expresses [the world] internally, she is eternally arisen as the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpatā*) by her own innate essence—that is, by her own imperishable essence whose body is repose in her own self. (196)

By the principle that "I am" is never extinguished, this consciousness—which consists of the reflective awareness as described—is the supreme speech (parāvāk) flowing by its own inherent nature. It is that very "I-ness" (ahantā), which withdraws the entire collection of phonemes from beginning to end;
this power of consciousness, whose form is supreme speech, is the primary sovereignty of the Self.
The supreme, perfect sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), lordship (*īśitṛtva*), and independence of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) are here described. In this state of Śiva, the supreme level (*parāvasthā*),
by way of the application of the term "supreme" (*param*), [the nature of] the supreme-non-supreme self...
And the supreme sovereignty has been implied; he states that very point with the words "But the higher and lower," etc.

The higher and lower sovereignty of the Supreme Lord—who consists of the manifestation known as *aham* (I)—is such that, for this very reason, even in the mere emergence of the thought "this" within the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) which is of the nature of existence, [that sovereignty is present].

The ellipsis is that [the yogin], suddenly perceiving "I am this, I am this, I am this," abides in the state of *paśyantī* on the plane beginning with Śiva. However, the supreme sovereignty of the Supreme Lord is distinct from that of Viṣṇu, Viriñca, Indra, and others who are governed by *māyā*.

Even that [attainment] of the true natures (tattvas) and their essential forms during the intermediate state and other stages arises solely from the grace of Viṣṇu, Viriñca, and the Supreme Lord; thus,
in the ultimate sense, the independence of the Supreme Lord is itself bliss and sovereignty.

It is called "sovereignty" (*svātantrya*) and it is called "consciousness" (*caitanya*). Because it is endowed with that reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) which is of the nature of consciousness and constitutes its very essence, this is indeed entirely logical.
This reflective awareness, which is the essential nature of this Light and serves as its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [is taught] in the principal scriptures (*pradhānāgama*).
It is demonstrated even in the *Mālinīvijayottara*, the *Trika*, and other scriptures (p.

154); he explains this with the words "se ti" (that). Starting from the aphorism "of the Lord who is established in the Self," [the text proceeds] up to "sphurattā" (vibration), which extends from Śiva down to the earth.
Because she transcends the universe—from Śiva down to the earth—which consists of the agency that causes the manifestation of all things;
because she pervades the prior and posterior limits of that entire universe; and because she is unconditioned by space and time, her nature is all-pervasive and eternal.
Furthermore, she is the cause of the creation of all space and time.

Because it pervades space and time through contact with them, its nature is all-pervasive and eternal; for this very reason, being characterized by space and time, the Great Being (*mahāsattā*)—which is of the nature of existence (*sadrūpa*)—pervades even non-existent things like a sky-flower, just as it pervades existent things like pots and cloths. Thus, it is a great, uninterrupted existence (*avichinnā sattā*). (197)

She is the one whose nature is the agency of creation, beginning from Śiva down to the earth. "That very same [power]" refers to her as perceived by the fortunate ones who possess the glance of a true Guru; she is remembered through hearing the scriptures (āgama-śāstra) heard from the mouth of the Guru, and meditated upon. "This" refers to her as being experienced through one's own direct realization (svapratyaya).
The experience of resonance is the Śrī Parā, who is the object of the venerable *Pratyabhijñā* and whose nature is "I.

Now, he begins the commentary on this aphorism with the word "iha" (here). When it is asked, "For what reason does a jar exist in this world, and for what reason does a sky-flower not exist?"—[the answer is given] individually regarding the jar...
People say, "The jar manifests to me.

If it is argued that this manifestation—this "jar-ness"—is the very nature of the jar itself and not something related to the subject (pramātṛ), then that jar would either manifest to everyone as "I am the jar" or it would not manifest to anyone at all; this was stated previously.

"By logic, the world must either be unborn or omniscient"— this is the consequence (*prasaṅga*). Therefore, because there is no such manifestation as "I myself am manifesting the jar," the jar investigates the meaning of "it manifests to me" as "my own manifestation."

"Being permeated by vibration" (*spandanāviṣṭa*) is precisely the meaning of the statement "this very jar is flashing forth to me. Therein, he also examines the meaning of "vibration": vibration is defined by the verbal root *spadi* in the sense of "slight movement," which refers to the manifestation [of the object] without ever abandoning its own nature as a mass of consciousness and bliss.
The manifestation as the universal self is like the manifestation of the ocean— which does not abandon its own nature consisting of water— as waves, distinctions, and bubbles; in this context,
the meaning of the word "kiñcit" (something/slightly) is simply the root-element "spadi," signifying slight movement.

Although its own nature (*svarūpa*) is immovable, it appears as moving through its universal self (*viśvātman*); thus, in its manifestation as the universal self, the light of consciousness does not deviate even slightly from its own nature, just like a seed and so forth.
The meaning is that it does not abandon its own essential nature. As it has been said:
"When the seed becomes the sprout, its state as a seed is no longer perceived;
likewise, when consciousness exists as the self of the world, its nature as consciousness expands even further.
(p. 155) Even though the manifestation as the self of the universe remains in the form of "I-ness" (ahantā), [it veils] the subjects through Māyā.

Because it manifests as the limit (*idantā*) of this entire universe, Māyā appears, as it were, as something transcendent; and it also appears as being endowed with the manifold diversity of the universe, which consists of the manifestation of "this-ness" (*idantā-ābhāsa*) within that which is accepted as the subject (*pramātṛ*). Regarding this point, he provides a corroborative statement:
The Self alone, manifesting within all existents, is the blissful body of consciousness;
with its unobstructed flow of will and its expanding vision and action, it is Śiva.
Thus it is said in the *Śivadṛṣṭi*:
"Therefore, one who is constantly diligent in discerning the reality of *spanda* attains his own true nature even while awake, without delay."
Whether extremely angry or greatly delighted, or reflecting "What shall I do?",
or running toward a distant place— the movement [of the mind] is established therein.
The fluctuations and non-fluctuations of the qualities (guṇas) and so forth, having acquired their own existence through their dependence on the universal fluctuation,
would constantly be obstacles for the knower.

Thus it is said in the *Śrīspandaśāstra*: "Even in the world, when there is a conjunction with the variety of joy, sorrow, and so forth, a person who does not waver or undergo transformation from the nature of the Self—which is the foundational wall of consciousness—is said to be 'possessed of power,' being one who possesses the vibration (*spanda*) of an undifferentiated reality. This much [is the definition].

The meaning of "throbbing" (*sphurattā*) is that the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*), having become throbbing in the manner described, likewise becomes existence (*sattā*). In this context, "existence" refers to the agency over the entire universe of worlds from Śiva down to the earth; and that [agency] is the supreme sovereignty (*svātantrya*) regarding the creative acts of emanation and so forth.

The non-existent form—such as a sky-flower or a double moon—pervades the world of existent forms, such as jars and cloths. When it is said to people that "a sky-flower appears," it appears to them as some kind of flower that exists, because of its insentience, being like the sky and resembling its color. Likewise...
Even a sky-flower or the like, when appearing [in consciousness],
pervades that object by appearing as being on the same level as it; however, the qualifiers of that object—
such as place and time, which are like bracelets [on Caitra]— do not appear on the same level due to the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).

When these two— space and time— are manifested through "this-ness" (*idantā*) as "this is space" and "this is time," even that power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*) is manifested through "I-ness" (*ahantā*); since it is impossible for both to possess equal status,
that very power of non-reflection, by not being touched by space, possesses omnipresence (*vibhutva*).

Because it does not touch time, it possesses eternity; thus, having become both manifold and eternal, through its conjunction with that [eternity] and its capacity for the manifestation of locations such as earth and so forth, it also comes to touch all locations and times.
Consequently, from that very fact of touching all locations and times, its pervasiveness [is established].
Regarding its permanence, it is stated in the venerable *Mālinīvijayottara*:
"The Great Being, the Great Goddess, is called the life-force of the universe. (p. 156)

"Essence" (sāra): This very power of reflective awareness (vimarśa-śakti) is the effortless form that constitutes the vital breath of the Supreme Lord (anuttara-bhaṭṭāraka). It is the presence of all objects of perception—beginning with earth and ending with the word "sound"—as well as the graspings of the external and internal organs, such as the pot and the act of making it.
Since even that form of the venerable Lord Paramaśiva— which consists of the light of all perceivers from Sakala up to Ādiśiva—
is itself the very nature of the venerable Lord Paramaśiva, its difference from the insentient must be demonstrated by means of its non-luminosity [in that limited sense].
"It has been established in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra* that this is indeed the power of discernment (*vimarśaśakti*).
'She who is the essence of this world is that supreme power, Mālinī.
Just as the great tree exists in the form of a potentiality within the seed of the *nyagrodha*,"
In this way, this entire world of moving and non-moving beings resides within the seed-syllable of the heart.

Thus, it is also stated in the *Śrītriśikāśāstra*: "She is this very one. By these two words—*smaraṇa* (remembrance) and *anubhava* (experience)—it is shown that the subject (*pramātṛ*) himself is thus constituted; as in the case of the *Maheshvarapratyabhijñā*, the recognition of His power is demonstrated. And what is called the "Heart" (*hṛdaya*) is...

The "foundation" (*pratiṣṭhā*) of everything is said to be its "abode" (*sthāna*). And that is so because, according to the principle stated as "of those things that have become insentient," the sentient is the foundation-abode for the insentient; and for that sentient [being] as well, the form whose nature is luminosity—expressed as "I"—is the foundation-abode, for that "I."

The power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*) is the foundation and abode of that which consists of Supreme Śiva and has the nature of light; thus, for the venerable Lord Parāśiva— who abides in the supreme, transcendent state of the sky of consciousness (*cidākāśa*), which is the station of the entire universe from the earth up to Śiva, and who rests there incessantly— the [power of reflection] is the support.
"Only this" refers to that which consists of the Supreme Goddess (Parābhaṭṭārikā), whose nature is reflective awareness (vimarśa) and whose essence is the supreme mantra;

it is the form of the full I-consciousness (pūrṇāhantā), as stated here and there in the Āgamas. "That power which is in the heart"—the heart is so called because it is said, "It resides in the void of my heart," and because it belongs to the self that is Bhairava.
"The Heart [mantra] of the God of gods bestows immediate liberation through yoga"—this means that it resides within the seed-syllable of the Heart;
it is "situated within the *hṛtpadma* (the heart-lotus)," as stated by the Supreme Lord—the ellipsis being supplied.
For every cognizing subject (*pramātṛ*), the mantra consisting of the form of "I" (*ahaṃ*) is indeed the Heart; that mantra, which is the form of "I," is the Heart.
Its nature is reflective awareness (*vimarśana*), and this reflective awareness consists of the power of the Supreme Speech (*parāvāk*).
The Supreme is the *mātṛkā* from *a* to *kṣa*, which is identical with the Supreme Goddess (*parābhaṭṭārikā*) who constitutes the Heart. Therefore it has been said:
"Without them, there would be no word, no meaning, nor even the movement of the mind."
Without those phonemes (varṇas), neither sound nor meaning exists, nor does the stability of the cognition of meaning exist. Furthermore:
Speech alone is their first form, since without you [Speech], they do not exist.
The manifestation of the phonemes occurs through them; without them, there is no cognition of words and the like.
Without that [consciousness], even conceptual construction could not attain its own existence;
and without it, there would be neither the arising nor the determination of entities.
Furthermore, because all activity and worldly transaction would cease,
this world would certainly become blind and mute.
Thus, in the *Śrī-tattvagarbha-stotra*:
"Therein, having first attained the state of the Mother (*mātṛbhāva*), she is divided;
Mālinī is twofold, ninefold, and indeed fiftyfold."

Due to the division consisting of the seed (bīja) and the womb (yoni), there are two types: the vowels are known as the seed, and the consonants are remembered as the womb, which is ninefold according to the division of the classes (vargas).
"Śiva as mere seed is that which is designated as Power (śakti), like fire;
she is radiant with half-extinguished rays through the differentiation of distinct phonemes," and so forth.
Thus [it is stated] in the *Śrī Mālinīvijayottara*. Regarding this, Bhartṛhari also [says]:
There is no cognition in the world that is devoid of the accompaniment of words;
all knowledge is perceived as if permeated by speech.
If the eternal nature of speech were to depart from consciousness,
manifestation would not shine forth, for it is that [speech] which performs reflective awareness.
"This very notion of those subject to transmigratory existence exists both externally and internally;
for upon departing [from the body], one is seen to be unconscious, like a piece of wood or a wall.
This entire passage establishes that they "know" this [Self] by means of the plural number.

Even by the Buddhists, who assert that the validity of the manifestation of an object— which is non-conceptual in nature— depends upon conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), this very object consisting of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) has indeed been accepted. For conceptual determination is the cause of the validity of manifestation.

This [determination] belongs to *vimarśa* (reflective awareness), because it consists of the verbal expression "this is indeed a jar. Now, regarding the Lord Paramaśiva, whose body is adorned by an infinite series of powers—such as consciousness (*cit*), bliss (*ānanda*), omnificence (*sarvakartṛtva*), and so forth; the states of *unmanī* and the rest; the principles beginning with *brahman*; and the elements beginning with earth—as taught in various scriptures:

The supreme Bhaṭṭārikā is the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśaśakti*) itself, which is the primary heroine; thus, according to the method stated in the *Śrī Mālinīvijaya* as "that which is the power...
and so forth, and according to the method stated in the *Śrī Spandaśāstra* and other texts as "whose opening and closing... and so forth.
And he is consecrated;
he is established as a vessel for universal sovereignty. (202) Having raised the doubt as to why this is so, [the author] proceeds to state the primacy of that very [initiation]—

[She perceives] herself as having a threefold form. Precisely for this reason, by virtue of her nature as the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*), she should make [everything] an object of knowledge in the form of the principles (*tattva*) beginning with Śiva and ending with the Earth. Although transcending the universe, she manifests by her own sovereignty as the very self of the universe. "Existing separately" means from that which has become thus.

For that which is established as separate from the Self whose nature is light— namely, the object of knowledge (*jñeya*)— such an object of knowledge cannot exist as something established separately from that light. However, in the case of maintaining the void (*khadhāraṇe*), if it were to exist as something distinct from the Supreme Lord by its own nature, [it would be impossible].
Because of its orientation toward the object of knowledge— which is characterized by making the knower itself the object of knowledge through its singular nature as the subject—

such independence, which consists in being oriented toward an external object of knowledge, would be shattered; therefore, by this orientation toward an external object, its state of dependence, consisting in subordination to another, is established.

Dependence (*pāratantrya*) is the opposite of independence (*svātantrya*), and independence— defined as not looking toward another— is the very nature of the Self (*ātman*). Therefore, due to the absence of such independence, the Self, by turning toward that which is distinct from itself, would become a non-Self (*anātman*).
An insentient entity, like a jar or other objects, does not turn toward an object of knowledge that is distinct from itself;

thus, there would be an over-extension [of the principle]. Therefore, by the reversal of this reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅgaviparyaya*), it follows that the Self, being inherently non-distinct [from consciousness] and turned toward itself, makes itself an object of knowledge; this is what has been established, and not merely—
Devoid of autonomy, it does not make itself an object of knowledge even in the form of blue and so forth;

rather, through its autonomy, it makes itself an object of knowledge even in the forms of Śiva, Īśvara, Paśupati, Bhairava, and others as described—thus he says, "through autonomy, as described," and so on. This...

The Lord, who is non-dual in nature, whose single form is pure consciousness, and whose essential characteristic is the performance of the most difficult tasks— through His sovereignty, which consists of the aforementioned power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*),
manifests Himself as the fivefold cosmic functions characterized by the creation of the universe and so forth.
The Śiva-liṅga, which is liberated in its absolute freedom, as described in the Śiva-āgamas regarding the Sthāṇu-liṅga, the maṇḍala, and so forth—

this conceptualization such as "this is Īśa" or "this is Paśupati" should be employed externally as an objectified "this-ness. It exists by itself in the form of that which is to be meditated upon, worshipped, and adored.
He who would conquer his own self through worldly activity, meditation, worship, and so forth—

[it is] thus the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*) that is the cause for the manifestation of one's own autonomy as the form of blue and other [objects], and for the manifestation of the autonomy of the Self as the form of the Lord (*Īśvara*) and others.
This is the meaning.
Having thus demonstrated the application of the sūtra, he states the explanation of this sūtra, beginning with "All powers," and so forth. All...

Thus, according to the method stated in the *Śrīmatstotrāvalīvyākhyā*, the powers beginning with consciousness (*cit*) and bliss (*ānanda*), which have been described in such a form, constitute sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) by virtue of their nature as lordship; that is, sovereignty is the state of being characterized by the autonomy (*svātantrya*) that effects the fivefold cosmic act.

In brief, the answer to the question posed by Bhartṛhari has been stated with the intended meaning that the power of agency (*kartṛtva-śakti*) is *vimarśa*. As for the literal meaning of the words: the Supreme Lord, whose nature is the full light of "I" (*pūrṇāhaṃ-prakāśātman*), is supreme because he transcends the universe while being of the singular form of the knower (*jñātṛ*).

It should be understood as being of the nature of the subject (*pramātṛ*). Even though it is not for the first time, the fact that it makes this [object] known through that [subject-nature] is what is intended by the term "sudden appearance" (*akasmikābhāsa*), according to the method stated in the *kārikā*, because no other cause is possible; for, as stated in the verse beginning with "The Lord is indeed the conscious self" (*cidātmaiva hi devaḥ*), [the Lord alone is the cause]. This is established firmly.

Because it has been demonstrated through the inference of possibility, there is that "possibility" (saṃbhāvana). For this very reason, according to the principle stated in the Sūtra—"the nature of manifestation"—it arises from the cause of agency characterized by the power of reflective awareness (vimarśa-śakti). That very possibility is the "reasoning" (yukti) by virtue of its being logical.

He establishes this with the words "for since he is this," and so forth. According to the principle stated that "light (*prakāśa*) has reflection-awareness (*vimarśa*) as its essential nature," this Supreme Lord reflects upon himself in the form of light; therefore, because that Self is the creator of the entire universe from Śiva down to the earth, how could it [not be so]?

"And how could the Self appear in the form of blue and so forth? [The author replies: "It does not. Anticipating the objection—"How can there even be such a possibility that the Supreme Lord makes the Self, whose sole nature is that of the knower, into an object of knowledge as the universal Self?"—[the author states] the essential nature of the object of knowledge as distinct from the Self:

He says that nothing whatsoever exists: in this vision of consciousness (*saṃvid*), there is no object of knowledge (*jñeya*) that exists as something separate from the light which is the nature of the Self; indeed, such a thing does not exist at all—the word "tu" has the sense of "indeed. There is simply no object of knowledge distinct from the light.
The arguments have been stated in the verses beginning with "vabhāsanām.

Now, he states even the argument consisting of a refutation that has been accepted: "If the object of cognition were distinct from its manifestation, then it would be established by the self-cognition of the Self, which is of the nature of the knower."

That orientation toward an object of knowledge distinct from itself cannot belong to this [consciousness]. Therefore, by virtue of its orientation toward an object of knowledge that is non-distinct [from it], there exists—
by means of that orientation toward a distinct object— a state characterized by dependence on another.
Dependence is attributed to this [consciousness]. And dependence is contrary to independence, which is its very nature as luminosity;
since independence is the defining characteristic of the Self, such independence is absent [in that which is dependent].

If the Self were oriented toward an object of knowledge that is distinct [from itself], it would be a non-Self (*anātman*). And being a non-Self, like a jar or other such things, it would follow as a logical consequence (*prasaṅga*) that it could not be oriented toward an object of knowledge that is not distinct from its own inert nature. Therefore, by the reversal of this consequence (*prasaṅgaviparyaya*), being independent and oriented toward an object of knowledge that is not distinct [from itself], it remains the Self.

The meaning of this single verse is that it follows that one makes the self itself the object of knowledge (*jñeya*). He states another [explanation] as well, beginning with "not merely," etc. As it has been said:
"Consciousness (*saṃvit*) everywhere, in every object, by way of its being that [object]..."

If this inert world were separate from consciousness and composed of the darkness of ignorance, it would be incapable of anything whatsoever— of existing, appearing, or acting— were it not for the Supreme Goddess, who, through her own sovereignty, vibrates as the nature of reflective awareness (vimarśa).
If consciousness, whose nature is vibration, were not all-pervasive, insentience would prevail;

and if the entire world were distinct from the Light of consciousness, it would be nothing but blinding darkness. Furthermore, because consciousness is the self-nature of the universe, the world is composed of consciousness.
Śiva is all, all is Śiva; thus, I go for refuge to Śiva.

The Self does not only create itself as independent, in the form of blue and so forth; rather, while remaining unliberated from its state of agency and capable of being liberated through its sovereignty, it creates itself in that manner— such as in the form of an invocation into a Śiva-liṅga or other objects— and thus engages in worldly transaction.

It is possible that [the Lord] unites the seekers of the Self with discourse through the teaching of meditation, worship, and so forth—by means of abiding, contemplation, adoration, and ritual offering—in the form of the object of meditation (*dhyeya*) and the like; this creation is also spoken of as such due to the sovereignty of this Self. Therefore, it arises from the nature of the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*).
The connection is with the word "by virtue of autonomy" (*svātaṃtryāt*).
In order to further strengthen this very point of emanation (*nirmāṇa*), he says, beginning with "But surely" (*nanu*).
It is a contradiction that the nature of the Self (*ātmasvarūpa*)—which is both liberated through autonomy and yet emanated—is [the object] here. Regarding the phrase "in this case":

To this question, he provides the answer: Because of the sovereignty (*svātantrya*) of one's own self—which is non-dual in nature and of the single form of consciousness—this creation, which is not liberated from that sovereignty, is not "not" tenable;
it is indeed tenable. For that very universe, consisting of jars, cloths, and so forth, [exists] in the state of *māyā*, whose nature is duality.
Because it is manifest, even its form as the "I" (ahantā) is extremely difficult to reconcile with the appearance of "this-ness" (idantā);

that very [difficulty] is what is expressed by the term "sovereignty" (svātantrya). Therefore, by the phrase "for this very reason," sovereignty is stated to consist of the power of reflective awareness (vimarśa-śakti), which constitutes a non-redundant formulation.

Alternatively, because of this very sovereignty (*svātantrya*), the two verses are to be construed in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the single form of sovereignty. Here, he demonstrates the fetching of water within the object created by the state of being unconditioned by sovereignty (p. 161): "If it is asked why, [it is because] 'this is blue,' 'this is...'"

"Yellow," [and so on], refers to the independent form of the term "emanation" (*nirmāṇa*), because emanation itself is not commonly established [as a distinct entity]. He clarifies this very point through an illustration: "This is the Lord (*īśvara*), this is the Blessed One (*bhagavān*), this is the Self (*ātman*), this is the Pervasive One (*vibhu*), this is the Eternal (*nitya*), this is the Independent (*svatantra*)" (206).

Thus, for the sake of the practitioner (*sādhaka*)— who is the knower (*pramātṛ*), who brings forth the Supreme, who is intent on worshiping, and who is intent on meditating— the nature of that Lord appears as something separate, manifesting respectively as the object of knowledge (*prameya*), the object of worship (*pūjya*), and the object of meditation (*dhyeya*); this much has been established.
Merely by being fashioned from the essential nature of Īśvara, it does not follow that it lacks the form of Īśvara. To explain "for thus":

if it were to lack the form of Īśvara, then the conceptualization and meditation regarding "this is Īśvara," "this is a jar," and "this is non-Īśvara" would become identical. And yet, such is not the case regarding the conceptualization of Īśvara.

The meaning is that there is no equality [between the two cases], because while one can form a resolution regarding meditation and so forth and obtain a specific desired result for the meditator, in other cases— such as when the resolution is not directed toward the Lord (anīśvara)— no such specific result is obtained in meditation and the like.

He concludes the meaning expressed in these two verses with the words "Therefore," and so forth: that the Supreme Lord, by means of both modes— namely, through the manifestation of blue and other objects devoid of autonomy, and through the manifestation of the Lord and others endowed with autonomy— renders Himself alone the object of knowledge.

Both of these constitute the means of knowing solely by virtue of the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*); thus it is established that this very power of reflective awareness is the primary form of the Supreme Lord’s own self.
[Objection: But [is it not] in the form of the light of the "I" (*aham-rūpa-prakāśa*)...?

The establishment of existence is as follows: according to the principle stated that "I am Being, and manifestation is the very nature of light," that which is manifest is not separate from light; and that light is not separate from reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
There is no other reflection than "I am," for Śiva alone is the indivisible and perfect nature of one's own being.

In such a reflective awareness regarding differentiation, it is appropriate to say that "that" is the nature of the "I," which is essentially light, and that "this very thing" is indeed the nature of the "I.
This occurs through the form of invocation within volitions such as "the Self of Īśvara" and so forth.
The reflective awareness of the emanated Lord as "this is the Lord" through the mode of "this-ness" constitutes his sovereignty.
To dispel the doubt—namely, how sovereignty could exist for the Lord in the absence of the sovereignty consisting of the reflective awareness "I"—he says: [207]
"‘Not “I” and so forth,’ etc.:

because of the very creation [brought about] by that which is perceived as "I," this Lord is the one who, through the mutual differentiation of the self being cleansed, performs the reflective awareness of "I."

Śaṅkara, Paśupati—[and so forth]—says thus: Furthermore, because the self being created is the object of the reflective awareness "I," it does not possess otherness. [This is so] because of the verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) which express the synthesis of the conceptual distinctions between action and its factors (*kriyākāraka*).

The construction of the sūtra is as follows: "Just as [the notion of] another vehicle arises from such conceptualization (parāmarśa), so it is here. The word "I" (*aham*)—[followed by ellipses]—is an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*). By the inclusion of the term "etc. (*ādi*), conceptualizations such as "self" (*ātman*) and "Lord" (*īśvara*) are understood. The mention of the *tiṅ*-suffixes is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the *sup*-suffixes.
The mention of "action" (*karman*) is an illustration of [grammatical categories] such as action (*kriyā*), agent (*kartṛ*), and so forth— such as "cooking," "the agent," "conjunction," or "option.

It is an indication of both that which is of the nature of a substance (*sattvarūpa*) existing as a potentiality (*śaktibhūta*), such as what is expressed by finite verb endings (*tiṅ*) or the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*),
and that which is of the nature of non-substance (*asatvabhūta*).
For this very reason, [I am] the self consisting of the reflective awareness of "I" (*ahaṃ-parāmarśa*) in its form as the creator (*nirmātṛ*),
and [the self] which is the locus of the reflective awareness of Īśvara and others in its form as the created (*nirmeya*); thus,
[I am] the creator-form consisting of the reflective awareness of "I," and the created-form is "this" (*idam*).
The distinction that was suspected—namely, that [the Lord] consists of reflective awareness (*parāmarśamaya*)—has been explained as being non-distinct. The reason for this is as follows:

the reflective awareness "this is the Lord" comes to rest in the reality of the knowing subject whose nature is sovereignty (*īśāna*). This is because both the state of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*) and the state of being a vessel (*kuṇḍatva*) reside in cognition and action.
Sovereignty (*svātantrya*). Sovereignty is defined as not looking toward another face. Not looking toward another face means the possession of the powers of uninterrupted knowledge and so forth.
And the non-interruption of knowledge and action rests upon the "I" (*asmat*) in the forms "I know" and "I act."

Thus, for this Īśvara, who is the Self, even that which is being created within the creation is precisely the object of the reflective awareness "I. Alternatively, in the phrase "of the creation," the ablative case with the suffix *ca* denotes the cause;
thus, even in the volitions such as "Īśvara" or "Paśupati" regarding the Self as the instrumental cause, there is only that which is fit for the supreme reflective awareness "I."

In the expression *sṛṣṭir ahaṃ-mṛśyate*, the suffix of the gerundive (*kṛtya-pratyaya*) functions in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). Just as the powers of action, the various grammatical relations (*kāraka*), and the conjunction of actions, as well as the forms of the verb endings (*tiṅ*) and the third case (*tṛtīyā*), are understood through usage—as in the statement "the cooking is the ultimate reality of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*)"—so too is the nature of the unreal [manifested] in dream. Thus, the ultimate reality consists in this reflective awareness.

Even when expressed by such words as "agent," "conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*), or "synthesis" (*samuccaya*), and thus brought to the state of being an existent entity, they finally rest within the fundamental reflective awareness (*mūlaparāmarśa*) in the form: "Caitra cooks" or "this is his speech. Thus...

In the absence of repose within the fundamental reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of Being, categories such as action and its factors would not even be perceived. Likewise, here too, the reflective awareness of "the Lord" or "the Self" and so forth comes to rest within the fundamental reflective awareness that takes the form of "I."
He states the summarized meaning of this verse with the words "this is what has been said," and so forth.
Here, "reflective awareness" (*parāmarśa*) is the place of rest for those entities that are being reflected upon.
Furthermore, the ultimate place of rest among those is the absolute one; that is its [true] resting place.

The locus (*sthāna*) is of the nature of "I" (*aham*). As it has been said: "When the object of knowledge, the means of knowledge, the knower, and the act of knowing are conceived within the Knower (*mātṛ*), even that Knower dissolves into the Great Knower (*mahatīmātṛ*)."

(p. 163) Regarding Devadatta’s journey to the village, there is a contradiction [in the opponent's view] because they claim that God’s state of being the creator is "intermediate" (madhya) with respect to that intermediate point of rest at the foot of a tree. By means of this [verse], however, one considers the fundamental rest in the "I" (aham) of the God who has been created.

It has been established that even for an object such as "blue," which lacks independence, its nature consists of the Self (ātman), because even in the intermediate reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*)—namely, "this is blue"—it ultimately rests upon the fundamental reflective awareness "I.
He demonstrates this very state of being constituted by the Self: "This blue is I, [the blue]."

By means of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), blue is embraced within the Self and shines; thus, even for blue and other objects, the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is the nature of "I. As it has been said: "Of this 'this'... and so forth. The object of knowledge (*vedya*), entering into the consciousness (*vitti*) established by its own sequence—consisting of the limbs, the sense objects, and so on—resides within the knower (*veditṛ*).

That characteristic belongs to what is dissolved through the gateway of cognition (*vitti*). However, the deluded person, through the very reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of blue and so forth, possesses the conceit of satisfaction regarding purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) such as bracelets or ornaments; thus, it is said that in the case of blue and so forth, there is a lack of autonomy (*svātantrya*). But in cases such as "the Self is the Lord," the nature is that of the "I" (*aham*).

Even a fool perceives that the cognition of an object such as "blue" reaches its completion without resting in a further reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), and likewise perceives the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) being performed by that blue object; thus, it is said that even this constructed self does not abandon its autonomy. [The objection begins with] "But surely... (*nanu*).
This [is] the cognition of "this is Īśvara," "this is Paśupati," "this is Mahādeva," "this is Gaṇapati," and so forth;
as well as "this is a jar," "this is a cloth," and so on,
up to "this is blue," "this is yellow," and so forth.

Furthermore, it has been stated that among all acts of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), the resting place within the single, non-artificial reflective awareness of "I" (*aham*) alone is the reality (*tattva*). Thus, for everything— [omitted]—
how can this distinction of the possessor of power (*śaktimat*) be described as "the one who possesses the power of memory and exclusion"?

Maheśvara is the possessor of power (*śaktimān*), and knowledge (*jñāna*) and so forth are his powers (*śaktayaḥ*); blue, yellow, and so forth are the objects of those powers. Furthermore, [this applies to] knowledge in the form of direct experience (*anubhava*), which is the root of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), memory (*smṛti*), and so on, as well as doubt (*saṃśaya*), ascertainment (*nirṇaya*), and the rest.

In response to this doubt, he states the resolution: "The power of *māyā*, etc. That very power of consciousness (*cit*), which was previously introduced as being of the nature of reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*), is the supreme sovereignty of the all-pervasive Lord Anuttara-Bhaṭṭāraka, his own self—the Great Lord’s capacity to accomplish the impossible.
Divine *māyā* is one's own nature (*prakṛti*), which—
acting as the cause for the manifestation of duality through its power of *māyā*, which brings about what is otherwise impossible to achieve—
is the sphere of objects of cognition such as blue and yellow, which are non-different from the subject and non-different from his senses.

The connection of the text is as follows: having come into being, [the powers] are designated by names such as "knowledge" (*jñāna*), "volition" (*saṅkalpa*), "determination" (*adhyavasāya*), and "emission" (*sṛti*).
Now, for the explanation: according to the stated principle that "whatever manifests is of the nature of a single manifestation," [all these are one].
(p. 164) Even though the universe is of the nature of the single light of the "I" (aham), its manifestation as "this" (idam)—despite being logically untenable—is called *māyā*. And thus:
because it has been described in this way, this manifestation as "this" is distinct from the light that is the nature of the "I."

The collection of appearances such as jars and cloths is called *māyā*. As it has been said: (210) "Even though in reality [everything] consists of 'I' and 'Me', whatever appears as 'this-ness' (*idantā*), that is *māyā*—so it has been stated by the Kashmiri teachers who know the truth."

Regarding the phrase "tatra ca" (and therein): within that arising manifestation, the sovereignty (*svātantrya*) of consciousness—which effects the manifestation of the differentiation of that which arises as the manifestation—is the power of *māyā*. By means of that power of *māyā*, there is that which is to be cognized (*saṃvedya*) which is distinct from the subject (*pramātṛ*) and from one another; furthermore, by the power of *māyā*...

She is that which has as its range of experience and locus of repose the objects of cognition— blue, yellow, and so forth— which are differentiated from the cognizer, differentiated from other objects of cognition, and differentiated from the entire group of instruments;
being thus one whose range consists of differentiated objects of cognition, she is indeed the Supreme Speech (parāvāk).

Consciousness (*citi*) is designated by such terms as "knowledge" (*jñāna*), "volition" (*saṅkalpa*), "ascertainment" (*avasāya*), "doubt" (*saṃśaya*), "memory" (*smṛti*), and so forth. He explains the true nature of knowledge, volition, and the rest through the passage beginning with "For instance" (*tathā hi*): [it is] by means of the sense organs, such as the eyes, which perceive clearly, and by that which is clear...

The state of being a cognition (*vittatva*) restricted by an object such as form and so forth is visual and other types of sensory knowledge; the state of being a consciousness (*saṃvittatva*) restricted by the mind and an indistinct object is volition (*saṅkalpa*), such as "this is indeed a jar. That which is restricted by an object through the intellect (*buddhi*), which possesses the quality of reaching to the limit of the objecthood [of the thing], is...

The nature of consciousness is determination (*adhyavasāya*). It consists in the distinctness of objects from one another, their distinctness from the subject, and their distinctness from the external and internal organs;
as well as the distinctness of the external and internal organs from the subject and their distinctness from one another.

Furthermore, that duality which consists of both [the subject and the object]—though such differentiation is logically untenable given its non-difference from Light—is manifested by the Supreme Lord through His absolute freedom (svātantrya) as consciousness (cittatvena).
Thus, the state of Māyā is the resting place of the subjects of Māyā in the perception "this is mine," within the sphere of duality; this is the level of Īśvara.
Since the repose of duality— expressed as "I am this" and "this is I"— occurs through non-duality, just as it does between Sadāśiva and Śivā;
for that reason, namely because of the repose of duality, cognitions, volitions, and so forth, though distinct from one another and distinct from the subject,
[attain their state] within that [consciousness] whose nature is the fully effulgent *ahantā*.
These are called the powers (*śaktayaḥ*) of Maheśvara, who is the one who continuously cognizes his own nature as the "I" in its entirety;
for that very reason, [all things]—doubt and so forth, as well as distinct entities such as blue and the like, and various phenomena—are entirely undivided. As it has been said:
Just as she manifests her own radiance as the non-self— the body, senses, and so forth—

so too does she manifest within her own self the "this-ness" of other things, such as a jar, through the act of flashing forth. This very power of the Supreme Consciousness, being the nature of absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), accomplishes what is otherwise impossible.
What does not appear through the power of the Illusion of the Blessed Maheśvarī?

Regarding the word "not": as it has been stated that consciousness (*citi*) consists of reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*), let that nature of reflective awareness belonging to the power of consciousness— according to the principle already explained— exist within the powers of speech-accompanied conceptualization (*vikalpa*),
such as imagination (*saṃkalpa*), memory (*smaraṇa*), and so forth, as something unconditioned by space and time.

Regarding that experience which is characterized by direct realization, inexpressible, and non-conceptual, how could there be even the possibility of the power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*) having the nature of reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśātmatva*) therein?
[This is because] with respect to objects such as pots and cloths, [the thought arises]: "This is a pot; it is located here."
The application of that particular word, which consists in the conceptualization of the distinction between words such as "the present one," is the connection [of the word].

According to the stated principle, "that which denotes the object directly designated by convention is the denotative (vācaka)," there is the postulation of various names based on authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

It depends on that recollection; for, according to the stated principle that "recollection arises from the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of a prior experience," it depends upon the awakening of the latent impression of a prior experience. That [awakening] also—
"Such" [a thing] requires the perception of an object similar to that which was previously experienced.
Thus, when from afar— [the power of memory arises]—
how could there be, in the first moment within the self of the power of experience, a reflective awareness (vimarśa) devoid of another [object]?
To dispel the delusion regarding awakening (*bodha*) and so forth, which are the ultimate reality consisting of mere cognition, he says:
"realization" (*sākṣātkāra*). Since awakening consists in the direct perception of each respective object, it lasts for only a moment. And as for "another": [it refers to another moment].

But for one who runs swiftly in the absence of reflective inquiry (*anusandhāna*), who rapidly grasps the words spoken by the mouth of the Guru and recites them, and who quickly reads a leaf or a book— how could that running, that reciting, or that reading truly be so?

The connection with the Sūtra is as follows: even in the absence of subsequent reflection (*anusaṃdhāna*), [this] certainly exists. Now, for the explanation: "here" refers to the self-nature, that is, the essential nature, of consciousness—which is awareness whose essence is the light of the "I"—namely, the union with expression (*abhilāpa*) whose essence is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).

That reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) by which the nature of each respective object is shown to both the seer and the one being informed— without the use of words consisting of specific conventions regarding those objects, but solely through the pointing of a finger—
and by which both cognition and knowledge are produced, is that which consists in the pointing of a finger.
Reflection: Thus, within one's own self, that which consists of the designation of the "head" (the initial term) is similar to its manifestation;
because the object of cognition is essentially composed of reflection (*vimarśa*), it is in reality of the nature of reflection.

It consists precisely of verbal expression (*abhilāpamayatva*). Having thus established that even the state consisting of non-conceptualization (*nirvikalpātmikā*) is composed of reflective awareness (*parāmarśamayī*), he says "staimitya," etc., in order to establish that even states such as torpor (*staimitya*) are composed of reflective awareness. For the subject (*pramātṛ*) who has ascended to *samādhi*, all thought...

If the state of inertia (*staimitya*), which is of the nature of withdrawal, does not consist of self-reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), then the very occurrence of that state of inertia is impossible; for there would be no emergence of the subject’s activity, which consists of conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and takes the form of the reflective awareness: "I remained in a state of inertia."

To claim that the state of the cognizer—which consists of the activity of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)—is ultimately unreal (i.e., a mere void) is impossible to maintain; for if that state of reflective awareness were not manifesting, how could its state of stillness (*staimitrya*) possibly arise? Furthermore, at the time of subsequent emergence, there would be no recollection of that experienced state of stillness.
If it is argued that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is not an activity of the subject, but rather arises as the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of objects such as form and so forth,

then what else could this "stasis" (*staimittya*) be for one who has ascended to meditative absorption (*samādhi*), other than the withdrawal of all thought consisting of conceptual construction, which constitutes its own inherent activity?
Therefore, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is indeed a property of the cognizer (*pramātṛ*), and not a property of objects such as form (*rūpa*).

Since conceptual construction lacks the nature of being a property of form and the like, and instead possesses the nature of being a property of the cognizer, reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*)—which consists of conceptual construction—is essentially a property of the cognizer; it is the state of stillness (*taimitya*).
It indeed exists.

Now, regarding the application of specific verbal expressions and the recollection of conventions—[the author] states its essential nature: "established by those who employ means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇika-kḷpta*).
Prior to the assignment of specific conventional designations, all objects are capable of being referred to by all words. In this regard, among those objects,
there is no fixed word such that one must think, "this is the designation for this object, and that other is the designation for that other."

He explains the very manner of the application [of the terms]: "After that reflective awareness"— meaning immediately following that innate reflective awareness which, prior to the grasping of linguistic convention, occurs as the delimitation 'I' with respect to one's own body and as the delimitation 'this' with respect to a cow standing before one— "the word 'this' [is applied]."

The word "cow" (*gaur*), which is common to both masculine and feminine genders, is superimposed upon that individual cow (*gopiṇḍa*)— just as the word "man," which is common to both male and female, is superimposed. This twofold word, being superimposed upon that individual cow, consists of the subject (*pramātṛmaya*) because it manifests through its appearance (*ābhāsāt*).
It occurs. Here, "superimposition" (āropaṇa) refers to the superimposition of silver upon mother-of-pearl—

as it has been stated— that on the surface of that [object], following the superimposition of the two kinds of words, there is the word *gaura* as the denoter of that red color, and the word *go* as the denoter of the feminine gender.
Another word, "the white ox to be excluded," is superimposed;

likewise, words such as "possessing long horns" and "possessing a white color" are also superimposed—this is the nature of the convention (*saṅketa*). Therefore, by the senior elder... [the child] is taught.

Having heard the linguistic usage such as "Bring the pot" being employed, and having seen the middle-aged person performing the act of bringing the pot and so forth, a reflective inquiry consisting of the synthesis— "This is a pot," "He should bring this," and "He brings this"— arises in the child; therefore, for that reason...

The reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) of the power of consciousness (*citi-śakti*) exists even at the time of direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*). The meaning is that even direct perception, from an ultimate standpoint (*paramārthataḥ*), culminates in nothing other than conceptualization (*vikalpa*), ending in the very activity of the subject’s conceptual construction such as "I see" and so forth;
thus, it results in conceptualization alone. Even the supreme conceptualization of the Buddha (*bauddha*) [is likewise].

One considers conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) to be the operation of perception whose nature is non-conceptual. It is logical that conceptual construction, being of the nature of an operation, is distinct from the perception that possesses that operation;
rather, it is the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) which constitutes the very essence of that perceiving perception.

Let it have the nature of a mere moment. Even in that direct realization which has the nature of a mere moment, there exists reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). And this—that even in direct realization there is necessarily reflective awareness—is certainly established; this is the basis for the use of the word "even" (*api*). Otherwise... [the following would not hold].

If there is no reflective awareness (vimarśa) even at the moment of direct perception, then how could one go quickly with a continuous mental synthesis such as "I am going," "I am reading," or "I am reciting," while rapidly moving,
swiftly reading a succession of syllables uttered by another, or quickly glancing over a leaf or a book?

And while reciting the desired sequence of phonemes on a leaf or in a book, one might go toward or utter [the destination]; furthermore, this very point—that even at the moment of direct perception there is reflective awareness—is established by the passage beginning with "tathā hi" (for instance). And for Caitra who is going, regarding the destination to be reached—(216) first...

The knowledge of the location suitable for the first placement of the foot, the desire to step upon that location, the actual stepping upon that location, the knowledge that the location has been stepped upon, and the act of taking up the plow or other tools by one remaining in that very location.

The pursuit of another purpose is the desire to abandon the occupied place due to constant exhaustion; therein, without the reflective awareness in the form of pursuing the connection with the destination and the disconnection from the current place— such as through the desire to go and so forth— [the movement does not occur].

"How can one who is traveling attain the desired destination? This same principle should be understood to apply to rapid grasping, recitation, and so forth. "Rapid grasping" (tvaritodgrahaṇa) refers to the reciting immediately at that very moment of the Āgamas and other texts heard from the mouth of the teacher; however, in that case—

In the case of rapid grasping and so forth, there is a sequence of effort involving the touching of locations such as the heart and so on. However, when there is a direct realization occurring at the very moment of that [process], then immediately following that realization, the coarse conceptual constructions cease for one who is running.
It is experienced;

therefore, the rapidity of that very running will be embraced within one's own self in that direct realization. The expansion of words, such as "this is forceful" or "this is supreme," is merely a conceptualization of sound by whatever means.

One must cultivate subtle discernment (*vimarśa*). By means of this subtle discernment, the latent impression of sound (*śabdabhāvanā*)—which has been made playful—is transformed through expansion such as "pot" or "cloth," and is thus extended into gross conceptualization (*sthūlavikalpa*), such as "the pot is white," and so forth. He demonstrates that very point: "Just as..."

The expansion of the subtle reflective awareness "this" consists of [cognitions] such as "the jar is white. In that context, the expansion of the reflective awareness "jar" consists of its broad base, belly, and shape;
the expansion of the reflective awareness "white" consists of the jar being entirely white, the whiteness belonging to the universal class, and the quality of whiteness.

The root *dhāv* (in *samavāyī*, etc. denotes swift motion by virtue of the power of the word itself; for that very reason, it is said [of the soul] that it "moves from the insentient. As for the phrase "let it be so": in the state of non-conceptualization (*nirvikalpa*), that which you have described as having a subtle form...

Let the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), which consists of the manifestation of the "I" as each respective subject engaged in activities such as running and so forth, enter into the body. Furthermore, in the state of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), where there is a clear state of conceptualization regarding an object such as blue—namely, "this is blue" in its gross form—therein, with respect to that object... (217) [text fragment]
Just as this [object] is grasped by her as "this is blue," so too the word "this is blue," which serves as the designator for those two—

the quality of blueness (*nīlatva*) and the indexicality of "this" (*idantā*)— is also grasped by the sense of hearing as its object. Furthermore, reflection (*vimarśa*) has sound as its very life, and thus the aforementioned blueness is of such a nature.
How could the word, which is the very life [of the object], not be non-different from the nature of the object? It must indeed be different.
Just as in the cognition "this is blue," the blue is perceived by the eye, so too is the word "blue" [perceived].

Because it is apprehended as an object by the sense of hearing, that which consists of such sound is accompanied by reflective awareness (*savimarśa*). Even in the case of a word, you maintain that the nature of "I" is a manifestation distinct [from the word]. How then can this be your own position?

Anticipating the objection that [the self] must be understood [as an agent], he says: "This is a jar"—this determination (*adhyavasāya*) belongs to the Supreme Lord who determines; it is called the power of determination, which is distinct from name and form, as in the case of "jar."
Having transcended form— which consists of two colors, which has the shape of a broad base and belly, and which is perceptible by the eye— the Supreme Lord exists as "I" (aham);
and just as He exists, so too does that [object] exist, because it is His power and thus shines through "I-ness" (ahantā) as non-different from Him.
Is this not the connection with the Sūtra: "This is that"? [The objection: "A jar" is a gross sound, an object of the sense of hearing, and an external form.
Who has said this—that even the gross sound "jar" is consciousness, whose nature is light, life, and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)?

Appearing as something distinct like a jar, it shines forth precisely as "this" (idantā). The two—the name and the form characterized by it—are the reflective awarenesses (*vimarśa*) of the ear and the eye; they are the word and its object, such as "this is a jar," perceived through the synthesis (*anusandhāna*) of "this is that."

The power of ascertainment (*adhyavasāya-śakti*) is that which, by means of a single form, simultaneously perceives all entities as a unity; this is the power of the Supreme Lord in the form of *vimarśa* (reflective awareness).
Like the Supreme Lord who knows Himself, it shines forth as the uninterrupted "I" (*aham*), and not otherwise.

At times, this [object] appears as if separated [from the subject] by the notion "this. Because of its capacity for determination (*adhyavasāya-śakti*), it is apprehended through the separation of "this-ness" (*idantayā*), since it is established as such; that is, because it is established as a jar or the like.
And of that [capacity], there is this reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)—just as of the jar being perceived in the form "this is a jar"—[expressed as] "this is [the capacity] of the jar."

If this power of determination (*adhyavasāya-śakti*) is itself being perceived as "a jar," there must be another reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) that takes that [determination] as its own object. If that reflective awareness were also to have such a limit, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Therefore—namely, precisely because of this infinite regress.

There would be only the manifestation of the blue object that has become an objective domain, because the attainment of a foundation for the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of "I" as form would be absent. Therefore— due to the absence of perception as something delimited by the "this-ness" (*idantā*)— every reflective awareness of blue, yellow, and so forth [is established].
It is indeed inseparable from the Light, as it has been said: "That which is manifest is not separate from the Light," and so forth.
It shines as a single consciousness; the perception of difference [is merely an appearance].
"Having the forms of blue, yellow, pleasure, and pain; with a deep navel and elevated breasts, she shines like [a figure] upon a smooth painted panel. Thus it is said.
[Here, a portion of the text measuring three folios has been lost.

(219) Regarding the word "nanu": according to the principle already stated—that for every cognition of blue, yellow, and so forth, that very reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is inseparable from the Light (*prakāśa*), and thus its foundation is established as "I" alone—it is appropriate that the locus is "I."

In the repose within one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*), there is no contact with the plane of objects of cognition such as "this is blue" or "this is yellow. For it is only on the plane of objects of cognition—blue, yellow, and so forth—that the connection with space and time is observed, such as "this blue [is here]. Now, regarding the aspect of the knower within the form of the "I":

In the absence of the conjunction of place and time, for those cognitions resting therein, there occurs— whether being experienced as a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), being remembered, or being synthesized— the thought "this," "this is blue indeed," "that is blue," or "this is that very blue."
Furthermore, sequence is not perceived in relation to its respective objects.

How, then, could that state of total sequence belong to cognitions that rest in the form of the non-sequential "I"? In the absence of sequence, there would exist in the ultimate sense nothing but the nature of the full "I-ness."

Regarding the phrase "tataśca" (and therefore): because He is of a single nature, the Supreme Lord is the possessor of powers (*śaktimān*) by virtue of His powers such as knowledge, memory, and so forth. As it has been said: "The Supreme Lord is the possessor of powers; knowledge, memory, and the like are His powers;
the universe is the object (*śakyarūpa*) of those powers."

(p. 171) To quell the doubt as to how [the world] can be an object [of cognition], he concludes all the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) mentioned in this chapter, saying: "In the repose within its own non-sequential nature, there is an absence of sequence"—this is indeed true. To demonstrate this, he says: "Only of that very Supreme Lord..."

From that Supreme Lord, by means of His power of *māyā* whose nature is absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), there arise objects of cognition such as blue and yellow, which are distinct from one another and from the powers of knowledge, memory, and so forth; [the terms] "belonging to those" (*tatsambandhin*) refer to these. Furthermore, the qualifiers "past" and "present" pertain to that specific class of objects of cognition.

Although there is a sequential order in accordance with space and time, by resorting to mere will, one first adopts the power of experience (*anubhava-śakti*), then the power of conceptualization (*vikalpa-śakti*), and thereafter the power of memory (*smṛti-śakti*), [all of which constitute] the multitude of powers such as knowledge, recollection, and ascertainment.
Immediately following this, there is the power of reflective synthesis (*anusandhāna*) consisting of memory and experience;
thus, the connection with the Sūtra is that [this power] proceeds toward transition (*saṃkrama*) in accordance with each respective time and each respective object.

(220) It has been stated that the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is such that there is no contact with the ground of objects of knowledge, because the cognitions [of things] as "this is true" are established as "I. Thus, in this manner, the sequence of the nature of consciousness (*saṃvittattva*) is exactly as described.
However, it is only by virtue of the power of *māyā* that [things appear] in the aforementioned manner as distinct entities. Those which [appear] as differentiated...
Nor is it [the difference] among them made by means of differences in form, such as having a broad base and belly; for instance,

"the jar is distant from the cloth," "the cloth is not distant from the wall," "the jar pervades a wide space," or "it does not pervade a wide space"— wherein "space" (deśa) consists of such forms as distance, proximity, extensiveness, and non-extensiveness.

The distinctions of action, such as "he stands" and so forth, are shattered by that very [consciousness]; and as for time— which consists of sequences such as slow and fast, produced by the differentiation of action—
[the Lord] conforms to space and time, which serve as specific qualifiers for those respective objects of cognition.

Because they are oriented toward the grasping of various objects of cognition, knowledge (*jñāna*), memory (*smṛti*), and ascertainment (*adhyavasāya*)— though they are partless and without succession— rely merely upon their reflection (*chāyāmātra*) by resting within the form of that [consciousness], even as those [objects] appear in such-and-such a way.

The manifestation of manifoldness, produced by the constituent parts consisting of space, time, and self, occurs through mutual dependence and in relation to their respective objective forms and own-parts (*svāṃśa*).
Although in cognitions such as experience and so forth, the past, present, and future—
There is no spatial sequence [in consciousness]. Nevertheless, for one who is deluded, the perception of a mountain appears as if it were extended because that mountain is extended;
however, the perception of a jujube fruit appears as if it were minute because that jujube fruit is minute.

The sequence of space has also been shown by that [means]. By this, because it is a manifestation of sequence, the spatial and temporal [distinctions] residing in the object of cognition—and consequently even those of knowledge and so forth—do not possess ultimate reality as being sequential. This is because the entity that is appearing...
Because it is the ultimate reality (paramārtha),
it is entirely logical that knowledge and the other qualities have been stated to be the powers (śakti) of this Blessed One.

(221) By the verse beginning with "māyāśaktyā," the mutual diversity of the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of cognitions is shown. The distinction [from the previous case] is that by this verse, the diversity [of cognitions] is shown through space and time associated with the respective objects of those cognitions, such as blue, yellow, and so forth.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the commentary titled *Śrīpratyabhijñāsūtravimarśinī*.
Now begins the sixth chapter.

Thus, having clearly explained in each individual daily lesson (āhnika) the power of memory and the power of knowledge as taught in the Sūtra beginning with "If not thus within," [the author] now seeks to explain in one daily lesson the power of exclusion (apohana-śakti), which serves to assist both of those.
Then, by means of praise, he enters into the Supreme Lord, whose nature is the object of daily practice (*āhnika-prameya*),
with the words beginning "the dense non-difference from one's own self" (*svātmabhedaghana*).
[This refers to] those entities from Śiva down to the earth (*kṣiti*), which are dense non-difference from one's own self and consist of the density of consciousness-bliss (*cidānandaghana*).

By means of His own will— the power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*)— which consists of the form of *māyā* and acts as a chisel through the fragmentation of that undifferentiated density, [the world] is differentiated from the Supreme Lord,
from the classes of subjects, and from one another, such that: "This is a jar alone, not a cloth, nor Caitra."

Thus, by delimiting [objects], this jar is a creator of diverse forms, as is this cloth; likewise, "this is the cognition of the jar," "this is the cognition of the cloth," "this is Caitra," and "this is Maitra"—
[the jar] is the creator of the nature of manifoldness consisting of mutually distinct objects of knowledge (*prameya*), means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and knowers (*pramātṛ*).
We praise that Śiva, who is constantly devoted to that [task].

Regarding the word "atha" (now): immediately after the determination of the powers of memory and experience, the power of *apohana*—which subsumes both of those—is determined by a series of eleven verses beginning with "the power of *apohana* is the reflective awareness of 'I'.
The nature of that power of *apohana* as being the subsumer of both is [as follows]:

Because objects such as jars and cloths—which are the domain of the powers of naming, experience, and memory—are identical with the universal consciousness (*saṃvit*), they are themselves composed of that respective consciousness; nevertheless, setting aside this fact of being composed of that consciousness, one brings about the state of being merely a single jar or the like, characterized by its specific place and time. (222)

Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*): in that chapter (*āhnika*), by the verse beginning with "I am the reflective awareness" (*ahaṃ pratyavamarśaḥ*), the specific conceptualization (*vikalpa*) whose nature will be described later pertains to the reflective awareness "I," which is the very life-force of the manifestation of the essence of the Lord Anuttara; it is a portion of that [awareness].

In the third [view], namely one's own philosophical system which asserts the existence of the Self as consisting of Maheśvara, it is argued that a single part (*taikadeśa*) cannot be pure in itself; because there is no object to be excluded (*apohya*) distinct from itself, it is impossible for it to possess the functional operation of exclusion (*apohana*).
The logical possibility of that exclusion (*apohana*) follows from this:
