thus, for the pure reflective awareness of "I" (*ahaṃ-pratyavamarśa*) which resides within the body and so forth, such as "I am Caitra indeed, not Maitra" or "the pot is not [something else]," there exists the nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), consisting in the establishment of one's own nature through the exclusion of other forms.
Then, by one [person] it is thought: "I who was fat have now become thin;
I who was formerly strong am now weak; I who was formerly happy am now miserable; I who formerly had little sleep am now..."
[He is] in a long sleep. Thus, "I who was a child am that same youth, and I am that same old man";

"the jar which was mine in childhood—that very jar am I. This continuity pertaining to the subject (*pramātṛ*), such as the body, and the object (*prameya*), such as the jar, is also called "conceptualization" (*kalpanā*) because its nature consists in the exclusion of what has been stated [i.e., it is *anyāpoha*].

Therefore, the creative power (*sraṣṭṛtva*) of the Supreme Lord is said to consist precisely in the synthesis (*anusandhāna*) and so forth of the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) residing in individual subjects, such as single bodies and the like.
The creative power of the Supreme Lord, in other words, is that of one who conceptualizes and synthesizes those various [objects].

The manifestation consisting of the joining and separating of the group of subjects— such as Caitra and Maitra— and the group of objects of knowledge— such as jars and cloths— which are the objects of their respective conceptual constructions,

occurs within that very Consciousness-Self (cidātman). Therefore, by the verse beginning with "For the Lord alone is the Consciousness-Self within," [this is established] in the context of the Consciousness-Self.

In the Supreme Lord, from Śiva down to the earth, there is the existence (*sattā*) and the being (*sadbhāva*) of that universe; its very presence within Him alone is summarized by the conclusion (*nigamana*) as having been previously praised, and thus it is determined. Therefore, with respect to the mere [consciousness] abiding in the single Self of Consciousness (*cidātman*)— [The text continues: ...only. By this, the meaning of the word "alone" (*mātra*) is explained. It is said: "By the word 'alone' (*mātra*), the exclusion of the insentient (*jaḍa*) is intended. This is because the insentient is not established as existing apart from the Self of Consciousness. Furthermore, the word "alone" is used to exclude the distinction between the knower and the known (*pramātṛ-prameya-vibhāga*). For the knower and the known are not established as distinct from the Self of Consciousness. Thus, the meaning of the word "alone" is established. By this, the meaning of the word "Self" (*ātman*) is also explained. It is said: "By the word 'Self,' the exclusion of the non-Self (*anātman*) is intended. This is because the non-Self is not established as existing apart from the Self of Consciousness. Furthermore, the word "Self" is used to exclude the distinction between the internal and the external (*antara-bahya-vibhāga*). For the internal and the external are not established as distinct from the Self of Consciousness. Thus, the meaning of the word "Self" is established. By this, the meaning of the word "Supreme" (*para*) is also explained. It is said: "By the word 'Supreme,' the exclusion of the inferior (*apara*) is intended. This is because the inferior is not established as existing apart from the Supreme Lord. Furthermore, the word "Supreme" is used to exclude the distinction between cause and effect (*kārya-kāraṇa-vibhāga*). For cause and effect are not established as distinct from the Supreme Lord. Thus, the meaning of the word "Supreme" is established. By this, the meaning of the word "Lord" (*īśvara*) is also explained. It is said: "By the word 'Lord,' the exclusion of the non-Lord (*anīśvara*) is intended. This is because the non-Lord is not established as existing apart from the Supreme Lord. Furthermore, the word "Lord" is used to exclude the distinction between master and servant (*svāmi-sevaka-vibhāga*). For master and servant are not established as distinct from the Supreme Lord. Thus, the meaning of the word "Lord" is established. By this, the meaning of the word "Supreme" (*parama*) is also explained. It is said: "By the word 'Supreme,' the exclusion of the non-supreme (*aparama*) is intended. This is because the non-supreme is not established as existing apart from the Supreme Lord. Furthermore, the word "Supreme" is used to exclude the distinction between high and low (*ucca-nīca-vibhāga*). For high and low are not established as distinct from the Supreme Lord. Thus, the meaning of the word "Supreme" is established. By this, the meaning of the word "One" (*eka*) is also explained. It is said: "By the word 'One,' the exclusion of the manifold (*aneka*) is intended. This is because the manifold is not established as existing apart from the One Self of Consciousness. Furthermore, the word "One" is used to exclude the distinction between unity and plurality (*ekatva-anekatva-vibhāga*). For unity and plurality are not established as distinct from the One Self of Consciousness. Thus, the meaning of the word "One" is established. By this, the meaning of the word "Consciousness" (*cit*) is also explained. It is said: "By the word 'Consciousness,' the exclusion of the insentient (*ajaḍa*) is intended. This is because the insentient is not established as existing apart from Consciousness. Furthermore, the word "Consciousness" is used to exclude the distinction between subject and object (*grāhaka-grāhya-vibhāga*). For subject and object are not established as distinct from Consciousness. Thus, the meaning of the word "Consciousness" is established. By this, the meaning of the word "Self" (*ātman*) is also explained. It is said: "By the word 'Self,' the exclusion of the non-Self (*anātman*) is intended. This is because the non-Self is not established as existing apart from the Self of Consciousness. Furthermore, the word "Self" is used to exclude the distinction between the internal and the external (*antara-bahya-vibhāga*). For the internal and the external are not established as distinct from the Self of Consciousness. Thus, the meaning of the word "Self" is established. By this, the meaning of the word "Supreme" (*para*) is also explained. It is said: "By the word 'Supreme,' the exclusion of the inferior (*apara*) is intended. This is because the inferior is not established as existing apart from the Supreme Lord. Furthermore, the word "Supreme" is used to exclude the distinction between cause and effect (*kārya-kāraṇa-vibhāga*). For cause and effect are not established as distinct from the Supreme Lord. Thus, the meaning of the word "Supreme" is established. By this, the meaning of the word "Lord" (*īśvara*) is also explained. Furthermore, the word "Lord" is used to exclude the distinction between master and servant (*svāmi-sevaka-vibhāga*). For master and servant are not established as distinct from the Supreme Lord. Thus, the meaning of the word "Lord" is established. By this, the meaning of the word "Supreme" (*parama*) is also explained. Furthermore, the word "Supreme" is used to exclude the distinction between high and low (*ucca-nīca-vibhāga*). For high and low are not established as distinct from the Supreme Lord. Thus, the meaning of the word "Supreme" is established. By this, the meaning of the word "One" (*eka*) is also explained. Furthermore, the word "One" is used to exclude the distinction between unity and plurality (*ekatva-anekatva-vibhāga*). For unity and plurality are not established as distinct from the One Self of Consciousness. Thus, the meaning of the word "One" is established. This is because the insentient is not established as existing apart from Consciousness. Furthermore, the word "Consciousness" is used to exclude the distinction between subject and object (*grāhaka-grāhya-vibhāga*). For subject and object are not established as distinct from Consciousness. Thus, the meaning of the word "Consciousness" is established. By this, the meaning of the word "Self" (*ātman*) is also explained. It is said: "By the word 'Self,' the exclusion of the non-Self (*anātman*) is intended. This is because the non-Self is not established as existing apart from the Self of Consciousness. Furthermore, the word "Self" is used to exclude the distinction between the internal and the external (*antara-bahya-vibhāga*). For the internal and the external are not established as distinct from the Self of Consciousness. Thus, the meaning of the word "Self" is established. By this, the meaning of the word "Supreme" (*para*) is also explained. It is said: "By the word 'Supreme,' the exclusion of the inferior (*apara*) is intended. This is because the inferior is not established as existing apart from the Supreme Lord. Furthermore, the word "Supreme" is used to exclude the distinction between cause and effect (*kārya-kāraṇa-vibhāga*). For cause and effect are not established as distinct from the Supreme Lord. Thus, the meaning of the word "Supreme" is established. By this, the meaning of the word "Lord" (*īśvara*) is also explained. It is said: "By the word 'Lord,' the exclusion of the non-Lord (*anīśvara*) is intended. This is because the non-Lord is not established as existing apart from the Supreme Lord. Furthermore, the word "Lord" is used to exclude the distinction between master and

It is said that there is a variety of forms— clearly clear, unclear-clear, and clearly unclear— in the experience and recollection of an object appearing externally, such as "this is a jar," "that was a jar," or "the jar will be. Therefore, [there is] a single [consciousness], independent of prior experience, such as in daydreaming and so forth.

The object of independent conceptualization (*svatantra-vikalpa*) is not something innate or natural, nor is it an object previously experienced that appears as the content of memory; rather, it is a construction produced by independent conceptualization, which accounts for the resulting variety of clarity and lack of clarity. Thus, the statement regarding the "creation" (*nirmāṇa*) of independent conceptualization is established.

We shall establish that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). It is employed for this recognition of the Lord as one's own self; the ellipsis is "it is the life of all. Such is the purport of this chapter (*āhnika*).
Now, in order to explain [the text] in sequence, he introduces the doubt regarding the first verse with the words:

"of the manifestation's own nature" (*svabhāvamavabhāsasya*). The *Sūtravimarśa* states: "being the very nature of the manifestation" (*avabhāsasya svabhāvabhūta*) means that it is accompanied by reflective awareness (*savimarśa*), through the word consisting of verbal expression such as, "this is indeed a jar, not a cloth."

It is indeed already joined. Since it has been stated that the nature of non-reflexive awareness (*avimarśa*), which consists of sound, is the very essence of even the pure, non-conceptual Supreme Śiva—this conceptual form produced by the joining of that word [“Śiva”] would thus apply even to Him; therefore, this state of being conceptual is not accepted in the case of that Supreme Śiva.

Anticipating the objection that "since that which consists of the nature of mutual exclusion (*anyonyāpohana*) arises within the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra-pada*), which is of the nature of the 'I' (*mayātmaka*), it follows that the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) of the 'I' is of the nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)," he states that this reflective awareness, which is the very life-breath of Supreme Śiva, is indeed conceptual in form: [He says: "The reflective awareness 'I', which is the life-force of Paramaśiva, becomes conceptual in form. (p. 174)

O Anuttara-Bhaṭṭāraka, for that consciousness which is light (*prakāśa*), even the conceptualization (*vikalpa*) consisting of the aggregate of phonemes grasped as beginning and end—namely, the self-manifestation "Haṃ"—does not exist as speech or body, according to the principle stated [in the scriptures]. That conceptualization is what projects duality, such as: "This is a jar, and not a cloth."

Since a definitive ascertainment (viniścaya) implies a pair of entities consisting of that which is to be established and that which is to be excluded, the reflective awareness of the notion "I" does not consist of such a conceptual construction (vikalpa); this is the meaning. Such is the connection [of the argument].

(224) Now, as for the explanation: because the Light is free from the stains of *māyā* and the rest, it is of the nature of pure consciousness; therefore, [it is distinct] from the body and so forth, which take the form of "I am fat," "I am thin," and so on.

The self of consciousness—which is the unsurpassed Lord, unsullied by sensory contacts—is its very life-force; like the burning power of fire, it is its essential nature. Because it is all-pervasive, eternal, and full, it is internally devoid of any limitation regarding space, time, form, or the senses.
The conceptualization of assent as "Om" is like a designation for the head, because it internally encompasses the entire universe from Śiva down to the earth; for this very reason,
since there is nothing external distinct from itself, it consists of the nature of sovereignty (*svātantrya*), which does not depend on looking toward another.
The reflective awareness "I am of the nature of rest" is not a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

He shows the reason for the doubt that this reflective awareness of "I," like the fragmented awareness of "this is a jar" and so forth which is animated by words, might also be a conceptual construction:

By this qualifying term "the womb of speech" (*vāgvapuḥ*), you investigate that speech which serves as the cause for the suspicion of its being conceptual (*vikalpa*). He says that this Supreme Speech (*parāvāk*) is not like that—by the word "speech" (*vāk*) here.
Unlike objects such as jars, which are perceivable by the eye, this [Supreme Speech] is not perceivable by the ear; therefore, it is not of the nature of an object.

This [notion] such as "this is a jar" or "this is a cloth" is indeed different from [the aforementioned] word. "Internal" (antar) refers to the internal reflective awareness (*parāmarśana*) consisting of the expression "I am everything," which is the nature of the Word (*śabdanātmā*), characterized by immersion into the form of consciousness manifesting as the self of the full I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhantātmatā*). Furthermore, that which...

The manifold world (*prapañca*), which is *māyā*, shines as an external form to the subject; having caused that [world], from Śiva down to the earth, to rest within himself, he expresses it—meaning he contemplates it—as the nature of the ego (*ahaṃ*) consisting of the reflective awareness "this is I. Thus, he is called *vāk* (speech).
If you accept that reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) has the nature of speech (*vāgvapu*), why is it not a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)? He replies:

this reflective awareness lacks the defining characteristic of a conceptual construction. He defines the very nature of a conceptual construction: having seen some object situated at a distance, [one forms a judgment] such as "this possesses color, brilliance, and so forth."

"Is it fire or is it a *guñjā* berry?"— such various conceptualizations (*vikalpa*) regarding a real object whose nature as fire is suspected through its manifoldness, such as "this is indeed fire" or "it is a *guñjā* berry," arise from the verbal root *kḷp*, meaning "to cut" or "to determine. Thus, it is another [meaning of the term].

The cutting away of that which has the form of a *guñjā* fruit is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); within that conceptual construction, its nature as fire must be determined. "And" (*ca*) means that the *guñjā* fruit, which does not have the nature of fire, is excluded.
This reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) is: "This is indeed fire, not a *guñjā* fruit."

Because there is no object to be excluded other than itself, conceptual construction (vikalpa) does not arise. He reiterates what was stated—that such conceptual construction entails a duality and is a definitive determination—with the words "and likewise.
It is possible that there would be the appearance of two things mutually distinct, as in the case of a jar and a cloth.

For one who is equal to the Light— which, like Śiva, fills the universe from the level of Śiva down to the earth— the appearance of another, a non-luminous counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), would be as if it were once again [the Light itself]. This is because if a counter-correlative were to exist, that too [would be of the nature of Light].
Since it is indeed of the nature of light, therefore the reflective awareness of "I" does not possess the form of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). This is the connection with the aphorism.

For when a jar situated at a distance is seen, one who intends to sit down upon it— having turned toward that jar which is habituated to moving [toward him]— finds that although the jar is not being perceived,
because of its distance there is no clear reflective awareness (*avamarśa*) of it; or rather, the jar [is not truly reached].

The notion "it is a cloth" is conceived through the presentation of a consciousness consisting of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of a previously experienced cloth, brought forth by a doubting intellect;
because it is being cultivated, that superimposition of "cloth" upon that [object] finds scope. Subsequently, upon that...

When a jar is perceived clearly, the cognitive operation of *apohana*—characterized by the negation of the false attribution of a cloth, such that one thinks "this is indeed a jar, not a cloth"—is present; thus, it is [the object] of a certainty (*niścaya*) sustained by that operation of *apohana*. In this regard:
The suffix *liṅ* is used here in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*).

Thus, he states that there is no such non-conceptuality for the Light: "But this Light, which is of the nature of 'I am Supreme Śiva,' is like a cloth in the place of a jar, or rather, [it is] in its own place."

That which is conceived as having the nature of the light of "I-ness" cannot possibly exist as something manifest, because it is of the same order as a manifest object; for that very [I-consciousness] is conceived as being on the same footing as a manifest jar by virtue of its being manifest, just like a manifest jar. (226) [The jar...]

Let there be an attribution [of existence] to that which is in a state of manifestation. However, for that which is unmanifest, since it lacks existence altogether, it cannot even be attributed to the status of manifestation, as it does not possess a level of being equal to manifestation.
Thus, having stated that there is no equality of status in terms of essential nature (*svarūpa*), [the author now argues] also from the perspective of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

He says that [the world] does not exist because it would be of equal status [to the non-existent]: whatever function such as illuminating the universe must be performed by light is never observed in that which is non-illuminating. That which is itself non-illuminating—
What else is capable of manifesting it? If one were to assume the attribution of that manifestation to the place of manifestation itself, then even its non-manifestation would be possible;
yet even that remains of the very nature of manifestation alone.

He concludes this very point with the words "ataḥ" and so forth: because [the object] does not exist as an external thing in its own nature, and because there is no equality of status [between them], it is like light;
for that which is other than light—being non-luminous by its own nature and distinct—is itself being made manifest as an object.
Because it possesses causal efficiency (*kāritva*), it belongs to the same category [as other things]. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "of those that are distinct":
there is no manifestation whatsoever of anything whatsoever that can tolerate an operation of differentiation (*bhedana*) consisting of exclusion (*apohana*) of the kind previously described.
In the absence of such a thing, there can be no exclusion of a single entity of that sort; nor is there any [exclusion] if a manifestation is impossible.

In the absence of that [object], there would be the exclusion (*apohana*) of such a thing even if it were non-existent; for when its manifestation is possible, that light too possesses the very nature of illumination. Thus, he shows another point regarding the meaning—that this belongs to the light alone and not to anything else—by saying, "just like the light."
He states that there is not even the manifestation of another light— distinct from the primary light and comparable to it— which is second to that light,
because the Great Light is full of the universe, pervades the universe, and has arisen from all sides of the universe.

In this way, there is no distinction in terms of its own nature (*svarūpa*), location (*deśa*), or time (*kāla*)—such as "belonging to this place" or "existing at this time"—by which a second manifestation could be excluded from this first manifestation. This is for the reason already stated: because of the absence of duality (*dvayābhāvāt*). Thus, the second [manifestation]...
Since there is no external object to be excluded, and because a conceptual construction (vikalpa) cannot exist in the absence of a real entity to be excluded,

[the notion] "I" is indeed not a conceptual construction; rather, it is the full reflective awareness within one's own self— the Supreme Śiva, the Supreme Self, which is pure consciousness and of a single, unitary nature of consciousness.

(127) Regarding the word "nanu": when a jar is perceived, even the nature of a cloth or other objects situated in that very same place is possible, as it is brought forward by the causal impressions (*saṃskāra*) consisting of one's own cognitions. Therefore, how can it be said that [the object] is negated precisely because of that?
When the form of the jar alone exists— fully established and distinct from other things such as cloth— how could [the negation] occur? Furthermore,

for one who relies upon this perception of the jar, it is simply impossible to effect the negation of a cloth that is not being perceived by the conceptualization "this is indeed a jar" at the time of perceiving the jar.
Let alone the fact that the form of a cloth—which does not possess the form of a jar—is an object of the eye located at a great distance;

even its name, which is an object of the ear, might not have been grasped by anyone at that time. For when a jar is seen, how could the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of the experience of a cloth possibly be awakened? This is a matter of dispute.

It is true that the Buddhists maintain that the continuum of consciousness alone is the reality; according to the principle stated thus, the Śākya, who is a proponent of selflessness (*nairātmyavādin*), should be questioned in this manner, but not the system (*naya*) itself. (p.
177) In our own position, for those who possess the manifestation of "that" and "not-that," there is no manifestation of a cloth where there is no cloth.
And since it has been stated that for those who rely on intuition (*pratibhā*), the determination of "that" occurs precisely here through the exclusion of the non-pot (*aghaṭa-vyapohana*),
such that the very ascertainment of the pot is what is called the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) "this is a pot," therefore, it is only they who can be questioned, not we.

In our system, the so-called cognizer (*pramātṛ*) is independent within well-established cognitions (*supramā*), which consist of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) that faces the path of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). It is this [cognizer] that performs the conjunction— such as "this is a jar" or "this is gold"— regarding this lump of clay, whether it pertains to the cognition of a jar or the cognition of gold.
Separation (*viyojana*), however, occurs in that very same jar; it is the disjunction from the cognition of silver, as in "this jar is not silver.
Since both are being perceived, the separation of the silver from that jar is its withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), because that [withdrawal] is also being perceived. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*)...
Furthermore, the existence of the jar and the gold, as well as their conjunction within a single jar,
constitutes the identity-form of the experience "this is that" and of recollection;
thus, when an object is present before one, there arises a non-conceptual, pure consciousness of "this is a jar."
The discernment [of the object] from the cognitions of conceptualization, memory, and synthesis, such as "this is that very cloth";
likewise, the discernment of conceptualizing cognition itself from the cognitions of experience, memory, and synthesis.

The disjunction of the consciousness that synthesizes conceptual constructions (*vikalpa-anusaṃdhāna-saṃvit*); the disjunction of the consciousness that synthesizes [even] the synthesis; the disjunction of the consciousness of direct experience (*anubhava-saṃvit*)—such as "this is indeed a jar"—and the disjunction of the consciousness of recollection (*smaraṇa-saṃvit*)—such as "that [is it]"—[constitute this]. Such is the joining and disjoining of these states of consciousness.

Thus, the agent has been demonstrated. If it is not so, then in such passages as "having internalized," for that cognizer (*pramātṛ*), the manifestation of objects—ranging from Śiva down to the earth—is internal, having consciousness alone as its body;
because it manifests as a unity in the form of "I," there is also the occurrence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that [consciousness].

Regarding the phrase "by the analogy of a city reflected in a mirror": just as a city situated within a mirror appears with a sense of distinction—as "this is the mirror" and "this is the city"—yet simultaneously appears as non-different from the mirror because it is situated within it; in that same way, it is said to appear [in consciousness], and thus the relationship of grasped object and grasping subject [is established].

Regarding the phrase "divided" (*bhinnau*): "In this way" means that, according to the analogy of the mirror, the universe exists within the cognizer. "The manifestation of the jar" (*ghaṭa-pratibhām*) refers to the manifestation of the jar; and "the non-that" (*atad*) refers to the manifestation of the non-jar. The cognizer "shines," meaning he indeed experiences them. Just as rivers already contained within the ocean remain within the ocean [prior to their entry].
Just as all rivers become one in the ocean, so too, in the state of non-conceptuality (*avikalpadaśā*), the jar—

being of the nature of consciousness (*cit*) which constitutes its perceiver— is full like that consciousness itself, its universal body being contained within that consciousness. Therefore, by means of this jar, which consists of the universe, no worldly activity such as the fetching of water is performed.

Regarding the phrase "tattad" (this and that): because there is an absence of practical usage regarding examples and so forth, the activity of *māyā*—which is the cause for the manifestation of duality—unfolds and, although the universe is inherently full, it carves out an entity consisting of a jar, making it limited by excluding other subjects such as cloth and so on. By means of that...

By means of exclusion (*khaṇḍana*), with respect to that jar, for the individual cognizer (*pramātṛ*) and for [objects] such as cloth, it is established that "this is indeed the jar, not the cognizer, nor the cloth, etc. Thus, a negation is performed in the form of the exclusion (*apohana*) of each respective cognizer, cloth, and so forth. For the jar itself has exclusion as its very life-force.

There is no certainty that "it is not a cloth," because the very possibility of such an object consists in its being the negation of another entity. Thus, the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) whose nature is certainty is, at that very moment, excluded from conceptualization;
it is so called because of its separation—that is, its cutting off—from both the class of subjects (*pramātṛvarga*) and the class of objects other than itself (*anyaprameyavarga*).

It is called "delimitation. For this very reason, it is rightly said that "ascertainment implies two things," as stated in the first verse regarding the two things: "I" and "reflection" are not conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); rather, conceptual construction is an ascertainment that implies two things. Regarding these two things mentioned in the first verse:

In the two subsequent verses, the reasons are stated in sequence. Therein, the half-verse beginning with "The manifestation belongs to light alone, and not to anything else that is differentiated," and the verse beginning with "That reflective awareness which is 'I', though its essence is light, has speech as its body," [are the reasons].
In this context, it is stated as a reason for the point that "this is not a conceptual construction.
The half-verse beginning with "for there is the appearance of two distinct [things], which partakes in the manifestation of that and not-that" is what is meant.
For that determination, which was stated as implying duality, is stated here as the reason for the established entity. Thus, in this [context].

In these three verses, the meaning of the great sentence (*mahāvākya*), which consists of a single reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*), has been shown by the proponents of selflessness (*nairātmyavādin*). In this verse— “The speaker, established in a single cognition called ‘reflective awareness,’ spontaneously emits those entities that are its causes”— the term “speaker” (*pravaktṛ*) [is used].
Even by the Śākyas, who assert "by itself" (*svayam*), this conceptual construction is stated to be the activity of a cognizer;
however, how can that cognizer be sustained by these proponents of a cognition devoid of a cognizer (*pramātṛ-śūnya-kevala-vijñāna-vādin*)? Let this matter rest for now.

Regarding the word "nanu": just as in the reflective awareness "this is a jar," the state of being a conceptual construction (*vikalpatā*) arises through the negation of its counter-correlate, the form of a non-jar; likewise, in the reflective awareness "I am," the state of being a conceptual construction arises through the exclusion (*apoha*) of its counter-correlate—the non-I-form—such as a jar or other objects that are to be excluded.

Anticipating the objection as to how this might not be so, he says "the state of consciousness" (*cittatvam*): because there is nothing to be excluded in the pure reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*), that which does not exist [as an exclusion] in the pure [awareness] exists in it alone.
Having discarded the state of consciousness—which consists of full subjectivity (*pūrṇāhantā*)—by means of *māyā*, whose form is the manifestation of duality; [it remains as such].

By not reflecting upon the internal variety [of objects], and by making that [internal state] primary, one perceives—distinct from other bodies such as the physical body or objects such as a jar—a body imagined within the intellect, the vital breath, and the void;
therein, one thinks: "I am indeed gross, not emaciated; I am not a jar; I am happy, not miserable."

"I am weak, I am not a jar, I am devoid of all forms"—in this way, through the exclusion (*vyapohana*) of the body and so forth, as well as jars and so forth, that reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) which occurs in the form of "subject" (*pramātṛ*) or "Self" (*ātman*) is indeed conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Why? Because [it refers] to another, something else.

The connection with the aphorism is as follows: because that reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of "I" has arisen through the negation of that appearance which is characterized by the superimposition (*samāropa*) of what is contradictory—namely, the mutual exclusion (*anyonyaparihāra*) between the body and so forth on one side and the jar and so forth on the other—as described in [the commentary on] p. 179.

Now, the commentary: The reflective awareness of "I" (*aham-pratyavamarśa*) is twofold—pure (*śuddha*) and pertaining to *māyā* (*māyīya*). Of these two, the pure reflective awareness is non-different from the entire universe, from Śiva down to the earth; it has internalized [the universe] within itself.
It exists within the nature of consciousness alone— the universal Lord— from Śiva down to the earth, in the form of awakening whose essence is the venerable Śivabhaṭṭārikā;
or alternatively, it exists as permeated by the shadow of the universe, from the earth up to Pure Knowledge (Śuddhavidyā).

In the pure Self, which is the nature of the venerable Lord Sadāśiva and consists of pure consciousness alone, there occurs the reflective awareness "I am. However, the impure reflective awareness "I" occurs when there is an absence of the body, within the form of the object of knowledge as "this. In that case, in the pure reflective awareness "I," there is no separate agent for the exclusion of what is to be excluded.

It is possible. Since even a jar or similar object, by virtue of having manifestation as its essence, lacks the status of being a counter-correlative (pratiyogin), it does not possess the nature of a conceptual construction (vikalpa) in the absence of anything to be excluded (apohya).
However, the impure reflective awareness (*ahaṃ-pratyavamarśa*), occurring in relation to the body and so forth which consist of the nature of the cognizable (*vedya*), [is indeed conceptual].

The meaning of these two verses is that [the self], appearing as delimited by other bodies, jars, and so forth, is nothing but a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). As for the meaning of the individual words, it is now explained: having abandoned the state of consciousness (*cittattva*), which consists solely of the full light of "I" (*pūrṇāhaṃprakāśamātra*), [it appears] internally as the wall-like foundation for the body and so forth, as well as for jars and so forth.

Even though [the Self] exists, by not making it primary and failing to grasp it, one says with the conceit, "I alone, in the form of a god or other [being], am the cognizer regarding objects of knowledge such as blue which are distinct from me," and thus the reflective awareness "I am gross" and so forth is merely conceptual (*savikalpa*) and not pure; it is not non-conceptual (*avikalpa*). For this very reason, it is not full (*apūrṇa*).

It is merely a retrospective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*). Regarding the phrase "herein," he states the reason for that awareness being a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*): "of that [awareness], 'I am Devadatta'. For this awareness, the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*)—such as Caitra, Maitra, or others distinct from oneself, as well as the body and so forth, or jars and the like—is of equal status (*tulya-kakṣya*), because it is equally manifest. And for such a [subject], which is opposed by its counter-correlate through mutual exclusion, there arises a reflective awareness of "I" (aham) that is animated by the negation of the appearance characterized by the superimposition of that very counter-correlate; [the awareness] being: "I am indeed stout, not thin."

The fact that [the object] is "a jar and so forth" is precisely the non-prioritization of the pure reflective awareness of "I," which serves as the cause for the mutual distinction between the body and so forth on one hand and the jar and so forth on the other; yet, because that pure reflective awareness of "I" is present within it, the Supreme Lord is identical with the universe.

The cause is the power of Māyā, which consists of absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), whose nature is the concealment of one’s own self that transcends the universe, and which takes the form of a delusion consisting in the non-manifestation of the non-difference of forms. Furthermore, for one who has not abandoned the state of being an object of knowledge, there arises the notion of "I" with respect to the body and so forth, as if they were distinct from one another, despite their lack of substantial reality.
That which is the conceit of being a knower (*pramātṛtva-abhimāna*) is itself the *vimarśa* (reflective awareness) that constitutes the rejection of the nature of consciousness. (p.

180) Now, in order to describe individually and separately each instance of the *ahaṃ-vimarśa* (I-consciousness) as it resides in the body and so forth, he says: "The body alone is the Self. This refers to the stage of the conceit of being the body (*dehābhimāna*).
The Cārvākas maintain that the body qualified by consciousness is the *puruṣa*;

they declare the body to be the self because women, children, and fools possess the conceit (*abhimāna*) that the body alone is the self. "Even beyond that" means even compared to the Cārvākas, those who possess discernment [hold a different view]; [the quality] called "produced by cooking" (*pākaja*)...

The body consists of the elements of semen and blood; from that [conception] arises birth, from that transformation, from that old age, and from that death. Thinking thus of the body as being subject to such states, they perceive its state of being infested by worms and its foul odor upon the departure of the vital force (*prāṇa-śakti*). (232)

Even for one who perceives hundreds of transformations, hunger and thirst [are experienced]; moreover, some who are learned in the Upaniṣads (śrutyanta-vidas) consider the vital breath (prāṇa) itself—which is fit to be connected with [the self]—to be the Self. Regarding the word "tataḥ" (from that): it refers to those who possess even greater discernment than the knowers of the Upaniṣads, because the vital breath is also impermanent due to its momentariness.

Not perceiving the fitness for the synthesis [of identity] as "I am that breath," "I am that," or "This is that," the followers of Kaṇāda maintain that the intellect (*buddhi*) alone is the locus of the nine qualities consisting of cognition,
pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit,
and mental impression.
The Sāṃkhyas and others say that it is the self...

Others, such as the proponents of the doctrine of the Void (Śūnyavādins) and Brahmavādins, [hold this] because, in the state of the womb which is the source of that intellect (*buddhi*), there is an absence of any object to be known; thus, it possesses neither posteriority nor audibility.

They conceive of that which is devoid of the aggregate of objects of cognition— such as the body, pots, and so forth— as being a state of non-perception of prior forms; and because it is thus empty, they regard it as the expanse of space,
which has become the nature of the great element of ether (*mahābhūtākāśa*), a void that possesses no form whatsoever.

They say that this very state is the nature of the knower (*pramātṛtattva*). When that void (*śūnya*) is an object of knowledge (*vedya*) as "this," another void, which is not an object of knowledge, must be postulated. When that other void is an object of knowledge, yet another void, which is not an object of knowledge, must be postulated—and so on, until it becomes infinite.

The meaning is that the form of the object of cognition (*vedya*) must be conceived as empty (*śūnya*). In this way, there is no infinite regress (*anavasthā*) in the conception of emptiness. [This occurs] by the power of the manifestation of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), consisting of the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) of the jar, the body, and so forth.

Light arises through the power of light; it does not arise from the body and so forth. The body and such are merely the nature of the conceit "I am fat," "I am thin," and so on, and they do not constitute the true subject. That which is called the "void" is [the state] below one's own [consciousness], whereas the reality of consciousness (*cit-tattva*)—which consists of the full light of the "I" (*pūrṇāhaṃ-prakāśa*)—resides above oneself.

Just as the ground, when distinguished from a jar, is the absence of the jar, so too, upon the contraction of that [absence], the very nature of consciousness (cittattva), permeated by the objective aspect (vedyāṃśa), arises as the intellect, vital breath, body, and so forth. These specific stages beginning with the body arise one after another; thus, having transcended the body, [one arrives] at the vital breath.
Having transcended the vital breath (*prāṇa*), having transcended the mind (*mati*), and having transcended emptiness (*śūnya*) within emptiness,

for the yogins ascending into the state of consciousness (*cittatva*), there are the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth (*turya*), as well as the categories of the body, word, form, and that which transcends form, according to the Āgamas.

They are so called. The rejection [of this objection] has already been stated and will be explained in the section on scripture (*āgama*) by the phrase "and this is intensified by *kalā*. Therefore, it is established that the reflective awareness "I am pure" is indeed a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

"Of two kinds" means: the reflective awareness of "I" which is said to be the very essence of light, and the reflective awareness of "I" as a deity (deva) and so forth, which is the vital breath of light and is described in the two verses beginning with "in the body, intellect," etc.

It is twofold, consisting of individual experience and the nature of synthesis (*anusandhāna*). Among these, the first is reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*): in the self that is Śiva, which is the very nature of Śiva, it consists of the experience "I am";
in the self that is Sadāśiva and Īśvara, it consists of the synthesis "I am this, this, and this."
That [superimposition] is of two kinds. The second, however, consists of the experience regarding the body and so forth in the form "I am stout," such as:
"I who was stout have now become lean; I who was a child am now a youth;
that very same I shall become an old man"—thus [the superimposition] upon states such as stoutness and leanness.
The nature of *svanusaṃdhāna* (self-connection) is also twofold.

Regarding that, since it consists of the connection with the aforementioned form, its status as conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is not established at all within the pure "I-reflection" (*ahaṃ-pratyavamarśa*), which possesses both natures; this was stated in the aphorism beginning with "the 'I'-reflection."

The nature of conceptualization (*vikalpatva*) has been established in the case of the impure reflective awareness of "I" (*ahaṃ-pratyavamarśa*) which consists of experience; this was shown in the passage beginning with "in the body and in the intellect. Regarding the impure reflective awareness of "I" which consists of synthetic recollection (*anusandhāna*), such as "I who was a child am now an old man," there is non-difference for the duration of that time.

Someone might suspect that because of its throbbing (*prasphuraṇa*), this [consciousness] is free from conceptualization (*avikalpatva*); in order to dispel that delusion, [the author] demonstrates that even the impure self-reflective awareness (*ahaṃ-pratyavamarśa*) consisting of synthesis (*anusandhāna*) is indeed a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). This is shown by the occasional manifestation (*kādācitkābhāsa*) which is precisely of the nature of "this," "now," and "thus."

Regarding "form" (*rūpa*): because of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of various states such as childhood and so forth within the aforementioned body and other objects—which appear as space, time, and form—and by virtue of the memory triggered by those impressions, [one thinks], "I who was a child am now a youth; I who was a youth..."

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), that very construction (*yojanā*)—which consists of a connection (*anusandhāna*) between successive appearances, such as "I shall become that same elder"—is conceptualization (*vikalpanā*). If it is asked how this is indeed conceptualization, [the answer is]: because even in that construction, there is the notion of "I" with respect to that body and so forth.

"I was a child, and that same person am I now a youth; yet [the body] is not Caitra, nor is it a jar," because it appears as something distinct, consisting of a different manifestation. This is the connection with the aphorism.
Now, the explanation: "occasional" refers to that whose manifestation is the body and so forth.

Occasional, it possesses a restricted place, time, and form; in that body and so forth, there is the conjunction with a prior appearance and so on—thus, by means of a subsequent appearance of youth, he is joined with a prior appearance of childhood.
By the inclusion of "and so forth" (ādi), [it is meant] that he is likewise joined with a subsequent future appearance of old age.

And that conjunction [of the subject with the object] is accompanied by conceptualization; it is indeed nothing but a mental construction (*vikalpa*). That conjunction, being of the nature of a mental construction, does not constitute the pure self-reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) "I am.
Here, the term "appearing as distinct" is an attribute of the body and so forth, insofar as they possess the nature of a mental construction.

Because that body and so forth appear as mutually distinct through the intentionality of causality—even at that time, namely, during that state of synthetic unification which consists of conceptual thought—there is an uninterrupted [consciousness] of it; thus, that body and so forth possess a universal fullness. For this very reason, they are devoid of limitation.
One should perform the synthesis (*anusandhāna*) thinking, "I perceive all this.

Thus, this very state, which consists of such synthesis, is the domain of Sadāśiva; because it is fullness and cannot be excluded, by what [means] could it be called a locus for conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)? As long as...

This is the meaning. Anticipating the objection—namely, how there can be a continuous recollection (*anusandhi*) regarding mutually distinct bodies and so forth when such continuity is actually limited to them—he says: "due to latent impressions" (*saṃskārāt*). It is solely by the power of the memory produced through the awakening of the predispositions (*vāsanā*) formed by experiences in previous childhood states that [one recognizes], "I am he."

The reflection based on the power and weakness [of the intellect] is: "I who was strong am now weak. In the intellect (*buddhi*), it is: "I who previously had little awakening am now possessed of complete awakening. In the void (*śūnya*), it is: "I who previously had little sleep..."

In this way, even the synthesis (*anusandhi*) of a jar and so forth— which thinks, "The very same jar that was previously seen in the state of childhood is now seen in the state of old age"— is indeed nothing but conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Even in the synthesis of a jar and so forth...

It should be understood as being conceptual in nature. It is not only on the planes of identification with the body and so forth that the power of *vidyā*, whose essence is non-duality, is perceived—shining like the splendor of a jewel—as the manifestation of the non-dual realization "I am He" (*so'ham*); rather, this occurs through the thorough cultivation of one's own full nature upon those very planes of identification.

In the context of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), the teachers have accepted that the body and so forth serve as the means (*upāyatva*). Regarding the phrase "the body and so forth": according to the stated principle, since the manifestation of everything occurs through the power of the light of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-prakāśa-bala*) and not by virtue of the body and so forth, the body and other such things are insentient (*jaḍatva*) because they are themselves objects of manifestation; thus, they are merely objects of knowledge for preceding subjects (*pramātṛ-vedyatā*).

It is so; for by virtue of that state of being an object of cognition (*vedyatva*), when the cognizer in the form of the body does not shine—that is, when the bodily cognizer is not perceived—the object of cognition such as a jar does not appear. Nor does the bodily cognizer appear when its prior form, the vital-breath (*prāṇa*) cognizer, is not perceived; that too is its prior form.
When the cognizer in the form of the intellect (*buddhi*) is being perceived, [the object] does not appear; that [cognizer] too does not appear when its prior form, the cognizer, is being manifested;

and that too does not appear due to the absence of a cognizer whose nature is a void other than the conceptualizable prior form of that [cognizer]. If there were an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), nothing at all would be manifest.

Therefore, the meaning is that neither the body and so forth nor the jar and so forth possess the quality of being perceivable by their respective preceding subjects; rather, it is the Light itself, whose nature is the fullness of the "I," which is the manifestation of the universe in the form of jars, bodies, and the like— thus describing it through each of those [forms].

By one [aspect], the unity with the subject (*pramātraikya*) is emitted; by another, the unity with the subject is withdrawn and the persistence of the mere object, such as a jar, is maintained. By the third, concealment (*tirobhāva*) is imposed through the closing of one's own nature (*svarūpanimīlana*), because fullness is distributed by that limited manifestation. Therefore, at every moment—

By the reasoning already stated— that the Supreme Lord does not manifest the universe through the diversity of joining and separating subjects (pramātṛ-saṃyojana-viyojana) in the form of emanation, withdrawal, and so forth— it is shown that the Blessed One is also said to be eternally inseparable from the powers of emanation and the rest.

The Lord alone is the Supreme Lord. In worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), within the sphere of *māyā* which is considered to be something to be abandoned, it is said that the conscious self (*cidātman*) alone enters into that which consists of the body and so forth. By this principle, [the self] shines within its own nature consisting of internal consciousness; therefore, the body and so forth take on the form of "I" and the like.

And by its will, the power of *māyā* manifests objects such as jars externally as "this"; therefore, the statement that [the world] exists within the body and the intellect, and so forth, is justified. Otherwise, there would be an infinite regress of the aforementioned nature.
The word *api* and the word *eva* are displaced in their sequence; the optative (*liṅ*) denotes the reason (*hetu*), and thus there is a single syntactical connection.
He states another point as well: "That which was said regarding 'in the body,' 'in the intellect,' and so forth"—it is for that reason.

Thus, even in worldly transactions such as buying, selling, viewing, and explaining, one first [projects] Caitra, Maitra, and others, as well as bodies and the like, which have been created by oneself, as the respective objects of purchase, sale, viewing, and explanation.

Entering as a unity—by way of the mutual agreement between various buyers, sellers, and so forth—into that which shines [externally] for the sake of objects, He would manifest that very flood of objects externally by His will, while not abandoning its internal luminosity.
This is another meaning. By this manifestation, even in worldly transaction, the five [powers] of the Lord...
The performance of what is to be done has been explained; such is the connection with the Sūtra.

Now, the explanation: immediately following [the previous verse], by the words "in the body, in the intellect," and so forth, that which was shown—the state of being a subject (*pramātṛtva*) consisting of the body, intellect, vital breath, and the void, and the state of being an object (*prameyatva*) such as a jar—is established in this way according to the manner about to be described; how is this so?

In the unfolding state of *māyā*, the Supreme Lord Himself— who transcends the universe and whose ultimate reality is the light of the perfect "I"— enters, by His will in the form of the power of *māyā* which causes the manifestation of duality, even the body and so forth that are considered fit for rejection as being gross, emaciated, and so on; thus, though He is perfect, He enters [into limitation].
Manifesting his own true nature through the predominance of the body, vital breath, and so forth— as in "I am stout," "I am powerful"—

he nonetheless shines within himself in his essential nature, which is pure consciousness and the self of perfect I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhantā*), according to the principle stated as "for [he] is indeed the conscious Self."
According to the principle stated as "of the Lord who resides within the self," [the Light] shines incessantly in that very place.
For this very reason, it manifests the flood of objects in the form of "I" as being permeated by its own nature;
and because it is established that it manifests each of those—such as Caitra, Maitra, and so forth—as "this" externally to the cognizer.
(p. 184) Only that which is [the cause] of that [cognition] is logically possible. If it were otherwise, there would be an infinite regress;
this is one meaning.
He states another meaning as well: "that which was said regarding the body, the intellect," and so forth.
For that reason, the object of knowledge (*prameya*) of the nature to be described has arisen in this way. If one asks, "What is it?", [it is as follows]:

by the principle to be stated—that the Lord (*prabhu*), who is of the aforementioned nature and capable, is experienced as such—the drama of buying and selling, consisting of both the impure and the pure, is observed.

At the time of mutual linguistic convention in the form of explanations and the like, they first take up the bodies and so forth belonging to Caitra, Maitra, and others— which they themselves have created—
and enter into them as if they were already situated within, by way of an identity consisting of mutual agreement regarding those very things they have created.
"It coheres with the external self. According to this stated principle, the entire flood of objects is eternally internalized.

That which is the single manifestation in the form of mutual agreement among various buyers, sellers, and so forth, such that [they perceive] "this is it" externally—this is what has arisen. This is the resultant meaning he expresses by saying "therein, therein."

For the purpose of buying, selling, and so forth, a unity in the form of mutual acceptance is created by each respective cognizer, such as a buyer and so on; and with a cognizer who does not accept it, that unity is withheld by the Supreme Lord, having taken recourse to the purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*)— such as the fetching of water— of each respective cognizer.

The state of abiding in the form of the subject (mātṛ) as the jar and so forth is established, because they are manifest. Even though they consist of Śiva, concealment is imposed by the closing of that prior nature which consists of Śiva.
To that extent, in the manifestation of the jar and so forth, [the thought arises] "this is indeed a jar," and so on for everything.
Grace (*anugraha*) is bestowed by granting fullness (*pūrṇatva*), which consists in the manifestation of identity with that which has been realized.

From the very beginning, within the great emanations (*mahāsṛṣṭi*) consisting of the manifestation of the thirty-six principles (*tattva*) from Śiva down to the earth, [there occurs] the withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) of the principles starting from the earth up to Śiva.
In the great dissolutions (*mahāpralaya*), within the great periods of maintenance (*mahāsthiti*) situated between such creations and destructions,

the great concealment (*mahātirodhāna*) and the great grace (*mahānugraha*) should be understood as being included within the aforementioned form of destruction. This occurs when there is a concealment of one's own essential nature (*svasvarūpa-tirodhāna*) produced by the wrath consisting of one's own self-restraint (*svanigrahātmaka-prakopa*).

Having assumed the form of a Guru, the Lord’s engagement with the fivefold cosmic acts (*pañcakṛtya*) is not limited solely to the bestowal of grace through initiation, knowledge, and so forth upon those who are fit for such favor;
rather, it extends even to worldly activity (*vyavahāra*) in its intermediate form, as it is said: "Always for the delight of creation," and so on.
In the *Śrīmatstotrāvalī*: Salutations eternally to Śiva, the performer of the fivefold cosmic acts,
the dense mass of consciousness and bliss, who illuminates the ultimate reality of one's own self.
Thus it is stated in the *Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya*. Regarding the phrase "resting at every moment," the venerable Bhaṭṭanārāyaṇa says:
"When you manifest sovereignty within yourself, assuming various manifestations at every moment."
By that very [means], even that Blessed One, whose conduct is generally that of the wise, partakes in meaningfulness through the proclamation of momentary destruction.
Thus [ends] the *Pratyakṣastava* composed by Avadhūta.

Regarding the word "here" (*iha*): according to the principle stated as "for those who abide within," the manifestation of objects beginning with Śiva and ending with the earth already exists within the Light, which consists of consciousness and is the nature of the full *ahaṃtā*.
Within that manifestation of objects, the sudden appearance of this or that [particular object] is the external.

Having stated that [the cognition] would cause one to infer [its object], what is the point of postulating another cause in the form of an eternally inferred prototype (*bimba*) which serves as the provider of the manifestation of that object?
That other cause is refuted by the statement "it is not logically possible through an external [object]," and thus its object of cognition exists internally.

"In the passage 'for it is indeed the conscious self alone' (*cidātmaiva hi*), that which was under discussion is precisely this [stability]. By the phrase 'for the sake of its establishment' (*tatsiddhaye*), it means for the sake of establishing that the object of knowledge (*prameya*) resides within [the subject]. An argument is stated to the effect that without an object of knowledge—which resides within oneself, is desirable, and is to be reflected upon—the Lord’s reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) in the form of will (*icchā*) would not exist. This follows from that context."
(239) This follows from the context of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) whose nature is will.

By the passage beginning with "the own-nature of manifestation" and ending with "that which is the reflective awareness 'I', whose essence is light itself, is not a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)," [it is established].

The very nature of that reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*)—consisting of cognition, volition, determination, and so forth—has been established by the passage beginning with "For that [reflective awareness] is joined with... dependent on duality" and ending with "...appearing as differentiated. This applies both to that which has the form of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and non-conceptualization, and to the synthesizing awareness (*anusaṃdhātṛ*).

Having established its essential nature (*svarūpa*), [the author] states "situated within" (*antaḥsthitam*) in order to settle the minds of the disciples, which have been distracted by other objects of knowledge (*prameya*). While establishing the subject matter at hand, he determines that the universe is indeed situated within [the Self], according to the principle previously stated regarding the body and the intellect; for it is the Supreme Lord alone [who is thus situated].
Since [the Lord] has entered into bodies and so forth and exists in the form of various subjects (*pramātṛ*), for this reason— namely, because of this cause—

the manifestation of an object (*arthāvabhāsa*) appears even in memory, in a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) which is intent on exclusion (*apohana*), and even in knowledge whose nature is experience, whether it be being remembered, being conceptualized, or being directly experienced. Therefore...
It is certain that [the subject] is established and rests precisely within the light of the fullness of I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhantā*).

Indeed, this connects with the aphorism [beginning with] "in the body and so forth. The Supreme Lord alone, whose nature is light—both consisting of the universe and transcending the universe—is [perceived as] the body and so forth in forms such as "I am fat" or "I am thin."

Even in the state of the conceit of being a cognizer (*pramātṛtābhimāna*), the Lord enters the body and so forth according to the principle stated above; therefore, the entity is the cognizer. For this reason, [the Lord] possesses the powers of knowledge, memory, and exclusion (*apohana*).
[This applies] even to a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) which, though its life is exclusion (*apoha*), is a manifestation of the power of Maheśvara in the form of recollection (*smaraṇa*).

In the knowledge of experience (*anubhava-jñāna*), the appearance of an object (*arthāvabhāsa*)— manifesting as "this is that jar," "this is indeed a jar," or "this is a cloth"— rests precisely within the luminosity of Maheśvara, just like that [prior cognition];
this is what is meant by "the appearance of an object."
(186) There is no doubt whatsoever regarding this point: that [consciousness] rests in manifestation.

If the body and so forth—expressed as "I am fat," "I am thin," and so on—were themselves the ultimate subject (*pramātṛ*), then it would be established that the body, the vital breath, and so on, reside within objects such as a jar. (240)
It is so. For even this body and so forth are indeed produced from *danu* (ignorance), because they are insentient like a jar;

for, as in the case of "I am not a jar, this is Caitra alone," the body and so forth persist only by being excluded from jars and the like. Therefore, according to the principle stated that [the self] is distinct from the grasped and the grasper—

But the manifestation of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-prakāśa*) is all-enduring; [it is] the cloth and so forth, the body and so forth—thus, by this it is established that the entire universe resides within that manifestation of ultimate reality. As it has been said:
"The nature of light, completely full, consisting of great bliss through its repose in its own self..."
It is filled with will, consciousness, and action, and is completely replete with infinite power.
In that Supreme Reality— which is devoid of all conceptual construction, pure, peaceful, and free from arising and passing away—
the world consisting of thirty-six principles shines forth.
Thus, in the *Śrīparamārthasāra*.

Now, as for the word "nanu" (but surely): if it is argued that the external manifestation of the multitude of appearances residing within the Light exists everywhere—in all instances of memory, conceptualization, and direct experience—by way of taking on the form of their respective objects, then [the response follows].
One might object: "How can there be a difference in manifestation (*pratibhāsabheda*) when both [manifestations] are remembered within the same act of recollection?

For this very difference in manifestation is clearly perceived in acts such as recollection, since they manifest in distinct forms—clear and indistinct. Anticipating this, [the author replies] by virtue of [the Lord's] sovereignty (*svātantryataḥ*).

He states that there is a distinction in manifestation consisting of its clear or unclear form with the words "But that... (*taṃ tu*). The word "but" (*tu*) indicates the specific difference in the clear or unclear form of that manifestation situated within, when it is externally manifested in experience and so forth. He explains this very point with the word "that" (*sa*): [it refers to] the previously introduced [subject] situated within the Light.
The appearance of an object (*arthāvabhāsa*) exists naturally (*naisargika*), established by its very nature, within the experience of cognition (*jñāna*) as it manifests externally;
however, in cases such as memory (*smaraṇa*), it exists having arisen from the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of a prior experience.
According to the stated principle that memory, conceptualization (*vikalpa*), and so forth have experience as their life-force, these [appearances] relate to their respective objects.
In the case of manifestation, it depends upon experience; however, experience itself does not depend upon another cognition—this is the consistency of the aphorism.

The manifestation within [the cognition] of that form, such as blue, which exists in its own interior—belonging to the experiential knowledge (*anubhavajñāna*) that projects this object appearing immediately as "this is blue" externally through mediation—is innate and self-established. "Innate" (*nisarga*) means "emission" (*nisṛṣṭi*); it is so called because it has come from that.

"Natural" (naisargika) means established independently. However, the internal manifestation of recollection and so forth always occurs solely by the power of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the knowledge of experience;
likewise, [the objection that] the knowledge of experience depends on another cognition for the illumination of its object—[is refuted].

It does not exist. Therefore, in memory, in imagination, and in the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that follows upon direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), such as "this is a jar," "I consider it to be that very jar," or "this is indeed a jar"— that appearance of a jar and so forth which must be manifested by those [cognitions] such as memory as being external, that [appearance] belongs to memory and the rest.

It does not belong to itself; rather, it arises solely from the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of previous experience. Regarding the word "therein": since it is established that the object appearing in memory and the like is born from a latent impression, the latent impression that produces it consists in the persistence of the experience even at a later time; this is its inherent nature.
This is its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Thus, even as it persists over time in the form of saṃsāra, this experience—
because it is inseparable from the appearance of blue and other objects that have become its own objects— is therefore the [means of knowing] the experienced object.

Because it is luminous, even memory and other such cognitions—which have attained identity with the experience—manifest as inseparable from the appearance of the blue object and so forth that has become their content. "Precisely for that reason" means: because they manifest through their fusion with the appearance of the blue object and so forth that has become the content of the experience, they are [perceived] as being accompanied by that blue object and so forth.
Since the appearance (*bhāsa*) cannot exist at the time of recollection, it must belong to a previous time consisting of that very experience;

thus, recollection and the like are devoid of an object for themselves. Furthermore, it is proclaimed in the scriptures—this being the ellipsis—that they apprehend what has already been apprehended by experience. "This very [point]" refers to their lack of an object for themselves, because [the object] was already apprehended.
The very state of being grasped (*grāhitva*) is the lack of clarity (*asphuṭatva*) of an object appearing in memory and so forth;
thus, the distinction between clear and unclear forms of appearance in experience (*anubhava*) and memory is established.
The non-intervention (*avyavadhānatva*) of an object appearing internally [in experience] is [established] by this experience.

External manifestation is clarity; in recollection and the like, there is a lack of clarity because the object, which appears with the intervention of a prior experience, does not exist at the time that recollection arises.
[The objection begins with] "But surely": "This is a jar," "this is a taste," "this is a smell," "this is a touch."
Anticipating the objection that conceptual cognitions such as memory— arising from perceptual experiences produced by the external senses regarding objects like "this sound" and so forth—
would appear as external objects of their respective domains by way of experience, with experience acting as an intermediary, [the author asserts] independence (*svatantrya*).
He states the distinction, saying "that [conceptualization] does not exist in that way," with the word "sa" (it).

The previously introduced appearance of an object is an independent conceptualization (*svatantra-vikalpa*) that arises by its own impulse, acting according to its own will without depending on prior experience; it is indeed innate (*naisargika*). It is autonomous.

It is indeed established. Here he states the reason: "because it moves" (*cara*). [This refers to] what has been experienced within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is like a mirror of pure intellect. "Just as intended" means because of the manifestation—that is, the illumination—of the desired form or configuration of one's own preference. Such is the connection with the aphorism.

That conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) which functions as the operation of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)— namely, the conceptual construction consisting of mental desire, resolve, and so forth, arising from the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of experience— is [so called] because of the root-meaning of *īraṇa* (to move) as "moving at will" or "impelling."

(188) By its own impulse, independently of any external instigation such as grace, and through its own sovereignty, delight arises and passes away; thus it is called "moving according to its own will" (*svairacāriṇī*).
Having descended from the ground of the Mother (*mātṛbhūmi*) into the domain of the intellect, that which appears externally as "this" is—
It is indeed innate. He establishes this innateness with the words beginning "for instance" (*tathā hi*).
Even though never seen before, [the elephant] was endowed with a hundred white tusks and possessed a pair of trunks;
and within [the mind], Caitra and Maitra perceived the elephant created by themselves.

Upon the ground of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which consists of the mirror of the pure intellect (*svacchadhīdarpaṇa*), conceptual construction (*savikalpa*) manifests this external object as "this" at that very moment. Therefore, independent conceptual construction does not depend upon the face of experience, such as recollection and so forth, [just as one sees] an elephant situated within oneself.

By the phrase "it manifests externally," it is stated that even here, the manifestation of the object in the form of a tooth remains situated within; otherwise, for that [object], the intellect would not be manifesting it as being external in the mirror.
Thus, through both the creation and the manifestation of such an entity—

It has been stated that the powers of knowledge and action are self-established for everyone; because all possess the powers of knowledge and action which constitute the attributes of the Supreme Lord, it is established that the nature of every being is indeed that of the One Lord alone. He demonstrates this very point with the following verse, beginning with "asmād" (from this).
Thus, it is certain that whether in memory, or in conceptualization, or even in cognition intent upon exclusion (apohana),
an internal appearance remains present.

Thus, [the author] has established the possibility of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) as a secondary consequence. "From this" means from that which is intended as such a configuration, having the aforementioned form. In this *Īśvarapratyabhijñā* treatise, independent conceptualization (*svatantra-vikalpa*) becomes the object through the investigation of the various manifestations (*ābhāsa-bheda*).
Even the Lord perceives within His own self— which shines as "I, I" to every cognizer such as Caitra—
that "I too know and act," because that very nature, characterized by knowledge and action, which constitutes the attributes of the Lord, is observed in me as well; thus He Himself has said.

Since it was stated at the very outset that "I shall establish the recognition of that [Lord] by making the recognition of the Lord the primary form," this *Pratyabhijñā* (Recognition) is presented through the manifestation of that power; such is the purpose already declared.

The purpose consisting of that recognition is that which, when another matter is not established, is established by way of its necessary consequence (*anuṣaṅga*). According to the principle stated as "the substratum is established [as a] tenet (*siddhānta*), such as the Lord being the creator of the world," this is likewise according to the logic of the *adhikaraṇa-siddhānta*, which consists of the investigation into the distinctions within the manifestation of existence (*bhāvābhāsa*).
He shows that [this] is accomplished without effort for people. In the phrase "having the desired configuration," he demonstrates—
in the case of an independent conceptual construction— the manifestation, the delineation, and the illumination of the form of the created object of one's desire.
For this reason, for every living being, knowledge and action alone are clearly established; such is the connection with the Sūtra.
Just as the eyes and other [senses] are directed outward toward what is desired.
Even for an object that has been experienced as "this" despite its non-existence as an external referent,
the correct delineation within the sphere of the intellect, the manifestation of a created existence (*nirmāṇabhava*),
and its illumination belong to independent conceptualization (*svatantravikalpa*). However, this is what is meant by the term "innate knowledge" (*naisargika-jñāna*) mentioned in the verse.

This has been shown by way of the discussion on the objects of knowledge (*prameya*). "For this very reason" means: because of the manifestation as such a description, this too is established. If one asks what that is: whatever it may be, whether a mere insect or Brahmā, as long as it is living and engaged in the activity of living, for all of that—

It is established that the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), which consists in the manifestation of the entire universe from a worm to Brahmā, and the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), which consists in the delineation of the universe, are innate [to the Lord]. Consequently, Caitra, Maitra, and others,
upon that ground of His autonomous conceptualization (*svatantra-vikalpa-bhūmi*), subsist upon a prior creation fashioned by the Lord as distinct from themselves.

"There is not even the possibility [of such a thing]"— by this, the sovereignty characterized by independence in action (*kriyā-svātantrya*), expressed as "I cause the world to arise," is clearly recognized through this singular form "this living one" (*jīvataḥ*).

By means of this singular number, the fact that the entire multitude of living beings, from the individual soul (*sakala*) up to Śiva, is in ultimate reality the nature of the One Lord (*ekeshvara*) is established.
It indicates Śiva.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the commentary *Pratyabhijñāsūtravimarśinī*.
Now begins the seventh chapter.

Infinite— that is, unconditioned by space and time— the powers such as memory and so forth are themselves "jewels" because they illuminate the universe which constitutes their respective objects; [He is the one] who is the single, non-dual substratum (āśraya) and the worthy vessel (bhājana) for those jewels, that very illumination of the universe.

Through reliance—that is, through abiding correctly right there—there is the accomplishment of that very [joy], which is diverse like moonlight; for by bestowing the taste of the nectar of various objects, it casts off the gloom and brings about the manifestation of the exultation associated with each respective entity, thereby becoming "this," "this one," and "this very thing. Thus, it is the source of bliss.

Right accomplishment (*samyak-siddhi*) becomes the attainment [of the goal]. Thus we praise Śiva as he truly is. In this manner, the essential nature of the powers such as memory (*smṛti*) has been demonstrated at length by means of each individual daily lesson (*āhnika*).
Here, among the powers beginning with memory, that [power] is the accomplishment of an object previously experienced.

By such statements as "this is that," "in the one who desires [to know], there is vision," "the grasped and the grasper are non-different," and "the Lord is indeed the conscious self (cidātman)," and so forth, that which is the nature of consciousness (citsvarūpa) of the cognizer (pramātṛ) has been revealed; this is intended to establish their status as powers (śaktitva).

And since "power" and "the possessor of power"— [as the saying goes]— cannot exist such that power is independent of the possessor of power, the nature of the cognizing subject (*pramātṛ*) who possesses those powers must also be disclosed in order to establish their status as powers. [This applies to] their memory and so forth...
That which is the single substratum of the powers (*śakti*), their state of division and their place of rest—

that very thing is the variety of the modes of knowledge [of these powers], which is a conceptual construction of manifoldness. This capacity is sovereignty (*svātantrya*), independent of anything else, the primordial great majesty (*mahadaiśvarya*) created by that [Sovereignty].

According to the stated principle that [this] is spoken of in relation to the sovereignty of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and others, because they possess the freedom (svātantrya) to conjoin, disjoin, maintain, and so forth, that single form— expressed as "this is that" or "this is the very one"— exists even within those subjects (pramātṛs) regarding their respective objects such as pots and cloths.

Maheśvara is not merely the substratum of powers such as burning and cooking— like fire and the like— which are insentient by nature due to the absence of the reflective awareness "I am," and which are thus solely dependent on that [power]; rather,
he is also independent even in the acts of joining and separating those [powers], and this is his power.

In this sūtra, "na ced antaḥkṛtā," both the sovereignty (*māheśvarya*) and the unity (*ekatva*) of the subject—who is the locus of the three [powers]—have been introduced. Now, both of these must be determined. Regarding the word *tatra*—"among those two"—the following is intended to determine first that which has a single locus.
This chapter is introduced by fourteen verses beginning with "caiṣā pratibhā" (246).
