Among these, the first verse introduces that single substratum (*āśraya*) as its essential nature. Then, the two subsequent verses present the reasons—such as the relationship of cause and effect—that will be explained [later], establishing that the single substratum is indeed of such a nature.

The reasoning (*yukti*) is said to consist of both positive concomitance (*anvaya*), in that all worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*) are possible only when a single substratum exists, and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), in that they are not possible when it does not exist. Therefore, although the nature of worldly transactions such as rejection and acquisition is extensive, for one who recollects them through the relation of cause and effect:
And it occurs "by way of the distinction between the real and the unreal," as summarized by one verse for each [of the two].
Furthermore, that very distinction between the real and the unreal is established in detail through seven verses.
Then, with one verse, the entire subject matter discussed in this chapter is concluded; such is the summary of the chapter's contents.
Now, demonstrating the connection of this daily lesson with the preceding one,

he introduces a doubt in order to explain the first verse: "How is it that what was stated— that the individual soul (*jīva*) is established as possessing both knowledge and action— is [possible] if [the soul] were distinct from cognition, conceptualization, and so forth?"
Who is this other living self (*jīvātman*) to whom knowledge and action could belong?

Therefore, by the passage beginning with "among distinct attributes" (*tatobhinneṣu dharmeṣu*), those who maintain the existence of a self through the relationship of quality and qualified (*guṇaguṇībhāva*)—including [the proponents of] causes and so forth—have been refuted. Having raised the objection regarding the doctrine of the continuum of consciousness (*jñānasantāna*):
If it is not "internally constituted," then, according to the perspective already stated, he introduces that [consciousness] as having a single locus by its very nature, saying:
"it reveals the nature of the manifestation of that very locus;
and this is she," and so forth. [He further describes her as] "colored by the sequence of those various objects."
"Of these objects, this is the one here,
this is the one now, this is that immediately following, this is prior to that"— thus this entire age has manifested simultaneously.
In this way, by means of each respective spatial nature, temporal nature, and nature of priority and posteriority, [it is perceived].

And although it is colored by succession through its simultaneous nature (p. 191), in the ultimate sense it is also non-successive— like the Supreme Lord— because of the absence of succession in space and time.

Thus, because it is oriented toward the apprehension of various objects distinguished by their respective sequences, it is "colored" (*rūṣitā*)— meaning it is affected by the nature of a reflection— and is therefore described as being merely "distinct from the object of cognition. This [consciousness], established as self-luminous for everyone, is the "I" with respect to the meaning "this is a jar" (247).

And [the cognition] "I experience the jar" refers to the experiencer; "I remember the jar" refers to the rememberer; "the jar alone, not the cloth" refers to the jar as the object of conceptualization; and "I conceptualize the jar" refers to the conceptualizer.

The manifestation that expresses external objects is itself the infinite form of consciousness; thus, the Great Lord (Maheśvara), who is the subject (pramātā) whose nature is consciousness—unlimited by space and time, all-pervasive, eternal, and perfectly full—is independent (svatantra) in the joining and separating of cognitions (pramāḥ) and so forth. This is the connection with the aphorism.

In the cognition "the jar appears," although that manifestation appears as conjoined with the jar, nevertheless that manifestation is not the jar's own nature; rather, it is the consciousness itself which is the subjecthood (*pramātṛtva*). And in the form of that manifestation, [it is said]: "It exists for me" or "it appears to me"—that is the jar.

Because the image (pratimā) is joined with its material cause (mātṛlagna). And so says the Veda: "Tameva... [referring to] the Supreme Lord who transcends the universe, shining incessantly, manifesting as "all"—that is, from Śiva down to the earth. This is the very explanation of [the word] "vi-"; by His light...

"All this shines"— by this [statement], the word *bhāntam* (shining), formed with the present participle suffix *-śatṛ*, illuminates the unceasing radiance (*sphuraṇa*) of that Supreme Lord. Through the karmapravacanīya *anu*, which functions as an agent of experience, the creative act (*nirmāṇakriyā*) produced by the sovereignty (*svātantrya*) of the Supreme Lord is indicated.

The relationship, which is of the nature of a defining characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*), has been illuminated. The relationship, which is of the nature of light, has been illuminated for the Supreme Lord—the light of the universe whose self consists of the known and the knower. Of that *pratibhā* (intuitive flash of insight)...

Although, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), there is no succession because of the non-difference from the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), the appearance of succession alone is established [in the empirical world]. It is said that "cognition, memory, determination, and so forth appear as possessing succession"; in this context, [this appearance] is colored by the succession of various objects, consisting of their respective prior and posterior states.
Succession, simultaneity, and so forth; slowness, speed, extension, and non-extension— whatever variety of forms exists among entities due to the diversity of their material manifestations,
that succession is fashioned by the two factors of space and time, which are themselves the very form of the Lord’s sovereign freedom.

Now, regarding the passage beginning with "this present one here" (248): that which is colored by the sequence of space and time, and thus embellished as being like a reflection—only that which is distinct [from the object] and possesses awareness, etc., is the perceiver; this very one [is the subject], because it manifests right before [the mind]. Sva... [text fragment]... because it flashes forth right before [the mind].

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the manifestation [of the world] is not established; for, by virtue of resting within the essential nature of the "I" (*aham*) as the supreme mouth [of consciousness],
that "I" is, in its ultimate sense, pure luminosity (*prakāśa-mātra*), and thus transcends the limitations of space and time.

Because there is no division, that [consciousness] is without succession; it is declared to have the characteristic of being "reflexive awareness" (*pratibhā*). Maheśvara and His power (*śakti*) are non-different from the possessor of power (*śaktimat*); thus, He is the infinite form of consciousness (*anantacid-rūpa*). For this consciousness, there is no limitation (*pariccheda*) by means of space, time, or form—no "end. Thus, that infinite consciousness is the Supreme Goddess (*Parā Bhaṭṭārikā*), whose nature is pure awareness (*saṃvid-rūpa*).

"Of whom such [a nature] exists. For this very reason—because he is of the nature of infinite consciousness (*ananta-cid-rūpa*), and because he is oriented toward grasping external objects such as pots and cloths, he himself is also of the nature of an outward-turned light;
thus, he will later state that his essential nature consists of the cognitions of various pots and so forth, characterized as "this is such-and-such."

Thus, that by virtue of which an object is established as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is itself a fresh arising of its own manifestation; according to the principle to be stated later, it is a means of valid cognition that establishes the object of cognition (*prameya*) both generally as "this" and specifically as qualified by such attributes.
He is the life-force of the group; thus, by the method to be described, he is the internal reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

This refers to the manifestation of objects such as pots and cloths, and their conjunction in the form of qualifier and qualified—such as "the crown is silver"—which arises from the consciousness of silver. It is like [the appearance of] gold.

According to the stated principle, the pure "I" (*śuddhāhaṃ*) is the sovereign self-reflection (*pratyavamarśa*) which possesses the freedom to perform various types of conjunctions— such as the conjunction of one cognition with another, of a cognition with redness, or of a cognition with the cognition of a jar— and so forth. It is this [pure "I"] that is [the subject].
That aforementioned Maheśvara, who consists of reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*), is called the subject (*pramātṛ*).

He states this summarized meaning with the words "Therefore," and so forth. "Therefore" means: because the true nature of the object of knowledge (*prameya*), the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), valid cognition (*pramā*), and the subject (*pramātṛ*) has been thus explained, first [there arises the thought] "this is a jar."
That light which, as the external means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), is oriented toward the object of knowledge consisting of a jar,

and which, "within"— that is, within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)— has assumed its prior form; [it is] that very light which, having assumed the prior form consisting of the means of knowledge that establishes that object of knowledge consisting of the jar, is of the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), and thus constitutes valid cognition (*pramā*).

The conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) "I"—this very nature is the locus of rest for both [subject and object]. The meaning is that this nature of the light called "I" is full; it is full of the objects of knowledge, the means of knowledge, and the acts of knowing, such that everything is composed of that alone. "Right here" refers to the subject whose nature is a single substratum.

When, by way of the aforementioned manifestation (*pratibhā*), there occurs a resting in the form of mutual interconnection consisting of the causal relation— such as that between clay and a jar, seed and sprout, or fire and smoke—
he first expresses this positive concomitance (*anvaya*) in the form "this is a jar" with the words "tattad... (that-that...).

For me, objects such as jars and the like exist only insofar as they are grounded in a single cognizer— the substratum of those experiences and so forth— who, through the doors of the mutual differentiation of experiences and other cognitions, takes on the forms of the experiencer and the conceptualizer,
and in whom those aforementioned states consisting of cause and effect are established.

(193) Regarding the passage beginning with "it appears" (*pratibhāti*) and so forth: while these [meanings] possess their primary resting place, *jñāteya* is the state of being known (*jñāti*). Within that very state of being, it is the activity of the cognizer’s conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which determines: "this is the cause, this is the effect, this is the qualifier, and this is the qualified."

The relationship characterized by mutual interconnection is established; it is not possible [otherwise] in the case of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Furthermore, the duty (*karma*) consisting of the mutual maintenance of welfare and security among kinsmen, which is kinship (*jñāteya*), is also shown with the intention of demonstrating the convergence of all entities within a single cognizing subject (*ekapramātṛ*); such is the consistency of the aphorism.

It is asserted by all proponents of philosophical systems that the determination of objects such as jars and cloths consists in their being grounded in the respective cognitions of those jars and cloths; yet, that determination of objects is not established through a mere resting in pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*) that is distinct from and mutually different from the experiences resting upon individual subjects (*pramātṛ*).

Moreover, "that" refers to those various distinct and mutually differentiated forms of certainty, which consist of determinative judgment (*adhyavasāya*) and whose nature is valid cognition (*pramā*). These are essentially cognitions themselves, appearing as inward-turned reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). They are the "faces," that is, the doors, the means, or the paths.

By means of those forms of consciousness, which are like the currents of rivers flowing toward the ocean, if these objects of the external and internal organs— being perceived— come to rest within this great ocean of supreme consciousness (*mahāsaṃvit*), which is the nature of the subject (*pramātṛ*) and is unconditioned by space and time, as "I" (250).

They attain rest through the direct presence [of consciousness] in the manner described. "From that" means: when these objects have thus attained rest in the subject, their mutual interconnection is established by way of that logical necessity; the word "that" (tat) is employed [to refer to this].

*Jñātīya* refers to the state (*bhāva*)—in the form of cognition—of relatives who mutually recognize the basis for the application of the term "relative" (*jñāti-śabda-pravṛtti-nimitta*). Furthermore, *jñātīya* also refers to the activity (*karma*) of relatives, consisting of the mutual maintenance of their welfare and security (*yogakṣema*). And that [activity] is of the nature of action (*karmarūpa*).

And this "relation" (*jñāteya*) is shown with the intention of indicating the nature of repose through the process of unification. If one asks how this is so: that "relation," which is of the nature of action, consists in the prior non-production of a sprout—which was previously non-existent—within the objects [of the seed], such that the sprout and so forth arise from the seed and so forth.

It carries security and well-being (*yogakṣema*). Since there is no causality for a sprout and so forth without a seed and so forth, the carrying of security and well-being—which consists in establishing even the sprout and so forth as having that [seed] as its cause—indeed exists with respect to the seed and so forth.
In the same way, even between a pot and gold, there is a mutual relationship consisting of the qualifier and the qualified.
The maintenance of security and well-being (yogakṣema) is to be understood as follows:
for insentient things, there can never be an intrinsic integration without resting upon a cognizing subject;
this is what was shown in the passage beginning with "of those mutually distinct. As it has been said:
"Thus, although these insentient things appear as if they were non-existent in relation to the Self, they exist only within the Light;
for the Light alone exists by its own nature through itself and others. (p.
194) "The jar does not know the cloth, nor likewise does the cloth know the jar."
"The knowledge of those two depends on Caitra; its persistence [in them] is through him.
Having stated this very point, he says "of those characterized by spatial and temporal succession" (*deśakālākramajuṣām*) in order to establish it even by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
Here, "present" (*idānīntana*) and so forth refers to the sequence of space and time.
Of objects such as jars and cloths that have not been abandoned by cognition; furthermore,

of each of those cognitions directed outwardly toward the apprehension of their respective objects, and of the conceptual constructions (vikalpas) associated with those objects, when they are individually absorbed within themselves.

For those [entities] that rest solely in their own essential nature, what kind of synthesis (*samanvaya*)—in the form of a merging—could there be without resting in a single cognizer? The meaning is: none at all, because they rest only in their own respective forms. "This" refers to the aforementioned synthesis, which is a "single manifestation" (*sakṛdābhāsa*).

By means of a single manifestation, through the subject (*mātrā*) whose light is uninterrupted because of the absence of space, time, and form in its own self; furthermore, through the appearance of unification (*yojanābhāsa*) effected by a single cognizer, which consists in the mixing of space and time— such as [the thought] "this is that very thing" regarding various objects here and now.
This is the point to be established. "Otherwise" means that in the absence of such a simultaneous appearance (*sakṛdābhāsa*), there can be no positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
Regarding this, he provides an illustration: "Having reached the ocean, [the rivers] remain separate in the middle."

When the currents of the streams have been exhausted, grasses, reeds, and the like, being carried along by them, naturally attain a state of conjunction; with the intention that the difference consisting of place, time, and form produces manifoldness in entities,
the word "simultaneously" (*sakṛt*) is employed in the sense of negating the multiplicity caused by differences of place and so forth, [and thus it is said] "one" (*eka*).

The meaning is that for the appearance which is the nature of the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) and which manifests all at once, there is no multiplicity produced by space and so forth. In that regard, having raised the doubt as to what the connection is between fire, smoke, and so on, within that cognizer,
[it is shown that] the seed does not know its causality toward the sprout, nor does the sprout know the seed.
The selfhood of the effect [consists in] its dependence on a single cognizer; the relation of cause and effect between those two [the cognition and the object] depends upon that [single cognizer].
In this way, the entire continuum of relations resides within a single cognizer.

According to the principle thus stated, he demonstrates the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), which consists of a connection, pervades numerous places, times, and persons, and takes the form of a synthesis (*samanvaya*).

This occurs when that [causal relation] is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) within the essential nature (*svabhāva-ātman*) of each respective instance of smoke and fire as its objects.

In each respective portion of form (*rūpa*) and in each respective portion of its own nature consisting of cognition (*jñāna*), for those who "fall"— that is, for those who move, according to the verbal root *pat* meaning "to go" or "to move"— who cause their own existence to be understood as having the form of existence and as consisting of their own objects, within each respective portion of cognition; [for them, there is no difference].

Let it rest: with respect to fire, there is one positive concomitance (*anvaya*) in the form of perception (*pratyakṣa*), and one negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) in the form of non-perception (*anupalambha*). Thus, among these five types of perception and non-perception regarding smoke and fire, this smoke is the effect and fire is the cause.

Regarding the term "cause" (*kāraṇa*): the causality that establishes the relationship of the nature of cause and effect is born of a single cognizer (*ekapramātṛ*). At the initial moment of perceiving fire, if smoke is also perceived, it is impossible at that time to determine which is the cause and which is the effect.

The non-perception of smoke must be admitted. "From that" means immediately after the non-perception. For the sake of establishing the causal relationship—that smoke arises only from fire—one perceives the smoke through direct perception; in this sequence of logical connection, if one does not perceive the fire, then [the smoke] is also [not perceived].

How could the statement made in the world—that "the causal relationship between smoke and fire is established from the fivefold set of perceptions and non-perceptions, consisting of two types of non-perception in the form of negative concomitance (vyatireka), namely 'fire has not arisen' and 'smoke has not arisen'"—be possible? It is not possible at all; thus he says: *agni*... [etc.]

Just as a jar is perceived by means of smoke that is directly perceived, so too is a cloth. He demonstrates this very point: because that direct perception of fire rests upon a portion whose nature is knowledge distinct from the smoke, it does not penetrate beyond itself; therefore, it is distinct from itself.
And because it does not apprehend the specific nature (*svarūpa*) of the cognition of smoke— due to this fourfold set of reasons—
the cognition of that [smoke] with respect to its object, which is smoke,
is of a different form from that [object], since it possesses certain distinct parts that are excluded [from the object].

The term *pati* signifies that which rests upon its own respective portion of knowledge (*jñānāṃśa*) within the domain of objects (*viṣayāṃśa*). Furthermore, the word *pati* is employed here according to the *tantra* (esoteric system) as a secret terminology (*guptabhāṣā*). This same principle should be applied to the fourfold [negations] such as the non-perception of smoke (*dhūmānupalambha*), and so forth. For example, first:

The non-perception of smoke is "other-referential" (*aparaviṣaya*) because it serves as the cause for the cognition of fire— which is distinct from the presence of smoke that has been somewhat intensified— as a defining characteristic; since it rests upon the cognitive aspect in the form of its own intrinsic nature, it has fire-cognition as its object.
Because fire is not directly perceived [in the smoke] and because the nature of the cognition of fire— which is distinct from itself— is not entered into [by that cognition],
the presence of fire is inferred to some extent through the direct perception of smoke; for,
while the presence of fire is distinct from the specific characteristic of smoke, it serves as the cause for the cognition of that [fire] in its own essential nature.

Because that [non-perception] is the cause for the cognition of its own objective component, and because it does not involve the non-cognition of the existence of fire as the object of the cognition of fire,
and because it lacks the entry of a cognition of the existence of fire distinct from itself,
there is no absence of smoke through the cognition of the non-perception of fire.

This has been explained somewhat. Otherwise, since [the non-perception] would be the cause for the cognition of that [absence] in a portion distinct from smoke—which serves as the indicator of the state (bhāva)—it would follow that the knowledge of the non-perception of smoke does not grasp the absence of smoke, which is its own object;
thus, it would consist of a knowledge whose nature is the non-perception of smoke distinct from itself.

And because there is no penetration of its own nature (*svarūpa*): by the cognition of the non-perception of smoke, which is accompanied by the absence of fire, [the non-perception of fire] rests upon a portion distinct from the absence of fire within the definition of the non-perception of smoke (p.
196); therefore, it is the non-perception of fire.

The fourfold [defect] has been explained as follows: because it does not penetrate the absence of fire within the object of cognition, and because it does not enter into the nature of another cognition consisting in the perception of fire. Regarding the phrase "and therefore":
it is because the causal relationship between smoke and fire is not established by that mere fivefold cognition alone.

The absence of fire and smoke, the absence of smoke and fire, and the absence of smoke— these five objects, which constitute the domain of the five cognitions thereof, are each individually cognizable by a knower. First, when the existence of fire is the object of one cognition, at that time, if there is the existence of smoke...

The existence of smoke following [the presence of] one thing is also the object of that same one. Thus, through various cognitions such as perception and so forth, there arise specific determinations (niyama) to be individually experienced by each individual knower. Now, regarding those cognitions, just as it is with those two—smoke and fire—...

Just as [cognitions] do not establish a causal relationship, so too, according to your position, since the continuum of cognition alone is the reality— as stated by the Sugatas— and because, according to the logic of the Sautrāntikas, only a single cognizer consisting of the continuum of cognition perceives them,
smoke and fire, though perceived by that cognizer, do not establish a causal relationship.

If it is asked how [this applies] to your position—that it is merely a continuum of cognition—the answer is as follows: for a cognizer who perceives fire, because of momentariness, the non-perception of smoke and so forth exists at the time of the [fire-]cognition; since the cognizer is momentary, [there is no continuity] between the smoke and the fire.

Suppose it is argued that the cognition of the causal relationship between the two does not occur [through perception], but rather that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) alone makes their causal relationship known. [We reply: Even in the conceptual construction that follows upon the direct perception of fire, there is no apprehension of the presence of smoke and so forth as something distinct from the fire experienced in that direct perception of fire.
If he were to make it known [as such], then that direct perception (pratyakṣa), which constitutes the very operation [of cognition],
would have as its object only the object of direct perception;
for this reason, having thus refuted the position of others, [he establishes] cause and effect within his own system alone.
He states that there is the arising of existence: when the stream of cognition, consisting of perception and non-perception,

is pervaded by the fivefold [senses] with respect to those five entities— beginning with fire— and their presence, etc., due to the reality of place, time, and form, [all] within the one ocean of consciousness which is "I," eternally full and complete, by the knower.

When they have come to rest, they then become unified and mutually intermingled. Precisely from that state, they are conceived by the subject through its sovereignty as being mutually dependent by way of the relationship of cause and effect; however, this is not like a jar or a cloth, which lack mutual dependence. A jar— [is not like that].
Even when two objects rest within a single cognizer, there is no mutual dependence between them.

Their mere appearance as cause and effect is unified into a single appearance by the cognizer, who causes them to rest within the ocean of a single consciousness. For this very reason, it is a single appearance that is mutually dependent.

The mere appearance of the unification of those factors, such as the existence of fire and so forth, is itself the appearance of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). Since this causal relation is produced by a single cognizing subject (*pramātṛ*), there is nothing defective and no loss whatsoever [to the theory]. [This is established through] perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*).
That which has been accomplished by the five cognitions through their own respective objects— the illumination of smoke [by the cognition of smoke],
and the illumination of the absence of fire and smoke by the cognition of the non-perception of fire and smoke— [is as follows].
All this will be unified through the power of recollection by way of mutual dependence;

thus, even the causal relationship between smoke and fire is established. [The question] "Is there one cognizer?"—[is answered by noting that] perception and conceptualization are like two conceptualizations.

Since conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) follows after [perception], it does not constitute a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by itself when it makes known something beyond the immediate experience;

according to the principle stated in the immediately following verse, and by the logic that all such conceptual construction is rooted in experience, this conceptualization does not operate upon an object that exceeds the experienced content consisting of the conceptual construction itself. (255)

By the principle that "I" alone is the internal-facing nature of the consciousness of aesthetic relish (*rasa*), there arises a single entity consisting of the experiencer, the conceptualizer, and the rememberer; this is of the nature of a synthesis of the Vijñānavāda school, wherein experience and other such phenomena consist of preceding and succeeding moments of consciousness.

It does not establish the existence of the knower (*pramātṛ*). Regarding the phrase "and in memory itself, self-awareness" (*smṛtau caiva svasaṃvittiḥ*): "in memory" means when memory occurs within one's own self; that is, at the arising of memory, there is self-awareness consisting of the nature of the knower who remembers. This very self-awareness—which is one's own indestructible consciousness—is what establishes memory.
That very [subsequent cognition] is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that establishes even the occurrence of a prior experience;

there is no other means of valid knowledge— such as perception, inference, and so forth— apart from the consciousness consisting of mere measurement (*mātrātmaka-saṃvitti*), which can establish the existence of a prior experience.

Regarding the word "here" (*iha*): in the world, because memory itself lacks its own object, it is only an already experienced object that appears. In that case, regarding the appearance of the experienced object, that memory does not constitute a new manifestation such as "this is the object of that [experience]"; rather, it is within this memory [that the object appears].

The very prior experience of an object that is manifesting is the illuminator; it becomes the illuminator by means of memory. And that experience which illuminates the object, being itself of the nature of knowledge, lacks the status of being an object of knowledge [in that moment], and thus exists in the form of memory.

Like an object experienced by another cognition, it is not self-cognized. If it were cognized [by another], it would not be self-luminous. Therefore, it is simply not cognized at all. Furthermore, if that luminosity were non-existent at the time of experience and recollection, how could it manifest, given its very non-existence?

Even when there is recollection at the time of memory, this pair of cognitions— "that" as the manifestation of recollection and "this" as the manifestation of direct experience— arises simultaneously as mutually distinct; thus,
"that" is distinct from the manifestation of direct experience as "this."

(198) No recollection whatsoever could exist that is not of the nature of light. "Therefore" means: because memory and experience cannot arise by themselves apart from the subject (*pramātṛ*). "In this way" refers to what is about to be stated. "This" refers to the fact that the manner of their arising is logically established. "Memory," etc.

That very self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) which is the cause for the arising of memory and constitutes the nature of the cognizer (*pramātṛ*), is itself the self-awareness that is the cause for the arising of experience; thus, that self-awareness has the form of the rememberer at the time of recollection, and the form of the experiencer at the time of experience. (256)

Apart from such self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). In that regard, [the object] cannot even stir to move by means of a prior experience. That self-cognition which, from the time of the experience until the time of recollection, remains uninterrupted as "I," is itself indestructible.

It is established that the very nature of the subject (*pramātṛ*) is consciousness itself. By the implication that "the rememberer is one thing and [the experiencer] another" is untenable, the proof of the subject was previously stated in the passage beginning with "now, the destruction of experience. For that [subject] is the one who [possesses] the object previously experienced.

And so on. Now, however, the distinction is that memory and experience have one and the same self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) as their cause; thus, the subject (*pramātṛ*) is established by way of another mode, namely, through the identity of the causal self-awareness.

Regarding the word "nanu": it has already been stated that even in the case of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), if it makes known something beyond direct experience (*anubhava*), it is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) at all. Therefore, how could conceptual constructions be valid cognitions with respect to an object that is distinct from what was experienced? For their lack of validity arises solely through the force of a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-jñāna*).
"In the absence of a subverting cognition (*bādhakajñāna*), how could that [prior cognition] lack validity? Thus,

this very relationship between the sublated and the sublator among cognitions— such as "this is a cognition of mother-of-pearl" being true and "that was a cognition of silver" being false— is established for all people through the production of true and false appearances.

Having stated in one verse that the life-force of all empirical transactions (*vyavahāra*) cannot be established without a single subjecthood (*pramātṛtva*) which serves as the point of rest for cognitions such as that of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell,
[the author] then explains in seven verses how cognitions, in the absence of resting in a single subject, [cannot be valid] by themselves alone.
He demonstrates at length that there is no relationship of the sublated and the sublator by stating:

"bādhyabādhaka... [The sublated and the sublator]. For those things which are not contradictory because they are established in their own nature—being established (*niṣṭha*) within their own object (*sva-viṣaye*), within themselves (*ātmani*), and within this aspect of cognition (*jñāna-rūpeṃśe*)—there is no contradiction.

The relationship between the sublated and the sublator— wherein this cognition of mother-of-pearl is the sublator and this cognition of silver is the sublated— can only arise or be possible through being established within a single cognizer; that is, because it must rest and find its finality within one and the same cognizing subject.

"In this world"—that is, in the universe—there may be the sublation (*bādhā*) of one cognition by another cognition. The validity (*prāmāṇya*) of that [sublated] cognition consists in its having an object; whereas the validity of [the sublating cognition] consists in its having as its object that which is not unreal (*satya-viṣayatvena*), given that its nature is sublation. That which must necessarily be established... that too is one.
The meaning of the word "how" (*katham*) is also: "How could it be [otherwise] without resting in the subject (*pramātṛ*)?

(p. 199). First of all, no sublation whatsoever is observed being performed by the mother-of-pearl, which is the object of the cognition of mother-of-pearl, upon the silver, which is the object of the cognition of silver.

Since insentience (jaḍatva) implies the capacity for movement, let there be no sublation by the mother-of-pearl (śukti), which is the object of the cognition of silver. Anticipating the objection that the cognition of silver is sublated by the cognition of mother-of-pearl,
and considering that this too is not tenable, he says that even this is indeed tenable:
Regarding the phrase "of those that contradict their own self-abiding": "In its own" means in its own object; "in the self" means in one's own nature consisting of a portion of cognition.

This is because there is no mutual contradiction between the two cognitions of shell and silver when they have come to rest [in their respective objects], just as there is none between the cognitions of a jar and a cloth.

Now, regarding the phrase "of those that are contradictory to abiding in their own nature": the contradiction between those two cognitions is of the nature of mutual exclusion, which is itself an instance of abiding in their own nature. [The word] "then" [is used as follows]:
if the contradiction is indeed abiding in their own nature, then for all things considered to be real...

Since even cognitions such as those of a jar or a cloth possess this very same mode of mutual exclusion, it would be impossible to establish a definitive, limited system regarding the relationship between the sublated and the sublator— determining that "this is the sublator" and "this is the sublated"— and thus the [proposed] position utterly collapses.

In the phrase "the distinction between the real and the unreal, which contradicts abiding in one's own self," the meaning of the particle *iti* should also be understood through *tantra* (economy of expression) as being conveyed by a single utterance.
To conclude the point already stated, he says: "If [it were] silver..."

If a cognition perishes by itself without being sublated by another cognition, then what sublation could there be for this cognition of silver by means of another cognition, namely the cognition of mother-of-pearl? He says that it is impossible for the cognition of mother-of-pearl to even remove its object: "silver..."

Since that [subsequent cognition] is impossible at the time of the [initial] cognition, it cannot effect the removal of the silver-form object from the cognition of the mother-of-pearl, because it does not arise at that time. Let there be no sublation (*bādha*) of the cognition of silver and its object by the cognition of the mother-of-pearl. [The cognition] "this is silver... [is thus established].
He says that even if silver is absent, let the cognition of silver that occurred previously, along with its object, be sublated;

however, the cognition "this is not silver," while taking as its object the absence of silver inherent in itself, would not remove the object of that previous cognition of silver. For that [previous cognition] also...
Because it is impossible at that time.

He states the refutation regarding the counter-position with the words "athāpi" (even so). Even in the absence of such a refutation, if the position is held that one cognition is destroyed by another cognition, then for all [cognitions]...

Since this very same principle applies even to cognitions of jars, cloths, and so forth—which are regarded as true—the path is simply mutual sublation; thus, how could it be that "some are to be sublated and some are sublaters"?
It would follow that anything at all [could be either].
Having thus demonstrated that the relationship of the sublated and the sublator exists only among cognitions regarding objects beyond the senses, [the author] states—
on page 200— that this relationship of the sublated and the sublator is established within his own position alone: "But when..."

In the past, the cognition of silver and immediately thereafter the cognition of mother-of-pearl both rest within the single self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) consisting of the cognizer; he demonstrates that this establishes their relationship as the sublated and the sublator by saying, "For instance" (*tathā hi*). One...

Even for cognitions that come to rest within the state of the subject (*pramātṛtattva*), that resting does not take a single form; rather, it is experienced as having a manifold nature. He demonstrates this very manifoldness:
there is a pair of cognitions, namely "this is blue" and "this is a lotus."
Through the appearance of the mutual coloring of the qualifiers of those two blue lotuses, [the cognition] comes to rest in the subject (pramātṛ);

whereas in cognitions such as "this is a jar" or "this is a cloth," which come to rest without mutual contact, there is no reciprocal relation—just as in the case of "this is mother-of-pearl" or "silver. And [in the latter], it is silver...

The absence of another cognition— that is, the two-fold consciousness which uproots the previously arisen cognition "this is silver"— is called "consumption" (*kṣī*) according to the analogy of a painting on a wall;
it consists of the nature of the subject (*pramātṛ*) who reflects upon the silver that was the object of that cognition of silver.
By destroying the persistence of functional activity, it establishes itself within the cognizer.
Thus, regarding the causal relationship between smoke and fire and so forth,
the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) consisting of "this is the effect" and "this is the cause" would be impossible.

That very [object] created by the non-independent cognizer must be said to provide a variety of resting points for its independent means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Thus, in the manner described, within a single cognizer, there occurs the abandonment of the prior cognition "this is silver" in favor of the present cognition "this is mother-of-pearl. Since...

The certainty of that [cognition] is established because it rests in the repose of a single cognizer; thus, the relationship of the sublated and the sublator among cognitions is logically possible. Just as He creates blue and other objects, so too does He alone create the conventional usage of the relationship between the sublated and the sublator associated with them.

Because the Supreme Lord causes them to appear through His own sovereignty, they too are indeed real. In this worldly transaction, which consists of the relationship between the sublated and the sublator, it is precisely the subsequent cognition of mother-of-pearl— occurring within a single cognizer— that [sublates] another prior cognition of silver.

Thinking, "I shall refute with the following verses the opponent's view which anticipates [the objection] that 'the cognition of a bare ground is the cognizer of its own validity,'" [the author states]:
"Just as the cognition of a ground devoid of a jar establishes the apprehension of the absence of the jar, so too..."
"And the subsequent cognition of the previously perceived silver is the awareness of its lack of validity"—this connects with the aphorism [which states] "by resting in the cognizer" (p.
201). Thus, even the cognition of mother-of-pearl arises independently by itself from its own nature.
"By the principle that 'validity, which is non-different from its own nature, is cognized and thereby delimits that [object],' it follows by the principle that 'it delimits the object of knowledge,
namely the form of the mother-of-pearl,' that there is a delimitation of the cognition with respect to the object. This is incorrect, because of the cognition of the mother-of-pearl.

The cognition of the mother-of-pearl as distinct from the cognition of its validity is itself said to be the cognition of the invalidity of the previously occurred cognition of silver. However, the subsequent cognition is of the nature of the jar; the subsequent non-apprehension is of the form of the jar—thus [it is].
It is well known that the cognition of the absence of a jar is simply the cognition of a previously [perceived] secluded spot; likewise,
the very experience of the invalidity of the cognition of silver produced by the cognition of mother-of-pearl is said to be the sublater of that cognition of silver.

The relationship of the sublated and the sublator exists between those two cognitions. If it is argued that this is according to the manner described above—namely, by us who, following the Sautrāntika doctrine, maintain that the continuum of cognition alone is the self, and thus assert that cognition itself is the self—then [the question arises]:
what is the basis for the unity of the knower among these various cognitions? In this context, there is the relationship of the sublated and the sublator.

In the context of establishing the conventional usage of non-existence (*abhāva-vyavahāra*) as a consequence, intending to demonstrate its essential nature (*svarūpa*), [the author] first refutes the very example stated as "the cognition of a bare ground" with the words:
"Just as the cognition of a bare ground is the apprehension of the absence of a jar. He shows that this is not so. As for the example...

If it is asked how that very [absence] was thus stated, it is said: "From the knowledge of the locus as pure. From the knowledge of a portion of ground devoid of a jar, the state of that ground as being non-jar—or rather, its nature as something other than a jar—is established. Only this much is established: "There is no jar on the ground. In this case, regarding the ground...

Furthermore, the non-existence of the pot— which is perceptible and capable of being seen by visual perception— and even the non-existence of the self in the form of the pot, cannot be established [by mere non-perception]. The illustrative example (dārṣṭāntika) is that, without a single cognizer, the very cognition of mother-of-pearl becomes the cognition of silver.

If it is asked why that very same counter-example was stated, it is said in reply: Just as one might say "the jar is not a cloth," so too is non-existence to be designated through identity (*tādātmyena*) as "the ground is not a jar"; and just as one might say "there is no jar here on the ground," so too is non-existence to be designated through difference (*vyatirekeṇa*). Thus, there are these two types of non-existence.

From the knowledge of the pure ground, the first [type of non-existence]— the linguistic usage of non-existence in the form of identity, namely "there is no jar on the ground"— is established. This occurs where the object to be negated, such as a jar,
would otherwise be made an object of visual perception through its functional characteristics, such as its broad base and bulbous shape.
The linguistic usage of the absence of identity [is as follows]:

even for that which, such as a ghost or the like, lacks attainment through its own nature or through the power of creation such that it is not fit to be perceived, its absence as an identity must nonetheless be expressed by itself; [for example,] "the ground is not..."

Regarding the phrase "piśācādi": Alternatively, the example that was stated—namely, that just as on the surface of the earth there is the cognition of the absence of a jar caused by sound and so forth—is itself not tenable. [For] sound and so forth are [already] associated with the cognitions of other objects, such as sound, which are produced by the sense organs like the ear and skin that grasp them. (261)

There is no certainty because of the absence of proximity. Furthermore, the absence of sound and so forth through identity (*tādātmya*) is what is conventionally expressed when one says, "The ground is not sound. In that case, where the qualification of being perceptible (*dṛśyatva*) is necessarily required for the object to be negated, there [it is understood]: "There is no jar on this ground. It is not [the case that] "on this ground... [without such a qualification].

We say that by the words "sound," etc., if it were not accepted that the absence [of sound] is the means for the linguistic usage of identity with that which is to be treated [as absent], it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
This so-called "over-extension" refers to the [linguistic usage] of the floor even while a cloth exists [upon it].

It is precisely the distinctness from the jar, because there is no mutual intermingling of entities. Furthermore, even when a jar is not present, it would be impossible to say that "there is no jar on the ground. This very point demonstrates the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), as shown by the phrase "even [when the jar exists]"—for even while the jar exists, the ground...

The phrase "the ground is indeed devoid of the jar" means that because entities such as the ground and the jar are established in their own selves—that is, because they are each established in their respective natures—there is no mutual commingling;
thus, even while the jar exists, the ground remains distinct, and this is the cognition [of the ground]. As for the word "jar": [it refers to the jar itself].
The cognition of a secluded portion of ground occurs only at certain times, specifically in a state characterized by the non-proximity of a jar. Regarding the phrase "of that which is distinct":
this refers to the absence of a jar that is distinct from the ground. As for the term "means of proof" (*sādhana*): how can it be said to prove non-existence?
Even when a cloth is present, [the floor]—the floor does not become mixed with other entities, because there is no mutual intermingling between the floor and the jar. "Tataśca" means "therefore.
"Tadāpi" means "even then"; that is, even while the jar exists, there is cognition of the distinct floor. Thus, even though [the jar] is present...

"In this pot on the ground, there is no pot"—this is the cognition [of absence] by way of exclusion (*vyatireka*). "The cognition of the ground as distinct from the pot. "At some time" means only in a certain state characterized by the non-proximity of the pot; it is the absence of the pot, which is distinct from the ground.
In what manner could it be established that [the absence] exists? It should be understood that even in the state when a jar is not present, [the absence] would exist here on this ground;
for even when a jar is present on the ground, there is no mutual intermingling between the ground and the jar.

In this case, it is appropriate to say, "There is no jar on this ground. However, when the jar is not present—because the jar is not perceived here on the ground—it follows that even the statement "There is no jar on this ground" is not established;
such is the meaning.

But is it not the case that when a jar exists on the ground, it is said that "the ground is distinct"? Likewise, in this instance, the linguistic usage "there is no jar on this ground" is based on the absence of a distinct entity; [how then can it be] with respect to some jar...?
In the state consisting of proximity (*sannidhāna*), it is perceived by all; this has been experienced by the untrained as well.

Anticipating the doubt, "What is the way [to explain] that? the ancient masters, such as Akṣapāda and others, demonstrate the method for establishing the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) of non-existence (*abhāva*) with the words beginning "But... and so forth. "In this case" means in the place devoid of the jar.
On the surface of the earth, for one possessing sight, there exists a mass of sunlight perceivable by the eye;

yet for a blind person situated in blinding darkness, there exists— indicated by sound— a soft or warm touch, distinct from the hard touch appropriate to a jar, which is the object of the sense of touch.

There also exist sound and other objects perceivable by the sense organs such as hearing. Regarding that [object], there is a cognition of its own form as distinct from a jar or other things—such as when one says, "this is light," or "this is touch"—which constitutes the absence of the nature of a jar. [For example: "There is no jar here on this ground."
The statement "it does not exist" indeed establishes the absence of a jar distinct from the ground.
The meaning is that, by relying on the presence of each individual object among the various sensory objects upon that ground, it is possible to apprehend the absence of another— the jar.

The principle that "the very absence of a jar is to be designated as the absence of other entities such as a jar" is a path established by experience that cannot be abandoned by any proponent of philosophical views. Regarding the word "therein":
in such a case, [it refers to] the jar and other entities together with another entity, namely the ground.

The relationship consisting of the nature of the supported and the support is that very same [relationship] between the presence and the absence of that [thing]. Thus, there is a relationship of supported and support between both the presence—the ground—and its absence—the absence of a jar—[as well as] Śiva and so forth. "And from that" means: in this way.
In the case of what is known through the relationship of locus and located— whether it be stones and so forth on a ground distinct from a jar and the like,

or whatever such as a mass of light appears in visual cognition— that very stone or the like [appearing] on the ground is designated as the "absence of the jar," either by way of the non-existence of a reflective awareness of an action.

The absence [of a jar] on the ground is conventionally expressed through the presence of a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the activity [of perceiving] its non-existence. Even in cases where there is no operation of the eye— such as when the eyes are closed or in deep darkness—
the absence of a jar on that ground, which is within the range of visual perception, is characterized by the cognition of a specific hard touch.

Perceiving a tactile sensation such as softness or warmth that is invariably absent [from the object], one conventionally designates that very sensation as the "absence of a jar. Regarding the phrase "of the omnipresent": the summarized meaning of the verse is that the tactile sensation of air, which exists in all places and times, must necessarily be present there on that ground. As for the meaning of the individual words:

(p. 204) It is explained: the word "but" (*kiṃ tu*) indicates a specific position within one's own system (*svamata*). This [word] "but" serves to set aside [the opponent's view] in one's own system; having made one's own intuition the respondent for the sake of establishing one's own tenet (*svasiddhānta*), [the author asks] along with that [intuition]: "What, then, is the correct [position] here? according to the author of the Sūtras.

The meaning of the word *kiṃtu* ("but/however"), which indicates this specific distinction, is that reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) takes the form of a question. Regarding the word *tatra* ("therein"): when such a reflective awareness in the form of a question has arisen, he himself says "therein.
On a ground distinct from a jar, there is first of all for one with eyes a mass of light perceivable by his own eyes.
It should be understood that for one who is blind and situated in blinding darkness, there is no perception of heat or other such tactile qualities.

Regarding that light, touch, and so forth, by way of their own forms— that is, through the cognition which grasps them individually in the form "this is light," "this is touch," and so on— that cognition, acting as the agent, [perceives] that light and the rest.
The meaning is that the cognition of a stone or similar object on that ground establishes its nature as the absence of a jar— that is, its nature as the non-existence of a jar—
and thus it is capable of establishing [that absence].

Having thus stated that the very absence of stone and so forth, or light and so forth, is the existence of a jar and so forth, he says the following in order to state that the absence of sound, taste, and so forth is likewise the existence of other sounds, tastes, and so forth:
"The external vibration consisting of inhalation and exhalation is distinct from internal vibration."

From hearing one's own subtle sound produced by the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa), one infers the completeness of the causal complex consisting of the auditory organ and other factors; thus, imagining that the auditory faculty possesses the completeness of the causal complex for the apprehension of sound,
one perceives that very internal sound as a single cognition in the form of audition.

By apprehending the associated [sound], it negates any other external sound; thus, the thought arises that "the sound exists only internally, not externally. At that time, based on the absence of subtle internal sounds—[the sound] which is the most subtle sound of the ear, permeated by the *nāda* up to its subtle limit—there exists only the subtle sound itself.
One perceives non-existence through the thought "sound does not exist. Thus, due to the absence of other tastes and so forth,
at the very moment of perceiving the non-existence of those respective external sounds and other objects,
auditory and other sensory cognitions arise from one's own internal sounds and so forth— distinct from their respective external forms.
Even though it does not touch any other object, while experiencing the taste of its own saliva, it perceives that "there is only the taste of my own saliva, and nothing else. Likewise,
while smelling its own state of being moistened by the three [tongues], it perceives the absence of any other taste, thinking, "there is only the scent of my own palate, and nothing else."
In this way, while experiencing its own bodily touch, it perceives that there is no other touch;
[this is] due to the perception of other objects such as sound, which are capable of being associated with auditory and other types of cognition.

It is an absolute certainty that there is no determination of the absence of other sounds and so forth with respect to the collection of auditory and other organs, which are the causes for the perception of sound and the rest. Therefore, having apprehended each individual sound and so forth, [one proceeds].
The meaning is that the non-existence of other entities such as sound and so forth can be asserted.

By the experience of objects like sound that immediately follows, there occurs at that very moment the destruction and dissolution of the collection of instruments, such as the ears, which were previously imagined to exist.
Since there is an absence of other sounds and so forth from time immemorial, there is indeed a certainty regarding that possibility.

If it is asked, "At the time of perceiving the absence of each respective denotable sound and so forth in its own [perceptual] moment, why is there not a single locus consisting of one's own auditory and other sense organs for the aspect of non-sound?"—he refutes this, saying: "No."

For one who desires to perceive the absence of this or that sound and so forth is observed to be actively employing the respective bases of the auditory and other sense organs—which serve as the causes for the apprehension of those specific sounds and so forth—by means of effort.
(265) Now, [it may be objected]: "Is it not the case that [this applies] not only to the objects of the auditory and other senses, such as sound and the like?"

The conventional practice of negation by way of exclusion (vyatireka) is established. Consequently, it follows that even for something invisible, such as a *piśāca*, there would be a conventional practice of negation by way of exclusion. If one asks how this is so:
just as that mass of light situated on the ground is other than a jar, so too is it other than a *piśāca* and the like.

Having grasped that mass of light, one might think it reasonable to say that there is no *piśāca* here on this ground; anticipating this, he says: "A *piśāca* might exist," and so forth. It might be that even something other than light—a *piśāca*—being invisible due to being beyond the range of the senses, appears within another part of the ground.
In the same way, it is indeed possible that he exists within the light;

for just as a *piśāca* cannot be denied when it is said "there is no *piśāca* here" because it remains invisible while existing within the ground, so too, because the *piśāca* exists within the world, its existence there likewise cannot be denied.

"In this way, in every respect" means that just as the linguistic usage regarding the non-existence of identity— such as "the ground is not a jar"— is established everywhere by its own nature, so too is it for a *piśāca* and the like; according to the logic you have stated,
although a mass of light is distinct from a *piśāca*, and although the light is of a non-*piśāca* nature...

The existence of identity in the form of "it does not exist" is established. Even so, it is impossible to determine here that "there is no piśāca in the midst of this light. For a jar, like a piśāca, cannot be conceived as invisible in the middle of a space filled with light. If one asks why, it is because when a jar is present there...

Because, when the ground is occupied by a jar, the flood of light residing on that ground recedes; and for this reason—namely, because the presence of a jar in the midst of the flood of light is impossible—it is said: "There is no jar here in the midst of the flood of light."

This is established: for a *piśāca* that exists either in the midst of the earth or even in the midst of light does not obstruct the presence of a jar because its nature is such that it is not obstructed by the dense mass of light; and therefore, there is no obstruction caused by that density.

Since the existence of that *piśāca* is impossible in the midst of light, how can there be a conventional negation through exclusion (*vyatireka*) such as "there is no *piśāca* here"? In the same way, [how could one negate] taste and so forth, which are objects of the gustatory faculty, within the color-form (*rūpa*) that is the object of the visual faculty, such as milk?
Since color, taste, smell, and so forth are not perceived, it is impossible to formulate a negative exclusion (*vyatireka*) stating that they do not exist.
Having thus explained the intended meaning (*tātparya*), he explains the words of the verse, beginning with "Even though" (*yadyapi*).

In the same way, it is possible to conceive that this [Piśāca] exists within the light as well; thus far, the application of the Sūtra has been explained. Then, with the words "And therefore": because the Piśāca is conceivable even within the light, the light is other than the Piśāca; by this, [the relationship] is shown to be one of identity (*tādātmya*).

The meaning of the verse is as follows: "Even though the piśāca has been prohibited, and even by all means [it is said] 'there is no piśāca here,' since it has not been prohibited even by way of exclusion (apoha), how can worldly transactions based on the dense latent impressions (vāsanā) regarding the non-existence of piśācas and the like proceed with respect to that ground?"

Thus, having demonstrated the ultimate reality of the conventional usage of "the sublated and the sublator" as it arises from the context— beginning with "evam bādhya-bādhaka-bhāva-vyavahāra-prasaṅgāt," followed by "kiṃ tv āloka-caya" and so forth, up to "bādhyabādhaka" and so forth, ending with "āloka-caya"— it is not the case that [this is so].

With the half-verse beginning "śuddhasthala-jñānāt" (from the knowledge of the pure locus), he applies the state of identity (*tādātmyabhāva*) to the subject under discussion—namely, the object of love (*premeya*)—saying "evam" (thus): just as the cognition of light and so forth is of the nature of the cognition of the absence of a jar, so too the cognition of nacre in a place containing nacre would be of the nature of the absence of the cognition of silver; it is not [otherwise].
It would serve as an indicator of the invalidity of a previous cognition of silver.

Just as when one perceives that light itself is of the nature of the absence of a jar, once that light is grasped, nothing is gained for the jar that existed prior to it by that cognition of the jar which was previously held.

Even in the case of the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) regarding its sublation, it has not occurred. "In this way" means: just as the cognition of mother-of-pearl is not the cognition of silver—so too, a pot-cognition does not [validate] its own validity by itself through its own nature, since it is the very cognition of the pot which is its own object.
At that very moment, the present consciousness—the absence of the cognition of the cloth—is the validity of the absence of the cognition of the cloth;
thus, by means of the cognition of the jar and the cognition of the absence of the cloth, [the former] previously... [becomes established]. "This is a jar," this...

The reflection on the cognition of a jar (*ghaṭajñānacintā*) and the reflection on the absence of the cognition of a cloth, namely "this cloth does not exist" (*paṭo nāsti iti paṭajñānābhāvacintā*), all of this is merely a reflection on the intrinsic nature (*svarūpacintā*) of the cognition of the jar. By means of this, nothing at all has happened to the previously arisen cognition of the cloth; such is the meaning. Thus...

"This is mother-of-pearl, not silver"—in this sequence, [the subject] says, "I am the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the mother-of-pearl; I am the means of valid cognition regarding the absence of silver. Let it be that [this] is manifested by itself through its own self.
By means of those two cognitions alone, [there is no sublation] of the previously arisen cognition of silver.

Since some sublation has indeed occurred, how could the silver that was made the object of the previous cognition of silver be real? The meaning is that the relationship of the sublated and the sublator does not exist among cognitions alone, independent of a cognizer.

Having thus stated that the cognition of silver is sublated by the cognition of mother-of-pearl through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), he says the following in order to establish that even through inference (*anumāna*) there can be no subsequent sublation of either of the two cognitions without their both resting upon a single cognizer (*pramātṛ*):

Regarding the word *nanu*: "this" (*idam*) refers to the present shell (*śukti*), which, without a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) resting upon a single subject, brings to mind that previously experienced object of knowledge.
It means: "in that very same object where the cognition 'this is silver' occurred, [silver] does not exist now."

Two cognitions—“this is silver” and “this is mother-of-pearl”—have arisen as valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Because both of them are valid with respect to that very same object, it is inferred from this pair of cognitions that the prior cognition of silver is invalid. [This is because] the cognition of silver apprehends silver as its object...
Furthermore, it is simply not possible for a cognition apprehending mother-of-pearl as its object and a cognition apprehending silver as its object to occur with respect to one and the same object;
because two cognitions cannot exist regarding a single object,
there is an empirical sublation of the cognition of silver by the cognition of mother-of-pearl.

Anticipating this objection, he says: "The sublation of the cognition of silver by the cognition of mother-of-pearl is not established merely through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) via self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*); rather, it is not established even through inference (*anumāna*), because at the time of the cognition of mother-of-pearl, the subject (*dharmin*)—the prior awareness of silver—is not established."

In that subject (*dharmin*) which is the cognition of silver, the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*)— namely, invalidity— is established by means of reasons such as "because it is the cognition of mother-of-pearl," or "because it is the cognition that 'this is not silver,'" or "because the object [of the cognition] is that which is made the object of that very cognition. Wherever there is a cognition of silver, [there is invalidity].
In that case, since invalidity is established by self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), there is no sublation even by means of inference;
rather, it is established at that very moment through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) without any interval, as in the cognition "this is mother-of-pearl, not silver.
Furthermore, it is said to arise from a single cognizer when those two—the cognition of mother-of-pearl and the cognition of silver—come to rest within a single cognizer.

This cognition of mother-of-pearl, being of the nature of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), cannot establish a sublation (*bādha*) in the form: "The previous cognition of silver was a valid means of knowledge.
[Rather,] the subject (*dharmin*)—the prior cognition of silver—must possess the property (*dharma*) of invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*). Of that...

Now, regarding the subject (*dharmin*), which is the cognition of mother-of-pearl (*śuktikā-jñāna*): there are three reasons—namely, because it is a cognition of mother-of-pearl, or because it is a cognition [of something] that is not silver, or because it has as its object both [the shell and the silver]. Wherever there is such a cognition of mother-of-pearl with respect to an object, there is invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*). This is established by the word "also" (*api*) and by the logical pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason.

Since sublation (*bādhā*) is established even through inference from the proof [of the object], and since this sublation— namely, "this is mother-of-pearl, not silver"— is established at that very moment by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) without mediation,

it is logical that this sublation arises from a single cognizer (*pramātṛ*). Having stated that it arises from a single cognizer, [the text proceeds] regarding those two, the mother-of-pearl and the silver...

Because the two cognitions rest upon a single cognizer, sublation (bādha) is established in the form: "This cognition of mother-of-pearl is valid, whereas the previously existing cognition of silver was not valid.
The particle *api* is also to be understood as applying to both the reason (*hetu*) and the pervasion (*vyāpti*) in the case of inference.

"Here" means: when the subject (*dharmī*) exists in the world, the function of inference is the exclusion of the non-connection of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) with that subject, by means of a proven reason whose pervasion (*vyāpti*) is being recollected. In this case, regarding the inference stated by you, [the function is] the [exclusion of the non-connection of] the property to be proven with that subject.

The probans (*sādhaka-hetu*) for each respective property (*dharma*) consisting of validity is the cognition of mother-of-pearl and so forth. At that time— that is, at the time of the cognition of the mother-of-pearl—
because of the existence of the subject (*dharmin*), namely the cognition of silver which is to be attained, the [properties] of that subject, the cognition of silver, are present.

Properties such as the cognition of mother-of-pearl do not establish the probandum through the reason of being properties whose nature consists in the awareness of silver. Nor is it correct to say that the cognition of that form, when being remembered, would be the property-possessor (*dharmin*);
for even in that case, because it is not part of the subject (*pakṣa*), the probandum is not established. Now, as for the mother-of-pearl...

It is already established, and not something yet to be proven, that silver is not the object of the cognition of silver. If it is then argued that at the time of the cognition of silver, that cognition of silver has mother-of-pearl as its object, then the status of having that [mother-of-pearl] as its object would have to be established by the cognition of mother-of-pearl within the self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) of that prior cognition of silver, regarding whichever object [is intended].
Now, by whom has this pervasion been grasped—that at that time, another cognition was not previously present? Since the cognizer is not admitted [as a real entity], let there be no cognizer;
if it is argued that this stated pervasion was grasped by another inference, then for that too there would be a dependence on yet another inference.

This leads to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). By this, the argument that "two cognitions cannot exist because it is impossible to grasp the pervasion (*vyāpti*) without a single cognizer" is refuted. Who could know the identity of object between those two cognitions—the cognition of mother-of-pearl and the cognition of silver—since they arise merely from experiences occurring at two different times?
In that case, the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell would rest within its own nature as a ray of cognition and within its own object in the form of silver; thus, without a cognizer,
there is no mere cognition of the mother-of-pearl shell.

There is no sublation of the cognition of silver even by means of inference. In this context—regarding the sublation-cognition “this is not silver, this is mother-of-pearl”—no mediation such as the apprehension of pervasion (vyāpti), which is required for inference, is perceived; rather, it occurs through perception alone: “this is not silver, this is mother-of-pearl.”
Furthermore, it is impossible to say that sublation does not occur simply because [the cognition] appears immediately as established by its own experience;
for in this way, in the opponent's position, the relationship between the sublated and the sublator consists solely of the stream of cognitions (*jñānasantāna*).

Having thus demonstrated the inconsistency within the Buddhist position— which, according to the statement "The Sugatas [teach] reality," asserts that the self is merely a continuum of cognitions— he concludes his own position with the sentence "one single cognizer," stating: "If that sublation [occurs] from a single cognizer..."

In that case, it would follow that at that very moment, this cognition of mother-of-pearl is true and this cognition of silver is false; thus, it has been explained that the cognizer alone constructs even those conventional transactions consisting of the sublated and the sublator, just as he does with blue and other objects. This being the case—

Since it is established that "there is only one subject," this state of affairs constitutes the *anyathānupapatti* (the impossibility of being otherwise) for the practical establishment of the relationship between the sublated (*bādhyam*) and the sublator (*bādhakam*);
for if one does not accept the sublation of false knowledge by true knowledge, the relationship between the sublated and the sublator would be untenable.

If it is argued that "practical activity (vyavahāra) would be impossible," let that be as you wish; however, by now accepting a single cognizer (pramātṛ), everything— including the relationship between the sublated and the sublator, and the reality or unreality [of things]—
is established.

"Not merely" means that these conventional practices of remembering the causal relationship— consisting of perception and non-perception as described by the phrase "beginning with perception and non-perception"— which constitute the entire course of worldly life and common usage,
do not pertain solely to a single cognizer, but extend even to intermediate [entities].
Worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*)— whether impure ones such as buying and selling, or pure ones such as the relationship between teacher and student—

are all grounded solely in a single cognizing subject (*ekapramātṛ*). Thus, he concludes the chapter by stating that the proof for the synthesis of all worldly transactions is their resting within a single cognizing subject.
Thus it is said.

By the manner of logical justification consisting of positive and negative concomitance expressed in the two verses beginning with "tattadvibhinna," and likewise by the manner of illustrating conventional usage expressed in other verses beginning with "pratyakṣānupalambha," and so forth.

By means of the manner of illustrating worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) as also stated in other verses beginning with "perception and non-perception" (*pratyakṣānupalambha*), [the world] is inlaid with the manifestations of objects— ranging from reflections and conceptual constructions down to the earth and up to Śiva— which, through the power of *māyā*, are distinct from the knower and from one another.
Resting within the all-pervasive [Lord], who is untainted by any alteration of His essential nature and is unconditioned by space and time,
worldly transaction— whether characterized by impurity or purity— is experienced in the manner described.
Therefore, for those people,
their own experience alone is the firm proof that destroys [their doubt], such is the meaning.
"In this way" means that this too should be understood according to the manner stated in the verse beginning with *tattadvibhinna*.
In the Great Lord (Maheśvara), who is transcendent to the universe and unconditioned by space and time— and precisely because of this omnipresence—
he is veiled by Māyā through the power of which [entities] exist as non-different from him, since otherwise they would lack any resting place, being animated solely by duality.
All linguistic usage, which consists of verbal expression, rests upon that which is not colored by any alteration of its own nature;
it is experienced in such forms as "I experience," "I conceptualize," "I remember," and "I synthesize. Such is the nature of this experience.

This indeed is the most firm means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*): until, through the instructions of a true guru and by means of the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of one's own self as the Great Lord (*Maheśvara*),
everything appears within me alone with focused attention, like jars and other objects in a stainless mirror.

By means of that form and that attentiveness through which the state of worldly transaction—consisting of those teachings identified as "this"—is regarded as saṃsāra, that very state becomes the resting place of the reality of the subject (*pramātṛtattva*), whose nature is the manifestation of "I," the ground of Śiva. As it has been said: "The grasped and the grasper..."
By the words beginning with "consciousness" (*saṃvitti*), [it is meant that] for those for whom the succession of appearances has not been recognized as their own self and as the state of the Lord,
the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is a defiled worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), accompanied by the impurities such as the *āṇava* and others; whereas for others,
for whom that very ultimate reality has been recognized as their own self and as the Great Lord (*maheśvara*), that same [reality] is Śiva.
Because it manifests as its own essential nature, it is stainless; thus all is auspicious.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñāsūtravimarśinī*, the commentary.
Now begins the eighth chapter.
The realization of the perfected ones (*siddhas*)—
who have directly perceived their own essential nature as the Great Lord (*Maheśvara*), who have attained fullness,
and who possess the self-awareness that "I experience," "I conceptualize," "I remember," and "I synthesize"— is established.

By the force of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). Furthermore, for that which is perfectly established and accomplished from the very beginning as the manifestation of Maheśvara through one's own self-awareness in the form of the full *ahaṃtā* (I-consciousness)—namely, the worldly course of life consisting of the manifestation of all things according to one's own will—there is salutation, according to the principle stated as "namaḥ" (salutation). This is the worldly course of life.
