By the power or capacity of conventional usage regarding form— that is, by some means attained according to the stated principle— He is established as Maheśvara, characterized by speech due to the impossibility of otherwise accounting for such worldly activity; Him, thus proven, one recognizes in His own essential nature.
We praise Śiva. (p.

211) (272) Having established cognition, recollection, and exclusion through the fifth, fourth, and sixth chapters respectively, [the author] proceeds with the seventh chapter to show that these cannot exist without a single substratum.

It has been established that conventional usage—consisting of the relationship between cause and effect, the relationship between the sublated and the sublator, and so forth—is not tenable. By this much, through the examination of a single substratum (*ekāśraya*), that "oneness" which was mentioned in the sūtra *na cedantaḥkṛtā* is fully integrated; [it applies] only to those things that exist within [the same substratum].

"It functions through the external self. For the Lord is indeed the conscious self (*cidātman*), and because He is the master who identifies with His own self, this is so even in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). Thus, by supporting the internal manifestation as stated in the verse beginning with "In memory there is conceptualization" (*vikalpa*), the infinite forms of the universe are made internal.
Thus it has also been determined.

Regarding the phrase "in this very [context]": that which was stated in the sūtra *na ced antaḥkṛtaḥ* as "Maheśvara" must now be established as the sovereignty (*svātantrya*) whose nature is *māheśvarya*. Of Maheśvara...

Since its nature consists of the states of being the knower and the agent, its autonomy (*svātantrya*)— which, according to the stated principle, is of two kinds, pertaining both to cognition and to action— is,

by virtue of the non-manifestation of its own nature, essentially of the single form of consciousness (*citi*), whose essence is the fullness of "I-ness" (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*) and which consists of the awareness (*saṃvit*) characterized by light and reflective awareness (*prakāśavimarśa*).

Although [the Self] is indeed of the single nature of pure consciousness (*bodha*), nevertheless, for the purpose of explaining its ultimate reality (*pāramārthika-svarūpa*), the distinction between the object of knowledge (*jñāna-viṣaya*) and the object of action (*kriyā-viṣaya*) has been fashioned by that very Great Lord (*maheśvara*). Even at the time of perceiving a jar or other objects... [perceives] the jar.

One knows that "it is accompanied by action"; therein, the internal application of exertion (*saṃrambhayoga*) shines forth as the thought "I know. By means of this, the body attains the nature of consciousness (*citsvabhāvatā*). And according to the stated principle, that exertion is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), which is called the power of action (*kriyāśakti*); thus, even knowledge consists of action.

Although sovereignty, which has knowledge as its essence and action as its object, takes the form of the power of action within the domain of the section on action, it must nevertheless be determined within the section on knowledge itself,
because it falls within the domain of the section on knowledge. Thus, the meaning of the word [svātantrya] is not [to be understood] according to its primary etymological sense.

And it is determined through its conditions (*pratyaya*). (273) It is determined in its fullness and completeness through its nature (*prakṛti*), that is, through the essential nature of the knower, and through its conditions, that is, through the essential nature of the agent.
"Therein" means between knowledge and action. Knowledge is [the power] of the Lord who possesses the form of the universe.

The light that constitutes the three worlds in the form of absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), as well as its reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), are what are called "knowledge and action" according to the principle to be explained later; these two, though uncontracted, are [manifested] by the Great Lord himself through his own nature— that is, by his own freedom— by means of the power of *māyā*, and not from any other source distinct from the subject (*pramātṛ*).

When there is a differentiation of appearances such as blue, yellow, and so forth, which are contracted by space and time, one relies upon that [limited] consciousness; however, it does not exist there in the nature of knowledge itself (jñānasvarūpa), which is uncontracted by constraints.
This being the case, [it does not exist] in instances such as "I experience," "I conceptualize," or "I remember. (p. 212)
That very sovereignty which consists in the conjunction and disjunction of blue, yellow, and so forth, becomes the sovereignty that is the object of the Lord’s power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*).
This sovereignty itself is what is defined by the eleven verses beginning with "tātkālikā" (momentary). In that regard, [the first] daily lesson (*āhnika*)...

By the first verse, it is stated that the manifestation (*ābhāsa*) of blue, yellow, and so forth, at times during the illumination provided by the sun and other sources, depends upon another manifestation; that is, it depends upon the contemporaneous sensory perception (*akṣasāmakṣya*). "Otherwise" means that it does not depend upon contemporaneous sensory perception. Having said this, [the text continues] with the entities such as blue and yellow.

The second [verse] states that the manifestation (*bhāsa*) is one, being of a single nature and neither deficient nor excessive, whether it pertains to the immediate sensory perception (*tātkālikākṣasāmakṣya*) or to the non-sensory [mental] perception (*asāmakṣya*). This is because the manifestation of causal efficiency (*arthakriyābhāsa*), whether it be an external object such as blue produced by the external senses or an internal state such as pleasure produced by the internal sense (*antaḥkaraṇa*), is exactly the same; thus, just as with blue and so forth...

[The text explains] with two verses that [the subject] is dependent upon the immediate perception of the external senses (*akṣa*) and likewise dependent upon the immediate perception of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Regarding the verse beginning with "In one" (*ekasmin*):
between the states of being external and internal, there is the appearance of blue, yellow, and so forth as being external. Regarding the word "that" (*sā*): [it refers to that appearance].

The aforementioned nature of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is not "I. By means of two verses, [it is shown that] in the form of identity with the subject (*pramātṛaikya*), there is an internal manifestation (*antarābhāsa*). Because consciousness (*cinmaya*) is always variegated by internal manifestations such as blue, yellow, and so forth, even when there is an external manifestation, internality stands as its foundation; this is stated regarding blue and the rest by means of one verse.
The externality of the knower is described in a pair of verses through the division [of consciousness] into the internal organ and the external organs according to their own nature.
This is the withdrawal into the form of the single knower, who is the substratum of the powers of cognition, memory, and exclusion. (274)

Then, by means of the next verse, while concluding Maheśvarahood in the form of knowledge and action, an introduction to the section on action (kriyādhikāra) is also made within this very section on knowledge (jñānādhikāra); such is the summary meaning of this daily lesson (āhnika).

Now the meaning of the verse is being determined—starting with "nanu" (but surely). Therein, he presents an introductory objection in the form of a doubt in order to introduce the first two verses, beginning with "nanu" and so forth:
"In this way, within the all-pervasive [consciousness] which is inlaid with the appearance of objects that are extremely diverse, there is both the stained and the stainless..."

According to the principle thus stated, if every transaction (*vyavahāra*) of the aforementioned nature were grounded solely in the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), then the variety of worldly experience— well-known in its predominance of clarity and lack of clarity regarding such acts as "I see," "I will," "I imagine," "I remember," "I act," and "I speak"— would be untenable. By what [agency] is this transaction [accounted for]?

(p. 213) [This] is animated. We perceive that this very one, being of a single form and distinct from the Supreme Lord, is itself some reality whose nature is origination for worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).
Therefore, it is appropriate that the transaction resting upon that [reality] should likewise be of a single form, and not otherwise.

Anticipating the objection regarding this diversity, he states that the Supreme Lord’s sovereignty consists precisely in the production of that diversity: "Appearances"—such as blue, yellow, and so forth—occur in some cases, such as at the time of sunlight, depending solely upon the subject's immediate sensory perception at that moment; in other cases—

"At times when the light of the sun does not illuminate, such as in blinding darkness and the like"—this means "otherwise. They do not depend on the immediate perception of the senses at that moment; rather, [the cognition] occurs regarding blue, yellow, and so forth. "In the past"—this refers to those cognitions directed toward objects that are future, present, or past. "In some cases"—this means even in certain instances.

Regarding the existence of the appearance of objects such as blue or yellow within conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), there is no difference in their intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*). In all conceptual constructions, blue remains simply blue; there is neither deficiency nor excess in its intrinsic nature. "To this extent" means according to the manner that will be explained hereafter.

The distinction between clarity and lack of clarity belongs solely to the appearances of experience and so forth (275); it does not, however, pertain to the appearance of the object which constitutes the domain of those appearances of experience, for there is no distinction whatsoever within its own nature, even in any conceptual construction. Otherwise, you would not be yourself.

The connection between these two joined verses is as follows: that appearance of blue, yellow, and so forth, which manifests at a time conjoined with the light of the sun and other sources, exists at that very same time.
This is the direct perception (*pratyakṣatva*) of the external senses belonging to the subject (*pramātṛ*).

In certain conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), there arise appearances of blue, yellow, and so forth, which are mixed with that [consciousness], dependent upon it, and contingent upon the direct perception (*sākṣāt-karaṇa*) of those sense organs, such as when one thinks, "I see a knower.
In such a conceptualization, where there is the clear linguistic usage, "This is blue; this is yellow," [the appearance occurs] for one who is blind from birth.

For one who possesses [wrong] views and has become blind, there remains only darkness; however, that other conventional usage which exists therein consists of mere appearances. In that conventional usage, there is no dependence on the immediate sensory perception of the eyes as they actually are. He explains this very point as follows: "In that manner..."

By the words "hī" and so forth: for one who is blind from birth, there is no other semblance characterized by external sensory perception; however, for one who was previously sighted but has become blind, there is no external sensory perception [of that object]. In both cases, it is simply the former state.
They maintain that [the object] is perceived by the external senses. Therefore,
in the conceptual cognitions such as "I see" regarding the existence of the manifestation of the object in certain instances,
there would be no distinction in its own nature— consisting of blue, yellow, and so forth— in terms of deficiency or excess.

Furthermore, those conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) of yours that grasp objects—whether they refer to future things, reside in the present, or rest upon past things—should not be performed. For there is no distinction in the existence of the manifestation itself; it remains the same regardless.

In some places, he concludes what has been said with the words "this is what is meant" (*etaduktaṃ bhavati*) and so forth: in conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) such as "I see this blue," "I resolve," "I imagine," "I remember," "I act," or "I speak," this appearance of blue is, in its own nature, neither deficient nor excessive compared to yellow and other colors. (276)

In conceptual constructions such as "I see," these appearances of "I see" are additional to the knowledge [of the object] by virtue of their own nature; when the Blessed One, through his sovereignty, joins and separates those appearances of blue and so forth within those [constructions], then the conventional usage of the clarity and other qualities of the blue and so forth occurs.
He explains this very point with the words beginning "blue" (*nīlam*). When one perceives the manifestation as "blue" by means of the exclusion of other manifestations— thinking "I see"—
there is the conventional usage of "clarity" (*sphuṭatā*) upon the blending of manifestations, such as [the thought] "I shall see blue."
The occurrence of the diversity of linguistic conventions regarding the clear and unclear forms of both present and past time— as in "I saw blue"—

is established by the fact that even the manifestations of blue and so forth possess full subjectivity (*pūrṇāhantā*) when they are contained within the interior of the Supreme Lord, whose nature is full subjectivity.

Because it is of the nature of form (*rūpatva*), there is no exclusion from anything through conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Nor is there any confusion with any conceptualization, because they are complete and thus not within the domain of conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*). This diversity, consisting of clarity, lack of clarity, and so forth, is thus established in respect to blue and other such objects.

Where there is the operation of external senses such as the eyes with respect to blue and so forth, one might ask: "Since there is no operation of external senses with respect to pleasure and so forth, how can there be variety [of cognition]? Anticipating this, he states that there is indeed variety even in that case: "with respect to the objects of the internal organ—pleasure, pain, and delusion."

Even though objects such as garlands and sandalwood—which serve as causes for pleasure and so forth—are present, there is no stability [in pleasure], because pleasure itself perishes in its own nature and because it exists as past or future. Just as at the time of experience there arose the state of "I am experiencing pleasure," such a state does not persist; thus, it is called "happiness" (saukhyam).

The suffix -ya is used in the sense of the base word itself; thus, *saukhya* means simply "pleasure. When pleasure and so forth are intensely and repeatedly delineated within by an independent conceptualization (*svatantra-vikalpa*)—which, as stated in the verse, does not look toward direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) because such [perception] does not exist by its very nature—one remains established in the thought, "I am experiencing it in that way."
"Likewise" means that there arises the state of [the thought], "I am experiencing [this] in the manner described," because the intended configuration appears.
This is because this pleasure and so forth are clearly perceived— that is, seen— in proximity to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
Upon perceiving pleasure, its causes such as garlands and sandalwood, or pain, its causes such as snakes and thorns— whether past or future— the manifestation (*ābhāsa*) of that pleasure,

pain, and so forth, as well as the manifestation of their causes, remains the very same; thus, even when associated with the manifestations of pastness or futurity, it [the manifestation] is identical.

There is no loss of its essential nature (*svarūpa*). Nevertheless, even though there is no change in its essential nature, because it is intermingled with other appearances of its own form— such as "this is past" or "this is future"— in the form of pastness and futurity, [the object appears as such].
Because there is a delimitation [of the subject] from the appearance "I am experiencing," it is said "by that.
When those pleasures and so forth exist through association with the appearance of the past or future,
for that cognizer whose nature consists in the experience of pleasure and so forth, at the time of experiencing that pleasure and so forth—

The [notion] "I am now happy" or "I am suffering" is a false proclamation; for the causes of that happiness and so forth—such as garlands, sandalwood, and the like—are brought about just as they were previously established. Now, existence does not occur in that manner. Therefore, even regarding happiness and the rest, [the notion of self] is clearly [unfounded].
A variety of forms, such as vividness and so forth, certainly exists.

This cognizer, within his independent conceptualizations, intensely and repeatedly delineates those objects consisting of pleasure, pain, and their causes within himself. At that time, due to this repetition—

"Distinct" means that, as one repeatedly desires further excellence, there occurs an entry into a semblance of a cause called "highlighting" (*ullekha*)— which is the ground for the arising of pleasure and its causes— and which exists as such through the very process of being mixed with other appearances; thus, it is "in that very way," according to one's own intention.

By what we have stated—that there is an appearance of configuration—in the manner of "I am happy" and so forth, such a state of being exists; it does not exist in any other way. A state of being in that manner does not occur in mere conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*) alone, which is devoid of repose in the subject (*pramātṛ-viśrānti-śūnya*). [This refers to] pleasure and so forth as they are being delineated.
It is entirely appropriate for the counter-subject (*pratipramātṛ*) to abide in such forms as "I am happy.

At that time, when there is an intense manifestation, this subject (*pramātṛ*) enters into a state mixed with the appearance [of the object] by means of the flash of the thought "I experience the appearance of pleasure"; he perceives it within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and directly realizes it.

[He] acts. The mention of the "past" is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the "future. By saying "when [the object] is being intensely delineated," what is meant by this much of a meaning? Only this much is stated:
that the objects of the vital breath and the senses, such as sound and so forth, are the causes of pleasure and the like; they possess external forms.

Pleasures and the like produced by garlands and such are the causes of the various forms of self-identification in the cognizer, such as "I am happy"; in that regard, because of that very [fact], in the conceptual construction, the external garland and so forth lack external existence.
And if pleasure and so forth lacked that quality of being "seized" (*tajjittva*), then the expression "I am happy" and the like would not occur.
In that case, regarding independent conceptualization (*svatantra-vikalpa*), it is precisely this [that is meant]: garlands and the like, as well as pleasure and the like, do not exist at all.
And from that: because of the non-existence of objects such as garlands in those cases, [this applies] to the conceptualizations of things as if they were real (*bhūtavat-bhāvi-vikalpeṣu*).

It has been stated that there is no distinction in the manifestation of the object; how then can there be the existence of the manifestation of the object within that conceptual construction? Anticipating this objection, he clarifies here as well that the manifestations themselves reside within [the subject].

There is blue, there is pleasure, and "this is mine"—thus there is the manifestation of external and internal objects of the senses as positive existents; likewise, there is the manifestation of non-existents such as "even yellow does not exist" or "suffering does not exist.
Furthermore, externality and the state of being external function as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) merely by way of coloring [the consciousness].

—They [say]: "The jar is external... Just as that externality is not the self, which is their own essential nature (*svarūpa*), so too, because externality lacks the status of being an essential nature, according to the stated reasoning, there is always the existence of those very things which exist internally, as if situated within.

Regarding its own nature (*svarūpa*): [statements such as] "there is vigor," "there is no vigor," "there is suffering," "there is no friend," "there is no enemy," and so forth—those which are appearances of existence (*bhāvābhāsas*) and appearances of non-existence (*abhāvābhāsas*), their being external is not the essential nature of the Self (*ātmasvarūpa*). [For instance,] that which is called "pleasure" is cognizable by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

The nature of the self-essence does not appear as "external" in this physical form; rather, the very essence of pleasure is pleasure alone, and what is called "externality" is merely another manifestation appearing as pleasure.
By the power of His sovereignty, the Lord manifests externality within the manifestation of pleasure through a process of intermingling.

In the case of "the jar is external," externality is not the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of the jar. Rather, it is superimposed by the cognizer as a qualifier upon it—just as in expressions such as "the hand possesses a bracelet"—and thus appears as something mixed with it;
that is its externality at that time.

The appearance of pleasure (*sukhābhāsa*) undergoes the state of being an adjunct (*upādhi*), a coloring factor (*uparañjaka*), or a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), just as in the case of "Devadatta with a staff" (*daṇḍī devadattaḥ*). And from that—that is, from its becoming a qualifier—in the expression "blue lotus" (*nīlotpalam*), when the appearance of blue is absent, nothing occurs by way of its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*). [This is] like [the absence of] a king’s...

In the case of the term "person" (*puruṣa*), just as there is the appearance of a king within the state of being, so too, even though the appearance of pleasure does not exist externally, there is likewise an absence of the appearance of pain; for the appearance of a beloved, which is of the nature of pleasure,
there is no fading whatsoever in its own essential form— this applies only to internal appearances.
The perpetual existence of all things within the Lord who abides in the Self has already been explained previously by such statements as "within the self" and so forth.
[This refers to] those things appearing as reflections within the internal organ, which is like a mirror of the intellect (*buddhi*).

Blue and other [objects], which are related to the objects of the eyes and so forth, possess internality in relation to their externality; this is because they exist within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Therefore, it is precisely within that internal organ that [the cognition] "this is mine" arises for the knower.

Because they appear as distinct [from consciousness], externality also exists; thus, while there are two kinds of externality for blue and so forth, there is only one kind of externality for pleasure and the like. And here, in these two states—consisting of being objects of the internal organs and the external organs—these [objects] such as blue and so forth [function] in purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
Indeed, they perform functions externally in the form of bracelets, ornaments, and so forth, and internally in the form of pleasure and so forth; thus,

for the cognition of blue and the cognition of pleasure, their respective causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) consists precisely in being the instrument for those [objects], such that the cognition of blue has blue as its object and the cognition of pleasure has pleasure as its object.

Furthermore, regarding that internality characterized by identity with the subject whose nature is full *ahantā*, one might suspect that within such internality, these [objects] such as blue and so forth would perform some kind of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*); however, even such causal efficiency is [subject to] the aforementioned externality.

He states the nature of the objects of cognition (*vaninīlādi*): (280) Because these entities possess internality—which is caused by their identity with the subject consisting of full self-awareness (*pūrṇāhantā*)—and because they are thus composed of that full subject, no objective causal efficiency whatsoever belongs to them. This is the distinction regarding their causal efficiency.

This is based on differentiation (*bhedanibandhanā*). Therefore, from this basis of differentiation—differentiation being the distinctness of the jar from the cloth and so forth, as well as its distinctness from the cognizer—such differentiation does not exist even when the jar is internal; consequently, the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) associated with it does not occur. [This refers to] forms such as "this is my beloved," and so on.

Even though it is external, because of the difference in the manifestation of the causal efficiency consisting of joy related to its beloved, when another manifestation capable of embracing it disappears, she seems to "go far away"; and when another manifestation arises, she appears as something different, having a different form, and lacking joy.

The meaning is that the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) of entities is not restricted; thus, even causal efficiency is not the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of entities. If it were their essential nature, then in the absence of that causal efficiency, the entities themselves would also be non-existent. Regarding the phrase "in the unity of the cognizer" (*pramātraikye*): [this refers to] entities...
The internality of entities is caused by their identity with the subject whose nature is full I-consciousness; that is, they consist of the single essence of full I-consciousness.
For this reason—namely, because of such internality—there is no external causal efficacy for these things, whether in the form of bracelets and ornaments or in the form of internal joy and so forth.
The meaning is that causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) occurs when there is difference, being based upon that difference.

He establishes the nature of this difference: "That which appears as blue, being the cause of causal efficiency such as [producing] a bracelet and so forth, is distinct from that which appears as yellow. And "from that" means from that very difference.

It would perform for the cognizer—while making that blue appearance its object—the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) of his own goal, such as the ornament of a bracelet; yet at that time, this distinction does not exist in the state of internality. The reason for this is that [the blue] is that very appearance of blue.

Because of the identity of the subject (*pramātṛaikya*), that causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) belongs to the beloved and other such objects; for this very reason, it is considered to be the cause of delight. When that [identity] has receded—in the absence of the appearance of embracing and so forth—a different [efficiency] is perceived, one which is contrary to the previous delight. This is due to the identity of the subject.

(281) Since such a distinction in the manifestation of entities as being "thus" does not exist precisely within their internal nature, therefore even the manifestation of causal efficiency is not a separate manifestation like blue and so forth; thus, even the capacity for causal efficiency does not belong to entities.

It is their intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*). If it were their intrinsic nature, then in the absence of purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*), there would be the non-existence of things by virtue of their very nature. Therefore, the meaning is that purposeful activity is also the intrinsic nature of things.

Regarding the word "nanu": at the time when there is a mixing of the appearances of externality—such as "this is blue" or "this is yellow"—with respect to blue and other objects, [the subject] is... because it is opposed to externality, [it is] "severed"; thus, for internal [objects], that [externality] does not exist. As it has been said. How is that so? This is the objection.

He offers a rebuttal by stating that even the appearance of externality possesses an internal appearance; otherwise, their very "this-ness" would consist of light, for they are of the nature of being. Thus he says: "consisting of consciousness" (*cinmaya*). And as for the consciousness-nature of appearances, their abiding place is the light of the subject itself; this is the internal state.
Because of "externality"— that is, by relying on that externality manifested through the sovereign power of the appearance of separation from the subject and from other entities—
there certainly exists [this state] even for those things appearing as "this. Therefore, this [world] is of the nature of Light.
Since that [intermediate manifestation] also possesses externality, it is entirely logical to say that there is always the existence of other [manifestations] within it.
Here, the appearance of blue, yellow, and so forth as manifestations is always characterized by externality.

The state of those two absences also exists only within [the subject], which is the very abiding of the light of the knower; this is what is meant by "consisting of consciousness" (*cinmayatva*). For it has been stated that these [objects] consist of consciousness, otherwise they could not manifest at all. Since the light whose nature is manifestation is the object, the power of autonomy (*svātantrya-śakti*) which is the cause for the emergence of duality has been called *māyā*, and she is eternal.
When, by means of the power of Māyā whose nature is sovereignty, there occurs the manifestation of things as distinct from the subject and from one another; and when,
by means of the power of Māyā whose nature is sovereignty, there occurs the manifestation of externality in relation to the subject of Māyā.

When externality is manifested in relation to the subject (*pramātṛ*), then at that time, this state belonging to those things being perceived by relying upon that externality—though it is external, even though it has become external—is also internal; "even internally" means that even at that time it is internal. This [is what is meant].
The internal manifestation in the form of the light of the subject (*pramātṛ-prakāśa*) is not incompatible with externality;
on the contrary, it is the very foundation for the externality of all manifestations— including blue and the like— which reside within it, as well as for their qualifiers such as space and time.

p. 219) "That" means: because it has become a wall [of separation]. Since there is no appearance of externality, how could there be a contradiction with the internal appearance? Thus it is rightly said that internal things always exist.

Regarding the word "nanu": for blue and other such things, causal efficiency exists provided they possess externality; and that externality—namely, being perceivable by the external senses such as the eyes—is not possible for those objects which, though appearing in conceptual thought, are actually the domain of the internal organ.
Therefore, since these [entities] lack the quality of being perceivable by the external senses, how could they possess causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)?

Anticipating the objection that causal efficiency— such as the fear caused by demons— is observed even in the case of things delineated by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), [the author replies] that this is so for the subject (*pramātṛ*) even regarding those things delineated by conceptual construction within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

Because it appears as something separately constructed, its externality indeed exists; for this very reason, its causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) also exists—as he says: "in conceptual construction" (*vikalpe*).
This is the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the cognizer, which is the mental representation (*ullekha*) within a specific conceptual cognition.
Even an object such as a beloved or a thief, when being delineated, is external and distinct [from the subject].
This is because even in that case, it manifests within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as "this," appearing as separate from the cognizer.
"This" means it appears as distinct from the cognizer. Internality, moreover, consists in being of the nature of the full I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*).
Identity with the subject (*pramātṛ-ekātmya*). "From that" means: from that identity with the subject, whatever distinction or state of separateness exists, that alone is externality (*bāhyatā*).
"In reflective awareness" (*vamarśa*) means: in the form of a specific reflective awareness produced by the internal organ of the subject.

In conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*), that which is this "mental image" (*ullekha*)— this object such as a beloved woman or a thief being delineated according to one's desire— that too is an external image;
for it is not only an object perceived externally that is external and distinct, since even this [object] is being delineated.
Since this object (*padārtha*) manifests as something entirely distinct from the knower (*pramātṛ*), such that its state of resting within the knower as "I" alone constitutes its internality;
and since that which is "internal" is proximity relative to something else— [this being true] everywhere, whether in the case of blue, pleasure, or the like.
In the absence of an intermediate state dependent upon objects, that [object] has attained proximity through identity with the cognizer; therefore,
whatever is distinct and separate from that identity with the cognizer is indeed external— this is the meaning pertaining to the "mention" (ullekha), that is, the object being mentioned.

It is indeed connected with action. Now, [one might object]: "Let objects such as a jar, which reside within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), become external through the activity of a potter and the like;
however, what of that object which is being delineated [as an object] of the internal organ within that very internal organ?"

The externality of the cognizer has been established. Anticipating the question "By which cognizer was this done?", [the text explains that] objects such as jars—which are the objects of the external organs—and those things being delineated as objects of the internal organs, such as pleasure and so forth, are externally projected by the will of the Supreme Lord in each respective case; it is not, however, by a potter or the like.
He explains this through its function: "of the delineation" (p.

220). This refers to the external nature of blue and so forth—which is not being delineated within the internal organ by an independent conceptualization—as well as pleasure and so forth, which are produced by external garlands, sandalwood, and the like. [The text continues: "This is blue, this..."
"This is yellow," "this is suffering," "this is happiness"—such is the illusion for the subject.
In that regard, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is that externalized manifestation which exists as a distinct [entity] within it. Regarding the word "of the Lord" (*bhartuḥ*):
it refers to one who sustains the entire universe, from Śiva down to the earth, within his own essential nature consisting of consciousness; and therefore, from that very [source].

The meaning is as follows: just as by the will of the Lord who nourishes the external creation, there is the manifestation of the objects of the senses— such as the eyes and so forth— as well as of blue and other colors within their perceptual range, appearing in the form of direct perception as "this is external," even so [is the case here] through the will of the Sustainer (Bhartṛ).

This external manifestation is not like a jar or other objects produced by an illusory potter and such subjects, because even the potter and others are manifested solely through the will of the Supreme Lord. As he will say:

For instance: "In this way, the potter, by means of his sovereign power alone, produces a jar through a sequence of refinements applied to various clays and other materials. Regarding the word "internally": it refers to that which is reflected within Māyā, concealed by the subject.

Regarding that [blue and so forth] which is established as a reflection, the manifestation of it as "this is blue" or "this is yellow" in that very place by way of an external nature belongs to the Sustainer— that is, to the Lord (Īśvara), who sustains the internal manifestations from Śiva down to Earth and nourishes them in the form of an external creation.
By means of an illustration, he clarifies the very same point already stated regarding the will of Paramaśiva himself:

"Just as the direct cognitions of forms and other objects that have become dear [to the senses], such as 'this is blue' or 'this is yellow,' are denoted by the word 'perception' (pratyakṣajñāna) in relation to the eyes and other [senses]..."
Manifestation as an external self occurs solely through the will of the Supreme Lord.
Just as the manifestation of "this pot," "this sound," "this touch," and so forth, which appear external to the subject,
occurs by the will of the Supreme Lord, so too does the manifestation of that which is within the scope of the internal organ [appear] externally.
[The author] states the summarized meaning: "I am manifested by that [will]," meaning I am manifested by the will of the Supreme Lord.

From the initial ego-sense of "I shall create" down to the vibration of the internal organ and the body, the entire activity—such as that of a potter—is, in the ultimate sense, nothing other than the will of the Lord; even that activity is not distinct from Him. Furthermore, the heart [remains] non-conceptual and eternal.

"Towards making [them] go" (gamīkaraṇāya). And "therefore" (tataśca): and therefore, although blue and other objects do not exist outside of the light—which, by virtue of being manifest through the will of the Lord, is in ultimate reality the nature of the full I-consciousness (pūrṇāhantā)—they are nonetheless [perceived as such] through Māyā.
Objects that have become the domain of the cognizer’s external organs appear as external in the form of spatial separation.

Even those objects that have become the domain of that cognizer’s internal organ appear as external within that very internal organ solely by the will of the Lord; thus, [it is established] regarding the objects of the internal organ.
The meaning is that for objects of the external senses, there is no specific quality whatsoever that causes them to appear as external, other than the will of the Supreme Lord. Furthermore,
it is not the case that pleasure and other states— which are objects of the internal organ and are universally recognized by all people— are themselves external.

He explains this with the words "pleasure and pain": for the Bharatas, those states such as despondency (*nirveda*) and the like—which are described in the treatises on drama as consisting primarily of suffering—appear externally as if they were pleasure. Therefore, while this bliss of consciousness (*cidānanda*) exists, [there is no] suffering.

The eyes expand and become tremulous with tears of joy; by such signs as the expansion of the face, the nature of the bliss consisting of *rati* (pleasure) residing within can be inferred. Likewise, the *nirveda* (world-weariness) residing within is to be discerned by a withered face and eyes clouded by tears of sorrow.
As it has been said:
"The person who is dear to the Teacher shows the beauty of the instruments reflected in the face by means of the primary [sense] and the rest."

Regarding the phrase "in volitions": although it is the Māyā of the *kṣetrajña*— that is, the sovereignty of the subject alone— that serves as the cause for the mental representations (*ullekha*) of this or that beloved woman, elephant, and so forth within those volitions, nevertheless,
from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), there is the non-conscious ultimate reality (*acit-paramārthatā*) which is the cause of the agency of the universe.

Since it is impossible to cause [the body] to cease its activity, that autonomy—even though it pertains to the *kṣetrajña*—belongs in reality to the Lord alone. As stated by the author of the treatise himself:
"Even though the persistence of the object is constrained by the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the *puryaṣṭaka*..."
When dissolved in the individual soul (jīva), it likewise remains established there in the Supreme Self (paramātman).
"Then how could there be control over the vital breaths by that very [limited] self?
Thus, the existence of objects such as blue, pleasure, and so forth, occurs within one constrained by the body, the vital breaths, and the *puryaṣṭaka*.
Here, *puryaṣṭaka* refers to the intellect (*buddhi*); in the case of the individual subject (*jīva*) who is under the influence of *māyā*, it is *māyā* that constitutes the subjects.

"Even though it appears as if ceased, even there— (286)— in the living soul (*jīva*), having transcended the individual soul, she remains and finds rest in the Supreme Self, whose essential nature is full subjectivity (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*) and consists of consciousness. To that Self— that is, by means of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) which is her ultimate reality (*paramārtha-svarūpa*)— "
And how can there be restraint or obstruction of that Supreme Self by means of the differentiated body or the *puryaṣṭaka*? As it has been said:
"Even by means of the body and so forth, consciousness cannot be concealed."
If consciousness, which is its own very foundation, were to veil its own manifestation;
"Then what is the state of this dissolved body and so forth? What shines forth? [To this it is replied:

In that kingdom of the mind (*manorājya*), even for the knower of the field (*jñātṛ*) who does not desire it, by his own natural inclination and will, there occurs—within that very kingdom of the mind—a purely volitional [state] whose essence is the passing of time as it flows, and so on; [this belongs] to the Lord himself.

The activity is manifest because it proceeds even without [prior] desire. Therefore, the established conclusion (rāddhānta) is that for objects fashioned by volition— which exist within the internal organ— the very will of the Supreme Lord is the cause of their external manifestation.

Now, however, he concludes the previously mentioned unity of the subject (*pramātṛaikya*)—which is the single substratum for experience, memory, and exclusion—as well as this sovereignty (*māheśvarya*) spoken of in this context. "Conclusion" (*nigamana*) means the establishment of the matter proposed at the outset. "That" (*tat*) refers to that aforementioned [unity] of the previously experienced object and so forth.

For the reason stated in the previously cited text—that there is no unity among cognitions occurring at different times according to the logic already set forth—the worldly course of life, consisting of the worldly activities of rejection, acquisition, and so forth, would not be possible without the unity of the cognitions (saṃvid) such as perception and the rest, by way of their being of the nature of the knower. This is indeed observed. Therefore:

Thus, their identity is not difficult to establish. Why? Because that light, which is the root of those consciousnesses and is devoid of space, time, and so forth, is one due to its unity. That identity—that oneness—is the very unity of those consciousnesses; it is that single light alone. "These" [refers to] what follows now by way of logical proof.

Established as the nature of light, that one subject alone is the Great Lord (Maheśvara) by virtue of being composed of unconditioned reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), which is constant, non-deviating, and innate.
Reflective awareness itself belongs to the Great Lord, who takes delight in the play of creation and so forth within the pure [state], wherein duality [is absent].

Since knowledge and action pervade the entire aggregate of principles from Śiva down to the earth when free from the turbidity of *māyā*, the subject (*pramātā*) who possesses such reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is the Great Lord (*maheśvara*).

Indeed, lordship (*īśvaratva*) consists precisely in the possession of knowledge and action; therefore, even the subject under the influence of *māyā* is indeed the Lord, by virtue of possessing knowledge and action.
As it has been said:
"The Supreme Lord, while living, must act with knowledge;
for vision and action, as well as the states of existence and non-existence, are indeed the causes of sovereignty and insentience."
"Whoever is permeated by knowledge and action, all such a person is the Great Lord;
whatever appears by itself, that very thing is [the Absolute]—this is the unsurpassed vision."
"Whoever knows and acts upon this—whether god or man—is the Lord, the Master of the world.
This is the characteristic of sovereignty proclaimed by the ancient teachers.
According to the stated principle that "the nature of manifestation is such," reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) constitutes the very life-force of light.

Thus, in the supreme state (*parāvasthā*) whose nature is Śiva, within pure knowledge and action which consist of the form of full subjectivity (*pūrṇāhantā*), that very reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) exists. On page 223, in the intermediate state (*parāparāvasthā*) whose nature is the form of the venerable Sadāśiva-Īśvara,
it is "I am this, this is I"— the essential nature of which is the reflective awareness of subjectivity.
The pure state is another state within the impure; that very reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) exists in the realm of illusion (*māyāpada*).

The distinction is this: in the impure state, which manifests as "this" and operates primarily through the predominance of objective existence due to its connection with objects, there are cognition and action. This is so because of what was stated previously in the preceding text.
This refers to that which has been established as the object of knowledge (*prameya*). For this reason,

without the repose within a single cognizing subject (*pramātṛ*) through the unity of the experiences and cognitions of consciousness, worldly transactions such as "this is a jar," "this is a cloth and not a non-cloth," "it is a jar with [other things]," or "this is that very jar" would be impossible.

This worldly convention certainly exists through direct perception. Therefore, because such worldly conventions are possible, there is indeed a unity among those cognitions. Yet, this unity is difficult to establish.
The reason for this is that consciousness is said to be nothing other than the manifestation of jars, cloths, and so forth.

That manifestation whose nature is consciousness, which merely reflects the objects, arises solely through the power of the external object; by virtue of that outward orientation, the manifestation of blue is one thing and the manifestation of yellow is another, and thus its diversity as mutual forms appears.

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), because the light of consciousness (*saṃvidātmanaḥ prakāśasya*) possesses a nature that is all-pervading, eternal, and perfectly full, it is one due to the absence of any limitation regarding space, time, or form; thus, it rests within the internal fullness of the I-consciousness (*ahantā*). That is Light.
It is said that the subject (*pramātṛ*) is indeed the light (*prakāśa*).
Now, by means of the reasoning stated in the verse beginning with "tattadvibhinna" (distinct from each of those), it is established and certain:
the nature of this subject, characterized as light, is the form of "I" (*ahaṃ-rūpa*), and [the object] is attached to that.

Furthermore, when a crystal gem—which is insentient by nature—is colored by blue or other hues, its very self remains devoid of self-reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*). Rather, it is that which serves as the substratum for the powers of various experiences and so forth, such as: "I experience," "I conceptualize," "I remember," and "I synthesize."
Objects such as jars and cloths, which are the domains of consciousness—consisting of experiences and so forth—shine forth as being fixed within one's own nature (*svasvarūpa*).

Thus, even while reflecting upon jars, cloths, and the like that are mirrored within his own self, he remains in a state of constant awareness; therefore, he possesses the nature of *vimarśa* (reflective awareness). That is his nature of *vimarśa*.

At all times, this very state of uninterrupted self-reflection (*vimarśatā*) is embraced within [the Self], because it is filled with the entirety of the universe. For this very reason, due to the absence of orientation toward external objects, there is no orientation toward anything other [than the Self]. Therefore, with respect to an object distinct from itself...

The state of being whose sole wealth is bliss, resulting from the absence of desire—this very reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is the supreme sovereignty (*māheśvarya*) of this subject. That very sovereignty is the reflective awareness whose essence is the state of "I" (*ahambhāva*). It is precisely through this reflective awareness that the Lord's [activity] of emanation and so forth occurs.
"For one intent on play, it is I alone. In the pure state, knowledge and action are ultimate.
He states the ultimate nature of knowledge and action: "Knowledge is indeed 'I'."

The reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of Māyā is action (*kriyā*), arising from such sovereign freedom (*svātantrya*) as: "I am the creator in this very state of luminosity through the nature of luminosity; I am the sustainer, I am the destroyer, I am the concealed one, and I am the one who bestows grace. As it has been said:
"The Lord who is the agent of creation and destruction, the cause of dissolution and maintenance,
intent on bestowing grace, and the destroyer of the suffering of those who bow to him. Thus,
according to the stated principle that "that [consciousness] is reflective awareness (vimarśa), which is the Great Being (mahāsattā)," light (prakāśa) is internalized.

Even for luminosity, reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) itself is the state of rest; in the supreme state (*parāvasthā*) appropriate to Śiva, it takes the form of "I" alone. In the intermediate state (*parāparāvasthā*) appropriate to the venerable lords Sadāśiva and Īśvara, however, it takes the form "I am this, this is I. In the state of manifestation (*prakāśa*), reflective awareness alone constitutes knowledge and action.

In the state of Maya appropriate for the subject of limited cognition (māyā-pramātṛ), the reflective awareness whose nature is the self-awareness of "I" as being in grammatical coreferentiality with "this-ness" (idantā)— that very awareness, when existing in the secondary state at the level of Maya, operates primarily as objective existence ("this") due to its orientation toward the objects of manifestation such as "this is this."

"Knowledge and action" are indeed reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). In every way, knowledge is precisely this reflective awareness, occurring through the mode of its own self as the essence of knowledge, and through the mode of the object of knowledge as its form.
It has been stated that without such reflective awareness, this [consciousness] would be insentient, as in the passage: "Even though the light of the object is external... and so forth.

"Reflection itself, having become the means of valid knowledge (*jñāna-pramāṇa*), is action. By this demonstration of the essential nature of action, he provides an introduction in the form of a thematic connection for the forthcoming *Kriyādhikāra* within this very chapter. May there be auspiciousness!
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the *Vimarśinī* commentary on the *Pratyabhijñāsūtra*.
Thus ends the chapter on Knowledge;
now begins the ninth chapter, the chapter on Action.

(290) Since it has been stated that [the agent] is the knower (*jñātṛ*), the primacy of the section on action (*kriyā*) would logically follow. Likewise, [it is said]: "Knowledge and action belong to the elements. In that regard, since knowledge is self-established, both knowledge and action are indeed manifest. As it is said: "For the Lord, pure knowledge and action are nothing but reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)."
In each case, by means of the very method already stated,
one who perceives oneself and this [other] through their correct knowledge and action knows and accomplishes desired objects exactly as intended.

(p. 225) Furthermore, according to the principle stated in the concluding verse, the qualification for knowledge (*jñānādhikāra*)—which consists of the capacity of the knower’s power of cognition (*jñānaśakti*) and not its form—has been determined. Now, the qualification for action (*kriyādhikāra*), which is the very life-force of that qualification for knowledge, is determined—beginning with the words "vitata" and so forth. [This pertains to] everything from the earth up to Śiva.
Because it provides space for all things, it is "expanded" (vitata);
where the six paths are unified, there exists that state of Bhairavī.

According to the principle thus stated, the supreme covering (*paramāvaraṇa*) is the subtle impurity (*mala*), which consists of the expansion of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhva*) and provides space for the entire universe from earth up to Śiva; the gross [covering] is the external form consisting of the fivefold *māyā*.
According to the principle that the Self is indeed enveloped by three sheaths (*kośa*), it consists of five elements— namely *parā*, *rūpa*, *aṇava*, *mala*, and *māyā-kalā*—
which constitute its subtle form; this is inherently stainless because it is free from the gross impurities found within bodies such as those of *prakṛti*.
In the pure "mother-aspect" (*mātṛsvāṃśa*), which is capable of reflecting the expansion of the taught reality, there is the duality of the object of knowledge (*meyatā*);

thus, the Mother, who is Supreme Śiva himself, constitutes one shore. Because it shines forth therein, the object of knowledge (*prameya*)—the "own-aspect" extending down to the earth—is the other shore. In this way, [the Mother] is accompanied by these two vessels.

One's own self alone is the object of knowledge (*prameya*), consisting of the expansion (*prapañca*) of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the knower (*pramātṛ*). Therefore, it is called a "mirror" (*ādarśa*) because it displays [all things] everywhere as if they were reflections. Within that mirror of one's own self, [it perceives] its own power as radiant with essence; thus, the internal organ...

"By excluding the temporal sequence from oneself, you, being full of sovereign power, assume a state of independence. According to this principle, [the Goddess] is radiant within the universe with the essence of freedom consisting of exclusion; elsewhere, she is brilliant and ablaze with the quality of the nature of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).

Regarding the phrase "the ground of the manifold modes of existence" (*bahutarabhavadbhagībhūmim*): it refers to the manifold modes of existence (*bhangīnām*)—that is, the various ways of being—which range from Śiva down to all [lower levels], corresponding to the respective gradations of subjects (*pramātṛtāratamyānām*). Furthermore, it refers to the general relationship (*sambandhasāmānya*) of those [categories] which are about to be described.

For substances and so forth, as well as for cognitions of time, their relationship and the like constitute the "life-force" (prāṇabhūta) of the universal; it is precisely that which consists of the measurement and its fruit, having the nature of a determination.
This is the causal relation (kāryakāraṇatā), which is the very life-force of the relationship consisting in the state of the signified and the signifier.

And by the term "mode" (*bhaṅgī*), which consists of a relationship, [is meant] the ground— the locus of arising and resting— of that relationship characterized as cause and effect which precedes the state of the signified and the signifier; elsewhere, it refers to the ground of the many and more abundant waves of existence.

This wheel of power (śakticakra) of the Blessed Lords Bhairavanātha, having an uninterrupted continuity according to the stated principle, is indeed the river of action (kriyā) because it flows through all forms from Śiva down to the earth; it is that supreme and perfect [power], and not merely when Śiva and the others possess action.
The higher and lower, the full and the incomplete—Māyā is not [inherently] other than the activity of the subject; rather, it is incomplete.
He who manifests such a river, remaining as its agent, reveals it. By the use of the present tense, his agency as the revealer is shown to be uninterrupted.

This has been shown. He who possesses that supreme *śrī* (glory) consisting of omniscience, omnipotence, and so forth—he is the *Viśvaprakāśa*, the Lord of Gaurī, the Master of Parābhaṭṭārikā. For us, who are worthy of His grace, there is *ṛtam*—the supreme [reality] consisting of the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of one's own nature as the Lord.

May [the Lord] manifest the full ultimate reality that resides within; may He reveal it by means of the thorough withdrawal of the illusory power (*māyā-śakti*) which is considered to be the state of cessation; may He reveal it incessantly. Here, by means of the two words "yat" and "tat," the Supreme Lord is [described as being] unceasingly [active]. (292)
By means of these two forms of established renown (*prasiddhi*), the Teacher has indicated that his own self is solely intent upon self-reflection (*parāmarśa*).

Regarding the phrase "wherein" (*yatra*): therein, in the section on Action (*kriyādhikāra*), he praises the Supreme Lord, whose nature is the object of knowledge to be presented in the first daily lesson (*āhnika*), with the words "wherein. This is like the expression "lights, lights" (*tejāṃsi tejāṃsi*).
That which is the substratum for the powers of the first [case] and so forth is "that which is absolute.

By the statement "the agent is the knower," since agency alone is primary, even the power of knowledge is surpassed by the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*). "Having attained rest" means having reached its own substratum.

"Having attained the supreme, immovable state consisting of bliss within the Agent (kartṛ), and having reached fullness, it is 'wonderful' (acitram). It is 'wonderful' because it consists in the manifestation of the manifold world of objects of knowledge (prameya-prapañca) in various ways, corresponding to each respective subject (pramātṛ), beginning with Sadāśiva and ending with the Sakala."
"Consciousness alone is the supreme ground; it alone is the agent of emanation and the other [cosmic functions].

According to this stated principle, one should demonstrate that authority consisting of the fivefold activity, beginning with emanation and ending with grace. It demonstrates this incessantly, for it is the very locus of such power.

It is auspicious and of the nature of the highest good for the one who remembers it. Now, the section on knowledge (*jñānādhikāra*), which concerns the power of knowledge that serves as the reason for establishing the status of being a knower, is determined in detail; [and] its life-force is this very knowledge.

In order to determine the nature of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) by expanding upon it, another section, the *Kriyādhikāra*, is commenced. Therein, in the first chapter (*āhnika*), [it is shown that] because he is not limited by time, the Supreme Lord exists in a form that is non-successive;
thus, unlike the Supreme Lord as he is in the present moment of action, he is untouched by non-successive time.

Even though it is contracted by place and time and consists of mutually distinct illusory subjects within transmigratory existence, it is established as "possessing succession" because of its connection with the manifestation of a temporal sequence consisting of prior and posterior states;
such is the purport of these eight verses, just as [explained] in the *Jñānādhikāra*.

Indeed, the prima facie argument concerning the object of the power of knowledge—stated in the passage beginning with "nanu svalakṣaṇābhāsam" and ending with "caitanyam ajaḍā saivaṃ jāḍye nātmā prakāśate"—has been refuted. Likewise, by the first verse, [the objection regarding] the action of the object, such as the body and so forth, has been addressed. By that...

The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) concerning the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), as stated in the preceding section of the text on page 227— namely, that even the agent is imagined— is refuted. Then, by means of a verse, [it is shown that] the non-sequential nature (*akramatva*) of action in the Supreme Lord is due to *māyā*.

The distinction between succession and non-succession consists in [the fact that] for subjects there is non-succession, while for others there is succession. Regarding this, by means of two verses, [it is shown that] action possesses succession in terms of space, time, and form, whereas its non-succession—devoid of those—is present in the Supreme Lord; yet with respect to subjects under the influence of Māyā, it possesses succession.

The purport of this chapter is as follows: although there is a distinction between objects, the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*)— namely, the repose within the one Supreme Lord of both succession and non-succession— is established by means of this verse.

Now, the meaning of the verse is analyzed in sequence, beginning with "It is true, however... and ending with "...the reflective awareness itself is the Lord's pure power of knowledge and action. By means of this passage, the object of cognition (*prameya*) which is useful for establishing the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) is established.
By the very establishment of that [power], another object of knowledge (*prameya*) useful for supporting the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) is also established without effort;

this he shows with the first verse. "For this very reason" means: because it is useful for supporting the power of cognition (*jñānaśakti*), as stated in the present chapter (*āhnika*) in the passage beginning with "Truly, however... (*satyaṃ kintu*).
If the series of causal factors, which serve as the means for establishing the power of cognition,
does not constitute a single [unitary] action because it is successive, then a successive action cannot belong to a single entity— that is,
to that which is intended to be unitary.

Because the cognizer lacks unity due to being unconnected with [specific] place, time, and form; for this very reason, because of momentariness, and because that which resides here and there becomes this or that, and because that which is related to two [terms] possesses multiple forms— thus,
the refutation previously stated regarding the power of action and regarding the related entities also applies here.

This is rejected. For, in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), the oneness [of the subject] is established by the passage beginning with "if [the object] were not included within" and ending with "since the pure knowledge and action of the Lord consist in reflective awareness alone," which establishes that a single [entity], which is the nature of the knower and the substratum of the power of action of cognition, exists.
Now, regarding the passage beginning with "nanu svalakṣaṇābhāsam" and ending with "śarīrādyavasāyinī":

it has been stated immediately prior [in the verse beginning] "athānubhavavidhvaṃse" that there exist only cognitions in the form of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), and that there is no self (*ātman*) whatsoever that serves as their substratum.

Having refuted the position of the proponents of the self (*ātmavādin*) by means of the argument that the existence of some self must be admitted because otherwise memory would be inexplicable, [the author] then, with three verses beginning with "Even if there were a self" (294) and ending with "the rememberer is merely imagined as the seer," establishes that memory is accomplished solely from mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), and thus the self in the form of a seer is not established.

Regarding what was stated— that the self in the form of a knower is unestablished— it is argued in the verse beginning with "and cognition is of the nature of consciousness" that if cognition, like the self, is of the nature of consciousness, then why is it not eternal, just as the self is?

(228) If both the self and knowledge were eternal, there could be no relationship such as that of cause and effect between them. Furthermore, as for what was stated in the verse beginning with "athārthasya" regarding how knowledge—which is not of the nature of consciousness—could illuminate an object: [knowledge]...

To the Sāṃkhya who asserts that even an insentient entity becomes an illuminator of objects by receiving their reflections, [the author replies]: if knowledge, which is insentient in nature, were primarily the receiver of those various reflections, then it too would become essentially conscious like the Self and thus eternal.
In that regard as well, all the criticisms directed against the power of cognition on the grounds that there is no mutual relationship have been refuted.
If one asks, "Where were they refuted? [the answer is: in the section concerning mutual [dependence].

Because it has been demonstrated at length that separate experiences and so forth cannot be accounted for without their resting in a single cognizer, through a single chapter consisting of the determination of a single substratum;
therefore, that which was previously stated regarding this very point— that memory is established from latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) alone— remains as it was.

By the seven verses beginning with "dūṣayitum satyam" and ending with "jñānasmṛtyapohanaśaktimān," as well as by the previously mentioned passage, it has been stated that memory does not arise from latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) alone; rather, cognition is indeed non-inert, just like the Self, and possesses a contracted form.

Although his nature is uncontracted, due to the influence of the coloring by the objects of knowledge— which appear as external space and time through the sovereignty of his own consciousness— there occurs for him the manifestation of contraction; thus, by the power of Māyā, the All-pervasive Lord [appears so] only when the object of cognition is differentiated.

And in that regard, it has been shown by the passage beginning with "Since [the Lord] is Truth" and ending with "Because the very deliberation (*vimarśa*) of the Lord is His pure knowledge and action," as stated in the text. Therefore, from this collection of reasons,
there are merely objections in the form of refutations concerning the objects of the power of knowledge, and nothing else.

They have been refuted. (295) For this very reason, by means of the arguments consisting of the establishment of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), even those objections concerning the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) have been set aside according to the logic of the *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* (the established conclusion of the context).
This is also indicated by the word "api" [in the phrase] "if [action] were one," regarding the statement that action is also the effect of the object, such as the body and so forth.
How can it be successive? Now, if it is successive, how can it be one?
Since its substratum possesses a single nature, how can that substratum—which is endowed with moments of action characterized by different locations, times, and forms—be one? How can it be so?
Regarding the phrase "it might be" (*syāt*), the refutation directed at the capacity for action (*kriyā-śakti*) and its substratum—

which was stated starting from "situated therein" (*tatra sthitaḥ*) up to "the agent is also imagined" (*kartāpy akalpitaḥ*)— establishes the connection that there is no mutual relationship between cognition and action,
nor between cognition and the self whose nature is that of the cognizer. This is the connection [of the argument].

And as for that refutation which was stated regarding the object (*viṣaya*), that too refers to perception (*pratyakṣa*) itself. If one asks how so, it is because [the passage] beginning with "Indeed, in this much [it is] the appearance of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)" and ending with "therefore, even the agent is imagined," addresses the proponent of consciousness (*saṃvidvādin*).

(229) My dear friend, life itself consists in offering a counter-refutation: how could that which is one possess a manifold nature? To this it has been said: for a single entity whose nature is consciousness, just as in the case of a mirror, when its unity is realized, the appearance of the various manifestations from Śiva down to the earth becomes possible; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever.

The two objects, which appear as distinct from one another as the grasped and the grasper, are non-different from the cognizer; for even though a diversity of appearances in the form of the universe arises within him, there is no loss of his own essential nature. Thus, by the power of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), he alone is the Supreme Lord, the one who possesses the form of the universe.

To the extent that one accepts mutually contradictory things— such as the earth and other elements characterized by distinct natures— as existing together in a single place like heaven, those very contradictions, while manifesting, bring about that single manifestation as the locus of activity. And from that, [arises] the relation of cause and effect and so forth.
This means that the logical consistency of the relationship and other factors to be discussed is established. In this regard, the statement "What contradiction could there possibly be?
expresses the resolution of the objection regarding the consistency of the relationship and so forth.
[The Lord] desires the one supreme reality to assume manifold forms through His will.

"Thus it plays with the emergence and submergence of its own powers. In this way, the very nature of action (*kriyā*)—such as the movement of the sun and other celestial bodies—is precisely its sequential character (*kramikatva*), consisting of a succession of prior and posterior moments. (296) Of such an action, [the state] is *aruṇā*...

Following the manifestation [of the agent], there is the manifestation of arising; following that, the manifestation of joy and so forth. In such cases as "Caitra cooks," first there is the preparation of the hearth, and immediately thereafter the gathering of fuel and so forth.
Immediately following that, Caitra is understood through the sequence beginning with the installation of the fire and ending with the cooking of the rice;

thus, "sequentiality" consists in the form of casting forward the subsequent term immediately after casting forward the preceding term, and so forth— a process devoid of the reckoning of time such as past, present, and future.

Raising the doubt as to how there could be for this [Lord]— who is the Blessed One, the Lord of Beings— a sequential action related to the succession of time beginning with the elements, it is stated that even the possibility of such sequential action does not exist in Him, because He is devoid of sequential form.
He states that [this] occurs only in relation to Caitra, Maitra, and so forth: "The sequential nature of worldly actions such as going or cooking, which relate to Caitra, Maitra, and others,
[is derived] from the Supreme Lord, through His power of supreme vision, by means of the manifestation and dissolution of the aforementioned form."

It is possible; it is logically consistent because of a specific power (*śaktiviśeṣa*). "Eternal" (*śāśvatī*) means untouched by time, and for that very reason, constant. "Belonging to the Lord" (*prābhavyā*) means related to the Sovereign (*prabhu*). However, even that power of manifestation belongs to the Knower who is the Ruler; therefore, the distinction between the knower and the knowable appears as something manifested by Him.
According to the principle that will be explained, for an action whose nature is manifestation—being known by the omniscient knower—there would be no sovereignty, as in the case of a Lord;
since such a Lord is devoid of succession (akrama), even the possibility [of such an action] does not exist. [For example, one] raises the hand.
Immediately following that, it "casts down"; because it exists for only a moment through the nature of raising and lowering the hand, these moments possess a sequence of prior and posterior forms,
which constitute the non-cognitive action of worldly people.

For those who consider themselves possessors of some degree of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*), such as the Vaiśeṣikas, that action appears through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) itself, just like a jar or a cloth. Others, however, such as the Naiyāyikas and others, hold that it is "to be inferred" (*mantavya*);
likewise, [the Sāṃkhyas] hold that it is "perceived as such" (*tathābhūta*) in direct perception.
Consciousness (cit) is that which brings about the distinction of sequence in the forms of upward movement (utkṣepaṇa) and downward movement (avakṣepaṇa), consisting of prior and posterior states.

It is beyond the senses, yet it is the object of the senses such as the eyes; residing in the hands of Caitra, Maitra, and others, it takes the form of the awakening of activity consisting of upward and downward movements.

Like the sense organs, power (*śakti*) is eternally inferable; since it is that [power] which is the action (*kriyā*), its state of being a sequence of prior and posterior stages is also inferred. Thus, through the modes of perception and inference, worldly action possesses succession, and this is due to the power of time (*kāla-śakti*).

It is established that the manifestation of a distinct mass of clear light and so forth arises from the Supreme Lord—due to a specific power (*śakti*) consisting of the capacity to perceive the cessation of the manifestation of [colors] such as red and the appearance of [other] manifestations. This occurs in the case of a jar;
for that which belongs to the Lord (*prābhavī*), being inseparable from Him, is eternal like His own sovereignty.

Since the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) is untouched by time, there is not even the possibility that it possesses succession; the word "but" (*tu*) has the sense of "even. "Like the Lord" means: just as succession might be conceivable for the Lord because he lacks the sequence of time, so too is it inconceivable for her. As it has been said:
"Hi" [is used] in the sense that "he raises" and "he lowers"; here, because the hand possesses sequentiality (*krama*), the action residing therein is also sequential.
As for "nanu": it was stated [previously] that this is due to the power of time (*kāla-śakti*); now, [the question arises regarding] things that possess time.

By assuming the status of a qualifier in such forms as "this body is mine" and so forth, it delimits those entities—such as the elements and the like—in their own specific form at each respective moment, [determining that they] have been, are, or will be. This delimitation consists in the fact that the entity cannot endure the intrusion of any other time; this is its qualification.
Since time is a qualifier residing in the qualificand, time is not perceived apart from the qualificand; therefore,
having raised the doubt as to what this so-called "time" is, the very nature of time [is explained].
To define it, he says: "Time. Time is the movement of the sun, the moon, and so forth.

By becoming the various seasons such as spring and the rest, it is the cause of the birth of those respective objects of the sense organs—such as the fragrance of mangoes and jasmine—and of fruits such as the jackfruit.

(298) Alternatively, time (*kāla*) is perceived through cold and heat, which are apprehended by the tactile faculty (*sparśendriya*). In reality (*tattvataḥ*), from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthataḥ*), time—characterized by the movement of the sun and consisting of the forms of "prior" and "subsequent"—is itself sequence (*krama*); and sequence itself is time. The particle *eva* ("itself") is placed out of its syntactic order (*bhinnakrama*). As it has been said:
The sun is known to have set by the birds settling down, the lotuses closing, and the jasmine flowers blooming.

Those which are determined by their extent are as follows: the moon’s transit through one zodiac sign, such as Aries, takes slightly more than two days; the sun’s transit through one sign takes one month; and Mars’ transit through one sign takes forty-three days.

Bṛhaspati moves through one zodiac sign in one year; Budha and Śukra move through one zodiac sign in twenty-five days; and Śani moves through one in two and a half years. For flowers and fruits, the period lasts for only two months, corresponding to their respective seasons.

The measure of the six seasons, consisting of cold and heat respectively, is established by way of their extent: the moon and the sun, the mango and the jasmine, and the *kuṭaja*—these are the manifestations that constitute the very essence of the playful display of the supreme seasons of cold and heat.
These appearances are established; they alone are time. If one asks how this is so—it is because [time] is not otherwise established.

Even by means of movements such as walking and reciting, or by the movements of the sun and other celestial bodies, [the world] remains unestablished and devoid of finality; for example, Devadatta walked ten yojanas in a day,
recited a thousand verses of a treatise in a day, and wrote three thousand verses of a treatise in a single day and night.

That which is measured by her as "a hundred *niṣkas* of gold" or "a thousand *niṣkas* of gold" through the use of weights and measures is, in ultimate reality, merely a specific movement of the sun, moon, and so forth; thus, sequence is indeed time, and time is indeed sequence.
The particle *eva* (only/just) is to be applied separately and in a different order [in the following analysis]: even though these two appearances— the jar and the cloth—

are manifest as simultaneous at the present moment, they are nonetheless sequential when compared to the appearances of other jars, cloths, and so forth, which were permeated by a different time [the past].
"This jar was made long ago by Time," "this jar was produced recently," "now this fruit has ripened recently," or "this has ripened after a long time"— even in such notions of duration and brevity,
