there exists only a distinction in the manifestation of a sequence consisting of prior and posterior states, determined by the extent of its expansion or non-expansion.

Succession (*krama*) consists in the non-manifestation of one thing while another is being manifested. Since, while the cognition of the long duration of a crystal is present, there is at that very moment no cognition of its short duration, the cognitions of "long," "quick," and so forth, are also simply succession. The notion of priority (*paratva*) related to time has been experienced.

Because it qualifies a specific object, the cognition of "otherness" is clear; because it qualifies a future object, it is unclear in that very same case. Thus, in this sequence, Devadatta—who stands in the place of gold—is measured by means such as the movement of the sun, which acts like a scale-pan.

The distinction regarding the appearance of the form of going is stated thus: "He goes for a day. The accusative case is used here according to the rule *kālādhvanor atyantasamyoge*. An action such as going, which is not yet completed by Devadatta, is brought to completion in this way by time alone.

Regarding the word "nanu": since [time] is perceived as residing in various states—such as "this is the present time" or "that was the past time"—just like hardness and other qualities reside in their respective substrates, let time be of the very nature of those states themselves; for apart from those specific states, there is no such thing as "time."

Nothing [independent] exists. Because it lacks inherent stability by its very nature, he says that time is not merely a distinction within the intrinsic nature of entities: "That sequence which consists of prior and posterior forms is the locus of difference; for 'difference' is defined as the exclusion of mutual appearance."
At that time, the flashing forth of multiple individual appearances makes their difference manifest.

Furthermore, this difference exists because the collection of [qualities] such as redness, existence, and so forth, is non-existent [in isolation]. And the variegated appearance is produced by the existence and non-existence of those two appearances.

The concealment of the Lord’s true nature occurs through manifestation from the Supreme Lord Himself, who is by nature the source of all power. This so-called "wondrously manifesting nature" of the Lord refers to each individual manifestation that appears within His own self as a distinct, integral flash of light.

The capacity to apply specific attributes— such as "this jar is high" or "this is firm"— through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) consists in establishing them within its own self as distinct entities, due to the absence of any appearance of mutual contact between the appearances of the jar and the appearance of the cloth. As it has been said:
"Purchase is that which consists of space and time and is the life-breath of the distinctions of cognitions;

from its division comes this manifold appearance for the knower. Thus, if time were essentially sequential and existence were merely the state of being one's own nature, then [it would be like] a finger.
Since the four [states] differ from one another in their nature as short and long, a single finger would have to possess different natures at different times;
therefore, it is not merely a difference of time and nature. What, then, is the nature of time?

If one asks, "Of what kind? he says: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). Because time has no existence as an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), there is the non-existence of the state of being red and the non-existence of the mass of light that clearly manifests the state of being.
Thus, it is based on that distinction which is animated by the existence of these appearances; therefore, it is produced by that distinction.

The sequence is the nature of time. This is what is meant: for time is the sequence that consists of the manifestation and non-manifestation of entities, and it is the delimiting factor. These two—existence and non-existence—are manifested by means of that which is external to light, eternally inferable, and causeless.

In such passages as "The object intended as a reflection is not produced by an external thing; for God is indeed the consciousness-self," "The [powers] of the Lord abide in His own self," "This [world] is known as the Self alone," and "Entities are the manifestations of non-entities," it is stated that manifestations consist of consciousness (*cinmayatva*).

It has been explained in detail that the Self, whose nature is consciousness, is the sovereign and powerful creator who fashions the various appearances of elephants, horses, and so forth in dreams and in mental constructs;
for He is known as such because He abides as the very self of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
This is established by one's own experience (*svānubhavasiddha*). "From that very [source]" means that those two arise from that very Lord.

For this very reason, as previously stated, having embraced within His own nature another object of a non-differentiated form, He manifests some particular object as emerging from His own nature, while still maintaining it within Himself.
By means of that [power of] Nīti, that Lord— like the emerging and submerging of blue and other colors—

having grasped within Himself another appearance consisting of a mass of manifest light and so forth as a temporal manifestation without distinction, that Lord, from Śiva down to the earth, causes each individual appearance, such as red and so on, to emerge.

Because it provides space for everything, it is like the sky; by its own will, it withdraws the universe into its own self according to the principle that "it swallows" (*nīla*). Thus, while manifesting appearances such as blue and so forth, it shines there even in a variegated manner, that is, in manifold forms. He clarifies this very production of variegation:

Taking as its locus the manifestation of a jar appearing within its own self, it manifests that very [self] as having the manifestations of redness, solidity, height, and so forth— as those respective universal manifestations— acting as their qualifying attributes. Furthermore, within that very same self, like the surface of a mirror...
Just as the appearance of mutual contact and the appearance of a cloth manifest separately within that which consists of consciousness,

so too this appearance of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) regarding redness and so forth, as well as the appearance of mutually distinct objects such as jars and cloths, [manifest] without internal separation due to the identity of the subject (*pramātṛaikya*), according to the principle already stated.

He manifests [objects] within his own self—which consists of identity with the subject—in a single flavor. In that case, within this manifestation of identity, there is no relation of qualifier and qualified among the manifestations, nor is there any appearance of separateness, because they shine forth as identical with his own self. Immediately following this, through the variety of forms...

Thus, the sequence of space (*deśakrama*) which is about to be described is indicated right here; for even the sequence of space depends upon the sequence of time that serves as its own qualification. This occurs within the manifestation of the light of vision (*dṛktvābhāsa*), which consists of a state of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) such as "this much," and which pertains to manifestations such as pots, cloths, and so forth.
There would be no arising of temporal succession based on a distinction created by the unreality of appearances.

He states the ultimate nature of temporal succession: "But when [the mind] causes the appearance of autumn to appear as the appearance of winter—by being entirely devoid of its properties such as coldness and so forth—"

In the same way, when the winter season makes the light appear as empty through the appearance of autumn, then the sequence consisting of the nature of those respective times arises; thus it expands upward. This is the power of the Blessed One for the manifestation of the variety of appearances such as autumn and so forth.
The power of time (*kāla-śakti*) is said to be that which is related [to it]. Furthermore, in the explanation of this "intuition" (*pratibhā*),

the sequence— consisting of succession, simultaneity, and so forth— of entities, which is fashioned by the powers of space and time that are forms of the Lord’s sovereignty (*īśvara-svātantrya*) to be described hereafter, is space and time.

Regarding what was called "succession" (*paripāṭī*), it refers to the sequence of space and time, which is to be understood in this very chapter. As it has been said: "Heaven and earth are space; day and night are time. The expansion of these two consists in the manifestation and concealment of the power of the multitude of entities."
This clarifies the indication that the Blessed One alone is the projector of diverse appearances:

Is this Lord the house, the courtyard, and so forth, of objects such as trees situated on the ground—which serves as their support—or the trunk, branches, and feet? Or is He the house, the courtyard, and so forth, of Caitra, Maitra, pots, cloths, and the like? [He is the source of all these.]
Through the variety of forms such as broad bases and bellies, it manifests spatial succession (299) and incessantly reveals it—
by the power of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) that "this is that very [deity]," because there is no diversity [in the ultimate sense],
even though each possesses a single nature, due to the differentiation of actions such as birth, existence, transformation, and so forth.
He also manifests even the succession of time, which bestows various and distinct forms, solely by virtue of His sovereignty.
As it has been said:
"External differentiation is created in two ways: through action and likewise through form."
The sky is beyond in terms of space.
And he will state that it is that very [consciousness] which creates space and time, just like blue and other objects: "In the absence of space and time,
it bestows the state of being a particular mode of presence— characterized by the refutation of all-pervasiveness and eternity which are the causes for having a universal form."

The "own form" (*svam svarūpam*) of a category such as time is its "body" (*mūrti*); [the author] now demonstrates that very diversity (*vaicitrya*) belonging to that incorporeal [time], which consists of its various divisions.
On a single floor, first there is the floor itself, and then, distinct from the floor, there is the house.

The courtyard is one thing, the house another, the marketplace another, and the forest yet another; all these are distinct from that which is manifested by the Supreme Lord. Therefore, due to this diversity of houses and so forth, the forest is far from the house, and the courtyard is far from the house; the forest is far from the house.
"Extended" [refers to] the courtyard and so forth, while "unextended" [refers to] what is beyond;
thus, on page 235, the Lord manifests a sequence of being extended or unextended at a distance or nearby.
However, when this very same single ground is perceived as manifold and diverse in the form of houses, courtyards, and so on—

"It is divided, yet it is 'the ground' (bhūmiḥ)"—due to the force of intense recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), there is no difference in the form (*mūrti*) nor any diversity. Now, as for "and so forth" (*atha ca*): because of the absence of diversity, even though an object such as the ground possesses a single nature, in each individual form [one thinks], "this too is the ground."

When one form appears as another, although it is non-existent— meaning unmanifest and even illogical— due to the contradiction between unity and multiplicity, it is called "action" (*kriyā*) because it arises through the sovereign freedom of the Lord (*īśvara*). Of this action, there is swiftness, slowness, limitation, and lack of limitation.

That which is the manifold variety consisting of form— [determining] that "this will happen quickly" and "this will not bear fruit for a long time"— is the nature of Time (*kāla-rūpa*), which manifests by means of a continuous, uniform, and uninterrupted synthesis (*anusaṃdhāna*) based on the constraints of the accomplishment of results as they are conceived according to one's desire.

It manifests the succession; you should not say, "How can one thing have another form? If you ask why, it is because this entity, which possesses both singular and manifold forms, does not arise by itself independently of consciousness. [This applies] to that which has a singular nature.

How is it that there is no other form? That entity which is conceptualized by you in this way is indeed consciousness alone, manifesting with a nature of both unity and multiplicity. This very manifestation as unity and multiplicity is its sovereignty. Since unity and multiplicity are mutually contradictory in their appearance, [some might argue] that nothing [can exist].
It prevails. Because of the mutual contradiction between pleasure, pain, and so forth, nothing else prevails.
This mutual contradiction between pleasure, pain, and so forth is produced solely from the manifestation of what has arisen in another;
just as there is the manifestation of pleasure, the manifestation of their contradiction is likewise produced by that very same [consciousness]. It is because they manifest in such a way.

Regarding the term *bhāva*: the manifestation (*bhāsa*) of pleasure as having the nature of pleasure is its *bhāva*; likewise, the manifestation of pain as having the nature of pain is its *bhāva*. This very [manifestation] constitutes the nature of contradiction. Regarding the word *etad* ("this"): it refers to the manifestation of mutual forms within each individual essential nature (*svarūpa*), even though this is not explicitly stated in the Sūtra.
This has been shown by the word "sound" and by the word "Lord.
Now, as for the phrase "in this way": the Lord manifests the spatial form and sequence of a single entity—the nature of the ground—as a variety of things, such as a house, a courtyard, and so forth.

In that very [consciousness], by means of the manifestation of the variety of actions, it causes the succession of time to appear; according to the manner thus described, the succession of time and space must exist solely through the objects of manifestations such as a jar,
while the subject (pramātṛ) is non-manifested, not being of the nature of an object of knowledge (prameya) consisting of manifestation like a jar.
It is not so.

That cognizer does not appear as "this" (idantayā) to anyone, like a jar, because he possesses the nature of the "I" (ahantā) within his own self; for it is from that very cognizer that all objects of cognition (prameya) manifest. Therefore, he...

The meaning is that the cognizer (*pramātā*) never appears as "this" (*idantayā*) to anyone. And therefore: since those two—temporal and spatial succession—are objects of manifestation in the form of the cognizable (*prameya*), those temporal and spatial successions [do not apply] to the cognizer; for [the cognizer thinks], "I was, I am, I shall be," or "I stay in the house, [I stay] in the forest."

"How can it be seen that 'I stand in the temple'? For in that case, there is no possibility whatsoever of a sequence of time and space. Furthermore, since the void itself possesses the sequence of space and time, and because it is itself all-pervasive, from every side...

Because it is said [to be such], blue, yellow, and so forth are devoid of the sequence of space and time as previously defined; they are neither distant nor near. Since time itself is its own illuminator, what object distinct from it could exist—whether characterized by that time—as present, past, or future? Thus, it is complete.

Depending upon the cognizer, even within his own self, such things as distance created by the sequence of space and time, or states such as being past and so forth, are not possible. This is what is meant: this very nature of the sequence of space and time does not occur within the ultimate cognizer (*paramārtha-pramātṛ*), who is full of the universe and manifest as the universe from every side.
However, in order to establish that [the property of] being limited to a specific location and so forth applies only to cognizing subjects (*pramātṛ*), he says:

"everywhere" (*sarvatra*). This refers to that which consists of a collection of multiple universals (*sāmānya*), appearing as individual forms through the nature of particularity (*svalakṣaṇa*), and as various forms consisting of respective universals such as gold and the like.

Even regarding entities (*bhāva*), this temporal sequence—which exists in the form of "past" and so forth—is its *ākāra*, meaning its ground of origination. This has been demonstrated in the verse: "Difference, though based on the non-difference of sequence, appears as both existent and non-existent" (302). Of the one...
The differentiation of appearances—

such as "I am weak," "I am strong," "I am happy," "I am suffering," or "I am empty"— which is produced by the existence of one thing and the non-existence of another, and which possesses the form of temporal succession, [is so called] because the state of valid cognition (*pramā*) is fragmented.
This refers to the state of the cognizer beginning with the "weak" (durbala) and so forth; when there is the manifestation [of the Self], even the status of the cognizer as "I am gross" is severed.

Thus, for that which has a fragmented appearance—such as the void, the vital breath, the intellect, and so on—there occurs [this state]. Regarding the phrase "of that which has manifested once": [it refers to] the fragmented... gross.

One conceives within one's own self in such forms as "I am the form of the bodily appearance" or "I become the form of the bodily appearance," and so forth. Furthermore, if there were no possibility even of a distinction in that appearance, then [the same would apply] to related entities as well, just as in the case of one's own self.

There exists a distinction in manifestation characterized by temporal succession, such as: "I who was a child [am now] accompanied by the manifestation of a jar and so forth," even within the objects of one's own senses.

(237) According to the principle stated as "O Lord, when the body is entirely filled with the essence of the nectar of consciousness, there is no affliction," and according to the principle to be stated later— "The subject is called the Lord (pati) with respect to gross objects"—
because those objects manifest as being limbs (*aṅga*) of him.
For the limited subject whose nature has been described, spatial succession— just like temporal succession—
does not exist within his own self in such forms as "I stay here" or "I stay there.
From his own perspective, this object exists as being "far" or "near," yet even regarding these objects, [this distinction] appears only through the light of consciousness.

However, because the entities of the limited cognizer (*pramātṛ*) manifest from all sides as his own self—that is, through the state of "I" (*ahaṃbhāva*)—the meaning is that they manifest as his very own self, which is full, precisely by virtue of being the non-self. The particle *tu* (however) indicates this specific kind of manifestation. This [is stated] in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā-vivṛti-vimarśinī* composed by Śrī Kṣemarāja.

Recognition has been shown in the *Hṛdaya*: "The manifestations of the Lord, whose sole body is light, are as if transcended, because they lack the nature of being solely light. Regarding the word "everywhere":
in all things, whether their nature is one or many, they are of a single form by virtue of having the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their essence.

This temporal succession, manifesting as "this was past," "this is present," and "this is future" within various forms such as gold and the like— which are not of a single nature due to their commonality—
is the very form of that succession which is the basis for origination; thus, succession rests upon difference, and difference, too, [rests upon it].
"And regarding the existence or non-existence of appearances, [it is] due to the Lord’s creation of variegated appearances"—this has been explained in this sūtra.

As for the phrase "of the appearance": the distinction caused by the presence or absence of autumn and so forth—meaning the distinction produced by the presence of autumn and the absence of winter—is devoid of temporal succession and free from any differentiation within the appearance itself.

It is possible that [the state] arises for the subject (pramātṛ) consisting of the means of knowledge (pramāṇa), cognition (buddhi), the body, and so forth. First, the supreme subject (parapramātṛ) is of undivided manifestation; because of [the power of] knowledge (vidyā), there is divided manifestation, yet for that subject of divided manifestation, there is no appearance such as "I am empty."
The manifestation of that subject—the manifestation consisting of consciousness—is not its innate nature.
Because it would otherwise be insentient like blue and other objects, the manifestation of this subject is simply the flashing forth of consciousness;
[the text] explains the very fragmentation of that manifestation: "When that manifestation of this subject..."

Just as when one is asleep there is no appearance of "I am empty" regarding the body in the state of the emptiness of the subject (*pramātṛ*), so too, while that subject remains within the course of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra-yātrā*), there is no such manifestation as "I am empty," "I am weak," or "I am defiled. Thus, [the connection] is severed.

In that subject, such as the void and so forth, there exists a temporal sequence produced by the presence or absence of appearances in the form described above. He demonstrates this very point: "I, who previously had the appearance of a child's body, now exist in the form of the appearance of a youth's body," and so on with the void and the rest. (p. 238)

Since the cognizer (pramātā) arises from the immersion into the state of "I am full" (paripūrṇāhaṃbhāva), therefore that state of being full is, by virtue of being the reality of the cognizer whose nature is immersion into one's own essence,
characterized by an intensified temporal sequence even with respect to objective entities, just as it is within one's own self.

It manifests the succession of time. By the reasoning that "I who was a child—the manifestation of the jar coexisting with that [childhood]—also existed," all is manifested simultaneously (*sakṛdvibhāta*). Through this method—that the cognizer, whose nature is consciousness, is manifesting incessantly—it follows that he does not possess the succession of time.

For him, even though existence has arisen within his own self in relation to that [object], it does not truly exist [as separate]. Because that state of being an object of knowledge appears there, within the subject, as non-different from him and as his own limb (*svāṅga*), this is the meaning of the single verse.
Thus, for the limited subject, even regarding objects within his own self, there exists the succession of time.

Having established that for the unlimited (aparimita) there is no [temporal sequence] within itself nor even among objects, he states— “In this way, spatial sequence as well”— that spatial sequence belongs only to the limited subject (*pramātṛ*) regarding its objects, but not to the unlimited one, neither within itself nor regarding its objects.

Regarding the phrase "due to the variety of forms" and so forth: even the aforementioned spatial sequence belongs to the limited subject—consisting of the void, vital breath, intellect, and body—who experiences within his own self the thought, "I stand here in a temple," or "I stand there in a forest. Whatever is an object of knowledge (*vedya*) relative to himself appears thus.
Through my conjunction, by way of proximity, [the space] extends; that which is near is one thing, while the other is distant.
Thus, even among objective entities, there is a spatial sequence.

However, in the case of the nature of consciousness—which has set aside its own limited form, is devoid of such [spatial] limitation, and is full of the universe from Śiva down to the earth—the objective entities exist as its very self.
Because they shine with the sense of "I" according to the principle stated as "I am this," they are therefore full;

for in their unlimited essential nature (*svarūpa*), they possess the measure of the fullness of the state of "I-ness. The reason for this is that the immeasurable Self is of such a nature—that it possesses the measure of fullness within its unlimited essential nature. Thus, it is unlimited.

When, through the self-restrained self, these very selves shine as one with his own self— this immeasurable reality of the subjects (pramātṛ-tattva)— then all things within that reality, which previously appeared in the form of distinct bodies such as "this is the house" and "that is the courtyard," [are unified] through the activity consisting of the movement of the sun and other celestial bodies, and through the time produced by that activity.

An object such as blue or yellow is complete in every respect because, by virtue of being composed of consciousness (*saṃvinmaya*), each single object possesses the nature of all things, just like consciousness itself. Here, in the context of the discussion on action (*kriyā*), the temporal sequence is relevant because, in this section defining the power of action, [the object] consists of the unfolding of action; therefore, it is mentioned first.
It has been stated that time is the movement of the sun and other celestial bodies, as it is fit to be defined.

In connection with the sequence of time, the sequence of space (*deśakrama*) has also been explained by way of illustration through the passage beginning with "due to the variety of forms" (*mūrtivaicitryataḥ*). This is the illustration.
According to the principle that between two examples, the first example must be stated first,

the nature of spatial sequence was demonstrated by the passage beginning with "due to the variety of forms" (*mūrtivaicitryataḥ*) at the occasion of describing variety, prior even to temporal sequence.

By the phrase "due to the manifestation of the variety of subsequent actions," the temporal sequence in its form as the illustrated subject (*dārṣṭāntika*) is also shown. In the conclusion, however, by the phrase "the differentiation of manifestations everywhere," the temporal sequence relevant to the present topic is first mentioned; immediately thereafter, the spatial sequence is also [mentioned].
By the word "in entities" (bhāveṣu), the incidental sequence of locations is also indicated.

"Now, if this is so": according to the principle stated that "in all cases there is a difference in manifestation," a fragmented manifestation belongs to the subject within the sequence of time, whereas it does not exist in the subject who is an unfragmented manifestation;
thus it follows that even action does not exist in such a [subject]. Of that [action]...

Anticipating the objection that this is due to dependence on a temporal sequence, he states that such an appearance of a fragmented manifestation—the very appearance of the distinction between the subject and its object—is indeed His power of action (*kriyā-śakti*):
"In that way, the distinction between the knower and the knowable is manifested. The word "in that way" (*tathā*)...

The distinction between the knower and the knowable is characterized by the difference in spatial form for those who act in space, and by the difference in temporal action for those who act in time; this refers to the mutual distinction between the subject—the cognizer who is empty of [external objects] such as a jar—and the object, such as a jar, expressed as: "I am Caitra alone, not Maitra, nor am I a jar."

In the same way, regarding a jar or other objects, there is a distinction from one another— such as "this is indeed a jar, not a cloth, nor Caitra"— and the manifestation of that twofold distinction [between the object and the subject] is what is meant by "manifestation. This manifestation consists of the Supreme Lord himself appearing as the knower and the knowable in such a manner.
When there is the manifestation of duality, that shadow is the Lord’s power of emanation (*nirmāṇa-śakti*), which is his power of action (*kriyā-śakti*).

Action does not belong solely to the relationship between subjects such as the void (*śūnya*) and their objects; it also belongs to the Lord, who is the creator of both, and likewise to the one who knows in this manner. Thus.

Having established upon its own ground the distinction between the knower and the known—which it has itself projected—it knows that [distinction] by itself alone, because that [distinction] does not manifest apart from itself; thus, even this act of knowing is its power of action (*kriyā-śakti*).
For, according to the principle stated as "at the time of grasping a jar and so forth," even the act of knowing consists of action; therefore, [this belongs to] the Supreme Lord.

Thus, it follows that He is the knower who illumines this entire universe, from Śiva down to the earth. However—this indicates the specific nature of the two types of creative powers (*kriyā-śakti*) belonging to the Blessed Lord. "In this"—that is, in this Anuttara system, in reality, [He is the knower] even of Sadāśiva and the others. (306)
Within the collection of principles (tattva) beginning with Śiva and ending with Earth, which constitute the causal state, [this power] consists of unimpeded sovereignty;
it is undivided because it is distinct from the sovereignty of Brahmā and others, and because it is devoid of space and time.

Consisting of the uninterrupted self-reflection (*svātmavimarśa*) that is all-pervading and arises from every direction, it is "will alone" (*icchā eva*) that constitutes "action" (*kriyā*), because— due to its being filled with the infinite universe internalized within it— there is nothing whatsoever existing apart from itself, and thus it is not directed toward anything other than itself. In this way, will alone [is action].

The nature of causality, agency, and action will be concluded in the section on the subject; even in the context of the state of *māyā*, it establishes that the will (*icchā*) is essentially of the nature of action. For instance, even in the case of a cognizer such as Caitra or Maitra, before the procurement of fuel, a stove, and so forth, there arises within them the will, "I am cooking."

That very [process], because it extends from the cooking of the rice to its final completion, is called "action" (*kriyā*). However, in that case, no sequence consisting of the interruption of that [activity] is perceived. Thus, since there is an absence of a sequential process of action for Caitra and others in the act of cooking, the same applies to the Supreme Lord regarding [the creation of] everything from Śiva down to the earth.

I am the creator in the fashioning of the universe; I appear as such through the universal self (viśvātman). I am the illuminator of that which shines; having withdrawn the entire universe within, I manifest. Salutations to You, who are eternally satiated by the consumption of the three worlds.

In accordance with the principle thus stated, I manifest within the Full because of fullness; by virtue of being a mass of bliss and through my surging forth, I am in the very state of *spanda*. I thus reflect upon myself as having become such;
I perceive and contemplate myself as abiding as a mere residue of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) while existing as the self-nature of the universe.
The fivefold activity beginning with emanation is the ultimate reality; this much alone is the reality, which is the reflective awareness whose essence is will.
In that regard, there is no sequence whatsoever, for by the supreme Lord's power, the sequence of subject and object may manifest in this manner.
By the word "this," it is precisely this reflective awareness (*vimarśana*) that is expressed. Regarding the phrase "even there":
in the supreme Lord’s reflective awareness, there is no sequence whatsoever, unlike the reflective awareness consisting of speech such as "Caitra" or "Maitra.
Just as the reflective awareness consisting of the will [in the form] "let me cook" encompasses everything from the preparation of the hearth up to the final cooking of the rice.
Having attained the nature of vibration within the center, that [consciousness] proceeds through the sequence of the feet and so forth;

likewise, the will of the Lord extends from Śiva down to the limited subject (sakala), from the intellect and the senses up to the subtle elements such as sound, smell, and the like, ending with the ether and so forth.

By the phrase "concluding with the differentiation of the category of gross objects of cognition," the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) in its form as emanation (*nirmāṇa*) is described. Having reached that limit, the power of action in its form of perception (*vedana*), consisting of the cognizer, the means of cognition, and the object of cognition, is described in sequence. In the phrase "it appears as conjoined with that sequence... [the following is stated].

He provides an illustration: "like the surface of a mirror. Just as a river, though expanded within [the mirror] in the form of a reflection, appears as if closely joined with the flow of the stream through the sequence of its current—by this illustration, the subject (pramātṛ) consisting of the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) and the object of knowledge (prameya) is fashioned by the Blessed One.
The meaning is that the manifold world (*prapañca*) appears as the form of the Lord’s own reflection.

As he will state: "For it is an established tenet that the conscious [subject] causes objects to appear within itself like reflections. Thus, because a mirror is insentient (*jaḍatva*), [it cannot do so] within itself.

There is no desire in the form of the capacity for the sequential movement of that river's flow. Furthermore, the mirror does not even know the sequence of that flow—that is, the sequence of the river's current. In this context, the mirror is used as an illustration based solely on its purity; however, [the case] of the Supreme Lord is different.

The power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), whose nature is will, exists in two ways: as the capacity for the manifestation of everything from Śiva down to the earth, and as the experience of being colored by the act of reflecting the universe created by itself. Thus, just as there is a temporal sequence, spatial sequence also belongs solely to the Lord.

It must be stated that there exists an emanation (*nirmāṇa*) in the form of a variety of forms, and there is also the perception of the coloring (*uparāga*) by the sequence of those emanated places. In that regard, concerning the perception of the coloring by means of a sequence, it is said by others that desire itself becomes the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*). However, in this [our] system, at the time of perceiving a jar or other objects—
According to the principle stated as "he knows the jar," that power of vision (*dṛk-śakti*) is appropriated by the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) alone;
the summary meaning is that the power of action itself is the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), and that very same [power] is the power of will (*icchā-śakti*).

The literal meaning of the passage beginning with "tathā" and ending with "tasya kriyāśaktiḥ" has been shown in the *Anvaya* [section]. As for the word "ataḥ": since the Lord, the true subject (*pramātṛ*), exists, there can be no interruption in manifestation due to the absence of temporal succession; therefore, [the sequence] depends upon succession.

Although there may be a suspicion that action is untenable from the perspective of a gross view of activity— nevertheless, in this way, action is established through the capacity for the production of action in the form of succession and through the experience of being colored by action in the form of succession. All is auspicious.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the commentary on the *Pratyabhijñā-sūtra-vimarśinī*.
Now begins the tenth daily lesson.

"Contradiction," and so forth: [this refers to] the relation of entities consisting of the knower and the known, which, although each possesses a single form within itself, exhibit difference due to being differentiated by space, time, and form;
yet they exhibit non-difference because they are the objects of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) in the form "this is that very same thing. Such is the nature of difference and non-difference.

Furthermore, there is the contradiction of a single entity having a manifold form, and again the non-contradiction of that very same manifold entity having a unitary form as the object of recognition—
that power of the Creator of the world which is said to be inherent (samavāyinī).
O Goddess, you become the will of that [Lord] when he desires to create.

According to the principle thus stated, by means of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*)— which is imperishable, non-different from itself, and whose nature is that of the Supreme Goddess (*parā-bhaṭṭārikā*)— the knower of the reality of mantra (*mantra-tattva-vid*) unfolds the universe within his own self upon his own screen; as it has been said, "unfolding [it] within his very self," he is a jar.

The various appearances (*bhāsa*) have passed away; indeed, the very vision of difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābheda-dṛṣṭi*) is the means (*upāya*) to be relied upon for entering the vision of ultimate non-duality (*paramārthādvaya-dṛṣṭi*). For, according to the principle that will be stated later, even this conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is not in contradiction with the immersion into the nature of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara-svarūpa*). Thus, [it is] itself...

Because it consists of both the one and the many— being both transcendent of the universe and identical with the universe— it knows the reality of mantra, which is composed of its own nature as both one and many and is the form of perfect I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*) pertaining even to those entities that have become its own limbs; thus, this is indeed the power of action (*kriyāśakti*).
According to the principle that will be explained by the phrase "the expansion of all," we praise that very Śiva who is the source of that expansion.

As it has been said: "But that is the power of manifestation"—by this, it is meant that the Blessed One’s power of manifestation is unimpeded sovereignty. And by the principle to be explained later, it is precisely this sovereignty of manifestation that constitutes the entire expansion of the power of action (kriyā-śakti).

This very unimpeded sovereignty, which constitutes the expansion of that [consciousness], is not possible for the collection of categories such as action and generality according to the previously stated principle— that there is no practical transaction whatsoever with an eternally inferable external object— for those who maintain the view of an eternally inferable external reality. (309)
The daily lesson is introduced with seven verses beginning with "kriyāsaṃbandha" in order to carry through the exposition by way of justification.

Therein, by the first verse— beginning with "In that regard, one internal reality... and so forth, which functions as a set of six verses like a sūtra— it is shown that because [the opponent's view] rests upon both one and many entities, even for action and the like, which are themselves manifold in form, if it were a single [entity] according to the externalist (bāhyavāda) position, it could not be manifold.

By the second [verse], it is demonstrated that even though the nature [of the object] is untenable due to the refutation based on the attribution of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*)— namely, that "if it is manifold, it cannot be one"— this very [nature] must nevertheless be accepted. In that regard, [the verse concerns] that which resides in both unitary and manifold entities.
By the third [verse], the arising of action and so forth in both singular and plural forms is indicated. Although action and the rest— such as the object of cognition (e.g.,

a jar) and the cognizer (e.g., Caitra)— are experienced in non-conceptual awareness (*nirvikalpaka-saṃvedana*) by virtue of their ultimate reality, they become clearly manifest only at the time of conceptualization (*vikalpaka*).

By the fourth [verse], it is stated that "it has form. By the fifth, the distinction between unity and multiplicity is considered: their internal unity and external multiplicity, as well as their state of being both one and many externally.
Therein, internal unity is established by its very nature; by the sixth, it is established through connection with action.

It pervades the seven grammatical relations (*kārakas*), such as the relationship between action and its factors (*kriyākārakabhāva*), which are accepted as being indicated by the first aphorism; it begins with the relationship whose nature is that of action and its factors.

In brief, by means of the seventh [case], the nature of the two relations— namely, the relation of the limit and the limited and the relation of space and time, which are based on the cognition of direction and duration— is expressed through the word; furthermore, it is stated that actions and so forth have utility in purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*), just like a jar or other objects.

Regarding the word "nanu": however, by the phrase "that is the power of manifestation" (*nirmāṇa-śakti*), the power of manifestation of the Lord—which consists in the appearance of the differentiation between the diverse knower and the knowable—is described as His power of knowledge and action (*jñāna-kriyā*).
Likewise, there is the subject (*pramātṛ*) and the object (*prameya*) of that entity which is being manifested.
"May the manifestation of variety arise!"—according to this principle of the statement, manifestation alone is the creation and nothing else.

Thus, just as with the letter *ba* and others, no other activity such as that of hands or feet is possible in the creation of the universe; this is precisely what is meant. And "that" [refers to] the manifestation of the experience of the form of creation.

Because even the double moon and so forth appear in that very same way; and because there is existence for blue and so forth residing in the blue, as well as for the connection with action and universals (sāmānya) and so forth. And "therefore":
due to the similarity in their manifestation, [the double moon] and so forth—[and] in succession...

One might object: "How can the conventional usage 'this is real' and 'that is unreal' be consistent, since all three [of these categories] are equally non-existent? Anticipating this objection, [the author] first determines that the reality of blue and so forth—that is, the reality of blue and other such objects—is accepted by all disputants.
Stating that the unreality of action and so forth as asserted by the Vijñānavādin is not tenable,
and indicating that the reality of the double moon and such phenomena occurs in the manner to be described, he says: "Relations based on single or multiple entities..."
The cognitions of universals, substance, space, time, and so forth, are considered valid due to their stability and functional utility;

by the phrase "stability and functional utility," the impossibility [of validity] for such things as the double moon is indicated, because they lack both stability and functional utility. In this context, "stability" refers to [the cognition] in the case of "Devadatta is walking."

Up until the attainment of the village, there is no interruption in the middle, just as in the case of the perception of two moons and so forth; the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) consists in reaching the village and so on,
and its utility is [seen in] "a golden jar," where the quality of being golden persists up until the cognition of the jar.

Utility (*upayoga*) consists in the stability of the relationship between what has been heard and what is subsequently heard, and so forth; for example, [the cognition] "my jar is golden" possesses the quality of being delightful. In this same way, it should also be understood regarding the universal (*sāmānya*).
Where, according to the stated method, having attained rest, the manifold universe from Śiva down to the earth [is perceived].

From the state of consciousness (*cittatva*), which serves as the foundational wall for the repose of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*)— the cause manifested through the play of creation and so forth— there arises, within the sphere of *māyā*, a cognition of action (*kriyā-buddhi*) directed toward the agent, object, instrument, and so forth, such as "Caitra goes," "the rice grains soften," or "the fuel burns. It is within that cognition of action [that this occurs].

According to the stated principle that "they are considered to have a single or multiple substrata," the fact that the objects such as Caitra— which are the objective supports— possess both a single and a multiple form demonstrates precisely the single-and-multiple nature of those objects such as Caitra; for instance, the body of Caitra, while moving, is indeed multiple due to its differentiation by various locations, times, and shapes.

The objects of recognition, such as "this is that very same [person]," appear without abandoning their single form; it has been stated that action consists of both a single and multiple form, because that very object— both single and multiple— is the action, since it resides in Caitra’s body, which possesses both a single and multiple form.

(244) A single entity is not itself manifold in form; however, by relying on Caitra’s body—which as it moves appears both single and manifold—the cognition of action manifests as being both single and manifold, and is therefore ultimately real and true. But the case of a double moon and so forth is different, for although it appears in that way, it is due to a defect of the sense organ.

Even though it appears as two moons, at a later time it is considered unreal because its stability—which consists in the persistence of the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the form "two moons have arisen"—is uprooted by some [subsequent cognition] in the form "there are no two moons. Regarding the word "here": furthermore, in the case of the cognition of action, such as "Caitra moves,"...

An investigation that has arisen and persists is perceived as being uprooted by some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it does not waver in the interim— just like the [perception of] two moons and so forth. However, in the case of two moons and the like,
this is due to a defect in the visual organ (*akṣi-doṣa*) existing at that time for the one who sees the two moons.
If [the cognition] is useful for causing later disillusionment— according to the principle to be stated below, such as "one whose eyes are afflicted by the power of *timira* sees two moons"—
or else, if it is useful even at that very moment for one who is about to see those two moons; or...
Thinking, "This very person has become one whose eyes are afflicted by disease," one feels distressed;

yet, regarding that [second moon], one determines it to be such through the sight of the moon. For another [person], because of the capacity for causal efficiency (arthakriyā) performed by the single moon, there is a twofold causal efficiency in that sight of two moons.

He does not resolve upon it; thus, with respect to that second purposeful action, this [person] is not of use, just as the double moon is not. However, regarding the act of walking—the action of going—Caitra does not [resolve upon] the purposeful action consisting of reaching a village in the same way that he does not [resolve upon] the perception of a double moon.

Regarding the phrase "two moons": in this state of having reached the village—which is free from conceptual construction in the interim—there is the application of this renunciation. Because of its stability and its application, the cognition takes as its support the reality of single and multiple forms and actions, based upon entities such as Caitra, whether they be one or many.

Because it serves as a basis for stability, this "truthfulness" must be predicated of cognitions extending up to the time of the relationship [between word and object] and so forth; this will become clear in the subsequent verses.
(312) Now, as for the word "nanu": regarding any given object whatsoever...
If the coexistence of unity and plurality, which are mutually contradictory, were admitted,
then the plurality of a single entity would constitute a sublation, and the unity of multiple entities would constitute a sublation; thus,
there would be a sublation of both unity and plurality by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Anticipating the objection that this would result in the uprooting of stability, he says "therein" (*tatra*) in order to refute it.

"Therein" means among those [factors] such as action and so forth. "That" refers to that which has become the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). "Internal" means having the nature of being inward-turned. "The one" means that very reality itself, having attained the state of being perceivable by the senses. "In this world or the next" refers to space; "now or then" refers to time.
In terms of time, [an object] is thin, thick, and so forth; by its very nature, that [object] undergoes multiplicity.

"Therein" means: while their reality remains established. "Therein" means: among those two—oneness and multiplicity—the application of oneness itself as multiplicity is according to the manner to be explained.
(p. 245) When there is a mixture with the appearances of space and so forth, [the object] is cognizable by the internal organ alone;

when it is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), it is manifold; when there is a mixture with other appearances, it is cognizable by both organs; and when it appears as something distinct from consciousness, it is [cognized as such]. Thus, there is no clear distinction between the objects of unity and multiplicity.

He demonstrates, by way of a negative example (*vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta*), that the unity or plurality of an action which rests upon a single or multiple entity is real: "In this world, regarding the action of walking performed by Caitra, Maitra, and others, when Caitra is seen moving, the cognition never arises that 'this Caitra is not moving.'"

Therefore, because Caitra, as he moves, is qualified by various locations, times, and forms, he possesses multiplicity; yet, because of the appearance "this is that very same person," he possesses unity. Since the action resides in Caitra, who thus possesses both unitary and manifold forms, the action itself is also of a unitary and manifold nature. Such is its true form.
Just as the cognition of silver is sublated in the interim—even before reaching the destination intended by the action—so too is this [cognition].
He further confirms this with a counter-example: "As in the case of the cognition of silver, so it is not [the case] even in the case of the double moon."
When one whose vision is impaired by *timira* perceives two moons, the thought "I know only this: there are two moons" constitutes a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Regarding the question you raised—namely, how it is that what is actually one becomes many—therein [lies the answer].
The manner in which one [cause] produces many effects is stated:

how is it that seeds and the like, which serve as the instrumental cause for sprouts and so forth, become the cause for jars and the like? Now, if it is argued that this is so because of the difference in objects—that the sprout produced by the seed is one thing, while that produced from clay is another—[the response follows].

If it is argued that, because of the difference between the two objects consisting of their respective effects, the seed is said to be the cause of the sprout alone and not of the jar, then— given this stated distinction of characteristics— it is not contradictory for the seed to possess causality toward the sprout and non-causality toward the jar and so forth.

By whom was this occasion or rule established— that the causal and non-causal nature of a seed and so forth is determined such that only a perceived seed is the cause with respect to a sprout, and not a jar? If you say it is by one's own experience, then in cases such as "he moves," [experience likewise establishes] that the moving Devadatta [is the cause].

Because it is differentiated by various places, times, and forms, there is multiplicity; yet because it is the object of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) as "this is that very same thing," there is unity. In reality, we have accepted self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) itself as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding both unity and multiplicity; why, then, is this not tolerated? In this regard—
Once multiplicity has been established, it is indeed possible to speak of a difference in objects as well. To explain:

when space, time, and so forth are not perceived through another manifestation, that [object] such as Caitra consists of nothing but a single manifestation. It is for this very reason [that the distinction is made].
Because it consists of a single manifestation alone, there is no possibility of dependence on space; thus, it is internal, inward-turned, and shines forth without interruption as such.
This is because it is perceivable by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), which is suited to grasping a single manifestation that is not qualified by space and so forth.
And likewise, when there is no lapse from that inward-facing nature,
reality— which is the ultimate truth—
remains; furthermore, the outpourings of the vibration of the qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth arise from their reliance upon the universal vibration.
According to the principle thus stated, because it consists of the nature of universal vibration (*sāmānyaspanda*),
because it is conjoined with the manifestations of all individual forms, and because it cannot tolerate [the existence of] anything other than that,
the reality (*tattva*) is perceived as one that is woven through everything. "That very same" means that the internal reality of these [individuals] is indeed that [one reality].

It is mixed with the appearance of space through "here" and "there," with the appearance of time through "now" and "then," and with the appearance of nature through "grass," "thick," and so forth; for this very reason, it is perceived as manifold when it is cognizable by the external senses. Furthermore:

In the passage beginning with "of the Lord who resides within the self," it is stated that for one who revolves within such a universe— which, like the true Lord, is unitary and undivided— the state of being perceivable by both sets of organs [the internal and external] occurs according to the principle of the relationship between cause and effect to be described later; thus, regarding the unity and multiplicity of the reality, once again—

Having clarified the unity of that very [object] whose space, time, and so forth have been made manifest— by means of the section beginning with "the mixing with other appearances" and ending with "the distinction of objects is clear"— the difference in objects is once again [examined] from the perspective of the unity and multiplicity of the thing-in-itself.

In the same way, you [should understand] that the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*)— that "this very thing is that same innate unity"— does not occur by force alone, just as [the relationship between] a seed and its sprout involves both material and auxiliary causes.
Now, regarding the single entity that is the seed itself, it is the cause of the sprout, while [factors such as] soil and so forth are [auxiliary causes].
Thus, it follows that [the entity] would possess two forms: being both a cause and a non-cause.

Furthermore, for a single entity whose nature is clay, there would likewise follow two forms—namely, being the material cause (*upādāna*) with respect to a jar and being a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*) with respect to a sprout—and this applies to a single entity in general.
Because [the Self] is a single object solely within the internal organ (*antarantaḥkaraṇa*), it possesses unity;
yet because it is delimited by external space, time, and form, it possesses multiplicity. Thus, the contradiction between unity and multiplicity is not a sublation.
Now, the seed is the cause with respect to the sprout, but it is not the cause with respect to a jar or the like;

by the inclusion of the word "etcetera," [it is meant that] with respect to a jar it is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), while with respect to the sprout it is the cooperative cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*).
Such is merely conventional usage; it does not reflect the investigation into the actual nature of things.
In that case, even here at the level of *māyā*, although the reality is composed of consciousness (*cinmaya*), there exists internally the one and externally the many—

namely, blue, yellow, the non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*), and the conceptual (*savikalpaka*)— as well as everything such as the knower, knowledge, and so forth, characterized by oneness and multiplicity, blue and yellow, non-conceptuality and conceptuality.
"Everything you have said and everything we have said is the same in that it is merely conventional usage (*vyavahāra-mātra*).
Regarding the phrase "that very thing": by the word "only" (*eva*), he states that "oneness and multiplicity" is precisely that which is perceptible by the senses;

he then explains this very point with the words "in that regard" (*tatra*). This means: among those aforementioned [categories] such as action and so forth, that which is the internal reality (*antara-tattva*).

The connection [of the passage] is as follows: that single reality which is the nature of the *ahaṃtā* (I-ness) serving as its substratum, having reached the state of being perceived by the senses, becomes manifold—possessing distinctions of place and so forth—and yet proceeds toward external unity.
Alternatively, the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) extends up to this point, with the phrase "therein" (*tatra*) meaning "abiding in truth," and so on.
This has been shown.
[Objection: "Now, if it is admitted that unity and plurality have distinct objects by virtue of being internal and external forms, then at the very moment that object appears as one..."

The manifold does not appear. When that very [entity] appears as manifold—that is, when it appears as manifold—then the appearance of unity is absent; how, then, could a single entity possess the nature of both unity and multiplicity?
If unity and multiplicity were perceived simultaneously in a single entity, then unity and multiplicity would exist at one and the same time.
The meaning is that for an entity, neither oneness nor multiplicity is possible.
He demonstrates this very point with the words "For instance" (*tathā hi*). Caitra, while moving and going to various different places, is perceived solely by means of the external sense-faculty.
And within that single body, Caitra, there occurs a blending of appearances such as place, time, and so forth— which serve as the causes for multiplicity—
with respect to that which consists of the mere appearance of each individual object and has as its domain the mere object itself, undifferentiated by place, time, and so forth.

There is no activity of the non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*). That which arises by the power of an object suddenly encountered would be non-conceptual, characterized by that object, because it does not investigate the place, time, and so forth that occur at the moment of the subsequent conceptualization (*bhūtavikalpa*). And all this—
According to the principle that "conceptual construction (vikalpa) is rooted in direct experience," even by a mental conceptual construction following upon that [experience],
an object— whether unitary or manifold— that exists in such a manner is not touched at all; rather, [it is touched] in natural cognition, which consists in the external manifestation [of the object].

"However, that which consists of a prior experience remains present in its recollection and so forth"—according to this stated principle, because it possesses an object of non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*), by what means [is it known]? By the statement "by which excellence?"—that is, by a conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) as if it were a non-conceptual one. Thus, for the proponent of the doctrine of non-duality (*anātma-vādin*), there is only a continuum of cognitions (*jñāna-santāna*).
To dispel the delusion of another who considers this [duality] to be reality, he says: "taddvayā" (those which rely on that duality).

"Taddvayam" means the duality of that; namely, of an entity such as Caitra or a jar. "Tat" refers to what was previously mentioned. By the phrase "etāḥ... taddvayāvalambanāḥ," the connection with the action is shown: these [notions] are those which rely upon the duality of unity and plurality.

The *grahaṇaka-sūtra* indicates that cognition (*buddhi*) consists of the activity (*vyāpāra*) of the subject (*pramātṛ*), the object (*prameya*), and the action (*kriyā*), which is essentially the nature of that very activity.

Now, [it may be asked]: "Is it not the case that [this cognition] is of the nature of a determinative judgment (*adhyavasāya*) occurring immediately after non-conceptual reflective awareness (*nirvikalpa-vimarśa*)? (316)

The internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) itself performs the function of determination (*niścaya*). Thus, volition (*saṃkalpa*), which consists of self-conceit (*abhimāna*) and resolution (*adhyavasāya*), makes the internal organ itself the means for accomplishing its respective operations.
Here, [the phrase] "in the garland of knowledge" refers to that which takes the form of experience (*anubhava*) and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "within" (*antar*): there exists a certain subject (*pramātṛ*) who, as the very life-force, wears the thread-like form of the garland of knowledge (*jñānamālā*) described in the three daily lessons beginning with the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*). Regarding the word "previously" (*prāk*): [it refers to what was stated] before.

This has been established in the chapter titled "The Determination of the Single Substratum. Furthermore, by means of the eighth chapter, which is the "Determination of the Great Lord," it has also been concluded that this cognizer (pramātṛ) is autonomous. And when he becomes one whose impurity of māyā has dissolved through the glance of a true guru, [he attains liberation].
Then, although his essential nature is Śiva, when he is in the state of *māyā*—which consists of the manifestation of "this-ness" (*idantā*)—he is once again concealed from that [Śiva-nature].

Consequently, though his form is one with Śiva, he becomes a bound soul (*paśu*) whose nature is contracted, thinking "I am Caitra," "I am Maitra. This [state] is declared to be the mind of this subject who possesses the form of a bound soul.

The "opportunity for the manifestation of the internal organ of form" refers to the occasion when resolve, egoity, and so forth properly manifest according to their respective functions; at this time, the triad of "I-nesses"— existing in this manner— is clearly manifested on the plane of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

Even in the non-conceptual sensory perception (*nirvikalpaka*) of "I am this," which is not yet qualified by space, time, and so forth, because there is as yet no recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), at the initial moment it appears simply as "this" unqualified by space and time;
subsequently, at the time of manifestation, there arises the state of Sadāśiva and Īśvara, characterized by the very forms "I am this" and "this is I. Thus...

The meaning is that the real, sensory object, being non-conceptual, does not perform functions such as connection with action when it possesses the form of conceptual cognition. According to the stated principle that even at the moment of direct perception there is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), such non-conceptual cognitions of reality belong to one who has gone outside [of himself].

The function of reflection (*vimarśa*) is that which possesses subsequent determination (*anuvyavasāyin*); because it occurs subsequently, the internal organ (*manaḥ*), by performing the verbal expression "determinative" (*vyavasāyi*)— that is, the determination (*vyavasāya*) consisting of certainty (*niścaya*)— the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and the binding of these actions such as [the aforementioned], brings them about and accomplishes them.

"Having those two as their objective support" means that those conceptual constructions take as their objective support that pair consisting of unity and plurality. Here, in the case of a conceptual construction based on memory, the object is first determined (*adhyavasīyate*); otherwise, there would be the consequence of falling into a state like deep sleep or fainting. And thus, as long as there is a determination of the object...

To that extent, it must be accepted by implication (*sāmarthyāt*) that "it is from the object itself. For if the object were not manifest, then when there is something to be determined (*adhyavasātavya*), determination would be as if one were blind; for it has been stated that in conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) there is no manifestation [of the object], and thus existence is only what is manifested by consciousness.
According to the principle stated in the *Śrīmattantravaṭadhānikā*, the very nature of a thing (*vastu*) is its manifestation; thus, the essence of a thing is its being manifest.

Regarding a thing that is not manifest, there arise conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) such as: "Is this a *guñjā* fruit or fire?", "This is indeed a *guñjā* fruit and it is fire," or "This *guñjā* fruit belongs to me alone."

Successively having dispelled the mind (*manas*), the intellect (*buddhi*), and the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), it is not logical for there to be any other activity. Therefore, [it is said] "the external, the external," and so forth. "From this" means because the manifestation of the object is the ultimate reality; thus, even though external blue and so forth do not exist *per se* within the internal continuum of cognition, as in the case of mother-of-pearl [mistaken for silver].
Statements such as "it superimposes like silver" and so forth are devoid of objective reality and are not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
This has been stated [in the following passage]: "And this—namely, that this object of cognition (*prameya*) is determined as being an error.

With reference to what was called "the reflective awareness" (*anuvyavasāyin*), he says: "by means of the non-conceptualizing knowledge that is the instrument of valid cognition (*nirvikalpakapramāṇa-jñāna*)."

The opponent might say: "How could conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) touch upon the object to be manifested, since their objects are distinct? [The author replies: "It would indeed be so. If conceptual construction were itself independent, existing without a cognizer (*pramātṛ*), then that conceptual construction would [grasp] the object of non-conceptual [perception].

It is not capable of touching the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). "As far as" means that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is not independent with respect to the nature of the object without the cognizer (*pramātṛ*). Therefore, this conceptual construction—the mental knowledge of conceptualization—is the very activity of the cognizer; and this cognizer [perceives] "this is a jar."

It consists of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) whose nature is a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) turned inward toward a prior experience. For that cognizer, in the non-conceptual operation following upon the [initial] experience—[expressed as] "this is indeed mine"—there is the state of being a prior experience; thus, the object previously experienced, that place, that...

"Time"—this refers to that very object, as well as to space and time which serve as its qualifiers; not abandoning the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of these, there remains this very *vimarśa* as a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) within the subject.
Existing in the subject in the form of a latent impression, it is the prior experience (*pūrvānubhava*) as far as its own object extends.
Since even memory and the like, having attained identity with that which is of the nature of manifestation, appear in that same way according to the principle already stated,

conceptual thought (*vikalpa*)— which is an activity of the subject (*pramātṛ*) that has attained identity with such a prior experience— is likewise directed toward the very object of that prior experience. For this very reason:
The reason for this has been stated by the venerable teacher Utpaladeva:
"This very [consciousness] of the knower is the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of prior experience,
which persists as the state of *apohana*."

This and so forth: because this very latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of the previous experience belongs to the cognizer (*pramātṛ*), and since the cognizer remains established even at the time of exclusion (*apohana*), [it follows] "therefore. Because it consists of the activity of the cognizer, in each individual object there is both unity and multiplicity—

The nature of conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is non-activity. "Consisting of activity" means that those conceptualizations of action and so forth have as their fundamental form precisely activity. Regarding the word "gone" (*itā*): it is established that the mind alone performs the conceptualizations of action and so forth indicated by the summary statement (*grahaṇakavākya*). By the third [verse], the non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*)...
Even though these [objects] are objects of cognition within consciousness, their form is clearly manifest only at the time of conceptualization;
thus, according to the previously stated principle, because there is only the manifestation of the jar as qualified by its qualifiers,
even in that non-conceptual state, although there is no manifestation of the connection with a universal (*sāmānya*) and so forth, it remains as such.

Nevertheless, universals and the like do not manifest clearly. He demonstrates this very point with the words "nevertheless, [the universal] such as generality," etc. Although it possesses a common coloring factor (*uparañjaka*), the universal residing in a jar—which persists through all jars located in all places—is said to have a relation that resides in two loci (*dviṣṭhasambandha*).

Since a relation, by its very nature, resides in two terms— as will be stated in the rule "the king's man" (rājñaḥ puruṣa)— it arises from two related entities in the form of "king-man. Furthermore, for Caitra who is moving,
it consists of a succession of moments characterized by the displacement of his feet into prior and posterior positions.
If there were no abandonment of the continuum, then regarding a jar or similar object, when its constituent parts such as the mouth and so forth are accepted, one could say:

"This is a jar," or "This cloth is situated in the front part," or "This is in the back part. Likewise, regarding Caitra and others, one could say: "Maitra was born right in front," or "This one was born behind."
Thus, because of the apprehension of the non-limit and the limited, and so forth, in this sequence, universals (*sāmānya*) and other entities manifest at different times;

therefore, it is established that universals and the like are of both unitary and manifold forms, being graspable by mental conceptualization (*mānasavikalpa*). "And thus" means: the unreal, the real, and the real-in-the-present.

According to what you have stated, conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) is conceptual cognition (*vikalpa-jñāna*), and it is by virtue of that [conceptualization] that even ultimate reality (*paramārtha-rūpa*)—because it consists of conceptual thought—is said to possess the nature of conventional truth. Thus, according to your own statement, this conventional truth is merely a mode of the real itself; for conventional reality, which has the form of truth, is [nothing other than] the real.

Actions and so forth are not unreal, just as the appearance of two moons is not. Even when speaking of conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) therein, this entire sequence of relations, extending from action up to time, is the very process of the descent of consciousness (*saṃvit*) which possesses the power of action; consciousness consists of the power of action.
The meaning is that [consciousness] manifests by descending into the form of action and so forth. As it has been said:

"Since there is no such entity whatsoever that is thus conceptualized, for it is consciousness alone; indeed, its sovereignty consists in appearing in such a manner. In that regard, even within action and the rest, there is an action and so forth that serves as the root.

Every relation whatsoever has time as its limit; this very point is demonstrated by the passage beginning with "tathā hi" (for instance). That which appears as a single, continuous [entity] among similar individual objects such as jars is the universal "jar-ness.
Just as Devadatta, while moving from one place to another, [perceives it] spatially and temporally...

And in terms of configuration (*ākāra*): that which is the extension of a jar or the like, consisting of its parts such as the mouth and so forth, because they rest within the single nature of the jar; and that unity which, through the pervasion of the supporting ground, constitutes the extension—this is the "whole" (*avayavin*). Taking this mountain as a limit, [one perceives] "this mountain is thus."

"Eastward" (*purastāt*) refers to the eastern direction and so forth. This expansion of action belonging to Caitra exists simultaneously with him; the "present time" is that which takes the form of "he goes," existing together with Devadatta during the expansion of actions such as going. [The terms] "was" and "will be" refer to this same expansion of action.

Time, which begins with the primary elements (*bhūtādi*), although it is one because it resides in a single substratum such as Devadatta, possesses both a unitary and a manifold nature due to its pervasion of various locations during action. In this same way, universals (*sāmānya*) and the like also possess a unitary and a manifold nature; this is the objective reality (*vastutattva*) of things such as trees.

Whatever form appears, beginning from that which follows upon the meaning of the nominal stem— as in "the tree stands" (*vṛkṣastiṣṭhati*) or "it is stood by means of the tree" (*vṛkṣeṇa sthīyate*)— and extending up to the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), all that is indeed relation (*saṃbandha*). This relation, in some cases, constitutes the linguistic usage of universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth.
It tolerates other designations; at that time, it is designated by such terms as "universal" (*sāmānya*) and so forth.
Here he provides an illustration:

just as the continuous relationship in the form of "cowness" (*gotva*), which runs through individual cows such as the tawny one (*kapilā*) characterized by the dewlap and other features, is expressed as "cows."

Because of the use of the plural number, [the Self] is capable of being designated as one; therein, when other designations are tolerated, there is the conventional usage of a "relation" by means of universals and so forth.
In the absence of such a complex of designations, the relation is simply the verbal expression of the relation itself—that is, the relation is just "that."

It is so designated. Regarding this, he provides an illustration: just as among individual cows such as Kapilā and others who possess dewlaps and other characteristics, there is an underlying connection consisting of the universal "cowness" (gotva), which is capable of sustaining the single designation "cows" expressed in the plural; for it does not tolerate any other alternative designation in that context.

Regarding the existent, when there is an absence of the aforementioned form of designation—that is, the knot [of conceptualization]—the conventional usage of a relation through universals and so forth is merely a verbal expression of relation; it is simply treated as "this is that relation.
For this very reason, because the factors of action (*kārakas*) consist of the nature of relation, they are measurable by means of the sacrificial ladle, the hand, and so forth.
The measurement of a field is its connection with the two measurements [of length] from front to back;
the connection of a field measuring only a *diṣṭi* is with its two front and back boundaries;
and the connection of a *prastha* and its substance is the connection of the measure residing in the *prastha* and the substance.

Connection is established through prior and posterior measurement (*parimāṇa*). The connection of fruits and the like with their weight (*unmāna*) is with gold and other such standards. And by means of both prior and posterior weight, there is the form of measurement consisting of dimension (*pramāṇa*), circumference (*parimāṇa*), and weight (*unmāna*). Among these, the measurement of vision is as follows:

Furthermore, whatever exists within the scope of measurement—such as minuteness, magnitude, number, distinctness, and so forth—all of that is of the nature of worldly convention; all of it is merely the manifestation of relation itself.
Whatever universals and so on exist, they are related like a jar.
They considered it to be a distinct category (padārthāntara), and they also accepted inherence (samavāya) therein.

Furthermore, since inherence is of the nature of a relation and is supported by that [category] as its life-force, according to the view of some, inherence is "supported by a relation" (saṃbandhānugrāhya). He states that very point:

The relation called "inherence" (samavāya) favors that power which is termed "relation. He clarifies this very point already stated: "And even that which is a causal factor (kāraka) is the coordination of causal factors, which is the object of the reflection upon action"—according to the principle that will be explained hereafter.

That action as well, which looks toward actions such as "staying" and so forth, depends upon Time— the Lord of its own life-force— which consists of the elements and so on. And that Time, through the medium of actions such as "staying," effects the connection with the Self of all entities that serve as the substrata for those very actions of staying and so forth.

This manifold course of worldly affairs is dependent upon relationship. As the Teacher himself has said: "The course of worldly affairs is the activity of Him whose relationship consists of both difference and non-difference, who accomplishes all purposes by His own will; I bow to that Śiva."
