(p. 252) — Because manifestation (*rūpa*) consists of relation, he first defines relation itself:
entities consist of the manifestations of kings and the like, as well as the manifestations of persons and the like.

Established in themselves, they rest in their own very form; for this very reason, they possess distinct appearances, being manifestations differentiated from one another. When they attain unity—characterized by mutual interconnection—within a single cognizer who grasps the manifestations such as "the king's man," then those very [manifestations]...
The word "related" (*saṃbandhi*) refers to that which serves as the objective support (*ālambana*).

The phrase "the state of being isolated" (*viviktābhā*) means that, prior to the resting of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) within the cognizing subject (*pramātṛ*) who grasps both [subject and object], the two remain standing apart externally, unmingled with one another, and established in their own self-nature. For this very reason...

In the state of complete fulfillment, which is resting solely in one's own essential nature (*svasvarūpa*), that identity— which consists of attaining oneness with the subject (*pramātṛ*) who perceives both [the object and the means]—
does not constitute an identity with that subject, as is the case with those two, the king and the man.

For otherwise, there would be the consequence of the dissolution of the status of being a "king's man" (*rājapuruṣatva*). Rather, in the case of "the king's man," there is a unity characterized by a conjunction consisting of a mutual interpenetration, wherein two currents of difference and non-difference—appearing as the simultaneous and instantaneous submergence and emergence of the forms of "man" and "king"—are marked by the surging of their tide. This is the nature of the synthesis (*samanvaya*) that constitutes oneness.
As they proceed, those two—the king and the man—then become the relational objects (*ālambana*), as in the expression "the king's man.

He explains this very point: for prior to the perception of the man, although the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) whose intellect grasps the appearance of the king has already apprehended him, he is [at that time] devoid of the appearance of the man.

When the King is not satisfied by resting within his own self, he then becomes fulfilled by entering into union with the Puruṣa through another form; likewise, the Puruṣa also is not satisfied by resting within his own self, and he too becomes fulfilled by entering into union with the King through another form. He.

The mutual proximity (*ūpaśleṣa*) of the king and the man exists as one alone within the cognizing subject, the conscious Self (*cidātman*), by means of that aforementioned unity. In the expression "the king’s man," it remains established upon the previously attained consciousness of the king; for this very reason, the man is [perceived] as subordinate.
Due to the immersion of consciousness, the characteristic of non-manifestation of the distinctness between the king and the servant rests in sovereignty;
there, it shines forth in that very independent conscious self (cidātman), even though the ultimate reality is [identical to] the person who has been integrated.
Immediately following the appearance of the king and so forth, [the cognitions] take as their object the single form—namely, the nature of "cowness," "potness," and so on—which is non-dual;

yet they simultaneously apprehend the difference and multiplicity of those two through the external individual (vyakti) such as Kapila, by way of the face and other features, and by way of parts. Thus, there is both difference and non-difference between the two.

Only externally; the cognitions of the subject’s conceptualizing intellect, which grasp the universal (*jāti*) as having a manifest form once it has been apprehended, do not [perceive] only the relation.

Within the word itself, they maintain a single form; even externally, when associated with individual instances such as those of the followers of Kapila, it leads one—just as if it were an object of perception—to the nature of "cowness" and its unity. (p. 253) He demonstrates this very point briefly with the words: "gāvaḥ" (cows). [This occurs] when there is the appearance of plurality externally.

Separated from one another, they appear externally as distinct individuals, such as Kapila and others; by which manifestation the plural number indicates their multiplicity. Furthermore, the form of these cows appears as a recurring [commonality], such that "this is a cow, this is a cow, this is a cow. But when the single nature of *gotva* (cowness) [is considered]...
The reference to the meanings of the individual words is the conclusion;

following this, the body [of the text] shows that both unity and multiplicity are indeed external, and by the pointing out with the finger in the phrase "these," it demonstrates through direct perception that the nature of both is more external.
Even though there is externality, the ultimate reality is the prior connection with one's own self;
for when they are included within the Light, they shine. In that state, the distinction or non-distinction of objects by virtue of their externality does not constitute a flaw.

On one hand, because manifestations consist of consciousness (*cinmaya*), their existence is always within [consciousness] alone; yet, because they appear as external through *māyā*, that [existence] is also outside, just as in the case of the perception of a painting. In a painting, there is both the unity and the differentiation of a bird in its form as a bird, as well as [the differentiation of] blue.

The state of having blue-colored wings constitutes multiplicity. By this principle, even in a substance such as a jar, the contradiction between one part being golden and another being silver, or between being red and not red, is resolved. Every object is consciousness itself, because it consists of consciousness.

The meaning is that she endures the state of being all forms. Through her connection with this genus (*jāti*), there is also one internal aspect. It is not only externally that she is "everywhere"; she is also internally within all entities through her connection in this manner.
Regarding the conceptual constructions (*kalpanā*) which grasp the composite substance (*avayavidravya*) appearing as "a jar"— which appears as if it were a genus—
these conceptual cognitions do not have a single object internally while having multiple objects externally.
Even externally, those conceptual cognitions have both single and multiple things as their objects.
It further demonstrates that even external objects possess both unity and multiplicity:

they are of a single form by virtue of being a unified construction, yet they are manifold through their various parts— such as the primary characteristics of a whole like a jar— and thus they assume multiple forms, appearing as "a jar."

Existence (*bhava*) appears as a single form consisting of a unique collection whose sole basis is its own nature, and it manifests as having an extended form through its various parts, such as the mouth and other limbs, which pervade their respective locations.
This refers to substances such as trees, which serve as the substrata for the potencies of agents (*kartṛ*) and so forth.

The connection between Devadatta, the firewood, the pot, and the rice— as agent, instrument, locus, and object— which occurs in such expressions as "he cooks," has as its sole cause the investigation of the action.
The cognition grasping direction and time establishes this limit: "In relation to this, that was born before;
therefore, this is its elder brother. Day is the sun’s journey up to the mountain of sunrise, and night is its journey starting from the western mountain up to the mountain of sunrise.
The cognition of direction and so forth, based on the relation between a limit and that which is limited—as in "the night"—is [an instance of] the [cognition] of *kārakas*;

that is, of *kārakas* such as Caitra, Maitra, and others, who are the substrata of the powers (*śakti*) of the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth, ending with the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), beginning with the nominative case (*prathamā*). (p. 254, 324)

Furthermore, the mutual correlation observed among substances such as trees and so forth— expressed in forms such as "Devadatta [cooks] with wood, in a pot, rice"— is that very correlation; it consists of that cognition which is internalized within the cognizer, namely the action of cooking and the like.

He provides an illustration for the point that the coordination of the factors of action (*kārakas*)—which has deliberation (*parāmarśa*) as its sole cause—has as its object the deliberation regarding an action, stating: "Just as [the relation] of the knower, the object of knowledge, and the means of knowledge...
[referring to] the knower Caitra, etc., and that which resides in both of them, directed outwardly.
Just as there is a mutual correspondence between the cognition in the form of "I" and the act of knowing in the form of valid cognitions such as "seeing," so too here,
in the case of Devadatta, [the self] remains apart from the reflective awareness of valid cognition (*pramā-parāmarśa*) which consists of internal acts such as "seeing."

In cases such as "the tree" and so forth, there is no direct, intrinsic reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of two entities possessing form; rather, the coordination of the case-factors (*kārakas*) has as its sole cause the reflective awareness of an action, such as "he cooks," and thus, without an action, this [coordination] does not occur elsewhere.

The meaning of "nimittatā" (causality) is the state of being unable to endure existence [as separate entities]. The point is that the mutual connection of the factors of action (*kārakas*) cannot occur by themselves without an activity consisting of the subject's reflective awareness (*pramātṛ-parāmarśa*). This applies even to the powers of the first and other case-roles (*kāraka-śakti*).
The mutual inherence (*samanvaya*) that exists between its own substrata, such as trees and so forth,

is caused solely by the reference to actions such as "standing" and so on— as in: "the tree stands," "he sees the tree," "it is stood by means of the tree," "he gives [fruit] from the tree," "he falls from the tree," and "this belongs to the tree."

"Everything exists as 'a tree' and 'stands'. Thus, there is a direct relationship between substances and their powers with action; and this much indeed is the venerable [relation] that serves as the cause for all worldly transaction.

It manifests the relationship [of the case-roles] as they unfold through the grammatical factors (kārakas), beginning with the nominative and ending with the locative. Having perceived two external objects, the cognizer [distinguishes them] by their external differentiation, thinking: "This mountain is to the east of that; this is to the west."
Because the two entities being grasped by the eyes and other senses rest together within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*),
there is first non-differentiation; then, emerging again outwardly, in the middle, at the central limit,
there occurs the manifestation of mutual differentiation— such as "this from that" or "prior"— and yet again, non-differentiation.

If that which is rested upon is firmly perceived, it is generally called "direction" (*dik*). Here, within this general direction, by means of the reference to the front, back, right, and left parts of those two entities, there arises the possibility of the division of directions such as east and so forth; [this refers to] their parts.
By the phrase "the determination of facing toward or facing away from," the possibility of specific distinctions such as intermediate directions (*vidig*) and so forth is established.

"Conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) is that which is conjoined with this mountain; "conjunction with the conjoined" (*saṃyuktasaṃyoga*) is the connection of the [mountain] thus conjoined with trees and other objects.
p. 255) Furthermore, the proximity between two entities and their mutual inclusion are useful when referring to direction (*dik*).
Thus, for a cognition whose nature consists in the reference to direction—which rests upon the relation of the limit and the limited—the forms "east," "west," and so forth [arise].

Having demonstrated the relationship between the limit (avadhi) and that which is limited (avadhimat), he shows the nature of priority, posteriority, and so forth by means of the passage beginning with "the reflection of time" (*kālaparāmarśa*), etc.: "This was born before this one;
this [was born] after. Even therein, [one distinguishes] "born after a long time" or "born after a short time"; immediately following birth, this [remains] for a long duration...
Śiva [is the cause] of "not long ago" (acirakāla); this reflection on the shortness of birth, duration, and so forth, regarding two entities, is useful—
such as in the case of "this jar was made in just one *ghaṭikā*," or "this bowl was made in just half a *ghaṭikā*"—
even when there is a distinction between long and quick, such as "this elephant was born twelve years ago," while this...
The reflection on birth as being slow or quick— such as "the pig was born six months ago"—
is useful for such purposes. However, in cases such as "he will cook," "he cooks," and "he cooked," there is,
respectively, the future form of the present, the present form of the future, and the past form of the future.
The manifestation of that which was previously conceived and made manifest consists of one's own prior consciousness;

it is the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) in the form of inhalation and exhalation, as well as other activities such as the circulation of the sun and so forth, and the specific results of actions such as cooking, characterized by their being slow or quick.

Apprehension (*parāmarśa*) is employed in all worldly transactions, such as: "This number belongs to that which possesses number," "This measure belongs to that which possesses measure," "This is separate from that," "This is conjoined with this," and "This is disjoined from that," and so forth.
Or rather, it is the very nature of the relation itself that must be expressed.
(326) Having thus demonstrated the essential nature of the relation in detail, he once again shows the ultimate, absolute nature of the relation in brief:
"In every way, that which is its summary," and so forth. "In every way" means by way of all places, times, forms, and natures;
thus, this nature of the relation is seen as manifest through perception for everyone. Even when [the object] has been grasped by a prior cognition such as "this is a king,"...
When one is not satisfied by resting in one's own self, then, seeking union with a person of another form,

one becomes fulfilled; in this very context, according to the previously stated principle, at that moment, for a king or similar person who does not find contentment through resting in their own self as distinguished from a man corresponding to themselves—

The manifestation of an object is incomplete so long as it does not find its rest in a reflective awareness of another manifestation in the form of the subject; thus, its establishment in its own nature [is achieved only through this]. In that state, the very nature of the relationship—which consists of the performance of a purposeful action characterized by mutual satisfaction and which is composed of the unfolding of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*)—must be expressed. Furthermore, in that regard:

In cases such as "the king's man," even when it takes the form of a relation, if one considers the man to possess a bracelet— as in "the man has a bracelet"— let there also be another relation; for number and so forth reside upon substance, which is based upon a relation.
Some accept the relation of inherence (*samavāya-sambandha*), arguing that since unity and other qualities inhere within it,
there is no fault of infinite regress;
just as the creation of a subsequent kalpa occurs after the creation of a preceding kalpa.
It does not constitute a defect in the form of a loss of the previous creation of the kalpa;

he clarifies this very point already stated: "In the absence of the appearance of a subsequent connection, there is no loss whatsoever of the appearance of the previous connection," by which [means]...

Without non-existence (*vinābhāva*), one might suspect a fundamental destruction of the prior relationship; however, such a loss does not exist, for [the relationship] consists of the manifestation of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*). In this manner, as stated, the abundant life-force of all worldly activity (*lokayātrā*) is sustained by the relationship.

Having described the state of being a relative (*bandhurībhāva*) as swelling (*ucchūnatva*), and having established that it is connected to an action (*kriyā-sambandha*), he says— beginning with "in this very way" (*evam eva*)— that actions which serve to establish stability are to be defined for the mother who seeks purposeful activity (*arthakriyārthinī*), according to the manner stated in the passage beginning with "connected to an action" (*kriyā-sambandhinī*).

The accomplishment of the object—the accomplishment of the effect—would occur through an object such as a jar that possesses both difference and non-difference by way of having the nature of relations and so forth; however, causal efficiency does not arise from an object that consists merely of its own appearance. Therefore, [the object must possess] stability.

Furthermore, a cognition that apprehends a relation by virtue of its performing a function cannot be an error—such as the cognition of two moons—and so forth. In this context, existence (*sattā*) is not the nature of the relation;
thus, the essential nature of the relation is not the connection with existence in the sense that "entities exist."

If the existence (*sattā*) of a jar or similar object is its very nature (*svarūpa*) consisting solely in a relation to existence, then in cases such as "the jar does not exist," "pleasure does not exist," or "it does not exist," there would be no relation to existence regarding the objects—namely the pleasure and so forth. Consequently, since the relation to existence would require another relation to existence, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). This constitutes a second fault.
This is a fault. Even causal efficiency, such as the fetching of water and so forth, does not exist [in the ultimate sense] because it is a distinct entity from existence (*sattva*).
As it has been said: "Causal efficiency also belongs to things that are not co-nate. He states another fault:
if it is accepted that its very nature (*svarūpa*) consists in performing that [causal function], then [the question arises] regarding the actual existence of that causal efficiency.

Even causal efficacy (*arthakriyākāritva*) exists [in the pot]; yet, in the absence of that [pot], causal efficacy does not exist. Since causal efficacy is understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is not itself perceptible; therefore, even on that basis, the pot would have to be perceived. Consequently, the capacity for performing causal efficacy is also not the [true] nature [of the pot].

It occurs as follows: regarding that capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākaraṇatva*), whether it be "real hair" or "unreal hair," because at the time of the determination of hair and so forth, there is the apprehension [of it], and because all this—
such as its connection with existence— is not manifest, causal efficiency is equivalent to a human horn.
If its own nature (*svarūpa*) is its causal efficiency (*kāritva*), then that causal efficiency would depend upon another causal efficiency, resulting in an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

The existence of an entity consists solely in its being manifest, just like the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, wherein the vibration of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) has not yet been uprooted.

Since this state of manifestation exists for relations and so forth by way of a connection characterized by both difference and non-difference, these [relations] lack reality, just like jars and other such objects.

Without hesitation. "Nevertheless" (*tathāpi*): even though causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is real, people in this world for the most part, seeking the purposeful action of fetching water and so forth through various objects such as jars, dwell as seekers of that purposeful action and engage in worldly affairs (*vyavahāra*) for its sake; such is their capacity for performing that purposeful action.

The opponent, the Vijñānavādin, might argue that [the categories of] relation and so forth do exist. If, however, his heart is now set at ease beyond doubt by this [argument], then— provided he does not become angry—
the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) has been established for all objects, whether they consist of difference, non-difference, or both, along with their relations.
According to the stated principle, "he whose activity consists of worldly conduct," there exists worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) consisting of relations and the like;

that is, there exists worldly transaction wherein jars, cloths, and so forth reside, and which consists of universals (*sāmānya*) and relations. This is because, in such worldly transaction, the cognition of relations and the like is not being directly reflected upon (*aparāmṛśyamānatvāt*).
Even in that case, the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) does not arise clearly; rather, it is the object—

which possesses both difference and non-difference by virtue of being the substratum for the universal and other relations that constitute the conceptual cognition of the cognizer— that is the basis for the aforementioned form of causal efficiency.

In that which is devoid of the conceptual construction of objects such as action and so forth— which consist of the activity of the cognizer— or even when not touched by them, because it has entered into the cognizer through the medium of the aforementioned conceptualizing intellect and rests solely upon its own manifestation, no purposeful action whatsoever occurs.

He demonstrates that very point with the words "tathā hi" (for instance). In the world, first there is a longing once again for that beloved object because of the pleasure previously experienced—and therefore subsequently remembered—and by the word "ādi" (and so forth), the attainment of the object and other such things are included; thus is the sequence.

All worldly activity arises [from this]. That very cognizer by whom a manifestation of pleasure was experienced desires that very same one; however, it is not that another person who possesses a manifestation of pleasure is obtained. Rather, when everything desired has arrived, he is satisfied, thinking, "That pleasure is indeed this very thing."

If it is something already experienced, why is it desired? For it has already been attained. Alternatively, if it is something not yet experienced, how can it be sought? For that which is unknown cannot be remembered; thus, it would be unattainable.
Therefore, this [objection] must be unavoidable for one who maintains the non-existence of the knower (*pramātṛ*).

"This is thus" means that it becomes so in the manner about to be described; the summary meaning of "that very happiness, that indeed, that alone," and "experienced as such, not experienced as such," is as follows: "both that and not that" means that although that happiness has been experienced, it is again [regarded as] experienced because it remains an object of longing.
It occurs. Regarding "in the means to happiness" (*sukhasādhaneṣu*):

[the word] *sādhaneṣu* [is used]. Thus, it should be stated that [this applies] even to garlands, sandalwood, and so forth, which serve as causes for happiness and the like. In the desire for a desired object—that is, in the desire for happiness—or [simply] in the desired [object].

It might be argued that "perceived" means something produced by experience—namely, pleasure or the means of pleasure such as garlands, sandalwood, and so forth—which is contemplated by the knower. This should not be said; for what is perceived does not become the object of desire.
Even though heaven, the locus of specific enjoyment, is unseen, this world is the locus of enjoyment here, characterized by the fitness of the senses.

Because it is a ground where enjoyment has been seen, even heaven is desired; for happiness that has not yet been experienced is lost through the very act of seeing—that is, through experience—and thus there is a longing for it once again.
The meaning is that such happiness is contemplated as being one with the seer (*draṣṭṛ*). This is because it has been contemplated as being one with the seer.
Furthermore, the meaning is that it is capable of being remembered as "this is that very same thing" and of being recognized through re-cognition (*pratyabhijñā*).

Regarding this object, which consists of a relation characterized by both difference and non-difference within its appearing nature, even that which is unperceived— that is, not clearly manifest to direct perception— is another relation, namely the universal (*sāmānya*).

It has entered [into the world] by way of being its very nature of relationship. "Otherwise" means that without such relationships and so forth, no worldly transaction whatsoever can occur in any manner;
thus, [the categories include] the space from Śiva down to the earth, the elements which serve as its specific qualifiers, time, and the states beginning with waking.

"Beginning with Śiva and ending with the Sakala, [all levels] are useful for the subject. Thus: if everyday practice—consisting of the notions of action, relation, generality, substance, and so forth, as well as time—is not real, then even things like pots and cloths, which are the substrata of such practice and are considered real even in your own system, would also lack reality.
One should not be deluded by the thought that the cognition "we do not know" is an erroneous perception because it grasps a relation between actions and so forth; may there be auspiciousness.

Therefore, that which is the internal [principle] of the category of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), whose nature is consciousness manifesting toward external objects— consisting of an infinite variety of conceptualizations such as "this is this" with respect to each individual manifestation— is the *vimarśa*-natured vital breath (*prāṇa*).

According to the principle stated previously, that cognizer who is full of manifold forms of sovereignty— ranging from a distance of a *yojana* to the infinite— and who consists of the pure reflective awareness of "I," is so designated; whereas the means of knowledge (*pramāṇas*), such as perception and the rest, are of the nature of consciousness whose essence is outward-turned manifestation.

"By the sequence of entering into one's own nature" means by means of one’s own form, which is consciousness devoid of sound (niḥsvana-bodha-rūpa). "Yellow" refers to the process of entering into one’s own respective objects of cognition;

thus, it is the internalization [of consciousness] within each respective object of cognition, such as blue or yellow, which constitutes the very life-force of the class of its corresponding means of knowledge, directed inwardly.

Consisting of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), it establishes objects such as "this is blue" or "this is yellow" at the moment of the entry into valid cognition (*pramāveśa*). For the Supreme Knower, Śiva, during the occasion of this entry into cognition, [the power] called "looking at the speaker" refers to the inward-turned rest in the "I-ness" (*ahantā*) expressed as "I see," in relation to which [the object is established].

[All things] are dependent on another. Thus, we praise Śiva, who is the ground of rest for the phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*) consisting of the object of knowledge (*prameya*), the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the act of knowledge (*pramā*), and the knower (*pramātṛ*). As it has been said by the learned: "The emergence and manifestation of the expansion consisting of the knower, the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the act of knowledge... (p. 259).
"Salutations to Tryambaka, the beloved of Ambikā, whose abode is rest, and whose name destroys all misfortune when recited.
Thus, his essential nature has been described. In connection with that, by means of the second chapter (āhnika)...

Having preceded this with an investigation into the relationship consisting in the expansion of the power of that activity, the true nature of the universals (*sāmānya*) and other categories— which constitute that expansion of the power of activity— has been established. Now, however,
the very nature of that relationship itself must be explained primarily by way of its unification.

According to the principle stated that "it must be investigated as residing in the agent and the knower," because it resides in the subject (*pramātṛ*) whose nature is both knower and agent, that relation itself is twofold: the state of being the signified and the signifier (*jñāpya-jñāpakatā*), and the state of being the effect and the cause (*kārya-kāraṇatā*). Regarding the phrase "in that [case]": it refers to the form consisting of the signified and the signifier.

Regarding the objects of cognition and the means of cognition— which serve as the basis for the cognizer’s reflection— the nature of one's own self that was described [in the previous chapter] through such statements as "the connection with action" and so forth,
as well as everything that will be explained in this present chapter, all depends upon the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This is just like the case of an object such as a jar.

Just as [the establishment of an object] depends upon means of valid cognition such as perception, so too does the establishment of the nature of relations and the like residing in things such as jars depend upon those respective observations; for it is well known that the establishment of a real entity depends upon the means of valid cognition. And "in this way" refers to the dependence on the establishment of each respective entity.

Just as there is no operation of an agent upon that [Self], so too there is no operation of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) upon it, because eternality and self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) are present therein; for according to the principle stated, how could such a means of knowledge apply to the Blessed Lord who is of such a nature?
Furthermore, regarding the reality of the nature of Paramaśiva, which is to be established according to the method about to be explained,

it is not tenable that the aforementioned [limited] means of knowledge— which establishes delimited objects of cognition such as jars and cloths while being attached to a delimited subject of cognition— could apply here; this is what is to be established in the present context.

It must necessarily be investigated in two ways: by virtue of its utility as an object and by virtue of its nature as a relation. Through the formulation of "means of knowledge" and "object of knowledge," the conventional usage of "this is such-and-such" is set in motion in order to define the essential nature of the knower.

Thus, with seventeen concluding verses, another chapter (āhnika) begins. Therein, the essential nature of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the result (*phala*) is defined by two verses. The means of knowledge consists of perception and so forth, while the result is the manifestation (*prabhā*). In order to define the essential nature of the object of knowledge (*prameya*), which is the objective domain of those means of knowledge—

In that case, with respect to objects of cognition such as jars and cloth, there occurs no operation of a distinct means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the appearance of forms such as jar-ness, gold-ness, redness, or brilliance; rather,
this is not restricted by the rule of being grounded solely in a single entity whose nature is the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), and thus it is not merely a matter of multiple universals (*sāmānya*).

To demonstrate that the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) pertains solely to the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is qualified by space and time within the form of a composite whole, [the author] states, by the power of the cognizer’s retrospective synthesis (*pratyavamarśa*),
that it pertains to the universal nature (*sāmānyātman*).

(260) The establishment of the object of cognition (*prameya*) as an appearance whose nature is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is stated in ten verses. Regarding the phrase "in connection with that" (332): in connection with the discussion of reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*), the nature of false cognition (*mithyājñāna*) is stated in a verse [as being] both universal in nature (*sāmānyātmaka*) and particular in nature (*svalakṣaṇātmaka*).
The accomplishment of the two-fold object of knowledge (prameya) occurs only by relying upon the nature of the Lord as the agent and the knower; this is demonstrated by the following verse,
and that very [nature], consisting of the means of knowledge (pramāṇa), its fruit (phala), and the object of knowledge (prameya), is defined in these fourteen verses.

That differentiation which was demonstrated by the preceding verse occurs when the subject (*pramātṛ*) exists in the form [described]. Therefore, it would be a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it serves as the ground for its manifestation; it does not become an object of knowledge (*prameya*), like a jar or similar things.
For if it were an object of knowledge, then even here—in this case of the subject who transcends the universe—[the same consequence would follow].

The possibility of the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to this Self consists in the fruit of establishing a mere conventional usage— such as "I am the Lord," "I am full," "I am eternal," and "I am all-pervading"— which has not occurred previously; thus, the scripture consisting of the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā* is the means of valid cognition.

The intended meaning is that this is stated by means of three verses. Therefore, by the phrase "such is the error," it is established that the cognitions—regarding the connection with action and so forth—are not of the nature of error;
rather, this is said in order to determine that they indeed possess the nature of error, [and to refute] the view that their nature consists of outward-directed consciousness.

Regarding "the fruit of that means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇasya tatphala*): he first restates the nature of the fruit—which is the very life-breath of that means of valid cognition—and of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) which consists of valid knowledge (*pramā*), is inward-turned, and is well-known in systems such as the Nyāya. [This nature is] the object [presented as] "this is such-and-such."

"Blue, yellow, and so forth"—this [refers to] that which is established by virtue of two modes: first, as a universal form (*sāmānyarūpa*) permeated by the nature of "this-ness" (*idantā*) throughout all things, such that they are perceived as "of this kind"; and second, as a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) distinguished by space and time, associated with various universals. It is by means of these two aspects that [the object] is determined.

The ellipsis to be supplied is: "that by whose power one does not overstep the fixed limits of manifestation pertaining to each respective thing is designated as 'pramāṇa' (the means of valid cognition) in the verse. As for the phrase "so'pi" (even that): even that cognition in the form of *pramāṇa*, because it is oriented toward ever-new objects of knowledge (*prameya*) at every moment in terms of space, time, and so forth...

Being himself ever-new, with a constantly arising manifestation, he is the self-luminous one; thus, Māyā is that manifestation which is intended as a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), conceived as real by the subject (*pramātṛ*) as being non-different from him.
"Internally" means: just as blue, yellow, and so forth exist externally, so too internally they become of the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).

In a case where there is no distinction of place, time, and so forth— where [the object] is not differentiated by place, time, or form, and for that very reason appears as a universal— in regard to a real entity such as gold, which is the referent of each individual designation like "the pot" or "golden-red," the cognition "it is not silver" is uncontradicted; thus, being of the nature of the fruit of that means of valid cognition, it becomes a valid cognition (*pramā*).

"By whose power" (yadvaśāt): by whose power— that is, by whose efficacy— the object (*vastu*), such as blue and so forth which is the domain of the external organs, and pleasure and so forth which are the domains of the internal organs, are [cognized] as "this" (*idam*)— that is, in the form of a universal (*sāmānyarūpa*) permeated by the all-pervading "this-ness" (*idantā*)— as "of this kind" (*ittham*), meaning "located here," "at this time," and "having such a form."
And it is established through its connection with various other attributes in the form of specific qualifiers;

as "blue" or "pleasure," it does not overstep its own determined and appropriate limits of self-luminosity. Such knowledge that establishes an object of this kind is what is called "valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) in the world.
It remains established—this is the remainder of the sense, namely that it has been determined by those headed by Akṣapāda.

Having investigated that [reality] with one capable of investigating the nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by means of an analysis of the nature of the means of valid cognition, observe the manner of that investigation. Here, the nature of objects such as pots and cloths is the cognizer (*pramātṛ*).
Without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consisting of activity, [consciousness] does not establish itself by its own power alone.

As it has been said: "For indeed, of those things that have become insentient," and so forth. If it were to establish itself by its own power simply because of its insentience, then there would be no distinction between the appearances "blue is manifest" and "Caitra’s blue is manifest."

How could this be? Therefore, because there is no establishment [of the object] by its own power, it is established by the power of another; thus, that other thing which pervades it—even if it is a fallacy of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāsa*)—would be insentient (*jaḍa*), just like that object. This is like one blind man leading another blind man.

The gift of the hand. The meaning is that an appearance of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāsa*) which is insentient in nature is not capable of establishing a real object. Therefore, that appearance of a means of valid cognition which has arrived for the purpose of establishing a real object is itself of the nature of consciousness (*saṃvidātman*). "That too" refers to that which is of the nature of consciousness.
Even a semblance of valid cognition (pramāṇābhāsa), by virtue of having consciousness as its very essence, becomes submerged in the pure ocean of Great Consciousness, the Supreme Śiva.
If it is thus pure, identical to Him, undifferentiated, and perfectly full, it could not be the cause for the establishment of even a single object such as "blue. At that very moment—

Because that pseudo-means of knowledge (pramāṇābhāsa) is pervasive even in the case of yellow and so forth, and because it is submerged in the Great Light (mahāprakāśa), it simultaneously establishes the entire universe just like the Great Light itself. "From that" means: from the very simultaneous determination of blue, yellow, and so forth.

Because it would follow that [the cognition] would be a determiner (*vyavasthāpaka*). This semblance of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāsa*) is distinct from the Great Light (*mahāprakāśa*), being colored solely by blue; for this very reason, it is directed toward the blue.
Consequently, having the nature of the manifestation of blue, it is the determiner of blue alone—the manifestation of blue.
The very nature of that which appears as a semblance of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāsa*) is its capacity to establish that [object] as blue. And that is the manifestation of the blue.

If the manifestation of the blue were distinct from the Great Manifestation (*mahāprakāśa*), then it would follow that there would also be a manifestation of yellow. That manifestation of yellow is the essence of consciousness (*cittattva*).

Because there is no distinction in their identity (*tādātmya*). Therefore, for that blue which is distinct from that Great Light (*mahāprakāśa*), there occurs an appearance that is a semblance of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāsa*). If blue is also thus, then that which is capable of being conjoined with an appearance non-distinct from the Great Light is the illuminator of blue.

If that false means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāsa*), which manifests as blue and is capable of appearing as something empty because it lacks even the slightest distinction from the Great Light, were to be distinct from the Great Light, then for that false means of knowledge...

For otherwise, it would follow that there is no distinction between blue and other objects from the Great Light (mahāprakāśa), since they too would lack distinction from it. Since there is not even the slightest distinction from the Great Light, neither the object of knowledge (prameya), nor the means of knowledge (pramāṇa),
nor the knower (pramātṛ) can withstand [separation] from the Great Light, which is identical with Supreme Śiva (paramaśiva).
Due to its sovereignty, the fullness of the I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhantā*) is the very nature of consciousness within its own self.
As the life-force (*prāṇanā*) that manifests the contraction of objects and their mutual distinctness, I am the Great Lord (*maheśvara*).
"I am not the jar," or "I am Caitra"—this is the manifestation of contraction. This contraction is "not I."
Because Maheśvara and the others are characterized by mutual limitation, they are called "void" (*śūnya*). Such a manifestation of limitation is the emergence of the subject belonging to *māyā*;
it occurs through this single, non-dual creative power (*sṛṣṭi-śakti*) of the Great Light itself.

Through the manifestation of the contraction of one's own self at precisely the same time as the manifestation of the subject’s contraction— which is Māyā, since it is the cause of the subject's emergence—

there occurs, from the ultimate perspective (*paramārthataḥ*), the unfolding of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of knowledge (*prameya*). Therefore, because of that, [one thinks], "I am asleep."
"I am fainted," "I am happy," "I am miserable," "I am hungry," "I am thirsty," "I have colic," "I am emaciated," "I am prosperous," "I am poor"— this is, in sequence,
the contraction consisting of the appropriation of supports such as the void, the vital breaths, the body, the jar, and so forth.

However, because the perceiver— namely the body and so forth— is contracted by appropriation (*parigraha*), it is precisely that objective portion (*vedyāṃśa*) which is created and withdrawn by the Lord; for even when the agent-nature, whose essence is the light of non-otherness and I-consciousness, enters into the body and so forth, it remains of the singular nature of the Lord, according to the principle already stated.

Because it is inseparable even at the fall of the body, that manifestation— which is accepted as the vital breath (prāṇa)— belongs to the subject of Māyā from the beginning of creation until infinite time, consisting of an inward-turned self-awareness in the form of "I. As long as its nature is directed toward objects of knowledge such as jars and cloths, it belongs to the object of knowledge.

Because it possesses a distinct nature due to its differentiation from the appearances of place, time, and form, that [means of knowledge] as well—namely, the semblance of a means of knowledge that establishes that [object]—must be seen to have a mutually different nature in every moment, just like the object of knowledge. This [semblance of a means of knowledge]... [is characterized by] a new arising at every moment.

By the words of the Sūtra: he states the meaning of the term *abhinava*— because it itself is momentary by virtue of establishing objects as qualified by their respective momentary times, it does not suffer even the slightest exhaustion from the mere duration of a single moment in any object whatsoever.

It is not stained. Because of that unstained nature, although it is said to be "ever-newly arising," such a manifestation of vital breath (*prāṇābhāsa*), being attached to the subject of *māyā*, would [otherwise] be so; in that case, there would be no cognition for someone that "the yellow manifestation has arisen for me alone," whose blue manifestation had previously arisen.

The statement "this blue appearance is mine" is established by everyone's own experience; it is uncontradicted at all times and in all places, and thus is not illusory (*amāya*). Here, "illusory" (*māyā*) refers to that which appears as belonging to the subject (*pramātṛ*) by way of its own nature, yet possesses a new and ever-renewed emergence because of its constant orientation toward ever-new objects of knowledge (*prameya*).

The appearance of cognition (*bodhābhāsa*). Since it establishes the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that is about to be described along with its authority, if one asks, "What is the nature of that [appearance]? he says: "That very thing, which has the form of cognition, is the appearance of the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇābhāsa*);
the connection is that it is the result (*phala*) in the form of valid cognition (*pramā*). This is like the case of "pot" and "jar" being synonyms.

It has been stated that *pramā* is another synonym for *pramāṇa*. It has not been stated that this [cognition] is of the same form as *pramā*, which consists of the fruit of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇaphala*).
Here, within the nature of cognition as appearance (*abhāsabodharūpe*), "appearance" refers to that which is directed toward external objects such as a jar.

It is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by virtue of its nature as luminosity. That which was previously established here as this "intuition" (*pratibhā*)—namely, the inward-turned self-nature consisting of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)—is [perceived] solely through its own essential being, though it appears contracted in the state of an object; the word "solely" (*kevalam*) refers to one's own self.
Although there is no contraction in its nature as pure consciousness (*saṃvid-rūpa*), when it is in a state of contraction consisting of an outward-turned certainty toward objects,
that very cognition of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa-bodha*)— by virtue of its inward-turned reflective awareness (*vimarśa-svabhāva*)— is the fruit, the light; it is indeed one and the same.
The manifestation of consciousness (*bodhābhāsa*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) when it is extroverted; it is *ra* when it is introverted.

He confirms this by illustrating it with an example: "He who is brave is the very same person who is victorious. Since bravery and victory reside in one and the same person—such that because "I am brave," therefore "I am victorious"—[the two are non-different].

It is established by way of the relationship between cause and effect. "In this way" means: just as there is a relationship of cause and effect between heroism and victory, so too, because for a single cognizer there is the manifestation "this is blue" externally with respect to a single blue object, there follows from that the internal reflective awareness "this is blue. Thus, [it pertains] to those things related to the blue.

Although the Blessed One is of a single nature, there exists a relationship of cause and effect through His manifestation as the internal and external forms of light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). By virtue of that—that is, by virtue of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—there arises an internal reflective awareness in the form of valid cognition (*pramā*), whose essence is the determination of the object of knowledge (*prameya*). Furthermore, the result is of the nature of an operation; thus [it belongs to] the subject (*pramātṛ*).
The result,

which consists of the operation of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) related to the cognizer (pramātṛ), is the operation of the means of valid cognition related to the cognizer; and since that operation belongs to the cognizer who is performing the operation, by means of it, the object of cognition (prameya) [is apprehended].
Because it appears in a different form when being directed toward its object, there is non-difference between the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and its fruit (*phala*).

Furthermore, even the means of knowledge becomes a means of knowledge only through the power of the cognizer’s reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). Reflective awareness is the very essence of all means of knowledge.

(337) That [consciousness], which is the very life-force of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is untouched by other appearances such as space, time, and so forth. Therefore, even in the case of an entity whose nature is universal (*sāmānya*), which is of a single form and pervades everywhere—
such as in the notions "this is a jar" or "it is red," and in the jar-ness, redness, and so forth residing in the jar— [it remains untouched].

The word functions as a form of denotation because it is not mixed with the two appearances of space and time— which are intent on establishing the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of things as "being here" and "being now"— due to its pervasiveness.

Precisely for this reason, when the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) operates toward a universal that is eternal, it functions by way of a reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) whose life-force is the respective designating word, as in the appearances of "pot-ness," "gold-ness," and so forth. For even the appearance "this is located in a pot" is like the appearance of "gold-ness" and the rest.

It has been stated by the venerable Teacher himself that [consciousness] rests solely upon the appearance of being present before one— the essence of which is "this"— which pertains to all entities and is unmixed with other appearances such as space and time. Thus,
whatever entity appears to the cognizer as determined before him, in the form "this is this," [that is what constitutes its manifestation].

Therefore, just as the appearance of "gold-ness" arises through the universal of "this-ness" (idantā-sāmānya) which extends to all existents and shines forth as permeated by gold existing in all places, so too this appearance of "this is a jar" arises precisely through the universal of "this-ness" that is permeated by jars, cloths, and so forth, existing in all places. Thus...
This very limit (anta), because it possesses a universal form, is merely the appearance of a universal form;

however, the specific individual characteristic (*vastu-svalakṣaṇa*) such as "gold-ness" (*kāñcanatva*), because it is a universal form, is merely the appearance of a universal form that serves as the locus of manifestation. These alone are each...
It is another appearance of something else; for this very reason, it is distinct from universals (*sāmānya*).
In that regard, regarding that manifestation as its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which grasps that particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the authority.
When those [objects] to be mixed together within that particular characteristic have been apprehended by each respective means of valid cognition...
"In this case, a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does not apprehend what has already been apprehended regarding appearances such as 'gold-ness' and so forth.

In that regard, it will apply to the remaining [object], such as fire and the like; for, according to our stated principle, conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), which is of the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), is animated by that reflective awareness, and reflective awareness is the very life-force of language.

Even for the Vijñānavādin, who— though unwillingly— asserts that the validity of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in his own system depends on the determination (*adhyavasāya*) regarding the respective [appearances] such as "jar-ness" or "gold-ness" when each appearance comes to rest, [validity] must necessarily reside in each individual appearance (*pratyābhāsa*). (338)

Let it be granted that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must be accepted; however, what is the use of this intermediate digression, other than the reflection on the essential nature (*svarūpa*) which is the subject at hand? It is intended solely to demonstrate the non-sublated nature of the "cognized" (*miti*), which consists of the fruit of the means of valid cognition and has the form of inward-turned reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
He dispels this doubt with the words beginning with "nanu" (but surely).

If reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) alone were the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then it would exist even in the case of a double moon. Not so; such a reflective awareness [is not the same].

A double moon does not exist at all. That reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), termed "gold," through its connection with the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the experience of gold, manifests itself as its own nature—
the attainment of the purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) well-known in the world, such as bracelets and other ornaments.
Proceeding toward its conclusion, if its function is not uprooted by any other intervening obstructive reflection, it remains firm for that very reason and becomes such [as it was intended].
If it were to tolerate being uprooted again in the interim— as in the case of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell— it would have been so even previously.
In the discernment of gold, just as in the discernment of silver,

even the relationship of sublated and sublator arises among cognitions because they are grounded in a single cognizer, according to the principle stated: "The relationship of sublated and sublator [occurs] for those who are opposed to abiding in their own self."

By means of the very single cognizing subject— the inward-turned "I"-form which is unconditioned by space and time and serves as the foundational wall for the repose of the two cognitions in the form of the sublated and the sublator—
[the former] has already [effected] the uprooting of the cognition of silver prior to the latter.
"It is not gold"— this very self-awareness, one's own direct experience,

is the witness. Having first perceived a piece of mother-of-pearl from afar due to its brilliance and seeing it as having the form of reality, for one who has engaged in the error regarding the mother-of-pearl, thinking "this is indeed silver," [the silver is negated].
After the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), once that [silver] has been extracted for the sake of ornaments such as bracelets,

one experiences the non-reflection (*avimarśīkaraṇa*) that "this is not silver," even prior [to the extraction]. This non-reflection— the cognition that "it is mother-of-pearl" and "it was silver"— is the uprooting of the silver.

Or rather, by means of inquiry, it will be explained in the passage "the single reflective awareness of silver" (*rajataika-vimarśa*) that [the cognition], while destroying the persistence of the operation in the form of valid knowledge consisting of reflective awareness regarding that [silver], attains its establishment in the subject (*pramātṛ*). This being the case, even for another person, there is the perception of two moons.
While he was still desiring to display to him the curiosity known as the sight of a previously unseen object,
even before that desire could be fulfilled, [the Lord] saw that this ignorant man— deluded and under the sway of objects such as enemies, friends, derision, and grief— was being uprooted.
The prior reflective awareness, "the rising of two moons," is perceived by one's own self-awareness even as it is being uprooted upon hearing the words of another person, "this is not two moons."

As for the word "nanu": let it be that the cognition "this is a double moon" is erroneous because, at the time of performing a purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) characterized by curiosity, it is sublated by the cognition of a single moon. However, in a case where one does not seek a purposeful action regarding a certain object—there...

How can there be the conventional usage of "sublation" (bādhā)? Is it not the case that nothing is destroyed, because of the absence of the conventional usage of sublation and non-sublation? For in every action, the engagement of cognizers is based solely on what is authoritative, through a certainty of the form: "This will be thus. It is not otherwise.
If it is asked, "By what means do knowers engage in their respective actions? he replies: "Or [one acts] with the thought 'there will be a result'.

In the case of agriculture and the like, even one who is hungry engages with hesitation; yet, because of the predominance of the objective of removing the affliction of hunger through eating, his engagement occurs despite that hesitation.
For some, when such an act has been committed through their own understanding, this negligence occurs; thus,
when the transgression is determined by the intellect, when the sin is conceived by the mind,
and when the visible sin consists of impaling one on an iron stake, even afterwards the King [punishes] him.

Because we observe activity directed toward theft [and other such ends], therefore, the world’s excessive desire for an object is precisely the excessive hope that is the cause of engagement. Consequently, it is the knower’s own excessive desire for an object that is the cause of engagement in agriculture and so forth; thus, he occasionally engages in agriculture and the like.
The knower, until the attainment of the fruit, possesses a cognition that has not been uprooted by anything— just as in the case of "this is silver"—

and thus he is one who possesses the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) that "this will be so. He states that this *vimarśa* constitutes the validity of activities such as agriculture, culminating in the fruit, and its very reality.

In some cases, it is understood otherwise; that is, while that activity possesses the nature of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as previously described, because it lacks its [expected] fruit, it is understood as a misconception (*viparyaya*), even though it is [actually] true. By this cognizer—either from this present life or from previous hundreds of births—this...

It becomes a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because, through long-term investigation, the distinction between what is a valid means of knowledge and what is not is established according to one's practice;

that is, through practice, one who knows the true nature of gems and gold [discerns] the nature of a valid means of knowledge upon merely seeing it, just as one does with jewels and silver at the very first glance.

He perceives [the knower] as distinct from other people. Thus, for a cognizer who knows the distinction between valid and invalid means of knowledge, there certainly exists a distinction from other people, produced by a difference in causes such as the practice of previous births. And therefore, such a distinction—
Having made the limited desire that clings to suffering—which naturally flows forth—subservient to his own will, he considers it bearable, meaning capable of being endured;
however, he does not consider it to be that which uproots itself. Precisely for this reason, because of the pride of having abandoned such seeking, there is no longer that seeking for it.

In this world, regarding agriculture and other such activities, one who is not impelled by a great seizure (mahāgraha) or a great elemental influence (mahābhūta), and who— due to doubt as to whether it will bear fruit or not— is afraid of contradiction, nevertheless arrives at a certainty of validity through the cognition "this is mine" and "it is exactly thus," based on the means of valid cognition such as direct perception (pratyakṣa).

One who acts with regard to perceptible things such as agriculture, or toward goals such as heaven, is not deceived by the attainment of those results— namely, agriculture, heaven, and so forth— and thus becomes one who has correctly understood [the means]. Such a cognizer is called "one who acts with foresight" (prekṣāpūrvakārī), because he perceives a future object even beforehand.
"One who acts with foresight" is what is said in the world by those who know the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); this is the ellipsis.

For those who, out of delusion, think that knowledge such as that of universals (*sāmānya*) and relations (*saṃbandha*) is not a valid cognition, [the author addresses] their doubt regarding its lack of validity.

(p. 267) In order to establish that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) operates even with respect to universals (*sāmānya*) and the like—which reside in things such as jars—just as it does with respect to those jars themselves, we have followed the nature of the means of valid cognition as described by Akṣapāda and others as being "non-worldly" (*alaukika*); this is the remainder [of the sentence]. [This applies to] action, relation, and so forth.

The nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been stated solely for the purpose of establishing the reality [of the self]. Therefore, the distinction between perception and other means of valid cognition as taught in external treatises— such as the division of the world into hearers and so forth— is merely a distinction of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

The apprehension of sensory objects such as pleasure and so forth is one means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); the apprehension of external objects such as blue and so forth by means of the external organs is another means of valid cognition; the definition is simply perception (*pratyakṣa*) itself; and the repeated examination of what constitutes such inference (*anumāna*) and what constitutes such [perception] is [the process of investigation].

He has not been exhausted by [arguments] such as "by merit there is contemplation" (*punyena carcanam*). He states the general definition of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*):

whatever cognition is uncontradicted—like [the cognition of] silver in mother-of-pearl—and because it possesses stability, is characterized by unimpeded continuity, and results in reflective discernment (*vimarśa*).

It establishes that each respective means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is itself of the nature of consciousness, resting upon objects in the form of the cognizable, and finally grounded in the essential nature of the knower (*pramātṛ*). And that means of knowledge in the form of perception consists of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) [engaged] in the knowledge produced by the external senses, which arises from the senses of the knower through *māyā*.

In the self-awareness of sensory pleasures and so forth, which is omnipresent, the knowledge of the yogi is indeed non-contradictory; there is no contradiction in it. He states the reason for its non-contradiction:
"precisely in the primary sense," that is, by way of predominance alone, without dependence on the appearance of anything else.

For this [consciousness] rests directly— without mediation— in the object of knowledge (*prameya*), which consists of appearances such as blue and so forth, pleasure and so forth, and the nature of the universe itself.

Having thus defined direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*), he speaks in order to define the nature of inference (*anumāna*) and the other means of knowledge. The particle *tu* indicates the distinction of inference from direct perception. Such being the case, inference is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), arising from the inferential subject (*anumātṛ*), who is the knower (*pramātṛ*).

Cognition, however, is the apprehension or determinative awareness of one thing— such as smoke or a *śiṃśapā* tree— within another appearance, such as fire or "treeness," based on another appearance that has become its effect (in the case of smoke) or its essential nature (in the case of a *śiṃśapā*). This occurs through the mediation of those other appearances.

Therefore, by means of [specific properties] such as "smoke-ness" and others, and by means of [general properties] such as "tree-ness" and others, there is a restriction regarding the relationship of cause and effect (*sahakāryakāraṇabhāva-niyama*) and a restriction regarding co-inherence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya-niyama*). It is precisely fire that has smoke as its effect, and it is precisely a *śiṃśapā* tree that possesses the nature of being a tree; such is the determination (*niyati*) of the Lord (*īśvara*).

It must be understood that [the yogi] subsists solely upon the power of *niyati* (destiny), and not otherwise. Since nothing occurs without the power of the Lord’s *niyati*, the Lord, by virtue of the yogi’s subsistence upon the power of *niyati*, [determines] in whatever place or time a yogi might effect a transgression of destiny; and in whatever place or time there might be smoke or other things produced [by him], apart from [ordinary] smoke and so forth.

The sovereign power of necessity (niyati-śakti) has arisen such that inference is a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) only with respect to a specific place or time, and not in any other place or time. Scriptural authority (āgama), however,
is distinct from the sound grasped by the ear— which is the form of the object— and consists of the nature of consciousness itself.

The innermost [consciousness], whose nature is the most firm reflective awareness that "this indeed belongs to the Supreme Lord," is incessant and inseparable; because it consists of such reflective awareness as "this is a jar, not a cloth" or "this mountain possesses fire," it is the very life-force even of perception and other means of knowledge.

[This is] conventional usage. (342) As it has been said: "Since the arising of cognition does not occur without the interpenetration of words," therefore, that which is perceived by the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) whose nature is scripture is true exactly as it was seen. Regarding this, he provides an illustration with the word "just as": "I am indeed Garuḍa."

Therefore, regarding this matter, even that mass of sounds in the form of scripture— which, when such internal sound has arisen, maintains its conformity with the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the Self— is also a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), just like that reflective awareness itself.

Regarding this, he provides an illustration: "I shall attain heaven through the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice"—in this reflection, the Vedic statement "one desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma" serves as a favorable support; likewise, in the reflection "I am the consecrated one who partakes in non-return."

The word in the form of the Śaiva Siddhānta accords with [the seeker's disposition]. In the reflective awareness, "I, enduring intense afflictions, shall go to the state of a Buddha," the word "homage to the Buddhists" (bauddhān namaḥ) accords with that disposition.
Regarding the inquiry, "Shall I, being capable of enduring intense afflictions, attain the state of an Arhat?", the scripture says that in that regard—

such as in the case of heaven and so forth— the qualification of that seeker does not undergo reversal. This is because when there is an injunctive statement such as, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," [the result follows] from that statement.
This is because tomorrow alone is suitable for its performance there; in this same way, it should be understood in other cases as well.
The verbal expression in the form of reflection—such as "I shall go to heaven, which is the fruit of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice"—belongs to another qualified person (the sacrificer).

Because it lacks the nature of firm conviction, it is simply not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*). It follows, then, that this single scripture would be a valid means of knowledge for some and not a valid means of knowledge for others; yet this is not tenable, because a means of knowledge in the form of a scripture cannot be partisan.

To him who speaks thus, he gives this reply: One who knows the truth of the way of the world—that is, the established worldly conduct—is not [merely] a knower of that. Nevertheless, you are not to be neglected by us;
for it has been said that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is impartial. What is the meaning of that statement? Of one...

A cognition of blue has arisen in the form of perception; does that cognition of blue manifest the blue object to every cognizer? (343) Does the cognition of smoke, which is perceptual for one person, manifest the presence of fire to every cognizer? Is this method [applicable] even to a treasure found in the morning?

"Obtained by one who does not exist" refers to the scripture (*āgama*) in the form of a prediction from a perfected being (*siddha*). Without such an instructor, what would be the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for all of it?
(p. 269) Now, even in the case of that very instruction, at some time, through great effort, there may likewise be the acquisition of wealth.

Furthermore, verbal testimony— defined as the act of signifying which conveys its own internal object through the medium of words— is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for every qualified person (*adhikārī*).
It is just like the eye, light, and so forth, which serve as auxiliaries to perceptual false knowledge.

Invalidity becomes accompanied by the absence of validity. "To this extent" means that, due to defects in the light, the sense organs, and so forth, there is no status as a valid perception for a perception whose nature is correct knowledge. "In the same way" means that, just like perception, that very word such as *jyotiṣṭoma* [is established].

Precisely because Śūdras and others lack qualification, [the scripture] consists of a firm reflective awareness; for this very reason, even though it provides assistance to what is not a means of valid knowledge— that is, to a semblance of scripture— it serves the purpose of the means of valid knowledge characterized by verbal testimony in the form of true scripture, which consists of firm reflective awareness, with respect to the qualified person.
Possessing validity, it becomes capable of rejecting the fault of partiality.

What need is there for more? For indeed, every scripture consists of prohibitions such as "one should act thus" or "one should not act thus," [specifying] a restricted authority, a restricted place, a restricted time, and restricted auxiliary factors.

It establishes a restricted deliberation. "For this very reason" means that because its authority is restricted, that very worldly consensus which is uncontradicted is considered the true speech of the Lord (aiśvarī vāk). By the verse beginning with "by that," it is stated that there is a restriction of place and time: "in whatever place" (*yatra yasmin deśe*) and "at whatever time" (*yadā yasmin kāle*). As it has been said: "to whatever extent... (*yāvati*).
The power of destiny (*niyati-śakti*) arises such that, within a specific place and time, inference (*anumāna*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

For that reason, Bhartṛhari, the author of the *Nyāyabhāṣya*, and others have stated that when there is a pervasion (*vyāpti*) across all places and times, perception (*pratyakṣa*) and scripture (*āgama*) are the sublaters (*bādhaka*) of inference.

Therefore, since the entire nature of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is known within a single moment of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), what is the use of specific definitions? According to the Sautrāntika principle that "non-contradictory cognition is valid cognition" (*avisaṃvādi vijñānaṃ pramāṇam*), for one who [holds this view]...

He states that non-contradiction (*avisaṃvādakatva*) is the defining characteristic of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). By that [non-contradiction], there is the capacity to lead the cognizer toward the object of cognition (*prameya*); that is, the attainment of the object of cognition, which consists in being the cause of engagement (*pravartakatva*) with respect to that which is fit for engagement, capable of being attained, and attainable.
By stating that the "manifestation of the object" (*vastuna upadarśatvam*) is also a characteristic of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*), the Buddhist—

according to the principle stated [in his own texts] that "it is a self-manifestation arising anew"— has not said anything at all regarding the true nature [of cognition], which consists in its resting within the knowledge accepted as valid cognition, the very form of the subject’s own manifestation (*pramātṛ-svābhāsa-rūpa*).

[It is] a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). If it is established by this definition stated by us, then it is successfully resolved; that is to say, it is thoroughly examined. "Otherwise" means: if it is not established by this definition, then what was stated by him [as] the definition of a means of valid cognition cannot be so called, because it is impossible to state [it as such].
(270) Without words, there is merely the contortion of the face, the shaking of the head, the wriggling of the toes, and so forth; enough of this excessive detail.
Having thus defined the nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*), [the author now addresses] the object of that means of valid cognition and its result...

He demonstrates at length for the sake of reflecting upon the true nature of the object of knowledge (*prameya*), beginning with the word "nanu" (but surely). Regarding the term "ghaṭa" (pot), as well as "this" (*idam*) and "such-like" (*etādṛk*), which establish external objects, that which is internal—the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) itself—is merely a semblance of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāsa*). This is so in each case of singular designation, such as "red" and so forth.
Regarding the statement that cognition occurs with respect to an object that is undifferentiated by space and time, and is therefore of a universal nature:

therein, each individual designation such as "jar" refers even here [to the object] which consists of a collection of appearances such as gold and so forth, and is characterized as being present at this very moment.

If [the universal] resides in a particular characterized by place and time— namely, in an external *svalakṣaṇa* such as a jar, which is the object of an outward-directed means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes such a thing— then, for that very reason, in that very jar and so forth, prior even to the apprehension of that thing consisting of the *svalakṣaṇa*, [it would have to exist] in all places.

It is logical that [the cognition] occurs in what is permeated by the jar. Furthermore, regarding gold-ness and the like, which are permeated throughout all locations, there is a single appearance of a universal (*sāmānyābhāsa*) as the object of each individual designation—such as "jar," "gold," or "red"—and a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) operates therein. How, then, can it be said that [the object of perception is] the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)?

Dispelling the doubt that [the object] consists of the appearance of various universals such as "gold-ness" and so forth, he says— beginning with the word *kāñcana*— in order to show the ultimate nature of the object of knowledge (*prameya*), which is the domain of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the reality of things.
When the identity of an object— such as "red" and so forth— is established through the synthesis of its appearances,

then according to the desire of the cognizer who acts as he pleases, there arises a state of "seeking" (arthitva) that conforms to his wish; and in accordance with that seeking, there occurs a process of linguistic acquisition (*vyutpatti*) based upon the conventional usage of elders who establish conventions such as "this is gold" or "this is red."
Successively, one conceives of various common appearances as "gold," "copper," or "red";
externally, this perceived object such as a jar is conceived through its broad base and belly-shape, and its nature as a warp and woof.
Even though each [element] is individually a single self, it is not merely that much; that is, it does not exist as a single, unitary form alone.

Rather, it also undergoes externalization—being differentiated separately through various manifestations such as "golden," "red," and "solid. This is what is meant by "differentiation" (*nirbhajyamānatā*).
He establishes this very point with the words "For instance" (*tathā hi*) and so forth: within each individual object, such as a jar,
according to the will of the knower— either through his autonomy, or according to his desire,
or according to his proficiency— the conventional designation (*saṃketa*) established by authoritative persons [occurs].
Alternatively, by relying on what was previously established, there occurs an individual analysis in such forms as "golden," "red," or "elevated.
(p. 271) Thus, according to the sequence stated by the knower, when there is a threefold analysis based on preference and so forth—
When [the pot] is being analyzed, reflections such as "gold" and so forth appear as distinct entities.
Now, if the pot—which is of a single nature—is divided according to the forms of various universals such as "gold-ness," then only that division remains; how can its collective form be one?

The *svalakṣaṇa* (particular characteristic) is said to be that reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) belonging to the cognizer which serves as the vitalizing principle for those various appearing manifestations, such as "gold-ness" and so forth; for those seeking the true value, this [awareness] is sometimes called "the reflection upon each manifestation."

It rests upon the appearance of gold residing in the jar; for one desiring water, it rests upon the jar alone; for one desiring brilliance, it rests upon the brilliance residing in the jar. Thus, they come to rest upon each individual appearance. "At that time" means at the moment of resting upon each appearance, accompanied by reflective awareness (*savimarśa*). "Supreme and non-supreme" (*parāpara*)... [refers to this state].
