When that same cognizer [perceives] the touch of gold as existing in all places and times, there arises the conventional usage of "higher" and "lower" universals (*sāmānya*), because [the former] is the touch of gold characterized by specific space and time,
while [the latter] is the particularity (*svalakṣaṇa*) consisting of the specific gold present before one. Thus, there occurs the linguistic convention of a universal that is both higher and lower.
Sometimes, when qualities such as the appearance of gold and so forth are manifested,
there occurs a blending of space, time, and form— expressed as "this is here, this is thus"— by establishing the predominance of the jar which serves as the substratum for that manifestation.

When the vital breath (*prāṇa*) becomes reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), then that object consisting of a jar becomes a single particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) qualified by the appearance of gold and so forth. Having thus demonstrated the intended meaning of the aphorism, he states the application of the aphorism: "The particle *api* is displaced [in its position]. [It refers to] synthesis (*anusandhāna*)."
"Established" means that which is established as a single identity through reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)— as "this is that very same thing"— by mixing with the appearances of gold and so forth;
that [object] whose nature is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), even though it exists as a single entity such as a jar or the like,
possesses therein *ruci* (inclination), *svātantrya* (autonomy), *arthitva* (desire), subjection to the longing for purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), and proficiency (*vyutpatti*).
And the phrase "yathā" (just as) refers to taking refuge in the aforementioned usage of the elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*);

the meaning is that the appearance of gold and so forth is indeed differentiated, just as was stated in the passage beginning with "according to one's preference" (*yathā ruci*). Now, regarding the word "atha" (now):
it confirms that [the appearance] is indeed the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) by first presenting what is well-known through established perception.

Someone, in accordance with their own preference, contemplates only length within a particular individual person who is well-known for being conscious— a length that pervades many parts and exists even in young people— while regarding that very same [person] as having a nature devoid of joints and bonds.
It reflects upon circularity itself, which belongs even to such things as a stone;
it contemplates a certain verticality consisting of the act of ascending from below to above.
Even in a pillar, there exists a certain capacity for independence, such as moving or not moving.

Since the very nature of being a person (*puruṣatva*) is common to all persons, even the appearances of "Brahmin-ness" and so forth must be determined within their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*); thus, a well-known example that pervades both the insentient and the sentient has been shown.

p. 272) Likewise, even in the case of a single particular instance of smoke (*dhūma-svalakṣaṇa*), the property of smokeness (*dhūmatva*) residing in all smoke located in every place must be divided by way of its generalities—such as "being sandalwood" (*candanatva*) and, within that, further distinctions such as "red sandalwood," "white sandalwood," or "jatuka sandalwood. This too is a well-known example.

Just as appearances such as length and so forth— which are well-known in relation to a single specific particular (svalakṣaṇa) like a person, being qualified by place and time— as well as [appearances] such as "smokeness" and so forth,
are differentiated individually according to one's own preference and so on, in the same way, within that very same [particular].
Since the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a jar is as unestablished as the specific characteristic of a person and so forth,
[the opponent]— seeking to avoid the first "shattering of the heart" regarding the illustrative example (*dārṣṭāntika*)— first analyzes existence itself,
which also exists in cloth and other things; whereas one who seeks to fetch water analyzes the appearance of "jar-ness."
That which is also pervasive in other jars: for one desiring an object suitable for being brought or not brought, it is the substance;

for one desiring its price, it is the appearance of gold; for one desiring its core, it is the appearance of brilliance; and by the inclusion of "and so forth," for one desiring extreme firmness, it is the solidity. Thus...

This should also be applied to aesthetic relish (*ruci*) and proficiency (*vyutpatti*). Thus, the various manifestations (*ābhāsa*)— such as "existent," "jar," "substance," "sandalwood," and "brilliance"—

act to produce both distinct and non-distinct effects, such as the avoidance of heartbreak and so forth, according to the manner described above, within the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of sound (*dhvani*) such as "existent," "jar," or "red."
The word becomes the locus and the object of the designation "form.

Here, first of all, within the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the person, which is established as being conscious, one may distinguish appearances according to one's own will and autonomy, or according to the form of one's preference or desire. As it has been said:

Because distraction is its essence and the wasting of time is its essence, one should act according to that very inclination (*ruci*) of a mind that rises spontaneously as it desires; this is the remainder of the sense. (348) "According to its state of need" (*yathārtitvam*):
in that very person, who is a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), [the mind] is extended while seeking the purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) of that particular characteristic.

One should distinguish objects that pervade a specific location, according to how they are conventionally understood. For example, when an elder wishes to instruct someone who desires to learn— asking, "What is called 'long' in common usage?"— he would make a distinction between the appearance of length and so forth, even though that [object] is a single entity.

The distinction between appearances such as specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and length arises from the fact that those appearances possess a single specific characteristic (*ekasvalakṣaṇatva*), which is not limited to this place or this time; thus, because they rest upon objects such as jars qualified by space and time, there occurs the appearance of space (*deśābhāsa*) and the appearance of time (*kālābhāsa*).

When the universal nature of things and the pervasiveness of the causal factor are both refuted, they yield their presence as particular natures or unique specificities (*svalakṣaṇa*). Thus, like the determination of "manhood," there appear [distinctions such as] "Brahminhood" and "Kṣatriyahood."
They are indeed to be distinguished.

Here, among the particular characteristics of the person (*puruṣa*), this well-known differentiation of appearances, such as "long" and so forth, is the locus of a great many properties common to both the insentient and the sentient. By means of this—

By means of more well-known examples, [such as] "smokiness," "sandalwood-ness," "being sought after by Śrīkaṇṭha," and "white sandalwood," these—though being the referents of other words—are established as distinct manifestations (*ābhāsabheda*) because they are pervasive and because they abide in their own respective forms. (p. 273)

They are to be distinguished. By means of this well-known example of "smokiness" and so forth, even in the case of a jar whose existence is unestablished—because it lacks a connection with the nature [of smoke]—there occurs a differentiation of appearances (*ābhāsa-bheda*).
Within that [jar], existence and the other [attributes] are differentiated into various appearances.

He demonstrates that very point with the words "tathā hi" (for instance) and so forth: someone, having entered his own house, not seeing any object there whatsoever that was pleasing to the heart, experiences as it were a breaking of the heart, thinking "there is nothing here at all"; yet, upon seeing a jar before him, he thinks of it, "this exists."

One perceives the appearance of "existence" (*sattvābhāsa*) alone as the primary thing to be accepted. Regarding the phrase "others": one does not even acknowledge by name—let alone respect—the appearances of "pot-ness," "gold-ness," and so forth, which are distinct from the appearance of existence; it is just like that.
One who desires to fetch water perceives only the appearance of a jar as the locus for qualities such as being self-dependent, substantial, and golden; likewise,
one who desires an object suitable for going and coming, or for bringing and taking away, perceives that which corresponds to those requirements.

One sees only the substance itself. One who seeks its value sees only the appearance of gold; one who seeks its beauty sees only the appearance of brilliance. By the inclusion of "and so forth," one who seeks extreme firmness sees only firmness. This applies likewise to taste (*ruci*) and proficiency (*vyutpatti*).

Some say that this should be applied as follows: among the aforementioned appearances of existence and so forth, someone might—either out of personal preference or through a specific analytical understanding consisting in not overstepping the reliance on the linguistic usage of elders—distinguish a particular pot as a unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*). In this way, these...

The manifestations such as "being" (sat) and so forth are indeed nothing but specific appearances; because reality consists essentially in appearing in this or that way by virtue of being the object of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), the reflective awareness (vimarśa) which constitutes the means of valid cognition for every manifestation— including the manifestation of the means of valid cognition itself— is also [valid] like the means of valid cognition.

It proceeds precisely toward each individual manifestation (*pratyābhāsa*). For the cognizer—who has consciousness as his life-force, who is characterized by the life-force of light, whose nature consists of internal discourse (*abhijalpa*), and who is composed of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)—words such as "jar" or "red" find their rest in each respective manifestation; thus, these manifestations of existence and so forth [are established]. Their reality...

Through the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with the appearance of existence, the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) is also restricted to the appearance itself;
for by the mere appearance of existence, the prevention of the heart’s breaking is accomplished.
In that regard, concerning the causal efficiency consisting of the fetching of well-water, which is to be accomplished by the appearance of a jar—
Just as in the case of a study hall there is a requirement for a vessel that serves as a support for the eyes,

so too, because of the necessity of another appearance— namely, the appearance of the rope— which is invariably concomitant with the appearance of that jar, [the cognition] depends upon it; thus, in the performance of a causal function (*arthakriyā*), by means of each individual appearing object...
In the case of that which is to be proven (*sādhya*), there is indeed a dependence on another appearance (*ābhāsa*) situated in a corresponding place.
(p. 274) (350) Likewise, by whichever primary path an object is investigated, that very thing appears as a mere appearance in that very manner.

It is established [that there is a distinction] because of reflective discernment (*vimarśana*) and because of the performance of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). With the intention of defining the particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a well-known person, smoke, and a jar, as well as the less well-known [objects], even a single object such as a jar is defined in a manifold way— as "long," as "functioning," as "smoke," or as "jar"— despite being one.

Now, if it is admitted that reality consists solely in individual appearances— such as "existence," "jar-ness," or "gold-ness"— then the single appearance that constitutes the essence of the jar, which serves as the substratum for those [particular] appearances,
would not be a real entity; for its own nature would not exist apart from those various appearances.

Furthermore, due to the distinction between appearances— such as "the jar," "golden," or "red" with respect to objects characterized by jar-ness, gold-ness, redness, and so forth— the causal efficiency (arthakriyā) consisting of functions such as preventing the heart's breaking is restricted to each specific form; thus, a single jar is the common locus (samānādhikaraṇa).

Having performed [this], let it rest within that very [consciousness] as a qualifier; through the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) produced by its connection, [let it rest] toward the manifestations— such as "this jar," "it is here," or "now it has such a form"— which are directed toward objects and arise from the manifestation that is light.

Furthermore, for those appearances that do not differ and rest upon a single [substratum], their causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is restricted; for example, the collective form: "This is a jar, made of gold, firm, and bright;
therefore, it is suitable for fetching water from a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) fit for the cleansing of the head of a Śiva-linga. This applies to appearances.

Regarding that form which is a mixture and a collection of qualities such as goldness and so forth, some manifestation among them must be established as the resting place by virtue of its predominance; this is the manifestation of the jar. By means of that common substratum (samānam adhikaraṇam), through that identical locus...

The relation between these is their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); by means of that coreferentiality, the manifestation— which is oriented toward the object and is the illumination [of it]—
is that which subsequently shines forth as the various objects such as gold, and which constitutes its vital breath (*prāṇaka*).

Because there is a rule that every appearance and every reflective awareness— such as the one directed toward grasping the meaning of the Veda, thinking "some entity of this nature exists right here and now"— must ultimately rest upon a single manifestation in the form of a particular (svalakṣaṇa).

Therefore, because it rests upon a single manifestation, the sentence-meaning "here and now this jar exists"— characterized by a location standing before one, by the present time, and by forms such as its broad base, belly, and shape— is the external self (*bāhyātmā*), owing to its orientation toward an external object.

Vimarśa, whose nature is reflective awareness (parāmarśa), is declared to be the defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa); it animates (anuprāṇayati) that grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) and provides it with internal support (upodbalaka). For that reason—namely, because of its animation of that coreferentiality—those [qualities] such as "whatever-ness" (kāñcatva) and so forth...

The distinct [particulars] have attained the state of being that single particular (*ekasvalakṣaṇa*). Even there, not abandoning their own internal differentiation such as "gold-ness" and so forth, their resting in that single particular is certain;
yet, another [activity], consisting of a single appearance in the form of various universals, performs the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) characterized by those [particulars].

Furthermore, if there were a difference between the appearances— such as gold and so forth that have arisen in a unified form— and their respective reflective awarenesses (*vimarśa*) on account of their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*),
then causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) would be restricted to one or the other alone;
this is indicated by the two terms *ābhāsa* and *pratibhāsa* found in the Sūtra.

It should be understood that even *vimarśa* (reflective awareness), being of a single nature encompassing all forms, is also implied. Furthermore, the word "again" (*punaḥ*) indicates the distinction between the universal manifestations (*sāmānyābhāsa*) and the particular manifestation (*svalakṣaṇābhāsa*) regarding their causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*).
By the use of the plural "of non-differentiated things," it refers to the individual essence (*svalakṣaṇa*).
In the manifestation of unity, there exists a dependent distinctness among the manifestations of gold and so forth;

yet even within that dependent distinctness, because it serves as the coloring factor for the individual instances— which are of the nature of specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) consisting of the manifestation of unity— it possesses an ultimate nature as a universal (sāmānya).

This gold and so forth—[which is] essentially nothing more than the mere fitness for the reflective awareness “this is a jar” [arising] from that which is independent, characterized as a reflection manifesting as many [aspects], pure, and serving as the substrate of common designation—is, in reality, [merely] gold and so forth. (352) ———— [The rest of the sentence continues: ...the jar.

Its nature as a universal is indeed a distinct category from the substance that is the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), because it consists of the single form of the individual; for that category other than substance, which has dependence as its essence,
possesses dependence with respect to its resting upon a single substance, such as the nature of a jar.

The manifestation whose nature is the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) is indeed real, just like the manifestation of the universal (*sāmānya*); for it persists as having that very nature of a unique particular by virtue of its manifestation, its reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), and its causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

In that case, within the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) which consists of a collection of appearances, no single purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is accomplished by each individual appearance alone; rather, from the collection of appearances such as gold and so forth, there arises a collection of purposeful actions. These are the appearances.

He also raises the objection: "If these appearances, though mutually non-different, nevertheless mingle in order to perform a single purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), then what is the limit (*avadhi*) consisting of their specific measure? [The response is:
"Of those appearances which are mutually contradictory and exist separately..."
Furthermore, when lights of intense radiance have their essences merged within a single dwelling,

there occurs a unitary cognition capable of perceiving extremely subtle objects through a single, unified form as its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), which performs a purposeful function (*arthakriyā*). This is just as it happens for [drops] falling into the ocean.

Just as through the flow of a single stream, which is the collective form of many streams, there occurs a causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) consisting of the initiation of many waves; likewise, there is a cognition of unity within a single particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) regarding a jar, its redness, and its golden nature, which appear without contradiction.
The functional efficacy (*arthakriyā*) consisting of the act of taking [water] from sacred bathing sites suitable for the consecration of the head of the supreme Śiva-liṅga becomes unified;
this is like the lights of separate lamps existing in different locations.

Those very lamp-lights, which— because they fell separately— did not perform that purposeful activity characterized by the capacity to perceive extremely subtle objects for the cognizer of the lamp and the water-trough, [are now seen to do so]. That very [capacity] is the perception of the extremely subtle.

It performs a purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) characterized by the conferral of capacity within a single dwelling; however, when those lamp-lights coalesce within that same dwelling, there is no collective performance of purposeful action among them.
The causal efficacy [of these cognitions] does not consist in multiplicity;

rather, it is indeed unity, because they manifest a single object through their subtle forms. This is just as when streams that previously existed separately later come together and fall into the ocean, becoming even more abundant.
Even in the case of that which performs a single purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) in the form of a wave, the collection [of causes] does not itself constitute that purposeful action. Similarly,
when a jar is perceived as qualified by the appearance of multiple qualifiers— such as "golden," "red," and "solid"—
it is seen immediately that it is suitable for the ritual placement of a *śivaliṅga* and fit for the fetching of water.
Thus, it is established that [the cognition] possesses the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) characterized by complete conviction;
therefore, the capacity for a single causal efficiency is proven even for appearances such as a jar or gold.

Regarding what you asked—namely, what constitutes the limit of performing a single causal efficiency—in that regard, those [appearances] which are not in contradiction with one another in the performance of a single causal efficiency are precisely [what constitute that limit].

Forms become the objects of the eye, and they mingle with the wind—which is the object of the sense of touch and possesses luminosity. Although there is a mutual contradiction because each belongs to a different sense-object, that very contradiction is brought forth by the power of *niyati* (the principle of necessity) which ordains: "Let it be thus. Having stated the meaning with this underlying intention, [he continues].

He states the application of the sūtra: "The single collective form belonging to those various lights of lamps existing separately, and the single collective form of the streams falling into the ocean— by each of these, the meaning of the stated definition [is illustrated]."

The connection is as follows: just as the cognition of unity (*aikyadhī*) has its form in an action (*kriyārūpā*) because it is produced by that [action], so too the cognition of unity regarding those appearances—such as "jar," "red," and "golden"—which are mutually contradictory, is produced by their single underlying particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Thus, the cognition of unity arises from the jar, the red, and [the gold]. Regarding these cognitions of unity, the jar, the red...
The threefold nature— namely, the collective external manifestation of gold and so forth, the internal reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), and the causal efficacy consisting of the form of experience—
is accepted [as the object]. Thus, according to the principle stated, for each individual manifestation of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)...
Because they rest upon their respective appearances— such as that of gold and so forth— even in the appearance of fire,

the cognition of fire itself is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and the cognition of smoke is the means of valid cognition only in the mere appearance of smoke, not in the appearance of fire; for there is no causal relationship between those two, smoke and fire.

Since even cognition is merely an appearance of cause and effect, for that reason, even the appearance of smoke produced by fire might deviate from the appearance of fire as its cause; likewise, every other category of effects, such as sprouts and the like, might deviate from their respective appearances of causes, such as seeds and the like.
To dispel the doubt that "because there would be no inference of a cause from its respective effects, there would result an excessive proliferation of errors," he says: "In that regard" (*tatra*).
This refers even to this position [of ours] that "the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) comes to rest in each individual manifestation."

There is no fault whatsoever. For when a manifestation of fire (*vahny-ābhāsa*) is not qualified by place, time, and so forth—and is thus appearing as a universal—therein resides the fire's status as the cause of smoke (which is the effect of fuel), its nature of being hot, and its denotability by such terms as *vahi*, *anala*, and *vaiśvānara*. By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [other attributes are also implied].

The nature of fire—consisting of the illumination of objects such as jars, its upward flaming, and its being devoid of smell and taste—is its selfhood (*ātman*), which is its essential property (*dharma*). This very essence is cognized through a single means of knowledge, namely, the cognition of fire itself. However, its status as an effect, its status as a cause, and its denotation by various specific words are distinct [from that essential nature].
The notion of separateness is intended to indicate a distinction between classes of properties—such as being produced or unproduced—pertaining to fire, in relation to other entities such as fuel.
In this context, fuel is characterized by its status as the effect of [fire] and the cause of smoke, and it constitutes the referent of its respective linguistic expressions. As for smoke...
Furthermore, with respect to the denotators established by the conventions of various cognizers, [the letters] are artificial;
whereas the group consisting of heat (*uṣṇatā*), upward flaming (*ūrdhvajvalanatā*), odor (*gandha*), taste (*rasa*), and emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is an unartificial group.
This is for the purpose of indicating the distinction between groups. He demonstrates this very point with the words "For instance" (*tathā hi*), and so forth.
Now, although the appearance of fire (*vahnyābhāsa*) is undifferentiated because it consists of the nature of a mere universal— being unconfounded by place, time, and form as "this very thing here"—
it is nonetheless invariably concomitant with all the appearances of causality and so forth that will be described below.
Having accepted those appearances of causality and so forth— which are produced by the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) and constrained by the power of the Blessed One’s *niśati*—
as being accomplished and brought about by that very single means of perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*) regarding fire.

It enters the domain of the cognizer’s certainty. And thus: by being established in this way in the domain of certainty, that appearance of fire [is understood] through the appearance of its own self as the effect of fuel, the appearance of its causality for smoke, and the appearance of its nature as heat.
And being perceived as having an inherent, non-deviating concomitance (*avyabhicarita-sāhacarya*),
it is thus perceived everywhere— in every place and at all times—
as having such a non-deviating concomitance. By those [means], that appearance of fire...

Due to the identity of the word, this nature of fire—such as its being produced by effort—is determined through fallacious appearances of "being an effect" and the like; yet even that nature which is not inherent, being dependent on human convention and so forth, is also ascertained from the very perception of a single fire. Having perceived that fire...

For the cognizer who acts, the manifestation of fire— accompanied by other various manifestations such as being denotable by artificial words like "fire" and being the effect of fuel, which are non-artificial— is perceived just as it was previously.

It exists in all places and times; likewise, it is cognized as being invariably concomitant with every place and time. "Therein" refers to the artificial nature consisting of being denotable by words such as "fire," which—distinct from the means of valid cognition regarding fire—is the state of being the effect of that smoke, established by the means of valid cognition.
There is no purpose whatsoever for another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) to establish that divine state;

for all those aspects, the measure of fire alone is sufficient [to determine]: "This is the effect of fuel," "This is the cause of smoke," "This has the nature of heat," and "This is what is denoted by words such as 'fire'."
For a person being directed by convention toward each respective word,

there is only one object— fire— with a throbbing, radiant form; thus, it is the power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*) itself that manifests the inseparable connection with the appearance of being an effect of fuel and so forth, belonging to fire alone.
The Teacher indicates that [the term] "refuge" applies everywhere, in every conventional transaction.
He clarifies the very point already stated with the words "this is what is meant" (*etaduktaṃ bhavati*), and so forth.

For any manifestation of an entity whatsoever, whether artificial or otherwise, there appears an inseparable connection (*nāntarīyakatvam*), that is, an invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvaḥ*) with another manifestation. In that case:
In the state of being inseparable from those various artificial and non-artificial appearances,
it is solely the power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*) that unfolds; indeed, the power of necessity itself brings about that inseparability,
since inseparability constitutes the nature of the effect produced by fuel.
The meaning is that, appearing as the cause of smoke, it becomes a determinate form (*niyatarūpa*) and thus pervades all time, spanning prior and subsequent moments.
The ellipsis to be supplied is "inseparability" (*nāntarīyakatva*) with respect to being denotable by words such as "fire" and so forth. And from that, [follows] necessity (*niyati*).

By the force of its capacity, even a semblance of smoke would not deviate from a semblance of fire; thus, there is no flaw whatsoever in the discourse on inference. Having stated the meaning of the verse in its entirety, he explains its connection: "The causal relation of that [semblance] is its status as the object of the word."
The state of being denotable by those respective words; by the inclusion of the term "etcetera," [it includes] the non-emptiness of the texts.

Such an Ātman, which is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) in fire and so forth, is held to be all-inclusive in its own nature; it becomes known through a single means of valid cognition regarding fire alone. This is the established convention (*samaya*) known as "the cutting of blindness."

However, in poetry— and not in a technical treatise (*śāstra*)— there is no fault even when there is a totality (*sāmastya*) consisting of cause and effect in the second and third quarters, or identity (*tādātmya*) between the respective word and its meaning in the first and second halves; for in such totality,
there is simply the relation of cause and effect, heat, and the respective word-meaning.

The application of the term "separateness" (*pṛthagbhāva*) as a condition is indicated in order to demonstrate the distinction between categories— namely, those things that are produced and those that are unproduced— based on whether they depend upon other entities, such as being denotable by the words "fuel," "smoke," or "fire," or whether they do not so depend. (357)

In this regard, heat is its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and is therefore unconditioned (*akṛtaka*) in itself; whereas its being an effect of fuel and its being a cause of smoke are, in dependence upon other entities such as fuel, for the most part conditioned (*kṛtaka*). Likewise, its denotability by words such as "heat" is entirely conditioned. This has been established by the six verses beginning with "This is such-and-such."

He clarifies briefly, with the words beginning "In this way," the means of valid cognition for the universal (*sāmānya-pramāṇa*), which establishes the appearance of a commonality such as gold, and the means of valid cognition for the particular (*svalakṣaṇa-pramāṇa*), which consists in the establishment of the particular characterized by multiple appearances such as gold.

By each individual means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) resting upon its respective appearance of gold and so forth, the determination of that specific appearance of gold and so forth is effected. Among those appearances of gold and so forth, [there is] their mutual [relationship] as appropriate.

The state of inseparable concomitance (*avinābhūtatva*) between the qualifier and the qualified, as appropriate, belongs to that reality which consists of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); this [reality] is, by means of a single nature of consciousness undifferentiated by space and time,
designated as "this" and "that" through various [cognitions], such as "this is golden," "this is red," or "this is bright."
When an object appearing as gold or the like has been measured by means of valid cognitions (*pramāṇa*) and internally determined, there arises—

by way of the inward-turned nature of the "I" (*ahaṃ-bhāva*)— a subsequent cognition that is animated by the awareness of the valid cognition of that appearance as gold or the like, which had previously occurred.

It is determined by that which has become the ground of rest. Consequently, with respect to that particular (svalakṣaṇa) consisting of various appearances such as gold and so forth, there is a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) in the form of a synthesis, such as "this pot is golden and red.
That means of valid cognition which apprehends the particular is [active] when synthesizing the gold and other qualities.
If it operates upon the appearances of qualifiers, it is invalid due to the fault of apprehending what has already been apprehended; in that case,
regarding each of those appearances such as gold and so forth, it is precisely the same as before.

The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is precisely the consciousness that consists in the determination of common objects such as gold; for the cognizer, it is the mental activity consisting in the determination of those respective entities—such as "this is gold" or "this is bright"—which is distinct from [the initial sensory perception]. (356)
For one who is intent on grasping a jar characterized by its own specific nature (*svalakṣaṇa*) for the purpose of fetching water,
there is a connection with form (*rūpa*) in the activity of the body; and likewise, [there is a connection] with that which consists of visual and other types of cognition.
In order to demonstrate the manner in which [an object] becomes the object of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), he says:

for a cognizer who seeks the purposeful action of fetching water, there arises at that time—that is, occurring at that specific moment—a desire to fetch water directed toward a jar, such as "this is a jar. This [desire] is produced by the occasion.

The activity that consists of speech, consists of mind, and possesses organs and other limbs is indeed distinguished by internal differences such as place and so forth; thus, with respect to the place which serves as the locus for a jar,
and by the inclusion of the word "and so forth," with respect to the time which serves as its qualification, and the gold and so forth which serve as its further qualifications.

In its other form, this very jar is "fit for fetching water"; and regarding such considerations of its own nature, there are many distinct perceptions for each, as well as many distinct acts of fetching water— by means of those various distinct perceptions, [the object] is indeed differentiated and yet integrated.

It would exist as the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) whose nature is the jar. Such a thing, which is the basis for the activity of speech, mind, and body—such as "this is a golden jar" or "this is red"—cannot arise from a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends a universal entity (*sāmānyavastu*), because [the universal] is of a single nature. Furthermore...
The aforementioned definition and means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) arises precisely from the aggregate [of cognitions].

Alternatively, the construction may be understood as follows: when there is a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) that is non-different from the internal state of the knower and possesses multiple perceptions of place and so forth in the form described, there occurs the aforementioned activity. This is by means of the various direct perceptions (*adhyakṣa*) of place and so forth that have become manifest.

Alternatively, it may be said that the aforementioned engagement occurs when the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)— the cause— is differentiated by other appearances such as place, time, and gold-ness. In this case as well, the collection of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-samūha*) is designated as following that [particular characteristic] by way of defining the many objects of knowledge, such as place and so forth.
The threefold application is that [the object] is said to be the cause (*nimitta*).

Thus, regarding the object of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) which is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)— namely, the specific particularity (*svalakṣaṇa*) such as a jar, which is differentiated by space and so forth— the embodied activity of the cognizer who seeks purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) [proceeds].

He demonstrates that activity occurs in exactly the same way even with respect to an appearance of fire within the domain of inference—by stating, "even through inference. Activity does not occur solely toward a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) perceived directly, which is distinct from other perceptions such as place and so forth; it occurs through inference as well.

The meaning is that when there is a manifestation of fire (*agnyābhāsa*) distinct from other direct perceptions (*adhyakṣa*) such as those of places like mountains, the aforementioned kind of activity occurs. In this case as well, the manifestation of the mountain, which constitutes the subject (*pakṣa*), is the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); and that which consists of the manifestation of smoke and fire, which is the mark (*liṅga*) residing therein, is the means of knowledge.

The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding deviation, however, is that inferential means of cognition which consists in the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*)— namely, that fire exists in something other than the mere appearance of a mountain and so forth as apprehended by you.
When this [means of cognition] is combined with the collection [of other factors], there arises for the seeker, even from an inferential appearance of fire, a temporary [cognition].

The connection is with the word "activity" (*pravṛtti*). However, the particle *tu* indicates the distinction between the causal efficiency of a particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the causal efficiency of its general form, such as being gold. For the cognizer, external causal efficiency—which is distinct from mental activity—arises from that which consists of a collection of multiple universals.

p. 281) Because its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is precisely its own nature, [the aspects of] place and time are internal [to that characteristic], insofar as they are "located here" and "occurring now. In that regard, when [an object] is qualified by the forms of place and time, there arises for the cognizer a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) such as: "this is such-and-such," "it is located here," "it is occurring now," and so forth.
Apart from that, the specific nature (*viśeṣa-rūpatā*) of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), which constitutes its being a *svalakṣaṇa*, does not exist in itself;

rather, through the medium of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), it comes to rest in the cognizer who is the object of that awareness. For the cognizer, whose sole form is consciousness and who is unconditioned by space and time, there is an internal unity due to the absence of space and time.

A particular characterized by its own attributes necessarily abandons its own specific form as a particular. As it has been said: "established in its own sequence," and so forth. Thus, in every respect, from the perspective of ultimate reality, [all things] are non-dual and consist of the subject; nevertheless, regarding that particular, whatever its specific...

The manifestation of form within that [consciousness], for the purpose of bringing about its specific forms, has as its sole cause the sovereignty of the Supreme Lord, which is called the power of *māyā*. Here, the words "yat" and "tat" indicate what is well-known. In that regard, specifically in the unfolding of the power of *māyā*:

For a cognizer who has arisen [with a cognition] characterized by a specific causal efficiency— such as the fetching of water— which is conjoined with a particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) that is itself the probandum,
there occurs at that time a verbal, mental, or physical [activity] directed toward that very particular characteristic, which is the object in the form of a qualifier.
That activity occurs in the place which serves as the locus for that particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*);

by the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), it also occurs in time, which serves as its qualification, and in other intrinsic natures such as gold, which serve as its qualifications—[as in the thought]: "This very jar is fit for the purpose of carrying water and so forth."

Furthermore, regarding the investigation of one's own true nature (*svarūpa*) and so forth, when there is a distinction, a convergence, or a conjunction of other means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it occurs;

it does not occur otherwise. It does not arise through each individual means of knowledge such as space (*deśa*) and so on; rather, it arises through the [synthesis of] the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

It arises precisely from a collection [of means of knowledge]. For the opponent, the proponent of a stream of cognitions (*jñānasantānavādin*), the state of being a collection of means of knowledge is not tenable, because he does not admit that they find their rest in a single essential nature.
For us, however, it is logical that the collection of means of knowledge consists in resting within a single self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).
If it is not [already] included within that which has been stated here as "this," then this very resting in one's own self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is called *yojanā*,
*vyamiśraṇā*, *yojikā*, *yojayitrī*, *yukti*, and *yoga*.
It consists of the activity of joining (*yojanā-vyāpāra-rūpā*), the agent of the activity of joining (*yojikā-vyāpārayitr-rūpā*), and *yukti* is the act of uniting (*sammelana*).
All three of these also come about solely through resting in one’s own self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). As it has been said:

"In the single cognizer, by means of the various distinct modes of consciousness... and so forth, up to: "...this principle is established. This reasoning is like the logic of [the extraction of] fragrance from its substance and so on.
It brings about a specific purposeful action consisting of the satisfaction of the cognizer's heart.
Thus, the intended meaning is that activity toward the particular (svalakṣaṇa) arises from the very aggregate of perceptions (pratyakṣasamūha) of the aforementioned form.

The construction is as follows: even when the knower experiences other perceptions such as those of space and so forth in their previously described form, there occurs therein either activity or a connection toward the particular (svalakṣaṇa) which is non-different from the interior [of consciousness].
This occurs in that which is differentiated—that is, mixed—with other appearing objects of knowledge (prameya) such as space and so forth that have become manifest to perception.

Alternatively, the construction may be: "When the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) exists as the cause (*nimitta*), there is [cognitive] activity. Even in this construction, by way of describing the multiplicity of the objects of cognition (*prameya*) such as place and so forth, it is precisely the collection of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-samūha*) that follows after those respective objects of cognition—place and so forth—that is stated to be the cause. (361)
Now, one might ask: is the aforementioned collection of means of valid cognition useful only in regard to activity connected with perceptual valid cognition? To this he says:
"Not only in the case of perception for the knower."
Activity is caused by a collection of means of knowledge consisting of the perception of various locations and so forth;

inferential activity is likewise so. Thus, it demonstrates that very same thing: [inferential activity] is caused by a collection of means of knowledge consisting of the perception of various locations such as mountains and so forth.
Because they are remote, in that which is devoid of qualification— namely, in the mere appearance of smoke,

in the mere appearance of fire corresponding to it, and in the appearance of the mountain which serves as the locus for those appearances of smoke and fire when they are subject to deviation— those appearances of smoke and fire [are not established].
If there is deviation, then even in the case of the mountain-appearance which serves as the locus for this [inference],

those other perceptions that apprehend the respective appearances of smoke and fire— beyond the appearance of smoke and so forth grasped by those various means of valid cognition— in relation to such a state as "there is fire here on the mountain," [the inference would fail].

In the *Ayogavyavaccheda*, the connection is as follows: that which is a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consisting of inference, and that very collection of means of valid cognition, leads to an immediate activity toward the appearance of fire for one who seeks it;
this occurs precisely through the power of deliberation (*vimarśa*) regarding objects.

The foundation for the determination of difference and non-difference, consisting of the particular (svalakṣaṇa) and the universal (sāmānya), is the power of that reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) [of the Supreme Lord]; thus, the nature of the Supreme Lord, who is consciousness itself, consists of full subjectivity (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*), wherein things possess the nature of both the particular and the universal.
Even for Sadāśiva and the others, [this state] is the manifestation of the power of absolute freedom (svātantrya-śakti) of the Lord Śiva.

Therefore, as for what is asserted by other Buddhists— that there is no distinction between objects such as a jar in terms of distance, proximity, and so forth, and that consequently the nature of the jar and such things does not undergo any alteration— that too is non-difference.

This is established solely through the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). It is demonstrated that without the power of reflective awareness, that non-difference cannot be established by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), whether objects are distant or near, or whether they are beyond perception or directly perceived.
Whether by way of being external or internal, or due to defects in the manifesting agent such as a lamp or light,

or due to the acuity of the sense organs and so forth, or due to factors such as being on one side or facing [the object], there occurs— in respect of shadows that appear as non-different— the cognition "this is that very same thing" in a single form.

Because its manifestation is primary—meaning that it is "known all around" (*pratyavamarśena-ākhyātam*) through a pervasive renown and a manifestation of a single form—the unity [of the object] as "this is indeed that very thing" is unimpeded. (362) p. 283) From this manifestation of a single form, unity is not obstructed.

Regarding the phrase "by mere appearance": for one who establishes the reality of an object according to its appearance, how could there not be a difference between that object as it stands far away and as it stands near?
This is because the appearance of that object is complete when nearby, whereas it is obscured when at a distance.
And "not far" means by way of being unobstructed; "in whatever way" means by whatever manner—such is the distinction.

Now, one might object: even reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is likewise differentiated according to whether it concerns what is distant or near, and in each manifestation (*pratyābhāsa*), it is divided into the categories of *sakala*, *asakala*, and so forth. True. Reflective awareness that conforms to the manifestation is indeed differentiated.
Even so, there is another [form of manifestation] consisting of a single unifying reflection (*ekapratyavamarśa*),

which is of the nature of synthesis (*anusandhānātmā*). By means of that single unifying reflection, there is a complete manifestation (*prathana*)— that is, a full disclosure— of that which possesses this quality.

Since even the single reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) of the primary manifestation—the manifestation of a single form—is arisen from that [consciousness], it is said to be "arisen from the primary manifestation. Thus, there exists indeed the light of "I" (*ahaṃprakāśa*), which is of a single form. Furthermore, due to the mutual union of manifestation and reflective awareness, or of light and reflective awareness, [the self is established].
From that primary manifestation, which is vitalized by reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*),
the unity of objects— whether distant or near— remains unimpeded.
He states the oneness of those things whose shadows of manifestation appear distinct, whether they consist of the imperceptible or the perceptible:

"That which has not yet arisen is that very same thing which has been seen"—thus [they are one] in the form of being manifest or unmanifest, and so forth. Their secondary manifestation consists of the diverse shadows of appearance within their own self-nature.
Their unity, however, arises from the primary manifestation which is animated by a single reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*); such is the connection.

The very unity that is observed among appearances— though they appear as distinct through being external or internal— as when one thinks, "I am perceiving the same internal [object]," is due to the defects of the manifestors and so forth; for instance, the unity of distinct appearances in the word *raktotpalam* (red lotus) [is seen] by means of a lamp stained with defects.

"Even though blue is seen, one perceives it as red due to the rays of the sun. Regarding the phrase "even for others": this refers to those for whom the appearance of the shadow is not distinct, whether due to a defect in the sense faculties or because of the direction from which the light falls. (363) Even for them...
It is established that, by the power of the nature of the manifestation of the persistence of the primary reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*), there is indeed identity.
Now, one might object: let the object be the very same whether it is distant or near, or whether it is hidden or manifest;
for in the aspect of the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) determined by the subject as "this is that very same object," [the object remains identical].

"In the same way" means through application corresponding to what has been determined, such as in the case of "externality" and "internality. You have stated that whatever is seen externally is precisely what I delineate internally.

Therefore, in order to dispel the delusion that an internal object, when determined by the cognizer, possesses functions such as carrying water, he says: "Even the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) of objects is not innate."

(284) "That [activity] is restricted by the will of the Lord. This is the meaning: for it is because the specific group of objects has been determined by Him—[determined] thus, "let this causal efficiency (arthakriyā) be performed, let it not be performed"—that there is no deviation from that causal efficiency, due to its non-performance or its performance otherwise.
If a jar lacks causal efficiency such as the fetching of water, it is not a jar;
for its very nature consists solely in its manifestation.

In that regard, concerning a specific fire and so forth, where "the effect is heat due to its cause," by means of this statement—"the capacity to produce the cognition of a jar"—the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is enumerated as if it were the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the fire; however, that [action] is not its innate, essential nature (*sahaja-svarūpabhūta*). Whether the object exists or does not exist...

And its being "that which performs" means that the performance of purposeful action (*arthakriyākāritva*) is necessarily determined by the will of God (*īśvarecchā*). Regarding the word "therefore" (*tena*): because of the non-performance—that is, the non-acting—of that purposeful action, one should not suspect the alteration or destruction of the entity (*bhāva*). This is because when the specific nature of an object, such as a jar, dissolves, [the entity itself does not cease].

One should not suspect that this is merely a state of being like a threshing floor; nor has it been said that the essential nature [of consciousness] consists in causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), for that will be explained in the passage beginning with "because of its internality, there is identity with the subject" (*antaratvāt pramātraikya*). Furthermore, as in the passage beginning with "the insentient lacks that power," by the force of the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) that "this very same thing exists both externally and internally," [consciousness is established]. (364)
The essential nature (*svarūpa*) is indeed one alone. Now, if it is as stated— that by the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) alone,
the distinction between difference and non-difference, consisting of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the universal (*sāmānya*), is established for entities— then [what follows]?

Even in the three worlds, the conventional usage of delusion has ceased; even in the case of mother-of-pearl, it is indeed mother-of-pearl that appears as silver, because it is being examined as "this is silver. And therefore:
since there is no delusion when real silver falls upon mother-of-pearl, [the cognition] "this is silver" [would not occur].
Since it is impossible for the subsequently arising cognition of mother-of-pearl to sublate the perceived reflective awareness of silver, for what purpose was this stated?
[The answer is: "Cognition regarding an object that is the referent of a single designation is uncontradicted with respect to the thing-in-itself."

Thus, he dispels the doubt that— since there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of silver— the term "unsublated" (*abādhita*), as a qualifier of the cognition (*miti*), would have no excluded object (*vyavacchedya*) such as a reflective awareness of silver that is incapable of being sublated; [he does so by noting that] when there is a single reflective awareness of silver regarding a mother-of-pearl shell at a distance...

Having seen this [shell], although there is an identity with the cognition of silver—as in "this is indeed silver"—the persistence of silver in the shell is due to the location of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) because of its correspondence; thus, [the cognition] ceases in the form of a reflection of silver arising from mere clarity.
Subsequently, at a later time, regarding the nature of the limiting adjunct which is the nature of the shell, [there arises the cognition]: "This is silver."

Due to the absence of reflective discernment (*vimarśa*), even in the cognition of a double moon—where the cognizer perceives "this is a double moon" because of a defect—the sky is occupied by the double moon.
Otherwise, it would not subsequently be occupied by the double moon. [The sky] is occupied by the double moon.
Due to the convergence of spatial points in the sky, even the cognition that "this is a double moon" is indeed an error.

Similarly, having seen a mother-of-pearl shell from a distance, because of the similarity in its color consisting of whiteness, one perceives it as "this is silver," stable, and common to all perceivers.

This [cognition] pertains to the aspect "this," the aspect "silver," the aspect "stable," the aspect common to all cognizers, the aspect of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), and the aspect of the synthesis of "this" and "silver" and so forth— [all of which are] capable of the purposeful action of serving as a bracelet, an ornament, and the like.

By the force of the appearance "this is silver" and by the force of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of that appearance, at that very moment— that is, at the time of the initial reflective awareness— there is no falsity whatsoever in that portion of "this" and so forth; rather,
[it is only realized later that] "this is not silver," it is not stable, it is not cognizable by another subject, and it does not perform the intended purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).

The reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) that will arise at a later time—that which is to be reflected upon as "this is not silver"—is not [the same as] the reflective awareness at the time of the initial awareness; rather, that form [of the object] was [already] present at the time of the prior awareness. Thus, having first perceived the power (*śakti*), with respect to it...

At the very time of the reflective awareness "this is silver," that [silver] is not perceived by the subject in the same form as it was previously reflected upon; it should not be present in its first moment in the form of that which is to be negated later in such reflective awarenesses as "this is not silver."

At the time of the first reflection, there is indeed the subsequent reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) that "this very mother-of-pearl became silver," as in the phrase "in that which has arisen and immediately subsided. This refers to something that, like a flash of lightning, has arisen and subsided at that very moment; [the word] "now" (*idānīm*) [refers to the present time].

At the very time of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the mother-of-pearl, not only was there no silver— nor even at the time of the reflective awareness of silver, when one thinks "this is silver"— did silver exist. Therefore, as long as it is incomplete, it cannot serve as a bracelet, an ornament, or the like.

The ellipsis implies that [the object] must be manifested through a form capable of performing functions such as silver and so forth; this continues until the completion of that purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*). It is not manifested. In this philosophical system, non-manifestation (*aprakhyāti*) is simply a state of incomplete manifestation, which is itself a form of non-cognition (*akhyāti*). It is not merely a lack of shining forth. In this view...
This is the nature of delusion. As it is said in the *Virūpākṣapañcāśikā*:

"Through the firmness of immersion (*samāveśa*), one destroys the full manifestation of the full [limited] manifestation; create worlds at will, establish them, withdraw them, and illuminate them with speed. Thus it is said.

"By its power" means by the power of *akhyāti*, which consists of the non-apprehension of what is not fully manifested. Let it be said that there are also the other types of non-apprehension (*akhyāti*): the non-apprehension of the unreal (*asat-khyāti*), the non-apprehension of the contrary (*viparīta-khyāti*), and the inexpressible non-apprehension (*anirvacanīya-khyāti*).
Non-apprehension of the unreal (*asat-khyāti*) is the manifestation of things such as a mirage, which are empty of essence in themselves.

*Viparītakhyāti* (misapprehension) consists of the reflective judgment "this is silver" regarding a mother-of-pearl shell standing before one, due to the similarity of color, even though the silver has gone elsewhere. *Anirvācyakhyāti* (indescribable apprehension) is that which cannot be described as either existent or non-existent.
(286) Now, if it is argued that non-apprehension (*akhyāti*) in the form of incomplete apprehension (*apūrṇakhyāti*) is indeed error,

then even the cognition of a jar and so forth— which is of a true nature because it does not fail to produce purposeful action such as fetching water— would also be incomplete apprehension. This is because the jar and so forth...

Even though it is of the nature of "I" (*ahantā*) by virtue of being manifest, its manifestation as "this-ness" (*idantā*) through *māyā* is "incomplete cognition" (*apūrṇakhyāti*). Regarding the word "thence": [it refers to] the cognition of a real jar. What follows from complete cognition? If one asks "what?", [the answer is that] the notion that "everything is an error" would arise. Excellent! Excellent!

"O long-lived one, by your good fortune and through the turn of fate, your vision—meaning the knowledge of ultimate reality—is about to open; that is, it desires to open. In that case, this entire realm of illusion perceived through such [vision] is nothing but delusion. Even therein—in that which consists of delusion—"

Even in the state of *māyā*, although it consists of consciousness and is of the nature of the "I" (*ahaṃtā*) which is the essence of self-savoring, there occurs the cognition of silver— "this is silver"— in relation to mother-of-pearl, which is perceived as "this" (*idantā*) through an error fashioned by *māyā*; this is because [the cognition] is unstable and not common to all people.
In the case of an error, like a dream, there is no remedy; regarding the object, it is like a foul-smelling, great ulcer.
That which distinguishes it is called another error, like a boil (sphoṭa) upon that [ulcer].
Like a jar or similar objects, this extends to the fulfillment of purposeful action, such as serving as a bracelet ornament.
Because the reflective awareness (vimarśa) that conforms to the cognition "this is silver" is stable with respect to both the "this" aspect and the "silver" aspect,
for that very reason which was stated previously, there is no error whatsoever in appearances such as "this is silver" or "this silver is stable."

Because, unlike the cognition of two moons and so forth, there is no uprooting [of the error]; for in the case of the "this" portion perceived in the cognition "this is silver" regarding mother-of-pearl,
from the very moment the reflective awareness arises— "this is not silver, this is mother-of-pearl"— in respect to the aspect of their mutual conjunction, this...

The sublation by a sublating means of knowledge—such as "this is not silver, this is mother-of-pearl"—effects the eradication of the persistence of the reflective awareness "this is silver. In that very context, it is stated: the status of error lies in the aspect of the conjunction between the mother-of-pearl and the silver; thus, the meaning of the Sūtra is established in detail.
Having established the application [of the principle] to the Sūtra, he says:
"Even when there is a single reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of silver, there is no status of silver in the mother-of-pearl.

This means that regarding the object which is mother-of-pearl, there is a reflective awareness of the form of identity—namely, "this is indeed silver"—involving the silver together with the mother-of-pearl.

Even so, although there is the cognition "this is silver" by means of that knowledge—which consists in the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of silver—that existence of silver in the mother-of-pearl does not exist at all. The reason for this is:
"because of the non-correspondence with the location of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). Regarding the word "here": it refers to the mother-of-pearl situated in front.
The region of the mother-of-pearl shell, being an adjunct (*upādhi*) itself, colors the self with the appearance of silver— due to the similarity of color— and thus,
at the time when the cognition "this is mother-of-pearl" subsequently arises, there is no persistence of the reflection upon that former silver in the form "this is silver."

(287) Here, "correspondence" (*saṃvāda*) refers to the manifestation that follows upon the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of this [silver]. Because of the absence of such correspondence—that is, for that reason—the silver exists in the mother-of-pearl only as a manifestation;
therefore, the meaning is that there is no actual persistence of silver in the mother-of-pearl.

Now, it might be argued that in the case of silver in mother-of-pearl, because there is no subsequent correspondence with the locus of the mother-of-pearl— which serves as the coloring factor for the appearance of silver— the cognition of silver must be erroneous, since the persistence of the reflective awareness "this is silver" is uprooted regarding the aspect of the conjunction between the mother-of-pearl and the silver.
In the case of the two moons appearing constantly, there is no convergence with any object whatsoever distinct from those two moons— such that a sublation (*bādha*) would occur. However,
it has been stated that sublation occurs regarding the individual portions of the appearances, namely "this" and "silver."
By you yourself it has been said that in the appearance "two moons," there is no conjunction with anything at all.

"This being so" means in the absence of conjunction. "In its own specific character" (*svālakṣaṇyena*) means that in this particular region of space, the two moons are now [perceived] as being restricted to that specific spatial location and characterized by that specific time.

What is the appearance? In that appearance of "two moons," there is an appearance of the simultaneous conjunction of two [moons] across extended space and time. This is what is meant by "reflection" (*vimarśa*):
the desire to subsequently express this conjunction in the form, "At this place in the sky, right now, these are two moons."

The deliberation (*vimarśa*) desires to follow [the truth]: here, just as there is a negation that "there is no double moon in this sky," so too must the negation of the appearance of duality be stated even regarding the appearance of the conjunction of the two appearances of the moon;
for one whose vision is impaired by cataracts (*timira*) does not see a double moon.
Because it was previously stated, "I have indeed known [it] as such.

Thus, in the context of explaining the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), the reflective awareness perceived in cases such as mother-of-pearl appearing as silver or two moons does not persist until the fulfillment of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
Having established that this is an error, he confirms the very subject at hand with the words "Thus, appearances," and so forth.
Appearances are not qualified by space and time; therefore, they are all-pervasive and eternal, and they take the form of universals such as "pot-ness" and the like.
Furthermore, regarding the question of what the limit is for the blending of appearances (*ābhāsa*),

it has been stated that only those appearances which are non-contradictory blend together; thus, [the object] consists of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) not limited by space or time, and is vitalized by the rule of mutual non-contradiction among appearances.
And that is their union. "Only this much" means that the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is indeed twofold;

these entities, which consist of the universal (*sāmānya*), are precisely what will be discussed in the section on scripture (*āgama*) within the first chapter (*āhnika*) concerning the internal and external functioning [of consciousness], just like the terms *ghaṭa*, *karīra*, and *kumbha*.

“Object” (*vastu*), “reality” (*tattva*), and “object of knowledge” (*prameya*) are synonyms. He briefly explains how even in a single object such as a jar—which appears as something distinct from each [of the principles]—there exist all thirty-six principles, beginning with the words "For instance" (*tathā hi*). The appearance of solidity present in the jar is the earth-principle (*pṛthivī-tattva*).

In the passage beginning with *ghaṭalohita* (p. 288), the appearance of redness, the appearance of form, and the appearance of moisture constitute the water-principle (*ap-tattva*), while the appearance of solidity and so forth in the jar, along with the appearance of their mutual conjunction, is *rajas*; by this, [the nature of *rajas*] is characterized.
The principle of *prakṛti* (primordial nature) is accepted as "this is such-and-such. The principle of *niyati* (necessity) is the specific arrangement of a jar;

for *niyati* is the restriction that "this must be exactly thus. And this [restriction] has its life-force in the non-existence of other appearances, such as cloth, within the jar; for it is precisely the manifestation of the non-existence of other appearances, such as cloth, [that constitutes necessity].
The manifestation of the earth’s appearance as variegated, shining with the form of a broad base and belly,

and the perception of mutual difference between a jar and Caitra and so forth, is *māyā*. Following that, the manifestation of reality in the form "this is a jar" immediately after the illusory appearance is the *śivatattva*.

This serves as an illustration because even those principles not explicitly mentioned here are included within this jar; (369) let this investigation of the principles suffice for now, as it will be treated in detail later. In every way and by all means, regarding the object of knowledge described as "this is such-and-such" and so forth:

In each individual object such as a jar, there exists the Lord’s very sovereignty over both the differentiation of the appearances of universals— such as "jar-ness" or "golden-ness"— and the non-differentiation within the nature of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) which consists of the aggregate of those [appearances]. Thus,
the perception of the differentiation of appearances such as "gold" residing in the jar is itself the appearance of that gold.

The vision of the non-difference of the collective form and the vision of the non-duality of the Supreme Lord are to be relied upon as means for entering into the essential nature of the Supreme Lord— which, though dual in aspect, is one in its transcendent universality and consists of the manifold universe— as a way of entering into that very self-nature.

It has been established by this that even the worldly convention regarding jars, cloths, and so forth— which possess both unitary and manifold natures— is not in contradiction with the penetration into the essential nature of the Supreme Lord, who likewise possesses both unitary and manifold natures.
"This very [point]" means making clear, that is, manifesting explicitly, the very meaning already stated.

He explains that the establishment— that is, the existence— of the entire range of objects of knowledge (prameya), from the earth up to Śiva, which consists of both specific and universal characteristics, is dependent upon the Supreme Lord, by means of the phrase "by the qualities" (guṇaiḥ). This refers to the qualities of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell belonging to entities that take the form of both objects of knowledge and subjects of knowledge.

By means of its qualities acting as qualifiers— such as the stick and so forth— or even by these [attributes], this lump of clay, characterized by a broad base and a bulbous belly, is denoted by the word "jar"; it possesses a hard touch,
has a form consisting of seamless joints, possesses its appropriate taste, and is composed of earth.

By means of innate qualities such as sound, which serve as qualifiers— as in "because of its odor"— and by means of adventitious qualifiers— as in "Devadatta is staff-bearing" or "he is umbrella-bearing"— there is a differentiation consisting of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) in the form "this is here, now, and of such a shape," which is woven through everything in space and time.

And there is the universal (*jāti*), such as "pot-ness" or "Brahmin-hood," which is woven through those respective individuals. By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is also similarity (*sādṛśya*) in the form of non-difference, such as "the face is like a lotus. Furthermore, there is the non-apprehension of difference; by these [factors], non-distinction is established. And non-difference is thus: [The text continues: "Just as a single moon is perceived as many when reflected in various vessels of water, so too is the one Self perceived as manifold due to the diversity of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). This is the meaning. It is not that the Self is actually manifold; rather, it is perceived as manifold because of the diversity of its limiting adjuncts. Just as the one space appears divided by jars and other objects, so the one Self appears as many through the diversity of bodies and other adjuncts. Therefore, the conclusion is that the Self is one. Thus, the identity of the individual self (*jīva*) with Brahman is established. This is the purport. Thus ends the section on the identity of the individual self and Brahman. Now begins the section on the identity of the individual self and the Lord (*Īśvara*). Therein, the following doubt arises: if the individual self is identical with Brahman, then since Brahman is omnipresent, the individual self must also be omnipresent. If that were so, then since all selves would occupy the same space, there would be no distinction between them, leading to the confusion of experiences—just as when many people occupy a single house, their joys and sorrows become intermingled. To resolve this, the author says: "Just as the one space is divided by jars and other objects, so the one Self appears as many through the diversity of bodies and other adjuncts. (Verse 17) This means: just as the one space appears divided into many parts such as "the space within a jar" or "the space within a cloth" due to the diversity of limiting adjuncts like jars and cloths, even though in reality space is one and undivided; in the same way, the one Self appears as many—such as Caitra, Maitra, Devadatta, and Yajñadatta—due to the diversity of limiting adjuncts consisting of bodies, sense organs, and the like. Therefore, although the Self is omnipresent, there is no confusion of experiences, because each individual self is associated with its own specific set of adjuncts. Consequently, the experience of pleasure and pain remains distinct for each person. Thus, the identity of the individual self and the Lord is established. This is the purport. Thus ends the section on the identity of the individual self and the Lord. Now begins the section on the identity of the individual self and the material cause (*prakṛti*). Therein, the following doubt arises: if the individual self is identical with the material cause, then since the material cause is insentient (*jaḍa*), the individual self would also have to be insentient. If that were so, then since the insentient material cause is common to all, there would again be a confusion of experiences for all beings. To resolve this, the author says: "Just as the one sun is perceived as many in various vessels of water, so the one Self is perceived as manifold due to the diversity of limiting adjuncts. (Verse 18) This means: just as the one sun is perceived as many in different vessels of water due to the diversity of the limiting adjuncts—the vessels—even though in reality the sun is one; in the same way, the one Self is perceived as manifold due to the diversity of limiting adjuncts consisting of the intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), mind (*manas*), and the senses, even though in reality the Self is one. Therefore, although the material cause is common to all, there is no confusion of experiences, because each individual self is associated with its own specific set of adjuncts. Consequently, the experience of pleasure and pain remains distinct for each person. Thus, the identity of the individual self and the material cause is established. This is the purport. Thus ends the section on the identity of the individual self and the material cause. Now begins the section on the identity of the individual self and the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*). Therein, the following doubt arises: if the individual self is identical with the enjoyer, then since the enjoyer is distinct from the body, the individual self would also be distinct from the body. If that were so, then since the enjoyer is eternal, the individual self would also be eternal and distinct from the body. But this contradicts the scriptural teaching that the Self is non-different from the body. To resolve this, the author says: "Just as the one moon is perceived as many in various vessels of water, so the one Self is perceived as manifold due to the diversity of limiting adjuncts. (Verse 19) This means: just as the one moon is perceived as many in different vessels of water due to the diversity of the limiting adjuncts—the vessels—even though in reality the moon is one; in the same way, the one Self is perceived as manifold due to the diversity of limiting adjuncts consisting of the intellect, ego, mind, and the senses, even though in reality the Self is one. Therefore, although the enjoyer is distinct from the body, there is no contradiction with scripture, because the Self is taught to be non-different from the body only insofar as it is not separate from the aggregate of the body and its adjuncts. Consequently, the identity of the individual self and the enjoyer is established. This is the purport. Thus ends the section on the identity of the individual self and the enjoyer. Now begins the section on the identity of the individual self and the object of enjoyment (*bhogya*). Therein, the following doubt arises: if the individual self is identical with the object of enjoyment, then since the object of enjoyment consists of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, the individual self would also consist of these qualities. If that were so, then since these qualities are diverse, the individual self would also be diverse. To resolve this, the author says: "Just as the one space is divided by jars and other objects, so the one Self appears as many through the diversity of bodies and other adjuncts. (Verse 20) This means: just as the one space appears divided into many parts such as "the space within a jar" or "the space within a cloth" due to the diversity of limiting adjuncts like jars and cloths, even though in reality space is one and undivided; in the same way, the one Self appears as many—such as Caitra, Maitra, Devadatta, and Yajñadatta—due to the diversity of limiting adjuncts consisting of bodies and other factors. Therefore, although the Self is one, there is no multiplicity of the individual self, because the distinctions are merely due to the diversity of the adjuncts. Consequently, the identity of the individual self and the object of enjoyment is established. This is the purport. Thus ends the section on the identity of the individual self and the object of enjoyment. Now begins the section on the identity of the individual self and the knower (*pramātṛ*). Therein, the following doubt arises: if the individual self is identical with the knower, then since the knower is dependent upon the instruments of knowledge such as the eyes and ears, the individual self would also be dependent.
