If that were so, then since the instruments of knowledge are subject to production and destruction, the individual self would also be subject to production and destruction. To resolve this, the author says: "Just as the one sun is perceived as many in various vessels of water, so the one Self is perceived as manifold due to the diversity of limiting adjuncts. (Verse 21) This means: just as the one sun is perceived as many in different vessels of water due to the diversity of the limiting adjuncts—the vessels—even though in reality the sun is one; in the same way, the one Self is perceived as manifold due to the diversity of limiting adjuncts consisting of the intellect, ego, mind, and the senses, even though in reality the Self is one. Therefore, although the knower is dependent upon the instruments of knowledge, there is no contradiction, because the Self is taught to be eternal and independent in its true nature. Consequently, the identity of the individual self and the knower is established. This is the purport. Thus ends the section on the identity of the individual self and the knower. Now begins the section on the identity of the individual self and the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Therein, the following doubt arises: if the individual self is identical with the means of knowledge, then since the means of knowledge are diverse—consisting of perception, inference, and testimony—the individual self would also be diverse. To resolve this, the author says: "Just as the one space is divided by jars and other objects, so the one Self appears as many through the diversity of bodies and other adjuncts. (Verse 22) This means: just as the one space appears divided into many parts such as "the space within a jar" or "the space within a cloth" due to the diversity of limiting adjuncts like jars and cloths, even though in reality space is one and undivided; in the same way, the one Self appears as many—

(289) By means of the extensive passage beginning with "kriyāsaṃbandha," difference and non-difference are established as existing in one [place], namely in the cognizer who is unconditioned by space and time; for this very reason, in that [cognizer] which is all-pervading and eternal, there occurs the joining and disjoining of all cognitions and means of knowledge, and so forth.

This is possible and logically consistent only when there exists that which is designated by the term "Śiva," characterized by absolute freedom (svātantrya) appropriate for the manifestation of the fivefold cosmic functions and the proliferation of the world of phenomena (prapañca). It is established through valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa),
as the principle of earth (pṛthivī-tattva) is observed to persist continuously in mountains, trees, cities, and so forth.
The nature of water is pervasive throughout rivers, streams, oceans, and so forth; in this manner, it persists as a recurring feature.

Now, regarding that which is present here: by which [of the two] is it characterized—as that which is excluded from other places, times, and forms, such as mountains, trees, cities, and the like, or as rivers, streams, oceans, and so forth? Is it by way of the recurring [universal] or by way of the excluded [particular]?
Let it be said that truth consists in having a form; nothing lacks truth by virtue of having some form or other.

Regarding both cases—namely, in the case of a persisting form and a non-persisting form—since there is no mutual sublation between them, if truth were to reside in either one form, whether persisting or non-persisting, then the other would necessarily be a sublater. If...

"Upon its arising" means upon the arising of that sublater (*bādhaka*). "That very [thing]" refers to the sublated entity (*bādhyo bhāvaḥ*), which, being devoid of the capacity for re-emergence, would be unable to rise again and would thus dissolve like a flash of lightning. However, it does not dissolve in this way, because both [the sublater and the sublated] are manifest. "For this very reason" [is said].

By those who consider the contradiction between difference and non-difference to be difficult to resolve, because entities— whether they are universals in the form of non-difference or particulars in the form of their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*)— manifest without mutual exclusion. "By some" refers to this group.

By some proponents of the doctrine of external objects (*bāhyavādins*), it is determined to be "inexpressible" (*anirvacanīya*) because it consists of false ignorance (*avidyā*); by others, namely the proponents of consciousness-only (*vijñānavādins*), it is considered "present" (*sāmpratatva*) due to its being attached to appearances—
that is, its being attached to cognitions of blue, yellow, and so forth— and thus it is that which is attached to those cognitions of blue, yellow, and so forth.

The world, consisting of blue, yellow, and so forth, which possesses the nature of both difference and non-difference, is real for the time being, but it is real only as conventional usage (*vyavahāramātra-satya*) and not ultimately real; thus they call it "indescribable" (*anirvācya*).

By saying "for the time being," he implies that the self (*ātman*), as well as the speaker who utters this, the listener who hears it, and the other person to be enlightened, are likewise [only conventionally real].
He is deceived and robbed [of his true nature]. By the will of the Supreme Lord, both are indeed non-dual, their own essential natures being concealed.

The objects of knowledge (*prameya*), such as jars and bodies, which consist of both difference and non-difference, appear as resting within consciousness, which serves as the foundational ground for the subject (*pramātṛ*).
(371) As it has been said: "The distinct states of being the grasped and the grasper appear as two objects within the cognizer.

Due to the sovereignty of that consciousness (*saṃvedana*), the multiplicity—which rests within the internal consciousness whose nature is the cognizer—such as "water" and "fire," is brought to a state of unity with that very consciousness.
Water and fire are mutually opposed;

this is established by one's own self-awareness even for every animal. "For that very reason" means precisely because they are mutually opposed when resting within the consciousness of the subject. It has been said: "For this very reason..."
Regarding the phrase "the delineation of whatever is intended":

having established the meaning of the aphorism through this underlying intent (*tātparya*), he explains it in detail, preceded by a formal application (*yojanā*), starting with the words "And therefore" (*ataśca*). As for "And therefore": [this is] because of the repose within consciousness.
Because they are distinct, that aforementioned type of differentiation— produced by qualities (*guṇa*) functioning as adjuncts (*upādhi*),
and by intended objects such as sound and so forth, or even by [external marks] such as a staff— which serves to qualify the substantive entity (*vastu*) by bestowing specific distinctions—
is [illustrated] by the case of "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and "Brahmin-hood" (*brāhmaṇatva*), which, by virtue of their respective universals (*jāti*), are like the orb of the moon appearing as "vast."

Or, according to the principle stated as "the cognition of objects as they exist due to similarity," there is a non-difference between entities resulting from the non-apprehension of their distinction. This is described by the phrase "connected with action" (*kriyāsaṃbandha*) and so forth; and this [non-difference] is both differentiated and non-differentiated. "In one place" means...
In the one, non-dual cognizer, who serves as the foundational ground for the repose of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*),

the knowledge (*pramā*), and the cognizer (*pramātṛ*); from this very fact, the manifold expansion of the fivefold group of actions (*pañcakṛtya*)— numbering countless varieties such as the joining and separating of all the means of knowledge and knowledge residing within the cognizers from *sakala* up to *sadāśiva*— is manifested.

In the case of absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), it is only when [the Lord] is designated by the term "Śiva"—who dwells exclusively within our hearts purified by the glance of the Supreme Guru, and who is not within the range of the hearts of dualistic Śaivas, Naiyāyikas, Buddhists, and others—that this is logically established; it is not otherwise. Such being the case...

This is not tenable if the cognizer (pramātṛ) is not admitted. For entities whose nature consists of the object of cognition (prameya) and the cognizer, it is precisely the qualifiers such as "being made of gold" or "being a Brahmin" that bring about their qualified state; this [qualified state] does not arise from anything other than these [qualifiers], such as "being made of gold."

Since these ultimate particulars (*viśeṣas*) are not manifest, what purpose is there in distinguishing the object by means of them? (372) This is because they cannot be apprehended through perception. He demonstrates the qualifying attributes that would differentiate it: "This [atom] possesses another atom; that..."

Now, at the time of the commencement of this jar characterized by its specific location and so forth—immediately after the second dyad formed from the first conjoined dyads—at the moment of the conjunction of the third dyad, it is distinguished from the first [dyad].
Thus, this jar is measured by such atoms; this is that very self which existed previously.
By this very fact— that he thus embraced the celestial damsels in the abode of heaven—
the appearance of difference regarding atoms, the self, and so forth, is established for the yogins, the omniscient ones, and others; such is the intermediate subject matter.
It is established that the reality of the object of knowledge, which consists of both difference and non-difference, attains freedom from doubt by resting in the single cognizer. As it has been said:
"The cognition of difference shines within the single consciousness."
"Blue and yellow, pleasure and pain, embodied; with a deep navel and elevated breasts—this woman is like a figure upon a flat painting board. Thus it is said.
Furthermore: "With a deep navel and high breasts, walking with the gait of an elephant"—in this way, the manifold play of the world's variety appears within consciousness, as if upon a wall.

If this cognizer— the very foundation upon which the entire phenomenal expansion consisting of objects of knowledge, means of knowledge, acts of cognition, and cognizers rests— is itself of the nature of both difference and non-difference,
then one must strive to demonstrate the means of knowledge precisely within that cognizer, and not within something that is insubstantial.
Regarding the object of knowledge (*prameya*): he states that effort directed toward the primary subject matter is fruitful— namely,

this very object of knowledge (*prameya*) which was first introduced at the beginning of the treatise as "the knower" (*jñātṛ*) in relation to the agent, and which is now addressed as the most intimate internal factor, having been raised both as a question and as a point of doubt.
The Teacher causes [the student] to remember what has long been forgotten and establishes it in the mind by means of the words "tathā hi" (for thus) and so forth.
As for the question "Who would bring about its accomplishment?"— it refers to that reality which was previously introduced,
namely, the nature of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the nature of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), within the knowledge described in the aforementioned manner.
It is now indeed fit for its conclusion: "Thus it has become.

Previously, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) was that which establishes the mere object of knowledge (*prameya*)—which was unmanifest, limited by space and time, and therefore circumscribed—as "this is a jar" or "this is a cloth."

It is appropriate to investigate how [the categories] could proceed within that Supreme Lord, the subject (pramātṛ), who is the foundational wall upon which the entire manifold of objects of knowledge (prameya), means of knowledge (pramāṇa), and acts of knowledge (pramā) come to rest; the meaning is that no means of knowledge can apply to that subject.
To clarify this, he says: "of the variegated painting of the manifold universe" (*viśvavaicitryacitrasya*). "The object of knowledge, the means of knowledge" (*meyamānam*):
[this refers to] that which consists of the circle of subjects (*mātṛcakra*), beginning with the earth and ending with Śiva—the variegated painting of the manifold universe.
It is "like a level wall-surface," meaning it is the locus of repose in non-differentiation; for this very reason, it is "level" (*sama*).

Because it is like a surface of a wall devoid of the gradations of high and low, and because it serves as the very wall for the manifold variety of the universe, it is untouched by any state opposed to its own nature; thus, since there is no contact with any entity whose non-existence is not admitted, it is therefore ultimately real.
"In the Lord, the subject, who is in essence reality from the perspective of ultimate truth, whose form is eternally manifest"— that is to say, in the Lord,

the independent subject who performs the fivefold acts such as the creation of the universe, who is the substratum for the entire cycle of objects of knowledge, means of knowledge, and subjects, and whose form is eternally manifest at all times.
Even at the prior, posterior, and middle limits of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*), there shines the common,

perfect *ahantā*-constituted nature whose essence is Light; for this very reason, it is described in the Purāṇas as "unconditioned by time" and "the partaker in all cognition," [encompassing] everything from the *sakala* state up to Śiva.
Residing above the entire range of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) belonging to the subject (*pramātṛ*), and partaking in the inward-turned aspect of cognition (*pramiti*),

it manifests as the nature of each respective subject with a new appearance; thus, because of its orientation toward ever-new objects of knowledge (*prameya*) qualified by space and time— such as "this is a jar" or "this is a cloth"— it is itself also new.
If that form is momentary and newly appearing, what is the purpose of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) therein?

There is neither utility nor justification for a means of valid cognition in that case. As it has been said: (374) "The means of valid cognition exists between the limited object and the knower; it is established in relation to the object of knowledge."
"And the consciousness of another cognizer is not capable of being delimited.
For it has been determined that even that [other's consciousness] depends upon consciousness for its establishment.
Here, by means of the passage beginning with "this is such-and-such" and so forth, [the author refers to] limited entities such as Caitra, Maitra, and others.

"This is a jar," "this is a cloth"—it is that which establishes the limited objects of knowledge (*prameya*) as they adhere to the subject (*pramātṛ*). For this very reason, it is said that there is a "constantly new manifestation. Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*): [it refers] to the Supreme Lord Śiva, the subject whose nature has been described, extending from Śiva down to the earth.

It is said that [the Lord] is established prior to the emergence of the manifold world— which consists of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*), the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and the act of knowing (*pramā*)— within His luminous body, whose nature is pure light and which consists of a full subjectivity (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*) capable of embracing the universe; for this very reason, He is described as being that which transcends that manifold world.

What is the utility of a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) or a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), what is its purpose, or even what possibility or logical justification (*upapatti*) exists? This is the meaning:
it is precisely for this reason that he demonstrates [the point] with the words "And thus," and so forth. Even in the world, such as in the case of Caitra, Maitra, and others...

The means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) bestows only that established cognition which consists of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) inherent within the light of consciousness—consciousness which is essentially bound to the subject—and which pertains to the object of knowledge situated below that [subject], in such forms as "this is a jar" or "this is a cloth. This is because [the object] is already primordially established within the uninterrupted light [of consciousness]. Therefore...

Since the Supreme Lord, the supreme subject, is already established even prior to the emergence of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*), what need is there for the establishment of Him? Let there be, for now, the establishment of jars, cloths, and so forth.
And let that establishment of jars, cloths, and so forth be contingent upon subjects such as Caitra and Maitra, by means of the instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that determine those objects.

If even the Supreme Lord (Prameśvara) were to be established by means of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as a jar, a cloth, or the like, then that establishment would be contingent upon that cognizer (*pramātṛ*). For, according to the principle that "there is nothing whatsoever beyond the Supreme," there is no existence beyond Him; thus, from the very beginning, [He is established] in the Blessed Lord.

Having indicated by way of summary that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is being rejected, he demonstrates at length (375) the uselessness and the logical impossibility of such a means of valid cognition with respect to that Supreme Lord,

beginning with the words "the manifold variety of the universe" (*viśvavaicitrya*). For the manifold variety of the universe consists essentially of the objects of knowledge (*meyamātra*) and the means of knowledge (*mānamātra*).
In the Blessed One, whose singular nature is the light consisting of full subjectivity— just as a painting [requires] a wall—

[the author] states with the words beginning "that which" (*yad*) that the manifold variety of the universe would not be possible without the Supreme Lord, who is the wall-like subject, were he not admitted as the cognizer. Without the subject who serves as the wall...
If these [objects]— such as "this is blue" and "this is yellow"— are reflected upon by the subject as being strictly distinct from one another,

then, while those [objects] such as blue and so forth remain resting solely within their own selves, the cognitions that grasp the blue and yellow likewise [rest] in that very same way; thus, the cognition of blue [rests] upon its own object.

It perceives only blue and not yellow; being like those blind from birth or deaf regarding the objects of cognition, they are incapable of seeing, hearing, or speaking concerning the objects of others. Each [cognition] rests within the cognizer (pramātṛ) upon its own respective object, such as blue and so forth.
(p. 293) Following that cognition, the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) that arise immediately thereafter are likewise [of the same nature];

like blue and so forth, and like the cognition of blue and so forth, they rest solely within themselves. Thus, in the absence of a cognizer (*pramātṛ*), how could there be the realization that "this variegated world consists of the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), the cognition (*jñāna*), and the knower (*jñātṛ*)"? How could it be?
It would be so; for even in the world, it is established that a painting is not seen without a wall.

Thus, on a surface that is level—devoid of depressions, elevations, and the like, and uniformly high in one place—it is nevertheless perceived as having deep navels and elevated breasts, divided by lines imagined by the painter, which possess the distinctions of depth and height.
A variegated manifestation is logical; likewise, because it is not limited by space and time,

there arises the possibility of the diversity of the aforementioned universe as a differentiation adhering to the wall of the Great Light, which consists of a pervasive, eternal, unitary, and perfect *aham*-nature.

Because it devours time—which brings about birth in the lower realms—it is eternal. For this very reason, he declares that his own self is an uninterrupted self-luminosity; otherwise, the resting place for the aforementioned variety of existents would be untenable. "Therein" means in that which serves as the variegated wall for the diversity of the universe.

In the self-luminous Supreme Lord, there is no purpose whatsoever for the aforementioned means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), which establishes limited objects of knowledge; for such a means of knowledge resides within the subjectivity of *māyā*, whereas [the Lord] transcends the universe and is the very foundation of the universe.
Because it is impossible to transfer [the nature of] the self-luminous Supreme Lord [into other categories]. As it has been stated in the *Śrī Tantrāloka*:
"Even the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), which extend the very life-force of objects..."
"Even for them, that very Supreme Lord is the other who is the life-force.

Thus, let there be some Supreme Lord who serves as the foundational wall for the manifold variety of the universe; however, He is not the light of the former [the individual soul]. Therefore, in order to manifest Him, there must be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) directed toward Him.
If it is argued that "let it proceed," and thus its manifestation did not exist previously,

then it would follow that it does not exist at all; for since this Supreme Lord has no form other than mere manifestation, even the contact with non-existence is untenable regarding everything from the earth up to Śiva.

For even at the time of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), this very [Lord] alone exists in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), because the Supreme Lord, who is Light, is eternally existent, and because that which is existent cannot possibly have the nature of non-existence. The meaning is that contact with non-existence is not possible for Him. This Lord, due to the impossibility of contact with non-existence, [remains].

Let it be self-luminous. If it is argued that his lordship—which was previously unperceived—is now to be cognized by a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and that the lordship of the knower (*pramātṛ*) who is established in a means of valid knowledge, though previously unperceived, will now be cognized by a non-means of valid knowledge (*apramāṇa*), that too is not possible. This one is the Lord.

If [the Lord] does not manifest as a knower (*pramātṛ*), then whose effort would there be consisting of affirmation and negation toward the Lord? In this regard, who here [could have] the establishment characterized by knowledge, such that one might know "the Lord exists" by means of some kind of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or [know] "he does not exist"?

If it is argued that the knower (*pramātṛ*) performs the negation characterized by cognition, then is that [knower] the same as the insentient body and so forth, or is it something else denoted by terms such as "Self" (*ātman*)? Furthermore, is that [Self] of the nature of self-luminosity or not? If it is the insentient body and so forth, then it is that very [body].

How could that which is unestablished in itself bring about establishment in another? If it is argued that the self, though non-self-luminous and indeed insentient (*jaḍa*), shares the same status as that [other] and is thus of the nature of self-luminosity—then in what form does it shine?
If it shines in the form of established pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*) alone, then... (377) ...at that time, [it would not be established].

The differentiation of cognitions and the non-differentiation of those differentiated [cognitions] would not occur through internal synthesis. Therefore, it first shines forth as having the nature of self-luminous autonomy.
And while shining forth in that manner, what other [object] could it establish or negate? [It is only] the agent and the knower.
If you say it is its *svabhāva* (intrinsic nature), then surely it is the subject (*pramātṛ*) itself that has become such; what else could it be?

This much alone is to be investigated as the object of knowledge (*prameya*). Therefore, if you say it manifests as the subject, then its very state as subject is its lordship (*īśvaratā*). That indeed is the "I" in the Lord, the subject, whose body consists of the manifestation of all things.

The analysis of the compound is as follows: "the uncommon, essential nature—which consists of full subjectivity (*pūrṇāhantā*) and is of the nature of light—is grasped with distinction and excellence. For this very reason, because its form is that of the independent space consisting of full subjectivity, there is no contact with the aforementioned limited forms.

By the phrase "through entry into non-existence" is meant that the conventional usage of time, which consists in the entry into impermanence, does not exist in this Supreme Lord; thus He is called "Ancient" (*purāṇa*). In such a cognizer, what is the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and for what purpose is there a need for a means of knowledge? In that regard, what is the utility of a means of knowledge?
What is the meaning? Furthermore, what is the proof for that? The meaning is that nothing is established by logical reasoning.
He states the very definition of proof (*pramāṇa*): "Proof, namely..."

The means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is that which, being itself of the nature of a novel manifestation, effects the repose of the cognition of the object within the limited subject; for the supreme subject,
whose manifestation is uninterrupted, [encompasses] all cognitions residing in subjects ranging from the *sakala* up to Śiva.
"In the form of being turned inward" means it rests within the Self that is the perfect I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*). Regarding the word "that":

how could that which is of the nature of an internal manifestation, proceeding toward the subject who is the Great Light, be a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)? How could it be a means of knowledge with respect to a subject other than that [Great Light]? Where [else] would such a means of knowledge exist?
Once that supreme divine cognition has been established, where could it possibly find rest within a cognizer?

For there exists no cognizer whatsoever situated above it, as it alone transcends all. Therefore, [it rests] within the body composed of grossness, weakness, strength, pleasure, pain, and their absence.

Let it be granted that a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is applicable even to the cognizer (*pramātṛ*), who is essentially [empty] like the eightfold group of means of knowledge, just as it is in the case of jars and other objects. Even in that case, however, [the means of knowledge applies] only to a portion consisting of the body and so forth, just like a jar, and not in any way whatsoever [to the true nature of the cognizer].

The ellipsis is "a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) operates. However, in no way whatsoever can a means of valid cognition be established with respect to that portion of consciousness which is the nature of the light of the "I," [identifying it] as that body and so forth. In that regard, even when the body and so forth—which are the knowing subject—are directed toward objects such as jars and cloths, a means of valid cognition is established. This...
When one says, "This is a jar" or "This is a cloth," because the mind is directed toward objects such as their parts,
there is a contraction within the body and so forth; however, in comparison with the attachment to the true subject— which consists of uncontracted consciousness—
let self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) be declared the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the ultimate subject who consists of consciousness.

There is no purpose whatsoever for a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) at any time; furthermore, since a means of valid cognition is not possible with respect to the ultimate knower (paramārtha-pramātṛ), I too have said in accordance with this that "every person has been made an object of knowledge (prameya)."
"I am desired by myself"—one feels shame at this; how then could Maheśvara tolerate that making [the world] an object of cognition, which brings shame even to people?
Indeed, the tenfold objects of cognition consist of the gross and subtle forms of earth and so forth, ending with sound.

The wheel of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇacakra*), consisting of the ten external instruments— beginning with the secret organ and ending with the ear, which are the forms of the intellect (*buddhi*) and the organs of action— and the threefold internal instruments consisting of the mind (*manas*) and so forth up to the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), [perceive] from the earth up to the jar.

The group of twenty-three forms ending in the suffix -kāra consists of the seven types of subjects— namely, the *sakala-pralayākala*, *vijñānākala*, *mantra*, *mantreśvara*, *mantramaheśvara*, and *śiva*— which are essentially divisions of the single form that is *pradhāna*, and which revolve within the nature of *paramaśiva*.

In the Blessed Lord, who is the subject (*pramātṛ*), both non-utility and impossibility apply; for in that Blessed Lord, a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is both unnecessary and impossible. Therefore, the means of knowledge consisting of the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of such a Blessed Lord—and consequently the scripture (*śāstra*) which has him as its object—is established.

Anticipating the question at the end—“For what purpose [does this diversity exist]? according to the stated principle that the Blessed Lord is beyond the scope of even the scripture as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), just as He is beyond perception and the other means of knowledge—the author says:
“In such a state, the Blessed Lord [acts] by His own will alone.”
Thus, even within empirical transaction (*vyavahāra*), the Lord does not enter the body and so forth.

According to the principle stated [in verse 379], having entered the body and so forth, and having concealed His own Self—which is both immanent in the universe and transcendent of the universe—by means of the power of His own *māyā*, [He thinks]: "I am the Lord."

Having concealed even such conventional expressions as "I am independent," "I am complete," "I am eternal," and "I am free from [worldly] attachments," one superimposes upon one's own self such conventions as "I am Caitra" or "I am Maitra"; this is that supreme sovereignty which accomplishes the impossible.

The divine power of Māyā belonging to Maheśa is the veil of Śiva’s own self; by virtue of this Māyā being grasped, the person (puruṣa) becomes a bound soul (paśu), his consciousness defiled by time, death, necessity, and passion.

The connection [between them] is by virtue of knowledge (*vidyā*). According to the principle stated in the *Paramārthasāra*, "one knows this very thing as 'just this' and 'nothing else' through one's entire being," she relies upon the stage of the non-animal (*apaśu-bhūmikā*) and thus remains with her own true nature un-recognized; for this very reason, of this [true] nature—
When indeed a longing for Śiva arises among bound souls (paśus),
then those atoms (paramāṇavas) arise as possessing Śiva and other [attributes].

"Then, at that very moment, they receive initiation from the Guru. According to the principle stated in the *Nandiśikha*, those who have not previously been initiated [into the higher levels] become liberated from the bonds of *māyā* only when [the knots] have dissolved through the falling glance of the true Guru, who is non-different from Paramaśiva.

Since this scripture initiates for this person— the three impurities of *āṇava*, *māyīya*, and *kārmika* having fallen away through the falling glance of a true guru impelled by the will of the Supreme Lord— the previously uninitiated worldly discourse such as "I am the Lord," it is [the means].
Immediately after hearing this, he remains reflecting thus: "I am eternal, I am perfect, I am independent, I am the all-pervading Lord"— not merely by the words of the Guru,
but in accordance with this very method, he abides as one who has recognized his own true nature as being identical with the Supreme Śiva.

Therefore, because it initiates such worldly transactions as those concerning Ishvara and so forth, that scripture is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Every scripture consists of an inference whose purpose is the form of the hearer who is distinct from the author of that scripture; this is also the case with that particular scripture.

In reality, its nature consists precisely of the sixteen categories beginning with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); this is the remainder [of the thought], namely that "its nature" is such. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the Buddhists—who maintain that an inference consists of only two members, the example (*udāharaṇa*) and the application (*upanaya*)—[are included] as those who hold that there are five members beginning with the proposition (*pratijñā*).
Furthermore, the objection that [the Nyāya system] consists of sixteen categories is merely a dogmatic prejudice;

for when the sixteen categories are being examined, the object of knowledge (*prameya*) pertaining to the science of logic (*tarkaśāstra*) is established as "the other" (*para*). Thus, the charge that the scripture is possessed by the demoness of sophistry (*tarkapiśācikā*), which causes the throat to wither, is baseless.

Having been instructed "correctly," one proceeds without error. What is the purpose for another—the listener—by means of this passage beginning with "useful for the attainment and avoidance [of what has been stated]"?
That purpose belongs to the other, the listener of the treatise, for the sake of comprehension (*pratipatti*). And that comprehension...

It arises from that scripture alone which consists of inference regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Even in that scripture, the five-membered syllogism beginning with the proposition (*pratijñā*) is employed; thus, that scripture, complete with its five members, brings about understanding for the listener. In reality, however, [it is] Īśvara...

Everything other than the scriptures proclaimed [by the Lord] is a human treatise; thus, it was established by Akṣapāda, the creator of the system of Nyāya, in the two sūtras beginning with "the diversity of the universe" (*viśvavaicitrya*), that such [human treatises] are merely inferences based on the ultimate reality (*paramārthānumāna*). (p. 297)
The meaning stated in the verse beginning with "kartari jñātari" has been recalled. Regarding the phrase "atrāpi":

even in this treatise known as the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*, which will be discussed immediately hereafter and which initiates the linguistic usage of "Īśvara" and so forth, [the teaching] has not been previously set forth—this being expressed by a single verse.
However, in order to recall the meaning stated in the verse beginning with "but through the power of delusion" (*mohavaśāt*), he says: "herein.

Although [the true nature] exists within the subject whose nature was described in the two immediately preceding verses, due to the power of delusion—and as will be explained, due to the power of *māyā*—[one fails to perceive it] until the glance of the true Guru, who is non-different from the Supreme Lord, falls upon them.
In the *Śaktiprakāśa*, conventional expressions such as "I am the Lord who was not previously set in motion," "I am full," "I am all-pervasive," and "I am eternal" do not apply.
For those existing in this [state], these belong to the category of the Lord (*īśvara*).

The *Pratyabhijñā-śāstra* is set in motion by the illumination of the powers of will, knowledge, and action through its own illuminating light. By hearing this scripture, people engage in worldly activity and [recognize] the worldly usage of "Lord" and so forth within their own selves.

"Let them proceed"—this is the first meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*). Furthermore, by means of the scripture composed by the Teacher—which, as an instrument, reveals the powers of will, knowledge, and action—the worldly convention regarding Īśvara and so forth is set in motion; this is the second meaning of the causative suffix. In this world... [iti]

The capacity to accomplish the impossible (*durghaṭakāritva*) is indeed his unsurpassed [power]; this alone is his sovereignty (*svatantratva*), his lordship (*aiśvarya*), and his nature as consciousness (*bodharūpatā*). According to the principle stated in the *Bodhapañcadaśikā*, this very capacity to accomplish the impossible is the supreme, perfect sovereignty of the Supreme Lord, which is now—

For those like us, who have been recognized as Great Lords of the Self through the falling glance of the True Guru, there exist in the various states of bondage (*paśubhāva*) acquired during hundreds of previous births in former times;
yet, due to the current absence of the True Guru’s glance, these [states] are now impossible for us to conceive.

Indeed, the accomplishment of a difficult task from afar demonstrates precisely that accomplishment of a difficult task by that Supreme Lord—by means of the sentence beginning with "from here" (*itaḥ*). What could be more difficult than this? That is to say, what could be more difficult than the performance of what is exceedingly hard to accomplish, as is being set forth?

If it is asked what that is like: it is when, while the light of the nature of the full "I" (pūrṇāhaṃ-rūpa)— that is, while the light whose essence is that very indivisible identity— is shining forth as one's own unconditioned nature of such full subjectivity, [the soul] remains concealed, having assumed a human body.
Maheśvara, according to the principle stated in the scriptures, having entered Caitra, Maitra, and others, as well as [objects such as] space and so forth by his own will,
remains as if concealed; he manifests within himself in such forms as "I am not," "I am not the nature of full subjectivity (pūrṇāhaṃtā)," "I am not the Lord," "I am not the Master," and so forth.

"Because manifestation is an appearance of prohibition"—thus, due to its possession of such sovereignty, this [world] is "this" (idam), while that [Absolute] is "the Beyond" (tat). Therefore, this is something other than the aforementioned sovereignty.
It is not merely that the Supreme Lord manifests within His own self in the form described above.

Only the manifestation of negation is made manifest; such is its manifestation. Within that very self, in the portion of "this" (idam-bhāga) regarding creation, the intellect and so forth have been brought by him to the state of the reflective awareness of "I" (ahaṃkāra-parāmarśa) as the subject. That is his own essential nature.

The person is considered manifold, consisting of various forms of thorough cognition, such as "I am Caitra" or "I am Maitra. According to the principle that will be explained later— that which is called the manifestation of the form of a bound soul (paśu)— it is through the emergence of the subjective aspect (grāhakāṃśa) that Māyā, for the subject, presents [the object] as perceived through the "this-ness" (idantā).

The manifestation within one's own self of the objects of perception, such as jars and cloths, as well as the manifestation within one's own self of the perceiver in the form of a bound soul (paśu) corresponding to that manifestation of the object—
this very dual manifestation is the Māyā-śakti of the Lord. Thus it has been said:

"The pair of the grasped and the grasper is created simultaneously," as it has been said: "She is named Māyā, the Deluder. Thus, from such a state—namely, from the sovereignty (svātantrya) which consists of the power of Māyā in the form of latent impressions (vāsanā), the Supreme Lord assumes the state of a bound soul (paśu). This is the state of being a bound soul taken up by the Supreme Lord.

He states the ultimate nature of that delusion— the state of full consciousness consisting of supreme *ahantā* (I-ness) which has destroyed the nature of the Supreme Self— by means of the passage beginning with "svātmavartinaḥ" (residing in one's own self). "Residing in one's own self" means existing within one's very own self.
The manifestation of the multitude of entities residing within the Self exists indeed as the Lord's own;
without that, the reflective awareness of will does not proceed.

According to the principle thus stated, [the reality] is to be contemplated as terrifying when the vibration of the group’s own will arises— [a vibration] that clearly manifests from the beginning with Śiva until the end— as the self that is filled with the manifestation of the universe (which consists of the three powers), namely, the fullness of autonomy characterized by memory, experience, and exclusion.
Because it possesses power, [it is] sovereignty consisting of those three powers abiding within its own self—[as stated]:
"The Self alone is the one Great Lord of all living beings;
I am the universal form, nourished by the unbroken awareness that 'this is I'."

Thus, according to the principle to be explained, if there is the conceit that the attributes of omnipresence, eternity, and so forth— which exist within one's own self, are effortlessly established, and are devoid of the limitation of space and time due to their oneness— though manifesting within one's own self, are not manifest, that indeed is *yama*.

"By the power of his delusion" means by the power of the conceit consisting of delusion; "here" refers to the subject (pramātṛ) mentioned in the two immediately preceding verses concerning the manifold variety of the universe and so forth,
in whom [the state of] Īśvara and the rest had not previously been set in motion through the falling of the glance of a true Guru.

Regarding the term "empirical usage" (*vyavahāra*): if one asks what kind of empirical usage is that which is expressed by [attributes] such as lordship (*īśvaratā*) and so forth— namely, fullness, autonomy, omnipresence, and eternity—
it is indeed that which shines as "I," being full, autonomous, omnipresent, and eternal.

"In this manner and so forth, may people engage in that worldly transaction within their own selves. By "that manifestation of power" (śaktiprakāśena), [it means] of the powers belonging to the Lord. Nevertheless, for this cognizer who is to be made to recognize [his own nature], there are the powers of will, knowledge, and action residing within his own self.
The author [states]:
"Those people who know him as 'This is Śiva'— as described in the Purāṇas and other texts, like the Lord (Īśvara)— and act accordingly upon hearing such words..."
Knowing this for myself and acting accordingly, I constantly contemplate thus:
"I am Śiva; I am the God; I am the Lord; I am Bhairava."

According to the principle stated by the learned, for those people who— by means of the scripture consisting of a parārthānumāna (inference for others) that establishes the conventional usage of "Lord" and so forth within their own self through the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of their own self as being Śiva—
initiate that very convention within themselves, [there arises] that conventional usage...

The activity of setting [the world] in motion is performed by those who are capable. The teachers, by means of this treatise, set in motion for the world the conventional usage regarding the Self, God, and so forth. Regarding the term "pravartyate" (is set in motion), there are two [explanations]: [it is derived from the root *vṛt* with the prefix *pra*,] and [it is derived from the root *vṛ* with the prefix *pra* and the suffix *ṇic*].
When this worldly transaction involving Īśvara and so forth has thus proceeded, for the cognizer,
that which exists remains exactly as it is— whether external or internal— just as it was before.

According to the position stated by the learned, nothing whatsoever arises that exceeds one's own true nature, which consists of Śiva. Furthermore, it is not the case that this Śiva-nature—which, though established from the very beginning, was not manifest in reality—is now being manifested; rather, for this [individual],...

The meaning expressed by the word *kevala* is simply this: even though the Self— which is Śiva himself, the ground of the empirical usage of "I" and so forth, and which shines as one's own nature— is being manifested for the cognizer, that conceit [of the cognizer] which holds that it is not manifest due to concealment by the power of *māyā* is removed.
"One whose sovereignty is made manifest through knowledge and higher realization (vidyā-abhijñā) is called liberated (mukta).

According to this principle to be explained later, liberation consists precisely in the removal of the mental representation [of duality] through the word of the Lord Teacher, which consists in the unfolding of the power of knowledge (vidyā-śakti).

Bondage is precisely the departure from such a state of self-identification that results in assuming the form of a limited being (*paśu*). From the very beginning, within the Śiva-nature of one's own true essence, there is both the state of being bound—due to the obscuration by *māyā* through thoughts such as "I am Caitra" or "I am Maitra"—and the state of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), characterized by the realization "I am God," and so forth; both of these [conditions] exist through the grace of the True Guru.

Through the unfolding of the power of knowledge (*vidyā-śakti*) consisting of the sidelong glance (*kaṭākṣa*), the two—namely, "I am Śiva" and "I am the Lord," as well as liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*)—have as their sole essence mere self-conception (*abhimananamātra*). That is to say, both have as their sole essence mere self-conception. This refers to both of these types of liberation associated with that [state].
The Lord alone manifests through this twofold nature as the unfolding of the Blessed One. As it has been said: "Salutation to the one who is eternally bound and yet eternally liberated."

Thus, in the *Śrīmatsrotraratnāvalī*. By the phrase "it has been said by you," he clearly establishes the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*) itself, preceded by the presentation of the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), with the words "of one possessed by an element" (*bhautasya*).
Just as in the case of Caitra who is possessed by an elemental spirit, there arises the notion "I am Caitra."

Even though [the being] appears as the self, for one who, due to being seized by a spirit, thinks out of delusion "I have been carried away by a spirit," that delusion consisting of the spirit's possession is removed by a practitioner capable of that task; this is the remainder [of the sense].

He describes the manner of its removal: "Indeed, who are you that [address] one possessed by a spirit? This means: for you, who consider [me] to be possessed by a spirit, [this person] is intent upon such objects as a jar; thus, [he speaks] to one capable of discerning the presence of a spirit, in due order.

When the proof has been stated, [the opponent]—possessed by a spirit—says: "The multitude of objects such as pots and cloths directed toward me are directed toward the Lord alone, and not toward me. To this, the proponent replies: "Child, look! This orientation toward the universe belongs to you as well," and he says this again and again.

Just as one who speaks while possessed by a spirit— though his speech is not a proof [of his identity]— does not perform any new action different from his previous state, but rather resumes exactly what he was doing before once the possession has been dispelled; in the same way, the world of bound souls (*paśu*) is also characterized by the concealment of its own nature through the power of *māyā*.

Regarding the removal of the animal-like possession (*pāśavāveśa*), he says— starting with "In that way, in the world of bound souls" (*tathā paśuloke*) and so forth— that even after abandoning conventional designations such as "I am Caitra" or "I am Maitra," one initiates within oneself the usage [of terms] such as "I am eternal" and "I am all-pervading. In that [state], "I am Caitra..."

When the cognizer perceives himself as "I am loving," he is, due to the force of delusion, unable to engage in the conventional usage of "Lord" and so forth that has not previously occurred; [the author] therefore makes him recognize this by demonstrating the members of the syllogism, such as the proposition, beginning with the words "He who... (385): "You are the Lord."

Because of being endowed with the sovereignty of knowledge and action: for he who is endowed with the sovereignty of knowledge and action is indeed Īśvara, just as [Īśvara] is well-known in the Siddhāntas and Purāṇas; and in that same way, you are endowed with the sovereignty of knowledge and action. Therefore, you are indeed Īśvara—thus [the teacher says] to the disciple.

Because He possesses the powers of knowledge and action, His status as the Lord (Īśvara) is established through a five-membered syllogism as a process of recognition: "You are the Lord of the Universe;
for You consist of the objects of knowledge and the effects [produced] by those powers of knowledge and action," and so forth, up to Śiva.

Because the entire universe is dependent upon you: in whatever cognizer (*pramātṛ*) a particular field—such as the world of becoming and so forth—is manifested by *māyā*, he is the Lord (*īśvara*) therein, just as a king is within his own domain. Likewise, the entire universe from the earth up to Śiva is dependent upon you;
therefore, you alone are the Lord of the Universe (*viśveśvara*). This is the universal lordship of the cognizer.

Recognition is the state of the subject as Lord; worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) has no other cause [than this], but rather has as its cause the sovereignty (*svātantrya*) consisting of that knowledge and action (p. 301). Furthermore, it has as its object that knowledge and action, and it has as its cause the entire universe, from Sadāśiva down to the earth.

It is so; however, this is not to be understood as having any other cause. To demonstrate this, it is established that he who possesses sovereignty over knowledge and action is the Lord (Īśvara). Furthermore, as it is well-known in the Siddhānta Purāṇas, there is a pervasion (vyāpti) expressed thus: "He is the Lord with respect to that which depends upon him, just as a king is within his own realm."

Furthermore, you are filled with the entire universe from Sadāśiva down to the earth; for according to the stated principle that "He unfolds the universe by His own will upon His own wall," you are its very foundation because you are rooted in the nature of consciousness (*saṃvit*).
Indeed, whatever appears as being rooted in something else is filled by that [foundation], just as a treasure chest is filled with jewels.

The universe is attached to Him; therefore, He Himself is indeed full of the universe. This is the manifestation of the knower’s recognition of His own perfection. Furthermore, You are the pervader of the universe, because He exists within it. Whatever appears within something is pervasive over that extent, like a casket [containing its contents].
Within you, who are the nature of consciousness, resides the entire universe—from Īśvara down to Śiva—as described in the systematic exposition of the scriptures.
Therefore, you alone are all-pervasive; this is the demonstration to the cognizer that you pervade the entire universe from the earth up to Sadāśiva. Furthermore, you are eternal.

Because the universe, which possesses the nature of arising and dissolving, pervades both prior and subsequent states; for that in which something arises and dissolves while it remains must pervade its prior and subsequent states, just as a sprout [arises and dissolves] upon the earth. And so, the entire universe arises and dissolves within You; therefore, You are That.

Because it pervades the prior and posterior portions of the arising and dissolution of the universe, it is indeed eternal; for, since the cognizer consists of consciousness (*saṃvit*), its eternity is made manifest as being untouched by time, as it has been said:
"When You, the primordial and eternally established Self, shine forth..."

"The entire universe, both moving and unmoving, arises and dissolves within this subject. Thus, because this subject consists of the excellence of the dharmas established by the scriptures— even if they number in the thousands— such states as Śivatva, Paśupatitva, Devatva, Bhairavatva, and so forth, [are all present].

He should be meditated upon because He possesses qualities such as being a protector of cattle (paśupāla), because His primary concern is the sport of creating the universe and so forth, and because He bestows fearlessness upon those who are afraid.
Thus, when the subject (pramātṛ) has been deluded by the delusion consisting of Māyā in the manner described, once again—

In the case of the body and so forth, there is first of all the conceit that they are not the self; yet, when that delusion is merely sustained by its own latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), there arises the conceit of them being the self in such forms as "I am fat" or "I am thin. Furthermore, in the case of objects like a jar, because they appear [to consciousness], there is likewise the conceit that they are the self.

Just as for one who has realized the truth of a magician’s trick, even when that trick is being performed again, a delusion arises from the perspective of reality; so too, for the Supreme Lord whose nature is self-recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), there is no delusion from the standpoint of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Therefore...

Furthermore, because of the nature of returning [to the source] immediately thereafter, for this subject— once the body has generally reached its end and become delimited— the state of being composed of the universe and transcending the universe arises, just as the space contained within a jar or a wall returns to its original condition of pure space when those limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the jar or the wall dissolve.

From the supreme Śiva down to the earth, that which transcends [the levels] from the supreme Śiva down to the earth is the state of supreme Śiva consisting of pure consciousness (*cinmaya*). As it is said in the *Svarūpapraveśikā* (387): "Viśvānara..."
Or let the fire consume my fallen body;
being Śiva, the self of all, I rest in my own abode, the space of consciousness.
Thus:

"Even while living, I am Śiva myself, because through the words of my Guru, I have been established by the recognition of the powers of knowledge and action; thus, although I move about like an ordinary person,"

"Upon the exhaustion of the experience and enjoyment of all previously commenced good and evil karmas, when this body has fallen, he alone—the Self of the moving and unmoving universe—is the Lord. Thus [it is said].
Whoever desires certain supernatural powers (siddhis) [should practice] according to the nature of the Supreme Lord as taught in the Śiva scriptures...
By the power of the practice of the self-identification with the absorption of *dhāraṇā*,

one perceives the state of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvaratā*) as having entered into either the body or an object such as a jar; thus, having brought about the entry of a portion of the Supreme Lord into one's own body, another's body, or a jar and so forth, one perceives the Supreme Lord in each of those respective locations.

For one who realizes here in this very body the supreme sovereignty endowed with infinite attributes— such as omniscience, omnipotence, omnipresence, and omnipervasiveness— the emergence of a portion of those attributes constitutes a dharma that consists of a single part.
As long as the body exists, the state of incompleteness— consisting of [limitations such as] non-omniscience and non-omnipotence— does not truly cease.

Only upon the dissolution of this "bodiness," which is a contraction consisting of space, time, and form, and which is merely eight *aratnis* in measure, does one become the Supreme Śiva himself, existing exactly as he is, comprising the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*).

Regarding the term "prapañca" (the manifestation): according to the principle stated in the *Svarūpapraveśikā*, it refers to the attainment of the state of being the universal self—consisting of the entire universe from Śivā down to the earth—which is the very nature of Paramaśiva. For whichever cognizer there is a descent of grace (*śaktipāta*) of varying intensity, that [cognizer] is the means for establishing the conventional usage of "Lordship" (*īśvaratā*) and so forth, which consists of five members (*pañcāvayava*).

Even when the collection of causes is present, the conceit of having attained perfection—such as "I am the Lord" or "I am independent"—does not arise. Even for one who possesses that conceit of having attained perfection, it occurs only through the repeated application of the means of worldly activity; however, this is not so for one who [possesses] the collection of causes for the worldly activity of lordship and so forth.

Even when demonstrated in every possible way, this delusion does not depart. In that state, due to the power of the Lord’s energy (*īśvara-śakti*) which consists in the concealment of one's true nature (*svarūpa-tirodhāna*), there is only stupor—the very state of being a bound soul (*paśu*).
For one who is possessed by such stupor, even though [the teacher] repeatedly says, "You are the Lord," "You are full," "You are eternal," and so forth—
Because the conventional usage employed by the Supreme Teacher reaches the path of one's ears,
the ripening of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) will necessarily occur at some time or another;
the meaning is that even after a long interval, that very conventionality— such as "Lordship" (*īśvaratva*) and so forth— will indeed proceed within oneself.

(p. 303) That very object of knowledge (*prameya*) which was stated at the beginning of the treatise by the two verses beginning with "the agent" (*kartṛ*) is now thoroughly and extensively re-examined by the three verses beginning with "the manifoldness of the universe. If one asks how [this is so], it is because [it is described] as being "of such a nature."
The means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is that which establishes objects of knowledge (*prameya*) such as pots, which are manifest and limited;

it is of such a nature. How, then, could this be applicable to the Blessed Lord, who transcends the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) consisting of the object of knowledge, the means of knowledge, the valid cognition (*pramā*), and the knower (*pramātṛ*)? Therefore—and for this reason—it is because the means of knowledge cannot be established in relation to Paramaśiva.

The object of knowledge (*prameya*) which was stated at the beginning of the treatise by the two verses beginning with "the agent" (*kartṛ*), that very same [object] is now determined by the three verses beginning with "in the manifoldness of the universe" (*viśvavaicitrye*). [May there be] auspiciousness.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter (*māhnika*) in the *Pratyabhijñāsūtravimarśinī*.
It is finished.
Now begins the twelfth chapter.

Just as a variegated array of cities, villages, and so forth appears without division within a stainless mirror— that is, one free from the impurities of *āṇava* and the rest— yet appears as if divided from one another and even from the mirror itself,
so too does [the universe] appear within the supreme consciousness of Bhairava, which is more stainless than the mirror; for although it is devoid of such division, it appears as if divided.

"And from that [Śiva], everything appears as mutually distinct, yet not separate from the form of Śiva" (Paramārthasāra 3.89). According to this statement, [the universe arises] from within one's own indestructible mirror—the mirror of the Self—which is capable of reflecting the entire universe and whose nature is the plenary I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*). From that mirror of the Self, all things manifest.
From the earth element up to Śiva, this [universe] is permeated by hundreds of internal subdivisions of the insentient and the sentient;

according to the principle stated previously, for an insentient object such as a jar, the potter is the cause, and for an insentient seed and so forth, the effect is an insentient sprout and so forth. For the non-insentient, such as Caitra or Maitra, [the cause is likewise non-insentient].

The cause [of the world] consists of Caitra, Maitra, and so forth; moreover, it is diverse in form, such as the fact that for a non-insentient creature like a scorpion, the insentient cow-dung is the cause. We praise that Śiva, whose very agency consists in manifesting the causal relationship between these things—that is, whose agency is nothing other than this manifestation itself.
Therefore, that which was also stated—namely, "The sequence does not belong to a single [agent];
'it is one,' etc."—is refuted by the demonstration that it is indeed one, and so forth.
Likewise, the distinction between the knower and the knowable which appears...
Thus, following the discussion of the expansion of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) as stated in the first chapter on action,

and in connection with the description of the relationship between the general action (*kriyā-sāmānya*) and so forth— as taught in the second chapter beginning with "by that, such an error arises"— and continuing with the passage beginning "of this kind," [the author] proceeds.

By the end of the third chapter (*āhnika*), up to page 304, [the author] has established that the relationship between the knower and the known (*jñāpya-jñāpaka-bhāva*)—which must necessarily be determined by the statement "in the knower" (*jñātari*) in the *Sūtra* "The Great Lord is the agent, the knower, one's own self, eternally established"—is as follows: conventional practice (*vyavahāra*) proceeds... [as previously stated].

Having established and determined that reality (*tattva*), he now speaks of the "agent" (*kartṛ*)—which is the very life-breath of the relationship between the signified and the signifier—in order to establish the reality of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) which is dependent upon the agent. This begins with the words "And this... and ends with "...the will itself is causality, agency, and action."
A new chapter begins with twenty-one verses.

Therein, by the first verse, [the author states] "our own doctrine" (*svamata*): according to the doctrine of the proponents of consciousness (*saṃvidvāda*), the state of being agent and object belongs solely to the Lord; thus, the status of agent belongs only to Īśvara, while the universe—extending from Sadāśiva down to the earth—is [his object].
The state of being an agent and an object is thus established;
(390) it is proposed and summarized that the very relationship of agent and object is the relationship of cause and effect, meaning that Īśvara alone is the cause and the universe is his effect.

Then, with three verses, the Lord refutes the causality of primordial matter (*pradhāna*), atoms (*paramāṇu*), seeds (*bīja*), and so forth—entities distinct from Him—with respect to the universe. Then, with six verses, [He refutes it] because of the undesirable consequence that only the conscious Supreme Lord could be the cause in the form of fire, seeds, and so on; [therefore], fire and the like...

In these three verses, it is stated that when one infers a cause such as fire from an effect such as smoke, the power of the Lord’s necessity (*niyati-śakti*) must necessarily be relied upon. For example, the Supreme Lord, having entered the body of a yogin, [manifests] fire and other causes through His own sovereignty.

If it were to produce smoke and so forth without the form of its specific effect— meaning it would produce smoke even from fire alone— it would transgress its own causal necessity (*niyati*). Consequently, when one infers fire from smoke that is devoid of the smoke produced by that [specific] cause, the smoke would belong to fire alone [and not to other fires].
The meaning is that the power of non-determination (*aniyati-śakti*), in the form "the sprout arises only from the seed," must necessarily be relied upon.
For if one were to deny the causality of fire and so forth in such a causal relationship as "smoke arises only from fire" or "the sprout arises only from the seed," then even when fire is present...

The Buddhist assertion of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*)— namely, that "when there is smoke, there is fire," meaning the existence of smoke and so forth arises immediately following the existence of fire and so forth— is, by this very fact,
adopting our own position that the universe is the effect of that very [Supreme Lord] as its agent. It is not [otherwise].

It is stated in three verses that nothing whatsoever exists [independently]. Since, in the absence of our position, the world lacks existence (*sattva*), the very nature of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) pertaining to that world does not even come into being; therefore, the twenty-three principles of the Pradhāna, beginning with Mahat and ending with the earth—

From a subtle perspective, the nature of the seed is its being composed of reality (*tattvamayatva*) with respect to the aspect of reality, and its being primarily composed of each individual element; and from a gross perspective, it is shown through enumeration to consist of the mutual natures of one another, such that the nature of the sprout is the nature of the seed (p. 305).

Even the relationship of cause and effect is not tenable. (391) It is stated in three verses that if the agency of consciousness as asserted by us is accepted, [the following occurs]: when the seed exists, the sprout arises; the sprout is the nature of the seed, and its [nature] is the seed.

It has been stated that even according to the causal relationship accepted by the Buddhists and the Sāṃkhyas— namely, "intrinsic nature" (svabhāva)— it is logical for an insentient entity such as a seed to be the instrument; this applies equally to Brahman, who is of the nature of pure consciousness, were He not to be the Lord.

In this system, the Supreme Lord is essentially light (*prakāśa*); and light has the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). For reflective awareness is indeed the spontaneous vibration of "I" as the universal form or as the manifestation of the universe. If there were no reflective awareness, it would follow that He would be neither the Sovereign nor conscious, but rather insentient.

The *Svarūpapraveśikā* states that if one does not accept the innate freedom (*svātantrya*) whose nature consists of the manifestation of "I" (*aham*), which is essentially the Lord, then it would be impossible for Brahman alone to be the cause of the entire universe— extending from Māyā down to the earth— which is its effect; this [point] is concluded by means of two verses.

This is the summary of the daily lesson (*āhnika*). As for the meaning of the text, it is now explained: through the relationship characterized by the nature of the known and the knower, which arises by way of the determination of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), [the text establishes] the state of being of a single form as the subject (*pramātṛ*).

Having established that the previously mentioned state of being a single nature as the knower applies to the Blessed One— who is to be engaged with in worldly discourse and who is the knower— it was stated from the outset that "He is the agent," because that state of being the knower constitutes His very life-force.
He now demonstrates that since the nature of being an agent arises from that very source, His state of being the knower is accomplished without effort through that very means.

"And this [is the case]. The very subject (*pramātṛ*) whose nature is described in the three verses beginning with "the manifold variety of the universe" is [the Lord], because he possesses infinite powers.
"All this world is his power, while the Great Lord is the possessor of power."

Thus, according to the principle stated in the *Śrī Sarvamaṅgalāśāstra*, this manifest world, consisting of objective categories (*padārtha*), is indeed eternal; it is submerged once again into that very [source], the unmanifest which consists of power (*śakti*) and is attached to it. And according to the principle stated in the *Śrī Virūpākṣapañcāśikā*, that which possesses infinite internal powers—
"Abiding by resorting to the state of being composed of power (*śaktimayatva*), which is not limited by space or time due to its own nature" (392).

"In this way" means: as those respective forms. "Previously manifested" means manifested by one's own self at the beginning of past creations and so forth. "Entities manifesting immediately thereafter by one's own self" refers to entities such as earth (*kṣiti*) and the rest.

By means of the power of *eṣaṇīya-icchā* (the will to desire) and its capacity (*sāmarthya*), [the Lord] causes that group of objects to be desired— beginning with the earth and ending with Sadāśiva, which He has inwardly appropriated within Himself by His own will—
to manifest; this use of the present tense indicates that the manifestation is an uninterrupted continuity.

This has been illuminated. The meaning is that the Supreme Lord, as the seeker (*eṣitā*), incessantly manifests through the medium of His will the entire universe, which is the object of seeking (*eṣaṇīya*) contained within His own will. The word "thus" (*evam*) indicates that His very will, as it is manifesting, constitutes His creative activity (*kriyā*) in the form of the creator of the universe. As He will state: [p. 306]...

Thus, desire alone is the causality, the agency, and the action. The word "ca" (and) is used for emphasis; the "ca" found in the aphorism functions as an emphatic particle. [The Lord] is ancient, unconditioned by time, and is indeed the knower. For this very reason, He brings about the states of being (*bhāva*)—those which are to be brought forth and accomplished—by His own self. For this very reason, there is no such thing as time, beginning with the past (*bhūta*).
Because it is already determined. Regarding the word "these" (*amūn*): it manifests in a continuous stream those things previously manifested as well as those currently being manifested.
Precisely because of this—due to having been previously manifested and due to being manifested—the [nature] of that which is being manifested...
The state of having a severed continuity is illuminated. How so? "By the power of will" (*icchā-vaśāt*).

This is because will is non-different from the Self, which is the desirer; therefore, it is non-conceptual (*avikalpa-rūpā*), does not follow the sequence of being a desirer, and encompasses the entire range of objects of desire from the earth up to Sadāśiva.

The meaning is that by its own power (*vaśena*), it does not manifest [them] through external capacity. Anticipating the question—"Where were those entities situated prior to being manifested?"—he says: "Relying upon infinite power within."

The meaning is that they are "established" [in Him]. In the aphorism, "And of the Lord who is established in Himself," all entities from earth up to Sadāśiva indeed exist as the very nature and power-form of that Lord alone.

It has been stated that [they] "are established. This manifestation of the states beginning with Earth and ending with Sadāśiva—this very will to manifest in such a manner is the creative agency (*nirmātṛtā*), which is the form of the action (*kriyā*) of this Blessed Lord.
(393) Now, [one might object]: "A sprout is seen arising from a seed, etc. Here...
"Someone who, entering through consciousness, causes this sprout to appear from the seed is not perceived.
Therefore, anticipating the objection—"How can it be said that consciousness alone makes things appear?"—he says:
"Because the sprout, though previously non-existent, subsequently attains existence in the form of a sprout."

It does not arise from insentient things such as seeds due to their lack of causal power; this is precisely because of their insentience. Therefore, since seeds and the like lack the status of being causes, sprouts and the like lack the status of being effects. Consequently, the universe lacks both the state of being an effect and the state of being a cause. Likewise, the reality of agency and the object of action is itself the reality of agency and the reality of non-causality.

The meaning is that for the sprout and so forth, the Lord alone is the cause, and not the seed; this is because he will later state that "being an effect consists in being an object of action. For this very reason, even in the case of the sprout, the Supreme Lord is the desired efficient cause (*nimitta*). Regarding the phrase "from the non-existent to the existent": [it refers to] the sprout, which was previously non-existent.
The power of a non-existent seed does not exist; nor indeed does the power of a seed exist for a non-existent sprout, or for an existent sprout.
This is according to the principle stated in the *Śrī-nijavṛtti*: "The insentient [is produced] from the primary matter (*pradhāna*), atoms (*paramāṇu*), or the seed."
That which is accepted by the Sāṃkhyas, Naiyāyikas, and others—namely, *pradhāna* and so forth—must indeed be stated as the cause.
Nevertheless, because that [cause] lacks perceptibility, like a seed, it is said to be "of an insentient seed. Thus, of an insentient seed...

Regarding the statement "the capacity of the elements": that which makes a sprout, which previously existed as a mere form (*sad-rūpa*), subsequently possess manifest existence (*sattā*)—this kind of capacity does not belong to an insentient seed.
For it is because of the presence of the sprout's existence within the seed that the sprout arises from the seed; this is what is meant.

The greatness of the sprout does not belong to the produced [effect] itself. Since the sprout did not previously exist, how could the greatness that "the sprout is born" belong to the seed? Just as the greatness expressed by "the pot is born" never belongs to anything else, likewise, the greatness that "the sprout is born" cannot belong to the seed in any manner whatsoever.
It exists; like other objects, it exists within that [consciousness]. Because it is other than the sprout and so forth.

Since this is so—because, according to the stated principle, insentient things such as seeds lack causality—therefore, that which is to be produced by the action and pervaded by it, namely the effect, extends from the earth up to Sadāśiva, according to the established rule.

Because the universe is manifested through the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), it is indeed an object (*karman*); thus, in the context of cause and effect, the term "effect" (*kārya*) is explicitly indicated by the verbal suffix (*kṛtya*). By this agent, who is capable of bringing about creation, the agent is not made an object; therefore, causality also resides in the conscious agent.

It comes to rest. Consciousness alone is the cause of the universe. As it has been said: "The Self is indeed the root of the universe; no one seeks a means of knowledge for it. Regarding the phrase "from the non-existent to the existent":
the existence or production of a sprout, which is itself of a non-existent nature, does not arise through its own inherent capacity.

Furthermore, in the phrase "of the non-existent and the existent," the meaning is also implicitly included: by implication, it follows that there is no causal capacity either for a non-existent sprout or for a non-existent seed. Moreover, there is no lack of capacity between the two existing things—the seed and the sprout—as he will state later: "And therefore..."
Whether the seed exists and the sprout does not, or conversely, or both exist, or both do not exist, and so forth—
[the opponent asks] "But surely" (nanu); [the author replies] that for an insentient thing such as a seed, that very [nature] has just been introduced immediately before.

He states that power (*śakti*), which consists of the capacity to produce a sprout, is what constitutes "becoming. Whatever entity is non-existent by its very nature remains non-existent; it is not logical for that which is non-existent to possess the nature of existence.
If it were already existent, there would be no purpose or necessity for it to acquire existence once again.

For him, that [doubt] does not exist from the very beginning, because [the object] exists. It is only reasonable that such a doubt as "Is the universe, which is an effect, existent or non-existent?"—namely, the doubt as to whether it was previously existent or non-existent—should arise; however, the notion that it is "of both natures" is not so.

"Consisting of both existent and non-existent, yet neither of these"—that is, consisting of the non-existent and the non-existent, being inexpressible (*anirvācya*). It is impossible to say it is "existent," and it is impossible to say it is "non-existent"; all of this is inherently contradictory. He clarifies this very contradiction: if it consists of the existent, [how can it] consist of the non-existent? (395)

It does not exist. If it is of the nature of non-existence, it is also not of the nature of existence. That which is neither existent by its own nature nor nonexistent lacks the very status of being a real entity (*vastutva*), because, being nonexistent by its own nature, existence is impossible for it from the outset.
Because even existence, which pertains to an object that has perished immediately after being seen, is impossible;

if it is argued that this ignorance (*avidyā*) is "indescribable" (*anirvācya*), they do not know to what it belongs as something indescribable, nor does it appear in its own nature. Nor is it the case that it cannot be described; for according to the logic to be stated later, even that which is "indescribable" possesses such a nature.

One should simply state the contradiction itself; so what is the use of this? Therefore, what is the purpose of [listing] other objects of cognition, such as "consisting of both" or "consisting of neither," which are contradictory to its own nature?
We shall attend only to that which is relevant to the subject at hand.
The pot exists by its very own nature. If it is existent, then its true reality (*tattva*) is simply its state of being existent;

how then could it admit non-existence, which is a property contradictory to its own nature? For in a thing whose essence is blue and whose form is blue, there can be no admission of non-blue, just as there can be no prostration at the feet of that very blue object.
"Even by hundreds of vows" means that not even a mere atom is seen; the meaning is that blue never becomes yellow.
He states another alternative: "Or rather, the jar exists. [It is] broad-based and bellied.
