If the pot, whose nature is to be produced, exists by itself (*svataḥ*), then why is another auxiliary cause—such as the staff, the wheel, and the cloth—sought for the purpose of its production? For it already exists by itself.
Manifestation, objectivity, clarity, and so forth should also be considered in terms of their being existent or non-existent; they too are [included in] existence.
The meaning is that they culminate in existence alone. A pot that was previously unmanifest becomes manifest through the activity of a potter;
what was previously indistinct becomes distinct again through the potter's activity. All such cases are to be considered as having the nature of both being and non-being.

Regarding the word "nanu": [the opponent] objects that if an effect such as a jar exists [prior to its production], it would require a staff, a wheel, a potter, and so forth; however, if it does not exist, it cannot attain existence, which is contrary to its own nature. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Let him remain silent. This refers to the statement of Prajāpati and others.

(396) "Not even this" means that even this remaining silent is not appropriate. Regarding that, he states the reason by means of a portion of the Sūtra: "And yet, it is said that causal relation exists in the world. The word "and yet" (*atha ca*) means: even though causal relation is asserted in the world, therefore (*tat tasmāt*), this matter consists of the nature of cause and effect.

This means that it must necessarily be established. And "therefore" (tataśca): because it must necessarily be established, he demonstrates that this matter is as follows: that which exists internally and revolves [within], its being perceivable by both sense-faculties—even though it is only one—is what is called in the world "the relation of cause and effect."
Regarding the phrase "of that certain one": by the power— that is, the sovereignty— of the Supreme Lord, whose majesty is inconceivable and beyond questioning,
[the elements] beginning with earth and ending with Śiva, which revolve within his own nature as the full *ahaṃtā* (I-consciousness), abide in that state of full *ahaṃtā*.

(p. 309) For those who perceive that this jar is fashioned by a potter—who is intended as its creator and who exists as something distinct from it—there is perceptibility by both sense organs (*ubhayendriyavedyatva*).

Thus, in this process of establishing perceptibility by both the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and the external organs (*bahiṣkaraṇa*), [the potter] is the potter of consciousness (*saṃvit-kumbhakāra*).

"In the heart" (*hṛdaye*) means "within," because it is the object of that potter's mind; "already as one with his own self-awareness" (*svasaṃvidekātmatayā*) means that the universe is full even through its identity with his own self-awareness, which is imperishable;
and "by way of variety" (*vicitratvena*) refers to the differentiation of all entities from Śiva down to the earth existing within that heart.

Regarding the term "parivartinaḥ" (of that which revolves): for a jar— which, while vibrating as a single form of movement, manifests through its own pulsation— there exists within it, for the potter and for others, a state of limitation and contraction in terms of space and time, characterized by its specific shape such as a broad base and a bulbous belly.
The state of being cognizable through both the internal and external instruments is what is manifested; yet, in this manifestation itself, that [duality] does not exist.

Thus is "causality" (kāryakāraṇatā) described. Regarding the term "both" (*ubhaya*) in the phrase "cognizability by both," it serves as the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of a real entity (*vastu*), because the full accomplishment of its purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is completed within that extent of the object's purposeful activity.

When the time for the fulfillment [of an object's causal efficacy] arrives— meaning, at whatever point in time the causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) of a given entity becomes complete, whether it is cognizable solely by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) or cognizable by both organs.

(397) He says that very thing: "The creation (*nirmāṇa*) of pleasure and so forth is precisely their being made known by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); the Supreme Lord creates pleasure and so forth as something to be known only by the internal organ.

Blue and so forth are to be known by both types of sense organs [the external and the internal], and they consist of the insentient nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), and what is mostly empty (*śūnya*)."
This [agency] does not reside in the potter with respect to objects such as the jar,

because that potter is also insentient (*jaḍa*). Therefore, according to the stated principle that consciousness alone, by its own will, unfolds the universe upon its own screen, it causes the universe to appear within itself.
"Due to the diversity of its own powers. This refers to the Supreme Lord, whose greatness—as previously stated—is inconceivable and beyond questioning, because He alone possesses infinite power.

Furthermore, the aforementioned quality of being perceptible by both types of sense organs in the case of a jar and so forth—whether that [perceptibility] exists or does not exist like the jar itself—[is likewise subject to the same analysis].

This must not be said by you. He states the reasoning for this: "Because this is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) here. In this context of the relationship between cause and effect, this is the ultimate reality;
because, in the reflection within a mirror of a jar or similar object produced by a potter in the form of an original (*bimba*), [the reflection is not distinct from the original].

Just as the appearance of reflections is the majesty of a mirror, and just as in a dream the manifestation of objects such as elephants and horses is the majesty of consciousness alone, so it is here as well. In the creation of jars and other things, it is by that very majesty— namely, by the majesty of that Supreme Lord alone.
Regarding the phrase "by this": the remainder of the sentence is that the conceit arises in the world that "this object, such as a jar, is being produced externally in a manifest form by the potter.
Thus, it is solely through the power of consciousness (*saṃvid*) that the potter, who is the causal agent, acts together with the co-operative causes.
While the causes— such as the staff and the wheel— and the effects— such as the jar— exist,
it is solely through the power of the consciousness of those [entities] that, although the insentient self is inherently a non-agent, there arises the thought:
"This was done by me," "This was done by him," "It flashed in my heart," or "It flashed in his heart."

The conceit "it has vibrated" arises. Regarding the word "therein"—in the context of this conceit, since insentient things such as clay are insentient by their very nature, the conceit is far removed from them. Agency is established solely in the Supreme Lord, whose essential nature is consciousness.

(398) But surely, since an entity such as a jar exists by the power of *saṃvit* (consciousness), let it be perceived externally in its manifest form; what is the use of its being cognizable by both sets of sense organs?
The mention of "both" is merely illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*). For whatever [entity] possesses a full completion of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), that much is its reality.

It has already been stated that by this [quality] of being perceptible by two sense-faculties, the form of a jar and so forth is described as clearly capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākṣama*); therefore, what contradiction is there in its being perceptible by both sense-faculties?

Furthermore, by means of this investigation into the relationship between cause and effect— establishing that agency belongs to the Lord alone due to His infinite power and so forth, and not to the *pradhāna* or other principles— the subject at hand is also addressed. Thus,
having established the counter-position through the argument that "agency [belongs] to the object of action such as the body," etc., [the author proceeds to refute it].

It has been established through its non-existence. Furthermore, by means of the passage beginning with "just so" (*evam eva*), he demonstrates that the very nature of action (*kriyāsvarūpa*) under discussion is also established—this being shown by the sūtra beginning with "in this way, one" (*evam eka*).
The word "thus" (*evam*) [is explained as follows].
In the world, the relationship of cause and effect belongs to that which revolves within [the body],
provided it possesses the capacity to be perceived by either of the two types of sense organs.
According to the principle thus stated, that succession exists as an internal and external state;
yet, in the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*), even that [succession] is not one, nor is it appropriate for a single entity.
Thus, it is perceived that [succession] does not exist either by way of its own nature (*svarūpa*) or by way of its substratum (*āśraya*). This refers to that which cannot endure both forms.

It has been established that for the cognizer— who is capable of sustaining both internal and external forms due to his autonomy, and who is not limited by space and time— this [oneness] exists as a relation; and having now set aside any subverting evidence,
it has been proven by means of subverting evidence that "that very same [oneness] belongs to action as well."

By the phrase "of the body and so forth," it is shown that [the action] is not tenable either in terms of its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*) or its locus (*āśrayataḥ*). That action, which constitutes the object of the critique, has been established as being endowed with logical consistency through its possession of sequence and unity. He states this very point with the words beginning with "since" (*yataḥ*): "since from within... (*yata āntarāt*).
Starting from the nature of consciousness which consists of full *ahantā* (399),

there exists a state consisting of manifestation that extends as far as *idantā*— that is, to the external limit— by way of the external creation of objects such as jars situated within that [consciousness], appearing through the range of both types of senses as that which possesses full *ahantā*.
(p. 311) For that very reason, it is established that action possesses succession. Furthermore, because of its identity with the subject whose nature is a single substratum, action is one;
that subject, who constitutes the single substratum of action, has arrived at the state of being consciousness through his two qualities of transparency and autonomy.

Transparency (*svacchatva*) is the capacity for the universe—which is created by one's own self as an external form—to be reflected within the mirror of one's own self; sovereignty (*svatantratva*), however, is the manifestation of that universe—which exists internally as consisting of consciousness—as "this-ness" (*idantā*) externally. By means of these two...
"By means of transparency and independence, both [unity and multiplicity] respectively; thus, it sustains both unity and multiplicity, as well as the state of being internal and external.
Now, regarding the phrase "in the case of a jar and so forth": at the time of the creation of a jar or the like, of that jar and so forth...

Because it is manifested by another conscious agent, such as a potter and so forth. "In this way" means: let each respective form, such as a jar and so on, be its effect, just like that [conscious agent]. However, in cases such as the seed and the sprout, where the entry of a conscious agent is not perceived through direct perception—that is, where a conscious being does not enter into the interior of the seed and so forth—[the same principle applies].

If it is argued that the sprout and so forth, though existing externally, are not perceived [as such] because of the absence of the entry of consciousness (*cetanā*) therein, [the author] says this in response to the doubt: "How is it that the sprout is not the effect of the seed alone?"—
whatever object exists internally for the Supreme Lord, that very object belongs to Him alone.

It is to be cast out. The meaning is that the Supreme Lord, who is capable of casting things outside, projects the universe—which is inherently within Him—as His own externalization. Therefore, the dual state of the universe—both internal and external—is described from the perspective of the subject (*pramātṛ*). For that reason, the subject alone is the cause of the universe.

But it is not the insentient *pradhāna* and so forth. The word "ca" (and) indicates the reason: that single subject alone is the cause for the existence of the two-fold manifestation—external and internal—of the universe in its form as an effect. Therefore, the activity consisting of the state of being the creator of the universe belongs to the one [subject].
It belongs precisely to the subject.

According to the principle stated [in the verse]: "The manifestation of the multitude of objects residing within the Self exists indeed for the Lord," the universe likewise manifests within the Supreme Lord.

"Form" (*rūpa*) refers to manifestation as "this-ness" externally with respect to the subject—that is, *māyā*—upon the relinquishing of internal form; this is *nirmāṇa*. Consequently, whatever object is said to be "internal" with respect to something else, it is merely a transformation of the form of that very object which exists immediately prior [to its externalization].
For an object that exists within one's own internal "I-ness," its mere externalization— consisting in the manifestation as "this-ness"—

is something fit to be made external by the subject alone. According to the principle stated as "the Self alone should make this [object] into a knowable," the Supreme Lord likewise [externalizes] the universe contained within Himself.

The meaning is that [the object] manifests externally by itself and vibrates as that very essence. With respect to the subject (*pramātṛ*) who consists of consciousness, these external manifestations exist only in relation to the state of internal manifestation. Therefore, it is by the subject alone that those [objects], which reside within himself, [are manifested].
It is logical that the manifestation of entities as external is [due to] the subject alone;

therefore, the subject itself is the cause of the universe, and not the insentient object. For that subject exists as the cause for the dual manifestation—both internal and external—of the universe which consists of effects. Indeed, "internal" means proximate.
"And that" refers to the fact that, according to the stated principle, the subject alone is everywhere both dependent and independent;

for without this [subject], the duality of internal and external manifestations—which depend upon it—would be untenable. "Therefore" means because it exists as the causal condition (*nimitta*). Its form has been established starting from the section on its activity (*kriyādhikāra*).

The status of being a creator is appropriate for a single cognizing subject alone; it is not appropriate, nor does it belong to an insentient entity such as *pradhāna* (primordial matter), because [the capacity to create] belongs only to the conscious. For this very reason, even the sprout [is considered a creation] by the Naiyāyikas and others.

The remainder [of the argument]: If the Supreme Lord is accepted as the efficient cause (*nimitta*), while others accept that seeds and so forth are causes distinct from Him, then—according to the principle already stated—that causal power does not belong to an insentient entity (*jaḍa*), and thus it is not tenable.
For even when the insentient causes such as seeds and soil are perceptibly present, [the effect does not arise].

Another meaning of the word "api" (also/even) is that because the sprout is insentient, the Supreme Lord, whose nature is consciousness, is stated to be its efficient cause (*nimitta*). The word "api" functions here as a restriction (*avadhāraṇa*); that is, the Supreme Lord alone is intended to be the efficient cause.
(401) According to the principle stated— that its effect exists externally— it is the conscious being alone who is the creator of the universe;

for this very reason, the Naiyāyikas and others accept the Supreme Lord, endowed with an excellent intellect, as the efficient cause (*nimitta*) in the production of sprouts and so forth, as well as in the creation of the universe.

But is it not the case that they accept that Supreme Lord is merely the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*)? [For they hold that] earth and the other elements— which are the inherent causes (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*) of qualities such as smell and taste—
arise through a sequence of disjunctions resulting from the actions that initiate their own respective constituent parts.
Regarding the phrase "of that which is other than that, by way of atoms, dyads, and so forth":

when it is objected that it is true that even things other than the Supreme Lord—such as seeds, water, and the like—are stated to be causes for sprouts and so forth, this is accepted as a partial admission (*arghāṅgīkāra*). However, an insentient thing does not possess that power.

According to the principle thus stated, that [position] is not tenable. Consequently— “For this very reason, he [the subject] would have to make himself an object of knowledge while remaining separate”—
according to this stated principle, the Lord alone is the intended causal ground, the seed-stage.
The ultimate truth here is simply this: that [the world] manifests as the nature of water and appears as the nature of a mirage.
(p. 313) As for the word "nanu": [it refers to] that which is unobserved, distinct from the observed causes such as seeds and so forth.

What is obstructed by the assumption of an intelligent Supreme Lord as the cause, if the production of the world occurs [without Him]? To dispel the opponent's delusion regarding what this obstruction might be,
he says "for instance" (*tathā hi*), preceded by the presentation of an illustration, [showing that] it is indeed the conscious [principle] alone...

He demonstrates the pervasion that has become firmly established by the words "asau" (this one). In the world, a potter is perceived through direct observation; by means of a sovereign arrangement—that is, a state of being in the form of a Lord—he would produce a jar through the sequence of processing various materials such as clay.

One interpretation is that the Lord himself, by his own will, having assumed the form of a potter, produces the effect in the form of a jar through the sequence of preparing the clay, the staff, the wheel, the cloth, and so forth, and then turning them.

"By means of sovereignty and fixed order": this potter shall produce a jar through the sequence of processing various clays and other materials; thus, by the power of necessity (niyati-śakti) fashioned by the Lord, according to the fixed order of sovereignty, he [processes] those respective clays and other materials.

[He] would produce the jar. Otherwise, if [the Lord] creates solely by His own independence, how could insentient materials such as clay conform to the will of the potter? Furthermore, regarding the restriction [of power] by sovereignty, since the potter is also insentient, [he too would act] only by himself.

Due to the absence of actual agency, he might produce a jar through a state of existence consisting of the false conceit of agency imagined by God; furthermore, according to the very arrangement of God, would even a potter think, "I am producing a jar," or "I am not producing it"? One [must conclude that such a distinction is impossible].

The fourth meaning is: "He should produce a jar" [is understood] from the state of being determined as a subject, from the cause consisting of the conceptualization of Īśvara, from the form of inquiry, from the various forms of concealing one's own nature, and from the state of manifestation.

By the phrase "for thus" (*tathā hi*), he establishes the pervasion (*vyāpti*) that the agent is indeed conscious. By the phrase "being such," he demonstrates [the point] preceded by an example in the manner that will be explained. By the phrase "for thus," he shows that insentient things such as clay, the staff, and the wheel—which serve as the causes for a jar—are [directed] by a conscious potter.

If clay and other materials, being impelled in this way, were to produce an effect such as a jar merely through their mutual proximity without the prompting of a potter, then what function would the potter have here? [For] the manifestation of a jar with a broad base and belly must precede its appearance.

If it is argued that the palanquin, the pillar, and so forth, produce the jar through a causal series, and that this series is dependent upon the potter, then these [materials] such as clay must depend upon the instigation of a conscious being for the production of the palanquin and the rest.

From this [statement], the point to be proven is established. Therefore, regarding "insentient causes"—that is, even seeds and the like—it follows that, by the logic already stated, the Supreme Lord is desired as the efficient cause (*nimitta*) even in the case of the sprout;
for without the impulsion of the conscious being whose essence is the Supreme Lord, nothing such as a sprout could ever function as an effect.
If consciousness were not to act as the instrumental cause for the production of a sprout by providing its impulsion,

then it would follow with certainty that even clay and other materials would not require the impulsion of a potter for the production of a jar; for an insentient thing performs its function only when impelled by a conscious being.
In order to demonstrate the pervasion (*vyāpti*) in the statement "it exists," he shows the five-membered syllogism with the words "tataśca" (and therefore).

Here, seeds and other such things, which are considered to be causes, produce effects such as sprouts only when impelled by a conscious being. This is because they are insentient (*acetana*). Whatever is insentient that performs an action depends upon a conscious being, just as [the example].

The principle is that even insentient things such as clay and the like, or seeds and the like, produce their effects only by depending upon consciousness. For the capacity of an insentient seed or similar object to produce an effect, such as a sprout, occurs only occasionally (kādācitkatvāt).
In this regard, it is precisely this particular form of the seed that produces the sprout.

Because it is not restricted by place, time, or form due to the power of the Lord’s destiny (*īśvara-niyati-śakti*), that [seed] is the cause [only] when accompanied by a cause distinct from itself; it is dependent upon that. In the production of a sprout from this seed, no other cause is possible apart from the impulsion of a conscious being (*cetana*). This is because no such [other] cause is perceived. Thus, [the cause is] conscious.

If one were not to take the impelling agent as the cause— namely, that clay and other materials perform their functions being impelled by a conscious being— then the previously mentioned pervader, "being without a cause," would absurdly follow for seeds and the like;
yet that is not tenable, because even in the case of clay and so forth, it is precisely this [conscious agent] that is the cause, and not the absence of a cause.

By way of a corollary: just as clay and other materials, impelled by the Supreme Lord who has assumed the role of a potter, perform their respective functions, so too do seeds and other such things perform their functions when impelled by the Lord; this is the meaning, and thus the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established. "Therefore" refers to this pervasion.

Because [this] is established, in that regard, regarding the creation of jars and so forth, the Lord Īśvara— the potter— is indeed Īśvara himself who, having assumed the form of a potter, creates the jar and so forth.
He clarifies the intended meaning stated [above] by means of two sūtras, beginning with "tadetad" and so on.
"By means of the arrangement of sovereignty" means: the arrangement (*vyavasthā*) is the state (*sthiti*) of that which has the nature of a Lord;

by such an arrangement, namely through the sequence of the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the respective clay and other materials. This refers to the potter’s refinement of the clay, staff, wheel, and so forth—such as the kneading of the clay and [the preparation] of the staff.

"Rectitude" (*praguṇatva*) means straightening; "the turning of the wheel" (*cakraparivartana*), and so forth—by that sequence which is the process of undertaking [the work], such as the form of a palanquin, a cart, and so on, one would produce a jar.

It produces it necessarily, and does not produce it otherwise; thus, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) occurs in the sense of an injunction (*niyoga*). Furthermore, it is the Lord (*īśvara*) alone [who acts].

Furthermore, he is proclaimed as the "maker" (kartā); yet even the potter, in reality, acts through sovereignty, which consists of the nature of autonomous awareness (svatantra-vimarśa), established by means of conceptualization (kalpanā) in relation to the processing of clay and other materials. Thus, this potter [employs] clay, the staff, the wheel, and so forth.

Having performed the ritual preparation (*saṃskṛtya*), let him not produce a jar—thus it has been shown that [the jar] would be produced only when manifested by the expansion of the power of *niyati* (destiny/limitation) of the Supreme Lord, which is designated as *niyati*. "Otherwise" means: in the absence of its being manifested by the power of *niyati*. "Inanimate" means: [produced] by itself, as "I."

If earth and other materials were devoid of consciousness, they would have to conform to the will of the potter himself, thinking, "I am myself [the agent]. In the absence of the power of divine destiny, such that [the potter thinks], "Let this potter produce this jar by means of these materials like earth," the earth and other materials [would act on their own].
The meaning is that they do not exist under the control of a potter. Furthermore, even threads, which are not the [direct] cause, certainly attend to the desire to produce a jar.
By this sūtra, "tathā hi" (for instance), it is shown that even the potter produces the jar only as an expression of the power of the Lord's destiny (*niyati-śakti*).
It has also been stated that "he produces" is an object of knowledge (*prameya*).

[Objection: "But if it is thus"—if the potter possesses no agency (*kartṛtva*) by his own nature, then how can there be the worldly distinction between dharma and adharma, such as "this person performs dharma" and "this person performs adharma"?

It would collapse. True; if you have conviction in both reason and scripture—that is, if you possess faith in the reasoning concerning the contemplation of the Supreme Self and in the scripture uttered from the mouth of the Supreme Lord—then it is exactly so: the Lord alone is the agent, and not the potter. Nevertheless...

This [universe] too has been created by the Supreme Lord within the very midst of the creation of the universe, from Śiva down to the earth. Although that bound soul (*paśu*) is like a potter who is not the true agent, he possesses this false conceit of agency—the thought "I alone am the creator"—which is like a guarantor’s false conceit of being the debtor for a loan he did not take. (405) When...
Furthermore, this false pride of agency belonging to this potter vanishes when joy arises;
if such is the will of the Lord, then that potter is no longer an agent— the meaning is that his pride of agency dissolves.

Indeed, by the sūtra beginning with "tathā hi," it is stated that even the potter’s construction of the conceit of being a false agent occurs; for the potter too thinks, "I shall produce a jar from clay and so forth through a sequence of refinements, or I shall not produce it"— one or the other.
The investigation consisting of inquiry for the purpose of determining a position occurs precisely through a divine arrangement (*vyavasthā*)—
that is, through an arrangement belonging to the Lord (*īśvara*), arising from the various states of abiding in the form of light due to the veiling of one's own nature. In this regard:
The potential suffix (*liṅ*) in the word "janayeyam" (I should produce) is used here in the sense of inquiry. Regarding the phrase "therefore":

since potters and the like lack the status of being the [ultimate] agent, the Lord of the universe alone is the agent of everything from Śiva down to the earth. And I am that very [Lord], not merely the agent of limited things such as a jar; this is the object of knowledge (*prameya*), and the reason for this is the [Lord's] being the material cause (*upādāna*) and so forth.
Whether it be with respect to the elements such as earth and so forth, or with respect to the potter Brahmā, it is established that one must in every way fix this in one's heart:
"Of this conscious being. And [this refers] to the one whose nature has been described by the passage beginning with "because of having infinite power" and so forth.

The absolute sovereignty (*svātantrya*) of the Supreme Lord alone is seen expanding everywhere throughout the universe, from Śiva down to the earth. For this very reason, according to the principle stated that "He should make even Himself an object of knowledge," He brings even insentient things to the state of His own self-nature. This power is of the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
"By the principle stated as 'He makes the entire non-sentient [world] His own body,' He assimilates even insentient things to Himself. However,
it is not that insentient things such as clay or seeds possess the capacity to manifest other entities like jars or sprouts—
as was stated in the passage beginning 'But the insentient has no such power'— but rather, this capacity belongs to the sentient alone."

Having established that [the world] is the manifestation of the objects of one's own internal mind, he confirms this by means of examples well-known to all disputants, such as the Cārvākas and Buddhists: "In the world, even without clay and seeds—which are known to be the causes of jars, sprouts, and so forth—each of those [effects] performs its respective purposeful action. (406) Thus, of each [effect],...

That effect, such as a jar, which is stable, connected with subsequent moments, and connected with other causal efficiencies (*arthakriyā*), arises solely by the power of a will as the cause for performing its own specific causal efficiency, such as the fetching of water; therefore, agency belongs only to a conscious being.
Not for that which is insentient.
In this section,

it has been stated and demonstrated that clay and other materials perform their function when impelled by a conscious agent; for instance, a pot and the like are well known to have as their cause clay and so forth, which are themselves impelled by a conscious potter and the like, whereas a sprout and the like do not depend on such [conscious agents].

If seeds and the like, which are conventionally recognized as causes, were causes in the ultimate sense, then how could their effects— such as jars and sprouts— be produced by the mere will of a yogi in the absence of those seeds and so forth? If jars, sprouts, and the like are produced by the mere will of a yogi...

In that case, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that jars, sprouts, and so forth lack a cause; or else, it would follow that those [well-known] causes such as clay and seeds do not produce jars, sprouts, and the like. If it is argued that the jars, sprouts, and so forth produced by clay, seeds, and the like are one set, while those produced by the will of a yogin are another, then even in that case...
When [the Lord] speaks as one who is awakened, you are awakened; having dispelled the darkness of ignorance, you are made perfectly manifest.

(p. 317) It has already been stated that because of the difference in the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) regarding the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), such as carrying water, performed by things created by a potter and so forth, there is indeed non-difference between the two, just like [the case of] a yogi.

It would manifest a collection of objects without any material cause (*nirupādāna*). To this, [the author] replies: "Even there" (referring to the case of the potter). It is well known that a yogi whose will is unimpeded does not require causes such as clay for his creation;
he is indeed a potter who, through the refinement of clay and other materials, produces objects capable of manifold purposeful actions, such as the fetching of water.

The activity of the instruments would become fourfold. Indeed, the desire of that yogin is: "Let even clay and other materials become a jar in exactly that same way. He clarifies the very point already stated with the words "tadeva" (that very thing):
"tattat-sthira-svārthakriyākāram" means [the capacity] of each respective stable object to perform its own purposeful action.

It is the cause for the accomplishment— i.e., the performance— of its own specific purposeful activity, such as fetching water, which persists over time and is accompanied by other purposeful activities such as the quenching of thirst.
Thus, things such as jars arise with a form that is conducive to performing specific purposeful actions (*arthakriyā*).

Even in the externalist theory of atomic aggregation (*aṇu-sañcaya-bāhya-vāda*), although there is no other entity apart from the aggregate, it is simply the atoms themselves according to the stated principle; this is the view of the Naiyāyikas and others who maintain the doctrine of atomic aggregation as the external object.

The production of jars and the like cannot occur without a material cause consisting of an accumulation of atoms. However, those who claim that a yogi, by the power of his own yoga, perceives even extremely subtle atoms and instantly assembles them into jars and so forth, must be refuted. [For example,] a potter...

If the causes such as the clay, staff, and wheel exist, the pot comes into being; if they do not exist, it does not come into being—this is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Likewise, from the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," it follows that only the performer of the Jyotiṣṭoma goes to heaven, and no one else. This is like [the inference regarding] a mountain...

The causal relationship between smoke as it is being perceived and fire concealed by a mountain— which is established through direct perception, positive and negative concomitance, scripture, and inference— is subverted, that is, becomes reversed, in the case of yogis. Therefore, for that reason:
It produces an effect even without [the necessary conditions].

Furthermore, when the causal complex such as fire and so forth is present, it would produce smoke—which is the very essence [of that effect]—and thus, according to the logic to be explained, it would bring about an effect that does not perform the function of an effect; such is your position.

If your heart attracts you and brings you under its control, then what is the purpose for the yogin who fashions jars and other objects to take up atoms? "If it were so" (*vo ced iti*) means: in the absence of such attraction, [the atoms] produced from a lump of clay would be present in the yogin’s creation of a jar.
The skull and other parts [of the body], as well as the hands, feet, and so forth—

each being its own respective limb— are capable of withstanding the transformation of things like jars into grass, straw, or sesame seeds, even without their own constituent parts, such as the skull and the rest.

Only a well-known worldly cause is to be relied upon; thus, for a yogin, in the specific creation of a jar or a wheel and so forth, there is a long-term cultivation observed over time, involving the conjunction of three factors.

(318) Since everything is dependent, the arising of the jar, the body, and so forth— which were just mentioned— would be impossible without the will of the Yogin; these are the powers of the Supreme Lord, who,
according to the principle that will be stated, is the Blessed One whose multitude of principles consists of manifold rays and infinite power.

Because he is the cause of the creation and other activities even of the gods beginning with Brahmā— who possess the authority for such tasks— he is the "Conscious One" (*cetana*), the Supreme Lord himself, who, by means of his own penetration, brings to consciousness the entire class of subjects from Mahādeva and Śiva down to the level of *sakala*. Thus, in various forms such as a potter and so forth, he is the Yogi.

In this view, where the Supreme Lord— who follows and transcends necessity through His intensely dense sovereignty— exists both in the form of a potter and so forth, and in the form of an omniscient yogi and so forth, He abides as one who conforms to necessity within the causal relationship well-known in the world.

Freedom (*svātantrya*) is the source; for one who, while abiding in the form of the omniscient and so forth, honors the transgression of that [ordinary] necessity, freedom shines forth within the supramundane relationship of cause and effect— which is well-known among yogis— as the "creation of the potter" (*kumbhakārasarga*) and the "creation of the yogi" (*yogisarga*).
In this world, due to ignorance, a distinction appears between these two worlds: "this is the creation of a potter" and "this is the creation of a yogi.
However, in ultimate reality, the Supreme Lord alone is both the potter and the yogi.

The fivefold cosmic activity, such as universal emanation, which consists of both sequential and non-sequential forms and depends upon the omniscient Lord and others, becomes conscious through the light of its own essential nature. This occurs within the expanse of the Great Light, which provides space for the entire universe from Śiva down to the earth, according to the principle stated as "the wide and clear mirror of one's own Self."

The established conclusion is that [the Self] causes entities such as mountains to appear within its own mirror, like the reflection of a jar or similar object within an external mirror. A reflection situated within an external mirror requires an original object (*bimba*); however, this [reflection] residing within the mirror of one's own Self does not.
There is no distinction [between the two] because the reflection does not exist [as a separate entity]. Thus said the former teacher, the venerable Bhaṭṭanārāyaṇa:
"They manifest [the world] without material cause and even without a wall."

"Salutation to Him, the wielder of the trident, who is praiseworthy for His artistic skill and by whom this variegated world-picture is displayed upon the wall-less [canvas]—the nature of the Supreme Lord (Anuttara Bhaṭṭāraka)—which is devoid of any material cause and consists of a spontaneous manifestation, incessantly unfolding in the form of creation and so forth. Thus it is said. Upon the "wall-less" [canvas], which is the very nature of the Supreme Lord (Anuttara Bhaṭṭāraka), they display the variegated picture of the world, which is free from the accumulation of material causes and takes the form of a spontaneous emergence, occurring unceasingly in the form of emanation and the rest.

She expands [the universe]. According to the principle stated as "by means of *kalā*," she is the Supreme (*parā*) who performs this process of manifestation (*prapañca-vidhāna*) through *kalā*. Thus, by means of *kalā*—which effects those fivefold duties (*pañcavidha-kṛtya*) and consists of emission (*visarga*)—[he offers] to the venerable Supreme Goddess (*śrī-parā-bhaṭṭārikā*), who is praiseworthy and supreme among the worlds, the trident-bearer (*śūlin*).
"Salutation to the venerable Śūlavatī, who consists of the fourteen vowels and whose nature is the powers of will, knowledge, and action. (p.
319) The meaning is: "Having submerged the state of the subject—the body and so forth—right here [in her], may I enter into her alone.
For indeed, from the seed alone is born the *śiṃśapā* tree, which does not deviate from its inherent nature.

The fire, by its own cause, has arisen with the very nature of producing smoke from the fuel itself. Therefore, since this causal relationship— which pertains to a yogi and transcends the necessity of such [ordinary] conditions— has now come to be thus, all this [is established], such as the nature of the *śiṃśapā* tree.
The [proposition] that fire has the nature of producing smoke and so forth falls apart.
He demonstrates this very point: by the will of a yogin, even a *śiṃśapā* tree could have the nature of being a non-tree;
as for smoke, the objection is twofold—namely, that the causal complex of fire and so forth could be produced by the will of a yogin.
[If one were to say that] smoke would produce fire, then by the mere will of the yogi, smoke might as well produce fire itself;

thus, there would be no inference of fire and so forth from effects such as smoke. Anticipating the objection that such inference does indeed occur in the world, he says: "For this very reason. Even for yogis, [the production occurs] without clay or seed, by will alone.

By that power, that jar and so forth are produced. According to this stated principle, the fact that smoke and the like possess the very nature of *śiṃśapā* trees, as well as the state of being created by a yogin, [is established] through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Now, if even by the mere will of a yogin, without transgressing well-known causes such as clay and seeds—(510)— [The text continues: ...it is not the case that [the effect] arises from something other than those [specific causes]. For example, when a yogin intends, "Let this pot arise from threads," the pot does not arise from those [threads]. Therefore, since the production of an effect occurs only when there is no transgression of its own specific cause, the capacity of the cause to produce its effect is established. Thus, the capacity of fire to produce smoke is established by the non-perception of the contrary (*bādhakapramāṇa*). Consequently, the inference of fire from smoke is not fallacious. Furthermore, in the case of a *śiṃśapā* tree, its nature as a tree is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), while its nature as a *śiṃśapā* is established by the exclusion of what is other (*anyavyavaccheda*). Therefore, the inference of "tree-ness" from "śiṃśapā-ness" is not fallacious. Moreover, regarding the production of an effect by a yogin, since the effect is seen to arise immediately following the yogin's intention, the causal capacity of that intention is established by the non-perception of the contrary. Thus, the inference of a yogin from the production of an effect is not fallacious. Furthermore, the production of an effect by a yogin is not observed to occur without the assistance of material causes (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) such as clay; therefore, the inference of a yogin from the production of an effect is not fallacious. If effects such as pots and sprouts arise as possessing causal efficiency identical to that of other effects produced by well-known causes— such as pots and sprouts— then it is established that in the world fire is to be inferred by smoke alone,
and the nature of being a tree is to be inferred by the nature of being a *śiṃśapā*; thus, the discourse on inference is established.
[Otherwise] they would be fallacious.
He demonstrates this very point with the words "tathāhi" and so forth. How could it be otherwise?
[That is to say,] how could a thing such as a *śiṃśapā* tree or smoke be restricted (*niyama*) to another [locus], such as a tree in general or fire, respectively?
Anticipating the objection that [the relationship] might exist through non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*),

the Naiyāyikas and others— who consider themselves more authoritative— posit identity (*tādātmya*) and origination (*tadutpatti*), such that for a *śiṃśapā* there is identity with "tree-ness," and for smoke there is origination from fire alone.

When it is accepted—that is, admitted—that the cause (*nidāna*) or primary origin (*ādikāraṇa*) of a restriction (*niyama*) or a magical spell (*abhicāra*) is [the intrinsic nature], he demonstrates that very acceptance: for no entity possesses an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) that is not distinct [from itself]; thus, having abandoned its own intrinsic nature...

It does not accept the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of an entity as distinct from itself. For if it were of a different intrinsic nature, this entity would necessarily be something else due to that difference in intrinsic nature. Regarding the term "successively" (*paryāyaśaḥ*):
a *śiṃśapā* tree is at one time of the nature of a tree, and at another time of the nature of stone.
If this is accepted, then there would be an absence of two natures; that is, if the *śiṃśapā* possesses the nature of a tree,
it lacks the nature of stone, and if it possesses the nature of stone, it lacks the nature of a tree— thus, it would be devoid of nature (*nisvabhāvatā*).

The term "consequence" (*prasaṅga*) refers to the conventional usage of identity (*tādātmya*). "In this way" means that even an effect such as smoke is not without a cause, nor is it without fire; furthermore, it does not have a different cause, meaning it does not have a cause other than fire. Moreover, an effect such as smoke is sometimes caused by fire, and sometimes...

Nor is it the case that [the smoke] has water as its cause; for if those two causes were absent, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of it being causeless—this must also be stated regarding smoke. "In both cases" means: in the case of the identity of the *śiṃśapā* with the tree, and in the case of the fire's nature of producing smoke, it is "caused by a cause" (*hetukṛta*) by means of that cause.

The determination of a *śiṃśapā* tree as having the nature of a tree by means of its own seed, which is its cause of production; and the determination of fire as having the nature of producing smoke by means of fuel, which is its cause of production.

He states that very point: "Produced by its own cause," "well-known in its own world," or "due to practice in another birth"— when these are not ascertained, [the reason] is an effect such as smoke, or a nature such as being a *śiṃśapā* tree, which is born from its own seed that is the root-cause of its production, in the inference of fire and so forth.
In the inference [of a creator] based on [the existence of] trees and so forth, this serves as the logical reason (*hetu*). The will of the Yogin is likewise of that same nature;

thus, it produces effects such as jars—which perform purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) as established in the world created by potters and others—and not in the manner of a scorpion produced from cow dung and so forth. Likewise, [The original Sanskrit text continues: *...ityādi* || *tathā* || (As for the phrase "and so forth," it is as follows: [The text continues with further examples of the Yogin’s power. **Note:** The provided source text was truncated after *tathā*. The potency (*vīrya*) of a scorpion born from another scorpion is different;

just as the taste, potency, and so forth of a scorpion born from cow dung are different, in that same way, an effect that differs in taste, potency, and so forth does not produce [the same] result. Thus is the meaning of its own stable nature (*sthirasvārtha*).

That which was stated by the phrase "the formulation of the reason" (kriyākaraṇam) is precisely for this reason: smoke and the like become the reason (*hetu*) when inferring fire and the like as the effect (*kārya*); and the nature of being a *śiṃśapā* and the like becomes the reason when inferring tree-ness and the like as the essential nature (*svabhāva*). "In this way" (*evam*) refers to that smoke and so forth.

If the nature of the effect, such as being a *śiṃśapā* tree, is not established by a supramundane means of valid cognition consisting of one's own direct experience (*svānubhava*)—which is free from causes [of error]—and is likewise not ascertained through worldly consensus, then it is otherwise; that is, it is not otherwise. It does not serve as a reason for inference. "For this very reason" [is said].
Since that effect can arise through the mere will of a yogi even without a well-known cause such as fire,

when one infers a cause like fire from an effect such as smoke, the means for the inferer to distinguish whether "this smoke was created by a yogi or not" is the practice of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) regarding the arrival [of knowledge] in other lifetimes, as is the case in the world.

Established consensus (*prasiddhi*) and one’s own reasoning (*svayukti*)—all of this must necessarily be relied upon; and that [consensus] is the seed for the cognition of scripture and inference. (p.
321) As for yoga, however, if it were to disregard even well-known causes such as clay and seeds...

By the power of the yogi’s will (412), effects such as pots and sprouts—which are produced by those well-known causes—indeed possess equivalent causal efficiency; thus, effects such as pots and sprouts arise. If that is so, then in the world, fire would be inferable from smoke alone, and [the tree] from its nature as a *śiṃśapā*.
If "treeness" were the object to be inferred, then well-known discussions regarding inference would be undermined.

He demonstrates that very point with the words "for thus" (*tathā hi*) and so forth. [The opponent asks: "How could it be otherwise? [That is to say,] how could a thing such as a *śiṃśapā* tree or smoke exist elsewhere, such as in a tree or the like, by way of necessity (*niyamāt*), i.e., without deviation?
Anticipating this objection, [the author speaks] of those who consider themselves more authoritative than the Naiyāyikas and others.

The identity of the *śiṃśapā* with "tree-ness" and the production of smoke only from fire—this rule of identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*), which is non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*), is accepted as the source, that is, the primary cause. He demonstrates that very acceptance: "For there is no object whatsoever..."

It would be without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), nor would it have a distinct intrinsic nature. For he does not accept that manifestation is a real entity (*vastu*) apart from its own intrinsic nature. If it were of a distinct intrinsic nature, then this entity would be something other [than itself] due to the difference in its intrinsic nature. Indeed, an entity such as a *śiṃśapā* tree cannot be without intrinsic nature.

It occurs as follows: having abandoned its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it accepts an intrinsic nature that is not distinct from the object itself. If it were of a different intrinsic nature, then by virtue of that difference in intrinsic nature, the otherness of that object would be possible.
Regarding the phrase "successively" (*paryāyaśaḥ*): at one time a *śiṃśapā* has the intrinsic nature of a tree, and at another time—
If it is accepted that the nature of stone is absent [in a śiṃśapā], then there is an absence of its two natures;
thus, while the śiṃśapā has the nature of a tree,
it lacks the nature of stone, and if it had the nature of stone, it would lack the nature of a tree— this leads to the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of being devoid of any nature (nisvabhāvatā).
The conventional usage of identity has been explained.

"In this way" means: in that case, even an effect such as smoke is not without a cause, nor does it have a different cause; that is, it does not have as its cause any entity other than fire. Furthermore:

The effect, such as smoke, does not sometimes have fire as its cause and sometimes have water as its cause; for if those two causes were absent, it would follow that it is causeless—this must be stated regarding smoke, and indeed regarding both cases. [This applies] to the identity of the *śiṃśapā* with "tree-ness," and to smoke [arising] from fire.

And regarding the state of having the nature of production, it is "caused by a cause" (*hetukṛtā*); that is, by its own seed—which serves as the cause of its own production—the *śiṃśapā* is established as having the nature of a tree. By means of fuel—which serves as the cause of its own production—the fire is established as having the nature of producing smoke.

He says that very thing: Patañjali stated that inference (*anumāna*)—which is called *bhara*—has as its object the yogin, [arising] from the cause consisting solely of his own seed (*svabīja*). Others, who know the reality of reasoning (*yuktitatvavid*), hold that there is a certain perception (*pratyakṣa*) in the form of one's own cognition, which is equivalent to yogic perception (*yogipratyakṣakalpa*), regarding the ultimate reality (*pāramārthya*) of all things.

"Those who have devised [theories] for the sake of comprehension are merely conventional (*sāṃvyavahārika*). We have placed our burden upon the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the form of worldly transaction (*loka-vyavahāra*). For us, indeed, the very nature of the Lord (*īśvara-svarūpa*) is the subject under discussion, and that is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*). In the aspect of cognizing objects of knowledge (*prameya*) such as mountains and the like, which are distinct from Himself..."

It has been wrongly stated that even the contradiction of other objects of cognition, such as fire and so forth, does not contradict this nature of the Lord; for He cannot be obstructed by those things commonly accepted as obstructors, and so on.
Indeed, there would be a difference in appearance between two distinct things, such as a jar and a non-jar.
There is no manifestation of anything other than light that is distinct from it.
Because, in such cases, even the object of cognition—which is intended to be distinct [from consciousness]—is manifest;
therefore, there is no obstruction whatsoever to the nature of the Lord, whose essence is manifestation. As it has been stated in the *Svarūpaprakāśikā*: "And by this world, of this Blessed One..."

Form is essentially luminous and can never be concealed; for, having attained its very foundation through this luminosity, how could this world—which is the life-breath of the Self—be able to obstruct that light which is manifesting itself? And even if it were to obstruct it, how [could it succeed]?
"Let it abide by itself. What is the point of this relationship between cause and effect regarding the essential nature (*svabhāva-hetu*)?

In the case of the essential nature as a reason, he first states its very own form: that which is the root—the seed—from which arises the *śiṃśapā* tree, which is non-deviant because it is pervaded by "treeness" inherent in all trees. (414)

Therefore, from that very seed as the cause, there arises the nature of a *śiṃśapā* tree, which is invariably concomitant with that specific tree. It has been stated: "The cognition of a non-existent [entity] such as color and so forth, which depends on a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīna*), occurs through the inference of the property of the cause, like the transformation of fuel by smoke. Thus, there is no distinction between color, taste, and other qualities within a single [entity].

When the causal assemblage for production— consisting of the conjunction and completion of earth, water, fire, air, and space— is present, there occurs, even without the sense organ, the cognition of color such as white or yellow belonging to mangoes and other fruits by means of their taste.

In that case, it occurs through the inference of the property of being a seed, which has become the cause of the mango grove. This is the logic of the *svabhāva-hetu* (essential-cause reason), just as the transformation of fuel such as sandalwood is understood through smoke.
Now, [one might object]: regarding creatures such as scorpions, their cause consists of things like scorpions...
(Without [the cause], p.
323) first of all, unity is observed even in the absence of things such as insects or cow dung;
for instance, when a scorpion is produced from [cow dung] and so forth, it is directly from those born as scorpions [that it arises].

To claim that there is a difference in taste, potency, and so forth, is irrelevant to the present argument. For it is conceivable that even smoke produced by fire—though not originating from a scorpion—might be produced by a yogin, just as a scorpion born from cow dung might exist without its own specific cause, the scorpion. This is because the nature of a thing, such as the *śiṃśapā* tree, is its very essence.

How can there be the possibility of error through the desire for a source [of knowledge]? No one who accepts valid cognition would ever understand that what is blue is indeed blue, yet becomes non-blue.
It is said: here, the *svabhāvahetu* (essential reason) is of two kinds; therein, one is...
There is the type where the relationship of cause and effect is internally implicit, and another which is the opposite of that. He demonstrates this very point:

in the case of the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*) where the relationship of cause and effect is internally implicit, as in "fire" and "smoke," there exist two entities in the form of cause and effect; [the inference being] "this mountain possesses fire."

Because it possesses smoke; "this is impermanent because it is produced"—in this case, both the probandum (*sādhya*), which is impermanence, and its proof (*sādhana*), which is being produced, reside in one and the same entity. Since the very root of the first type of reason, the essential nature (*svabhāva-hetu*), is the relationship of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), what else remains to be said there?
Regarding the word "tu" (but): this [inference], namely "this is impermanent because it is produced," is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) that is being examined with you.

If, first of all, the essential nature of "being produced" in the world is its dependence upon a cause, then by means of this "being produced," the probandum "impermanence" must be either the essential nature of coming into existence (*bhavana-svabhāva*).

If its nature were existence (*bhāva*), then how could that [existence] be the nature of "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*), which is a delimited entity? For there is a difference in the manifestation (*ābhāsa*) of both. Since the manifestation of both is non-different, once the reason—producedness—is established, the probandum—impermanence—is also necessarily established.
The statement "whatever is produced is impermanent" establishes merely a linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*).

According to the logic of "this is a tree because it possesses treeness," the convention that "whatever is produced is impermanent" is indeed what is to be established, both for one's own knowledge and for communicating it to another. In that case as well, whatever is produced...

Even in the linguistic usage consisting of the cognition and expression "that is impermanent," if it is produced, let it be indeed impermanent; it should be understood that "whatever is produced is impermanent" occurs without any distinction within its own nature. That this must be expressed by another as well—such is the sovereign necessity (*niyati*).
The capacity [of the reason] becomes accepted.

(p. 324) Therefore, the *śiṃśapā* has the nature of a tree because it arises from its own seed, which is the root of its own class and is pervaded by all trees; fire has the nature of heat; [and] earth...

In all cases of essential-nature reasons (*svabhāva-hetu*), such as "hardness" and so forth— specifically regarding the essential natures of the *śiṃśapā* tree and the tree itself, or fire and heat, or earth and the nature of hardness and so forth—
in all such essential-nature reasons, [the relationship between] the *śiṃśapā* and the tree-nature [is established].

Because there is no difference in the manifestation within their own nature between fire and heat as intrinsic natures, or between earth and solidity as intrinsic natures, one establishes merely the conventional usage that "the *śiṃśapā* has the nature of a tree," and so forth. In that case, regarding the reason of essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), the *śiṃśapā* itself is the reason in the form of the probans.

Precisely because it consists of appearance (*bhāsa*), the appearance of "tree-ness" is not something additional to that [appearance]; thus, Caitra is distinct from Maitra in the form of the probandum (*sādhya*). He is distinct due to qualities such as good character, because he is different from him;
that is, because he is excluded from him. For whatever is distinct from something is excluded from it.

This very same discourse concerning the nature of knowledge and designations applies to exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) as well: "This is eternal, this is impermanent," because it exists as a universal (*sāmānya*) by being woven through all individual instances (*vyakti*). This is the path for universals.
As it has been said:

"Generality (sāmānya) is eternal, one, existent, and inheres in many. Therefore, it is "previously established. This means by way of a beginningless principle through the force of the logical reason (*hetu*), that is, by virtue of the capacity of the seed which serves as its own cause of production; thus, the *śiṃśapā* tree is indeed of the very nature of a tree.

By the power of such natural necessity (*niyati-śakti*), there occurs that grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the appearances of "śiṃśapā" and "tree," such that one thinks, "This tree is a śiṃśapā. Therefore, this tree is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the śiṃśapā; because it is rooted in the relationship of cause and effect, the reason (*hetu*) is the cause of its own production.

The seed is the cause; the *śiṃśapā* possesses that cause, and their state (*bhāva*) is existence (*sattā*). The meaning is that it is precisely rooted in that [seed] that the *śiṃśapā* arises from the seed as its own origin, having arisen as the very nature of a tree.
It should be understood that this has been stated in a general sense for all things: "Every nature has its cause born from its own origin."
The word "by the wise" (*vipaścidbhiḥ*) is to be supplied [as the agent]. "Or rather, let them be mere appearances," as stated previously. Regarding the phrase "the object of a single designation":

likewise, in cases such as "an unreal pot" and so forth, or in cases such as "fire and so on being indistinguishable therein," the fact that smoke—which is not fire—is produced by that [fire] is its very nature, namely, its "compatibility" (*sahyatva*).

He states the very opposite with the words "tataśca" (and therefore) and so forth. When a single object possessing branches and other features— such as a *śiṃśapā* tree— is being created by the will of a yogin,
[there arises] that universal self which is the probandum (*sādhya*), namely the appearance of "treeness" (*vṛkṣatva*) and so on.

Even the name "śiṃśapā" does not exist [in that context]. At that time, it is indeed possible; for by the power of the yogin's will, such a reversal of intrinsic nature (svabhāvaviparyāsa) is produced. Since the other form is created by the yogin's will, it is permeated by all other trees; therefore, that specific tree-ness (tadvṛkṣatva) is a unique, singular form.

Since the nature of being a *śiṃśapā* tree is already established as being inherent even in a *śiṃśapā*, its "tree-ness" is proven; thus, this [example], such as a jar and so forth, which is dependent on causes like clay, does not serve as a probandum for that [appearance]. Even in the case of the fallacious argument [that sound is impermanent because it is produced], its impermanence is not something to be proven, as it is already established.

The meaning is that a jar and other such things are stable because they perform causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Thus, all these reasons based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) occur only in dependence upon God, necessity, and power; it is not otherwise.
However, the logic of reasons based on essential nature, even when considered in relation to their respective [specific] dependencies, is indeed contradicted by all [empirical] sublation (*bādha*).

Thus, the transgression of the necessity of elemental existence (*bhūtaniyati*) is the power of the yogi. As it has been said in the *Praveśaka*: "Because it is observed that for yogis who have transcended necessity, their mental representations are common to many subjects and possess well-known causal efficiency."

Regarding the word "nanu": according to the principle stated—that the very distinctions of manifestation (*ābhāsa-bheda*) constitute the reality (*vastu*), because the essence of reality consists in the state of being a manifestation—within this doctrine that manifestation is reality, fire, which is non-manifest (*anābhāsa*), is entirely (from all sides) non-real by virtue of direct perception. Therefore, how [can there be a relation] with that which is non-real and consequently appears only internally?

Having raised the objection— “How can this smoke, which is perceived directly as being produced upon a mountain, be generated [from fire], and how, then, can there be a cognition of fire, which is intended to be the cause, from such smoke?”— he says "bhūyaḥ" (again) in order to justify that very point.
First, in the kitchen, for the cognizers who have gone to that kitchen, there arises the cognition: "This is fire; from this [fire] smoke is born.
Thus, through direct perception, there is the pervasion (*vyāpti*) consisting of the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) between fire and smoke, which possess a single form.

Immediately after its perception on the mountain, for those perceivers who had previously gone there—such as Kṛmi, Sarvajña, and others—the mountain appears in a uniform manner; and for those perceivers situated along the path, it appears as fire due to the dominant cause of the "imperceptible" (parokṣa) [object]. Thus, fire indeed manifests.

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), it is understood that [the effect] arises immediately from the seed and so forth; it is produced at that very moment, and not like the play of a cowherd boy or smoke that has emerged long after a pot was left behind.
Only such an effect as smoke and the like is capable of manifesting [its cause], and not anything else. Therefore, this smoke and so forth...

Smoke is an infallible mark (*liṅga*) for fire and the like; therefore, the inference of fire is not possible through that alone—this is the meaning. First, one must once perceive smoke directly in the kitchen here.
They perceive by means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). However, if one does not apprehend fire, one likewise does not apprehend smoke;

thus, through the force of the aforementioned perception and non-apprehension (*pratyakṣānupalambha*), those desiring to understand the relationship between cause and effect grasp the causal relation between the appearance of fire and the appearance of smoke. In that regard:
If, in the relationship of cause and effect, other subjects were distinct,
then the appearances residing within them would necessarily be distinct from cognition;
consequently, because they would not reside within a single appearance, they could not rest upon a single appearance.

The conventional usage [of "other"] arises from their coalescence; thus, it has been stated according to the logic of the Vijñānavāda school that the world—consisting of the elements (*bhūta*) and primarily composed of primordial nature (*prakṛti*)—becomes "other" when it is not permeated by another. Furthermore, within each individual continuum (*santāna*), the appearance as Caitra and the appearance as smoke are distinct from one another.
The appearances of fire and smoke occurring within the continuum of a friendly person are distinct from the appearances of fire and smoke [perceived elsewhere]. Regarding "of their own appearances":
it is precisely the appearances of fire and smoke occurring within one's own continuum that are grasped as having the relationship of cause and effect.

But does one not directly perceive another continuum—whether that continuum distinct from oneself or fire? No, because one does not experience the events belonging to that [other continuum]. Therefore, at the time of inference, for the proponent of consciousness (*vijñānavādin*) who is the cognizer situated on the path:

It is certain that there can be no inference of the appearance of fire— which manifests as a single entity in the form "this is fire"— belonging to cognizers who are omniscient regarding the insects dwelling on that mountain, from the appearance of smoke seen on top of the mountain within one's own continuum, even though that fire is concealed by the mountain.

Regarding the phrase "In this case, however": in our system of consciousness (*saṃvid-darśana*), at the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the appearances of fire and smoke in a kitchen,
as many subjects (*pramātṛ*) as there may be who potentially exist in that kitchen location, for all of them, [it is established that] "this is fire" and "this is smoke."

Thus, this single form—the appearance as smoke—and likewise the appearance as fire, such as "Whose is this fire? in the externalist view—all of that shines forth as nothing but one. "To that extent" means:
within the mere appearances of smoke and fire, for those perceivers...

Unity has been created by the Supreme Lord. And He unifies subjects within the appearance of smoke and fire, as in the phrase "like spectators at a dance performed by a beautiful woman. For indeed, that Lord [unifies them] with one another during the time of worldly transaction, such as buying and selling, watching performances, or explaining texts.

(p. 327) It is conceivable that the [Light] manifests externally in the form of a single appearance that which belongs to Caitra, Maitra, and others— the body, vital breath, intellect, and void— which, while remaining entirely within as an internal manifestation and never abandoning its internal luminosity, appears as such.
Thus, this [cognition] arises here as well, and from that [cause] as well. In this way, unity resides within the stream of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*);

by abandoning the distinction between one's own and another's mental stream, the mere appearance of smoke is the effect of the mere appearance of fire, specifically in the case of the perceived particularity of the appearance of smoke.
Having fully cognized "this is smoke" together with other subjects who accompany his own self,

he becomes one with that very appearance of smoke as an effect; because of the non-cognition of the remainder— that it was produced from fuel such as sandalwood— it exists in a general form, being concealed by the mountain.

Because it possesses a portion of a form that is beyond direct perception, the manifestation of fire located on the mountain—which is of the aforementioned nature and distinct from other manifestations of specific qualities—becomes one with other cognizers who are different from itself, in the sense that [the thought arises]: "There is fire on this mountain here. This is what is meant.
Having demonstrated the meaning of the sūtra through its intended purport (*tātparya*), he states the application of the sūtra with the words beginning "furthermore" (*bhūyaḥ*).

"Furthermore" means that after the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*), smoke-appearance is again apprehended as being invariably concomitant with fire; by the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), sprout-appearance and so forth are also included.

The appearance of smoke, too, is fresh, having arisen at that very moment; it is not old or stale like the smoke produced by a cowherd’s bellows which has been smoldering for a long time. And that appearance of smoke [arises] from the mountain, its own dominant cause.

Or it may arise from the very appearance of fire (*vahnayābhāsa*) itself, which is not being perceived due to its being concealed (*tirohita*). That alone is capable of producing [the effect], and nothing else. Here, the particle *liṅ* functions in the sense of "doubt" (*viśaṅkā*). And that appearance of fire is one and the same for those various cognizers (*pramātṛ*), the subjects who act within their own selves as inferents (*anumātṛ*).

The intention is that if that fire lacks unity, this inference of fire is not tenable; therefore, there must be one sovereign appearance of fire for all cognizers which serves as the cause of the appearance of smoke. Consequently, once it is determined that the appearance of smoke is not produced by a yogin, it is established as non-deviant [from the fire].

The effect is the mark (*liṅga*) and the means of recognition; from that very effect, it [the cause] is inferred. That appearance of fire, which is the dominant cause (*adhipati*) of this appearance of smoke, exists beyond perception because it is concealed by the mountain.
For if fire is inferred solely from the appearance of smoke, [then even a cowherd...]

Anticipating the objection that one might infer the appearance of fire from the appearance of smoke—even though that smoke has been present for a long time within the interval of a *ghaṭikā* and has since departed—the author says: "another. This means that the appearance of smoke manifested at that time is different from the new [smoke], and it resides in another subject (*pramātṛ*).

(p. 328) [The cognition of fire] arises from the very appearance of smoke—which is distinct from the appearance of fire, apprehended by cognizers such as cowherds, and which is indirect (parokṣa) due to being concealed within the jar—but not from the appearance of fire itself, nor from such an appearance of smoke;
how then could there be [cognition of] fire?

"Let the appearance (ābhāsa) be inferred as a specific intention belonging to another. This refers to whether the appearance of smoke is new or old; it arises from its own cause, the appearance of smoke, which is imperceptible due to its being situated within a cowherd's water-clock (gopālaghaṭikā) and thus having the nature of a dominant condition (adhipati-rūpa). Thus, it is said to be "from such [an appearance]."

The underlying intention is this: how can the appearance of fire—which is not the cause—be inferred from the appearance of smoke that arises solely from the appearance of smoke? Regarding the term "skilled" (*kuśalāḥ*):
it refers to those who know the reality of inference. [They say: "This smoke has emerged from a jar; this [smoke] has emerged from fire."

Thus, doubts are indeed exhausted. Even the extensive inferential usage—such as "from seeds comes a sprout" or "from threads comes a cloth"—which pertains to this extremely intense manifestation in the form of smoke, occurs through the effort of the yogi. The established rule is that fire is inferred by means of smoke at that specific moment, and not by any other [smoke].
With the intention that it should be performed, that which was merely indicated by the word "new" (*nūtana*) would be the corresponding form.
Through the perception of smoke, which is the entity to be excluded, this has been made clear.
(421) Thus, from the mere appearance of fire, the appearance of smoke arises.

If this is accepted, then he manifests these entities solely by virtue of possessing infinite power; this manifestation occurs through the force of his will, and that is his capacity as the creator of action.

Regarding what was stated by such passages as "the agency belongs to the conscious being alone," how can that be so, given that smoke arises even without a conscious agent, from the mere appearance of fire? This very point is demonstrated by the phrase "for instance" (*tathāhi*).

Anticipating the objection— "If such is the case, how can the principle that 'when there is fire, there is smoke,' or 'when there is a seed, a sprout arises,' be a subject of disregard?"— he says: "Even that causal relation, expressed as 'this effect in the form of a sprout exists when this seed exists,' belongs to those who are devoid of [true] dependence."

This sprout arises from the seed. However, for seeds, sprouts, and so forth—which are devoid of the reflective awareness, "I am born from the seed" or "I am the sprout born from the seed"—such a relationship is not possible. In the world, a single entity in the form of a seed is not itself the causal relation; rather, it is the state of being an effect [that constitutes the relation].
Furthermore, the status of being a cause is not attained; for the relationship between cause and effect depends upon two distinct entities,
just as a jar and a cloth appear simultaneously, so too a pair of entities such as a seed and a sprout appearing simultaneously cannot constitute the nature of cause and effect.

(p. 329) Following this, although these [effects] arise in a sequence—as in "this which is here"—they do not constitute a cause-and-effect relationship with an indeterminate order, like the cognitions of blue, yellow, and so forth, even though it is possible for them to arise from this very [cause] in such a manner. This is because they possess a fixed order, in that "the production of this occurs from this very [cause]."
Nor is it the case that the effect exists prior to its cause.

For the opponent’s view is as follows: the seed, which is the cause, has a fixed existence as a prior state, while the sprout, which is the effect, has a fixed existence as a subsequent state. In that view, [the status of] priority...

And otherness does not come to rest in the cognizer. In that regard, the state of being prior and posterior belongs to moments due to the synthesis performed by the conceptualizing intellect. For, according to the principle you have stated, there is nothing prior or posterior within the self; it is merely the thing-in-itself (*vastumātra*), as in the case of the seed and the sprout.
If it were not distinct from its own nature, then there would be merely the two entities consisting of the seed and the sprout;

nothing more than that would exist. Furthermore, as for the word "and" (*ca*), even some sense of conjunction or coordination does not belong to the relationship between the seed and the sprout—of this very [nature]...

Because it depends on a subject whose form has been grasped, when the object is absent, there would be only two entities: "it exists" and "it is. That reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) as well is dependent upon the subject.
Now, what is called the "priority" of the seed is simply its state of being that which precedes the sprout which is to arise later.
The state of being the prompter (*prayojaka*) consists in having one's own existence as its cause. Furthermore, the posteriority of the sprout consists in having its existence prompted by the seed.
In that case, the first existence of the seed, which prompts the sprout, finds its rest in the sprout it has prompted;
