thus, it enters into the sprout and attains identity with it, because the sprout finds its rest in the seed.

The absence of the sprout would merely be the cause that brings about [the seed's non-existence], rather than being the producer of the sprout. Furthermore, even that "causality of the absence of the sprout" would be nothing at all. The same should be said regarding the existence of that which is to be produced.
He demonstrates this very point: even the sprout, by bringing into itself its own existence—which is brought about by the seed and does not rest within the seed—includes the seed within itself;
thus, because the seed has come to rest in the sprout, the sprout is indeed the absence of the seed.

There would be mere state-of-being-employed; yet even that is nothing at all. Since the seed is independent of the sprout, only the sprout remains, and the seed would not be anything at all. In this way, first of all, a single entity in existence cannot exist in isolation as a cause-and-effect relationship, nor can two entities exist simultaneously.
The positions beginning with "the nature of real cause and effect is like that of a jar and a cloth" and ending with "the state of being the non-efficient cause (prayojaka-sattākatva) for the former,

and the state of being the dependent existence (prayojya-sattākatva) for the latter," are untenable. For an insentient thing, such as an insentient seed, there is no such capacity [to produce an effect].
It is not so;

for according to the stated principle, this seed produces that sprout—which is non-existent in form and whose existence is not yet perceived—such that one might say, "this seed generates this sprout. And yet, the sprout...
According to the principle stated as "dependent upon the seed," this sprout depends upon the seed in its production in such a manner;
and according to the principle stated as "the insentient [seed] lacks that power," this sprout,
being of the nature of an effect, is produced by this seed which serves as its cause— thus the sprout is both the progenitor and the son of that seed.

The meaning is that it produces some kind of excellence; and according to the principle stated as "a sprout is born from a seed," this is the greatness of the sprout, while according to the principle stated as "this sprout is born from this [seed]," how can this be the greatness of the seed? Furthermore, [it implies] that "this sprout is related to this seed."

These and other such [relationships] are not only established through the relation of cause and effect; rather, by means of this locative case— “this seed existing”— the seed’s status as the efficient cause (*prayojaka*) with respect to the sprout is indicated,
as is the potentiality of the sprout itself, which is being brought into existence by the thought “this exists.”

Even that causal relationship which exists in relation to a beingness (*sattā*) that is itself non-causal—namely, the state of having a beingness brought about by a seed (*bījaprayojyasattākatva*)—does not arise. This is because, according to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), both [the self and the seed] are insentient (*jaḍatvāt*); [thus, one might think]: "The seed is my cause; therefore, I am dependent upon that very seed."
If it is argued that the sprout is the effect [of the seed] and therefore there is a relationship between them,
such that there is a mutual dependence between the seed and the sprout— this being the very lifeblood of their causal relationship—
and that this [dependence] is not possible for insentient things like seeds and sprouts, it is replied:
For those who abide solely in their own self and move within contemplation,
this meaning of the locative case is established even in the state of eternal existence.

This refers even to the state of existence and non-existence of seeds, sprouts, and so forth— which are described as being devoid of mutual correlation in the form of dependence on defined characteristics, and for that very reason, which are restricted solely to their own selves and rest only within their own essential nature, yet are conceived as having the form of cause and effect.

In the phrase "when this exists" (*asmin sati*), there is the state of existence (*sattā*) of the seed; and in the phrase "this sprout does not exist," there is the state of non-existence (*asattā*). For this very reason, according to the principle that will be stated later—that "the meaning of manifestation rests solely upon the subject"—the sense of the locative case expressed as "in me" (*ahammin*) is not possible. Both of these, moreover, constitute the meaning of the locative case.

It is not capable of accomplishing [this]. According to the principle stated thus: "O Lord, there is always the appearance of beings, and the manifold appearance is produced," both the existence and non-existence of that [object] depend upon the cognizer.
Inanimate things such as seeds and sprouts are indeed incapable of connecting their mutual forms, thinking, "I, who was born from the seed, am the producer of the sprout.
[Similarly,] I am not the one born from Caitra; rather, I am Maitra.

(331) "I am that very Maitra who was Janaka"—this mutual connection (anyonyānusandhāna), which is of the nature of mutual recollection, is of an insentient form; yet, this mutual connection in the form of dependence is pervaded by consciousness belonging to Caitra and Maitra, which is the opposite of the [insentient] nature of seeds, sprouts, and the like. Thus, for Caitra, there is this mutual connection consisting of dependence.

The very nature [of the seed] is not indeed a synthesis (*anusandhāna*). In other cases, such as with the seed and sprout, [the notion of identity] is metaphorical, like saying "the chariot goes. Therefore, because it lacks synthesis, the insentient state of the seed and so forth—having its body contracted by a satisfaction consisting of resting within its own seed—how [could it act]?
It might extend to other things distinct from itself, such as the sprout and so forth. Consequently, there would be the following possibilities: if the seed exists while the sprout does not;

or if the reverse is true, that the sprout exists while the seed does not; or if both exist; or if both do not exist; or if both the seed and the sprout are existent—or perhaps both are non-existent. Such is this state of being existent and non-existent.
[The term] "existent" (sat) implies that which has been internalized as the meaning [of the context]: namely, of the non-existent sprout and the existent seed.
Thus, it refers to the sprout itself or the seed itself, or even to the sowing of the seed; in this way, it possesses a designation (sopākhyam). Regarding the word "one" (ekam):
between those two, the seed and the sprout, it is one [the seed], because the sprout exists posteriorly [to it]. It is designated by its own name within itself.

"Accompanied by manifestation. "The other" refers to that which has the form of a sprout; because it does not exist while the seed—the real entity—is present, it is "indefinable" (*nirupākhya*). That is to say, it is devoid of manifestation within itself due to its lack of definition. Both [the seed and the sprout] possess definition (*sopākhya*), yet even so, they are merely the referents of their respective nominal stems. Nevertheless...

That pair—the seed and the sprout—existing merely as the reality of the seed and sprout, being of the nature of cause and effect, [exists] through a further property such as conjunction (*samuccaya*). By means of conjunction and so forth—as indicated by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "by way of conjunction and so forth"—the seed produces the sprout. Furthermore, the sprout depends upon the seed for its own production.
The sprout is produced from the seed; like father and son, the seed gives satisfaction to the sprout.

(425) From the seed the sprout is born. The sprout of the seed exists as the very essence related to the seed—this is established through the resting of the cognizer (*pramātṛ*), beginning with the nominative case and ending with the locative case.

It remains even when not embraced by another dharma. The seed and the sprout of that [process of] accumulation— such as "the seed produces the sprout"— have a nature that is perceived [as such], because they rest within the consciousness that constitutes the nature of that subject, due to their being of the nature of dependence upon that subject.

Regarding the phrase "in non-conscious things": because the aforementioned dependence on [causes] is not possible for seeds, sprouts, and so forth— which possess the nature of consciousness in the form of the manifestation "I"—
for this very reason, in this world one says, "this tree exists by means of this water," and "by means of the eye."
He sees the tree; shade is given by the tree to travelers; he gives water to the tree;
[the fruit] falls from the tree; this flower is related to the tree; [it is given] by many.

In the statement "the bird stays on the tree together with its branches," the meaning of the case-endings— ranging from the nominative to the locative— is characterized by the coordination of entities known as the relationship between action and its factors (kriyākārakabhāva). Such a state, whose form is apprehended through action and its factors, is logically possible only when it has the single subject (pramātṛ) as its sole substratum.

Regarding the word "asmin" (in this): it refers to the locative case (*saptamī*), as well as to other cases such as the nominative (*prathamā*) and so forth; in this [locative], birds stand together, and the very same meaning characterized by action, agent, and relation—such as "the tree stands here"—is present.
When entities such as trees and birds come to rest within a single cognizer through the medium of their respective distinct cognitions, this state of being known is established.
According to the principle thus stated, *samanvaya* (coherence) consists in resting within the subject (*pramātṛ*);

it is not something else, some dry [concept] devoid of rest in the subject. And that is the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhakti*). This is so if [the word] refers to the independent nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), which possesses the capacity for such acts as joining and separating.

Only then does the duality of existence, consisting of cause and effect, find its rest; otherwise—that is, in the absence of rest within the independent conscious subject—it is not possible in any way whatsoever. To explain: this is because there would be no rest within the subject.

"In any way whatsoever" (*kathaṃ cit*) means that it is not possible by any means at all. For instance, without resting in the subject (*pramātṛ*), even a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) occurring subsequent to experience cannot justify this meaning of the case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*) as residing in an object such as a jar or a cloth.
Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is indeed the vital breath that follows after objects such as jars and cloths already experienced;

it exists only by following after experience. And that [experience] does not exist here with respect to this object. Conceptual construction follows experience, experience follows the object, and the object itself does not follow experience.
It occurs thus: "This is a jar," "This is a cloth. Because these arise from the object (*vastu*), they follow that very object;
for in a subsequent verbal report (*anuvāda*) of objects occurring in a sequence of space and time, each object is self-contained.
According to this stated principle, the object is said to be established within its own nature. Therefore, when the seed exists, the sprout [arises].

The statement "there is smoke in the fire," and so forth, is logically tenable only when [the object] rests within the cognizer whose nature is entirely autonomous consciousness (*svatantra-cid-rūpa*), and not otherwise.
By means of the three verses beginning with "When this exists, that exists," [the author] discusses insentient entities such as seeds and sprouts.

Having refuted the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) taught by the Buddhists, [the author] says "But surely" (*nanu*) and so forth, in order to reject the causal relationship demonstrated by the Sāṃkhyas. Regarding the sprout and the seed,
which are characterized as the produced (*prayojya*) and the producer (*prayojaka*), their mutual dependence consists merely in their own respective natures (*svasvarūpa*).

If [the notion of] rest is not tenable, then, according to the Sāṃkhya school who maintain identity (*tādātmya*), there would be a mutual dependence between cause and effect— such as the sprout and the seed— wherein the seed possesses the nature of the sprout and the sprout possesses the nature of the seed (p. 333).

This is indeed possible because [the effect] abides in a state of insentience (*jaḍarūpa*). However, one might object: "All this is only logical when that [insentient effect] comes to rest within a conscious subject (*cidrūpa-pramātṛ*)," as has been stated by supporting the doctrine of the agent (*kartṛvāda*) whose nature is the unfolding of consciousness (*caitanyavijṛmbhātmaka*). Anticipating this, he says: "Of cause and effect, such as the sprout and the seed..."

Regarding "mutual intrinsic nature": if the sprout had the intrinsic nature of the seed, and the seed had the intrinsic nature of the sprout, there would be only oneness; thus, the state of being a seed would be identical to the state of being a sprout.
If they were of distinct and different forms, there could be no identity consisting of mutual intrinsic nature.

Regarding the phrase "mutual identity" (*paraspara-svabhāvatva*): if the sprout were the very nature and essence of the seed, then only the sprout would remain, and the seed would not exist as anything at all—or else there would be the opposite [of what is observed].
If the seed were the nature of the sprout, then only the seed would remain and not the sprout; thus, in the case of identity, [the two would become indistinguishable].

What is the cause? What is the effect? Because these two reside in both. For if there were difference—now, if the seed is other than the sprout and the sprout is other than the seed, then the seed and the sprout would not possess the nature of each other. [This implies] that the seed has difference from the sprout and non-difference [from it].
"Unity and difference at once": simultaneously, two objects having a single locus, such as the seed and the sprout, are indeed contradictory in their respective natures.
[Objection: "But surely... [Response: "Even so... If the seed and the sprout were of a mutually identical nature, there would be oneness.

In the absence of that [consciousness], because of insentience (*jaḍatva*), the relationship of cause and effect would not be possible. Nevertheless, the seed, sprout, stalk, branch, flower, and fruit appear in their manifold variety; thus, for those possessed of long and deep reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), it is like a stream originating from a mountain and reaching the ocean.
In the middle, its delimited nature is perceived as being for that very reason free from contradiction.

By the words "And thus," etc., he demonstrates the very state of delimitation [of the seed] starting from the production of the sprout up until the fruit. Regarding the transformation of the seed through the stages from the sprout to the final fruit:

When asked, "Where has the seed gone? since it is no longer visible, [the answer is that] having abandoned its form as a sprout and so forth, it has not gone anywhere; rather, it exists in the nature of a sprout, having become a sprout.
People say, "This sprout is that [seed]. In the same way, the *pradhāna* [exists] as the intellect (*buddhi*) and the rest.
The perception of those who grasp at the extended [universe] is that it consists of the earth and other elements in their essential state, as well as their modifications and manifestations;
and that it has attained the nature of an infinite succession of creations and dissolutions connected to those modifications— this is the Pradhāna, the cause of Mahat and the rest.

The conceptualization of causality arises from the imposition of parts such as "the effect" and so forth upon that [Prakṛti] which has transformed into the form of Mahat and the rest. For this very reason, fearing that it would be like the dismemberment or the violent mutilation of the complete nature of Pradhāna, he says:

(428) From the Great Principle (*mahat*) down to the earth (*dharā*), this diversity in the form of the Great Principle and the rest arises from a single cause, the *pradhāna*, which is of one nature and uniform; immediately after the *pradhāna* comes the Great Principle (*mahat*), and immediately after that, the I-principle (*ahaṃkāra*).

In this way, since action follows the temporal sequence of prior and posterior states, even the insentient *pradhāna* would possess agency by virtue of its transformation (*pariṇāma*) into the form of the *mahat* and so forth. If the single cause, which is the *pradhāna*, transforms into the form of the *mahat* and so forth, then despite its insentience—

Action would follow the sequence of time, which consists of prior and subsequent states. Since action rests in the agent, it would be the agent itself; likewise, because of its possession of the capacity for the action of transformation, it is Primordial Matter (pradhāna) alone that transforms into everything from the Great Principle (mahat) down to the earth.

Relying on recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), which is rooted in any one of the means of valid cognition— perception, inference, or scripture— for those who possess far-sighted vision, it is stated according to the principle that "Prakṛti is the state of equilibrium of the qualities (*guṇas*) of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*"; thus, this very thing consists of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, namely pleasure, pain, and delusion.

It is established that primordial matter (*pradhāna*), which consists of equilibrium, becomes the universe by assuming an infinite variety of states of disequilibrium, such as the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the rest. In this regard, the difference between that which is of a single nature— by virtue of the power of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) that "this is indeed that"— and its manifestation in the form of the Great Principle and so forth [is explained].

This very process of the Great Principle (mahat) and the others assuming successive forms is what is called "activity" (kriyā). For those other entities—the Great Principle and the rest—possessing natures that follow a sequence such as prior and posterior due to the characteristic of time, do not manifest simultaneously; for instance, the ego-principle (ahaṃkāra) arises immediately after the Great Principle, and the mind (manas) immediately after that.
Thus, appearing sequentially through a prior and posterior nature, that very state of being prior and posterior is what is called "action" (*kriyā*).

Since action is thus characterized by a form consisting of a sequence of prior and posterior stages, the agency (*kartṛtā*) would belong to *pradhāna* and the like; it would not be a mere causality (*kāraṇatā*) consisting of a dry, insentient nature.

Therefore, in that manner, you have not understood the activity characterized by transformation, which consists in the manifestation of the sequence of principles beginning with *mahat* and ending with earth— both prior and subsequent—
as the cause of the principles such as *mahat*.

Having set aside its own specific nature— which is to be excluded— and having transformed and abandoned some particular form consisting of the *pradhāna* itself, it establishes the form of the *mahat*, which is to be followed subsequently. (329)

If the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) and so forth were being produced as a third form, then by virtue of that subservience (*prahvatā*), which serves as the cause, there would be agency (*kartṛtva*) itself [belonging to them]. Regarding the word "and so forth" (*ādi*): it is not logical for insentient things such as seeds and the like to assume the form of sprouts and so on without abandoning their own nature. As it has been said:
"When the seed exists as a sprout, its state as a seed is indeed no longer seen.
Now, it may be argued that by this much, the *pradhāna* becomes the agent (*kartṛ*) in the act of transformation (*pariṇāma*) into the nature of the *mahat* and so forth.

If it is argued that [this] has been established, what is the fault? Anticipating the objection that we therefore accept the agency of this very Puruṣa as primary, he says: such an agency consisting of the act of transformation is not logical for the insentient Pradhāna alone, given the distinction of the Great One (mahat) and the rest.
There is a mutual contradiction between the nature of the primary [unity] and difference;

because that appearance of the primary nature is distinct, there is a contradiction in the single, uniform conscious Self possessing both the forms of difference and non-difference. Therefore, agency is not tenable.
Thus: according to the principle stated, it is illogical for that very substrate (*dharmin*) which is *pradhāna*— whose essential nature is non-different—

to possess the agency of action, characterized by the independence of undergoing the process of transformation (*pariṇamana*) through the grasping of a vast plurality of distinct attributes such as the Great Principle (*mahat*) and so forth, which flow forth continuously.
Because of its insentience (*jaḍatva*). For that which is called "insentient" is established as having a single, fixed nature such as "this-ness" (*idantā*) at this present moment;

it has fallen into the category of an object of knowledge (*prameya*), having reached the ground of "this-ness," and must be determined as distinct from its own essential nature due to the perception of differences in its own forms, such as the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the rest.
Just as when blue perceives a yellow or other form, its blueness is distinct and dissolved; yet,

because it does not abandon its blueness upon perceiving yellow and so forth, it remains a single, non-distinct form of blue due to its unitary nature— likewise, even when perceiving the Great One (*mahat*) and the other principles, [the Self] is "dissolved" as distinct because it perceives the difference in their own forms.

Its own essential nature must be established. Even when grasping [the transformations] such as the Great Principle (mahat), it is non-different because it does not abandon its own essential nature and possesses a single intrinsic nature; however, it is not the case that the very essence of the Pradhāna itself becomes differentiated in the form of the Great Principle and so forth.
It ought to be non-different from its own nature, yet let it be different;
likewise, it ought to be both non-different and non-different from its own nature, yet let it be both different and non-different—
thus [is there] the imposition of both affirmation and negation upon a single insentient entity.

If it is argued that, because of the contradiction in a single entity existing simultaneously, certain natures such as the "Great One" (mahat) and so forth are distinct while the nature of the Pradhāna itself is non-distinct, then there would be these two natures belonging to the single entity that is the Pradhāna.

But this is not tenable. If that were the case, then although Caitra’s body possesses multiple natures differentiated by various places, times, and forms, it would appear while not abandoning its manifold nature under the cognition "this is that very same person. Consequently, the established distinction between difference and non-difference regarding all things would be utterly destroyed.
According to the logical principle, the differentiation (*bheda*) of all things consists in their being distinguished by specific place, time, and form,
as well as in being the object of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) such that "this is that very same thing. However, for the Primal Nature (*pradhāna*),

non-differentiation (*abheda*) is the non-abandonment of its own essential nature, whereas differentiation is the assumption of the essential natures of the Great One (*mahat*) and the subsequent evolutes.

That [oneness] is not tenable in a unity that consists in the non-abandonment of one's own essential nature; for in such a case, it would not have fallen into the state of being an object of knowledge (*prameya*) as "this," but rather would be the ultimate reality as light, in the form of consciousness and the form of awareness as "I. Therefore, its sole inherent nature is consciousness.

(p. 336) That which is transparent becomes capable of reflecting the universe. In that state, while possessing the nature of differentiation—the universal self consisting of everything from Śiva down to the earth—it is also established as having a non-dual nature in the apprehension of the manifold universe, without abandoning its own essential nature. For this is evident from the very experience of all subjects regarding that which is transparent.

The body of a mirror or similar object, which is capable of reflecting images such as various pots and cloths, is perceived as possessing its own undivided nature, even though it is permeated by thousands of forms— such as mountains and elephants— reflected within it.
This is just as when one sees a mother-of-pearl shell from a distance...
Just as the silver perceived through the delusion "this is silver" due to the similarity of color,

and the double moon perceived due to an eye disease, exist by way of concealing the true nature of the mother-of-pearl and the single moon respectively; and just as mountains and so forth are perceived in a mirror.
Because its own nature as a mirror is concealed, it does not appear [as such];

for just as in the case of a mirror, even when there is a manifestation (*avabhāsa*) mixed with mountains, elephants, and so forth, the very state of being a mirror shines forth all the more clearly because, like a mirror, it provides non-manifestation. This mirror is stainless.

Mountains and all other objects are capable of being reflected; among those things capable of reflection, such as crystal, water, and so forth, [the mirror] is superior, pure, and purified by refinement. Thus, due to the conceit of the perceiving subjects who observe it, the mountain appears to be situated far outside.

The mountain does not itself come there to be reflected in the mirror; for if it did, it would follow that the mountain must abandon its own location. Furthermore, this mountain does not appear above the mirror by placing the mirror beneath itself; for in that case, it would follow that the mirror itself would not be perceived. Nor...

Regarding the word "in the middle": that mountain, having entered the mirror, does not exist within its interior; for it is impossible to conceive of the entry there of something dense and hard, such as its slopes, peaks, and ridges, which possess the quality of resistance (*pratigha*). Nor does it [exist] behind the mirror, as in the case of a mountain.

Having arrived, it appears at the lower part of the mirror. Since it is not seen there [within the mirror] but appears in its own place from afar, the external mountain is merely reflected by the mirror; for the rays of the eyes, having struck the mirror, turn back and proceed outward.
Nor is it the case that one perceives only the mountain as it stands [in reality]. This applies to both the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*).

For instance, when other objects are placed at the side of the mountain, there is the mountain in the form of the original object situated outside, and the mountain in the form of the reflection situated within the mirror.
Because of the observation of [objects] within the end of a mirror, this is the majesty of the mirror’s purity.

Therefore, even while the mirror grasps the infinite reflections of mountains, elephants, and so forth, its oneness remains unimpeded; and the mountain peak situated at a distance [is likewise perceived].
In the cognition "I" within a single subject, all objects situated in cities, villages, and so forth, manifest along with oneself; thus,
it is logically established that the nature of consciousness alone is the agent of the manifestation of the universe.

Because the one [Self], though inherently undivided, possesses the capacity to admit the penetration of distinctions from Śiva down to the earth, there exists the presence of the penetration of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), which consists in being the creator of those [distinctions]. This has been stated:
"And he, by virtue of possessing infinite powers, causes this [universe] to appear through that [power]."
"By the power of the desire for existence, this activity belongs to him; that is his state of being a creator.

[To the objection] "But surely," [the reply is] "to this extent": consciousness itself, which is the nature of Brahman, devoid of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) consisting of autonomy in the form of "I" as pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), is precisely what [is meant by] "this."
Let him embrace the manifold variety of the universal form, from Śiva down to the earth; for indeed,
in embracing that universal form, the Lord alone is the agent everywhere, and "I am He"— thus, according to the stated principle,
there is the knowledge and action characterized by sovereignty.
Anticipating the question, "What is the purpose of postulating a lordship characterized by absolute freedom (svātantrya)? he says:
"Even though the unity of consciousness (*cidekatva*)—the nature of Brahman as that which is manifest—is real, [it appears] as distinct through appearances.
This occurs through their respective forms of action: as the insentient self, as the agent, and as the manifestation of the conscious self.
"Without a single unifying reflection characterized by the desire to act— which pertains to the mobile and immobile worlds as distinct entities in the form of agents performing actions"—
according to the principle stated thus: "The manifestation of the multitude of existents, which reside within the Self and are non-different from it, occurs by way of the will-to-create."

For without the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the entire range of categories— from Śiva down to the earth— residing within one's own self, [the Lord] would not exist. Alternatively, there is the desire-to-act (*cikīrṣā*), which consists of the state of being a desirer (*eṣitṛtā*) and the state of being a creator (*kartṛtā*), pertaining to those two— the insentient and the sentient— which are differentiated by the aforementioned manifestation (*ābhāsa*).

The desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) is its very nature; without reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), action would not occur. Furthermore, as has been stated, there is a sequential relationship between the distinct conscious and insentient appearances, which constitutes the reflective awareness "I am this."

The form of resting within a single cognizer is the desire-to-act (*cikīrṣā*); without that reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), action would not be possible. Alternatively, it is the connection between the insentient and the sentient, which are distinct due to the aforementioned manifestation: "That state of 'I' makes this state of 'this' its own by means of the self-manifestation of the person."
According to the principle thus stated, how could there be an action characterized by the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) without the single reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of "I"?
In this way, the genitive case in the phrase "of the two [entities] distinct from manifestation" (*ābhāsabhinnayoḥ*) is used in dependence upon either the desire to act or the reflective awareness;

the compound *ābhāsabhinnayoḥ* is formed because it is a necessary relative term (*nityasāpekṣatva*). For what is called "reflective awareness" (*vimarśa*) is indeed the [consciousness of] the universe.

Through the manifestation of the universe, or through its withdrawal, there is the unartificial flash of "I-ness. Thus, for Brahman— which consists of pure light devoid of the aforementioned reflective awareness— oneness within its own self is the reality.

If it is argued that this distinction consisting of earth and so forth arises from the affliction of ignorance (*avidyopaplava*), then it does not cohere to say that such an affliction of ignorance belongs to that [Brahman]. How could Brahman, whose sole nature is pure knowledge, possibly possess the nature of ignorance? Apart from Brahman, [there is nothing else].

It does not exist as a reality distinct from sentient or insentient things—that of which ignorance could be predicated. If it is argued that "this is called ignorance," and thus it is impossible to say "it is such-and-such a thing," then we do not know to what this "indefinable" (anirvācya) belongs;
for since nothing exists apart from Brahman, there is no "ignorance" that appears as a distinct entity in its own right.

If it is argued that this "inexpressible" [nature] appears because it cannot be established through non-separation [from consciousness], then what indeed is this so-called "reasoning" that would set aside direct experience? For there is no reasoning that can set aside the manifest nature of ignorance while it is itself manifest.
What other "Kākhalu-yukti"—the subsequent logical impossibility of the nature of ignorance as it appears—could there be?
He states another position: "In non-conceptual cognition," [the expression] "Oṃ tat sat" is the designation.

According to the principle stated that "Brahman is remembered as being threefold," [the Self] shines forth as non-different from Brahman, whose nature is Being (*sadrūpa*). If it is argued that this differentiation, consisting of the universe, exists through the power of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), then at that time, to whom does this operation of conceptual construction belong? It cannot belong to Brahman, whose nature is free from conceptual construction.

If there were the activity of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), then there would be the application of ignorance (*avidyā-yoga*). Apart from Brahman, there exists no such thing as a "living soul" (*jīva*) or the like that possesses the activity of conceptual construction. From where, then, could this distinction arise—that Brahman, which is free from conceptual construction, is real, while the universe, which consists of conceptual construction, is unreal? For there is no difference between the two insofar as both are equally manifest.
If it is argued that although this [world] appears as the universal self, it is sublated by this form of Brahman; [we reply:

even this non-difference is sublated by the appearance of difference, because in the world, that which is sublated does so precisely because it appears, and not otherwise; thus, difference too appears.
How can ignorance, which appears as the very foundation [of experience], be disregarded? This non-duality cannot be established by either perception or inference.
If it is argued that scripture alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), even scripture consists of the distinction between the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge.
Since it is the cause for the manifestation of the universe, the entity is of the nature of difference; therefore, this [objection] is of no consequence.

Consequently, even while accepting the real unity of consciousness in Brahman, its characteristic as the creator of the universe does not consist in a form of the universe such as the earth and so forth that is distinct [from itself].

Action consisting of immersion (*samāveśa*) is not logically possible. For that which is called "reflective awareness" (*vimarśa*) has been described as having the characteristic of self-recognition in the form of the universe; it is only if its sovereignty (*svātantrya*) exists that [immersion] becomes possible. "Everything"—this refers to action characterized by universal agency and its effect.
The meaning is that even the universe arises [from it]. For the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) is the desire to create the universe, which is the will (*icchā*).
Regarding that will of yours, for whom this fruit consisting of the three worlds exists—by that [will], who can know what the extent of the destiny of those entitled to office may be?

Thus, according to the principle stated by the venerable Bhaṭṭanārāyaṇa, it has been said that within that will (*icchā*), which consists of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), the entire universe—from Śiva down to the earth—must be manifested; it exists through the conceptualization of internal distinctions.

This is because [the universe] is manifest to the Lord who is established in His own self, as stated in the passage beginning with "of the Lord... established in Himself" (verse 435). Therefore, it exists because it is being illumined.
The universe is indeed one's own self-nature; because it performs various purposeful actions (*arthakriyā*), it possesses a real form.

Its manifesting nature is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), which is the undivided "I"-form. Being non-different from manifestation, it is manifest as existence itself. Within the ultimate reality of manifestation, there is no such thing as "this" through the duality of separation.

"That which makes manifest, O Maheśvara"—this very [power] is called sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), characterized by absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), whose defining trait is the performance of what is otherwise most difficult to accomplish. In the phrase "of the two distinct from the manifestation," the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) depends on the action and denotes a general relationship; it is subsequently divided as appropriate.
The insentient appearance, such as a jar and so forth, which is distinct from the appearance of consciousness (cidābhāsa) by virtue of its own appearance, is the object (karman).

Therefore, the appearance of consciousness, being distinct from that, is the agent (kartṛ). Thus, the action pertaining to these two consists in the state of being acted upon for the one—the jar and so forth—and the state of agency for the other—the appearance of consciousness—both of which belong to Brahman.

It would not exist. Since the entire range of existence from Śiva down to the earth must be manifested in the form of will, how could this single [will]—which exists without the reflective awareness of duality—be the action itself?
Furthermore, how could it be the inherent nature of two things—one insentient and one sentient—which are mutually distinct, acting as agent and object of action?

He said: "The state of being acted upon belongs to one [factor], while the state of being the agent belongs to another; thus, in the context of the relationship between cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇatā*), the agent and the object are stated as the two *kārakas*.
Action is the object of investigation, and it is the coordination of the *kārakas* [that constitutes action]."

According to the principle thus stated, even other *kārakas* (factors of action) are, in the ultimate sense, participants in the action insofar as they possess the nature of having a single agent. Otherwise, if the collection of *kārakas* such as the instrument (*karaṇa*) were distinct from the action, how could they be non-distinct [from it]? Or rather, if the insentient and the sentient are distinct according to the aforementioned appearance—[then this distinction is merely phenomenal].
Regarding the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) of those two:

for one [object], such as a jar, there is the state of being desired (*iṣyamāṇatā*), and for the other, there is the state of being the desirer (*eṣitṛtā*). How could action occur without a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of their unity, which is their very nature?

Or rather, how could there be action on the part of Brahman without that reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*)— which takes the form of "I am this" regarding the manifest and the differentiated, the conscious and the insentient— which finds its rest in the subject who is the perfect I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*), and which consists of the will-to-act (*cikīrṣā*)? (436) [This applies] to the insentient and the conscious, as distinguished from the aforementioned manifestation.
Or rather, how could there be an action characterized by the desire to perform that [action] without the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of oneness as "raha"?
Thus, the genitive case is used in relation to either the action, the desire to perform it, or the aforementioned twofold reflective awareness;
and because these are always dependent, [the rule applies] even to those things distinct from the manifestation (*ābhāsa*).
Summary:
He concludes the subject matter taught in this chapter:
"The very will of Him who desires to abide as the world in the form of the manifestations of jars, cloths, and so forth, is the cause."
Agency is action.

However, by the statement "But the insentient [nature] lacks that power," and so forth, it is shown that it is not logical for the universe to have as its cause the insentient *pradhāna*, atoms, or the like; for even though that which is distinct from the insentient and consists of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) possesses this nature of being an obstructive agent, those who hold otherwise do not acknowledge its supreme agency.

It has been stated that "for this reason" (yata ittham), meaning that even for Brahman— who, according to the logic to be explained hereafter, is devoid of supreme agency, lacks sovereignty, and is consequently not the Lord— agency as the cause of the world is not asserted;
for it is endowed with such a manner, namely, with those various thousands of expansions such as birth, maintenance, and so forth.

For the Supreme Lord who desires to abide as the world through the manifestation of this or that— such as jars, cloths, and so forth— which is to say, who wishes to exist in those various forms; "thus" means that the very desire to abide in such a form is the causality toward the universe from Śiva down to the earth, which consists of agency and the activity of being a creator or fashioner.

"Thus it is said": however, by the logic already stated, the insentient—such as *pradhāna* or atoms—lacks that power; therefore, even though it exists, the insentient has no causal agency in the form of being the creator of the universe, because of the principle that consciousness is one. "Of the non-Lord" (*anīśvarasya*) means one who lacks the sovereignty consisting of the fivefold functions such as the creation of the universe.

If it is asked: "By this reasoning—that even Brahman, who is devoid of [external] objects, conscious, and consists of pure consciousness (cinmātra), lacks causality—how is it that this world has arisen? [The answer is: That very object, for that very subject, and in whatever way he desires to act—that desire to act belongs to him alone. Thus, this single creative action is sequential, both internal and external.

Abiding. According to the principle thus stated, that which has attained externality from the internal nature of consciousness is designated as "action" (*kriyā*). That very [consciousness] is the desire-to-act (*cikīrṣā*), the agency (*kartṛtā*); the universe is precisely the form of that desire-to-act, and there is no causality toward each [object] through agency and so forth apart from the desire-to-act. Therefore, in the world...

The meaning of the statement "the jar exists" (*ghaṭastiṣṭhati*) is as follows: it is the Will-to-Abide (*tiṣṭhāsuḥ*) in the form of the jar who, through his sovereignty, accepts that state of the jar; it is not, however, the Great Lord’s Light (*maheśvaraprakāśa*), as conceived by the pure Śaivas and others, which cannot tolerate the specific nature (*svarūpa*) of that jar or other objects.

It exists in the form of jars and so forth; for that which is indeed the world, appearing in the form of jars, cloths, and the like, He— being autonomous— desires to abide as that very world through its own nature, and thus [He remains] in the form of thousands of differentiated actions, such as the modifications of existence (bhāva-vikāra) including birth and persistence belonging to each respective world.
"Which is related. "In this way" means: the connection is that the very desire for various forms is itself action (*kriyā*).
This is precisely the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) which, through a progressive intensification, culminates in the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*).
"We shall demonstrate" was stated previously. "By that" refers to the insentient (*jaḍa*).

Since even Brahman, which is of the nature of consciousness and distinct from [insentient principles] such as *pradhāna*, lacks agency, the Blessed Maheśvara alone is the creator of the universe. May there be auspiciousness!
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the commentary on the *Pratyabhijñā-sūtra-vimarśinī*.
It is finished.
The section on ritual action is completed.
Now (the thirteenth chapter).

(438) The river-like flow of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) such as "I, I," and furthermore, the river-like flow of reflective awareness consisting of cognitions of jars, cloths, and so forth, residing within each respective subject (*pramātṛ*). Furthermore...

The flow of the river of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), which consists of the identity with the various forms of Garuḍa and so forth through the mode of contemplation such as "I am indeed Garuḍa," and furthermore, the awareness that "this [deity] is Sadāśiva of such a form," "this is Mantramaheśvara of such a form," and "this is Ananta of such a form"— [is the nature of the mantra].
"This is the time of consciousness, of such a nature; this is the Sakala [subject], of such a nature;

this is the category of its objects of knowledge, of such a nature"—this ocean of scripture, consisting of words spoken from the mouth of Paramaśiva, takes the form of an exposition of the subjects of knowledge (pramātṛ), beginning with Śiva and ending with the Sakala, along with their respective objects of knowledge (prameya).

All this which has been proclaimed by Bhairava consists of the nature of the fullness of I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhantā*). Just as the ocean is the essence of a multitude of jewels, so too is this ocean of the supreme scripture the essence of a multitude of wish-fulfilling gems (*cintāratna*); even within that, the Śāmbhava nature is the essence of a multitude of wish-fulfilling gems. Such is it.
Having reached the ocean of the supreme scripture (paramāgama) and resting therein alone, one attains fullness.

Generally, a multitude of rivers that have reached the ocean becomes full and achieves its ultimate purpose; likewise, one attains identity with the ocean of the supreme scripture. Being thus constituted—

I bow to the ocean of the supreme scripture (*paramāgama*). According to the principle that "the word *namaḥ* [expresses] the state of being bowed," it means that having submerged my limited subjectivity—consisting of the body and so forth—I become one with that [scripture]. (p. 342)

We praise that auspicious Śiva, from whose interior the wheel of internal principles shines forth— a beginning marked by an exalted and glorious blossoming that spreads as far as the earth of the illustrious Sadāśiva, reaching even to the very limits of the world.

It has been established that, through the two chapters on Knowledge (*jñāna*) and Action (*kriyā*), the Lord’s status as both knower and agent is demonstrated as the cause for the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of the subject as God. This applies likewise to the case of "pot" and "cloth. Immediately thereafter, at the conclusion of the chapter on Action, [it is shown] from Śiva down to the earth.
It has been stated that the characteristic [of consciousness] is the manifestation of all objective entities (*viśvapadārtha*). What, then, are these "all objective entities"? This is the question.

In that regard, when it is said that the characteristic is the manifestation of all objective entities, the entities characterized as subjects (*pramātṛ*) and objects of knowledge (*prameya*), whether insentient or sentient, are nothing but manifestations (*ābhāsa*). Let those entities be established.

Illusion (*māyā*) is apprehended by the subject through form, for perception (*pratyakṣa*) operates everywhere. However, inference (*anumāna*) does not operate everywhere for the subject, because inference follows upon perception. In whatever object exists, there the mark (*liṅga*) must be grasped as being pervaded (*vyāpti*).

"Indeed, there is no arising" means that the unconditioned, which is devoid of limitation, whose ultimate reality is the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the Great Lord whose nature is light— that [unconditioned] would not perceive the praise of the *Āgama*. "In accordance with that" means in accordance with the *Āgama*, by means of making the entire universe, from Śiva down to the earth, an object of cognition.

Having attained the definitive determination of the categories of reality beginning with Śiva and ending with the Earth, he now begins the third chapter on Scripture (*āgama*) in order to explain it. In that chapter on Scripture,
by means of eleven verses beginning with "Thus, internally and externally," [he explains] according to the distinction between the gross and the subtle.

By this [concluding] statement, that which is established through scripture— from Śiva down to the Earth— is shown to consist of individual manifestations (*ekābhāsa*). In the Nyāya system, this is what is conventionally designated as "generality" (*sāmānya*), whose nature consists in the state of being a single manifestation of earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*) and so forth, pertaining to the universe.

In the unification into a single collection of the group of principles (tattva-grāma) whose nature is universal— the group of principles beginning with earth and ending with Śiva— there occurs the manifestation of the specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) of jars and so forth, wherein the various universals such as "gold-ness" are gathered together.

The purport of this chapter is as follows: preceded by a specific arrangement, this entire aggregate—beginning with the body and the worlds—is the manifestation (*vibhava*) of the group of principles (*tattva-grāma*) established by the scripture of the Supreme Lord; it demonstrates that group of principles through reasoning, following them according to their true nature.
Connecting the sections on Knowledge (*jñāna*) and Action (*kriyā*) with the section on Revelation (*āgama*),
and concluding the refutation of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), he speaks in order to demonstrate the very nature of the *Śiva-tattva*:
(440) "Because even the eleven verses have a single meaning, the meaning of each individual verse is not [separate]."
It has been explained.

"In this way" means: because the relationship of cause and effect as stated in other philosophical systems (*paradarśana*) is not tenable, for that reason, by the principle already stated—that "this very [power] is action"—it is internal when sequential and external when non-sequential.
Since time consists of a sequence of prior and posterior moments, and action follows that sequence, it belongs only to the cognizer, the knower. Therefore,
because he is the knower, the reality of Śiva is the inseparable unity of knowledge and action within that knower.

The relationship of cause and effect as described in the systems of other schools, such as Buddhism— which is established as being insentient in nature and consisting of primary matter (*pradhāna*), atoms (*paramāṇu*), and so forth— is in no way tenable.
This is because [the former] exists as an internal sequence, whereas [the latter] exists externally as a sequential form.

Even though its ultimate nature is luminosity (*prakāśa-paramārtha*), that which exists as a body and as a self-nature (*svarūpa*)—a manifestation (*prakāśa*) whose internal and external forms are not [identical to] that [ultimate nature]—is designated as "action" (*kriyā*) because it projects the succession of time. It belongs to that which revolves within; its state of being perceivable by both types of sense organs is established.

According to the principle stated as "by the desire of someone," the causality of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) with respect to the universe and the fact that the universe is His effect— this very relation of cause and effect is designated as "action" (*kriyā*). Since He possesses the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), that action is a property belonging to the subject (*pramātṛ*) alone, because of His status as the agent (*kartṛtva*).
Since that [knowledge] is the very nature of that [subject], knowledge— which belongs to the subject consisting of the agent and the knower—
necessarily arises as a consequence of *vimarśa*, according to the stated principle that "the two activities of knowing and acting are mutually inseparable for the Lord.
Because they are mutually inseparable, knowledge follows upon *vimarśa*.
It is the form of knowledge and action inseparable from one another, which, through the medium of action,

is capable of sustaining within itself hundreds of thousands of cycles of emanation and withdrawal of the entire multitude of principles (tattvas) beginning with Sadāśiva and ending with Earth; yet it remains non-manifest, even in the absence of manifestation as "this-ness" (idantā).
For at the time of instruction, his state as the Supreme Lord is to be realized with one's whole being;

according to the stated principle, it is possible to avoid regarding him as an object of cognition (*prameyatā*). Thus, during the occasion of meditation, he appears in the form of the Guru, manifesting both as the one who instructs and as the object of meditation, while in reality [he remains the Supreme Lord].

It is said that this is the Śiva-tattva; therein, when [the individual] is thus separated from the Śiva-tattva, knowledge and action themselves constitute the Śakti-tattva, which occurs immediately after the Śiva-tattva.
"Thus constituted" means being inseparable from the powers of knowledge and action, neither of which is deficient or excessive relative to the other.
If the Śiva-tattva is non-different from the entire universe— extending from the yet-to-be-described Sadāśiva down to the earth (kṣiti)—

then what other principle could there be that is not distinct from that very Śiva-nature? When all principles from Sadāśiva down to the earth find their rest within the single Śiva-tattva, which is of the nature of consciousness, they possess no prior or posterior distinction.

How could there be a sequence? Because the principle of Śiva (śivatattva) is not subject to space and time; likewise, because the principles beginning with Sadāśiva and ending with Earth, when resting within the principle of Śiva, are non-different from it, and since they too are not subject to space and time due to that non-difference, how could the principle consist of a prior and posterior order?
There would be a sequence. It is indeed just so. Nevertheless, he says that a sequence occurs due to the sovereignty of the Śiva-principle:
(p. 344) "But what you have said is certainly true; nevertheless, there is a distinction," thus he demonstrates.

By the word "but" (kiṃtu): because of the predominance and slight expansion of the internal state consisting of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) toward the internal state of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), immediately after the principle of Śiva-Śakti, there is first the principle called Sadāśiva, which is *sāda*. Thus says the Śrī [Tantra].

The reality (tattva) called Sadāśiva is so named because it arises within that which is called "Being" (sādākhya). From the moment the manifestation of the universe—which is essentially Being—begins, there occurs the manifestation "I am this," and so forth; that is the manifestation. Such a manifestation is the cause of that reality, the Sādākhya-tattva.
Because it is the reality (bhūta), that principle is called Sādākhya. Furthermore, because it is the denotation (vācyatva) of Sādākhya— which is of the nature of the Sadāśiva-tattva—
that principle is also called Sādākhya or Sadāśiva, [being the ground] of the universe residing within it.
Because it is the cause of external existence, when the creative power (*kriyā-śakti*) within me— which consists of external existence— intensifies,
and because the creative power intensifies even from the cognitive power (*jñāna-śakti*), [the state] subsequent to the *Sadāśiva-tattva* is the *Īśvara-tattva*,
which is designated by the term "Lord" (*īśvara*) and is called Parameśvara. As for the *Īśvara-tattva*:
Although the principle of Īśvara is in reality non-different from the principle of Sadāśiva,
[the text] indicates the qualified object (viśeṣya) in the form of a differentiation;
for within the principle of Śiva, there is the realization of the entire universe— from Sadāśiva down to the earth— as "I" alone.

There is not even the possibility of [the universe] being its end. The principle of Śakti is not counted separately because it consists of the powers of knowledge and action inseparable from the principle of Śiva;
therefore, within the principle of Sadāśiva, it is connected to a single substratum in the form of "I" (aham). For this very reason...

Precisely because of this grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), through a cognition whose nature is coreferentiality— such as "I am this"— there occurs the perception of the universe, which is like a sprouting shoot, within the state of Sadāśiva; for while it is covered by the "I-ness" (*ahantā*) in the form of "I," there is the perception of the universe-related "this-ness" (*idantā*) as "I am this, thus."

The state of acting as a "kura" (sprout). Within the principle of the Lord (Īśvara-tattva), there occurs a cognition in the form of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) expressed as "I am this.
This is a cognition in which the "this"—which has sprouted forth—is covered by the "I-ness" of the universe, yet whose distinct "this-ness" remains clearly manifest.
Because it is undivided by space and time, the principle of Śiva (Śivatattva) is indeed one alone.

Nevertheless, even in its oneness, that very principle of Śiva is nothing but absolute freedom (svātantrya). Within its own self, in its innate form, it displays the differentiation of its own nature—extending from Sadāśiva down to the earth—in the manner of reflections. — Śiva.
The very manifoldness of reality as the universal self constitutes the sequence of space and time; according to the stated principle,

that this or that category of reality manifests the sequence of space through the manifoldness of the forms of the sequence of time— consisting of prior and posterior aspects— that space is composed of the manifoldness of forms.

Time consists of the variety of actions; the principle of Sadāśiva is distinct [from the preceding], and the principle of Īśvara is distinct from the principle of Sadāśiva— in this manner, spatial succession is precisely the variety of forms,
such as the principle of Sadāśiva immediately following the principle of Śiva, and the principle of Īśvara immediately following that.

Time consists of a sequence of prior and posterior moments and is composed of the diversity of actions. Consequently, within one's own self, there is a state consisting of the cognition "I" (*aham*), which—like a reflection—is distinct from its own nature; this state is internal and constitutes the innermost core of the Śiva-principle. (443) Of that [state]...

When there is an intensification of the state of knowledge (*jñāna-daśā*) through the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), and the preeminence of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) flashes forth— this being the nature of that which is called *sādākhya* (the "ever-existent")— that from which the universe, starting from that principle, is known as "existent" (*sat*), is the *sādākhya*. Furthermore:

"Sāda" is a synonym for Sadāśiva. It is appropriate that the reality which is the denotatum (*vācya*) of that [power] called Sāda—which is itself the nature of the Śiva-tattva and consists of the denoter (*vācaka*)—should be enumerated first in the sequence of the emanation of the universe; for even in the teachings, the Śiva-tattva alone is presented first as the Sadāśiva-tattva.

It is appropriate to first apprehend that reality called Sadāśiva in the form of the object of meditation (*dhyeya*) and so forth as it is taught; however, in the sequence of the emanation of the universe, at the time of instruction, it is the Śiva-tattva itself that first manifests in the form of the Sadāśiva-tattva. Following this come the Īśvara-tattva and the others.

In its form as *sādākhya*, that reality consists of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*); it is the state of swelling resulting from the predominance of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) over the universal external manifestation. It is the supreme lordly principle (*pārameśvara*), denoted by the term "Supreme Lord" (*parameśvara*). That which is called the *Īśvara-tattva* is the *Īśvara-tattva* of that *sādākhya*.
The subsequent manifestation of the appropriate [form] of that reality—this which is about to be described—is stated in its ultimate sense as follows:

the state (*bhāva*) of Sadāśiva is the *tattva* called Sādākhya; the state of Īśvara is the *tattva* called Aiśvara; and within the *Śivatattva*, there is the presiding subject (*adhiṣṭhātṛtā*) of that which has the form of the object to be presided over (*adhiṣṭheya*). The knower (*pramātṛ*)...

There is no arising of a group [of subjects] here. In the principle (tattva) of Sadāśiva, there is the presiding lord, the venerable Lord Sadāśiva-Bhaṭṭāraka; the group of Mantra-Maheśvaras as the subjects; and the principle called Sadāśiva, which consists of both and is that which is presided over—thus there are three divisions.

In the principle of Īśvara, the presiding deity is the venerable Lord Īśvara-bhaṭṭāraka, whose nature is that of the Mantreśvaras; the class of subjects (pramātṛvarga) is the form to be presided over. The principle known as the principle of Īśvara is that which is presided over by those who possess distinct forms as Mantramaheśvaras.

For the various groups of subjects who are distinct from one another, the nature of earth (*pṛthivī-rūpatva*), being itself a single entity, appears as divided according to the cause for their respective grouping. Likewise, the nature of water (*ap-rūpatva*) serves as the cause for the grouping of rivers, streams, oceans, and so forth, within their own category.
Even though it is itself non-existent, it appears divided into its own classes such as rivers, streams, oceans, and so forth.

(444) Having thus stated the illustration, he shows the illustrated point itself with the words "And therefore," etc.: the universe in the form of "this-ness" [appears] through the form of the "I," which is the sense of ego.

It is pure because it is capable of reflecting [the object]. Free from the impurities of the body and so forth, and consisting solely of consciousness, is the class of subjects known as the Great Lords of Mantras (mantramaheśvara).
At the initial creation of this universe, for this class of Great Lords of Mantras, for us— [p. 346]...
To all knowers known as *sakala*, that which is perceivable by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*),
presided over by the venerable Lord Sadāśiva,

and situated below itself— consisting for the most part of the impurity of meditation (*dhyānamala*) and being largely indistinct— is the principle of Īśvara and so forth, down to the earth (*kṣiti*).

The wheel of existence (*bhāvacakra*), which appears as a mere semblance of reality— just as a painting is when it has only just been unveiled— and which consists of a single conceptualization of indistinct parts and forms,
is [perceived] by him as being essentially like a reflection, due to its tendency toward dissolution and destruction even during the process of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*).

Because that group of subjects is contained within the mirror of its own self, it shines as if it were a reflection in the form of "I am this. For that group of consciousness called the Mantramaheśvaras, which resides in the level of Sadāśiva-tattva, it likewise shines as if it were a reflection in such a manner.

"Sad" (Being). Within the aggregate of existence, that which is the manifestation as "I" and "this"—namely, that specific state of consciousness (*cid-viśeṣatva*) or specific state of awareness (*bodha-viśeṣatva*)—is the reality called *Sādākhya*.
This belongs to one who resides in the *Īśvara-tattva*, presided over by the venerable Lord Īśvarabhaṭṭāraka.

For the group of subjects known as Mantreśvara, whose nature is consciousness, the wheel of existence (bhāvacakra) extending from Śuddhavidyā down to the earth has become manifest due to the predominance of the "I-ness" (*ahantā*) and "this-ness" (*idantā*) belonging to that group of subjects. The term "not-I" (*amadam*) refers to the previously mentioned group of subjects called Sakala.
And what exists as the circle of objective phenomena (bhāvacakra), such as jars, cloths, and so forth, which have reached the path of externalization?

This entire universe appears in the form of a reflection through the cognition "this is I," because the state of "this-ness" (idantā) rests within "I-ness" (ahantā). Within that category [of objects], while it is thus appearing in such a manner—

Regarding the phrase "likewise in the mass of existents (*bhāvarāśi*)," the manifestation as "this" and "I" is the *Īśvara-tattva*. Within that, the very reality (*tattva*) itself is designated by the names Sadāśiva and Īśvara; thus, the *Sadāśiva-tattva* and the *Īśvara-tattva* are spoken of, but the Lords (*bhaṭṭāraka*) Sadāśiva and Īśvara are not being referred to here. [This refers to] the class of subjects beginning with the Mantramaheśvaras.
When [the two] exist in the form of the object of meditation and the one to be worshipped, they are to be understood as the presiding deities,

the venerable Lords Sadāśiva and Īśvara (445), who are respectively equal to Brahmā and Viṣṇu, and distinct from Rudra. In that regard, because of the identity of name and form with their respective presiding deities, [they are called] Sadāśiva and Īśvara.
And one should not be deluded by the similarity of names;
nor should one be deluded into thinking that the venerable lords Sadāśiva and Īśvara are mentioned here [as the presiding deities].
Because they are of the same nature as the presiding deities of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, they should be understood as distinct from them in this way.

Because they possess the nature of presiding deities, these two—the *tattvas* of Sadāśiva and Īśvara—should be understood as distinct. By the words "Sadāśiva" and "Īśvara," the venerable lords (Bhaṭṭārakas) Sadāśiva and Īśvara are denoted. Similarly, why are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra not mentioned?

Thus they say: one should not be confused as if [the case] were the same for everyone. Therefore, just as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are not mentioned here, likewise Sadāśiva and Īśvara-Bhaṭṭāraka are also not mentioned; only the essential nature of the *tattva* itself has been stated.

Their form will be explained further on. In this regard, he also shows another designation for the two principles (*tattva*) known as Sadāśiva and Īśvara: the external unfolding (*unmeṣa*) of the principle called Īśvara is the name "the unfolding of that principle. That unfolding—

It is the cause for the manifestation of the universe outside [of itself]. The reality known as Sadāśiva is the "nimeṣa" (closing), which consists of the internalizing or withdrawing of the universe; it is given the name *nimeṣa* because through its *unmeṣa* (opening) and *nimeṣa* (closing), there is the emergence and dissolution of the world.

Thus, in this context, the principle of Īśvara alone is described. "Unmeṣaṇa" (opening) means the external manifestation of the universe. It is the state of that which exists internally as the nature of consciousness appearing externally in the form of "this-ness" (*idantā*); it is the opening. Since the arising of the universe occurs from this opening, the opening is the principle of Īśvara. "Nimeṣa" (closing), on the other hand, means...

The rendering of the universe indistinct is the "closing of the eyes" (*nimeṣa*), which is the state of Sadāśiva-tattva; for through this closing of the eyes, there is the immersion of this world of forms into the "I"—that is, the ego-sense (*ahaṃtā*)—which is dissolution. This is the principle known as Sadāśiva-Īśvara belonging to the Supreme Lord.

"Pure vibration (*śuddhaspanda*) belongs to the Immovable One" means that even when there is vibration in the form of objective awareness (*idantā-rūpa-bodha*), it does not abandon its own essential nature (*svasvarūpa*), which consists of the full subjectivity of "I-ness" (*pūrṇāhantā*). This is because, ultimately, for that pair of principles, there is no attainment of a form characterized by the emergence of "this-ness" (*aprarūḍhedantātmaka-rūpāpatti*).
"I am this, I am that, I am"—this sense of "I-ness" (ahantā) is the very limit [of consciousness], because it is there that [all things] find their rest.

It is pure vibration (śuddhaspanda), being free from the turbidity of Māyā. According to the etymological root-meaning (*dhātu-gati*) of the word *spadi*, which means "to move slightly," it is so called because its nature is to manifest as a slight movement; as it has been said: "Vibration (*spandana*)."
And there is not even the slightest movement; this alone is its "slightest form," namely, that although it is motionless, it manifests as the soul of the universe.

For the nature of Light does not deviate even in the least, yet it appears as if it were to deviate and as if it were endowed with a diversity of manifestations. This has already been stated previously in the passage beginning, "That is the very throbbing."
The entire collection of principles (tattvas), beginning with Sadāśiva and ending with the earth, are these very powers of the Supreme Lord.
As it has been said:
"Power and the possessor of power—these are declared to be the two fundamental categories."
"The entire universe is His power, while Maheśvara is the possessor of power.
Among these, one certain power is distinct from the others because it encompasses many powers; due to its being the innermost [aspect] of the Supreme Lord, it is different from the rest.
She is to be worshipped through her powers (*śakti*); just as the power consisting of "pot-ness" belonging to a pot—
which is inherent in it and serves as its specific qualifier— is itself worshipped by other powers,
so too is a certain power that encompasses a multitude of other powers.

The power of the Supreme Lord that resides in the jar—which is grounded solely in its own essential nature, exists as reality, and pertains to the jar—is independent of qualities such as hardness, height, or solidity belonging to that jar.
In this regard, it is said to be "distant" because it exists in the form of a universal presence, common to the existence of cloth and other things as well. (Ṭīkā p. 348)
In this context, the powers (*śakti*) consisting of the principles (*tattva*) beginning with Sadāśiva and Īśvara, which abide in the proximity of the Supreme Lord,
encompass within themselves the powers of the principles from Śuddhavidyā down to Earth situated below them;
because they manifest as "I am this" and "this is I," they are the Supreme Lord himself.

They become proximate. Because powers such as Māyā manifest with differentiation, they remain close to that which is established solely in its own essential nature; for they manifest as "this is this. (447)

Thus, the powers of closing (nimeṣa) and opening (unmeṣa) are themselves the principles of Sadāśiva and Īśvara; these very powers of closing and opening are the causes for the internalization and externalization of the universe within the principles of Sadāśiva and Īśvara. Furthermore, the presiding deities of those two principles are likewise designated by the names Sadāśiva and Īśvara.
The group of subjects (pramātṛvarga) residing within the two levels of reality, known as Mantra-Maheśvara and Mantreśvara, is likewise designated by those names.
Now, immediately following the state of Īśvara, there exists that which pertains to the two deities who preside over them.

Of those two, which consist of the nature of the governed (*adhiṣṭheya*), the *vidyā-tattva* is the cause, the presiding deity, and the sense-organ for the group of subjects known as the Mantra-Maheśvaras and Mantreśvaras— the form of the governed residing within that [category]— and it consists of the deities Sadāśiva and Īśvara who act as the presiders (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*).

Just as the group of sense organs such as the eyes constitutes the cause for the cognition "this is a jar," so too, for the cognitions "I am this" and "this is I," he states that the principle of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā-tattva*) serves as the sense organ for the presiding deities: "Pure Knowledge is both *sadvidyā* and *śuddhavidyā*; [it is expressed as] 'I am this' and 'this is I.'"

And he established the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the two cognitions. With respect to the previously mentioned reality of God (*īśvaratattva*), the reality of God is of such a nature; thus, both have one and the same substratum (*adhikaraṇa*). The state of that [shared substratum] is coreferentiality. That [he expressed].

The substrata for the cognitions of "I" and "this" belonging to the subject of impure knowledge (aśuddhavidyā) and māyā are two distinct substrata, each being separate. Among these, the body and so forth are the substratum for the cognition of "I," while the jar and so forth are the substratum for the cognition of "this. The cognition that apprehends these as two distinct substrata is impure knowledge (aśuddhavidyā).
"I am indeed the body and so forth," and "this is the jar and so forth"— thus,
the two cognitions of "I" and "this" each possess their own distinct natures.

He demonstrates this by showing that for the Supreme Lord, who is the light of the nature of consciousness, there is an absence of any contact with "objectivity" (*idantā*) within the pure Self alone.
Resting in pure consciousness alone.

That reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) which is characterized by the absence of "this-ness" (*idantā*), which is oriented toward one's own self rather than toward another, and which consists in resting within the light of one's own self in the form of a cognition that does not look outward toward "this-ness"—that is called "I" (*aham*). That reflective awareness which is not oriented toward anything other than itself [is the state where] what is distinct from it... (448)

That which is oriented toward the manifold is called "this" (*idam*). And this reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), though having the form of "this," ultimately rests once again within the nature of pure self-luminosity—the form of "I" (*ahantā*)—which serves as its own foundation and is not oriented toward anything else.
As it has been said:

(Ṭp. 349) "This" refers to that reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) which is [perceived as] distinct; thus it is said, and so forth. Among those, in the first reflective awareness of "I," there is the *Śiva-tattva*; in the second, the reflective awareness of "this," there is the state of a *Vidyeśvara*.
For those subjects who are mantras, the cognition "I am" is omniscient.

The cognition "this" occurs with respect to the conscious self—which is of the nature of the "doer of all" and so forth—and likewise with respect to the universe, the mass of objects of knowledge, which is distinct from that self; this is the view of both the Śaivas and the Naiyāyikas.
As he will state: "Just as for the dualists there is Īśvara, [so for us there is] Śiva."

Between the two venerable ones, Ananta and Bhaṭṭāraka, the cognition "I am this" is inferior to the cognition "this is I," because they share a single substratum. That reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) which is maintained with equal balance and parity— free from deficiency or excess— between "I" and "this is I," that is the reflective awareness [of the Supreme].

In due order, this occurs with respect to Lord Sadāśiva and the venerable Īśvara; although the state exists in both, what is the distinction between its turbid and non-turbid nature? There is a distinction made by its lack of clarity and its clarity. In the present context, these two are the cognitions "I" and "this."
The illusion regarding these two consists in their having separate substrates within the subject.

He demonstrates this very state of having separate substrates: the cognition "I" resides in the grasper in the form of the body and so forth, while the cognition "this" resides in objects such as jars that are distinct from oneself. By means of the negation of that [illusion],...

By means of the negation of separate substrates, there is a manifestation in a single substrate alone of both "I"-cognitions in the form of their connection; this is pure *vidyā*. That which consists of the manifestation of separate substrates residing in the limited subject (*pramātṛ*)—namely, impure *vidyā*—is other than that pure *vidyā*.

It is distinct. Therein, within the principle of Sadāśiva, that which is the locus of "I" in the form of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) causes the "this-portion" (*idamaṃśa*) to sprout within that locus of pure consciousness. Because that "this-portion" is not yet clearly manifest, it is the state of Sadāśiva. If one asks what that state is like, it is expressed as: "I am this," and "This is I."

When the substratum has become manifest through the reflective awareness of "this" (*idam*), and the reflective awareness of "I" (*aham*) is poured upon it, then there is the state of Lordship (*īśvaratā*) characterized by "this-I" (*idamaham*); such is the distinction between those two principles.
This Vidyā is the cause of the Lords Sadāśiva and Īśvara; for that reason [it is so called].

Because it is pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), he says this: for those who have reached the plane of the object of knowledge (*prameya-bhūmi*), precisely because these entities—beginning with *māyā* and ending with the earth (*kṣiti*)—are endowed with existence, they possess consciousness as their essence. Thus, from the observation of reality, that is, from the observation of the ultimate reality of consciousness (*cit-paramārtha*).
Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*).

That which is called "beholding" (*avalokana*) is manifestation; that very manifestation is awareness, and awareness itself is knowledge (*vidyā*), according to the reality of things as they are, in their ultimate form. Furthermore, it is the state of conforming to the reality of things.

Through knowledge (*vidyā*), there is non-deviation, conformity to the true nature of things, and the perception of the correspondence with reality; yet, even for that knowledge, there is a limited purity,
