and impure knowledge (*aśuddha-vidyā*) is the non-apprehension of an object as it truly is.

Of those things that have reached the state of being objects of knowledge (*prameya*)— that is, having become the objects of the sense faculties such as the eye— and which, precisely because they have attained the state of being objects of knowledge,
are endowed with their own appropriate reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) in the form "this."

For those things being reflected upon, the very essence is the reality consisting of the light of consciousness in the form of "I-ness" (ahantā). This light is "I" alone, not oriented toward another, because it lacks the light directed toward "this-ness" (idantā); thus, for these entities, it is of the nature of "I."

That which is the ultimate form— because the manifestation of "I am this" rests within that ultimate form, it has the nature of pure sensation (śuddhavedana), and the manifestation of "this is I" has the nature of pure knowledge (śuddhavidyā).
From the two deities, the presiding lords Sadāśiva and Īśvara,

the nature of the principles (tattva) of Sadāśiva and Īśvara is distinct because it is an object of cognition; although this was previously stated as "the Lord Sadāśiva and the Lord Īśvara," it is now [stated] according to the manifestation of the scriptures (āgama).
He shows it by another way:

because things do not appear as having the nature of "I" (*ahantā*) due to their lack of selfhood (*anātmatva*), there arises otherness, incompleteness, dependence on another, and the manifestation as "this" (*idam*). I...

Because it covers [all things] through its form, it is supreme fullness (*paratā-pūrṇatā*), which is independence from anything else and manifests as "I. In this regard, within the two principles consisting of Sadāśiva and Īśvara, that [state] is the "supreme-inferior" (*parāpara*) vision of entities; "that" refers to what is taught in the *Āgamas* as the nature of the mixture of "I-ness" (*ahaṃtā*) and "this-ness" (*idantā*).
The state of the higher and the lower (*parāparadaśā*): the "higher" (*para*) nature of entities is their fullness (*pūrṇatva*), which is independence from anything else, expressed as "I" (*aham*).
The "lower" (*apara*) nature is their incompleteness and dependence on another, expressed as "this" (*idam*). The state of "I" is the state of Śiva; the state of "this" is...
The states of the Mantra-kalā, Vijñānākala, Pralayākala, and Sakala exist here within the two principles of Sadāśiva and Īśvara;

they are designated as "para" (supreme) and "aparā" (non-supreme) because, respectively, they involve contact with both aspects— the "I" aspect and the "this" aspect— of objects whose forms range from indistinct to distinct.

Having stated the purport of the verse, [the author now describes] the two principles consisting of Sadāśiva and Īśvara, the class of subjects residing therein known as Mantramaheśvaras and Mantreśvaras,
and the two venerable lords (Bhaṭṭārakas), Sadāśiva and Īśvara, who are their presiding deities; [and finally] that which is the cause of these.

He explains the nature of each of these, including Śuddhavidyā, through their individual divisions: the state established in the objective portion consists of the essential nature of the *tattva*; that which has the nature of the object of knowledge consists of the essential nature of the *tattva* as its object;
and the quality of being the illuminator consists of the states of Mantramaheśvara and so forth, which are pure, beginning with Mantramaheśvara.

Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*) is that state of consciousness which, while common to all objects from Māyā down to the earth (*kṣiti*) as they are perceived by the subject, is nonetheless grounded in the pure subject. Just as the eyes and other senses, which constitute the causal basis for that class of subjects, possess their own true nature (*tattva*), so too does this [state].

Although [Sadāśiva and Īśvara] are the causes of the class of subjects known as Mantramaheśvaras and Mantreśvaras, they possess that same essential nature (svarūpatva) and preside over that class of subjects; thus, the state of being Sadāśiva and Īśvara Bhaṭṭāraka belongs to those residing in the region.
Just as a king is the presiding authority over his people, so it is here.

Regarding the phrase "of some": according to the view of the followers of the Āgama, in the expression "I am this, this is I," that which is the aspect of concealment (*ācchādaka*) is the manifestation of "this" (*idaṃ-prathā*), while the manifestation of "I" (*ahaṃ-prathā*) is the other aspect.

The primary *vidyā* is purity (*śuddhavidyā*). Others who follow the Āgamas maintain that this portion which is to be covered by "I-ness" (*ahantā*)—the covering of that portion—is what constitutes the primary [purity]. (451) This is it.

If pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), which consists primarily of the "portion" (*bhāga*) and is characterized by the manifestation of "this-ness" (*idantā*) that is to be concealed, were not predominant, then by what would the "this-portion" (*idamaṃśa*) be illumined?
The meaning is that the "this-portion" does not manifest because [pure knowledge] is predominantly the "I-portion" (*ahamaṃśa*).

Therefore, *śuddhavidyā* has this "this-ness" (*idam-aṃśa*) as its primary characteristic. In that regard, within the pure principles beginning with *śuddhavidyā* and ending with *Śiva*, which transcend *māyā*, *māyā* does not pervade them because of its absence. For if *māyā* were present, there would be the undesirable consequence of [the emergence of] sprouting even within the principles beginning with *śuddhividya*; thus, it is characterized primarily by the manifestation of "this-ness."

Māyā [is so called] because of its tendency toward the sprouting of māyā. For this very reason, since it is characterized by a predominance of the objective aspect (bhāga), this Māyā manifests "thisness" (idantā)—which is incapable of the sprouting of Śuddhavidyā—in a gross form that is incapable of sprouting. Therefore, for that reason...

And it is called "Vidyā" because of its pure manifestation; for Śuddhavidyā is so called because that which manifests as "this-ness" (idantā) is incapable of enduring separation from it, and thus possesses purity.
It is Vidyā because it is the manifestation of that very kind of "this-ness."
If it is asked, "Since this Śuddhavidyā is not yet fully developed and is like Māyā, is this not Mahāmāyā?", [the answer is] no, because even in the state beyond Māyā,
there is the suffering (raurava) arising from the manifestation of the aspect of "this-ness" (idantā).
By the teachers of the Sāra and other Āgamas, it is precisely Śuddhavidyā that is taught as Mahāmāyā.
This was already stated previously, in the commentary on the word "of Maheśvara" in the first verse of the first chapter:
"Even though they have crossed over Mahāmāyā, they have reached the pure [state]."

Regarding the phrase "of the pure mantra, its Lord, and the Great Lord": even for the subject who is all-creating and all-knowing, that cognition of difference among objects— which is the descent into the state of "this-ness" (idantā)— occurs solely through the power of Māyā, because of the reflective awareness of difference within the objective portion.

It is incomparable to the power of *māyā*. Not only is it not *māyā* alone— because there is no error (*viparyāsa*) in the aspect of the knower whose nature is pure consciousness (such as the errors "I am fat" or "I am thin")— but other followers of the Āgamas maintain that such a state is indeed *śuddhavidyā*.

The Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvaras), beginning with Ananta, who are the subjects of mantra, consider even their own sense of differentiation to be Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā). In the same way, when the subject of Māyā— consisting of the void, the vital breath, and the body— is not yet manifest, [one remains] in the pure consciousness (cinmātra).

Thus, while all entities are of the nature of pure consciousness because they manifest as the agent [of cognition], that supreme Lordly freedom— which consists in the manifestation of duality through the conceit "this is insentient" due to their being perceived as having an insentient form— is Pure Knowledge (Śuddhavidyā); it is equal to the power of Māyā by means of the power of Māyā itself.

If one asks how this is so: because differentiation is manifested in the objective aspect (*vedyabhāga*), it is not merely *māyā* alone. This is because in the subjective aspect (*grāhakabhāga*) of the Self, which is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), there is no occurrence of such errors as "I am fat" or "I am thin," by virtue of which [the powers] Ananta and the others function.

It is just like that; for those Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvaras), having grasped the state of "I" within pure consciousness alone—which is free from the stains of the individual soul (āṇava) and other impurities—perceive the object of knowledge as distinct from themselves. However, the subject under the influence of Māyā, having grasped the body and so forth as the reality of the "I," perceives objects such as jars as being distinct [from himself].

The distinction is that he perceives the object of knowledge (*vedya*). For the Śaivas and Naiyāyikas, although the Lord (*īśvara*) is omniscient and the creator of all, he perceives the universe as non-different from himself; the same applies to the Vidyeśvaras.
Therefore, for the dualists, the lordship of the Lord is ultimately restricted to the Vidyeśvaras alone. Thus...

Because, unlike Śiva, Sadāśiva, and others, there is no manifestation of the entire universe as "I" within the self— which, though consisting of consciousness in part according to the manner described, is not yet full consciousness—
the sense of "I-ness" (ahantā) appears only in the subject (grāhaka), since it possesses the nature of consciousness only in part.

Although the universe, which is graspable as the form of ultimate reality, possesses the nature of "I-ness" (ahantā) through its being composed of consciousness, the power of the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras) that manifests it as "this-ness" (idantā) despite this state of inversion is Pure Knowledge (Śuddhavidyā).
For the Supreme Lord, however, this [manifestation] of an object remains unestablished.

The manifestation of difference, which is merely the manifestation of an incipient differentiation, constitutes the state of Sadāśiva and Īśvara; for the Blessed One, Paramaśiva— who transcends the categories (*tattva*) consisting of the division between the principles of Śiva and Śakti— even when there is the emergence of the "this" (*idamaṃśa*) in the form "I am this, this is I."
Because this "thisness" (idam-aṃśa) manifests as concealed by the "I-ness" (ahantā),

the very manifestation of fully developed duality therein constitutes the state of Sadāśiva and Īśvara. In that state, due to the lack of clarity in the manifestation of duality— which is the principle of Aśuddhavidyā— there is [the aforementioned condition].

The power of will (*icchā-śakti*) of Paramaśiva is active [in the stage] where this portion, characterized by the manifestation of non-emergent duality, exists within the nature of the *Īśvara-tattva*. When that [portion] becomes manifest,
the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) of Paramaśiva is active, [expressed as] "I am I," "this is indeed I," and "this is indeed this."
In the absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), when duality has become firmly established as distinct from oneself,
even though there is a reversal regarding the object of perception, and even though the essence of "I-ness" (*ahantā*) remains as the foundational part within the Self—
which is pure consciousness (*cinmātratā*)— the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) of Paramaśiva is nevertheless maintained within the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvaras*).
Because both the subject—the body and so forth—and the object—the jar and so forth—possess the nature of pure consciousness (cinmātra), the two do not manifest as "this-ness" (idantā);
however, when they do manifest as "this-ness," the power of Māyā of Paramaśiva becomes active. That power of Māyā operates upon the limited subjects (paśu-pramātṛ).

When the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of both the grasped and the grasper— which exist in the form previously described— have ceased, there occurs the manifestation of one's own true nature as supreme Śiva, which is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). In that manifestation of the ultimate reality,
the yogi exists among those subjects who are no longer bound by the fetters (*apaśu*), having been graced by the glance of a true guru.
In the case of the Jñānins and others, the power of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā-śakti*) of Paramaśiva is active.

This very operation of the power of knowledge, which was described in the passage beginning with "that which has not previously set in motion the subsequent [state]," exists even in the state of being a bound soul (*paśubhāva*).
"Of him" refers to that which is previously described as having the nature of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) consisting of eternity, omnipresence, and independence.

That which is illuminated by the glance of the Guru is the power of knowledge (*vidyā-śakti*) of Paramaśiva, whose essence is grace (*anugraha*). In the state of the bound soul (*paśu-bhāva*), it consists of the subject (*grāhaka*) and the object (*grāhya*).

Because of the bondage [imposed] by the single characteristic of *māyā*-delusion, even though there is unity in consciousness from the perspective of independent ultimate reality (*svatantra-paramārtha*),
a mutual differentiation arises such that, despite the oneness of all, there is a distinction between the seer, the seeing, and the seen;
thus the seen is one thing, the seer is another, and knowledge is yet another.
Even so, she is that [power] consisting of grace belonging to Paramaśiva; you are the Lord (*īśvara*) because you are endowed with the powers of knowledge and action (*jñāna-kriyā*).

For whoever is endowed with the sovereignty (*svātantrya*) of knowledge and action is a Lord. Just as those well-known in the Siddhānta Purāṇas are Lords by virtue of being endowed with the powers of knowledge and action, so too [are you].

Therefore, because he is endowed with the powers of knowledge and action, he is indeed the Lord (Īśvara). Thus, those who are skillful, whose hearts are confident through reasoning based on such analogies as lordship, fullness, omnipresence, and eternity, become successful, fulfilled, and complete; that [grace] is of the nature of favor (anugraha).
The power of the Supreme Lord (pārameśvarī-śakti), which is the power of knowledge (vidyā-śakti), by means of the force of reasoning that sets worldly activity in motion,

illuminates that sovereignty which has been described as existing within the self— namely, the sovereignty consisting of eternity and so forth. It is by virtue of this, and by virtue of what has been stated, that "some" [say this].

Those fortunate ones who have been graced by the side-glance of the Guru and are in their final birth, having observed the logical arguments that establish [the soul's] eternality and so forth, and whose hearts are confident in those arguments, become accomplished, fulfilled, and complete. That supreme power of the Lord, which consists of grace, is the power of knowledge (*vidyā-śakti*). As it has been said:

As previously stated: this final fifth specific activity of the Supreme Lord (pārameśvara-kṛtya-viśeṣa), characterized by grace (anugraha-lakṣaṇa), brings about the supreme human goal (parapuruṣārtha), because ultimate liberation (paramārtha-mokṣa) is dependent upon it. "This very one" refers to the sixfold object consisting of the definition of the power of knowledge (vidyā-śakti).

The position seen in the *Śrītrikasāra* and other scriptures is stated here to win over the heart of the author of the Sūtra; for in this Sūtra, the word "another" (*anya*) is used in reference to one who maintains a different position.

Immediately after the principle of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā-tattva), the principle of Māyā is described according to the ascending order [of emanation]. He explains that very description as follows: "Furthermore, the power called Māyā is that which causes the concealment of His nature as sovereign lordship."

The distinction between Māyā and Vidyā is that the power of Vidyā, whose nature is sovereignty consisting of eternity and other attributes, reveals [the truth], whereas the power of Māyā conceals it. This applies to all subjects (*pramātṛ*) regarding those things—
earth and so forth— which serve as causes and are limbs of one's own self, which is essentially the Supreme Lord.

Regarding entities that are effects, such as jars, cloths, and so forth, these elements like earth and others [are distinct from me], and likewise, jars and so forth are distinct from me; similarly, within the class of subjects, Caitra is distinct from Maitra, and so on, both among subjects and among objects like jars and cloths. Thus it is with respect to jars, cloths, earth, and the rest.

The power of Māyā is that which effects the manifestation of duality among the various classes of subjects: "I am asleep," "I am in a swoon" [in the void]; "I am happy," "I am miserable" [in the intellect];
"I am awake," "I am hungry," "I am thirsty" [in the vital breath]; and "I am indeed a god or the like" [when rooted in the insentient due to its inertness].

In that very state, she bestows the conceit of subjectivity (*pramātṛtābhimāna*) which has taken root; though consisting of consciousness, she manifests even objective entities (*bhāva*) as objects of knowledge (*prameya*) through this form of differentiation, by means of the conceit of "I" with respect to everything that is non-self,
and by means of the conceit of selfhood with respect to the body and so forth.

Although the nature of the jar and other objects is essentially the Self because they are manifest, that power of Māyā conceals or covers their own true, ultimate nature; this concealment is what is described in the Āgamas as one of the fivefold cosmic acts (pañcakṛtya), such as creation and so forth. This concealment, which [concerns] whom—
Because it occurs within the interval between [the other stages], the fourth activity, which consists of occasional dissolution (*vilaya*), is to be honored.
Even for one who has been initiated, there is no activity consisting of dissolution such as the censuring of the Guru, the mantra, and so forth. As it has been said:
But someone who, by the will of the Lord, even though not fully confident in his mind,
should practice while censuring [the path], is said to be one whose nature is concealed.
The sin arising from the provocation of a Vidyācārya or others by one who reviles the Great Mantra shall always cast that person into a place of terrible torment.
This concealment (*tirodhāna*) is innate; it is precisely the veiling of one's own nature, the form of obscuration belonging to the Supreme Lord, a covering even of that which is manifesting.
It expands upon this concealment as the effect of *māyā*, pertaining to both the subject (*grāhaka*) and the object (*grāhya*).

Because it is manifest, even though consciousness is the ultimate reality, there occurs within one's own self— which consists of pure awareness— the superimposition of the ego-identification with the body, such as "I am a god" and so forth,

and likewise the superimposition of "this is a jar" and so forth upon objects distinct from oneself. (456) Thus, even while remaining in the self composed of consciousness, one identifies with the gross body and attributes objectivity to external things like jars.

Because it is manifest, even though [the object] is one's own self, there is the superimposition of "this-ness" (idantā) as distinct from one's own self; thus, while difference appears within the non-dual, single-flavored, uninterrupted light— which is the nature of both [subject and object] reversals—
there is the negation of non-self, which is like space, in the void of deep sleep, in the dissolution of the universe.

In meditative absorption (samādhi), one's own form, which is like space, appears as the Self in the form "I am emptiness. By the word "or" (vā), the vital breath (prāṇa) is implied in the middle. In the states of inhaling and exhaling, there is the vital breath resembling air, [experienced] as "I am inhaling" or "I am exhaling."

In the desire to devour among the stationary and moving beings, or in the blazing of anger and so forth, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), augmented by fire (*tejas*), perceives itself as "I" with the nature of the self (*ātman*). In internal states such as reflection, one perceives: "I know," "I am happy," or "I am miserable. Thus [the self] exists in various conditions.
The intellect (*buddhi*), which is like very clear water and possesses the reflection of the object of knowledge, becomes attached to the notion of "I.

In states such as "I am thin" or "I am fat," it becomes attached to the self-identity of what is called the body—which consists primarily of earth—as being "I. Furthermore, by the inclusion of [the other elements],...
Even regarding sons, wealth, wives, and so forth, which are themselves immeasurable, the boundlessness of attachment to their end is indicated;
thus, when the intellect and body have become as if void, they enter into the state of being a mother toward those very objects of perception— sons, wealth, wives, and the like— thinking,
"This son is mine," "These wives are mine," "This is mine."

"Wealth"— thus, regarding all these objects of knowledge such as sons, wealth, wives, and so forth, when they are perceived as being the Self (*ātman*), the power of *māyā* unfolds; by this, the unimpeded accomplishment of even difficult tasks is attributed to the power of *māyā*, which is the very freedom (*svātantrya*) of the Supreme Lord.

The capacity has been demonstrated. In deep sleep characterized by a short duration of manifestation, such as that of a jar or the body, the universe arises; likewise, in deep sleep characterized by a long duration of manifestation, which takes the form of the Great Deep Sleep (mahāsuṣupti), the universe arises; however, in dissolution, which is of the nature of the Great Deep Sleep, the universe of objects of knowledge does not exist.
Having reached the culmination of the meditation on emptiness, even the thought "I am not" ceases to exist.
Immediately thereafter, during the state of inhalation and exhalation, one does not perceive the self as being merely breath— like the wind— with the notion "I am inhaling" or "I am exhaling."

Furthermore, when there is an intense hunger leading to the desire to devour both moving and stationary beings, or during such states as the blazing of anger, the vital breath (prāṇa) itself— augmented by the fire-natured energy (tejas) of Vaiśvānara and intent on withdrawal—
is not perceived as the Self, because it serves merely as a reflection of the object of knowledge.
Like a vessel of clear water, I perceive within myself the entire collection of objects such as jars and the like;
for this very reason, I think "I am happy" or "I am miserable" during various states such as the contemplation of gain or loss.
Because that cognizable object—such as the jar or the cloth—is reflected therein, it is the intellect (*buddhi*) itself, which is like clear water, that is "I."

Thus one becomes attached. In states such as "I am thin" or "I am fat," it is the body alone—which serves as the foundational wall for the cognizer from the notion of emptiness up to the cognition of the self—that appears as the self, as "I.
As it has been said:
That which is called the life-force of the cognition of emptiness is created and destroyed;
its stability is merely relative to the body, but not in reality.

Thus, in the *Tantrapaṭadhānikā*, because everything beginning with emptiness (*śūnya*) is manifest, and because it was previously non-existent by its very nature, consciousness alone— appearing in those various forms— is, in ultimate reality, nothing but the essence of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), whose nature is "I-ness" (*ahantā*); such is the universe as one's own self-consciousness.
Māyā itself is indeed of the nature of the non-conscious (acid-rūpā); that which is manifested by it is manifested precisely as non-conscious,

and being manifested precisely as "this" (idantayā), even an entity such as "void" (śūnya) and so forth— which is a state of non-manifestation and "this-ness"— is [perceived] through Māyā as having the nature of consciousness in the form of "I" (aham).

The locus of attachment has been established. Thus, the accomplishment of such an inherently difficult task is the manifestation of the power of the Supreme Lord’s *māyā*, which takes the form of non-obstruction; this is the capacity that unfolds. By the word "or" (*vā*) found in the aphorism, [it refers to] those things related to the subject (*pramātṛ*).
It is indicated that even objects of knowledge, such as sons, wealth, wives, and so forth, are the objects of an incalculable attachment to the notion of "I" (ahaṃtā).
That which begins with the void (śūnya) is non-self (anātman) because it is insentient (acid-rūpa); yet this [non-self] is perceived as "one who is happy," "one who is thirsty," and so on.

(458) "I am devoid of all forms"— by this [realization], the state of "this-ness" (*idantā*) which manifests for transmigrating beings as the conceit of "I" (*ahaṃbhāva*) disappears, because, according to the principle to be explained, it lacks the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpatva*). For this very reason, since it is perceived in the form of "this-ness" like a jar or other objects, the void (*śūnya*) and so forth are not of the nature of the Self.
Therefore, those who are adhered to as the self in the form of "I" are indeed of the nature of consciousness; thus,

the subject (pramātṛ) consisting of Śūnya and the rest, once it has abandoned attributes such as limited agency and so forth, would become characterized solely by the pure sovereignty of omniscience and omnipotence.

Anticipating this objection, he says: regarding the object of knowledge (*prameya*), which possesses a distinction from itself and is therefore of the nature of "this-ness" (*idantā*), the subject (*pramātā*)—the cognizer who begins with the void (*śūnya*) and so forth—transforms the mental image (*pratimā*) of the jar and other objects, thinking, "This is a jar," "I am distinct from this," or "I am distinct from Caitra and others. Thus, the subject himself, like the jar and other objects, [is characterized by duality].

The object of knowledge (*meyam*), being existent, is enveloped by the pentad beginning with time (*kāla*); this is what constitutes its status as an object of knowledge—namely, its being enveloped by the pentad beginning with time. This applies even to the cognizable object that accompanies its master [the subject] in the body and so forth, such as when one thinks: "I who was thin am now fat, and I shall become fat."
At that very time, there was also a jar; [one says] "now the jar exists" and "the jar will exist.

Thus, both the body and so forth, as well as the jar and so forth, are enveloped by time, by *vidyā* in the form of limited knowledge (*kiñcijjñatva*), and by *kalā* in the form of limited agency (*kiñcitkartṛtva*). In this regard, there is attachment (*rāga*) in the sense of being colored by it, and even therein, precisely here.

By the principle that "the Red One is not elsewhere," and by being encircled by what is contradictory to eternality, omniscience, universal agency, fullness, and pervasiveness, the doubt as to who could be the one woven lengthwise and crosswise— possessing the attributes of omniscience and pure sovereignty— is cast far away.

He follows up on the aforementioned doubt by means of an objection: "Even though it is devoid of the nature of 'I', if the void and so forth, while being clung to as 'I', were to abandon its status as an object of cognition for itself, then at that time there would be a connection with the attribute of sovereignty."

If [the subject] were to abandon the state of being an object—as in "I am fat" and so forth—then alas, even blue and other objects would appear to the knower as distinct from that very knower; thus, the particle *anavah* indicates the non-existence of the intended object [of such a distinction]. (459) This [subject], beginning with the void, is the knower (*pramātā*).

The meaning is that even while being attached to the notion of "I," one does not abandon the state of being an object of knowledge (*meyatā*). He demonstrates this very point: from the void (*śūnya*) up to the subject (*pramātā*), as stated in the passage "in the void" and "in the intellect," for as long as [the subject] regards the object of knowledge (*prameya*)—such as blue and so forth—as distinct from his own self...

Like a jar or other objects, it is itself indeed characterized by difference; for, because it is delimited precisely by being cognized as "this" or "of such a nature," it is limited. Such a thing possesses a distinction established from another object of cognition that is of the form "this" or "of such a nature."

Because both are mutually distinct from one another. In this way, the cognizer Caitra is established as being distinct from the cognizer Maitra and so forth, as well as from objects such as a jar. For this very reason, the cognizer, whose nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*), does not become non-distinct from the category of objects of cognition (*prameya*)—such as a jar—nor from the cognizer himself.

Because [the Self] is full, the limitation—which is precisely the finitude—of the state of "I" (ahambhāva) regarding emptiness and so forth, namely the pentad beginning with time, first demonstrates its being enveloped by time; thus he says: "For by that...
Time, weaving together the non-sequential succession of "before" and "after," [resides] in the subject as the "I."
Thinking, "I was thin, now I am fat, and I shall become even fatter," the subject (pramātṛ), manifesting itself by projecting the sequence of time consisting of past and future,
extends accordingly even toward the object of knowledge (prameya) associated with that [body].
He describes that very process of its expansion with the words, "I who am fat," and so forth.

Thus, while [the consciousness] unfolds within itself and its own object, this subject does not perceive himself and that object through the expansion of time as: "I who was thin... [but rather as "I who am fat"].

Thinking, "I shall become even more gross than I am in this grossly coiled state," he perceives his own self—which consists of consciousness—as having the form of an insentient body; and though it is devoid of succession, he perceives it as if it possessed succession.

Consequently, even with respect to the object of knowledge moving within that body, such as a jar, there arises the notion of its being past, present, or future, in the form of "it was," "it is," or "it will be."
The meaning is that while the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) illuminates the object of cognition (*prameya*), time, though eternally existent, renders the cognizer non-eternal.
(460) Now, it describes the operation of *vidyā* [the power of knowledge]: [it acts] upon the insentient, beginning with the void (*śūnya*).

For a cognizer such as Caitra or Maitra, *vidyā*—which consists in the manifestation of limited knowledge (*kiñcijjñatva*)—reveals the multitude of entities, such as blue or pleasure, reflected upon the mirror of that cognizer’s intellect (*buddhi*).
This is experienced through the external and internal organs as "this is blue" or "this is pleasure. (p. 358)

When it manifests an entity consisting merely of blue, pleasure, and so forth, it renders even an omniscient cognizer as if he were a knower of only a little; at that time, the *kalā* (power), which consists in the reinforcement of the state of being a limited agent, brings about effects such as jars and cloths, thereby making even an omniscient cognizer appear as if he were a limited agent.
Regarding the thought, "I know something" and "I do something," although the objects of these acts—

namely, the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) and the effect to be produced (*kārya*)— are equally "something" (*kiñcit*), why is it that only this particular form of "something" becomes the object of those two acts, knowledge and action? In this regard, concerning that which takes the form of "something":
Regarding the two effects, knowledge and action, attachment— which takes the form of clinging toward the subject (pramātṛ) in the body and so forth,

and toward objects of knowledge (prameya) such as jars— consists primarily of the attribution of excellence through the intensification of regard for those objects; first, it manifests by withdrawing from the body and so forth.

Observe that it is passion (*rāga*) that operates upon the object. Therefore, this "passion-ness" (*rāgatva*) does not belong to the quality (*dharma*) of the intellect (*buddhi*). Rather, it is the gross passion residing in the intellect itself—this very state of passion—which arose previously during the time of youth for an old man, [and which now manifests] as a passion toward a young woman residing in the intellect.
It would not exist; however, the essence of passion (*rāgatattva*) is always present.

Within the eightfold nature of the intellect (*buddhi*), which consists of the qualities of knowledge, detachment, and sovereignty, the essence of passion is observed in the form of thoughts such as, "I am performing merit," or "I am performing demerit."
Attachment (*rāga*), which consists of an intense clinging to the eightfold [categories] beginning with *dharma* and *adharma*, is indeed perceived;

thus, the reality of attachment renders the subject (*pramātṛ*), though in essence complete, incomplete. In this very matter, why does this clinging occur here and not elsewhere? This principle of non-uniform clinging is the function of necessity (*niyati*).

"Restricted" (*niyamita*) means that because of *niyati* (the principle of necessity), due to the absence of fullness everywhere, [the subject] is restricted to only one object; thus, *niyati* renders the pervading cognizer non-pervasive, making him contracted to only one point.
In this way, being enveloped by time and the other principles, and having his entire sovereignty—such as eternity and so forth—stolen away by *māyā*, [he becomes a limited subject].

Afterward, having first withdrawn all sovereignty, it was subsequently bestowed [back]; thus, that which was formerly the entirety of sovereignty belonging to omniscience becomes now merely a fragment consisting of limited knowledge and so forth. Being such, this cognizer shines forth from here as will be described immediately below.

He explains that very point: "At this time now. At this time now, by means of limited ignorance (*tanavidyā*), he perceives himself as knowing only this little; by means of *kalā*, he performs only this little;
by means of *rāga*, he is attached to this [world] alone; and by means of *niyati*, he reflects upon this alone and not anything else.

"Thus am I. This cognizer appears enveloped by the pentad beginning with Time. Although one may be attached to something else, it is by Niyati (the power of necessity) that one is made to act upon another; thus, these factors beginning with Time also possess distinct objects. By this [process], there arises the autonomy of this body and so forth.

The absolute sovereignty of the Supreme Lord alone has been demonstrated. Furthermore, these factors—time and the rest—adhere solely to the subject (*pramātṛ*) according to the sequence already described, such as: "I am contemporary," "I am a knower of little," "I am an agent of little," "I am attached here," or "I am attached there and also right here. Thus, they are bound to the subject.
That which appears as "it shines" is his *māyā*, whose nature is the power of the subject (*pramātṛ-śakti*).

These [objects], which do not deviate from that [power], are indeed distinct from the subject; they do not constitute a single uniform category for all subjects, but rather remain distinct for each individual subject.
They do not constitute a single uniform category for all subjects, but rather remain distinct for each individual subject.

Even though they differ according to each individual subject (*pramātṛ*), time and the other categories would become one for all subjects in such cases as the viewing of actors or wrestlers. It has been stated more than once in passages such as "of the Lord abiding in Himself" (*svāminaścātmasaṃsthasya*) that the *kalās* and so forth have no innate life apart from the will of the Lord. This...

And it will be stated here that the cognizer is blinded by *māyā*. Regarding what was said in the previous verse— that when the object of cognition is distinct from oneself, one is called a "cognizer" (*pramātā*)—
it shows there that the object of cognition is indeed distinct from the cognizer.

The object of knowledge (*prameya*) consists of twenty-three types, beginning with earth and ending with sound, which are of the nature of both gross and subtle, and take the form of effects; it also includes that which is of the nature of external organs and that which is of the nature of instruments, all of which exist in the form of cause and effect.
That which is undivided from effects and causes, being itself one, and which is the root cause of these— the *pradhāna*—
all that is the object of knowledge (*meyam*).
That which consists of the nature of effects and causes, comprising twenty-three forms, is the entirety of all that is produced.

And because the cause consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion, that reality of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) which exists in an undifferentiated form with them—all that is the object of knowledge (*meyam*); such is the connection [of the text]. [This applies] to yogins who have transcended *māyā*, to those knowers (*pramātṛ*) of mantra, and to those lords of mantra who are of the nature of Īśvara.

And [the worship] of the Mantramaheśvaras, the Mothers, the five elements beginning with earth, the five subtle elements (tanmātras) beginning with smell, the five organs of action beginning with the organ of generation and ending with speech, the five organs of knowledge beginning with the sense of smell and ending with the ear, and the mind and so forth.

Because this entire triad of internal organs, ending with the intellect (*buddhi*), possesses the capacity for mastery through making everything its object, all that is knowable— even though it is not directly perceived by those subjects who are under the influence of *māyā*— is nonetheless [established] through the path of inference and the path of scripture, beginning with earth and the other elements.
Regarding the phrase "only the object of knowledge" (*prameyam eva*): that which is the object of knowledge consists of the principles beginning with earth and ending with *prakṛti*.

Although time, limited knowledge, limited agency, attachment, and necessity were mentioned in the previous verse, they are included within those [twenty-four] principles; this is because the present discussion defines the objects of knowledge as distinct from Māyā and the subject (*pramātṛ*).

At this juncture, even categories such as Time (Kāla) and others, though they are objects of knowledge (*prameya*), are not counted here as objects of knowledge; for in reality, the subject (*pramātṛ*) situated within the principles from Māyā down to Earth (*kṣiti*) is himself the object of knowledge. Yet, although that subject of Māyā is himself an object of knowledge, he [perceives] an object of knowledge distinct from himself.

Although it is being made an object of knowledge (*prameya*) by the Lord of Lords (*parameśvara*) through His power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*), which is of the nature of *māyā*, it is here said to have its state as an object of knowledge concealed (*ācchādita-prameyatāka*). Among the twenty-three principles (*tattva*) from Earth up to the Intellect (*buddhi*), what is the effect (*kārya*) and what is the cause (*kāraṇa*)? (p. 360) What...?
Having raised the question at the end [of the previous section] as to "and what is the cause," he says: "In this [system], within the twenty-three [principles],

there is the series of external organs, the series of internal organs, the thirteenfold knowledge, and the group of effects— divided by their gross and subtle natures— which consists of ten [categories] such as Māyā and the subject."
First, regarding the purpose of yoga in the form of the instruments (*karaṇa*), there is first the enumeration of the instruments.

They are thirteen. Among those instruments, in the order of descent, first is the intellect (*buddhi*), which consists of the mere universal form of determination (*adhyavasāya*)—beginning with earth and ending with sound. Determination is...
According to the liberated doctrine that "the means of cognition (*sādhana*) is the intellect (*buddhi*)," because it itself consists of the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of objects by the cognizer,
the intellect— which comprises the twenty-three principles— is essentially the universal form of whatever determination exists for the cognizer regarding whichever object it may be.

By this, the reality of the intellect (*buddhi*) as being of the nature of the pervasive [Self] is shown. According to the principle stated that "egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) is the means for the conceit (*abhimāna*) that 'this is mine' or 'this is not mine,'" because it is the means for such conceit, for whichever cognizer (*pramātṛ*), in whichever object to be grasped (*grāhya-viṣaya*), there arises the thought: "I am the grasper; this is mine."

The conceit that "this earth and so forth are to be grasped, they are mine"— this illusory conceit (*māyīya-abhimāna*) is the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) whose nature consists solely in the generality of such conceits.
According to the stated principle that "the mind is the instrument of resolve and doubt," it constitutes the resolve extending from the earth up to the word.

In all undertakings, the mind (*manas*)— which is the cause of volition (*saṃkalpa*), characterized by a general nature that presides over all agents of action, thinking "I do this" and "I do not do this"— these three constitute the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) of the knower. Within it, the objects ranging from earth to sound, both gross and subtle, are contained.

The internal organ [consists of] "I do" and so forth; the sense organs are those which serve as instruments for the intellect (*buddhi*), which is of the nature of knowledge and consists of the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of objects from sound down to earth.
Among these, the auditory organ is that which serves as an instrument for the knowledge consisting of the determination of sound.

The tactile sense organ is useful for cognition in the form of the determination of touch, and so forth; wherever there is cognition in the form of the determination of sound, there the auditory sense organ is useful. Thus, the nature of the auditory sense organ is pervasive in this manner, and so it is for all the sense organs in sequence.
The pervasive form of reality is to be understood as follows:
as it has been said—the ears and skin are the instruments for the sequential apprehension of the objects consisting of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. (464) [The nose, tongue, and eyes follow.]

The five sensory organs—eye, tongue, and nose—are useful for the actions consisting of speaking, grasping, moving, excreting, and sexual pleasure; these range from the organ of speech down to the organ of smell.
He demonstrates that the very utility of the organs lies in their function as instruments of action: "In the same way..."

By the words beginning with "hi," [it is meant that] abandonment and grasping—these two, namely abandonment and grasping, which constitute the activity of the external senses regarding their respective objects—involves the engagement of the instruments (karaṇas) in sequence: the anus, the hand, and the foot, for both abandonment and grasping. [This applies] to each of these, such as the organ of the feet.

"Relinquishment of the place" (*deśatyāga*)— both of these exist. By whichever sense organ this pair of relinquishments is performed within the internal subject who is the vital breath (*prāṇapramātṛ*), that sense organ,
starting from the *mūlādhāra* up to the extension ending at the tongue, undergoes a single expansion in the nature of its own unfolding.

By leaving one place and taking up another, there exist two actions consisting of relinquishment and grasping. Through the subsiding of the agitation caused by the activity consisting of relinquishment and grasping, the organ of generation (*upasthendriya*)— which is suitable for the action of resting in the nature of bliss— is distinguished from the class of the organs of cognition (*jñānendriya*).

The specific nature of the group of organs of action is as follows: the organs of action consist of the specific transformations of *tāmasa-ahaṃkāra* and pervade the entire body. Because they are pervasive, one whose hand has been severed still takes up [objects] with his arms; he does not take them with the hand alone. One whose foot has been severed [still moves] by means of his knees alone.

It moves; however, because it is the locus for obtaining conventional usage such as "grasping" and so forth, though indistinct and complete, it is called the substratum in the form of five fingers. Thus, the thirteen instruments beginning with the intellect (*buddhi*) and ending with the individual self (*upastha*), as well as the instruments beginning with the ear, are like the universals *gotva* (cowness) and *ghaṭatva* (potness).

Because they are interwoven within the auditory and other senses belonging to all subjects from Śiva down to the Sakala, these principles (tattvas) are indeed of a generic nature. Although these senses, such as the ear and others, function as effects with respect to the supreme subject, they are not designated as "effects" in their specific, individual capacity; it is precisely these [senses] that [are so designated].

The designation is by way of being the cause; however, no other group of agents or group of effects possesses the status of being the cause. Here, in the order of ascent, the mention of earth and the other elements while omitting smell and the rest is because the group of smell and the rest is included within earth and the others; [these refer to] gross effects.
The five elements beginning with earth are the subtle forms (*sūkṣmarūpa*) of those [gross] elements, earth and so forth, in their respective order:
smell, taste, form, touch, and sound. Space has sound as its sole quality;
O Mother, you are Space because it pervades that which has sound as its sole quality.
O Supreme One, that reality consisting of sound and touch, possessing those qualities, is the creator of the manifestations.
Vāyu, existing in the form of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth, is considered your prakṛti;
it is that which constitutes the structural basis for sound, touch, and form, as well as their respective qualities.
But the transformation of fire, which has your form, O Supreme One, performs effects such as cooking and so forth.
He who [is present] in Śiva together with sound, touch, and form, as well as through the nature of taste;
From that alone the waters arise; they have you as their source of containment, and they are characterized by the four qualities beginning with sound, as well as by smell.
The earth would be its effect, and you are said to be that very earth.

"Thus, by means of each single quality. Here, since it is not useful for the mere enumeration of the principles (*tattva*), first [the gross elements] such as earth and so forth—which are divided as earth, water, fire, air, and ether—are presented; they are the inferential indicators and revealers of the undifferentiated [qualities] such as smell.

The gross pentad has been shown. In that enumeration of the principles (*tattva*), the elements beginning with earth and ending with sound (*śabda*) are mixed. Furthermore, particular objects such as jars and cloths, having become specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), are projected by and grasped through the organs of action, such as speech and the rest.

The manifestations of earth and the other elements proceed in this sequence: they are first perceived by the sense organs such as hearing; they are conceptualized by the mind (*manas*); they are grasped as "this is mine" by the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*); they are determined by the intellect (*buddhi*); they are differentiated by impure knowledge (*aśuddhavidyā*); and they are colored by the four [tattvas] beginning with *kalā*.
The intended meaning is that [the universe] rests within the cognizer (*pramātṛ*). The sense is that all principles (*tattvas*) rest within the cognizer.

And this is stated in those primary works on the enumeration of principles—namely, the *Śrī Tantrāloka*, the *Trikasāra*, and so forth—which primarily focus on defining each respective cognizer for each respective principle.
Since it has already been determined, we have not elaborated here on what is of no use for the mere enumeration of the principles (*tattva*).
(466) Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the *Śrīpratyabhijñāsūtravimarśinī*, the commentary.
Now begins the fourteenth chapter.

In the first chapter of this section on the scriptures (*āgama*), the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) consisting of the principles (*tattva*) from Śiva down to the earth were defined. By this second chapter, [the principles] from Māyā down to the earth...

The exposition of the seven subjects of cognition, beginning with the limited cognizer (*pramātṛ*) and ending with Śiva; the demonstration of the mutual gradations among those states of subjectivity; the exposition of the three impurities (*mala*), beginning with the *āṇava* and so forth; the exposition of the three objects of cognition (*meya*);
and [the description] of transmigrating beings according to the distinctions arising from the manifestation and concealment of those three impurities.

The investigation of bondage and liberation is undertaken, as well as the exposition of the five states consisting of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, the fourth (turya), and that which transcends the fourth (turyātīta), which are composed of the vital breaths—prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna.
Regarding the term "unfragmented" (akhaṇḍita): it refers to that which is omniscient, the agent of all, eternally manifest, and characterized by omnipresence.

Even when the nature of the mass of consciousness and bliss is fragmented, there exists within oneself— in the indestructible, innate heart-center— the manifold conceptualization of subjects, which consists of the Sakala, Pralayākala, Vijñānākala, Mantra, Mantreśvara, and Mantramaheśvara, appearing diverse and mutually distinct within the circle of friends.

Because it performs the fivefold cosmic activity consisting of emanation, maintenance, withdrawal, suppression, and grace, that which manifests within the heart— the nature of the venerable Supreme Power (Śrīparāśakti) in the form of the Wheel—
though in ultimate reality non-different from one's own self, appears as mutually distinct, like cities, villages, and so forth reflected in a mirror.
We praise that Śiva, who manifests Himself as distinct from His own self.

Thus, when the aggregate of principles from Śiva down to the earth has been determined, although the principle of the subject (*pramātṛtattva*)— which is included within those respective principles— has not been explicitly mentioned, it is nevertheless set forth separately and in detail as the primary element. Therefore, having elaborated upon the principle of the subject alone, [the author explains] the essential nature of that principle of the subject.

Having demonstrated this in detail therein with the verses beginning with "This [power] is the motherhood" (467) and ending with "Vyāna is the supreme, whose essence is the universe," the chapter is introduced by twenty verses. In this [chapter], the nature of the qualified subject— the cognizer according to the Pratyabhijñā scripture, who has been purified by the glance of a true Guru— is [described].

Recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is taught. By the phrase "for thus" (*tathā hi*), through the means of defining the distinction between the reality of the subject (*pramātṛ-tattva*) and what is to be abandoned or accepted, both of those—the reality of the subject which is my own nature and the recognition of that very nature as being essentially the Lord (*īśvara*)—are presented in this [text] by way of the realization: "Therefore, I am indeed the Lord."

The scripture teaches this. That person to be instructed—the cognizer—through the medium of the scriptural teaching, comes to know what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted; having known the nature of the cognizer as his own essential being, he realizes both [the abandonable and the acceptable] as being his very own nature.
Entering into his own self, which is the nature of Śiva— the most supreme form to be attained— as non-different from it,

one becomes liberated even while living; thus, he who [realizes] his own self as having the nature of Śiva, characterized by the recognition of the defining marks of Śiva, because it is endowed with the powers of knowledge and action.

By entering into non-duality through the realization "I am that very Lord who is well-known from the Purāṇas, Āgamas, and other sources," one becomes liberated while still living; thus, by this verse, there is a description of the nature of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra as the presiding authorities over the three states of the withdrawal, creation, and maintenance of the entire class of subjects under Māyā, and even beyond that.

By means of this duality, there is that which is to be abandoned (*heya*) and that which is to be accepted (*upādeya*). The reality of the subject (*pramātṛtattva*) existing within *māyā* is to be abandoned; the class of subjects existing beyond *māyā* is to be accepted. Thus, the class of subjects whose nature is bound is to be abandoned, while those who have become liberated through the glance of the Guru are to be accepted. This pertains to the utility of what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted.

The description of the nature of the impurities such as *āṇava* and so forth, the differentiation of subjects caused by those impurities, the nature of immersion into one's true self which consists of the Supreme Lord— [all this is treated] in two [chapters], followed by five verses on the nature of immersion,
and then by the triad of states consisting of deep sleep, dream, waking, the fourth (*turya*), and that which transcends the fourth (*turyātīta*).

The Teacher explains therein that among those states— the determination of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted— the triad beginning with waking and so forth, along with the pair consisting of the Fourth (turya) and that which transcends the Fourth (turyātīta), are to be adopted. Thus,
when the nature of reality has been determined as established by scripture and supported by reasoning:

This is "Mātṛtā" (the state of being the subject): when the collection of objects of cognition, enveloped by the pentad beginning with Time (Kāla), is withdrawn and remains as mere subjectivity (mātṛtāmātra)— that is, during the stage of withdrawal (saṃhāradaśā)— Rudra [is so called] because he brings about that state by withdrawing the state of the objects of cognition.

The Lord Rudra, as the presiding deity (*adhidaivata*), is being worshipped by his own circle of devotees— who have attained immersion in that state through the bestowing of that state— and by the accomplishment of the presence of their primary master; this occurs through the expansion of distinct objects of knowledge (*bhinnaprameya*) in the form of "this [is the deity]."

In the state of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), He exists as the presiding deity (*adhidevatā*) Brahmā; in the state of maintenance (*sthiti*), when the objects of knowledge have been projected and consist of an expansion characterized by the continuous flow of their series, He exists as the presiding deity Viṣṇu. In that regard, [He exists] as the Lord Rudra with the sense of "I" (*aham*).

Because it is devoid of the state of being a limited subject (*pramātṛ*), and because it is free from the dualities of inhalation and exhalation, day and night, sun and moon, and so forth, there is no opening of the third eye of Brahmā and Viṣṇu.

Thus, when the category of principles (tattva-varga) beginning from Śiva down to the earth has been defined in the first chapter of the Āgama-kāṇḍa— starting from the passage "thus [it has] internal and external activity" up to "by way of the distinction between gross and subtle"—
that which is the subject (pramātṛ) consisting of the state of being a subject under Māyā, enveloped by time and so forth, is [now discussed].

In that state of the object of knowledge known as withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), the entire collection of objects of knowledge, such as the teeth and so forth, is withdrawn into form alone. For this very reason, [the subject] remains as pure subjectivity (*pramātṛtā-mātra*).
In that state, the presiding deity of that subject is his [own nature].

Furthermore, it is through the attainment of that state by the cognizer, which brings about the withdrawal of the entire range of objects of knowledge for his circle of devotees, and by bestowing the state of withdrawal consisting of pure subjectivity;
moreover, it is the manifestation of that [state] for one who has entered into the meditative absorption of the state of transmigratory existence.
And by means of this accomplishment, you— the presiding deity— having become Rudra,

the Lord, the Blessed One, the Supreme Lord, the Blessed One Rudra himself, remain as he who is Rudra even in the realm of *māyā*, consisting of prāṇa and apāna, dharma and adharma, sun and moon, day and night, and so forth.

I am free from duality, consisting of the *brahmanāḍī*, whose nature is giving, and which is composed of fire; it is the form of light within the center. (469) Through the touch of the true nature of the subject (*pramātṛ*), the third eye is opened—the middle light, the *brahmanāḍī*—which belongs to that subject of *māyā* as his own self.

In the expansion of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) which has assumed the form of differentiation during the state of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) and so forth, you are the presiding deity; and in the expansion characterized by the continuous flow of the stream of differentiated objects that have been projected, up until the reabsorption of that knower (*pramātṛ*), during the state of persistence (*sthiti*).

You are the presiding deity; Viṣṇu is the object of worship for both Brahmā and Viṣṇu, as well as for their respective worlds of devotees. The granting of the states of creation and maintenance to those worlds—specifically, the state of creation for the world of one's own devotees who are absorbed in meditation upon You—is Your manifestation directed toward them.

And there is also the accomplishment (*saṃpādana*). For this very reason, because the accomplishment of the object of knowledge—which consists of the creation and maintenance of the manifestation of forms as "this-ness" (*idantā*)—is primary, and because those two [creation and maintenance] lack entry into the state of the subject as "I" (*aham*), there is no unfolding or opening of a third eye; thus, there is a succession between the arising and the maintenance of the act of knowing (*pramā*).
(Ṭp. 365) When that nature of the cognizer (*pramātṛsvarūpa*) which was described by the preceding sūtra is under the influence of *māyā*, the transmigrating cognizer is called the "Lord" (*pati*).
This occurs when, according to the principle stated as "of that state of sovereignty," sovereignty is made manifest by *vidyā* within the cognizer.
When there is the conceit that the universe is one's own limb, the state of Sadāśiva and Īśvara—expressed as "I am indeed this 'I'"—is attained;
at that time, the designation "Lord" (pati) for that subject of Māyā is established by the Āgamas. This [state] is the cause of concealment.

Furthermore, according to the principle stated as "designated as Māyā," when the universe is conceived as distinct from one's own self by the power of Māyā, one is defiled by afflictions, karma, and so forth; this is the technical designation of the *āgama* as "the bound soul" (*paśu*).
Thus, there are these technical designations in the *āgama*: "the transmigrator," "those to be liberated," "the Lord," and "the bound soul"—and [it denotes] duality.

He explains [this] with the words "this one" (*eṣa*). Enveloped by time and the other factors, blinded by *māyā*, and for that very reason bound by karma—meaning one who perceives actions as being a bondage—"this one" refers to the limited subject (*pramātṛ*) beginning with the void (*śūnya*), who is enveloped by time and so forth; such a person is called a transmigrating soul (*saṃsārī*). This is the form previously described.

Because his sovereignty consists in the eternal nature manifested by knowledge and higher powers (*vidyā-abhijñā*), he is therefore a mass of consciousness (*cidghana*) and has the singular form of consciousness; thus he is called "liberated. When such a liberated one perceives objects—earth and other entities—which are in fact his own limbs, as being his own limbs, he is called the "Lord" (*pati*). This occurs through the power of *māyā*.

Because those entities, which are distinct from one's own self, are bound by various states that function as fetters (*pāśa*), they are therefore described in the scriptures (*āgama*) by the Supreme Lord— as is understood from the context— as being "defiled" by afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and so forth. One is utterly deluded by *māyā*, which effects concealment, such that one's own nature as the Lord is obscured.

For this very reason, the subject—deluded by time and so forth, enveloped by the void and other [elements]—wanders in saṃsāra, moving from one womb to another; thus he is called a "wanderer" (saṃsārī).
He states that the body also undergoes wandering with the words beginning with "the body too," and so forth.

(471) Not only in childhood, youth, and old age, but even in external objects such as forests, the embodied self transmigrates through states such as childhood by persisting in a similarity of essential nature; as it has been said:
Just as the embodied soul passes through childhood, youth, and old age in this body, so too does it attain another body; the wise are not deluded by this.

The body undergoes transmigration through various stages such as childhood and youth within a single lifetime, because it assumes different forms at each stage. However, the intellect, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and so forth, undergo transmigration even into other births, as it has been said:
"For the mind knows the connection between different births. By the word "also" (*api*), [it is implied that] these [factors] are momentary in each respective instance—

Because one is possessed by suffering and delusion, there is wandering in saṃsāra even within a single birth. By the aforementioned method, through that *vidyā* which effects the manifestation of one's own true nature as the Great Lord (*maheśvara*), the sovereignty of that subject is brought to the state of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). (Ṭp. 1)
365) Because of the vitalizing recognition of His sovereignty consisting of fullness and so forth, even the body and so on— though [ordinarily] devoid of body, life-force, and intellect—
as well as the entire universe of pots, cloths, and the like distinct from them, are nothing but consciousness itself.

He conceives of himself as consisting solely of a single consciousness; for this very reason, he is a mass of pure consciousness, a solid unity of the full "I-consciousness" (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*); for this same reason, other "I-consciousnesses" are void because they are mixed with the nature of consciousness. Thus, even when the state of union (*saṃbheda*) exists, his essential nature is consciousness alone.

After the fall of the body, one is fit to be designated as "liberated" because of being free from the bondage of rebirth; yet, once the body has fallen, he remains exactly as he was, consisting solely of Śiva. Since the body and other such factors—which serve as the cause for transmigratory existence—and that cognizer (pramātṛ) are both a single, dense mass of Śiva, who is liberated from what, and by what means? As it has been said:

"Salutation to Him whose form is *saṃsāra*. By the falling of the Guru’s glance, one who was previously unliberated—due to the state of being bound by the course of existence consisting of prior and subsequent conditions—and who is liberated in relation to other subjects such as Caitra or Maitra, receives the designation "Śiva.
This very one who is thus liberated, while still possessing a body, [perceives] the entities beginning with earth...

Not conceiving [of himself as the Self], he perceives—that is, performs the act of measuring—earthly entities such as earth and so forth through the method of thinking, "I am the earth," "I am water," "I am Vaiśvānara," "I am Marut," and "I am the sky"; thus, he measures them by regarding these states as his own body. This "measuring" (pramimīte) is the act of measuring (pramāṇa), which is to say, it is the process of reflection (manana) and comprehension (avagamana).

He acts; for this very reason, he is the master (*svāmī*), the lord (*īśa*), and the sovereign (*īśvara*) of entities such as the earth—these being synonymous meanings of the word *pati*. Furthermore, because he bestows upon them his own self—which, according to the stated principle, is their ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) that was previously unmanifest—he is the protector (*pālaka*).

The Lord of all beings is taught in the scriptures because He manifests Himself in their respective forms; He is taught in the scriptures by the Supreme Lord as the Protector and Guardian, the Master who,
through His power of Māyā, appears as distinct from others among those differentiated by Māyā, while remaining the Mother of His own Self.

[The Lord] perceives those objects as distinct from His own self precisely because they have been differentiated by the power of *māyā*. It is for this reason that He is called a "bound soul" (*paśu*), for He is bound (*pāśita*) by those very objects of knowledge which have been differentiated by the power of *māyā*. Because of being fettered [by thoughts] such as "this is my wife," "this is my field," and "this is my son," He is said to be bound.

The "bound soul" (paśu) has been described—[the word] "in battle" (maraṇe) is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. For by this [verse], he demonstrates that those objects of knowledge are indeed fetters (pāśa) for the primordial knower, solely due to the power of the mass of the knowable. Knowledge (vidyā) is the recognition of one's own true nature; [and] the sense of "I-ness" (asmitā).

In these [objects], there arises egoism (*ahaṅkāra*), attachment (*rāga*) which is clinging to them, aversion (*dveṣa*) which is the opposite of that, and obsession (*abhiniveśa*), which is a state of being possessed; thus the afflictions (*kleśa*) come into being. Due to the mass of objects of knowledge belonging to this knower, actions arise whose fruits take the form of heaven and hell. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), those in the form of hope (*āśā*) [are included].

The latent impressions (*vāsanā*) reside in their hearts; the residual trace (*saṃskāra*) residing in the heart is the fruition (*vipāka*) of the afflictions (*kleśa*), which takes the form of experience as a result. Thus, there is an infinite variety of turbidity in the form of ignorance (*avidyā*), egoism (*asmitā*), and so forth; this turbidity is the state of being clouded by the power of *māyā*.

Because it is bound by turbidity, it is called a "bound soul" (*paśu*). (Ṭp. 367) (473) Regarding this which has been described as the form of the bound soul, he states that the Supreme Lord has declared in the *Āgamas* that this very form of the bound soul is indeed the impurity (*mala*) consisting of *māyīya* and *kārma* [nature]: [The verse: "The impurity (*mala*) consists of *māyīya*, *kārma*, and *āṇava*; it is said to be threefold because it is divided according to its own nature. (Kārikā 2.10) [Commentary: The impurity (*mala*) is said to be threefold because it is divided according to its own nature. Among these, *māyīya-mala* is the power of concealment (*tirodhāna-śakti*), which is the cause of the manifestation of the world (*prapañca*). *Kārma-mala* is the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), which is the cause of the experience of the fruits of action (*bhoga*). *Āṇava-mala* is the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), which is the cause of the obscuration of the self's own nature. Thus, the impurity is threefold because it is divided according to its own nature. It is not that there is a separate substance (*dravya*) for each; rather, the single substance of impurity is designated as threefold based on its functional differentiation. Just as a single substance such as clay is designated as "pot," "plate," and so forth based on its functional differentiation, so too the single substance of impurity is designated as threefold based on its functional differentiation. Therefore, it is established that the impurity is threefold. Furthermore, it is not that the impurity is something other than the powers; rather, it is the very nature of the powers themselves that is designated as impurity when they are in a state of obscuration. Thus, it is said: "The impurity is the power itself, but it is called impurity when it is in a state of obscuration. Even though the nature of consciousness (*citsvarūpa*) exists, there is a loss of the sovereignty consisting of full subjectivity (*pūrṇāhantā*); and even though there is the sovereignty consisting of the identification with the body (*dehāhaṃbhāva*), there is a lack of awareness—thus the *āṇavamala* is twofold. The cause therein is the loss of the essential nature of consciousness, which consists of the state of being the knower and the agent. In that regard, of consciousness...

The distinction is as follows: in the cases of the *sakala* (the bound soul with all coverings) and the *pralayākala* (the soul dissolved in dissolution), there is a loss of autonomy; in the case of the *vijñānākala* (the soul of pure consciousness), there is a lack of awareness even regarding that autonomy. Thus, when these two types—the *āṇava* (atomic) and the *māyīya* (illusory)—are present, there occurs the manifestation of an object of knowledge that is distinct from one's own self, appearing as mutually differentiated and separate from oneself.

The very first of the objects of knowledge is the impurity called *māyā*. This *māyā-mala*, through its degrees of grossness and subtlety, is interwoven with the *sakala*, *pralayākala*, *vijñānākala*, and *mantra* subjects; it bestows birth and experience, while *kārmamala* bestows caste, lifespan, and experience.

According to the principle stated regarding *karman*, it grants repeated birth and experience to the subject (*pramātṛ*). When the subject, though performing meritorious and non-meritorious deeds, is devoid of awakened consciousness, there exists the impurity of action (*kārmamala*). These three [impurities] arise solely through the power of *māyā*. Indeed, the power of *māyā* alone is the cause of these three impurities.
The karma-mala exists in all subjects; even within that karma-mala of theirs,
by the principle of dissolution and subsequent re-emergence, the karma-mala exists in the form of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) directed toward Paramaśiva, Mantramaheśvara, and Mantreśvara.
In the sevenfold group of subjects known as the Mantra-vijñānākala, Pralayākala, and Sakala,
there is no gradation of the Āṇava-mala (the impurity of finitude) in the form of a progressive sequence of subtle and gross natures; rather,
the state of being a knower and agent is the awakening of the nature of consciousness, which consists of the fullness of the "I-consciousness" (ahaṃtā).

Even though the true nature of the Self exists as "I am omniscient" and "I am the creator of all," there is nevertheless—through *māyā*—an abandonment [of that nature]; by means of which *mala*, that cognizer (*pramātṛ*) becomes contracted and limited. Herein lies the *āṇava* [impurity].

The closing, that is, the contraction, of the essential nature of the Self which is full consciousness— that closing of its own nature occurs when it abides solely as the conscious Self in the form of pure awareness; it is the internal closing of the essential nature consisting of agency, which is of the nature of sovereignty, within the essential nature characterized by the state of being an agent.

When [the Self] remains, the Āṇava-mala— which consists of the closing of another essential nature characterized by pure consciousness, while that [consciousness] itself remains as the essence of full subjectivity— is a form that does not abandon its own nature; and since there is only one such [impurity] among the two types, when this Āṇava-mala exists, [there is obscuration] due to the loss of consciousness.

And due to the loss of sovereignty, when there is a contraction of one's own nature in two ways, there occurs the manifestation of an object of knowledge (*vedya*) that is distinct from one's own self. By virtue of this manifestation of a distinct object of knowledge, there arises the *kārmamala* (the impurity of action), which consists of merit and demerit; and from this *kārmamala*, birth and experience (*bhoga*) come into being. And that experience is as follows:

It has been stated that "caste, lifespan, and experience" constitute karma that is fixed as such at the time of its emission; this refers to the determinate, augmenting [karma]. In order to clarify the nature of the subject (*pramātṛ*), which is the very self of each respective substrate for these impurities (*mala*) beginning with *āṇava*, individually:

Regarding the first remaining state of the first stage, the *āṇavamala* (the impurity of individuality), which consists in the loss of the autonomy of consciousness, he says: those subjects known as *vijñānakevalas*, who, despite being of the nature of pure consciousness, lack supreme agency, [are] by the Supreme Lord...

They are created as distinct from one another and from the Supreme Lord; the cause for their creation as distinct from one another and from the self is the abandonment of the status of being a supreme agent.
Therefore:

Therefore, for those knowers (*pramātṛ*) for whom consciousness alone is the ultimate reality, there is no sovereignty characterized by bliss— the state of resting within one's own self as "I" with respect to the universe.
This is because, even while the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) exists, they possess the conceit of "not-this" (*atad-abhimāna*) arising from the imagined sovereignty of the Supreme Lord.

The supreme sovereignty consisting of the thought "I am the creator of the universe" does not exist [in them]. They have been separated and differentiated from their own self, which is the Supreme Lord—the perfect *ahantā* (I-consciousness) that is omniscient and the form of the universal agent. The cause of this creation as something distinct for them is as follows:

The remaining purport of this verse is that the Supreme Lord possesses the nature of consciousness by virtue of His supreme sovereignty, which consists of being the universal agent from Śiva down to the earth; whereas [the state] devoid of that supreme sovereignty consisting of the full *ahaṃtā* (I-consciousness) is characterized by the cessation of agency. This is due to the cause of the disappearance of agency.

Let them be distinct from the Supreme Lord; but how can there be mutual distinction among the individual cognitions (*vijñāna*) and the moments of time (*kāla*), since they are identical to one another in their possession of the quality of pervasiveness (*vyāpitva*) which constitutes spatial distinction, and the quality of eternity (*nityatva*) which constitutes temporal distinction?
Thus, he dispels the doubt as to how the plural number is used when they are created without mutual distinction by stating: "Because the eternity of consciousness is all-pervasive,
although it is one, its characteristics are mutually distinct."

By the specific will of the Supreme Lord, those [souls] possess mutual differentiation through the nature of their individual groups of cognitions at various times; and they are called "Vijñānakevalas" by the Supreme Lord in the scripture— those whose nature consists solely of cognition devoid of agency.

In the group of principles (*tattva*), desiring to exist as the nature of the principles beginning with Śiva and ending with Earth, and as the nature of subjects (*pramātṛ*) beginning with Śiva and ending with the *sakala*, He becomes and manifests in those respective forms. However, there is no other whatsoever—neither a supreme Lord distinct from Him, nor any group of subjects—that exists apart from Him. Whatever [is perceived] here...

Whatever flickers forth is merely the manifestation of the Lord’s own self, as will be explained; this has been stated repeatedly at the beginning of the commentary on such passages as "Therefore, this Self...
and "That consciousness which shines forth through the existence of the universe is 'I am Śiva' through the existence of the universe."
Thus it is said once by the teachers regarding Ākala; thus it is said repeatedly.

And therefore, because it has been stated once [in the scriptures]: "Even though I am by nature an all-pervasive and eternal consciousness due to being uncontracted by space and time, I am not able to manifest as distinct, mutually differentiated cognitions through the nature of the limited subject (*kalā*),"— it is by virtue of such a specific will of the Lord that [this occurs].

Although there is a unity among them regarding the entire collection of attributes such as consciousness—which have transcended the status of the insentient subject beginning with the body and ending with emptiness—there is nevertheless mutual differentiation between them. And they are described in the scripture as *vijñānakevalas*. Regarding this, the text states: "In that regard, the *vijñānakevala* is joined with only impurity (*mala*)," and so forth.
It has been stated: the meaning of the term *vijñānakevala* has already been explained previously.
Regarding the phrase "the loss of sovereignty of consciousness," this refers to the portion consisting of the *āṇavamala* and so forth.
Having abandoned the state of being a *vijñānākala*, there is also the non-awareness of sovereignty.

He clarifies this point by demonstrating its object: in consciousness, the *kalās*—characterized by the reality of the *kalās* and devoid of the instruments and their effects—are like those of a *sakala* subject.
