Therefore, upon arising from that state which is the nature of the great deep sleep (*mahāsauṣupta*), they become possessed of instruments and their effects.

Because they exist within the principle of *māyā*, there also exists for them the impurity of karma consisting of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), which serves as the seed for the causes and effects characterized by their re-arising;
this is considered by some to be an intellectual impurity regarding the object of distinct cognizable things.

In the deep sleep of the vital breath (*prāṇasuṣupta*), there exists the stain consisting of the manifestation of duality; in the deep sleep of the void (*śūnyasuṣupta*), which has as its object that which is beyond the range of objects of knowledge (*apavedya*), it does not exist. Thus, the domain of the *māyīya* stain is established. As he will say:

"That which is associated with the *māyā*-stain is [the state] with an object of knowledge (*savedya*), and that which is dissociated from it is [the state] without an object of knowledge (*apavedya*)."
For them, the atomic reality (āṇavavastu) exists by its own nature according to the stated sequence. This too is indicated by the word [“svataḥ”].

For those who, due to insentience (jaḍatva), possess the wonder of "I" (ahaṃ) within the void which is of the nature of non-consciousness, or within the vital breath (prāṇa) which is of the nature of consciousness, or within the intellect (buddhi).

Through yoga, agency belongs to you; at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), the *kalās* have not been made—that is to say, they are devoid of the instruments and effects characterized by the principle of *kalā*. She is "full" (*pūrṇā*), meaning devoid of the awareness consisting of the "I-feeling" (*ahaṃtā*). In that void and so forth, [there is the thought] "I am the void," and the agents are separated by the great deep sleep (*mahāsuṣupti*).

Since those very relationships between cause and effect remain established in that manner immediately after dissolution, therefore, for those who have remained in such a state until the limit of dissolution, there exists only the aforementioned *āṇava* impurity (*mala*), which consists of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and residual traces (*saṃskāra*), pertaining to future causes and effects. (477)

Because it consists of the impressions (*vāsanā*) and latent dispositions (*saṃskāra*), the self—whose nature is dharma and adharma—is the cause for the arising of cause and effect. Thus, there exists the impurity of karma (*kārmamala*), characterized by dharma and adharma, such that one thinks, "I am a partaker of merit," or "I am a partaker of demerit. If this is so—that is, if the impurity of karma also exists—then that [impurity] is the cause of karma.

Their manifestation as a separate object of knowledge, which consists of the impurity of *māyā*, is real; by this portion [of the reality], he describes it in the state of "vital-sleep" (*prāṇasuṣupta*), which is associated with the object of knowledge in the form of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). In that vital-sleep where there is no longer an object of knowledge, it exists.

It does not exist in deep sleep (*gāḍhasuṣupta*). Due to the presence or absence of the manifestation of distinct objects of knowledge (*vedya-prathā*) in the states of deep sleep—where there is both the knowable and the unknowable—the *māyīya-mala* (the impurity of Māyā) is conceptualized as having a fixed domain for these [states]. This is because, by the phrase "for instance" (*tathā hi*), the existence of the *māyā-mala* is established.

It reveals two states of being. Some *pralayākalas* rest in the portion of the unmanifest (*apavedya*) within the Void, rendered inert by a deep sleep; they abide in the state of profound slumber (*suṣupti*).
Others, however, these *pralayākalas*, reside in both the intellect (*buddhi*) and the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

For yogins, the objects of perception— which are of a universal nature, devoid of the remainder of pleasure and pain, and undifferentiated— are merged into the state of deep sleep; thus, the state of being yoga for all is equal, whether it concerns the gross body as the self, which is the effect, or the senses as the instrument, which is the cause.
"The loss of autonomy of consciousness" is the first part of the *āṇavamala*, residing in the *vijñānākala*;
"the non-awareness of autonomy" is its final part, residing in the *pralayākala*. This is mentioned here because of the context of the *āṇavamala*, which also pertains to the *pralayākala*.

The state of being the object of the *kārmamala* has been shown. Furthermore, it has been stated that the *māyāmala* is present only optionally (*pākṣikatva*) in the *pralayākalas*. Thus, the *āṇavamala* and *māyāmala* belong to the *vijñānākala*, while the *pralayākala* possesses all three impurities (*mala*) according to the sequence already described. Having thus explained the distinction [between the types of souls], we shall now again discuss the *āṇavamala*.

Even though the two karmic impurities (*kārmamala*) are absent in the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*), who are subjects of the mantras, he shows that there exists a pure object for the impurity known as *māyā*:
"I am a performer of meritorious deeds; I... [and so on]. This demonstrates that even for those who possess omniscience and the capacity to act as knowers, the impurity of *māyā* remains.

When there is the stain of karma characterized as "evil action" (pāpakarma), those who possess divided experience (bhinnavedya) have the stain of *māyā*; they are the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvaras*).
These subjects (*pramātāras*), perceiving pure consciousness alone as their own self, are the subjects of *māyā*.

They perceive that which has the form of impurity—the body and so forth—as the Self; yet, because of the emergence of the wonder of "I" within that very pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), they are agents. For this very reason, they are omniscient and omnipotent, since they see pure consciousness alone as the Self. Because agency resides in that very [consciousness], they are omniscient.

And those Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvaras) are the creators of all things. Even though they are of such a nature, he shows their distinction by means of the word "but" (kiṃ tu): the entire universe, consisting of worlds, states of being, and so forth, appears as an object of knowledge because it is the domain of cognition, and as an effect because it is the domain of action through its state of being knowable.
Just as on the plane of *māyā*, for creators such as weavers and potters, the universe— their created object of knowledge consisting of effects such as jars and cloths—
appears as distinct from their own self; so too, for the *Vidyeśvaras*, that [universe] appears as indeed distinct.
There exists a conjunction with the impurity known as *māyā*, which consists in the manifestation of objects perceived as distinct from that [pure Self].
In order to demonstrate the object common to all three impurities simultaneously, he says:
"Of those subject to existence (*bhavinām*), that is, of transmigrating beings (*saṃsāriṇām*) ranging from gods down to stationary beings."

Among the fourteen classes of beings enumerated in the scriptures— namely the Vidyādharas, Devas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Piśācas, Guhyakas, those born from eggs, those born from sweat, those born from a womb, those born from sprouts, and those ending with reptiles— there exists a threefold impurity. Even while these [other impurities] exist, it is the *kārmamala* (karmic impurity) that belongs to them.

The *āṇavamala* and *māyāmala* are primarily the causes for the wandering in *saṃsāra* for [beings] beginning with the gods. However, without the *kārma-mala*, these two do not constitute a cause for wandering. Here, among the class of subjects (*pramātṛ-varga*), the group consisting of the Vidyeśvaras and Vijñānakalas extends up to Māyā.
There is no state of non-existence through the process of dissolution for the two classes of Mantreśvara and Mantreśvareśvara,
who are presided over by the venerable Lord Īśvara and the venerable Lord Sadāśiva respectively; however, the *pralayākalas* [do not exist] because of the universal withdrawal [of the world].

Furthermore, regarding those deities existing within the *māyā-tattva*—from the beginning of the manifestation of the universe down to the immobile beings—who are devoid of [inherent] existence, even their three impurities (*mala*) exist simultaneously; thus it has been stated that they are all transmigratory beings (*saṃsārin*). Among those three impurities, which specific impurity is the cause of their transmigration?
Anticipating the objection that [the soul] brings about [transmigration], he states that it is indeed the *kārmamala* (action-taint) that effects transmigration:
"Even there" (*tatrāpi*) means "even while those [other impurities] exist. Even while those exist, the *kārmamala* becomes the primary cause of transmigration. As it has been said:
From the impurity of karma (kārmamala), bodies and sense-objects arise. At that time, their subtle essence consists precisely in the connection between the instruments of perception and the objects;
and this continues in an uninterrupted succession, existing now, and subsequently existing later and later.
Transmigration is thus described. However, the *āṇava* and *māyīya* impurities (*mala*) are merely the causes of transmigration.

Because they are devoid of the *kārmamala*, in the case of the *vijñānākala* souls, they lack the power to bring about the manifestation of various states such as the body and so forth; therefore, the *kārmamala* alone is primary [as the cause of transmigration].

It is stated in various scriptures that "impurity (mala) is the primary cause of saṃsāra. Precisely because it is stated thus, with the intention that once karma has been destroyed, the steps of the ladder of saṃsāra are rendered devoid of existence, [this is taught] in the Sāṃkhya, Purāṇas, Mahābhārata, and other scriptures.
The very abandonment of the conceit of being bound by karma is what is being described.

Through three bodies, each having a single form, and through three forms with two divisions—namely, by means of the single form and the threefold division—the seven subjects, beginning with Śiva and ending with Sakala, arise. They do so gradually, according to their respective degrees of excellence.

O Great Lord of Mantras, by which divisions of the three attained forms of *āṇava* do the *mantra*, *mantreśvara*, and *śiva* [levels] arise? [They arise] through the two divisions in the form of *āṇava* and *māyīya*, and through the single division in the form of *āṇava* and *kārmika*.
The Mantreśvaras, Vijñānākalas, and Pralayākalas arise in succession.
Among them, the Mantreśvaras and Vijñānākalas arise through the two-fold division of Āṇava and Māyīya [impurities].
The Pralayākalas arise through the two-fold division consisting of the Āṇava and Kārmika [impurities]. [The Āṇava...]

All [subjects] arise through a single division consisting of the *māyīya* and *kārmātman*. Thus, by means of the three divisions of each of the three impurities (*mala*), as well as by their two-fold and three-fold combinations, the seven subjects beginning with Śiva and ending with the *sakala* arise in sequence. In that regard, concerning the three impurities:

These impurities possess infinite modes through distinctions such as grossness and subtlety, through the distinction of predominance and non-predominance, through the distinction of alternation (*vikalpa*) and combination (*samuccaya*), and by the word "etcetera" [implying] the distinction of deficiency and excess.

Among those—Śiva, Mantramahesvaras, and Mantresvaras—the *āṇava* impurity (*mala*) is primary in varying degrees. Among them, the primacy of the impurity belongs to the Vidyeśvaras; for the Vijñānākalas, both the *āṇava* and the *māyīya* [impurities] are primary in succession; and for the Pralayākalas, [the *māyīya* is primary].

Among the *paśus* (bound souls), the *āṇavamala* (the impurity of limited subjectivity) and the *kārmamala* (the impurity of karma) are primary; among those possessed of *kalās* (*sakalas*), all three impurities are indeed primary.
Even there, the *kārmamala*, being the cause of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), is the most primary. This is the primary impurity.
One should observe the internal distinction that this is secondary, while that and this [other] are primary. And in this regard:
He demonstrates the two modes— bondage and liberation— for transmigrating beings through the differentiation between the manifestation and concealment of the three impurities (*mala*):
"Empowered by the principle whose nature is the power of *kalā*, yet suppressed by impurity..."

In such instances as "I am devoid of all forms," "I am thirsty," "I am hungry," "I am happy," "I am miserable," "I am emaciated," or "I am stout," the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*) exists as the primary reality, having made its own void-like interior of the body the principal locus. He states the reason for this: "Measured" (*mitam*).

Furthermore, when any object— from the body up to the void— has attained the state of "thisness" (idantā) and is submerged within the portion of the subject as an object of knowledge (prameya), then, since the primacy of the consciousness of the knowing self (cidātman) as the agent (kartṛtā) remains unestablished in the void and other such states due to the non-primacy of that knower's agency, that [object] is merely known.
This is characterized by immersion into one's own true nature, which consists of the Supreme Lord.

(481) Regarding this: the consciousness of worldly beings, such as the gods and others, consists of the aspect of agency belonging to the conscious form of the Self, because the cognitive portion of the Self has been submerged within the body and so forth.

"Reality" (tattva) means sovereignty. That reality which pertains to the subject of Māyā—ranging from the void (śūnya) to the body—is empowered and vitalized by the principle called "limited agency" (kalā), which is of the nature of a power of the Supreme Lord and consists of limited doership; yet, being suppressed by impurity (mala), it is now awakened.

Having made emptiness (*śūnya*) and so forth primary, that which exists as non-primary in itself attains the status of "this-ness" (*tad-idantā*). Furthermore, because it is submerged within the objective portion (*prameya-bhāga*) ranging from the body to emptiness, it is an object of cognition (*prameya*), just as the body is [the object] of the notion "I am happy."

"He who is thirsty" refers to the vital breath (*prāṇa*); "he who is devoid of all forms" refers to the void (*śūnya*). "He who is fair—I am he": having become these very entities such as the fair-complexioned one, which are the states of "I," they manifest within transmigratory existence; this is the state of transmigratory existence.

He who indeed shines as "I" in the forms of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep—he is complete, independent, all-pervasive, and eternal; by means of the reasonings of the Guru’s instruction, he is declared to be "complete, independent, and sovereign. "I am eternal, I am perfectly full, I am independent, I am all-pervasive."
Reflecting thus, the Guru remained with truthful speech.

According to this principle, when one— by means of that very [consciousness] which, through the reflective awareness of attributes such as autonomy, selfhood, and eternity, consists of the nature of consciousness— dissolves the object of knowledge (prameya), beginning with the void (śūnya) and so forth, into the nature of pure awareness by means of the state of "I-am-not" (nāhaṃ-bhāva) within that which is perfectly full, then at that moment there is the state beyond the fourth (turyātītāvasthā).
But when it is thoroughly realized, then— through the convergence of the reality of existence, permanence, sovereignty, and so forth—
the seven constituents from emptiness up to the body become [transformed] by means of that very nature;
just as mercury, through the power of a mantra-adept, turns copper and other metals into gold, so too do emptiness and the rest.
The body, including its constituent elements, is not pierced by the perfected elixir (*siddharasa*). That is the fourth state (*turyadaśā*);

in that fourth state, even that [subjectivity] such as emptiness (*śūnya*) seems to abandon the status of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatā*), because it consists of pure consciousness (*saṃvinmayī*).
Thus, both the state of the Fourth (*turyāvasthā*) and the state Beyond the Fourth (*turyātītāvasthā*) are states of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*).

It is called "immersion" (*samāveśa*). In the scripture—that is, in the *Śaṃvit-śāstra* and in various *Āgamas*—it is indeed the perfect immersion into the form of the "I-consciousness" (*ahantā*) that serves for the attainment of the primary immersion; other instructions, which take the form of specific means for immersion, must be relied upon. As it was sung by the Blessed One:

Having caused the mind— which here stands as a metaphor for the body and so forth— to enter and immerse itself within Me, who am the Self whose nature is the fullness of the "I-consciousness" beyond Māyā; those who, endowed with supreme faith, worship Me while their minds are thus absorbed in Me, are considered by Me to be the most perfectly disciplined.
Thus, those who are eternally disciplined, never ceasing in their exertion toward absorption into their own true nature, are considered great yogis.
"Then, O Dhanañjaya, if I am unable to make my mind steady within me through the yoga of practice, then I shall seek refuge in you."
Thus, it is well known that the body, vital breath, intellect, void, and so forth— when animated by a state of total surrender—

are the "limbs" (aṃśāḥ) of the Supreme Lord, consisting of praise, life-force, worship, meditation, absorption, and the like, which are the sprouts of immersion (samāveśa). One who is incapable of practicing this immersion [should resort to other means].

One who is devoted to my work is a true being; by performing actions for my sake, you shall attain perfection. Thus, upon the fall of the body, when there is the singular essence of the Supreme Lord, who could enter where, and how?

Because there is no other existence apart from oneself, and because one is oneself the Supreme Lord; this very point regarding the object of knowledge (*prameya*) has been stated: that which is the primacy of agency—consisting of the fullness of "I-ness" (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*)—is the inseparable state of agency, wherein the state of being a subordinate attribute (*guṇabhāva*) is empty.

Because the activity of *āṇavamala*— described as the non-awareness of even one's own sovereignty when [the subject] has become a subordinate quality within the nature of the acid-like void and so forth, and described as the non-awareness of the activity of *mala*— has been cast aside, consciousness (*cit*), which is essentially awareness, possesses that supreme enjoyment which had previously been rendered otherwise by *āṇavamala*.

Even for that aspect characterized by consciousness (*bodha*), at the present time when agency (*kartṛtā*) emerges, consciousness possesses primacy because it has emerged through the subordination of the *aṇavamala* which was its obscuration. [Thus] agency possesses primacy.
That which is the state of being emergent—the knowledge that has indeed emerged as the agency and consciousness—is this very knowledge characterized by immersion (*samāveśa*).

Because it is the antidote to the impurity consisting of ignorance, this constitutes the primary nature of agency and consciousness, which consists in immersion into one's own essential form (*svarūpa*). By means of this...
Although the subject remains within the body through immersion (samāveśa), he is called the Lord (pati) as stated in the scriptures.
Let the state of the subject in the condition of the Lord be of the nature of the Fourth (turya) and that which transcends it (tadatīta) in the manner described.
However, in the state of the subject as a bound soul (paśu), the states of deep sleep, dream, and waking are described in the Āgamas.
Anticipating the question, "How was this stated?", he first explains the very nature of deep sleep with three verses:
"The sense of 'I' (ahantā) as 'I am empty' arises because of the absence of the intellect, vital breath, body, jar, and so forth, within the Self."

The state of being an agent (*kartṛtā*) resides in that locus which is the indistinct void (*asphuṭa-śūnya*), characterized by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of consciousness, intellect, vital breath, and body; therein, the emptiness of objects of knowledge arises. That is the emptiness of the objects of knowledge (*jñeya-śūnyatā*) regarding the sense organs (*akṣāṇām*), such as the eyes and other faculties.

That inward-turned activity, whose nature consists solely of mental formations (*saṃskāra*), which impels the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, and which impels the wheel of winds consisting of *prāṇa*, *apāna*, *samāna*, *udāna*, and *vyāna*—that should be known as the Void;
it is considered to be called "life" (*jīvana*). It is that power (*śakti*) which is called "life" because one lives by means of it.

Alternatively, when the vital breath is in deep sleep, the egoity consisting of the *puryaṣṭaka* becomes what is called "living" (*jīvana*). When it abides in that alone—that is, when it abides in mere emptiness—it is said to be a deep sleep of the vital breath comparable to dissolution (*pralaya*), because it is joined with the impurity of *māyā* and accompanied by latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) and objects of experience (*vedya*). (484)

Precisely because it is joined with the impurity of *māyā*, the state of deep sleep (*sauṣupta*) is said to be the object of knowledge (*vedya*), consisting merely of that [state] or abiding in mere emptiness.
Here, the principle of consciousness (*cit-tattva*), concealing its own essential nature, appears in the form of the knowable through the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth.
The nature of the knowable appears through the body and through objects such as jars;

thus, this is the unfolding of the non-dual sovereignty of consciousness itself. In this unfolding of sovereignty, there is no real sequence or division in the form of an objective entity. Even therein—
Even though there is an absence of both succession and differentiation, succession and differentiation appear due to the sovereignty of consciousness (*cittatva*).

Since, in the ultimate sense, there is no differentiation or succession of space and time, even though there is non-differentiation, differentiation and succession appear. This being the case, that which belongs to consciousness...

That portion which conceals one's own essential nature is the "void-portion" (śūnyabhāga). When [consciousness] comes to rest within that very void-portion— remaining unmixed with other portions consisting of the progressively higher forms of intellect, vital breath, and body— therein lies the locus of agency in the form of "I-ness," which is reflective awareness (parāmarśa).
When the intellect, vital breath, and so forth— having attained the state of being an object of knowledge through their nature as the sixfold forms such as indistinctness,

and thus by means of that very pure residual impression (*saṃskāra*)— are joined with the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of "I-ness" in the form of agency, then that very [awareness] is the void (*śūnyā*).

It remains as the residual reflection on the non-existence of the locus. Even though there is a very clear intermingling of the intellect and so forth with the object to be negated— such as "there is no intellect," "there is no body," or "there is no jar"—
the occurrence of a fixed and necessary intermingling with a very clear reflective awareness in the form of negation is required and will come to pass.
Because of the connection with that which is to be negated— just as in the reflective awareness "I am nothing"—

the object of negation here is the general form accepted in the thought "I do not possess anything whatsoever. Precisely because it consists of the negation of a general form, it has the nature of an object of knowledge reduced to a mere residual impression (*saṃskāra*).

It is called the "state of emptiness" (*śūnyāvasthā*). Likewise, when the intellect (*buddhi*) and everything else down to the body have been reduced to mere residual impressions (*saṃskāra*), and blue and other objects have likewise been reduced to residual impressions, that which is of the nature of their absence is called "emptiness. For in that emptiness, there is the emptiness of all knowable things.
The nature of non-existence is the state of having only residual impressions (*saṃskāra-śeṣatā*), which is indeed a specific kind of impression; this is the "non-existence" everywhere.

For existing entities, there is no destruction in their entirety. In that regard, [these impressions] are conjoined with and inseparable from the void subject (*śūnya-pramātṛ*) within the wheel of wind consisting of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth.

The impelling power (*preraṇātmikā-śakti*) is of the same nature as that [consciousness]; that power is the ground for the expansion of the principles of *vidyā* and *kalā*. In sequence, the group of cognitive faculties (*buddhīndriya-varga*) is the manifestation of *vidyā*, and the group of active faculties (*karmendriya-varga*) is the manifestation of *kalā*.
Of those two groups— the group of the sense organs of cognition and the group of the organs of action— there is an intermediate function belonging to them; that is,
there is an intermediate function belonging to those two groups of sense organs of cognition.
The external function consists of the forms of reflection upon sound, touch, and so forth; the striking and other such actions against the locus that manifests sound, touch, form, taste, and smell;
the function of the general sense organs; and the five vital airs, beginning with prāṇa.

The five winds (*pañcavāyavaḥ*) constitute the common and general function (*sāmānyā sādhāraṇīvṛttiḥ*) of the organs; it is that which, in the void (*śūnye*), strengthens the wheel of the senses and is called "life" (*jīvana*). Thus, it is the void itself that transmigrates as the living being (*jīva*), or else it is that which consists of form and so forth. Alternatively, it is the internal, common principle of animation (*prāṇanātmikā*) belonging to the powers of the senses.

The function consisting of the impelling of specific vital airs such as *prāṇa* and so forth, which is denoted by the word *prāṇa*, is at that time itself the power (*śakti*). When this [power], being identified as "I," constitutes the life of the *prāṇa*-subject, then the *prāṇa* itself is the transmigrating individual soul (*jīva*); this is the meaning. Thus, there is both the subject of the void (*śūnya-pramātṛ*) and the subject of the vital breath (*prāṇa-pramātṛ*).

That which is designated by the term "pūryaṣṭaka" consists of the pentad of breath and so forth, the single group of the five sense organs, and the intellect whose nature is determination; since these are manifested from the knower who is of the nature of both the void and the vital breath, this is the "pūryaṣṭaka" according to our own system.

He states another opinion as well: "Others say that the five subtle elements (tanmātras), mind, ego, and intellect [constitute the body]; it is thus obstructed by the *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold city) which exists within the mind, ego, and intellect, and whose form is the emergence of the subtle elements."
"Earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect, and ego— thus my nature is divided eightfold," so say others. Furthermore,
that which consists of the void and the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the aforementioned group of eight, is to be known through touch.

Because of its existence, there is a resting of both—the pure [consciousness] and that which consists of both—aspects—within the void-subject and the vital-breath subject. When that resting occurs, the "I-ness" (ahantā) that is specifically deep-sleep-like, which is the nature of consciousness and whose form is existence, is the state of deep sleep; thus, deep sleep is so called because it is the existence of that which is deep-sleep-like.

That which is non-egoity (*ahantā*)—which is the nature of existence consisting of awakening—and that which is the activity (*karman*) of deep sleep, being of the nature of the state of being and the activity of that [state], constitutes the state of deep sleep. Even in the waking and dreaming states, the subject is as if asleep due to impurity; yet in deep sleep, through the immersion therein by means of a subtle power (*kalā*) whose form is slight agency, he remains as if not asleep.

The state and activity of one who is in deep sleep constitute "sauṣupta. In that state, within the void-like deep sleep (*śūnya-sauṣupta*), because of the existence of pleasure, pain, and so forth produced by the touch of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), there exists the impurity known as *māyīya-mala*.

Therefore, that deep sleep is to be considered both with and without objectification (*savedya* and *apavedya*); like a deep sleep with objectification, even dissolution (*pralaya*) is to be understood in this way.

The term *pralaya* refers to that which is produced by the destruction and non-arising of the body and so forth, and lasts for a long duration; it also refers to that which is produced by the disregard of the body and so forth while the body still exists, lasting for a short duration—this is the implied meaning. Among these, that produced by fatigue is *sauṣupta*; that produced by the imbalance of the humors (*dhātu*) is *suṣupta*.

The sub-divisions are as follows: the state of deep sleep caused by substances such as intoxicants, the state of deep sleep caused by independence [of will] such as intoxication and madness, and the state of deep sleep which is yoga or meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

However, some say that the state of deep sleep (sauṣupta) consisting of meditative absorption (samādhi) is accompanied by experience (savedya), whereas other states of deep sleep are devoid of experience (apavedya). This is because [in the former], one is completely liberated from the clear spheres of objects of experience, such as "this is pleasure," "this is pain," "this is the body," "this is the vital breath," and "this is the intellect."

(Ṭp. 377) Let the nature of the state of deep sleep be as described by the method stated in the three verses beginning with "In the void of the state of deep sleep, because of the absence of the intellect and so forth" (487). Now, [let us consider] the mutual relationship between the dream and waking states, which both possess the manifestation of clearly cognized objects such as "this is blue."

Anticipating the question, "What is the difference?", he states the distinction in two verses: "In the dream state, within the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), in the self, in the mind alone, and even on the path, [the cognition] 'I have seen the form of a beloved with my eyes' or 'I have heard a sound with my hearing,' and so forth, appears clearly through delusion."

The internal, unstable, and unique creation of entities belonging to the Supreme Lord, which is considered by the bound subject (paśu-pramātṛ) to be the state of dreaming, is that creation taught in the Āgamas by the Supreme Lord as being,
in ultimate reality, the object of all the senses, such as the eyes and so forth, for the subject.
That creation which is external in form, stable, and common to all subjects is the waking state. The seats of the senses, such as the eyes and so forth—
which serve as firm and fixed abodes— consist of the eyeballs, the ear-cavities, and so on.

In one who is sleeping, [the eyes] are observed to be closed. When the eyeballs and other such substrates have been closed, not even the slightest remnant of the activity of the external sense organs is seen. Therefore, due to the absence of being perceived, the sense organs such as the eye—

In a dream, when the mind is independent of external activity, entities such as the touch of objects of the senses like the eyes appear before it; though these are not capable of appearing with a clear form suitable for grasping by the physical senses, they are created by the Supreme Lord, and not by the individual soul (aṇu).

It is not like the dream state. If it were created by an atom (*aṇu*), there would be no perception of an object that has not been previously specified. Therefore, it is not created by an atom. Even when perceiving a desired object, [the mind perceives] the location presided over by one's own self, as well as the time existing therein.

Leaving aside the present form, because it is perceived through connection with another place, time, and so forth, it is not created by itself—as in the case of one in a dream-state; this is the implied meaning. Therefore, this creation of forms, touches, and so on, arises precisely from the aforementioned kind of emanation belonging to the Supreme Lord, and solely because it exists as mere mind.
It does not belong to another cognizer; rather, it belongs only to the dreamer himself.

In such an uncommon creation, the objects of the eyes and other senses—such as forms, touches, and so forth—are [perceived] by that dreamer alone, and not by other distinct cognizers such as Caitra or Maitra.

Commonality shines forth. As long as both of those exist, so long—up to the limit of their appearing in that way, up to the limit of their manifesting in that way—they are indeed the ultimate reality, because they are measured as such; nevertheless, even that ultimate reality [is seen differently] by one who has awakened at a later time.

In that dream of the sleeping cognizer who is deluded, the two-fold nature [of objects]— namely, being objects of the senses such as the eye and being common to other subjects such as Caitra and Maitra who are distinct from oneself— is perceived through subsequent reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) as appearing with the status of valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*), even though it has been uprooted.

Along with one's own self, other subjects such as Caitra and Maitra, as well as the external senses such as the eyes, appear; these [appear] as non-different from other subjects and the eyes and so forth that exist at the time of waking. In this regard, there is certainty in the dream state, but it is not so at the time of waking by means of these [latter].

The persistence of the certainty that [objects] are not non-different from other cognizers and from the eyes and so forth is indeed excluded; for both— the mere measure consisting of a certainty common to other cognizers and the measure consisting of the sense organs such as the eye—
are simply erroneous with respect to the mother-of-pearl.

Just like the cognition of silver [in a mother-of-pearl], both entities are indeed illusory; because the forms, touches, and so forth of instability have been created, their lack of commonality is implied by the absence of being objects of the three senses beginning with the eye, as stated in the Sūtra.
Thus, by the word "instability" mentioned in the Sūtra, it is indicated that this arises from delusion (vibhrama).

The meaning is that although it was not explicitly stated by the Teacher in his own words, he has demonstrated— and will further demonstrate— that the waking state is the counter-correlate of the instability of dreams. That unique creation of the aforementioned nature is the supreme creation of the Lord (pārameśvarī), because it exists during the time of dreaming.

Even at the time of dreaming, [the object] possesses the status of being an object and commonality with other subjects through the persistence of ascertainment. For this very reason, it shines as real by virtue of being free from sublation. Precisely because it shines as being free from sublation, it is an external sensory object common to other subjects.

And the creation [of objects] is the waking state of the bound soul (*paśu*). That subjectivity (*pramātṛtva*) of the bound soul which has that creation as its object is the waking state (489). As long as the stability of the continuous cognition that determines objects such as jars and cloths shines forth, for that long the waking state persists; and that waking state lasts until the limit of that shining.

Even during the interval between [waking states], because the persistence of certainty through memory is uprooted, one is indeed dreaming even while awake. This is because objects—whether appearing indistinctly or clearly—are essentially nothing but manifestations; for there is no clarity regarding an experienced object even at a later time through memory, and thus the nature of that experience is lost.
Even while awake, one may enter a dream at another time; therein, even that which is a very long internal dream—
compared to the long duration of the primary dream— is then experienced as being merely waking within the dream,
despite its being considered a very long waking state within the dream.
The persistence of certainty within a dream is its concealment; at that very time, what is considered waking by you should be understood as merely a dream in relation to the dream itself.
Demonstrating the worthlessness of these states, such as waking and the rest—
It indicates that the two states consisting of the fourth-and-beyond (*turyātīta*) are to be accepted by saying "this" (*iyam*).
The three states beginning with deep sleep (*sauṣupta*), which were mentioned in the five verses starting with "In the void, the intellect... (*śūnye buddhyādi*), are to be abandoned.
If one asks for what reason, it is because agency (*kartṛtā*) has become subordinate to the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth.

Due to the predominance of those two—namely, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth as the agent and the agenthood [of the self]—there occurs generally the increase or decrease of pleasure, pain, and so on. Thus, when the vital breath and so forth are subordinate, there is an increase in agency; when agency is subordinate, there is an increase in the vital breath and so forth. This refers to the three states [of existence].

He perceives the affliction consisting of the abandonment of one thing and the acquisition of another, the desire for those two— abandonment and acquisition— the effort toward the purpose of abandoning and acquiring, and so forth, including pride and the like. Thus, these three states of this cognizer appear as something to be abandoned, accompanied by affliction.

Since this variety [of experience] is produced solely through the diversity of the conjunction with pleasure and pain, and since that [diversity] occurs within the three states, therefore the three states are to be abandoned.
(490) He states the cause for their occurrence: "By means of resting in the Self in the form of agency..."

The body consisting of consciousness (*cinmaya*) has the characteristic of being oriented toward the Other and is a single mass of bliss (*ānanda-ekaghana*). When that conscious body becomes subordinate within the triad beginning with *prāṇa*, within the voids, within the eightfold group (*puryaṣṭaka*), and within the levels of the body and so forth, then, once that body whose nature is consciousness has become a quality, [the state of] *prāṇa* and the rest [arises].
To the extent that the diminution of the manifestation of the nature of consciousness occurs,
to that same extent there arises pleasure and pain; to the extent that there is some emergence of the nature of consciousness, to that same extent there arises pleasure.

He demonstrates that very possibility: at the time of hunger, there is suffering because the non-conscious aspect of the *prāṇa* predominates and the conscious aspect is submerged; upon satiety, there is happiness because the *prāṇa* and other vital functions become subordinate and the sense of "I" (*ahaṃtā*) predominates, just as for one who is weary, there is happiness from movement.

In the two states of vibration— namely, movement and stillness— there is predominance of the body during movement, and predominance of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*) during rest. For one who knows the reality of immersion into one's own essential nature, which is a mass of consciousness and bliss, there is simply the non-arising of suffering at the time of hunger during that immersion.
For even one who is weak, by assailing [the enemy] at the proper time, may prevail;
likewise, he who is extremely hungry should conceal his hunger until the right moment.
Having mastered that power whose nature is vibration, it proceeds toward its effect.

Thus, one accomplishes even an impossible thing. He who knows the reality of immersion (*samāveśa*) should cover over his hunger when he is intensely hungry; [he should practice] the predominance of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, the field of effort, and the conjunction with suffering—these three—while remaining in a state of subordination regarding agency, whether in the waking or dreaming state.

The triad consisting of deep sleep is indeed to be abandoned. When agency is predominant, there is the ground of exertion and the conjunction with suffering; when agency is predominant, there is the conjunction with pleasure. In the states of waking and so forth, there is the predominance of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and other factors, while agency remains subordinate.

Thus, this triad consisting of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep is entirely to be abandoned; however, from the state of the Fourth (turya) onwards— wherein agency is predominant due to its unfolding— up to the state beyond the Fourth (turyātīta), which consists of stability, that [state] is to be accepted as being of the nature of stability.
When the attainment of the nature that is a mass of the bliss of a single flavor occurs, the desire to grasp and the desire to abandon—these two states of being become powerless due to exhaustion;
the intended meaning is that the Fourth and the Beyond-the-Fourth are what must be imparted. This concerns the three states.
The predominance of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth has been stated as the cause for what is to be abandoned.

If that predominance of the vital breaths and so forth exists only within the triad beginning with the waking state (*jāgrat*), then, because of the absence of the predominance of the vital breaths and so forth in the fourth state (*turya*) and beyond, [the question arises] regarding the immersion (*samāveśa*) into the Self whose nature is the fourth and that which transcends it, concerning the vital breaths and so forth...
The impossibility of the non-falling away of that which consists of the subject would mean that there could be no ascending through the stages of Caitra, Maitra, and so forth.

Anticipating the objection that this is indeed possible because one has entered into the nature of one's own self-consciousness—which is of the essence of the Supreme Lord and free from the impurities of the body and so on—he says: "Beyond sleep and waking, [it is] full."
The supreme vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is the supreme power (*parā-śakti*) whose nature is vibration (*spanda*), consists of the universal life-force that extends from Śiva down to the earth.
Qualities and the like— whether vibrating or non-vibrating— exist by virtue of their dependence upon the universal vibration.
Having attained its own self-nature, it should always remain non-obstructive to the wise one.

Thus, according to the principle stated in the *Śrī Spanda*, for the cognizer in both the states of dreaming and waking, there exists respectively that which consists of prāṇa and apāna, that which consists of the sun and moon, and that which consists of the entire cognizer; furthermore,
even in deep sleep there is that which consists of prāṇa and apāna, and even in the waking state there is that which consists of prāṇa and apāna along with the supreme prāṇa.

In the state of deep sleep (*sauṣupta*), for some time during that condition of profound slumber, the subject becomes the *samāna*— characterized by the cessation of both prāṇa and apāna, consisting of their interruption— and characterized by resting for a while in the heart-abode, which is a region devoid of the senses. In this state of deep sleep, [the subject] is the sun consisting of prāṇa and apāna...
The dissolution-time called *samāna*, which consists of the repose of both moons,
is of the nature of the subject (*pramātṛ*). Like the equinoxes, it is equal to the time of the equinox,
consisting of a general state of day and night devoid of any excess of elevation.

The two paths of the equinoxes—the left and right paths, namely the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*—are so called because they are equal to the time of the equinox (*viṣuvat*), which consists of resting from the movement toward the south and north;

and because they incessantly impel (*suvati*) a slight distinction consisting of the decrease and increase of day and night. Having rendered these paths of the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā* barren (*khilīkṛtya*).
When that very vital breath (*prāṇa*) ascends through the middle path,
it then becomes known as *udāna*, moving with the sun, having reached the fourth state (*turyā*), consisting of fire,
and abiding within itself as the *vijñānākala*, the Mantreśvaras, and the Mantramaheśvaras.
And that vital breath (prāṇa), which is the form of the Lord Ananta who presides over it, is the state beyond the fourth (turyātītaka);

it is the universal self, the supreme, the vital breath whose essence is Paramaśiva. Thus, by means of its own immersion, it sustains the entire universe—from Śiva down to the earth—as the consciousness-nature of Paramaśiva.
That state which is the form of the Supreme Goddess (Parābhaṭṭārikā) is, for its part, a state of universal vibration;
it consists of the vibration common to the entire universe from Śiva down to the earth.
While this state exists—its essence being the imposition of autonomy such as "I am fat," "I am thin," "I am strong," or "I am weak"—it is for this very reason [that the individual soul appears].
The very form of reflective awareness, such as "I am indeed stout, not thin," which is of a manifold nature, assumes a fivefold state consisting of prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna.
In that process of assuming a fivefold state, it partially abandons and partially descends into its internal form.

Having abandoned [the internal] and falling outward, having abandoned the external form and falling inward, it gradually manifests the specific characteristics of being of the nature of *prāṇa* (out-breath) and *apāna* (in-breath).
*Prāṇa*, in the form of exhalation (*ucchvāsa*), having abandoned its internal form, falls upon the external object; so too does *apāna*.

In the form of exhalation (*niśvāsa*), having abandoned the external form, it falls inward; in both cases, abandonment and falling are equal. Thus, these two specificities—namely, the state of *prāṇa* and the state of *apāna*—are clearly manifest to the waking subject in the waking state as two distinct qualities of his own self.

He demonstrates this very clarity: [consciousness] proceeds from the body toward the object until it reaches the end of the universe, and from that object it proceeds back to the body where it comes to rest.

In the state of such experience, there is the state of recollective synthesis (*anusandhāna*), because the mind, having proceeded [outward], comes to rest within the internal object of knowledge itself. And from there, it proceeds into the non-mental (*amanasi*).

Because the prāṇa and apāna are perfectly manifest during the state of waking rest, they certainly exist as prāṇa and apāna even in dream; for even while dreaming, the prāṇa and apāna—which consist of exiting and entering—are clearly present at the sides of the perceiver. (493)

They are characterized by the subject. Even by oneself, through one's own self, a state consisting of rejection and acceptance is accomplished due to the internal flashing of the perception of objects within a dream. By emerging with the mind and falling back into that very same object of perception, a state consisting of rejection and acceptance is brought about.
Because he accepts these two specific types [of breath], there is no incapacity of the means of knowledge;

just as in the waking state there exists that which consists of the two specific types of prāṇa and apāna, so too in dream does that which consists of the two specific types of prāṇa and apāna exist. Dream is [the state] when the cognizer is asleep; in that very [state], it is sleep.
When that which is asleep becomes extremely manifest, then the subject is in deep sleep (*suṣupta*).

The state of deep sleep (*sauṣuptapada*) is twofold: the deep sleep of the vital breath (*prāṇasauṣupta*) and the [deep sleep] of the [supreme] Self (*anya sauṣupta*). It assumes the specific characteristic of the supreme vital breath, which is of a uniform nature.

In the state of deep sleep (*sauṣupta*), when the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is withdrawn, the movement of both *prāṇa* and *apāna* is still perceived. Nevertheless, that rest which occurs between those two—the *prāṇa* and the *apāna*—is a rest from the senses; by means of that, there is a rest in the abode of the heart.
Primarily, deep sleep consists of the *prāṇa* and *apāna*; therein, for some time, during that deep sleep...

The cessation of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths is rest (*viśrānti*). Its essence is the nature of rest; it is the essence of the equalizing activity within the upper regions and across the transverse directions of the body for a person who is being afflicted by the joints and other bodily constituents, because its nature consists in the function of equalization (*samānīkaraṇa*).

By causing the expansion of the heart-lotus, it effects the digestion of what has been eaten and drunk. The *samāna* [vāyu], because it maintains equilibrium for some time between the *prāṇa* and *apāna*—which take the form of day and night—and because it interrupts the flow of *prāṇa* and *apāna*, is equal to the time of the equinox (*viṣuvat-kāla*). It pervades (*viṣu*) [the body].
In the case of *samānīkaraṇamahatī*, because it has the sense of "deserving" (*arha*), it lacks the status of an indeclinable (*avyaya*).

For that [usage], such as in the well-known expressions *udgato nivataḥ*, is established by logic; being established by Vedic logic, it should not be employed [in ordinary discourse]. Or, in this instance, it is indeed employed because it is [part of] the technical treatise (*śāstra*).

Alternatively, it is called the *śatari-viṣuva* because it incessantly impels the breath (*suvati*) toward that specific distinction characterized by the deficiency or excess of day and night. In that *viṣuva*, there exists the state of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* being severed, persisting in the form of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*).

In passages such as "the very existence [of the breaths] in the form of mental formations (*saṃskāra*) is their cessation in the void" and "due to the absence of cognition and so forth," it has been stated that in deep sleep there is a state of latency for both exhalation (*prāṇa*) and inhalation (*apāna*) regarding the processes of rejection and acquisition;
in this much alone do all those belonging to the class of bound souls (*paśu*), from the *pralayākala* downwards, remain equal to the bound soul (*paśu*).

When the vitalizing function, which is the cause of life, flows through the central channel (*madhyamanāḍī*) in an upward form, having caused the paths of *iḍā* and *piṅgalā* to become stilled, then that upward flow of the path brings about the dissolution of all duality, such that one thinks: "I am Caitra alone; I am not Maitra."

The function of *udāna* is that which effects the flow— beginning from the *vijñānākala* up to the end of *sadāśiva*— of the essence of non-duality residing within all dualities such as "the jar is not the cloth," acting like the liquefaction of congealed clarified butter characterized by the act of giving. That [function]...
The state consisting of the fourfold *udāna-vṛtti* is above the stage of *māyā*, known as the *vijñānākala*.

Beginning from the *vijñānākala*, the dissolution of duality proceeds. When duality has dissolved, the entire aggregate of objects of cognition—such as pots, cloths, and so forth—is [perceived] as the *sakala* and other categories of reality.

The activity of vitalization (*prāṇana*), in the form of the upward-moving breath (*udāna*) which pervades the universal body consisting of the categories of the knower, objects of enjoyment, the earth, and the worlds, becomes the state beyond the fourth (*turyātīta*), appropriate for Paramaśiva who is the self of the universe; yet, as the very subject of cognition (*pramātṛ*), it takes the form of the inhaled and exhaled breaths (*prāṇāpāna*) during the states of waking and dreaming.

The state of deep sleep (*sauṣupta*) has the same form as [the *turya*], while in the *turya* it has the form of *udāna*, and in the *turyātīta* it has the form of *vyāna*. This grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established either with respect to the vital breath (*prāṇa*) or the cognizer (*pramātṛ*). Alternatively, that [cognizer] is *udāna*; he is the *vijñānākala*, and he is also the *mantra*, with reference to the class of *vijñānākalas*.

This [state] is designated in relation to the mantras, the subjects (pramātṛ), their lords, and the Great Lords (maheśa) alone, as well as in relation to the presiding deities over that group of subjects;
this is for the purpose of removing the doubt raised at the occasion of the introduction to these two verses.

He states the purport of the two verses with the words "this has been said. In the states of the Fourth (turya) and that which transcends it (tadatīta), the fivefold vitalizing power consisting of the vital breaths (prāṇa) certainly exists; otherwise, if it did not exist, then after the occasion of immersion (samāveśa), there would be no further state of being a cognizer (pramātṛ) characterized by the individuality of life and outward-directed activity.

Furthermore, because emergence is impossible [in those states], and likewise for the Fourth (*turya*) and that which transcends it (*turyātīta*), even though there is the destruction of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in the Fourth due to the withdrawal of differentiation, and in that which transcends the Fourth due to its primary nature as resting in non-duality,
there is an absence of the manifoldness of pleasure, pain, and so forth in these two— the Fourth and that which transcends the Fourth.

Because it consists of supreme bliss, whose nature is resting in one’s own self as a single form, it is indeed to be accepted. However, in deep sleep and similar states, because the diversity consisting of pleasure, pain, and so forth exists merely as latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), there is the manifestation of difference in the form of the vividly perceived objects of dream and waking.
Since diversity such as pleasure and pain exists because they are currently manifest, it is entirely appropriate to say that these three states—waking and so forth—are to be abandoned;

thus, what was stated regarding the "triad to be abandoned" is indeed logical. For the Supreme Śiva, whose body is the universe, his very nature as the fivefold forms beginning with Prāṇa constitutes the state of being the *sakala* (the one-with-parts).
The nature of the subject consists of the internal and external emergence and entry of exertion (*udyoga*) in the states of waking and dreaming;

it takes the form of the entire *prāṇa* and *apāna* in the state of deep sleep; it takes the form of the *samāna* breath, appropriate for the class of *pralayākala* subjects, in the fourth state (*turya*); and in the state beyond the fourth (*turyātīta*), it takes the form of bestowing (*dāna*), appropriate for the class of subjects beginning with *vijñānākala* and ending with Sadāśiva.
By these two sūtras, [the author states] that they have the nature of *vyāna*, which is appropriate for the state of Śiva.
As it is said in the Āgamas, beginning with "thirty-six," and so forth. Thus ends the second chapter.

even while accepting the manifold variety beginning with the infinite portions and so forth, the Self manifests itself as possessing differentiation by way of its own nature— as transcendent to the universe.
He who manifests himself as the Self consisting of full I-consciousness to his devotees— those who have recognized their own self as the Great Lord and are immersed in Him—
and who manifests the wheel of subjects (mātṛcakra) as composed of the infinite categories (tattvas) beginning with Śiva and ending with the Earth; [to him, I bow].
We praise that Śiva who, through uninterrupted and absolute identity, manifests himself even to his devotees, making him manifest in this manner— that is,
by means of self-awareness characterized by the authority of knowledge as previously described.

That very nature of Maheśvara, which has been established through one's own experience characterized by the authority of action, through reasoning, and through the scriptures proclaimed by the Supreme Lord, and which has been extensively determined, is now— having been condensed and established—
in order to instill it within the intellects of disciples; [this is] one's own self alone.
In this chapter, which consists of eighteen verses ending with the words "established for all beings like a blue lotus," he demonstrates the compendium of reality (*tattvārthasaṃgraha*),
that is, the compendium of the ultimate true meaning. Therein,
in this chapter consisting of the compendium of reality, having stated the ultimate intrinsic nature in the verse—

By means of nine verses according to the perspective of the "knower and the known" (*mātṛ-meya*), [the author] describes the nature of bondage consisting of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*); by means of seven [verses], the reality of liberation (*mokṣatattva*) consisting of the recognition of one's own true nature as Maheśvara; and by means of one verse, [he describes how] the Lord is of such a kind and the object of knowledge is of such a kind.
The intended meaning [of the text] demonstrates the summary of the meaning of the "mother-of-pearl" analogy:

for all living beings, this [world] is the resting place of the reflection of the insentient; thus, among all living beings whose essential nature consists of the reflection "I," there are the intermediate appearances of individual souls (*jīvābhāsa*).
According to the principle stated previously, for the subjects ranging from Śiva down to the Sakala, Maheśvara alone is their own self;

indeed, their very self is Maheśvara. And he is one alone, because his nature is consciousness unconditioned by space and time—truly one and without a second. Having internalized the state of "thisness" (idantā) [within himself],...

He is nourished by the undivided awareness of "I" (*aham*); thus, by manifesting his universal form through his sovereignty within his own self of such a nature, he possesses the universal form consisting of all things from Śiva down to the earth. The word *iha* ("here") is an indeclinable that indicates lack of dispute and is universally accepted; it refers to this very [reality].

In this world, insentient objects such as pots and cloths appear only as submerged within consciousness. He demonstrates that they appear precisely because they are submerged in consciousness: "this" is the reflective awareness of the insentient;
it rests only in the reflective awareness of pure consciousness, which is "I. Without that [consciousness], there would be no such thing as "this."
Because, according to the principle that "it is severed" (*vicchinna*), there is no resting in anything else;

and because, by the stated principle that "thus indeed for those who have become insentient," the insentient rest within the reflective awareness (*saṃvit-parāmarśa*) of "I"—and since the insentient lack selfhood, only living beings (*jantu*), that is, living souls (*jīva*), possess a self (*sātmān*); of them...

For living beings, one's own self alone is Maheśvara; there is no other whatsoever, because one's own self is of the nature of consciousness (*saṃvit*). Therefore, one's own self alone is Maheśvara, for there is no division in consciousness by way of space, time, or form, due to its being all-pervasive, eternal, and perfect in essence.
Let these factors— place and so forth— be mutually distinct from one another here and now as having such-and-such a form;
however, those things such as the body, vital breath, and intellect fall on the side of the insentient, and since they are submerged within consciousness itself,
the conscious Self alone exists as one, because it is devoid of place, time, and form, unlike objects such as a jar or the body which occupy a single location.

Since it causes the manifoldness of forms (*vaiśvarūpya*) to manifest within its own self, therefore, by means of that manifestation of manifoldness, having caused the "this-ness" (*idantā*)— which is the universal self— to rest within the form of the "I-ness" (*ahantā*),
one becomes full of the reflective awareness of "I," which consists in resting solely within one's own self that is not oriented toward "this-ness."

Therefore, because this self of mine is filled with the reflective awareness of "I" (aham-vimarśa) which permeates the entire range of subjects from Śiva down to the limited individual (sakala), its omniscience and omnipotence do not need to be established through effort; [it is evident that] "I am the hearer, I am the toucher, I am the taster, I am the smeller."

Just as the states of being a knower and an agent occur for a single Self with respect to the various objects of the cognitive and active faculties— such as "I shall speak," "I shall take," "I shall go," and "I shall release"— so too do they occur in the Supreme Lord with respect to His thousands of Rudra-fields, which are like the manifestations of the senses.

Knowledge and action pertaining to the aggregate of objective existence belong to the Rudras; the Rudras who have transcended Māyā are subjects (pramātṛ) graced by the glance of the true Guru. Furthermore, the individual souls (kṣetrajña) who reside within Māyā are subjects; for them, that respective knowledge and its instrument [of action] are unified in one place.

It belongs to the one alone within the conscious self (*cidātman*). The single conscious self alone, abiding as the class of subjects—the Rudras and the *kṣetrajñas*—has the sense of "I know" and "I act.
(498) If the one [self] in the form of the Great Lord (*Maheśvara*) is one's own self, then [objects such as] a jar and [the body] rest within it.
Because it is the ground [of all], if the self whose nature is that of Maheśvara were indeed one and non-dual,
then the cause of the self’s manifoldness— such as "I am fat," "I am thin," "I am Caitra," "I am Maitra," "I am a partaker of merit," or "I am an evildoer"— would be a fetter.
What is the substratum of that bondage? Since there is no bondage for the Self in its form as Maheśvara,
and because there exists nothing else whatsoever distinct from it, for whose liberation— that is, for the release from which connection— the instruction of the Pratyabhijñā-śāstra is intended.

(Ṭp. [386] 396) This knowledge has three sources: from the guru, from the scripture, and from oneself—according to the principle thus stated, it takes such forms as first the instruction of the guru, then the study of the scripture through his mouth, and thereafter one’s own direct experience, and so forth.
This effort is for the sake of liberating from that very bondage;
O Lord, this occurs either through the power of His grace or indeed through the arrival of a Guru.
Or from the scripture of the Supreme Lord; therefore, by means of that [scripture].
"This thorough knowledge of reality is liberation and supreme lordship;
that is the fullness of the awakened, and it is remembered as liberation while living.
Thus, when the Great Lord resides within one's own self in the form of that very light, [it is so].

Within the mirror of its own self—the Supreme Lord created by Himself—there exists, amidst His own creation, that which takes the form of "this-ness" (*idantā*), namely the intellect, vital breath, body, and so forth. This very [reality], by this Supreme Lord acting as the subject (*grāhakātman*), has been brought to the state of the reflective awareness of the "I-sense" (*ahaṃkāra-parāmarśa*). That [identification] with the intellect and the rest is bondage.
This is the remainder [of the sentence].

Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*): one meaning is that one's own self alone is the [self] of all living beings, as stated; thus, [the phrase means] "while the Great Lord resides within one's own self. Furthermore, [it refers to] that which has the nature of light (*prakāśa*).

In that mirror of one's own self— the Great Lord, who is the nature of full *ahantā* and capable of reflecting the universe— that [universe] was created by Him as this objective portion (*idambhāga*), preceded by the void consisting of the contraction of His own essential nature. In the midst of that, within this objective state, it is perceived as "this-ness" (*idantayā*).

That which consists of intellect, vital breath, and body—such as a jar and so forth—is distinct from oneself; for the sake of being an object of cognition, it requires an appropriate intellect and other faculties.
Because of its power to overcome [the self], by what means could there be the sense of fullness through the "I-feeling," such as "I am Devadatta" or "I am Caitra"?
Let it be so; let the term "I" be understood as referring to the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) consisting of the intellect (*buddhi*) and the rest.

Nevertheless, whose is the bondage? There is no other [agent] distinct from the Lord (*īśvara*), because the intellect and the rest, being manifest, are of the nature of the Lord. And that [Lord] appears in the form of the intellect and so forth belonging to Caitra, Maitra, and others.

The cognizer (*pramātā*) consists of the non-recognition of his own true nature; he is constructed through the non-recognition of the nature of perfect I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*). For this very reason, by grasping at various bodies, vital breaths, and so forth, he becomes a manifold person (*pumān*);
he is thus the enjoyer (*bhoktā*), meaning the experiencer of merit and demerit. In that regard, [this state] was created by the Lord (*īśvara*) within the person.
Activity (*kriyā*) and bliss (*ānanda*) are the qualities of *rajas* and *sattva* respectively; experience consists of pleasure and pain.
The quality of *tamas* serves as the locus of rest for both, and it too is considered a form of experience because it is composed of *prakṛti*, which consists of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
What you have said is true from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*): there is no connection whatsoever;

rather, it is the Supreme Lord alone who, through His sovereignty—which is most excellent and performs what is exceedingly difficult to accomplish—manifests His own Self, which consists of full subjectivity (*pūrṇāhantā*), as the contracted world of existence (*bhava*). (Ṭīkā, p. 387)

397) At whatever time, during that moment of manifestation, although one's own full form is appearing, there is non-recognition (*aparijñāna*) consisting of a lack of reflective awareness (*aparāmarśa*). That very non-recognition is what is posited as the cause for a person such as Caitra; however, he—
The *puruṣa* is said to be that which consists merely in the non-manifestation (*akhyāti*) of the fullness residing within—even such [notions] as "I am Śiva" or "I am Īśvara.
Because it is designated by the term "puruṣa," it is manifold. He demonstrates this very multiplicity with the words "that...
that": "I am fat," "I am thin," "I am weak," "I am strong."

"I am happy," "I am suffering"—thus, by assuming various contractions consisting of the body, vital breath, and intellect, the Self becomes manifold. For this very reason, the person (puruṣa) experiences bondage in the form of the cognition of pleasure, pain, and so forth.
This is what is called "enjoyment" (bhoga) for that person, fashioned by the Supreme Lord within creation.

Action and bliss. For imagined action is indeed suffering; [the text] shows that action has the nature of suffering through the passage beginning with "rajo 'pi" (even rajas). For *rajas* consists of a portion characterized by mobility belonging to both *sattva* and *tamas*—namely, light and non-light—and its nature is unstable.
Happiness is described as follows: *sattva* alone, whose nature is luminosity, is happiness.

The non-luminous form common to both sorrow and happiness—which serves as the locus for the dissolution of both—is the state of dissolution. He describes the conceptualization of that locus of dissolution: therein, in the process of creation, there is the bliss of activity (*kriyānanda*).
In this context, by the phrase "emitted" (*sṛṣṭā*), it is indicated that there is something unemitted as well.
Anticipating the question of what is to be excluded and what is to be accepted between those two, he says:
"Of the Lord, [the world] from Earth up to Śiva, who consists of the reflective awareness 'I' (*aham*)."

Regarding the Lord Śiva, that which is their "I-ness" (*aham-eva*) is the knowledge within them; and the activity (*kriyā*), which is of the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) that animates that knowledge, belongs to the Lords Sadāśiva and Īśvara— whose forms consist of the reflective awareness "I am this" and "this is I"— as well as to those known as the Mantramaheśvaras who are presided over by them.

Just as for the subject of Māyā, from the head down to the feet, all things that constitute his own body are of the nature of his own self, so too, regarding those objects that have become his own limbs, there is a lack of knowledge— that is, ignorance— concerning their status as being his own limbs. This occurs sequentially within the two classes of subjects with respect to those entities that have become their own selves or their own limbs.
The act of discernment (*avamarśana*) by means of that which has become one's own limb constitutes the knowledge and action of the venerable Lord Śiva;

and for the venerable Lords Sadāśiva and Īśvara, who exist in the form of presiding deities, [these consist of] "I am this" and "this is I," because of the manifestation of the first sprout of objectivity (*idantā*).

Knowledge and action exist together with Māyā. In that regard, for the bound soul (*paśu*), knowledge arises sequentially as *sattva* and action as *rajas*, while [the former] consists of the nature of Māyā. (501) As for the Lord Śiva of universal form (*viśvarūpa*), there is the light of "I" (*aham*) which pervades everywhere, from Sadāśiva down to the Earth.

The reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) that is the vital breath of the manifestation "I"—that indeed constitutes the knowledge and action of that venerable Lord Śiva; for, without ever abandoning the self-reflective awareness of His own nature as "I," He assumes the state of objectivity (*idantā*) in the form: "I am this, this is I."
Furthermore, that which has the nature of expansion, yet rests in the self-reflection of "I" as its own essential form—

that reflective awareness whose ultimate reality is the reflection "I am this, this is I, I am this"— is the Lord Sadāśiva-Īśvara, because it is characterized primarily by the sprout of "this-ness" (idantā).

That power of illusion (māyā-śakti), which was created by the venerable Lord Śiva and pertains to the venerable Lord Sadāśiva and Īśvara— namely, the three powers consisting of knowledge, action, and illusion— were emitted sequentially from the Blessed Lord Sadāśiva and the Blessed Lord Īśvara as their innate [qualities].
They are established by their own nature because the true form of that very Blessed One is concealed by His own power of māyā; thus,

when there is non-recognition of one's own true nature, [one perceives] even those entities which are one's own limbs as being distinct from one's own nature and from each other, thinking "I am I" and "this is this alone."

That knowledge which is of the nature of bliss is *sattva*; action associated with differentiated states is *rajas*, which is suffering; that which is devoid of both illumination (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), being of the nature of *māyā*, is *tamas*, which is delusion (*moha*). For the bound soul (*paśu*), *sattva*—which consists of the knowledge of illumination—is bliss, while illumination and non-illumination [constitute the other two].

Suffering is of the nature of *rajas* for both [the individual soul and the Lord]; delusion is of the nature of *tamas*, which is non-illumination (*aprakāśa*). Thus, in sequence, knowledge, action, and *māyā* constitute the *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* of the bound soul (*paśu*). Knowledge, action, and *māyā* themselves are the *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* of consciousness (*cetana*) in their respective order.

Just as knowledge, action, and *māyā* are called inseparable powers (*avyatirekiṇyaḥ śaktayaḥ*) of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), so too would it follow that *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* are inseparable powers of the bound soul (*paśu*). These [qualities] are insentient (*jaḍa*) because they are objects of experience (*bhogya*) in the form of pleasure, pain, and delusion.

They are said to be distinct from the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*) because they possess materiality (*pustatva*). To dispel the doubt as to how this is so, he says: "Of these [qualities]—sattva, rajas, and tamas—which undergo transformation into the internal organs such as the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) and so forth, and into effects ranging from sound to earth..."

The meaning is that although the qualities (*guṇas*) lack power (*aśaktimattva*), because they are suspected by you to possess power (*śaktimattva*), their status as power is not asserted; rather, because their distinctness is established— that is, because they exist as distinct— they are asserted to be merely qualities.
"What you have said is true"—this is a statement of objection. "In this way":

even *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* would possess the status of being powers (*śakti*). If there were no apprehension of the difference between them and the *puruṣa*, then this conventional usage of the distinction between *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* from the *puruṣa* [would not exist].
This is now being investigated. In this context of the conventional usage of difference, the *puruṣa* has a nature consisting solely of contracted consciousness (*saṃkucitacinmātra*).

For this *puruṣa*, the manifestation and reflective awareness (*prakāśavimarśana*) directed toward objects such as jars and cloths is neither innate nor natural. If it were innate for this bound soul (*paśu*), [then...]
Because [otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence of manifestation and so forth even in states such as deep sleep; because [the power] is produced by a connection with another—

that is, produced by a connection with the Supreme Lord— and therefore, since it lacks spontaneity, these [powers] do not exist in the *paśu* (bound soul), who, despite being conceived as possessing power, is distinct from that [Lord] due to his lack of power.

Since sattva and the other [guṇas] exist as distinct entities, they are not called "powers" (śakti) because they are free from differentiation. However, because they serve as instruments for the bound soul (paśu),
and because they take the form of the instruments of experience consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion, they are called "qualities" (guṇa).
Why are sattva and the other [guṇas] not accepted as distinct from the Puruṣa? It is said: they are not accepted as distinct;

if they are accepted as non-distinct, then the fault that will be stated hereafter occurs. The tenfold cause consisting of the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion is the tenfold effect, which is the form resulting from the transformation of pleasure, pain, and delusion.

And because that [unmanifest] consists of transformation, it is experienced as having pleasure, pain, and delusion as its essential nature; thus, pleasure, pain, and delusion— functioning through identity with the categories of instruments and effects— would share identity with the Puruṣa as well, just as they do with the instruments and effects, if that were the case, then the Puruṣa alone...

The [doctrine] that consists of creation, which culminates in the completion of the task and the completion of the process, is not tenable as a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of consciousness— just like the sequence of seed and sprout— and this transformation has been refuted by the three verses beginning with "if there were mutual identity of nature" (*paraspara-svabhāvatva*). Furthermore, even in the absence of the power of independence (*svātantrya-śakti*), the Person (*puruṣa*)...
The term "viśvarūpa" (the universal form) has been introduced. From primordial nature (*prakṛti*) down to the earth, it is called "viśvarūpa.

Likewise, when [the Self] possesses the universal form through the power of absolute freedom (*svātantryaśakti*), there is no such thing as a "puruṣa" (individual soul). For him, the state of being a *puruṣa* does not even exist; rather, he is nothing other than the Lord (*īśvara*). All of this has been stated.
This is the application of a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*). Therefore, because it results in a reductio,

according to the stated reasoning that "a single person is not held to consist of the non-recognition of his own true nature," when there is an investigation into the nature of the person consisting of non-recognition, the qualities such as *sattva* and so forth [are considered].
It is established that [the soul] is indeed distinct from the Puruṣa.

Anticipating the question at the end—how is it that the qualities (guṇas) such as sattva and the rest, which consist of knowledge, action, and māyā, come to belong to the bound soul (paśu)—he says: "Of knowledge, action, and māyā..."

He describes the very state of being subordinate to the *paśu* (the bound soul) by means of [the following]: the existence of the Lord (*pati*), the protector of the universe, who brings forth the world through emanation and so forth, is His very agency—the creative act of bringing the universe into being. That same [existence] is nothing other than the wonder of the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).

Because it consists in resting within one's own self through the supreme renunciation of the [worldly] bliss of mere existence, that [agency] belongs to the Lord; for the *paśu*, however, it is otherwise.

This is the state of being. Thus, for the bound soul (paśu), the very absence of existence, being, and bliss becomes the quality of darkness (tamas), which consists of delusion.
