The quality of goodness (sattva), consisting of pleasure and pain, exists in part as the nature of pleasure for the bound soul; that which is the mixed nature of both goodness (sattva) and passion (rajas) is the self of these two.
That [state] consists of *sattva* and *tamas* in mutual contact and is of the nature of suffering; it is the *rajas* of the Lord (*pati*).

In the state of the bound soul (*paśu*), *sattva* is the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) of the Lord, *rajas* is the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), and *tamas* is the power of illusion (*māyā-śakti*).

In this philosophy of consciousness (*saṃvid-darśana*), He who protects the universe through the fivefold activity (*pañca-kṛtya*)— characterized by the diversity of its manifestation— is called the Lord (*pati*), whose essential nature is self-luminosity.
This is that "vibration" (*sphurattā*) or "Great Being" (*mahāsattā*) previously explained in this context.

The existence of the Lord of the Universe as the agent of manifestation is the very agency of His own Self as the Universal Self; according to the principle stated [in verse 504], that very existence is the nature of the light of manifestation. Thus, the Lord’s sovereignty as the agent of the manifestation of the universe is the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) which constitutes His vital breath.

Through the process of exclusion (*vyatireka*), according to the principle stated as "I am that," the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) consisting of the form of the awareness "I" is called the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*). Existence itself, which consists in the manifestation of the universe, is called the power of action; for the Lord of the Universe, it is that very existence.

Because there is no other object distinct from itself, bliss arises as the state of resting in one's own self through the abandonment of orientation toward the "other. This very nature of the Lord consists of consciousness (*cit*), which is his form; it is his existence (*sattā*), his bliss (*ānanda*), and his activity (*kriyā*). For the bound soul (*paśu*), however, this exists only partially.

And there occurs both bliss (*ānanda*) and the absence of both. Due to the contracted nature of consciousness, there is an absence of existence (*sattā*) and bliss. In that state, by virtue of this contracted nature of consciousness, that portion of existence and bliss which pertains to the bound soul (*paśu*) constitutes the soul’s state of manifestation, pleasure, and being. Among these, regarding existence (*sattā*):

Aṃśa is the function of illumination (*prakāśavṛtti*). This *sattva*, which consists of both [illumination and bliss], is that in which there is an absence of existence (*sattā*) and bliss (*ānanda*); this is, respectively, *tamas* in the form of obscuration (*āvaraṇa*) and delusion (*moha*).
*Tamas* is the absence of illumination in the form of obscuration; *tamas* is the absence of bliss in the form of delusion. These two...

Just as the qualities *sattva* and *tamas* exist through mutual exclusion— just as an object consists of both a blue nature and a non-blue nature— and just as the states of cause and effect exist through mutual exclusion, even so, for a single cognizer who possesses both *sattva* and *rajas*, [these two] exist by means of one...

By means of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*)— in relation to the subject as the locus of the effect— the subject, the cognizer, shines forth in accordance with the principle of the blue-colored form residing in the subject (the butterfly) depicted in a painting;
therefore, because of this mixed manifestation, he is the self of the dyad.

Because its nature is a mixture of *sattva* and *tamas*, there is here a state of union between *sattva* and *tamas*, which are respectively luminous and non-luminous; due to this conjunction with the quality of *rajas*, it is characterized by suffering (*duḥkha*). Pleasure (*sukha*) is the intense, singular external manifestation of light—free from disease and free from affliction—belonging to a beloved son or the like, being a single, solid mass. "A single, solid mass" [means...]

Delusion (*moha*) is of the nature of non-reappearance and is unmanifest; however, that which is somehow manifest through the body’s state of being afflicted with disease— as perceived directly by the subject—
is somehow manifest as something desired and cherished by the cognizer, such as the absence of illness and so forth.

The non-manifestation of the possession of wholesome qualities (*kalyāṇadharma*) in some way is itself the manifestation of illness and the non-manifestation of health; thus both constitute the reality of suffering (*duḥkhatattva*). Of these two, the former is the manifestation of illness, while the latter is the future state of health.
"Manifestation" (*prakāśa*) is the essence of the temporal sequence of a disease; it is the ultimate reality of all actions.

By this, it is stated that *sattva* is of the nature of manifestation, *tamas* is of the nature of non-manifestation, and *rajas* is of the nature of both manifestation and non-manifestation. *Rajas* thus possesses the dual nature of both *sattva* and *tamas*.
Let it be so. For both [of these], there is no fourth quality of the bound soul (*paśu*) consisting of the absence of both.

If one asks why, it is because that quality which is neither-nor does not enter into the cognition—the intellect—of the knower, which consists of ascertainment and has the nature of being both imagined and non-imagined; for that [quality] lacks the nature of ascertainment.
For it is thus that [the text] illuminates precisely the lack of entry [into the object]: "This is blue. The presence of blue appears in the cognition determined by the knower;

however, the absence of blue—which is of a non-blue nature—because it appears as the word "blue" at the time of the manifestation of blue, is constructed by conceptual thought (*vikalpa*). This is because one thinks, "There exists some [entity] which is the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) of this blue."

Because it appears, it is the ultimate reality of conventional discourse; yet, through the intermingling of both— the blue and the non-blue, the perceptible and the imperceptible, and the blue and the non-blue— there is that entity called "neither blue nor non-blue," which is neither existence nor non-existence, consisting of the absence of both light and darkness, and possessing the nature of neither.
That unconstructed, perceptually manifest cognition of blue, which has not been made an object by logical reasoning,
pursues this non-dual entity that is neither [blue nor non-blue] as an unconstructed [cognition].
If it enters into the constructed cognition of blue through perception, then it would pursue the constructed cognition of non-blue.

Because it lacks substantiality (*vastutva*) by its very nature, the real entity does not enter into the non-conceptualized cognition of blue; for this very reason, the entity does not follow after the conceptualized cognition of non-blue either.
He raises an objection with "Now" (*atha*): [the opponent argues that] the entity, being of neither nature, [would follow] the conceptualized cognition of non-blue...

If it is argued that [existence] does not enter [into the object], then blue, being made an object by a non-imagined, perceptual cognition of blue, would be nothing other than blue itself. That [existence], which is neither of those two and is made an object by a non-imagined [cognition], being identical to blue, would be existence alone. There is no fourth quality belonging to the thread for a beast. The word "api" has the sense of "and."
That existence of the bound soul (paśu) is the state of Viśvapati; its presence is *sattva*, its absence is *tamas*, and that which consists of both is *rajas*—such is the connection.

Thus, in the manner described, the nature of the Lord (*pati*), the bound soul (*paśu*), and the principle of the subject (*pramātṛ-tattva*) have been determined. (Ṭīkā p. 392) To determine the principle of the object of knowledge (*prameya-tattva*) for both the Lord and the bound soul, he first speaks in order to determine the principle of the object of knowledge as it pertains to the Lord, whose form will be described below: "Those who..."

Entities such as "this is the Lord," "this is a jar," or "this is a cloth" are devoid of conventional linguistic usage; therefore, they are not within the scope of the conventional awareness of "this-ness" (*idantā*), but rather belong to the non-conventional *idantā*. What, then, are the *vibhāvas*? They are, for the bound soul (*paśu*), characterized by both mixed and unmixed forms.

Even for the Lord, who appears as variegated through a mixture of mixed and unmixed forms, there appear entities consisting of universals that are diverse, devoid of mutual intermingling, and whose nature consists of particulars (svalakṣaṇa) which are essentially collections of multiple universals.

In this philosophy of consciousness (*saṃvid-darśana*), it has been stated that objects are merely manifestations (*ābhāsa*) such as "this" or "of such a kind. These objects—such as "a white jar"—are sometimes mixed together in the form of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya*), when the objects possess the nature of specific individualities (*svalakṣaṇa*); and sometimes [they are not].

When objects, which possess a dual nature consisting of both the universal and the particular, are rested upon a single substratum yet perceived separately, they are apprehended in their universal form by means of a non-conventional,
unconstructed cognition such as "this is a jar" or "this is a cloth."

By means of the reflective awareness of innate differentiation— that is, by means of the reflective awareness of natural differentiation— such as the pointing with a finger and so forth, this [object] should be made an object of perception through its state of "not-this-ness," not only for the Lord, but also for one who has just been born at that moment.

For one who is indolent, unlearned, and accustomed to improper conventional usage, [the object] appears as a manifoldity (*citratayā*)—existing within the sphere of conventional reflection on "this-ness" (*idantā*)—in the form of both universal and particular, even for the Lord, that is, the Supreme Sovereign (*īśvara*), it does not appear as a manifoldity. As for what is called "manifoldness" (*citratva*): [The text continues: ...it is the state of being variegated through the simultaneous manifestation of various attributes. It is like the appearance of a painting, where diverse forms are perceived at once. This is the nature of the manifestation of the object for those whose cognitive faculties are limited by worldly convention. However, for the Lord, who is free from all such limitations, there is no such manifoldness; rather, everything is experienced as a single, undivided reality. Thus, the distinction between the ordinary perceiver and the sovereign consciousness lies in this very unity versus diversity.

And the state of being mixed with the nature of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) is a manifestation through simultaneous repose in a single I-consciousness, like [colors] on the surface of a wall. Because the state of Īśvara is inseparable from the emergence of the universe, it exists within the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), which consists of the contraction of consciousness characterized by full I-consciousness.
It is not manifest at all; for the object [of negation] is not colored by the thing to be negated.

Here, in the state of the Lord (Īśvara), this void—which is the manifestation of the "this-aspect" (idamaṃśa)—is the void that constitutes the "I-aspect" (ahamaṃśa) as something to be negated in some measure. It consists of the negation of the "I-ness" (ahantā).
He clarifies this conventional identity: such, then, is the case for Īśvara.

In this way, the reality of the object of knowledge does not exist as an object of knowledge within the Lord Paramaśiva; rather, the Lord’s very nature as Sadāśiva-Īśvara consists precisely in his being the one who brings forth the discourse concerning objects of knowledge.

Having described the nature of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) with respect to the Lord (*pati*), he describes the nature of the object of knowledge with respect to the bound soul (*paśu*) in three verses. The particle *tu* serves to indicate a distinction: the object of knowledge for the bound soul is of such a nature [as previously stated], but it is not, as in the case of the Lord, characterized by a mixture according to the logic already explained. (p. 393)

Objects appearing as distinct—whether in the form of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) or universal forms (*sāmānyarūpa*)—are traditionally held to be within the range of memory, imagination, and so forth; that is, they appear in memory, in imagination, in direct experience, in conceptualization, in volition, and so on, through such [notions] as "this is dear" or "this is an enemy. These [objects] are mutually...
They are to be conceptualized through distinct designations;

that is, they are to be conceptualized by means of various designations corresponding to the specific qualities of entities, which serve as the causes for respective pleasure, pain, and so forth. For that beast, [the thought] "this one is my friend" or "this one is my enemy" is unique to me.

The creation [of the notion] "my enemy is my friend" is restricted to each individual cognizer; this very creation—such as "Caitra belongs to me" or "Maitra belongs to me"—subsists upon objective reality and pertains to the bound soul (*paśu*) whose nature is that of the Lord (*īśvara*). Furthermore, it serves to obstruct the repose in one's own Self, which consists of full subjectivity (*pūrṇāhantā*).

He is beloved by that [power] which consists of the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is composed of the circle of deities beginning with Brahmā, which takes on the various colors and forms of this or that [letter], which exists as the very nature of the individual soul (*paśu*) through its state of knowledge, which is raised up by the power of the Lord (*īśvara-śakti*), and which is suited to the diversity of these respective letters. (508)

"Enemy," and so forth: that particular creation of the bound soul (paśu), unique to him, arises through the power of conceptualization (vikalpa-śakti) variegated by the diversity of those respective phonemes. This highlights the distinction between the creation of the Lord (īśvara) and the creation of the bound soul; he states this very point as follows:

The objects of the individual soul (pratyagātman), who is like a bound animal (paśu), are objects in the form of cognizable things (*prameya*) according to the nature that will be described hereafter, just as [objects belong] to the Lord (īśvara). Here, there appears to be a break in the manuscript.

(509) Objects whose identity as "this" arises from non-conventional [intuition] do not likewise arise from conventional conceptualization of "this. Those for whom light manifests as differentiated both in its particular nature (*svalakṣaṇa*) and in its universal nature (*sāmānya*) through a state of intermingling.
Objects, which consist of both the particular and the universal, incline toward and find rest in each individual person as distinct entities;
thus, the *pratyagātman*— the non-confused self-luminous "I"—
who resides within the body measuring eight cubits (*aṣṭāratni*), has [all things] as his objects of conceptualization.
They are not subject to the husband’s arbitrary will; rather, for every living being and for every individual,
they vary according to the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of their respective experiences— such as "this one is dear" or "this one is an enemy"—
in accordance with specific mental dispositions (*bhāvanā*) such as "this one is dear" or "this one is an enemy."

The connection is as follows: through the successive engagement with various pleasures, pains, and so forth, by means of designations, these [objects] are to be conceptualized in memory, in imaginative construction, in volitional thought, in conceptualization following upon direct perception, and in synthetic synthesis.

(Ṭp. 394) Here he states the intended meaning: "For the Lord, these objects—such as 'this is an enemy,' 'this is a friend,' and so forth—are not characterized by conceptual thought (*vikalpa*). Rather, objects are to be made the objects of pure reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) in the form of 'I am this,' 'this is I,' and 'I am this. For the bound soul (*paśu*), however, objects exist only through mutual exclusion (*anyonyāpohana*)."

They become mounted upon conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) due to curiosity. Because they are useful for worldly transactions such as the abandonment of the enemy that is saṃsāra and the bestowing of gifts upon a friend—namely, the practice of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted—those objects appear only when mounted upon conceptual construction. As long as the Lord remains free from conceptual construction, however great the object may be...
It is exactly the same for the bound soul (paśu). Therefore, what is the distinction regarding the object of cognition having the nature of an "other"?

For that [bound soul], the creation performed by the bound soul exists above the creations of the Lord; in this very sense, subsisting upon the creation of the Lord according to its own desire, it is "uncommon," being restricted to each individual subject.

The creation of a potter is one thing, while the creation of a tailor is another; thus, [creation] is restricted to each individual subject (*pratipramātṛ*). He demonstrates this very point with the words "tadyathā" (for example) and "idaṃ hṛdyam" (this is pleasing).
Whatever object is created by someone, that belongs to him alone; for instance, sugarcane is not desired by one who has phlegm disorders, nor is it desired by one who has leprosy.

(510) A person made of wool is dear to him alone and not to anyone else; yet, like the Lord, even the bound soul (*paśu*) possesses the power of creation. If that is so, then the Lord is just like the bound soul. True. He too is a Lord, for he is the creator of the bound souls; just as there is the creation of the earth and other elements, there is also the creation of the bound souls.

How is it not common to all? If he were to fully realize, "I too am the Lord; by the power of the Lord I create," then it would be common. However, such is not the case for us; that [power] is his own power, and though it is known to him, he does not know it as his own power, because he is dependent on another.

For that [subject], the power of conceptualization arises such that "this is an enemy" or "this is a friend. By what is that power of conceptualization obtained? He answers: "By 'A'. This is because it consists of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the perfect "I" (*pūrṇāham*).

I am the one who, through that power— which consists of the wheel of deities beginning with Brahmā, which serves the purpose of obstructing the state of Supreme Lordship characterized by resting in my own essential nature, and which is variegated by the diverse array of phonemes such as *ā* and so forth belonging to the Lord whose characteristic is the mass of sounds (*śabdarāśi*)— have been raised up.

The two tastes are the activity of conceptualization (*vikalpaka-kriyā*) belonging to the bound soul (*paśu*); because it is unstable even with respect to a single object, it is flickering like the moon in water, and due to its flickering nature, it is bound by the variety of mental constructs such as "friend" or "enemy.
By means of that activity of conceptualization, [the state of] that very bound soul—which is essentially the nature of the Lord (*īśvara-svabhāva*)—[is manifested].
The creation of the animal is unique: a five-tusked, four-faced elephant running through the sky.
Even when there is a mixture based on animals, such as "five elephants," that is a conceptual creation; these [numbers] beginning with five are created by the Lord.

It has been stated that "one subsists solely upon speech," meaning that the entire creation of the conceptual constructions of the bound soul (*paśu*) subsists upon the creation of the Lord (*īśvara*).
If, according to the manner described, the bondage-creating agency of the *paśu* is a creation consisting of transmigratory existence, then—
What could a creation authored by the Supreme Lord do for the bound soul (*paśu*)? Divine creation is twofold:
common and otherwise. That which is clearly manifest, such as a jar and the like, is the common;
"otherwise" refers to the uncommon, such as a double moon and so forth. Furthermore, "otherwise" refers to that which is already fully known.
If, through power (*śakti*), there is full realization of identity with the Lord (*īśvara-tādātmya*), then even for the bound soul (*paśu*), creation becomes common [to the Lord].

Although creation consists of both [subject and object], by abandoning the conceptualization that excludes one from the other (*anyonyāpohana-vikalpa-hāna*), and through constant one-pointedness like Śiva— thinking "I am this"— the state of lordship (*īśvaratā-pada*) gradually arises even for the bound soul.
It occurs.
That which is indicated by the word "otherwise" (anyathā)—such as a double moon and so forth—is the common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of both;
namely, the manifestation of a jar and so forth in the form of a jar and so forth, and the manifestation of a double moon and so forth in the form of a double moon and so forth.

Illumination: Even though the creation consists of both [subject and object], by means of the gradual abandonment of such conceptual constructions as "I am one, Caitra is another, and the jar and so forth are yet others," one grasps the object—which consists of both—as "this is indeed I" through a non-conceptual state that has been thoroughly embraced; thus, one becomes single-mindedly focused on the object consisting of both as "this is indeed I."

When the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the bound soul— that "this is indeed it"— becomes the locus of the supreme divine awareness (*aiśvara-parāmarśa*), then, for the object standing before one, there occurs within the heart a state free from the opening and closing of the eyes (*nimeṣonmeṣa*).

Through the sequence of instruction beginning with "the outward gaze" (*bahirdṛṣṭi*) and so forth, by means of the excellence of practice, the divine creation destroys the state of being a bound soul (*paśu*) and reveals the state of being the Lord (*īśvara*).
Furthermore, by the verse beginning with "her [power] is common," this which is the conceptualized creation (*vikalpasarga*)—

The extraordinary creation that is elevated belongs to the bound soul (*paśu*) who has not fully realized his own power and has not realized his identity with the Lord. "Otherwise" means: when it occurs through the opposite—that is, by the power of the Lord which is not fully realized [by him] while his identity [with Him] is fully realized—then it is the creation of the bound soul.
Nourishment, consecration, daily rites, and the strengthening of what is desired— likewise,

the malevolent rite (*abhicāraṇa*) for the destruction of enemies, the pacification of diseases, and so forth, become common to all when performed by a practitioner whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) has been purified by the deposited mantras; it is just like that.
The creation of even a beast is common [to all].

Thus, by abandoning conceptualization—which consists of mutual exclusion—in the manner described, through becoming one with the nature of non-conceptual awareness (*nirvikalpaka*), there arises the "I-ness" (*ahantā*) of the universe as "I am this, this is I. (p. 396)

Others maintain that liberation has been shown as something characterized by the state of being a "sat-kāra" (one who has attained the goal), established through one's own conviction and personal experience for the bound soul (*paśu*), occurring upon the abandonment of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Now, he demonstrates that liberation exists even in the absence of the abandonment of conceptual construction: "This entire collection of principles (*tattva-grāma*), from Śiva down to the earth..."

For one who fully realizes, "All this is my own manifestation," and who is therefore the Self of the universe, even the expansion of the animal's conceptual constructions becomes the state of the Great Lord.
Regarding the term "the inner self" (*pratyagātman*): it is that which, for each individual person, is its own unmixed...

I am that very Supreme Lord, a mass of luminosity, whose nature is the "I" as both the grasped and the grasper, embraced as my own limb according to the principle stated: "I am not some other limited being (paśu) characterized by the pursuit of sensory perception, but rather [I am He] within all entities that constitute my own limbs. I am He alone.

He too is indeed myself and not another; he does not exist as distinct from me. Therefore, because there is no mutual exclusion between us, even the conceptual creation of objects such as pots and cloths is my own power, characterized by absolute freedom (*svātantrya*). When such an awareness of reality has become firmly established, [the state of liberation is attained].

Even while his conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) are not yet fully exhausted, he is liberated even while living; he should not entertain even a doubt that causes transmigratory existence—such as the thought, "I am one, the Supreme Lord is another, and a jar or other objects are yet another.
This nature of the Self, which is identical with the Supreme Lord, is realized through the absence of doubt.
For what is called "conceptual construction" (vikalpa) is clearly not a state of unconsciousness; therefore,
it being established that even that which is being conceptualized is manifestation, it is indeed real— just like Brahman— precisely because it is manifesting.

Regarding the object of knowledge (*prameya*), what is the difference between the bound (*baddha*) and the liberated (*mukta*)? The liberated one, like the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), perceives the object of knowledge as distinct from his own self, yet as something common [to all]. The bound one, however, perceives the object of knowledge as being absolutely non-different [from himself]. [This is the state of] the venerable Sadāśiveśvara...

Beginning from the highest limit down to the smallest worm, one identifies as one's own self that very form which is the "I," the presiding subject over the entire class of perceivers. As it has been said:
"That which appears individually shines forth to each [subject] with the thought, 'This arises for me.'"

"The Lord Mārtāṇḍa appears as a single cognizer, Śiva, to each and every living being—whether they dwell in mountains, cities, villages, or forests—who traverses the path beginning with the earth and ending with Sadāśiva; thus, 'I am that'. So it is said.
Therefore, because of this non-difference, whatever is an object of knowledge (*prameya*) for the entire class of subjects (*pramātṛvarga*) is also my object of knowledge;

since I consist of the entire universe of subjects, that which is my object of knowledge is also the object of knowledge for the universe. This includes objects such as jars and cloths, as well as other objects of knowledge such as bodies and so forth.
It is indeed my own limb.

He demonstrates its very nature as a limb: "Excluded from one another and from the entire class of objects of knowledge (*prameya*), every object of knowledge rests in non-dual, single-flavored unity."

The ultimate reality (paramārtha) attains the status of being the object of the reflective awareness "I. For the bound soul (baddha), however, all this is an object of knowledge (prameya) that is distinct from the object of knowledge yet non-distinct from the class of subjects (pramātṛvarga); thus, the bound soul rests solely in pure differentiation.

By the passage beginning with "svāṅgarūpeṣu" (in the forms of one's own limbs) and that beginning with "ye 'pyasāmayikedaṃtā" (those for whom the sense of "this-ness" is not conventional), [it is shown that] Sadāśiva, Īśvara, Bhuvana, and the object of knowledge are common [to all], and the liberated one is [also common]. By the phrase "jīvanmuktapade baddhaḥ punarapyantabhedavān" (bound again even within the state of liberation, possessing internal differentiation), [it is indicated] regarding the bound subject, the *paśu*.

And the account of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) has been examined. Anticipating the question, "In what way is this account of the objects of knowledge [identical with] Supreme Śiva?", he says: "In every way—both by way of the objects of knowledge and by way of the subjects of knowledge—it is a mass of consciousness and bliss, overflowing with the infinite categories of reality absorbed within it."

The Supreme Śiva, whose form is the supreme unchanging (paramākṣara), is completely dissolved within his own essential nature, which is the internalized fullness of I-consciousness (pūrṇāhantā). He is the mass of the density of bliss consisting of pure consciousness, overflowing with the multitude of infinite principles from Śiva down to the earth, and whose manifest form consists of the phonemes beginning with 'A' and ending with 'KṢa'.
The fifty phonemes are the denotators (*vācaka*), while that which consists of the thirty-six principles (*tattva*)—beginning with Śiva and ending with Earth—is the denoted (*vācya*).
His form is the supreme syllable (*paramākṣara*), which is the causal source.
In Paramaśiva, whose nature is the fullness of pure I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhantā*), there exists no discourse whatsoever regarding objects of knowledge (*prameya*). The reason for this is as follows:

He said: Because the entire multitude of principles (tattvaugha), from Śiva down to the earth, has dissolved into that Supreme Śiva— resting solely in the nature of consciousness in every respect, both as the object of knowledge (prameya) and as the subject (pramātṛ)—
and because it has thus dissolved, that is the state of Supreme Śiva.
Because it is free from the impurities of the body and so forth due to its nature as consciousness consisting of full subjectivity (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*), it is uncreated;
for that very reason, it is innate; and for that very reason, it is natural, spontaneous, and characterized by the wonder of one's own self, the "I"—an undivided mass of bliss.

Embodied by the aforementioned supreme syllable (*paramākṣara*) as the nature of such bliss, she is Śivā; she dwells in the state that transcends the universe from Śiva down to the earth, yet consists of that very universe from Śiva down to the earth.
According to the principle stated as "the unsurpassed light" (*anuttara-jyotis*), she is of the form of the unsurpassed light, in which all discourse regarding objects of knowledge has dissolved.
The state that transcends all is designated as consisting of fourfold sections:
the section on knowledge, the section on action, the section on scripture,
and the section on the compendium of the meaning of reality.

He states the fruit of the result of reflecting upon this scripture— the reality that has been established as the object of knowledge (prameya) as taught in the venerable *Īśvarapratyabhijñā* treatise:
"In the manner described, [one realizes] this self as having the nature of the Lord."

Perceiving that his own self— which is of the nature of the Lord— is inseparable from those two [powers] which are like his very life-breath, and experiencing through direct realization that "his knowledge and action are distinct from him," he knows all desired and undesired objects as they truly are.
And he acts;

knowing himself to be of the nature of God, and knowing that within his own non-differentiated self there exist knowledge and action— which are the causes for the recognition of that divine nature— he becomes such as this.

My own self is indeed of the nature of Paramaśiva, as demonstrated by the Śeṣikas, Naiyāyikas, and others. Its knowledge and action are of such a nature that there are no other innate [powers] distinct from them;
reflecting thus, whatever one desires, one knows and acts upon it—remember this for a moment.

In this sequence, one who is intent on the practice of entering into the non-dual state (*advayasamāveśa*) for even a single moment knows and acts with this very body— this is the connection [of the words]. One who is devoted to this alone, according to the stated method "he who knows it as suchness," whereas one devoid of the practice of *samāveśa*, even while the body exists...

One who is liberated while living is Śiva even while alive, and upon the fall of the body, he is indeed the Supreme Lord. For this qualified student of the scriptures, whose own experience has established the meaning of the scripture, the lineage of gurus must be recounted by way of the authority of the Āgamas as a corroboration of that scriptural truth.

The experience established by the scriptures has been shown. This knowledge is threefold—derived from the guru, from the scripture, and from oneself—and thus this [point] is made firm. With this intention, he demonstrates the lineage of the gurus.

This path of the scripture (*śāstramārga*), which has been revealed by the words "having somehow attained," is new because it is contained within all the secret scriptures; this path of the scripture is [as taught] by the great masters, the venerable teachers Somānanda and his successors.

As it is stated in the *Śivadṛṣṭi* treatise, "it is very easy [to achieve]"; therefore, in this path of the scripture, the qualified practitioner, reflecting upon and establishing his footing, and bringing rest [to his mind], contemplates his own state of being the creator of the universe—which consists of the nature of Śiva—and thus becomes liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). Thus...

Entering incessantly that very path which is empty of body, vital breath, and intellect, and immersing oneself right there while entering that same path incessantly, one attains perfection and acquires the supernatural powers (*vibhūtis*).
From our supreme preceptor, the venerable teacher Lakṣmaṇagupta, from us...

The venerable feet of the teacher Śrī Somānandanātha, the supreme lord (parameṣṭhin) of the illustrious Utpaladeva Ācārya Bhaṭṭāraka; in the *Śivadṛṣṭi* treatise spoken by him, there exists an "inner practice" (*abhyantara-caryā*) which is novel, contained within all the secret scriptures, and because it is concealed, it is not well-known [outside]. As for the "outer practice" (*bāhya-caryā*):

Prāṇāyāma, āsanas, bandhas, and so forth; internal practice consists of meditation (dhyāna) and the like. Thus, the practice of both the external and internal elements—being free from the exertion and effort associated with prāṇāyāma and the afflictions—is easily accomplished; this very path has been described here in the venerable *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*.

Since this meaning— established through the teacher, the scripture, and one’s own conviction— has been brought to light by removing the stain of opposing doctrines such as those of the Buddhists, which consist of obscurations, in this treatise that dispels the suspicion of the stains of opposing doctrines; therefore, in this case, regarding this object of knowledge established by the scripture:

Establishing the state of reflective awareness and bringing rest, having contemplated and realized the sovereignty characterized by being the creator of the universe— having contemplated and understood the sovereignty characterized by being the creator of the entire universe from Śiva down to the earth— one becomes firm in the certainty of one's own self.

When one recognizes and reflects upon that which has resided within from the very beginning through the mouth of the Guru, then, by the mere reflection on that sovereignty, one first becomes liberated while living; for the Lord Śiva himself is thus realized, as stated by the venerable teacher Somānanda, the supreme preceptor, regarding gold once it has been known: "When gold is known even once..."

When gold is known as "this is gold," "it is thus," "its measure is this much," and "its color is such," that gold shall no longer undergo further processing, refinement, cultivation, or measurement; for its firmness arises from the state of a solid conviction that "this is it" through mere single cognition.

Once one's own father, one's own land, and so forth have been known once, there is no further need for a means of cognition (*jñāpaka*) or for cognition itself. When the Śiva-nature of the Self, which resides in all things, has been known through firm conviction— whether by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), by one's own realization, from the scriptures, or from the words of the Guru— the instrument [of action] is perfected.

Neither by means of postures, breath-restraints, and so forth, nor even through this cultivation of meditation— such as [thinking] "this is my father" or "this is my brother"— does the reality of one's own Śiva-nature become firm. Rather,
it is by awakening to and ascertaining one's own agency over the universe, which consists of the essence of Śiva, for a moment or longer...

If it enters incessantly in due order, it demonstrates that very entry: among the voids of body, vital breath, and intellect, it may enter one internal [void], namely the body alone; or two, namely both body and vital breath; or all three.
Whether it be the body, the vital breath, the intellect, or everything consisting of body, breath, and intellect— (517)—
he incessantly immerses all of that into that very state which consists of Śiva-nature and is the agency of world-creation; therefore, [one should worship] that.
One attains the sovereignty of being the creator of the universe, extending to its very limits.

If it is somehow reached [as described] by the words "having somehow attained," etc., and if that very thing is indeed the form of Śiva, then there would be no distinction between the recognition and non-recognition of that reality whose essence is Śiva; this is the seed [of the argument].

Even water and other such things, though unrecognized by the perceiver, do produce a sprout when all auxiliary conditions are present; likewise, even though unrecognized by the perceiver, the sprout is indeed produced.
In the same way, the reality called the Self, though unrecognized, is indeed Śiva in nature—the Self is the Lord.
Thus, what is the basis for recognition? Even in the absence of recognition, the Self is indeed the Lord.

He states the resolution: It is said that objects such as seeds, which consist of Umā and are insentient in nature, possess external causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), yet they culminate in the wonder of resting within the subject whose nature is "I."
The two types of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) consist of pleasure and so forth. What you have said is true.
Between those two, the first does not depend upon recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*); the second, the causal efficiency consisting of pleasure and so forth, necessarily depends upon recognition.
He demonstrates that very point with the word "here" (*iha*). Here, in this treatise known as the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*, [there occurs] the realization:

"I am Caitra; I am Maitra. Through the glance of the true Guru, there arises the essence of wonder—that "this one is indeed the Lord"—which consists of supreme accomplishment (*parasiddhi*), liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), and the sovereign power (*vibhūti*) of supreme accomplishment, manifested through creation and the other cosmic functions.
The Lord (Īśvara) is characterized by these two attributes: the power (*vibhūti*) capable of subjugating the universe and [the capacity for] this [consciousness].

He is the Lord consisting of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), well-known from the Purāṇas, Āgamas, and other sources. It is absolutely necessary to recognize him as "I am he"—this is the recognition of the Lord (*īśvarapratyabhijñāna*).

Again, he raises an objection: "The purposeful activity (arthakriyā), which has as its essence the wonder of resting in the subject, is not seen without recognition; yet when recognition exists, purposeful activity is seen.
Where has this been observed? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The beloved" refers to the desired hero from another island.

Although he had been long desired and was present nearby— having arrived at a certain pavilion during a great festival consisting of a vast assembly of people through various dispatches of messengers and prayers to the deities— nevertheless,
by the turn of fate, his beauty and other qualities [were not perceived].
Just as this Self was previously heard from the mouth of the messenger who is the perfection of virtues, saying "it is thus," yet it was not fully recognized—

because, while standing right before one, it was not identified as "this is that very person" due to being treated as equal to other people— so too is this Self not capable of being perceived by the world, that is, by the class of cognizing subjects.
One whose qualities are disregarded— even while remaining within— fails to recognize the characteristics of the Lord;

such a person does not recognize the majesty of their own Self, which consists of the qualities of being the creator of the universe, omniscience, fullness, the eternity of the universe, and its all-pervasiveness, [all of which reside] in the Lord of the Universe in the form of "I," one's own Self.
Even though the self of worldly people manifests as "I," it is not capable of knowing its own majesty, which consists of the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) that "I am the Lord.
Therefore, this [reality], which is eternally manifest and established by one's own experience...

The recognition "I am the Lord" has been proclaimed; it was taught by the Supreme Lord who had assumed a human form out of compassion. Then, due to the power of that vow made by the slender maiden, while her beloved was standing nearby, she looked at Avalokitā without any hesitation.

Her vision of her beloved— though it had attained a state of consummate aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) through the excellence of descriptions of his form and qualities, and though it had reached the path of heart’s recognition that "this is indeed he"— was nevertheless rendered common to everyone standing near her; thus, even while it was fully realized, it remained unattained by her.

It does not fill the heart. Even though the Lord of the Universe is constantly manifest within one's own self, the manifestation of one's own self as the Lord of the Universe—which remains unmanifest [to the limited mind]—does not bestow fullness upon the heart; for that reason, [it remains incomplete].

Although he is like a beloved son to people, perceived by them as "I," that very self—by virtue of being conjoined with the excellence of the Supreme Lord, characterized by omniscience and unimpeded power—is thoroughly grasped;
thus, it becomes an object of experience identical to a pot or other such things appearing before it. It is itself [thus transformed].
The meaning is that even the conscious subject, due to a lack of self-recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), becomes equivalent to the object of consciousness.

It is "wondrously arisen" (*adbhuta-saṃbhūta*), meaning born of marvel; by the logic of the blooming flower, through that very recognition, it reaches a state that is beyond the reach of words. This is like the recognition of one's own beloved by a woman [who has been separated from her lover]. *Ādi*... [etc.]

From the perfected word of the Guru, through the very recognition of the power of the Lord, there arises the exalted realization: "I am the Supreme Lord, who consists of the universe and yet transcends the universe. At that moment, one recognizes one's own Self as the Great Lord—the state of liberation while living, whose essence is supreme bliss.

In the essence of the practice of *samāveśa* (spiritual immersion), there is the attainment of the sovereign power (*vibhūti*) capable of bringing the entire universe—from Śiva down to the earth—under one's control;

thus, the very recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of one's own self as "I am the Lord" becomes the bestower of the two types of accomplishments (*siddhi*), which take the form of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) and sovereign power. As it has been said:

Whether it be stationary or moving, this great wonder is not born of the first taste of passion; for indeed, that source of the side-glances of the Guide—what is she not beloved, and what is he not beloved? Is it merely this much?
And if this noble-minded person alone were not present, with his voice modulated by expressive intonation;

By the phrase "of whatever person is being born," it is shown that there is no restriction whatsoever regarding the qualified recipient; this is according to the method stated in the commentary on the first sūtra.
Furthermore, by the expression "benefiting all castes" (*sarvavarṇopakāra*), it is indicated that this sūtra applies to "the person who has gone [to the teacher]" (*gatasya janasya*).

The explanation has been shown for the most part by following the meaning of the words. By the phrase "bestowing the great fruit," which consists of the glory of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) and takes the form of the supreme and subordinate accomplishments (*siddhi*),
the explanation of the word *ayatnasiddhyartham* found in the aphorism is shown according to its underlying sense.

By the two words "this treatise" (*idaṃ śāstram*), the explanation of the phrase "recognition of the Lord" (*īśvarapratyabhijñā*) is shown. By the two words "the name is established through connection with what is well-known," the son of Udayākara [Utpaladeva] has explained the two words "in Utpala."
The explanation has been shown.
Furthermore, the construction is "by the son of Udayākara";

by means of the well-known fact that [the word] does not apply to a blue lotus (*utpala*), and by means of the renown of his own name, it serves as a gateway for recollecting the excellence of his own lineage through his own name.

For one who has been born, this [result] occurs in this very way and not otherwise; thus, in order to direct people toward the application of the realization that turns back [suffering]— which is characterized by confidence consisting of the conviction that "this is so"— he applies the realization to the person and the person to the treatise he himself has composed.

While composing this treatise, he concludes with the words "of whatever person" (*janasya yasya kasyacit*) and "of a being who is being born" (*jāyamānasya jantoḥ*); by this, there is no regard for castes such as the Brāhmaṇas. By the word "etc.
(*ādi*), it is indicated that even therein, there is no requirement regarding specific qualifications (*adhikāra*) for this treatise.

The quality of being beneficial to all has been stated. By showing that through hearing this scripture, the attainment of both the higher and lower forms of perfection (*siddhi*) occurs for people without effort, the great fruitfulness for people is demonstrated. It is not that people are favored merely by being incited through the act of instigation, as people are already well-known [entities].

This is the designation of both names: by the word "this," which indicates its being based on one's own direct experience (*svapratyaya*), it is made heart-felt by people through hundreds of logical arguments;
thus, [it is called] *Śrīmad-Īśvarapratyabhijñā* (The Recognition of the Glorious Lord), for Śiva is auspicious because He has emanated from Śiva, who is the source of all people.

It is auspicious because it is the cause for attaining life and because it is itself the very nature of Śiva. It is the blessing that bestows both the supreme and the non-supreme perfections (*siddhi*), consisting of the glory of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*). "This" [refers to it]; it is established through one's own experience. Furthermore, "this" is so because it is established through the personal experience of people.

In the treatise known as the *Pratyabhijñā*, the commentary called the *Vimarśinī*— which elucidates the meaning of the aphorisms in their entirety and with excellence— was somehow brought to light by the venerable teacher named Abhinavagupta, beginning from the words "is being seen" and ending with "has not been established by Utpala."

It is a path that clearly illuminates the entire meaning of the concise scriptures by presenting it in summary; it is unbreakable, being impossible to be refuted by the tenets of the Buddhists and others.
That which was composed by Bhigu, being ancient and renowned, that very heart, through the supreme delights [of the teacher], vibrates of its own accord as the unsurpassed. (521)

Thus, according to the principle stated by himself, [this work] has been composed and expanded through the manifestation of the *sahṛdaya* (the sensitive heart) which consists of the Unsurpassed (*anuttara*).
By the word "brief" (*laghvī*), it is further indicated by his own mouth that there will be some extensive commentary (*vimarśinī*) on this treatise, which he himself will undertake.
The *Vākya* is the Mīmāṃsā treatise; the *Pramāṇa* is the Nyāya treatise;
the *Pada* is the Vyākaraṇa treatise; and the *Sadāgamas* are the scriptures proclaimed by Śiva.
From this "amutaḥ"—that is, from this excellent, supreme, and sublime treatise known as Pratyabhijñā.

From the scripture established by one's own experience: those [other scriptures], being without this scripture, do not reach— that is, they do not attain— proximity to the purpose, which is the utility for oneself consisting of the reflective awareness of one's own self as the nature of Maheśvara, for one who is devoted to the study of this scripture.
Treatises such as grammar and the like do not, by themselves alone, bring about their own utility for the self.
Regarding this, he provides an illustration: "the juices found in the earth" and "those consisting of water."

Who else besides the Sun is capable of withdrawing the rays that have withered during the summer and, having placed them within his own circle of rays, employing them as rain-giving beams for the nourishment of the crops?
[He alone is so capable,] conceiving of himself as "I" and manifesting his own self.

In the *Jñānakriyātmakaśaktipratyabhijñāna*, one who does not recognize the nature of the Lord cannot desire to discern other scriptures, such as verbal testimony and the like; therefore, by means of Māyā— which consists in the concealment of one's true nature and is like being possessed by a spirit— one is as if possessed by a ghost.

To the question "Who are you?", what should be said? The meaning is: "Nothing at all. Just as Caitra, possessed by a spirit, does not know his own name which was designated by his father and others, so too the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), being possessed by that spirit, does not know the Maheśvara who is the self's primordially established [nature].
The meaning is "he knows. (522) Thus ends the commentary *Pratyabhijñāsūtravimarśinī*.
Whatever syllable may have been omitted, or whatever may be deficient in its prosodic measure, the learned should forgive it; for who is free from transgression?

In that which is the nature of knowledge and action, whose essence is bliss, and which is free from conceptual construction; in that which is stainless, perfectly full, and in which all diversity of the phenomenal world— projected by *māyā*— has dissolved through *vidyā*.
O Śiva, may my experience of you alone be auspicious at all times.
In the forest of Vṛndāvana, during a night illuminated by the shimmering autumn moonlight,
that youth— who brings about the most intensely sweet *rāsa* dance with the cowherd women who are delighted by the melodious sound of his flute— [is celebrated].
I bow my head to Mukunda, whose limbs are dark like a sapphire that cleaves the clouds.
Thus all is auspicious.
